title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The ascetic Vālmīki questioned Nārada — the foremost among those devoted to austerity and sacred study, the best of the eloquent, the bull among sages.
"Who in this world today is truly virtuous, and also mighty? Who knows righteousness, and is grateful, truthful in speech, and steadfast in his vows?
Who is endowed with noble character, and who is a benefactor to all creatures? Who is learned, who is capable, and who is ever pleasant to behold?
Who is self-possessed, who has conquered anger? Who is radiant and free from envy? Whom do even the gods fear when his wrath is aroused in battle?
I wish to hear of such a one — my curiosity is boundless. O great seer, you are capable of knowing such a man."
Having heard these words of Vālmīki, Nārada — who has knowledge of the three worlds — addressed him saying "Hear me!" and, delighted, spoke thus:
"The virtues you have enumerated are many and rare, O sage. Having considered them fully, I shall speak of a man who possesses them all — hear of him.
Born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku, known among men by the name Rāma — he is disciplined in mind, of great valor, radiant, resolute, and master of his senses.
Intelligent, principled, eloquent, possessed of splendor, a crusher of enemies — broad-shouldered, long-armed, with a neck like a conch-shell and a strong jaw.
Broad-chested, a great archer, with well-concealed collar-bones, a tamer of foes — with arms reaching to his knees, a handsome head, a fine forehead, and noble gait.
Proportionate, with perfectly balanced limbs, of lustrous complexion, full of majesty — with a full chest, wide eyes, bearing the mark of fortune, adorned with auspicious signs.
Knowing righteousness, true to his pledges, devoted to the welfare of his subjects — illustrious, endowed with wisdom, pure, gracious, and possessed of deep concentration.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
A protector of the world of living beings, a guardian of righteousness — one who knows the true essence of the Vedas and their ancillary sciences, and is accomplished in the science of archery.
Knowing the true meaning of all treatises, possessed of a retentive memory and swift intelligence — beloved by all the world, virtuous, of undepressed spirit, and discerning.
Always sought out by the virtuous as the ocean is by rivers — noble, ever impartial toward all, and ever pleasant to look upon.
He, who increases the joy of Kausalyā, is endowed with all virtues — like the ocean in depth, like the Himālaya in steadfastness.
Equal to Viṣṇu in valor, pleasing to behold as the moon — like the fire of universal dissolution in wrath, and like the earth in forbearance.
Equal to Kubera in generosity, a second Dharma himself in truthfulness — him, Rāma, so endowed with virtues, of true valor,
his eldest son, endowed with the highest virtues, his beloved — king Daśaratha, the lord of the earth, wished out of affection to invest with the office of crown prince.
But seeing the preparations for his consecration, his wife Kaikeyī — the queen to whom a boon had previously been granted — asked him for this boon: the banishment of Rāma and the consecration of Bharata.
Bound by the snare of righteousness to his word of truth, king Daśaratha sent his beloved son Rāma into exile.
The hero went to the forest, honoring his pledge, acting upon his father's command and to please Kaikeyī.
His beloved brother Lakṣmaṇa, who increases the joy of Sumitrā, endowed with humility, followed him out of love as he departed.
Sītā too — endowed with all auspicious marks, the foremost of women, the most excellent of daughters-in-law — followed Rāma as Rohiṇī follows the moon.
Followed for a distance by the citizens and by his father Daśaratha, he dismissed his charioteer at Śṛṅgaverapura on the bank of the Gaṅgā.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Passing through forest after forest, crossing many swift rivers, and reaching Citrakūṭa by the direction of Bharadvāja,
having built a pleasant dwelling there, the three delighted in the forest and dwelt there happily, resembling gods and Gandharvas.
When Rāma had gone to Citrakūṭa, king Daśaratha, tormented by grief for his son and lamenting him, departed to heaven.
Upon his death, Bharata — of great might — though pressed to accept the kingdom by the twice-born led by Vasiṣṭha, did not desire it. The hero went to the forest to propitiate the feet of Rāma.
Rāma, the elder of Bharata, then turned him back, placing his sandals as a pledge for the kingdom.
Bharata, his wish unfulfilled, touching the feet of Rāma's sandals, administered the kingdom from Nandigrāma, longing for Rāma's return.
But Rāma, observing the arrival of townsfolk and others to that place, single-mindedly entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
Slaying the demon Virādha, he visited Śarabhaṅga, then Sutīkṣṇa, then Agastya, and Agastya's brother as well.
At Agastya's word, and greatly pleased, he received the Aindra bow, a sword, and two quivers of inexhaustible arrows.
While Rāma was dwelling in the forest among the forest-dwellers, all the sages came to him seeking the destruction of the Asuras and Rākṣasas.
While he was dwelling there, Śūrpaṇakhā — a Rākṣasī who dwelt in Janasthāna and could assume any form at will — was disfigured by him.
Then, at the instigation of Śūrpaṇakhā, all the Rākṣasas rose up — Khara, Triśiras, and the Rākṣasa Dūṣaṇa,
Rāma slew them all in battle, along with their followers — fourteen thousand Rākṣasas were destroyed.
Then Rāvaṇa, hearing of the slaughter of his kinsmen and overcome with fury, sought as his ally the Rākṣasa named Mārīca.
Mārīca repeatedly warned Rāvaṇa: "Conflict with one so mighty is not fitting for you, O Rāvaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
But Rāvaṇa, driven onward by fate, disregarded that counsel and went together with Mārīca to Rāma's hermitage.
That sorcerer, having lured both princes far away, abducted the wife of Rāma, slaying the vulture Jaṭāyus.
Finding the vulture slain and hearing that the Maithilī had been carried off, Rāghava was consumed by grief and lamented, his senses overwhelmed.
Then, consumed by that very grief, having cremated the vulture Jaṭāyus, he came upon a Rākṣasa while searching for Sītā in the forest.
Named Kabandha, grotesquely misshapen in form and dreadful to behold — him the long-armed hero slew and burned, and he ascended to heaven.
Kabandha told him of Śabarī, a female ascetic who walks the path of righteousness, skilled in dharma: "Go to her, O Rāghava." The greatly radiant slayer of enemies then went to Śabarī.
Duly honored by Śabarī, Rāma the son of Daśaratha met on the shore of Pampā with Hanūmān, the monkey.
Through Hanūmān's words he came to meet Sugrīva, and the mighty Rāma told Sugrīva everything that had befallen him.
Then the king of monkeys, out of affection and sorrow, told Rāma all about the origin of his enmity; and the monkey also recounted there the strength of Vālin.
Although Rāma pledged the slaying of Vālin, Sugrīva was always doubtful about Rāghava's valor.
To inspire confidence, Rāghava kicked the great carcass of Dundubhi with his toe and hurled it a full ten leagues.
He then pierced seven śāla trees with a single great arrow, penetrating through the mountain down to the netherworld, thereby inspiring conviction.
Then, his mind gladdened and his trust secured, the great ape together with Rāma went to the cave of Kiṣkindhā.
Then Sugrīva, the foremost of monkeys, golden-tawny in hue, roared; and at that great roar, the lord of monkeys, Vālin, came forth.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, at Sugrīva's word, slaying Vālin in battle, Rāghava reinstated Sugrīva in that kingdom.
That bull among monkeys, having assembled all the monkeys, dispatched them in all directions, seeking to find the daughter of Janaka.
Then, by the words of the vulture Saṃpāti, the mighty Hanūmān leapt across the salt ocean, a hundred leagues in breadth.
Arriving at Laṅkā, the city ruled by Rāvaṇa, he saw Sītā there, lost in thought, situated in the Aśoka grove.
Having presented the token of recognition, reported all tidings, and consoled the Vaidehī, he demolished the gateway.
Slaying five commanders of the army and seven sons of ministers, and crushing the valiant Akṣa, he was taken captive.
Knowing that the weapon had rendered him senseless by virtue of Brahmā's boon, the hero allowed the Rākṣasas to bind him as they pleased.
Having then burned the city of Laṅkā — excepting Sītā the Maithilī — the great ape returned to bring the welcome news to Rāma.
Approaching the great-souled Rāma and circumambulating him, that one of immeasurable spirit declared truthfully: "Sītā has been seen."
Then, going with Sugrīva to the shore of the great ocean, he agitated the sea with arrows blazing like the sun.
The ocean, lord of rivers, revealed itself to him; and at the ocean's word he had Nala construct a causeway.
Crossing by that causeway to the city of Laṅkā and slaying Rāvaṇa in battle, he consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa as lord of the Rākṣasas in Laṅkā.
By that great deed, the three worlds — with all moving and unmoving things, with all groups of gods and sages — were satisfied with the great-souled Rāghava.
Thus honored by all the gods who were supremely pleased, Rāma, his purpose fulfilled and freed from affliction, rejoiced greatly.
Having received boons from the gods and raised up the monkeys, he mounted that Puṣpaka vessel and then went to Nandigrāma.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
At Nandigrāma, having laid aside his matted locks, the sinless Rāma together with his brothers, reunited with Sītā, recovered his kingdom.
The world was filled with joy and delight, contented and well-nourished, deeply righteous — free from ailment and disease, free from the fear of famine.
No men anywhere will witness the death of their sons; women will ever be un-widowed and devoted to their husbands.
There will be no fear from wind, no creatures will drown in the waters, no fear from fire — even as it was in the Kṛta age.
Having offered hundreds of horse sacrifices and many other rites with abundant gold, and having given ten million cows to the learned in proper observance,
Rāghava will establish dynasties of kings a hundredfold, and will set all four orders of society in this world each to its own proper duty.
Having served as king for ten thousand and ten hundred years, Rāma will depart to the world of Brahmā.
Whoever recites this story of Rāma — which is pure, destroys sin, meritorious, and equal to the Vedas — is released from all sins.
A man who reads this narrative — the Rāmāyaṇa, which promotes long life — together with his sons and grandsons and his household, is glorified in heaven after death.
A Brāhmaṇa who reads it attains mastery of speech; a Kṣatriya attains lordship of the earth; a Vaiśya attains the fruits of his commerce; and even a Śūdra attains greatness.
Having heard that speech of Nārada, the great sage, righteous-souled and skilled in speech, honored him together with his disciples.
Duly honored by him, the divine seer Nārada, taking leave and receiving permission, departed through the sky.
A little while after he had departed to the world of the gods, the sage went to the bank of the Tamasā, not far from the Jāhnavī.
The great sage, reaching the bank of the Tamasā and seeing the ford free of mud, spoke to his disciple who stood at his side:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Behold, Bharadvāja, this ford free of mud — lovely, its waters clear, like the mind of a good man.
Set down the water-pot, dear boy, and hand me my bark-garment — I shall bathe here at this excellent ford of the Tamasā."
Thus addressed by the great-souled Vālmīki, Bharadvāja offered the bark-garment to that sage, attentively, as to a teacher.
Taking the bark-garment from the disciple's hand, with his senses restrained, he wandered about gazing in all directions at the vast forest.
Then near that spot the blessed one saw a pair of Krauñca birds moving together inseparably, calling with sweet voices.
Of that pair, a Niṣāda — one resolved on evil, a repository of hatred — struck down the male before the sage's very eyes.
The female, seeing her mate slain, writhing on the ground with his limbs drenched in blood, cried out in a piteous voice.
Seeing that bird, a twice-born creature, brought down by the Niṣāda, compassion arose in that righteous-souled sage.
Then, from that arising compassion, perceiving this to be unrighteous, hearing the female Krauñca weeping, the twice-born sage spoke these words:
"You shall find no rest, O Niṣāda, for all eternity — for you have slain one of this pair of Krauñca birds while it was in the grip of passion."
Even as he spoke thus and reflected, the thought arose in his heart as he looked on: "Moved by grief for this bird, what have I uttered?"
Contemplating this, that greatly wise and intelligent one formed a thought, and that bull among sages spoke these words to his disciple:
"This utterance of mine, born of grief, which is composed in metrical feet with equal syllables and suited to the rhythm of the lute — let it be a śloka, and nothing else."
His disciple received with great joy that incomparable utterance of the speaking sage; and the teacher was pleased with him.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The sage then performed his ablution at that ford according to rule, and returned, his mind still pondering that very meaning.
Then the disciple Bharadvāja — humble, learned, and obedient to the teacher — took up the full water-pot and followed behind him.
He who knows righteousness, entering the hermitage with his disciple, sat down and fell into meditation, while also engaging in various other conversations.
Then Brahmā himself came — the creator of worlds, the self-existent lord, four-faced, of great splendor — to see that bull among sages.
Vālmīki, seeing him, immediately rose, restrained his speech, stood with hands joined, composed and attentive, in utter astonishment.
He honored that god with water for the feet, an offering of welcome, a seat, and reverential salutation; and prostrating before him according to ritual, he asked after the imperishable one's well-being.
The blessed one then sat on the most worshipful seat and assigned a seat to the great seer Vālmīki.
When he who is truly the grandsire of all worlds had taken his seat, Vālmīki fell into meditation, his mind still absorbed in that same thought.
"What a vile deed was done by that evil-souled one, his mind set on enmity — who without cause killed such a sweet-voiced Krauñca bird!"
Grieving still for the female Krauñca, his mind turned inward and wholly absorbed in sorrow, he sang that verse again and again.
Then Brahmā smiled and said to that bull among sages: "What you have composed is a śloka — there is no doubt about this."
"By my will, O Brāhmaṇa, this speech has flowed forth in you. Compose the entire story of Rāma, O best of seers.
Tell the deeds of the righteous-souled, virtuous, wise, and steadfast Rāma as you heard them from Nārada.
What the wise Rāma did — both in private and in public — together with Saumitri and with all the Rākṣasas in every respect,

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And what befell the Vaidehī, openly or in secret — all of that which is not yet known shall become known to you.
No word of yours in this poem shall be untrue. Compose the holy story of Rāma, beautiful and bound in śloka meter."
"As long as the mountains stand and the rivers flow upon the earth, so long will the story of the Rāmāyaṇa circulate throughout the worlds.
As long as the story of Rāma, composed by you, shall circulate, so long shall you dwell in the upper and lower worlds."
Having said this, the blessed Brahmā vanished then and there. The sage Vālmīki, together with his disciples, was filled with wonder.
Then all of his disciples sang that śloka again and again with delight, and spoke, greatly astonished:
"This grief that was uttered by the great seer in four feet of equal syllables has become a śloka by being sung."
Then this thought arose in Vālmīki, whose spirit was cultivated and purified: "With such verses as these shall I compose the entire Rāmāyaṇa poem."
With hundreds of ślokas of equal syllables, adorned with noble subject-matter and pleasing words — the famous sage of noble intellect composed a glorious poem to the glory of the glorious Rāma.
Having heard all of that — the wholesome account filled with righteousness — the righteous-souled one seeks to see clearly, once more, what befell that wise man.
The sage, having touched water with restraint, stood with hands joined in salutation, on a cushion of kuśa grass with tips pointing eastward, and by dharma seeks the way.
The great birth of Rāma, his valor, his conformity to all, his belovedness to the world, his patience, his gentleness, his character of truthfulness —
The many and varied other stories in the journey with Viśvāmitra, the marriage of Jānakī, and the breaking of the bow —
The quarrel between Rāma and Rāma, the virtues of Daśaratha's son, the intended consecration of Rāma, and the wicked intent of Kaikeyī —

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The obstruction of the consecration, Rāma's exile, the king's grief and lamentation, and his resort to the other world —
The sorrow of the people, the dismissal of the people, the dialogue with the lord of the Niṣādas, and the turning back of the charioteer —
The crossing of the Gaṅgā, the visit to Bharadvāja, and by Bharadvāja's leave the sight of Citrakūṭa —
The building and setting up of the dwelling, the arrival of Bharata, the propitiation of Rāma, and the water-rites for the father —
The consecration of the sandals as regent, the sojourn at Nandigrāma, the going into the Daṇḍaka forest, and the meeting with Sutīkṣṇa —
The encounter with Anasūyā and the gift of the ointment, the conversation with Śūrpaṇakhā and her disfigurement —
The slaying of Khara and Triśiras, the rising up of Rāvaṇa, the slaying of Mārīca, and the abduction of the Vaidehī —
Rāghava's lamentation, the slaying of the vulture-king, the encounter with Kabandha, and the sight of the Pampā lake —
The visit to Śabarī, the meeting with Hanūmān, and the lamentation of the great-souled Rāghava at Pampā —
The going to Ṛśyamūka, the meeting with Sugrīva, the establishment of trust, the alliance, and the conflict between Vālī and Sugrīva —
The destruction of Vālin, the installation of Sugrīva, the pacification of Tārā's lamentation, and the sojourn of the rainy season nights —
The wrath of Rāma the lion-hero, the mustering of the troops, the dispatching in all directions, and the description of the earth —
The giving of the signet ring, the sight of the cave of the bears, the sitting in fast unto death, and the appearance of Saṃpāti —
The climbing of the mountain, the leaping of the ocean, the nocturnal entry into Laṅkā, and deliberating alone —
The going to the drinking-ground, the sight of the inner apartments, the going to the Aśoka grove, and the sight of Sītā —

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The presentation of the token of recognition, the conversation with Sītā, the terrifying of the Rākṣasī women, and the dream-vision of Trijaṭā —
Sītā's gift of the jewel, the breaking of the trees, the flight of the Rākṣasī women, and the slaying of the kiṃkara troops —
The capture of the son of the Wind-god, his roaring proclamation of Laṅkā's burning, his return voyage, and the plundering of the honey-grove —
The consolation of Rāghava, the handing over of the jewel, the meeting with the ocean, and the building of Nala's causeway —
The crossing of the ocean, the siege of Laṅkā by night, the alliance with Vibhīṣaṇa, and the disclosure of the means of slaying —
The death of Kumbhakarṇa, the slaying of Meghanāda, the destruction of Rāvaṇa, and the recovery of Sītā in the enemy's city —
The consecration of Vibhīṣaṇa, the sight of the Puṣpaka aerial chariot, the journey to Ayodhyā, and the meeting with Bharata —
The auspicious consecration of Rāma, the dismissal of all the armies, the delighting of his own kingdom, and the sending away of the Vaidehī —
And whatever things of Rāma's yet to come upon this earth — all this the blessed seer Vālmīki composed in the later portion of the poem.
The venerable sage Vālmīki, self-possessed, composed the entire life-story of Rāma who had attained his kingdom — a narrative adorned with wondrous words.
Having composed that work — complete with what was yet to come and with the Uttara-kāṇḍa — the greatly wise master then pondered: who indeed could perform this?
While the great seer of purified soul was thus reflecting, two wandering bards clad in the garb of ascetics — Kuśa and Lava — then clasped his feet.
He saw that those two — Kuśa and Lava — were royal princes endowed with righteousness, illustrious brothers blessed with melodious voices, dwelling in his hermitage.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing them to be gifted with keen intellect and thoroughly grounded in the Vedas, the master caused them to learn this poem as a supplement and amplification of the Vedas.
The one steadfast in his vow composed the entire poem — the Rāmāyaṇa — the great story of Sītā, known also as the slaying of Paulastya (Rāvaṇa).
Sweet whether recited or sung, composed in the three metres, bound in the seven classes of musical notes, and harmonised with the rhythm of the lute —
— this poem, infused with the rasas of the comic, the erotic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, and the repulsive and the rest, the two of them sang.
Those two brothers, skilled in the science of the Gandharva art of music, expert in the modulations and the proper placements of notes, endowed with melodious voices, resembled Gandharvas in their form.
Endowed with the marks of auspicious beauty, speaking with sweet voices, they seemed like two images drawn forth from a single original — as if lifted from the very body of Rāma himself.
Those two blameless princes, having made the entire poem wholly subject to speech — reciting the righteous and excellent narrative in full — sang it.
In assemblies of sages, twice-born ones, and holy men, those two great souls — supremely fortunate, adorned with every auspicious mark, knowers of truth — composed of mind, sang it in accordance with the teaching they had received.
On one occasion, standing near an assembly of purified-souled sages who had gathered and were seated together, those two sang this poem.
Hearing it, all the sages — their eyes brimming with tears — said to those two, 'Well done! Well done!' and were filled with the utmost wonder.
All those sages, joyful at heart and devoted to righteousness, praised Kuśa and Lava, those two who were indeed worthy of praise, as they sang.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Ah, what sweetness in the singing — and especially in the verses! Even these events long past are displayed as if directly before our eyes."
Those two, having entered fully and well into the feeling of the narrative, sang it together — melodiously, with deep emotion, rich with the wealth of their voices.
Thus praised by the great seers praiseworthy for their austerities, those two sang with even greater passion and with surpassing sweetness.
One sage, delighted, gave them a water-pot; another of great fame, greatly pleased, gave them bark garments.
"This narrative, proclaimed by the sage, is a wonder — the supreme foundation for all poets — and it is brought to completion in due order."
On one occasion, the elder brother of Bharata — Rāma — saw those two singers, who were praised everywhere, in the streets and on the royal highway.
Rāma, the subduer of enemies, then brought those two brothers — Kuśa and Lava together — to his own palace and honoured them, who were worthy of honour.
That lord, the scorcher of foes, was seated on a divine golden throne, with his ministers and brothers seated around him.
Seeing those two endowed with beauty, carrying lutes, Rāma then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata:
"Let this narrative be heard — sung properly by these two who shine with divine radiance, a narrative of wondrous meaning and verse, with sweet voices."
"These two ascetics — endowed with royal marks, Kuśa and Lava — are mighty in austerities. They recite a narrative of great power and glory that brings prosperity even to me. Listen to it."
Then those two, urged on by Rāma's word, sang with the perfection of the proper method and manner; and Rāma himself, seated in the assembly, gradually became absorbed in mind, eager to hear more.
This entire earth was formerly theirs alone — those victorious kings, beginning with Prajāpati himself.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Among them was Sagara by name — he by whom the ocean was excavated, whose sixty thousand sons encircled him as he journeyed.
In the lineage of those kings of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, great souls, a great narrative was born — known as the Rāmāyaṇa.
This I shall narrate in full, entirely from the beginning — replete with righteousness, love, and worldly purpose — and it is to be heard without envy.
There is a great and prosperous country called Kosala, joyful and abundant, settled on the bank of the Sarayū river, rich in wealth and grain.
There stood a city famous throughout the world, called Ayodhyā — a city that Manu himself, the lord of men, had personally founded.
That great and splendid city extended twelve yojanas in length and three in breadth, with its great avenues well laid out.
It was adorned with a great royal road, well planned, strewn always with scattered flowers and sprinkled with water.
King Daśaratha, who expanded a great realm, caused that city to be inhabited, even as the lord of the gods dwells in heaven.
It had gates and triumphal arches, its market streets were well arranged within, it was stocked with every kind of war-engine and weapon, and it was filled with artisans of every craft.
It was thronged with bards and panegyrists, splendid, of incomparable brilliance, furnished with lofty watchtowers and flags, and crowded with hundreds of śataghnī engines of war.
The great city everywhere was filled with troops of female dancers and theatrical companies; it was provided with pleasure gardens and mango groves, and encircled by a girdle of śāla trees.
It had a deep and formidable moat making it a fortress difficult for others to assail; and it was filled with horses and elephants, and with cows, camels, and donkeys as well.
It was surrounded by assemblies of subordinate kings engaged in rendering tribute, and it was adorned with merchants dwelling there from many different lands.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Adorned with palaces fashioned of jewels that rose like mountains, filled with pinnacled mansions — it resembled Indra's Amarāvatī.
Variegated and laid out in the form of a chessboard, filled with crowds of noble women, strewn with gems of every kind, and beautified with mansioned houses —
— densely packed with dwellings without gap, built on level ground, filled with śāli rice, and with water sweet as the juice of sugar-cane.
Resounding exceedingly — and beyond all measure — with kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas, lutes, and paṇava drums, that peerless city on earth —
— like the aerial palace of the Siddhas attained in heaven through austerities, its inner quarters of dwellings perfectly arranged, filled with the best of men.
Those who would not miss shooting — clearly, at moving targets, one after another, and at distant ones perceivable only by sound — light of hand and expert:
— slayers with sharp weapons of roaring, frenzied lions, tigers, and boars in the forest, and also by sheer strength of arm —
— with thousands of such great warriors, King Daśaratha at that time caused that city to be garrisoned and inhabited.
That city was surrounded by the foremost of the twice-born — maintainers of the sacred fire, men of virtuous excellence, masters of the six auxiliary sciences of the Veda, givers of thousands in gifts, devoted to truth, great souls equal to great seers, and by seers who were pure ascetics alone.
In that city of Ayodhyā dwelt one who was a knower of the Vedas, all-encompassing in counsel, far-sighted, of great splendour, beloved of the city-folk and the country-people —
— the foremost chariot-warrior among the Ikṣvākus, a performer of sacrifices, devoted to righteousness, self-controlled, equal to a great sage, a royal seer renowned in all three worlds.
Mighty, his enemies slain, rich in allies, his senses mastered, in his accumulations of wealth and other treasures comparable to Śakra and Vaiśravaṇa (Kubera).

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Just as the great and resplendent Manu was the protector of all beings, so King Daśaratha, dwelling there, protected the entire world.
By him — true to his pledged word, practising the three ends of life — that city was protected, as Amarāvatī is by the foremost of Indras.
In that best of cities, under that righteous-souled king, the men were cheerful, deeply learned, content with their own respective possessions, free from greed, and speakers of truth.
There was no householder in that best of cities who had small savings — none who lacked fulfilment of his aims, and none without cattle, horses, wealth, and grain.
In Ayodhyā could nowhere be found a man who was lustful, or a miser, or cruel; nor one who was unlearned, nor one who denied the existence of the gods.
All men and women were righteous in conduct, well restrained, joyful, pure in character and deportment — like spotless great seers.
None was to be found without ear-ornaments, none without a diadem, none without a garland, none of scanty enjoyments; none was without clean garments, none without anointed limbs, none without fragrant scents.
None was seen who ate without washing, none who was not a giver, none without upper-arm bands and golden neck-ornaments, none without hand-ornaments, none who lacked self-possession.
In Ayodhyā there was no brāhmaṇa who had not established the sacred fires, none who had not performed sacrifice, none who had not given thousands in gifts — and none who had allowed inter-caste confusion.
The brāhmaṇas were always engaged in their proper duties, their senses mastered, devoted to giving and to study, and restrained in receiving gifts.
At that time there was found none who denied the gods, none who spoke falsehood, none who was not widely learned, none who was envious, none who was incapable, none who was unlearned.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
None who was wretched or of distracted mind, or afflicted with suffering; in Ayodhyā no man nor woman was to be seen who lacked prosperity or who was of ill form, nor any who lacked devotion to the kṣatriya sovereign.
In the four varṇas foremost among them, all the men were worshippers of gods and guests, long-lived, devoted to righteousness and truth.
The kṣatriyas were guided by the brāhmaṇas; the vaiśyas were devoted in their vows to the kṣatriyas; and the śūdras, engaged in their own prescribed duty, were in service to the three varṇas.
That city was well protected by that lord of the Ikṣvāku line, even as it had been in former times by the wise Manu, the lord of men.
It was full of warriors equal to fire — skilled, intolerant of insult, their martial education fully mastered, like lions in their mountain caves —
— filled with the finest horses born in the Kāmboja country and among the Bāhlīkas, those trained in the forests and those born beside rivers, resembling Hari's own horses —
— filled with maddened elephants born of the Vindhya mountains and from the Himavat ranges — mighty elephants drunk with ichor, of surpassing strength, resembling mountains —
— that city was filled with elephants descended from Añjana and from Vāmana as well: of the bhadramandra, bhadramṛga, and mṛgamandra kinds.
Ever full of these ever-rutting elephants, mountain-like in form, that city — true to its name — shone forth for yet another two yojanas beyond.
That city of Ayodhyā — true to its name, with firm gates and bolts, adorned with variegated mansions, auspicious, thronged with thousands of men — was ruled by that lord of the earth equal to Śakra.
That heroic king had eight ministers, men of renown, pure of conduct and devoted, ever constant in their royal duties.
Dhṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, Arthasādhaka, Aśoka, Mantrapāla — and Sumantra was the eighth.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He had two highly esteemed officiating priests, both foremost among sages — Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva — and other counsellors as well.
They were prosperous, great-souled, learned in the śāstras, firm in valour, of established fame, ever attentive and obedient to command.
Endowed with splendour, forbearance, and fame, they spoke always with a smile preceding their words; neither from anger nor from desire of gain would they utter a falsehood.
Nothing was unknown to them, whether among their own people or among foreigners — whether an act being done, already done, or merely intended — not even through the work of spies.
Skilled in affairs of state, tested in matters of friendship, they would apply punishment proportionate to the occasion — even upon their own sons if need be.
Diligent in the accumulation of the treasury and in the maintenance of the army, they would not injure even an enemy who was guilty of no actual offence.
Valiant and of steady vigour, disciplined in the science of kingship, they were ever the protectors of the virtuous inhabitants throughout the realm.
Without harming the brāhmaṇa or kṣatriya classes, inflicting sharp punishment only after carefully assessing a man's strength and weakness, they filled the royal treasury.
Among all those who were pure, united in mind, and fully wise, there was not a single man given to falsehood anywhere in the city or in the realm.
There was none wicked there, no man addicted to another's wife; that realm and that finest of cities were utterly at peace.
Well-robed and well-attired, all of them were of fine character, ever watchful with the eye of wise counsel for the welfare of the lord of men.
Won over to their preceptor by his virtues, celebrated for their own valour, known even in foreign lands for their all-round firmness of judgment.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Endowed with such ministers, men possessed of every excellence, the sinless king Daśaratha governed the earth.
Surveying his subjects through his spies and delighting them with righteous rule, he could find no enemy equal to him, let alone superior.
Surrounded by those counsellors — versed in deliberation, dedicated, devoted, skilled, and capable — that sovereign blazed with glory, like the risen sun encircled by its effulgent rays.
Yet for him — of such great power, knowing righteousness, great-souled — who yearned ardently for a son, there was no son to continue the lineage.
As he pondered thus, the thought arose in the mind of that great soul: 'Why do I not perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice to obtain a son?'
Having resolved with certainty that the sacrifice must be performed, that wise, righteous-souled king, together with all his well-disciplined ministers —
— then spoke to Sumantra, best of ministers: 'Quickly bring to me all those venerable preceptors together with the chief priest.'
Having heard this, the charioteer Sumantra addressed the king privately: 'There is an account, formerly heard by me, related by the officiating priests —'
'— the blessed Sanatkumāra once narrated a tale in the presence of sages, O king, concerning the coming of sons to you.'
'Kaśyapa has a son known as Vibhāṇḍaka; his son in turn shall be renowned as Ṛśyaśṛṅga.'
'Always raised in the forest, that sage ever roams the woods; that foremost of brāhmaṇas knows nothing else, being perpetually devoted to attendance upon his father.'
'The twofold nature of that great soul's celibate life shall be proclaimed throughout the worlds, O king, and ever spoken of by brāhmaṇas.'
'As he lives thus — tending the sacred fire and serving his illustrious father — time passes on.'
'At this very time, the mighty Lomapāda, a king of great prowess, shall be celebrated in the Aṅga realm.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'On account of a transgression by that king, a terrible, exceedingly dreadful drought shall come — bringing fear to all living beings.'
'When the drought has come to pass, the king, filled with distress, will summon brāhmaṇas of learning and seniority and will speak.'
'"You are versed in sacred law and knowers of the ways of the world — prescribe for me the observance by which an expiation may come about."'
'Those brāhmaṇas, masters of the Veda, will tell the king: "O king, bring here by every means the son of Vibhāṇḍaka."'
'"And having brought Ṛśyaśṛṅga, duly honoured, O lord of the earth, give him your daughter Śāntā according to prescribed rite, with a collected mind."'
'On hearing their words, the king will fall into anxious deliberation: "By what means is it possible to bring here that one of great might?"'
'Then that self-composed king, having resolved after deliberation with his ministers, will despatch his chief priest and his councillors with due honours.'
'But they, on hearing the king's command, will be distressed, their faces downcast, and — afraid of the sage — will plead with the king that they cannot go.'
'Yet after reflection they will propose means fit for the task: "We shall bring the brāhmaṇa here — and no blame shall fall upon us."'
'Thus, by the lord of the Aṅgas himself, through the agency of courtesans, the sage's son was brought — and the god rained; and Śāntā was given to him.'
'And Ṛśyaśṛṅga as your son-in-law shall procure sons for you — this much has been declared by Sanatkumāra's account, as related by me.'
Then Daśaratha, overjoyed, replied to Sumantra: 'Tell me now in full detail how Ṛśyaśṛṅga was brought here.'
Sumantra, prompted by the king, then spoke these words: 'Hear from me, together with your ministers, how Ṛśyaśṛṅga was brought.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'The chief priest, together with the councillors, spoke thus to Lomapāda: "A stratagem free of risk has been devised by us."'
'"Ṛśyaśṛṅga is a forest-dweller, devoted to austerity and Vedic recitation; he is ignorant of women, of sense pleasures, and of enjoyment."'
'"By means of the objects of the senses that are pleasing and that overthrow the minds of men, we shall quickly bring him to the city — let it be decided upon."'
'"Let courtesans, beautiful and well-adorned, go there; by enticing him through various means, they shall bring him here, treated with honour."'
'Hearing this, the king consented and replied to the chief priest; and the chief priest and the ministers did accordingly at that time.'
'The leading courtesans, having heard this, entered the great forest; not far from that hermitage they made every effort to obtain a sight of the awesome sage's son who always dwelt in the āśrama.'
'He, ever contented in the service of his father, did not stray far from the hermitage.'
'From birth that ascetic had never previously seen a woman, a man, or any other creature belonging to city or country.'
'Then one day Vibhāṇḍaka's son came to that spot by chance, and there he saw those lovely women.'
'Those women, wondrously attired, singing in sweet voices, approached the sage's son and all spoke to him.'
'"Who are you, O brāhmaṇa, and how do you fare? We wish to know. Tell us why you wander alone in this desolate, fearsome forest."'
'Those women of beautiful form, never seen before by him in the forest, stirred his heart, and the inclination arose in him to tell of his own father.'
'"My father is Vibhāṇḍaka; I am his own-begotten son. The name by which I am known upon the earth, and my calling as well, is Ṛśyaśṛṅga."'
'"Our hermitage is close at hand — O you of auspicious appearance, I shall offer all of you honour there according to the prescribed rite."'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'On hearing the sage's son's words, all of them were disposed to see that hermitage, and all went there with him.'
'And when they had arrived, the sage's son performed the rite of hospitality: "Here is the arghya water, here the water for the feet, here are the roots and fruits of our āśrama."'
'Having received that hospitality, all of them — eager and also afraid of the sage — quickly resolved to depart.'
'"Take these choice fruits of ours too, O brāhmaṇa — good fortune to you; eat them, and do not delay."'
'Then all of them, filled with delight, embraced him and gave him sweetmeats and various beautiful confections to eat.'
'The radiant youth tasted them and took them for fruits — things never tasted before by one who had always lived in the forest.'
'Then, having taken leave of the brāhmaṇa and pleading their vows of observance, those women departed from that place, afraid of his father.'
'When all of them had gone, the brāhmaṇa son of Kaśyapa was ill at ease in his heart and tossed about in anguish.'
'On the very next day that man of great power went back to the place where he had seen those charming, well-adorned leading courtesans.'
'And seeing the brāhmaṇa approaching, all of them, their minds delighted, drew near and spoke these words to him.'
'"Come, gentle one, to our hermitage" — so they said to him — "there too this auspicious hospitality shall be offered, and more besides."'
'On hearing the heart-captivating words of all of them, he resolved to go; and the women then led him away.'
'And as that great-souled brāhmaṇa was being brought there, the god suddenly rained down, gladdening the world at that moment.'
'The lord of men went forth to meet the brāhmaṇa who had arrived with the very rains into his own realm; bowing humbly, the king touched the earth with his head before the sage.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'He duly offered him the arghya with a composed and collected mind, and begged grace of that foremost of brāhmaṇas, that no anger should enter the brāhmaṇa's heart.'
'Having led him into the inner apartments, and given him his daughter Śāntā according to prescribed rite, the king — his mind serene — was filled with joy.'
'Thus Ṛśyaśṛṅga of great radiance dwelt there, honoured with every desired thing, together with his wife Śāntā.'
And hear again, O lord of kings, my beneficial words — just as that foremost of gods spoke thus in the story.
Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus there shall be a most righteous king named Daśaratha — glorious and true to his word.
That king will have a friendship with the king of Aṅga, and this king will have a greatly fortunate daughter named Śāntā.
The son of the king of Aṅga is known as Lomapāda; the greatly renowned King Daśaratha shall go to him.
'I am without a son, O righteous one; let Śāntā's husband, directed by you, perform the sacrificial rite for me, for the continuation of my lineage.'
Having heard the king's words and reflected on them in his mind, that self-possessed one will give Śāntā a husband who will bring sons.
And having received that brāhmaṇa, the king, freed from his anguish, will perform that sacrifice with a heart full of joy.
And King Daśaratha, desirous of performing the sacrifice and knowledgeable in dharma, will choose with joined palms that best of twice-born, Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
For the purpose of the sacrifice, for offspring, and for heaven, that lord of men, that master of his people, will obtain his desired wish through that foremost of twice-born.
And he shall have four sons of immeasurable valour, establishers of the family line, renowned throughout all the worlds.
Thus did that foremost of gods, the blessed Sanatkumāra, the lord, narrate this story of old in the age of the gods.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
O tiger among men, O great king — go yourself with your army and retinue and bring him here, well-honoured.
Having taken Vasiṣṭha's leave and heeding the sūta's words, he set out with his inner-palace household and ministers to where that brāhmaṇa dwelt.
Crossing forests and rivers one by one, he gradually arrived at the region where that foremost sage resided.
Approaching that best of twice-born who was near Lomapāda, he first beheld the son of the ṛṣi blazing like a fire.
Then the king honoured him duly and with especial distinction, out of friendship toward that king, with a heart overflowing with joy.
And Lomapāda explained to the wise son of the ṛṣi the bond of friendship and kinship between them; Ṛśyaśṛṅga then honoured Daśaratha in return.
Thus well-honoured by him, that bull among men, the king, having dwelt there seven or eight days, said this to the king:
'O king, O lord of the people, let Śāntā, your daughter, go with her husband to my city — for a great task is at hand.'
Consenting with the word 'so be it' to the departure of that wise man, the king said to the brāhmaṇa: 'Go, with your wife.'
The son of the ṛṣi, agreeing, said 'so be it' to the king; then, given leave by the king, he departed with his wife.
The two of them — Daśaratha and the valiant Lomapāda — clasped hands with each other and embraced chest to chest out of affection, and were glad.
Then, taking leave of his friend and setting out, the joy of the Raghus sent swift messengers ahead to the citizens: 'Let the entire city be quickly and handsomely adorned.'
Then those joyful citizens, hearing that the king had come, did everything the king had sent word to do.
Then the king entered the handsomely adorned city to the sound of conches and kettledrums, placing the bull among twice-born at the head of the procession.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then all the townspeople were overjoyed, seeing that brāhmaṇa being ushered in with honour by the king who acts like Indra.
Having led him into the inner apartments and honoured him according to the scriptures, he considered himself fulfilled by the mere arrival of that sage.
All the women of the inner apartments, seeing Śāntā arrive thus with her husband — she of wide eyes — were filled with delight and joy.
Honoured by them and especially by the king, she lived there happily for some time together with the brāhmaṇa.
Then, after a long time had passed and a certain delightful spring had arrived, the king's mind turned toward performing a sacrifice.
Then, reverently bowing his head to that brāhmaṇa who was like a god in appearance, he chose him for the sacrifice — for the sake of progeny and the continuation of his lineage.
And he, well-honoured, said to the king: 'So be it.' 'Let your requisite materials be gathered and let the horse be released.'
Then the king spoke to Sumantra, the best of ministers: 'Sumantra, quickly summon the ritual officiants, the knowers of the Veda.'
Then Sumantra, of swift movement, went quickly and assembled all those brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Veda.
Suyajña, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, Kāśyapa, the family priest Vasiṣṭha, and whatever other best among twice-born there were —
Having honoured them, the righteous-souled King Daśaratha then spoke these gentle words full of dharma and purpose:
'For me, yearning as I am, there is no happiness without a son. For that reason it is my intention to sacrifice with the horse sacrifice.'
'I wish to perform the rite as prescribed by scripture. Through the power of the ṛṣi's son I shall attain my desires.'
Then all the brāhmaṇas, with Vasiṣṭha at their head, applauded that speech which had fallen from the king's mouth with the words: 'Excellent!'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
With Ṛśyaśṛṅga at their head, they spoke to the king: 'Let your requisite materials be gathered and let the horse be released.'
'You will certainly obtain four sons of immeasurable valour, since this righteous resolve has arisen in you for the sake of sons.'
Then the king was delighted hearing what the twice-born had said, and the king, with joy, spoke these auspicious words to his ministers:
'By the word of the preceptors, let my requisite materials be quickly assembled, and let the horse, guarded by capable men with its chaplain, be released.'
'Let the sacrificial ground be prepared on the northern bank of the Sarayū, and let the auspicious rites be performed according to proper procedure and rule.'
'This sacrifice can be performed by any king, but there must be no grievous fault in this best of rites —'
'For learned brahma-rākṣasas seek out any flaw here; the performer of a sacrifice that is deficient in proper procedure is instantly destroyed.'
'Therefore let the arrangements be made such that this rite of mine is completed according to proper procedure; let those who are capable attend to the execution.'
Then all the ministers applauded that speech of the lord of kings with the word 'so be it,' and carried out what had been commanded.
Then those twice-born praised the dharma-knowing bull among kings; having been given leave, they all returned the way they had come.
After the twice-born had departed, the lord of men, of great splendour, dismissed those ministers and then entered his own palace.
When spring arrived again, a full year had passed. Having saluted Vasiṣṭha and duly honoured him —
— he spoke these humble words to the best of twice-born for the purpose of obtaining offspring: 'Let the sacrifice be performed for me, O brāhmaṇa, as has been prescribed, O foremost of sages.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'Let it be arranged that no obstacle arises in the limbs of the sacrifice. You are my affectionate friend, and the greatest and most eminent preceptor.'
'The burden of this sacrifice, now set in motion, must be borne by you.' And the best of twice-born said to the king: 'So be it.'
'I shall do all of this that you have resolved upon.' Then he spoke to the senior brāhmaṇas who were established in sacrificial duties:
— to those well-established in architecture and construction, the senior and most pious ones; to the overseers of works, craftsmen, carpenters, and diggers —
— to astrologers and artisans, similarly to actors and dancers, to pure men who were learned in the scriptures and widely read —
'By the king's command, let all of you attend to the sacrificial work. Let bricks by the many thousands be quickly brought.'
'And let the reception halls for the kings, furnished with many amenities, be built; let auspicious lodging-houses for brāhmaṇas be constructed by the hundreds.'
'Provided with abundant food and drink and well-established — and for the townspeople as well, let many spacious halls be made.'
'Dwellings with abundant food, provided with all desired amenities — and let there be much splendour for the country folk as well.'
'Food is to be given according to proper rule, with honour — not carelessly — so that all classes of people are duly honoured and receive their proper respect.'
'And no disrespect is to be shown even under the sway of desire or anger toward those men who are diligently engaged in the sacrificial duties, nor toward the craftsmen.'
'They especially are to be honoured in due order, so that everything is well-arranged and nothing at all is neglected.'
'Act thus, all of you, with an affectionate and loving mind.' Then all of them assembled and said this to Vasiṣṭha:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'We shall do everything as instructed; nothing at all shall be neglected.' Then Vasiṣṭha, having called Sumantra, spoke these words:
'Invite the kings on the earth who are righteous, and brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras by the thousands.'
'Assemble and honour men from all lands. Bring the valiant lord of Mithilā, Janaka, true in his valour —'
'— who is versed in all the scriptures and likewise versed in the Vedas. Bring that greatly fortunate one, yourself, with due honour; knowing him to be an old kinsman, I speak of him first to you.'
'Similarly, the lord of Kāśi — affectionate, ever speaking pleasantly, of good conduct and god-like in appearance — bring him yourself.'
'Also, the aged and most righteous king of the Kekayas, father-in-law of this lion among kings — bring him here with his son.'
'The greatly fortunate lord of Aṅga, Lomapāda — who is to be honoured greatly and is the friend of this lion among kings — bring that illustrious one.'
'Bring all of them — the kings of the east, of Sindhu and Sauvīra, the kings of Saurāṣṭra, and all the lords of men in the south.'
'And whatever other affectionate kings there are on the surface of the earth — bring them as quickly as possible, with their retinues and kinsmen.'
Having heard those words of Vasiṣṭha, Sumantra at once dispatched capable men there to bring the kings.
For the righteous-souled Sumantra himself, acting swiftly by the sage's command, went to assemble the lords of the earth.
And all the overseers of the works reported to the wise Vasiṣṭha everything that had been prepared for the sacrifice.
Then the best of twice-born, pleased, spoke again to all of them: 'Nothing is to be given to anyone with disrespect or carelessly, for what is given with disrespect destroys the giver — there is no doubt in this.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then within a few days and nights, the lords of the earth arrived, bringing many jewels and treasures for King Daśaratha.
Then Vasiṣṭha, greatly pleased, said this to the king: 'O tiger among men, the kings have arrived at your command.'
'By me also all the best of kings have been honoured as they deserve. And the sacrificial ground, O king, has been made ready by men of concentrated minds.'
'And let your majesty proceed to the sacrificial enclosure nearby, which is provided on all sides with all desired offerings brought.'
In accordance with the words of both Vasiṣṭha and Ṛśyaśṛṅga, on an auspicious day and under an auspicious asterism, the lord of the earth set forth.
Then all those best of twice-born, with Vasiṣṭha at their head, placing Ṛśyaśṛṅga in the lead, thereupon commenced the work of the sacrifice.
Then, when a full year had passed and the horse had returned, the king's sacrifice commenced on the northern bank of the Sarayū.
With Ṛśyaśṛṅga placed at their head, the foremost of the twice-born performed the rites of the great Aśvamedha sacrifice for this most noble king.
The officiating priests, masters of the Veda, performed the rites according to injunction, proceeding in proper order and in strict accordance with the śāstras.
The twice-born performed the pravargya rite according to the śāstra, and likewise the upasad ceremony; they carried out every additional rite in conformity with rule and scripture.
Then, paying due honour and filled with joy, all those foremost of sages duly performed the rites beginning with the morning pressing of Soma.
There was nothing left unoblated, nor was any lapse at all observed; everything was done as befitting Brahman itself, carried out with full auspiciousness.
On those days none was seen to be weary or hungry; no brāhmaṇa there was unlearned, and none had fewer than a hundred attendants.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Brāhmaṇas ate freely, the protected and dependent also ate; ascetics ate, and wandering mendicants ate as well.
The aged and the infirm, women and children likewise — though eating without interruption, no satiation was perceived among them.
'Give, give food! Give garments of every kind!' — thus urged, the attendants did so again and again, many times over.
And many heaps of cooked food, resembling mountains, were seen there each day, prepared properly and in abundance.
The foremost of the twice-born praised the food — duly prepared and delicious — saying 'Ah, we are satisfied! Blessings upon you!' — and Rāghava heard this.
Well-adorned men served the brāhmaṇas, while others, wearing polished jewelled earrings, waited upon them with reverence.
In the intervals between rites, eloquent and steadfast brāhmaṇas propounded many reasoned arguments, each desiring to surpass the others.
Day by day there, upon the sacrificial ground, skilled twice-born men performed all the rites as enjoined by the śāstras.
No member of that king's sacrificial assembly was ignorant of the six Vedic auxiliaries, nor one lacking vows, nor unlearned in sacred lore, nor a brāhmaṇa unskilled in disputation.
When the erection of the sacrificial posts arrived, six posts of bilva wood and as many of khadira were set up, together with those of bilva combined, and others made of paṇin wood.
One post was ordained to be of śleṣmātaka wood and one of devadāru; two posts were appointed there whose circumference was as a man's outstretched arms.
All these were fashioned by those versed in scripture and skilled in sacrifice; for the glory of that sacrifice they were adorned with gold.
All were duly set in place by craftsmen, well made and firm, each with eight facets, all polished and comely in appearance.
Draped with garments and adorned with flowers and fragrant substances, they shone resplendently like the seven brilliant ṛṣis in heaven.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Bricks were also made in proper measure and proportion; there the sacrificial fire altar was built by brāhmaṇas skilled in the science of the cord.
That fire altar of the lion among kings, built by skilled twice-born men, was in the form of Garuḍa with golden wings, triple in extent and eighteen-layered.
The sacrificial animals were assigned there to their respective deities — serpents and birds as well, all as enjoined by scripture; and at the śāmitra post stood the horse and also the aquatic creatures.
All of this was assigned by the officiating priests in accordance with scripture; three hundred sacrificial animals were bound to the posts at that time, along with the chief jewel of horses belonging to king Daśaratha.
Kausalyā, having reverently attended upon that horse from all sides, slew it with three knives with supreme joy.
Then Kausalyā passed one night beside that winged creature, her mind composed and steadfast, out of her desire to fulfil dharma.
The hotṛ, the adhvaryu, and the udgātṛ then ceremonially united the horse with the mahiṣī, the parivṛktī, and the vāvātā in turn.
An officiating priest of the highest excellence, with his senses fully controlled, drew out the caul-fat of the winged creature and cooked it according to scriptural rite.
The lord of men then inhaled the fragrant smoke of that caul-fat at the proper time and in the proper manner, thereby expelling the sin from his own self.
All the limbs of the horse — every one — the brāhmaṇas cast into the fire in due order; all sixteen of the officiating priests together did so according to rule.
In other sacrifices the oblation is offered on branches of the plakṣa tree, but in the Aśvamedha alone the portion offered in the vaitasa manner is prescribed.
The Aśvamedha is reckoned to last three days according to the Kalpasūtra of the brāhmaṇas; the first day of it is appointed as the Catuṣṭoma day.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The second is reckoned as the Ukthya, and the following night as the Atirātra; many additional rites were performed there as ordained by the śāstra.
The Jyotiṣṭoma and Āyuṣī and the two Atirātra rites were also performed, as were the Abhijit, the Viśvajit, and the great rite Āptoryāma.
The king, increaser of his lineage, gave the eastern quarter to the hotṛ as his sacrificial fee, the western quarter to the adhvaryu, and the southern quarter to the brahman priest.
And the northern quarter was given to the udgātṛ — this is the southern (dakṣiṇā) prescribed of old by Svayambhū (the Self-born, Brahmā) for the great Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having completed the sacrifice with due ceremony, that bull among men, the king who had magnified the rite, then gave the earth itself to the officiating priests.
All the officiating priests then addressed the king, now freed of sin: 'You alone are worthy to protect the entire earth.'
'We have no use for land; we are not capable of governing it. We are always devoted to the study of the Veda, O lord of the earth — let Your Majesty give us some other ransom in its place.'
The king then gave them ten hundred thousand cows, ten crores' worth of gold, and silver four times that amount.
Then all the officiating priests together presented that wealth to the sage Ṛśyaśṛṅga and to the wise Vasiṣṭha.
Then those foremost of twice-born men, having made a lawful distribution of it, all spoke in reply with minds exceedingly well pleased and filled with delight.
Then the king, with a gladdened heart, having accomplished that unsurpassed sacrifice — which dispels sin, leads to the heavenly path, and is difficult of attainment even for the foremost of kings —
— then said to Ṛśyaśṛṅga, king Daśaratha spoke thus: 'O one of excellent vows, it is fitting that you accomplish the perpetuation of my lineage.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'So be it,' that foremost of twice-born men replied to the king: 'O king, four sons will be born to you, bearers of your lineage.'
That wise one then meditated for a moment on something excellent; having collected himself, the knower of the Vedas then addressed the king.
'I shall perform for you the putrīyā iṣṭi — the sacrifice for the sake of sons — accomplished with the mantras proclaimed in the Atharvaśiras, in accordance with the prescribed procedure.'
Then he commenced that putrīyā iṣṭi for the sake of sons; the brilliant sage poured oblations into the fire by the ritual action prescribed in the mantras.
Then the gods, together with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the great ṛṣis assembled in due order for the reception of their shares.
Those deities, having duly assembled in that sacrificial hall, addressed a great speech to Brahmā, the maker of worlds.
'O blessed one, through your favour a rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa oppresses us all with his might; we are unable to restrain him.'
'A boon was granted to him by you in times past, O blessed one, out of your pleasure; and out of constant respect for that, we endure everything from him.'
'That evil-minded one harasses the three worlds, hates the exalted, and desires to overpower Śakra, the king of the thirty gods.'
'He transgresses against ṛṣis, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and brāhmaṇas alike — that irresistible one, deluded by the power of the boon.'
'The sun does not blaze upon him; the wind does not blow at his side; even the ocean, garlanded with tossing waves, does not tremble upon beholding him.'
'Therefore, great is our fear of that rākṣasa of terrible aspect; O blessed one, it is fitting that you devise the means for his destruction.'
Thus addressed by all the gods, he reflected and then spoke: 'Indeed, the means of slaying that evil-souled one has already been ordained.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'By him the words were spoken: ‘I am not to be slain by gandharvas, yakṣas, gods, dānavas, or rākṣasas’ — and I assented to that request.'
'That rākṣasa did not mention human beings, out of contempt; therefore he is to be slain by a human being — there is no other death for him.'
Having heard this welcome speech pronounced by Brahmā, all the gods and great ṛṣis were then greatly rejoiced.
At that very moment Viṣṇu of great splendour arrived; meeting with Brahmā there, he stood in composed readiness.
All the gods, honouring him and bowing low, addressed him: 'O Viṣṇu, we shall appoint you for the welfare of the worlds.'
'O mighty Viṣṇu, become the son of king Daśaratha, lord of Ayodhyā — he who is learned in dharma, bountiful, and equal in glory to the great ṛṣis. Divide yourself fourfold and take birth in his three wives, who are comparable to Modesty, Prosperity, and Fame.'
'There, having assumed human form, O Viṣṇu, slay in battle Rāvaṇa — that thorn in the side of the worlds, grown mighty and invincible by the gods.'
'For that rākṣasa, the foolish Rāvaṇa, oppresses the gods together with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the foremost of ṛṣis through the arrogance of his might.'
'Therefore, deliver us from that haughty Rāvaṇa, blazing with splendour, swollen with pride, hostile to the lord of the thirty gods, ever-shrieking, truly a thorn to the ascetics — that fearsome one.'
Then Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, having been appointed by the foremost of gods, knowing it all already, spoke these gentle words to the gods.
'What means shall I employ for the slaying of that lord of rākṣasas, O gods, adopting which I might kill that thorn-in-the-side-of-the-ṛṣis?'
Thus addressed, all the gods replied to the imperishable Viṣṇu: 'Assuming a human body, slay Rāvaṇa in battle.'
'For he practised fierce austerities for a long time, O subduer of enemies, by which Brahmā — maker of worlds, worshipped by the worlds — was pleased.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'Being well pleased, the lord bestowed a boon upon that rākṣasa: freedom from fear from all manner of beings, excepting only human beings.'
'Human beings were despised by him of old on account of that boon; therefore his death at the hands of men has been foreseen, O scorcher of foes.'
Having heard these words of the gods, the self-possessed Viṣṇu then chose Daśaratha as the father into whom he would take birth.
And that king of great splendour, who was himself without a son at that time, was performing the putrīyā iṣṭi, longing for sons, he the slayer of enemies.
Then from the sacrificial fire of the sacrificer there emerged a great being of incomparable radiance, of mighty power and great strength.
Dark of complexion, clad in red garments, red-faced, with a voice like a kettledrum, with smooth tawny eyes, a body like a lion, and the finest beard and hair —
— possessed of auspicious marks, adorned with divine ornaments, of stature equal to a mountain peak, with the gait of a proud tiger —
— of appearance like the sun, comparable to a blazing flame, bearing a vessel of refined jāmbūnada gold with a silver lid —
— holding in both vast arms that bowl filled with divine pāyasa (rice-milk), like a beloved wife, or as if it were made of illusion itself —
— he gazed upon king Daśaratha and spoke these words: 'Know me, O king, as a man sent by Prajāpati, who has come hither.'
Thereupon the king replied with joined palms: 'O blessed one, be welcome. What may I do for you?'
Then that man sent by Prajāpati spoke again: 'O king, this has been obtained by you today through your worship of the gods.'
'This pāyasa has been made by the gods, O tiger among men — it is the source of progeny; take it, it is auspicious and enhances health.'
'Give it to your worthy wives to eat; from them you shall obtain the sons for whose sake you are sacrificing, O king.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Saying 'So be it,' the king, filled with joy, received upon his head that golden vessel filled with divine food, given by the gods.
He paid obeisance to that wondrous, fair-featured being, and filled with supreme joy, circumambulated him with reverence.
Then Daśaratha, having obtained the god-made pāyasa, was supremely delighted — like a penniless man who has received wealth.
Then that wondrous and supremely resplendent being, having concluded that act, vanished on the spot.
His inner palace shone ablaze with rays of joy, as the sky shines with the beams of the delightful autumnal moon.
Entering the inner apartments, he said to Kausalyā: 'Receive this pāyasa, which shall give you a son.'
The lord of men gave half the pāyasa to Kausalyā; of the remaining half he gave half to Sumitrā; the remaining quarter he gave to Kaikeyī, for the purpose of obtaining sons.
And the remaining portion of that pāyasa, comparable to nectar, the lord of the earth gave again to Sumitrā after reflection.
In this manner the king distributed the pāyasa separately to each of his wives.
Those most excellent wives of the lord of men, having received this pāyasa, all considered themselves honoured, their hearts uplifted with exceeding joy.
When Viṣṇu had entered into sonship with that great-souled king, Svayambhū — the Self-born Lord — spoke these words to all the gods:
"For the sake of Viṣṇu — the hero who is true to his vows and who desires the welfare of us all — create mighty helpers who can take any form at will.
Create warriors skilled in illusion, swift as the wind, versed in statecraft, endowed with keen intelligence, and equal to Viṣṇu in valour.
Create them invincible, skilled in every stratagem, possessed of divine physiques, proficient in the use of all weapons, and as it were nourished on immortal nectar.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Upon the foremost of the Apsarases, upon the bodies of Gandharvī women, upon the daughters of Yakṣas and Nāgas, upon female Ṛṣkas and Vidyādharīs,
upon the bodies of Kiṃnarī women and upon female monkeys — beget sons in the form of monkeys, equal in valour to one another."
Thus instructed by the Lord, they accepted his command and accordingly begot sons in the form of monkeys.
The great-souled sages, the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Nāgas, and Cāraṇas likewise begot heroic sons who roamed the forests.
Those created in their thousands, intent on slaying the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, were heroes of immeasurable strength, brave, vigorous, and able to assume any form at will.
Resembling elephants and mountains, handsome and mighty, they were born quickly as bears, monkeys, and gopucchas.
Whatever form, appearance, and valour belonged to each particular deity — with that entirety was each one's offspring separately born.
Some of approved valour were born of the golāṅgūlī females; others were born of female bears and monkey-women, and yet others of Kiṃnarī women.
All of them wielded rocks as weapons; all hurled trees; all were armed with claws and fangs; and all were skilled in every kind of missile.
They could dislodge the greatest mountains, shatter firmly rooted trees, and with their speed churn the ocean, lord of rivers.
They could split the earth with their feet, leap across the great ocean, soar through the vault of heaven, and seize the very clouds.
They could seize rut-maddened elephants roaming the forest, and bring birds plummeting down from the sky with their roar.
Of such monkeys of every form, hundreds upon hundreds of thousands were born — great-souled troop-leaders — and the foremost among those troops in turn begot further valiant monkeys.
Some by the thousands took up positions on the slopes of Mount Ṛkṣavān; others spread across many different mountains and forests.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
All those monkey-lords attended upon the two brothers: Sugrīva, son of the Sun, and Vālin, son of Indra.
By those mighty monkey-troop leaders — resembling clusters of storm-clouds and mountain peaks, formidable in body and form — the earth was covered over, for the sake of aiding Rāma.
When that horse-sacrifice of the great-souled king was concluded, the gods received their respective portions and departed the way they had come.
The king, his vows of consecration fulfilled, accompanied by his group of queens, together with his ministers, army, and retinue, re-entered his city.
Honoured fittingly by that king, the lords of the earth departed joyfully to their own realms, after bowing to the foremost of sages.
Once the lords of the earth had gone, the illustrious King Daśaratha re-entered his city with the foremost of Brāhmaṇas leading the way.
Ṛśyaśṛṅga, greatly honoured, departed together with Śāntā, followed by the wise king and his entire retinue.
Kausalyā gave birth to Rāma, endowed with divine marks, bearing half of Viṣṇu's essence, supremely blessed, the joy of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
Kausalyā shone with that son of boundless radiance as Aditi of the gods shines with Indra the Thunderbolt-bearer.
To Kaikeyī was born one named Bharata, true in valour — a direct fourth part of Viṣṇu, praised for all his virtues.
Then Sumitrā bore two sons, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna — heroes skilled in all weapons, jointly possessing a half portion of Viṣṇu.
Four great-souled sons were born to the king, each separately, virtuous and fitting, brilliant as stars in the month of Proṣṭhapada.
Eleven days having passed, he performed the naming rite accordingly: the eldest — the great-souled Rāma; and Bharata, son of Kaikeyī;
Saumitri as Lakṣmaṇa, and the other as Śatrughna — so Vasiṣṭha, deeply pleased, assigned these names. He also performed all the birth-rites and ceremonies for them from the beginning.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Among them, the eldest, Rāma, was like a banner — a source of delight to his father — esteemed even more by all beings as Svayambhū himself is esteemed.
All were learned in the Vedas, all were heroes, all were devoted to the welfare of the world, all were endowed with wisdom, all were filled with virtues.
Among them, Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of fortune, the greatly radiant Rāma of true valour — Lakṣmaṇa was deeply devoted to him from childhood onward.
He was ever doing everything agreeable to his eldest brother Rāma, the delight of the world — even as though he were another of Rāma's own bodies.
Lakṣmaṇa, endowed with auspiciousness, was like an external life-breath to that best of men. Without him, Rāma could not sleep; nor would he eat pure food brought before him without Lakṣmaṇa present.
Whenever the Rāghava mounted his horse and went hunting, Lakṣmaṇa would follow behind him, bow in hand, protecting him.
Śatrughna too — the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa — was always dearer to Bharata than life itself, and was equally beloved by Bharata.
Daśaratha with his four greatly blessed and beloved sons was supremely joyful, as Pitāmaha is joyful with the gods.
When they became endowed with knowledge, filled with virtues, modest, illustrious, all-knowing, and far-sighted —
— then the righteous-souled King Daśaratha, together with his preceptors and kinsmen, began to think about their marriages.
While that great-souled king was deliberating in the midst of his counsellors, the greatly radiant great sage Viśvāmitra arrived.
Desiring audience with the king, he spoke to the gatekeepers: "Announce quickly that the son of Gādhi, Kauśika, has arrived."
Hearing those words of his, all of them, their minds agitated, ran quickly to the royal palace, urged on by that command.
Going to the royal palace, they then announced to King Ikṣvāku — to Daśaratha — that the sage Viśvāmitra had arrived.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing those words of theirs, the king, composing himself, went out with his chaplain to meet him, rejoicing as Vāsava goes to meet Brahmā.
Seeing the ascetic blazing with lustre and firm in his vows, the king with a delighted countenance then presented the arghya offering.
He received the arghya from the king according to the rite prescribed by scripture, and then enquired of the lord of men about his well-being and about the eternal dharma.
Meeting Vasiṣṭha, that foremost of sages duly enquired about his welfare, and then addressed in proper order those greatly blessed sages present.
All of them, with gladdened hearts, entered that king's dwelling; honoured therein, they took their seats according to rank.
Then the king, his mind rejoicing, spoke to the great sage Viśvāmitra — supremely generous, joyful, honouring him:
"As is the attainment of ambrosia, as is rain upon a waterless land, as is the birth of a son to one who is childless and has a befitting wife, as is the recovery of what was lost, as is joy at a great occasion of rising — even so do I regard your arrival. Welcome, O great sage.
What supreme wish shall I fulfil for you? What does your joy require? You are a worthy vessel for me, O Brāhmaṇa; by good fortune have you come, O righteous one. Today my birth is fruitful and my life truly well-lived.
You who once shone by the title of royal sage, and whose lustre was illumined by austerity, have now attained the status of a brahmarṣi — you are worthy of my homage in many ways.
This, O Brāhmaṇa, is wondrous and supremely purifying for me; in beholding you, O Lord, I have entered upon auspicious ground.
Tell me what you desire and what business has brought you here. I wish to be graced by accomplishing that which is for your sake and advancement.
And you should not depart without deliberating on the matter, O Kauśika; I will carry out everything completely, for you are my very deity.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing those words — pleasing to the heart and the ear, spoken with humility by a man of self-mastery — that foremost of sages, whose virtues and fame were widely celebrated and who was distinguished by his qualities, attained supreme delight.
Having heard the wondrous and far-ranging words of that lion among kings, the greatly radiant Viśvāmitra, his body-hairs erect with joy, spoke:
"This is fitting for you, O tiger among kings, and for none else on earth — born of a great lineage and guided by the preceptorship of Vasiṣṭha.
The matter that lies in my heart — fulfil the resolve of that business, O tiger among kings; be one whose promise is true.
I am undertaking a vow for the sake of its accomplishment, O bull among men; but two rākṣasas who can change form at will are obstructors of it.
Even when my vow has been long observed and is near completion, these two rākṣasas — Mārīca and Subāhu, powerful and well-trained — defile that altar with torrents of flesh and blood.
When that firm vow is thus violated and overthrown, I — exhausted in effort and disheartened — withdraw from that place.
And it does not accord with my intention to release a curse in anger, O king; for such is the nature of that observance — no curse may be uttered there.
You ought to give me, O tiger among kings, your own son — Rāma of true valour, the hero who still wears the side-locks of boyhood, your eldest.
For he, protected by me and by his own divine radiance, is capable of destroying those rākṣasas who are the perpetrators of that desecration.
And I will bestow upon him manifold blessings, of no doubt, by which he will win renown across all three worlds.
Those two will not be able to stand in any way once they encounter Rāma; nor is there any man other than that Rāghava who would dare to slay them.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Those two wicked ones, intoxicated with their own power, are already in the grip of the noose of time; O tiger among kings, they are no match whatsoever for the great-souled Rāma.
You ought not to act out of paternal affection for your son, O king. I give you my solemn promise: know those two rākṣasas as already slain.
I know the great-souled Rāma of true valour, and so does the greatly radiant Vasiṣṭha, and all these others who are established in austerity.
If you desire the attainment of dharma and supreme and lasting fame in this world, O lord of kings, you ought to give Rāma to me.
If your ministers, headed by Vasiṣṭha, all give their assent, O Kākutstha, then send Rāma forth.
You ought to give willingly and without attachment your own son — lotus-eyed Rāma — for ten nights, the duration of the sacrifice.
The time of the sacrifice will not pass beyond its due limit, O Rāghava; act accordingly — may it go well with you — and do not give your mind over to grief.
Having thus spoken these words in accord with dharma and its purpose, the greatly radiant great sage Viśvāmitra, righteous in soul, fell silent.
Having thus heard those words of the sage — which rent his heart and mind — the lord of men was seized with great fear; his mind distressed, he trembled upon his seat.
Hearing that speech of Viśvāmitra, O tiger among kings, he was as though unconscious for a moment; then, regaining his senses, he spoke thus:
My lotus-eyed Rāma is not yet sixteen years old; I do not see him fit for battle against the rākṣasas.
A full akṣauhiṇī army of which I am the master and lord — covered by this force I shall go and fight those night-roaming demons myself.
These valiant and mighty retainers of mine are skilled in arms and capable of fighting the hosts of rākṣasas. You ought not to take Rāma.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
I myself, bow in hand, shall be the protector in the forefront of battle; as long as I hold life within me, I shall fight those night-roamers.
That observance of the vow shall be unimpeded and well protected; I shall go there myself. You ought not to take Rāma.
