He is still a boy, his learning incomplete; he does not know strength from weakness, he is not furnished with the power of weapons, and he is not skilled in warfare. Nor is he a match for the rākṣasas — for they fight with treachery, that is certain.
Separated from Rāma I could not endure to live even for a moment, O tiger among sages. You ought not to take Rāma.
Or if, O brāhmaṇa, O steadfast in vows, you desire to take the Rāghava, then take him together with me, equipped with a four-divisioned army.
Sixty thousand years have passed since my birth, O Kauśika, and he was obtained by me through great hardship and pain. You ought not to take Rāma.
My delight in all four of my sons is supreme, and Rāma — the eldest, foremost in righteousness — is especially dear. You ought not to take Rāma.
What is the prowess of those rākṣasas? Whose sons are they, and who are they? What is their stature? Who guards them, O foremost among sages?
And how are those rākṣasas, those treacherous fighters, to be countered — by Rāma, or by my forces, O brāhmaṇa, or by me?
Tell me everything, O blessed one — how I am to stand against those evil-natured ones in battle, for the rākṣasas are inflated with their own might.
Hearing his words, Viśvāmitra replied: There is a rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, born of the lineage of Paulastya —
— he is endowed with a boon granted by Brahmā, and he greatly oppresses all three worlds; of immense strength and immense valour, he is surrounded by many rākṣasas.
It is heard that the great-valoured Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, is the very brother of Vaiśravaṇa (Kubera), the son of the sage Viśravas.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When the great-powerful one does not himself create obstruction to the sacrifice, he sends forth two rākṣasas of exceedingly great strength — Mārīca and Subāhu — who will cause the disruption of the sacrifice.
Thus addressed by that sage, the king then spoke to the sage: I am truly not capable of standing in battle against that wicked-souled one.
Therefore show grace to my boy, O knower of dharma — gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, birds, and serpents —
— are not able to withstand Rāvaṇa; how much less then could mortals in battle? For that rākṣasa in combat seizes away the very valour of the valiant.
Against him I am not capable of fighting — neither with his forces, O foremost of sages, nor with my own forces together with my sons at my side.
How could I in any way give you my boy — a child, godlike in appearance, but inexperienced in battles, O brāhmaṇa, my little son?
Moreover, those two sons of Sunda and Upasunda who are like Death itself in battle and who are the disruptors of your sacrifice — I will surely not give you my boy for them.
Mārīca and Subāhu are both mighty and well-trained; against either one of the two, I might fight along with my band of allies.
Hearing his speech, which was confused with affection at every syllable, Kauśika, filled with anger, replied to the king of the earth:
Having first promised the thing, you now wish to abandon your pledge. This reversal is unworthy of and ill-befitting this lineage of the Rāghus.
If this be fitting for you, O king, I shall depart as I came. O Kākutstha, false to your promise — be happy with your kinsmen!
As the wise Viśvāmitra was overcome by wrath, the entire earth trembled, and fear entered into the gods.
Perceiving that all the world had assumed the form of fear, the great sage, steadfast in vows, the wise Vasiṣṭha, spoke these words to the king:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, like dharma himself made manifest, endowed with steadfastness, virtuous in vows, resplendent — you ought not to abandon dharma.
The Rāghava is renowned in the three worlds as one whose soul is dharma. Follow your own dharma; you ought not to bear adharma.
For one who has pledged 'I will do this' and then fails to do it, O Rāghava, the fruits of his ritual offerings and charitable works are destroyed. Therefore release Rāma.
Whether trained in arms or not yet trained, the rākṣasas will not be able to overpower him — guarded as he will be by the son of Kuśika, as ambrosia is guarded by fire.
He (Viśvāmitra) is dharma embodied in bodily form; he is the best among the mighty; he is supreme in intellect in this world and the ultimate resort of tapas.
He knows diverse weapons in all the three worlds, movable and immovable; no other man knows him fully, nor shall any ever know him.
Neither the gods, nor any sages, nor the asuras, nor the rākṣasas, nor the foremost gandharvas and yakṣas, nor kiṃnaras, nor great serpents —
— the all-righteous sons of Kṛśāśva gave all their weapons in former times to Kauśika (Viśvāmitra) when he was ruling as king.
Those sons of Kṛśāśva too, being the grandsons of Prajāpati's daughters, are of many forms, of great valour, radiant, and bringers of victory.
Jayā and Suprabhā, the two slender-waisted daughters of Dakṣa — they gave birth to one hundred supremely radiant weapons and missiles.
Jayā in former times obtained fifty excellent sons, immeasurable and able to assume any form at will, for the slaying of the armies of the asuras.
And Suprabhā in turn gave birth to fifty sons named the Saṃhāras — irresistible, impossible to assail, and most powerful.
And the son of Kuśika knows all those weapons rightly and fully; moreover he is capable of creating weapons never known before, being also learned in dharma.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Such is the valour and great energy of the great ascetic Viśvāmitra. O king, you ought not to entertain doubt about Rāma's going.
While Vasiṣṭha spoke thus, king Daśaratha, with joyful countenance, summoned his son Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Having had the auspicious rite of blessing performed — by his mother, by his father Daśaratha, and by the family priest Vasiṣṭha who consecrated him with benedictions —
— king Daśaratha smelled his beloved son's head and, with his inner soul well pleased, entrusted him to the son of Kuśika.
Then a wind, pleasant to the touch and free of dust, blew upon seeing the lotus-eyed Rāma depart with Viśvāmitra.
As the great-souled one set forth, there was a great shower of flowers, the sound of the divine kettledrum, and the reverberation of conch shells and drums.
Viśvāmitra went ahead; behind him followed the greatly renowned Rāma, bearing the kākapakṣa locks of youth, bow in hand; and Saumitri (Lakṣmaṇa) followed him in turn.
Adorned with quivers, bows in hand, illuminating all ten directions, the two noble princes followed the great-souled Viśvāmitra like two three-headed serpents, like the two Aśvins attending Brahmā.
With finger-guards and leather wristbands fastened, bearing swords, blazing with great splendour, the two princes were like the twin sons of Agni attending the unthinkable, immovable divine post.
Having gone one and a half yojanas to the southern bank of the Sarayū, Viśvāmitra addressed Rāma in a sweet voice: 'Rāma —'
'Receive water, dear child, lest the moment pass. Receive the group of mantras — receive both Balā and Atibalā.'
'Neither fatigue, nor fever, nor any change in your form shall afflict you; and the rākṣasas shall not be able to strike you down when asleep or when off-guard.'
'There is none equal to you in the valour of your arms on this earth, O Rāma, nor in the three worlds could any equal be found.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'In beauty, in grace, in knowledge, in the resolve of intellect, and in apt reply, no equal to you is to be found in this world, O sinless one.'
'When you have acquired these two sciences, there will be none equal to you; for Balā and Atibalā are the mothers of all knowledge.'
'Hunger and thirst shall not afflict you, O best of men; O Rāghava, as you recite on the path Balā and Atibalā — studying these two sciences — matchless renown on earth shall also be yours.'
'These two sciences, born of the granddaughters of Brahmā and endowed with brilliance, are fit to be bestowed upon you alone, O Kākutstha — for you are righteous and a worthy recipient.'
'Indeed, all these many virtues are in you — of that there is no doubt; and sustained by tapas, these sciences will manifest in many forms for you.'
Then Rāma, with joyful countenance, having touched water and become ritually pure, received those two sciences from the great sage of purified soul; gladdened by the sciences, Rāma of boundless valour shone resplendent.
Having entrusted all the duties of the teacher to the son of Kuśika, the three of them spent that night there on the banks of the Sarayū in great comfort.
When the night had brightened into dawn, the great sage Viśvāmitra addressed Kākutstha (Rāma), who lay sleeping on a bed of leaves.
"Kausalyā is blessed with a noble son — O Rāma, the eastern twilight is beginning; arise, O tiger among men, and perform the daily divine rites."
Having heard those most gracious words of the sage, the two sons of the king — those heroes — bathed, performed their water-offerings, and recited the supreme prayer.
Having completed the morning rites, those two of great valour saluted Viśvāmitra, the treasure of austerity, and, greatly delighted, presented themselves ready to depart.
As those two of great valour set out, they beheld there the divine river that flows in three paths (the Gaṅgā), at her auspicious confluence with the Sarayū.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
There was a holy hermitage of sages of fierce splendour who had been performing the highest austerity for many thousands of years.
Seeing that holy hermitage, the two Rāghavas were filled with the deepest joy, and they spoke these words to the great-souled Viśvāmitra.
"Whose is this holy hermitage, O Blessed One, and what man dwells here? We wish to hear — great is our curiosity."
Hearing their words, the foremost of sages smiled and spoke: "Listen, O Rāma, to whose this hermitage formerly belonged."
"Kandarpa — he who is called Kāma (Love) by the wise — once existed here in embodied form."
"The foolish one (Kāma) dared to assail Sthāṇu (Śiva), who was here performing austerity, collected in discipline, even as the lord of the gods was departing with his wedding train together with the host of Maruts; and that great-souled one (Śiva) uttered a wrathful exclamation."
"Burned by that terrible eye (of Śiva), O joy of the Raghu line, all the limbs fell from the body of that foolish one."
"His body destroyed, utterly burned by that great-souled one, Kāma was made bodiless there by the lord of the gods in his wrath."
"From that time onward, O Rāghava, he became renowned as Anaṅga ('the bodiless'); and that prosperous region where he abandoned his body is called the Aṅga country."
"This is his holy hermitage; these sages here were formerly his disciples, devoted to righteousness, O hero — no sin exists in them."
"Let us stay here tonight, O Rāma of auspicious appearance, between these two holy rivers; tomorrow we shall cross over."
As they were thus conversing there, the sages, perceiving them with the long sight of their austerity, came forward filled with the highest joy and delight.
Offering the arghya (water for the guest's hands), pādya (water for the feet), and hospitality to the son of Kuśika (Viśvāmitra), they then performed the rites of hosting for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Receiving that honourable welcome, they passed the time delightfully with stories and dwelt there in great happiness at the site of Kāma's hermitage.
Then, at the clear dawn, the two tamers of foes, having performed the morning rites, came to the bank of the river placing Viśvāmitra at their head.
All those great-souled sages of sharpened vows then drew up an auspicious boat and spoke to Viśvāmitra.
"Pray board the boat, preceded by the princes; go your way without mishap — let there be no reversal of time (delay)."
Viśvāmitra said "So be it," honoured those sages, and crossed together with those two the river that flows to the ocean.
Then in the middle of the river Rāma asked the foremost of sages: "What is this tumultuous sound of the water being cleft?"
Hearing the words of Rāghava filled with curiosity, the righteous-souled one explained the origin of that sound.
"On Mount Kailāsa, O Rāma, Brahmā fashioned a lake by the power of his mind, O tiger among men; therefore this is called the Mānasa lake."
"From that lake it flowed forth; it embraces Ayodhyā. The holy Sarayū, born from the lake, issued from Brahmā's lake."
"This incomparable sound approaches the Jāhnavī (Gaṅgā), born of the churning of the waters, O Rāma — bow in reverence without fail."
Both of them, those two of surpassing righteousness, made their bow to the two rivers and, reaching the southern bank, proceeded with swift strides.
Seeing the forest of terrible aspect, the son of the best of kings, the Ikṣvāku prince (Rāma), unperturbed, asked the foremost of sages.
"Ah, this forest is impenetrable, resounding with swarms of crickets, filled with fierce beasts of prey and birds with dreadful cries."
"It is thronged with various kinds of birds shrieking with frightful sounds, and graced with lions, tigers, wild boars, and elephants as well."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"It is crowded with dhava, aśvakarṇa, kakubha, bilva, tinduka, and pāṭala trees, and with jujube shrubs — what then is this fearful forest?"
The great sage Viśvāmitra of great splendour said to him: "Hear, my child, O Kākutstha, to whom this fearful forest belongs."
"These two prosperous territories, O best of men — Maladā and Karūṣa — existed here formerly, fashioned by divine ordinance."
"Long ago, O Rāma, when the thousand-eyed Indra slew Vṛtra, he was overwhelmed with impurity and afflicted by hunger, and brahminicide entered him."
"The gods and the sages, rich in austerity, bathed that Indra — they bathed him with their water-pots and released his impurity from him."
"Having deposited the impurity and also the bile from Mahendra's body here upon this earth, they then attained joy."
"When Indra became pure, free of bile, and clean, the lord, greatly pleased, gave the region an unsurpassed boon."
"'These two territories that bear the impurity and bile of my body — Maladā and Karūṣa — shall attain fame in the world.'"
"'Well done, well done!' — thus spoke the gods to Pākaśāsana (Indra), seeing that honour bestowed upon the region by wise Śakra."
"These two territories, Maladā and Karūṣa, O tamer of foes, flourished for a long time, rejoicing in wealth and grain."
"Then, at a certain time, there was a yakṣī who could assume any form at will, bearing the strength of a thousand elephants."
"Her name was Tāṭakā — blessings to you — the wife of the wise Sunda; her son was Mārīca, a rākṣasa of the valour of Śakra."
"She, Tāṭakā of wicked conduct, perpetually destroys these two territories, O Rāghava — Maladā and Karūṣa."
"She dwells there blocking the road, at a distance of more than a half-yojana; it is for that very reason that we must go to the forest of Tāṭakā."
"Relying on the strength of your own arms, slay this wicked creature, and at my command make this region free of thorns once more."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For no one is able to enter this region as it is, O Rāma, laid waste by that dreadful and irresistible yakṣiṇī."
"All of this has been told to you — how this forest became terrible, and how everything laid waste by the yakṣī has not recovered even to this day."
Then, having heard the excellent words of that sage of immeasurable greatness, the tiger among men spoke an auspicious reply.
"When yakṣas are said to be of little power, O foremost of sages, how does this weak woman bear the strength of a thousand elephants?"
Viśvāmitra spoke: "Hear by what means, though weak, she bears that superior strength — the valour wrought by the granting of a boon."
"Formerly there was a great yakṣa named Suketu, valiant and of good conduct, who was childless; and he performed great austerity."
"The Pitāmaha (Brahmā) was greatly pleased with that lord of yakṣas and gave him a jewel of a daughter, O Rāma, named Tāṭakā."
"The Pitāmaha also gave her the strength of a thousand elephants; but Brahmā of great renown did not grant a son to that yakṣa."
"That illustrious daughter, as she grew, resplendent with beauty and youth, was given as wife to Sunda, the son of Jambha."
"Then, in the course of time, the yakṣī gave birth to a son named Mārīca, who was irresistible and who became a rākṣasa by a curse."
"But when Sunda was slain, O Rāma, Tāṭakā, together with her son, sought to assault the most excellent of sages, Agastya."
"Agastya, in extreme fury, pronounced a curse on Mārīca saying 'Become a rākṣasa!'; and he also cursed Tāṭakā."
"'O great yakṣī who devours men, ugly and disfigured of face — abandoning this form, let a dreadful form be yours!'"
"She — this very Tāṭakā — enraged by the curse, senseless with fury, lays waste this region, once made auspicious by Agastya's dwelling in it."
"Slay her, O Rāghava — this wicked, most dreadful yakṣī of evil prowess — for the welfare of cattle and brahmins."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For no man is able to slay her who is bound by the curse, in the three worlds, except you, O joy of the Raghu line."
"You must feel no scruple on account of the slaying of a woman, O best of men — a king's son must do what is needed for the welfare of the four social orders."
"This is the eternal duty of those charged with the burden of kingship. Slay the unrighteous one, O Kākutstha — for righteousness does not exist in her."
"For it is told that in former times, O prince, Śakra slew Mantharā, the daughter of Virocana, when she sought to destroy the earth."
"And formerly, O Rāma, Viṣṇu slew the wife of Bhṛgu, Kāvya's mother, firm in her vows, when she sought to make a world without Indra."
"By these and many other great-souled royal heroes, women devoted to unrighteousness have been slain by the best of men."
Having heard the sage's spirited, undaunted command, the son of the best of men, Rāghava, stood with palms joined and replied—he who was firm in his vow.
"By the direction of my father's words, out of reverence for my father's command, the word of Kauśika (Viśvāmitra) must be carried out without any hesitation."
"I have been instructed in Ayodhyā, in the assembly of elders, by my noble-souled father Daśaratha himself—and his word is not to be disregarded."
"Therefore I, having heard my father's word and acting under the command of you who speak the truth of Brahman, will slay Tāṭakā—of this there is no doubt."
"For the welfare of cows and brāhmaṇas, for the happiness of this region, and to fulfill the command of you who are immeasurable—I am ready to act."
Having spoken thus, the subduer of foes gripped his bow in the middle and made the bowstring resound with a fierce twang that filled all the quarters with its sound.
By that sound the forest-dwellers were terrified and Tāṭakā herself was greatly enraged—bewildered by that sound.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Concentrating on that sound, the rākṣasī, overcome with fury, rushed with great speed toward the direction from which the sound had issued.
Seeing her—enraged, misshapen, disfigured of face, and of enormous stature—Rāghava spoke to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Look, Lakṣmaṇa, at the terrible and fearsome form of this yakṣī—the hearts of the faint-hearted would shatter at the mere sight of her."
"See how formidable she is, endowed with the power of illusion. Today I will render her harmless by severing her ears and the tip of her nose."
"I cannot bring myself to kill her—for she is protected by the nature of womanhood. My intention is only to cripple her valor and her movement."
While Rāma was speaking thus, Tāṭakā, frenzied with rage, raised her arms and roaring rushed straight at Rāma.
As she charged with terrifying speed, like a thunderbolt, he pierced her in the chest with an arrow. She fell and died.
Seeing her slain—she who had the appearance of one inspiring dread—the lord of the gods then cried "Bravo! Bravo!" and the gods honored Kākutstha (Rāma).
Purandara (Indra), the thousand-eyed, spoke with the utmost delight, and all the gods, rejoicing greatly, then addressed Viśvāmitra.
"O sage Kauśika, good fortune to you! All the troops of Maruts together with Indra are satisfied by this deed. Show your affection for Rāghava."
"Reveal to Rāghava, O brahmin, the sons of Prajāpati Kṛśāśva—those of true valor, endowed with the might of austerity."
"This son of a king, who is engaged in accompanying you, O brahmin, is worthy of them; and there is a great deed for the gods that the prince must accomplish."
Having spoken thus, all the gods, delighted, departed as they had come, after honoring Viśvāmitra; then twilight set in.
Then the best of sages, filled with joy and satisfied by the slaying of Tāṭakā, sniffed Rāma's crown in affection and spoke these words:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Let us spend this night here, O Rāma of auspicious appearance; at dawn tomorrow we shall go to that hermitage of mine."
Having passed that night, the greatly renowned Viśvāmitra smiled and spoke sweet-syllabled words to Rāghava.
"I am satisfied in my master, O greatly renowned prince of good fortune. Filled with the highest affection, I grant you all the weapons entirely."
"By these weapons you will, by force, bring enemies under control in battle and conquer the hosts of gods and asuras, together with gandharvas and serpents."
"I grant you all those divine weapons—good fortune to you. The great and divine Daṇḍacakra I shall give to you, Rāghava."
"Then, O hero, the Dharmacakra and likewise the Kālacakra; the Viṣṇucakra, which is extremely fierce, and likewise the Indracakra."
"The Vajra weapon, O best of men, and likewise Śiva's excellent Śūla; the Brahmaśiras weapon, and also the Aiṣīka, O Rāghava—I give to you, O mighty-armed one, the incomparable Brāhma weapon."
"Two maces also, O Kākutstha—Modakī and Śikharī, both blazing—I bestow upon you, O tiger among men, son of a king."
"The Dharmapāśa, O Rāma, and likewise the Kālapāśa, and also the incomparable Vāruṇa noose-weapon—these I give you."
"Two thunderbolts I bestow upon you, O delight of the Raghu clan—one dry and one wet."
"I give also the Pāinaka weapon, and likewise the Nārāyaṇa weapon; the dear Āgneya weapon named Śikhara by name."
"I give you the Vāyavya weapon named Prathama, O Rāghava; the weapon named Hayaśiras, and likewise the Krauñca weapon."
"Two Śaktis also, O Kākutstha, I give to you, O sinless one; the Kaṅkāla, the dreadful Musala, the Kāpāla, and the Kaṅkaṇa."
"Those weapons which the asuras wield—all of these I give you entirely; and the great Vaidyādhara weapon, named Nandana by name."
"A jewel-sword I give you, O mighty-armed son of the best of kings; and the dear Gāndharva weapon, named Mānava by name."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Prasvāpana and Praśamana I give, and also the Saura weapon, O Rāghava; Darpaṇa and Śoṣaṇa, and Saṃtāpana and Vilāpana."
"And Madana, which is irresistible and dear to Kandarpa (Kāma); the dear Paiśāca weapon, named Mohana by name—receive these, O tiger among men, O greatly renowned prince."
"Tāmasa, O tiger among men, and Saumana of great might; the irresistible Saṃvarta and Mausala, O son of a king."
"The Satya weapon, O mighty-armed one, and likewise the supreme Māyādhara; the dreadful weapon named Tejaḥprabha, which diminishes the radiance of enemies."
"The Soma weapon named Śiśira; the Tvāṣṭra weapon Sudāmana; and the terrible weapon of Bhaga, Śīteṣu; then the Mānava."
"These, O mighty-armed son of a king, that assume any form at will, of great power, supremely excellent—receive them quickly."
Then, standing and facing east, in a state of purity and self-restraint, Viśvāmitra, deeply pleased, bestowed upon Rāma the incomparable collection of mantras.
And while the wise sage Viśvāmitra recited the mantras, all those supremely worthy weapons presented themselves before Rāghava.
And all of them, delighted, stood before Rāma with hands joined and spoke: "We are here, O supremely noble Rāghava—your servants."
Kākutstha, having received them and touched them with his hand, urged them on, saying: "Dwell in my mind."
Then Rāma, with a joyful heart and of great splendor, having reverently saluted the great sage Viśvāmitra, prepared to proceed on the journey.
Having received the weapons, Kākutstha, with a joyful face and in a state of purity, as he walked along spoke to Viśvāmitra:
"I have received the weapons, O blessed one, and am now unassailable even by the gods. But I desire also the withdrawal formulae for the weapons, O bull among sages."
As Kākutstha spoke thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra—steadfast, of excellent vows, and pure—then imparted the withdrawals.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Satyavat, Satyakīrti, Dhṛṣṭa, and Rabhasa; Pratihāratara by name, Parāṅmukha, and Avāṅmukha—
Lakṣākṣa and Viṣama; Dṛḍhanābha and Sunābhaka; Daśākṣa and Śatavaktra; Daśaśīrṣa and Śatodara—
Padmanābha and Mahānābha; Dundunābha and Sunābhaka; Jyotiṣa and Kṛśana; and the two—Nairāśya and Vimala—
Yaugandhara and Haridra, and likewise Daityapramathana; Pitrya and Saumanasa; and the two—Vidhūtamakara—
And Karavīrakara; Dhana and Dhānya, O Rāghava; Kāmarūpa and Kāmaruci; Moha and Āvaraṇa—
Jṛmbhaka and Sarvanābha; and Santāna and Varaṇa—these sons of Kṛśāśva, O Rāma, resplendent and capable of assuming any form at will—
"Receive these from me—good fortune to you. You are worthy of them, O Rāghava. They are of divine and radiant form, embodied, and bestowers of bliss."
Standing before Rāma with hands joined, they spoke with sweet voices: "We are here, O tiger among men. Command us—what shall we do for you?"
The delight of the Raghu clan told them, "Go as you wish. Dwell in my mind, and at times of need you shall render me assistance."
Then those weapons, taking leave of Rāma and circumambulating him, saying to Kākutstha "So be it," departed as they had come.
And Rāghava, knowing them to have departed, as he walked along then spoke sweet and gentle words to the great sage Viśvāmitra:
"What is that grove of trees, resembling a cloud, shining not far from the mountain? I am exceedingly curious about it."
"It is beautiful, filled with deer, exceedingly lovely, adorned with various kinds of birds of sweet song."
"We have now emerged, O best of sages, from the hair-raising wilderness. By this I infer the pleasant nature of this region."
"Tell me everything, O blessed one—whose hermitage is this, where those sinful brahmin-slayers of wicked conduct came?"
Then, as that one of immeasurable greatness inquired about the forest, Viśvāmitra of mighty splendour began to explain it.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This, O Rāma, is the former hermitage of the great-souled Vāmana; it is known as Siddhāśrama, for here the great ascetic attained perfection."
"At that very time, king Bali, son of Virocana, having conquered the hosts of gods together with Indra and the Marut-bands, exercised sovereignty over the three worlds, renowned throughout them."
"While Bali was performing his sacrifice, the gods, with Agni at their head, assembled and themselves addressed Viṣṇu here at this hermitage."
"'O Viṣṇu, Bali son of Virocana is performing a supreme sacrifice; before that rite is concluded, let your own purpose be accomplished.'"
"'Whatever supplicants approach him from every quarter and ask for anything, wherever it may be, he grants all of it to them duly and in full.'"
"'Therefore, O Viṣṇu, for the benefit of the gods, resorting to your power of illusion, take on the form of a dwarf and accomplish the highest good.'"
"'By your grace this place shall become known as Siddhāśrama; when the deed is accomplished, O lord of the gods, O Blessed One, arise from here.'"
"Then Viṣṇu of mighty splendour was born of Aditi, and assuming the form of a dwarf he approached the son of Virocana."
"Having begged three paces of ground, and having received them with due respect, the soul of the worlds, devoted to the welfare of all beings, then strode across the worlds."
"He then gave the three worlds back to Mahendra, restraining Bali by his power; that one of mighty splendour brought the triple world once again under Śakra's sway."
"This hermitage, destroyer of toil, was formerly occupied by him; and I too, with devotion, have been dwelling here as a guest of that very Vāmana."
"It is to this hermitage that the obstacle-creating Rākṣasas come; here, O tiger among men, those evil-doers are to be slain by you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Today, O Rāma, let us go to the peerless Siddhāśrama; that hermitage-ground, dear child, belongs to you just as it does to me."
Seeing him arrive, all the sages dwelling in Siddhāśrama leapt up at once and in haste paid homage to Viśvāmitra.
They rendered due honour to the wise Viśvāmitra, and likewise performed the proper rites of hospitality for the two princes.
Then, having rested for a moment, the two princes — tamers of foes, the delight of the Raghu line — stood with joined palms and spoke to the tiger among sages.
"Enter upon your consecration this very day — may it be well with you, O bull among sages; may this Siddhāśrama be brought to fulfilment, may your word prove true."
Thus addressed, the mighty Viśvāmitra, great sage of brilliant splendour, then entered upon the rite of consecration, self-disciplined and with his senses fully restrained.
The two princes also passed that night with minds well-composed; and rising at the hour of dawn, they paid reverence to Viśvāmitra.
Then those two princes — tamers of foes, knowing the right place and the right time, skilled in fitting speech — spoke these words to Kauśika at the proper place and time.
"O Blessed One, O Brahman, we wish to know at what time those two night-roaming Rākṣasas are to be guarded against, so that we may not let that moment pass."
As the two scions of Kākutstha spoke thus, eager for battle, all those sages were pleased and praised the royal princes.
"Guard the hermitage, O Rāghavas both of you, for six nights from this day forward; this sage has entered upon the consecration and will observe a vow of silence."
Hearing those words, the two renowned princes, sleepless, stood guard over the ascetic grove for the full six days and nights.
The two heroes, ever watchful, supreme archers, maintained their vigil; tamers of foes, they guarded the foremost of sages, Viśvāmitra.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When that period had passed and the sixth day arrived, Rāma spoke to Saumitri: "Be vigilant, be fully composed."
While Rāma thus spoke, eager for combat, the sacrificial altar then blazed forth, together with the officiating priests and the ācāryas.
The sacrifice proceeded duly with the proper recitation of mantras; and in the sky a great and dreadful sound arose.
Like a storm-cloud that bursts forth in the rainy season covering the sky, those two Rākṣasas, conjuring their illusions, rushed forward.
Mārīca and Subāhu, and their retinue as well, arrived with terrifying aspect and showered down floods of blood.
Seeing those two rushing forward suddenly, the lotus-eyed Rāma glanced toward Lakṣmaṇa and spoke these words.
"See, Lakṣmaṇa, these ill-natured flesh-eating Rākṣasas — I shall scatter them with the Mānava weapon like clouds dispersed by the wind."
Rāghava, exceedingly wrathful, hurled at Mārīca the Mānava weapon — most noble and supremely brilliant.
Struck by that supreme Mānava weapon, Mārīca was hurled a full hundred yojanas away and cast into the ocean's surge.
Seeing Mārīca rendered senseless and spinning, tormented by the force of the numbing arrow, driven far away, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"See, Lakṣmaṇa, how the Mānava numbing arrow, charged with righteousness, only stuns him and carries him away — it does not separate him from his life."
"These others, however — the merciless evil-doers, those Rākṣasas steeped in wickedness, destroyers of sacrifices, feeders on blood — these I shall slay."
The delight of the Raghu line took up the mighty Āgneya weapon and hurled it at Subāhu; struck, Subāhu fell to the ground.
Taking up the Vāyavya weapon, the illustrious and most noble Rāghava slew the rest, bringing joy to the sages.
Having slain all those Rākṣasas who had disrupted the sacrifice, the delight of the Raghu line was honoured by the seers there, just as Indra was honoured of old after his victories.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, when the sacrifice was complete, the great sage Viśvāmitra, beholding the quarters free of all affliction, spoke these words to the scion of Kākutstha.
"I am fulfilled, O mighty-armed one; the command of your teacher has been carried out by you. Siddhāśrama is now truly made perfect, O Rāma of great renown."
Then Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, having accomplished their purpose, passed that night there — the two heroes joyful, with hearts filled with delight.
At the dawning of the night into morning, having performed their morning rites, the two together approached Viśvāmitra and the other sages.
Having saluted the foremost of sages — blazing like fire — the two who were sweet of speech spoke words that were sweet and noble.
"We two, O tiger among sages, stand before you as your servants; command us as you will — what order shall we carry out?"
When they had spoken thus, all the great sages, placing Viśvāmitra at their head, spoke these words to Rāma.
"O foremost of men, Janaka of Mithilā will perform a sacrifice most righteous; we are going there."
"You too, O tiger among men, shall go with us; and there you should see a wondrous jewel of a bow."
"That bow, O best of men, was formerly given in assembly by the gods — of immeasurable strength, fearsome, supremely brilliant in sacrifice."
"Neither gods, nor Gandharvas, nor Asuras, nor Rākṣasas, nor men of any kind are able to string it."
"Mighty kings and princes who wished to test the prowess of that bow were unable to string it."
"That bow, O tiger among men, belonging to the great-souled lord of Mithilā, you shall see there, O scion of Kākutstha, along with the sacrifice wondrous to behold."
"That bow with its fine nock, O tiger among men, was solicited as the fruit of the sacrifice from the lord of Mithilā by all the gods."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having spoken thus, the foremost of sages then set out for the journey, together with the assembly of seers and the scion of Kākutstha, having taken leave of the forest deities.
"Fare you well; I depart, my purpose fulfilled, from Siddhāśrama; I go to the Himālaya, the mountain mass of rock, on the northern bank of the Jāhnavī."
Having then circumambulated the peerless Siddhāśrama in the auspicious clockwise direction, he began to set out toward the northern quarter.
As that foremost of sages proceeded, some hundred carts belonging to the company of Brahman-reciters followed him in the procession.
The herds of deer and flocks of birds dwelling in Siddhāśrama also followed the great-souled Viśvāmitra, the great sage.
Travelling a great distance of road, when the sun was sinking low, the companies of sages made camp, composed and at peace, on the bank of the Śoṇā.
When the day-maker had set, those ones of boundless energy bathed, offered oblations into the fire, and then sat down with Viśvāmitra at their head.
Rāma too, together with Saumitri, having honoured those sages, then sat down in front of the wise Viśvāmitra.
Then Rāma of mighty splendour, filled with curiosity, questioned Viśvāmitra, the great sage, that tiger among sages.
"O Blessed One, what region is this, adorned with flourishing forests? I wish to hear about it — may all be well with you; please describe it truly and in full."
Prompted by Rāma's words, the one of excellent vows and great austerity, in the midst of the sages, narrated the complete account of that region.
There was a great sage born of Brahmā, named Kuśa, a man of immense austerity. In Vaidarbhī he begot four sons alike in their qualities: Kuśāmba, Kuśanābha, Ādhūrtarajasa, and Vasu.
Radiant and supremely energetic, eager to fulfill the duties of kṣatriyas, Kuśa addressed those sons of his who were righteous and truthful: 'Rule over your subjects, O sons; thus you shall attain the fullness of dharma.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing the words of Kuśa, those four foremost of kings, esteemed throughout the world, thereupon each established his own city.
The greatly resplendent Kuśāmba built the city of Kauśāmbī; the righteous Kuśanābha established the great city of Mahodaya.
O Rāma, Ādhūrtarajasa, that lord of the earth, built the excellent city of Dharmāraṇya; and King Vasu built Girivrajam.
This, O Rāma, is the land of that great-souled Vasu; and these five chief mountains shine forth on all sides.
The lovely river Śumāgadhī, renowned among the Māgadhas, flows through; amidst those five great mountains she gleams like a garland.
This, O Rāma, is the Māgadhī river, traversed of old by that great-souled Vasu—a region of fair fields, garlanded with crops.
The royal sage Kuśanābha, righteous of soul, begot in Ghṛtācī a hundred peerless daughters, O joy of the Raghu line.
Those daughters, in the bloom of youth, beautiful and well adorned, came to the pleasure garden, like a hundred lightning flashes of the rainy season.
Singing, dancing, and playing instruments, O Rāghava, adorned with the finest ornaments, they gave themselves over to supreme delight.
Those women, graceful in every limb and matchless in beauty upon earth, coming into the garden, shone like stars amid the clouds.
Seeing them endowed with every virtue and graced with beauty and youth, Vāyu, the all-pervading wind god, spoke these words.
'I desire you all; you shall become my wives. Abandon your human condition and you shall attain long life.'
Hearing those words of Vāyu, the tireless one, the hundred maidens laughed them off and then replied.
'You move within all beings, O best among gods; we all know your power. Why then do you treat us with contempt?'
'We are all daughters of Kuśanābha, O best of gods, and we are capable of casting you down from your station; but we protect our austerity.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'Let that evil time never come, O foolish one. Do not disregard our father, who is truthful. By the path of dharma we ourselves seek a husband.'
'Our father is our lord and our highest deity; he to whom our father gives us shall be our husband.'
Hearing their words, Vāyu was filled with extreme fury; the mighty lord entered into every limb of their bodies and broke them.
Broken by Vāyu, the maidens entered the palace of their father. Seeing them broken, the king was alarmed and spoke thus.
'Tell me, O daughters, what has happened. Who has disregarded dharma? Who has made you all hunchbacked? You are writhing in pain—speak to me.'
Hearing those words of the wise Kuśanābha, the hundred maidens touched his feet with their heads and spoke.
'O king, Vāyu, the all-pervading, wished to violate us; taking to an unworthy path, he did not regard dharma.'
'We have a father, blessings to you; we do not stand by our own will. You choose a husband for us; let him to whom you give us take us.'
'Because he would not accept our words, that one bound to sin—saying thus to him, we were all severely struck down by Vāyu.'
Hearing their words, that most righteous and greatly resplendent king replied to his hundred peerless daughters.
'O daughters, forbearance is proper for those who are forbearing; you have done a very great thing. You acted in unity and have upheld the honor of my lineage.'
'Forbearance is the ornament both of women and of men; and difficult indeed is the forbearance you have shown—especially toward the gods.'
'Such is the forbearance you all share equally. Forbearance is giving, forbearance is sacrifice, forbearance is truth itself, O daughters.'
'Forbearance is glory, forbearance is dharma; the entire world rests upon forbearance.' Having dismissed the maidens, O scion of Kākutstha, that king of godlike valor—

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
—versed in counsel, deliberated with his ministers about the giving away of his daughters in marriage, discussing the proper bestowal befitting time and place.
At that very time a great sage named Cūlī, who had preserved his vital seed upward and was of pure conduct, was performing Brahmic austerity.
A Gandharva woman named Somadā, daughter of Ūrmilā—blessings to you—attended upon that sage while he was performing austerity.
She, being devoted to his service, bowed before him and dwelt there in righteousness, season after season; the teacher became pleased with her.
And in due time he spoke to her, O joy of the Raghu line: 'I am fully satisfied; blessings to you—what may I do that is pleasing to you?'
Knowing the sage to be fully satisfied, the Gandharva woman, sweet-voiced and skilled in speech, replied most joyfully to that master of words.
'You are exalted with Brahmic splendor; you have become Brahman itself through great austerity. I desire a righteous son endowed with Brahmic austerity.'
'I have no husband, blessings to you, and I am no man's wife; since I have approached you through a Brahmic path, you ought to give me a son.'
The brahmin seer, pleased with her, gave her a peerless son—known as Brahmadatta, a mind-born son of Cūli.
That king Brahmadatta then dwelt in the city of Kāmpilya with the highest splendor, as the king of the gods dwells in heaven.
Then that highly righteous king Kuśanābha resolved, O scion of Kākutstha, to give his hundred daughters to Brahmadatta.
Having summoned him, the greatly resplendent king gave his hundred daughters to Brahmadatta with heartfelt joy.
Then in due order, O joy of the Raghu line, Brahmadatta, lord of the earth, took their hands one by one, as the lord of the gods would.
The very instant their hands were touched, all the hundred maidens became free of their hunchbacks, free of affliction, and endowed with supreme beauty.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing them released from the curse of Vāyu, the king Kuśanābha became supremely delighted and felt joy again and again.
The king, once the marriage rites were complete, sent Brahmadatta, lord of the earth, away with his wives and together with his assembly of teachers.
And Somadā, the Gandharva woman, greatly rejoiced at her son's worthy deed and welcomed those daughters-in-law duly according to custom.
After that wedding was done and Brahmadatta had departed, O Rāghava, Kuśanābha, who was without a son, arranged the pautrī sacrifice in order to obtain a son.
While the sacrifice was in progress, Kuśa, the son of Brahmā, greatly pleased, spoke to Kuśanābha, lord of the earth.
'A son worthy of you, O son, shall be born to you, most righteous; through him you shall attain Gādhi, and through him eternal fame in the world.'
Having spoken thus to Kuśanābha, lord of the earth, O Rāma, Kuśa rose into the sky and departed to the eternal Brahmaloka.
Then, in the course of time, to the wise Kuśanābha was born a supremely righteous son named Gādhi.
'That Gādhi, O scion of Kākutstha, supremely righteous, is my father; I am born of the lineage of Kuśa—I am Kauśika, O joy of the Raghu line.'
'My elder sister too, O Rāghava, of excellent vows, named Satyavatī, was given in marriage to Ṛcīka.'
'Following her husband, she ascended to heaven in her bodily form; the most noble Kauśikī then flowed forth as a great river.'
'Divine, of holy waters, lovely, resting upon the Himavat, my sister flows forth for the benefit and welfare of the world.'
'Therefore I dwell contentedly and happily on the slopes of Himavat, bound by affection for my sister Kauśikī, O joy of the Raghu line.'
'That Satyavatī is holy, established in truth and dharma, devoted to her husband, greatly fortunate—Kauśikī, the best of rivers.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'For I, O Rāma, have left her by vow and come hither; reaching Siddhāśrama, I have attained fulfillment through your splendor.'
'This, O Rāma, is the account of my birth, the fame of my own lineage, and of this region, which you asked me about, O mighty-armed one.'
'The midnight has passed while I have been telling these tales, O scion of Kākutstha. Go now to sleep; blessings to you—let there be no obstacle to us on this journey.'
'All the trees stand motionless; beasts and birds have settled to rest; the quarters are covered by the darkness of night, O joy of the Raghu line.'
'The twilight glow is slowly fading; the sky is like a face covered with eyes; it glitters with the dense mass of asterisms and stars and luminaries.'
'The cool-rayed moon, the hare-marked one, is rising, dispelling darkness from the world, gladdening the minds of living beings everywhere with his light, O lord.'
'All creatures of the night wander here and there; companies of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, terrible and flesh-eating, roam abroad.'
Having spoken thus, that greatly resplendent great sage fell silent; all the sages honored him with cries of 'Well done! Well done!'
Rāma too, along with Saumitri, somewhat overcome with wonder, praised that tiger among sages and then gave himself to sleep.
Having passed the remainder of the night on the bank of the Śoṇā along with the great seers, when the night had turned into a fair dawn, Viśvāmitra spoke.
"The night has brightened beautifully, Rāma; the morning twilight is beginning. Rise, rise — good fortune to you — make ready for the journey."
Hearing his words and performing the morning rites, Rāma resolved to set out and then spoke these words.
"Here is the Śoṇā, its waters pure, its ford shallow, adorned with sandbanks. By which path, O brahmin, shall we cross it?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by Rāma, Viśvāmitra replied: "This is the path I have pointed out — the very one by which the great seers travel."
Travelling a great distance, when midday had passed, they beheld the Jāhnavī, best of rivers, frequented by sages.
Seeing her sacred waters thronged with swans and cranes, all the sages together with Rāghava were filled with joy, and they took up their lodging on her bank.
Then, having bathed according to rule, having satisfied the ancestral spirits and the gods, having offered oblations into the sacred fires and partaken of the sacrificial food as though it were nectar,
They entered a pure spot on the bank of the Jāhnavī with gladdened hearts, surrounding the great-souled Viśvāmitra on all sides.
With a delighted mind, Rāma then addressed Viśvāmitra: "Revered one, I wish to hear about Gaṅgā, who flows through three paths — how did she, traversing the three worlds, reach the lord of rivers and streams?"
Prompted by Rāma's words, the great sage Viśvāmitra began to recount the origin and the growth of Gaṅgā.
"There is a king of mountains named Himavān, a great treasury of minerals. He had two daughters, Rāma, of unrivalled beauty in the world.
She who was born of Meru, of slender waist, charming in name and form — Menā — was the mother of both; the beloved wife of Himavat.
Upon her was born Gaṅgā, the elder daughter of Himavat; and a second daughter of his, named Umā, came to be, O Rāghava.
Then all the gods, wishing to accomplish the purpose of the deities, petitioned the lord of mountains for the elder daughter — Gaṅgā who flows through three paths.
Himavān, by the law of righteousness and for the good of the three worlds, gave away his daughter Gaṅgā — purifier of all worlds, free to course wherever she wills.
Receiving her for the benefit of the three worlds, those who promote the welfare of the three worlds departed, taking Gaṅgā with them, their inner selves fulfilled.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The other daughter of the mountain king, O joy of the Raghus, having undertaken a fierce vow, performed austerities, she whose wealth was asceticism.
On account of her fierce austerities, the best of mountains gave his daughter Umā — honoured by all the worlds — to Rudra, who was without equal.
These, then, are the two daughters of the mountain king, both revered by the worlds: Gaṅgā, best of rivers, and the goddess Umā, O Rāghava.
This righteous account has been told to you — how the river Tripathagā first ascended to the sky, O dear one, you who are the best among those who move."
When the sage had finished speaking, both heroes Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, expressing their appreciation of the narrative, addressed the foremost of sages.
"What you have told, O brahmin, is supremely righteous. Now it is fitting for you to speak of the elder daughter of the mountain king —
— in full detail, for you know how to expand a tale: her birth among gods and men, and by what cause she, the purifier of worlds, purifies the three paths."
"How is Gaṅgā, the renowned Tripathagā, best of rivers — endowed with what deeds does she flow through the three worlds, O knower of righteousness?"
As the descendant of Kākutstha spoke thus, Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is austerity, narrated the entire tale in full in the midst of the sages.
"Long ago, Rāma, Śitikaṇṭha — the blue-throated one — of great austerity, having married, and gazing upon the goddess with desire, approached her for conjugal union.
A divine hundred years passed for the god Śitikaṇṭha, yet still no son was born to him by her, O scorcher of foes, Rāma.
Then the gods became deeply anxious, led by the Pitāmaha: 'Whatever being is born here — who will be able to bear it?'
All the gods approached and, bowing low, spoke thus: 'O god of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are devoted to the welfare of this world — in response to the prostration of the gods, be gracious.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'The worlds will not be able to bear your seed, O best of gods. United with your brahmic austerity, practise asceticism together with the goddess.'
'For the welfare of the three worlds, restrain your vital seed within your own energy. Protect all these worlds; it is not fitting that you render the worlds void.'
Having heard the words of the gods, the great lord of all worlds said 'So be it' to all of them, and then spoke again thus:
'I shall restrain my seed within my own energy, together with Umā. Let the thirty gods and the earth attain peace.'
'But as for this unsurpassed seed of mine that has already been displaced — who shall bear it? Let the best of gods tell me.'
Thus addressed, the gods replied to the one whose banner bears the bull: 'This seed that has been displaced — the Earth shall bear it.'
Thus addressed, the lord of the gods released it upon the surface of the earth, by whose energy the earth with its mountains and forests was pervaded.
Then the gods again spoke to Hutāśana, the fire: 'Enter into it, O great blazing one — that which belongs to Rudra — accompanied by Vāyu.'
That which was pervaded again by fire became the White Mountain, and a divine thicket of reeds blazing like fire and sun — in that place was born the great-resplendent Kārttikeya, sprung from Agni.
Then the gods together with the hosts of sages, their minds exceedingly well pleased, worshipped both Umā and Śiva with great devotion.
Then the daughter of the mountain, Rāma, with eyes reddened in anger, wrathfully cursed all the thirty gods:
'Because I was prevented, when united with my husband for the desire of a son — henceforth none of you shall be fit to beget offspring upon your own wives; from this day your wives shall be without children.'
Having spoken thus and cursed all the gods, she cursed the Earth as well: 'You on the ground, taking manifold forms, shall have many consorts —'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'— and you, utterly foolish one, defiled by my wrath, who did not desire my son, shall never attain the joy that comes from a son of one's own.'
Seeing all the gods abashed, the lord of gods then prepared to depart to the quarter guarded by Varuṇa.
Going there, Maheśvara took up austerities on the northern flank of that mountain, on a peak where Himavat has his origin, together with the goddess.
This, Rāma, is the full account of the daughter of the mountain that has been set forth for you. Now hear from me, together with Lakṣmaṇa, the origin of Gaṅgā."
Long ago, while the god was engaged in austerity, the gods together with the hosts of sages, desiring a commander of the divine army, approached the Pitāmaha.
Then all the gods, led by Indra and preceded by Agni, having bowed down before the venerable Pitāmaha, spoke these auspicious words:
'He who was given to us as commander of the army by the Blessed One long ago — he is engaged in the highest austerity together with Umā.'
'Whatever must therefore be done next for the welfare of the worlds — arrange it, O knower of sacred ordinance, for you are our highest refuge.'
Having heard the words of the gods, the grandfather of all worlds, soothing the thirty gods with gentle words, spoke thus:
'What has been declared by the daughter of the mountain — that you shall have no progeny from your wives — that utterance of hers, unimpeded, is true; there is no doubt.'
'This Gaṅgā who traverses the sky — in her, Hutāśana shall beget a son who will be the subduer of enemies and commander of the army of the gods.'
'The elder daughter of the lord of mountains shall honour that son; and this will be greatly approved of by Umā — there is no doubt.'
Hearing his words, their purpose accomplished, O joy of the Raghus, all the gods bowed down and worshipped the Pitāmaha.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Going then, Rāma, to Mount Kailāsa adorned with minerals, all the gods commissioned Agni for the purpose of obtaining a son.
'Accomplish this divine purpose, O Hutāśana; O great blazing one, discharge your seed into Gaṅgā, daughter of the mountain.'
Having assented to the gods, Pāvaka approached Gaṅgā: 'Bear this embryo, O goddess — this is the wish of the gods.'
Hearing these words, she assumed a divine form; and seeing her greatness, he shed his seed all around.
Then Pāvaka anointed the goddess on all sides, filling all the streams of Gaṅgā, O joy of the Raghus.
Then Gaṅgā spoke to him, the priest of all the gods: 'I am unable to bear your uplifted energy, O god; burned by that fire, my senses are sorely distressed.'
Then the fire, the oblation-receiver of all gods, said to Gaṅgā: 'Let this embryo be deposited here at the foot of the Himālayas.'
Hearing the words of Agni, Gaṅgā — of great splendour — thereupon discharged that exceedingly brilliant embryo from her streams, O sinless one.
That which issued forth from her — gleaming like heated Jāmbūnada gold — when it reached the earth became pure, auspicious golden ore.
From its very sharpness of heat, copper and black iron were born; and its dross there became tin and lead.
That substance, reaching the earth, multiplied into various ores.
The moment the embryo was deposited, the entire forest clinging to the mountains, suffused with those energies, became golden.
From that time onward, O Rāghava, O tiger among men, gold has been known as jātarūpa — blazing equal to Hutāśana.
Then, when the boy was born, Indra together with the hosts of Maruts appointed the Kṛttikā stars to nourish him with milk.
They, making a solemn compact, gave milk immediately upon his birth, resolved: 'This boy is the son of all of us.'
Then all the gods declared: 'He shall be called Kārttikeya; he shall be the son renowned throughout the three worlds — there is no doubt.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing those words of theirs, they bathed with supreme splendour the one who had been born from the outflow of the womb, blazing like a fire.
The gods called him Skanda — 'the one who flowed forth' — born from the outflow of the womb: Kārttikeya of great fortune, comparable to the fire of the Kākutsthas.
Then the unsurpassed milk of the Kṛttikās welled forth, and he, becoming six-faced to match the six of them, drank the milk from their breasts.
Having drunk the milk in a single day, that tender-bodied all-pervading one then conquered by his own valour the hosts of Daitya armies.
Then the hosts of gods, gathering together led by Agni, consecrated him of spotless radiance as lord of the divine army.
"This, Rāma, is the full account of Gaṅgā that has been set forth by me — and likewise the birth of the Prince, which is meritorious and sacred."
Having narrated that tale to Rāma in honeyed syllables, Kauśika then spoke again to the descendant of Kākutstha with these further words.
There was formerly a heroic king, lord of Ayodhyā, a ruler of men named Sagara, righteous in soul, longing for offspring, yet he was without children.
O Rāma, the elder wife of Sagara was the daughter of the king of Vidarbha, named Keśinī, most devoted to dharma and truthful in speech.
The second wife of Sagara was the daughter of Ariṣṭanemi, matchless in beauty on earth, known by the name Sumatī.
Together with both those wives the king then performed ascetic practice, resorting to the Himavān mountain, at the peak called Bhṛguprasravaṇa.
Then, when a full hundred years had passed, the sage Bhṛgu, best among those steadfast in truth, gratified by the austerity, bestowed a boon upon Sagara.
O sinless one, you shall obtain an exceedingly great progeny, and you shall win incomparable fame in the world, O bull among men.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
One wife, dear son, shall bear a single son to continue your lineage; the other shall bring forth sixty thousand sons.
As that tiger among men was speaking, the two royal wives, greatly pleased, propitiated him and then spoke with palms folded in reverence.
O Brāhmaṇa, whose wife shall bear the single son, and which one shall give birth to many? We wish to hear this, O Brāhmaṇa -- may your words be true.
Hearing those words of the two, Bhṛgu, most righteous, spoke the highest pronouncement: Let the choice here be freely made by each of you.
Shall there be one perpetuator of the lineage, or many of great strength, famed and of mighty enterprise? Which of you desires which boon?
O delight of the Raghus, O Rāma, having heard the sage's words, Keśinī, in the king's presence, chose the single son who would continue the lineage.
Then Sumatī, sister of Suparṇa, chose the sixty thousand sons, mighty in enterprise and famed.
O delight of the Raghus, circumambulating the sage and bowing the head in reverence, the king departed to his own city together with his wives.
Then, when that time had come, the elder wife gave birth to a son -- Keśinī bore the son of Sagara who became known as Asamañja.
But Sumatī, O tiger among men, gave birth to a gourd-womb; and from the bursting of that gourd emerged sixty thousand sons.
Nursemaids nurtured them in pots filled with clarified butter; after a great span of time they all attained youth.
Then, after a long time had passed, the sixty thousand sons of Sagara were endowed with beauty and the vigour of youth.
And that eldest, O best of men, O delight of the Raghus, the son born of Sagara's own body -- he would seize children, hurl them laughing into the waters of the Sarayū, and watch them as they sank.
Engaged in the harm of the townspeople, he was banished from the city by his own father.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Asamañja's son was named Aṃśumān, a man of valour, esteemed by all the world, pleasing in speech to all.
Then, after a great span of time, there arose in the mind of Sagara, O best of men, the firm resolve: I shall perform the great sacrifice.
Having made that resolve, the king, together with his company of preceptors, learned in the Vedas in the matter of the sacrifice, began to prepare to perform the rite.
O delight of the Raghus, hearing Viśvāmitra's words at the tale's end, Rāma, exceedingly delighted, spoke to the sage who blazed like a fire.
I wish to hear this tale in full detail -- may it be well with you, O Brāhmaṇa. How did my ancestor perform that sacrifice?
Viśvāmitra, smiling, then said to Kākutstha: O Rāma, let the full account of that great-souled Sagara be heard.
The Himavān, the supreme among mountains, father-in-law of Śaṃkara, and the Vindhya mountain face each other in mutual regard.
Between those two the sacrifice was commenced, O best of men. For that region, O tiger among men, is celebrated for the performance of sacrificial rites.
O Kākutstha, dear son, Aṃśumān, firm of bow and great chariot-warrior, guarded the sacrificial horse, abiding by Sagara's command.
During that sacrifice's sacred juncture, Vāsava -- taking on a rākṣasa form -- stole away the sacrificial horse from the one performing the rite.
O Kākutstha, when that horse of the great-souled one was being carried away, all the companies of preceptors then addressed the sacrificer.
The sacrificial horse is being swiftly taken away at this sacred juncture -- O Kākutstha, slay the thief and bring the horse back.
This breach in the sacrifice is inauspicious for all of us; therefore, O king, let it be remedied such that the rite may proceed without defect.
Hearing the preceptors' words in that assembly, the king then spoke these words to his sixty thousand sons.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
O sons, O bulls among men, I see no passage for rākṣasas here, for this great rite is guarded by the greatly blessed ones who are purified by mantras.
Therefore go and search, O dear sons -- may it be well with you. Traverse the entire earth garlanded by the ocean.
O sons, each of you traverse one yojana in extent.
Dig up the earth as far as you see the horse, searching for the very one who stole the horse, by my command.
For I, having taken the sacrificial initiation, along with my grandson and the company of preceptors, shall remain here -- may it be well with you -- until the horse is found.
O Rāma, having heard these words, the mighty princes went forth with joyful hearts upon the surface of the earth, governed by their father's command.
O tiger among men, each one dug through the surface of the earth to a depth and breadth of one yojana with arms whose touch was like the thunderbolt.
O delight of the Raghus, as the earth was being cleft by spears like unto lightning-bolts and by most terrible ploughshares, it cried out.
O Rāghava, there arose an uproar from creatures difficult to overpower -- from nāgas, asuras, and rākṣasas being slain.
O delight of the Raghus, those heroes cleaved through the earth for sixty thousand yojanas until they reached the netherworld, Rasātala.
O tiger among kings, thus digging, the royal princes traversed Jambūdvīpa in all its mountain-thronged extent on every side.
Then all the gods together with the gandharvas, the asuras, and the nāgas, their minds deeply troubled, came to the Pitāmaha.
Having propitiated the great-souled one, with downcast faces and greatly terrified, they then spoke these words to the Pitāmaha.
O Blessed One, the entire earth is being dug up by the sons of Sagara, and many great-souled beings that move in water are being slain.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Declaring 'This one has ruined our sacrifice -- this one has stolen the horse' -- the sons of Sagara are slaying all creatures.
Having heard the words of the gods, the blessed Pitāmaha replied to those greatly terrified ones who were bewildered by the power of Fate.
This entire earth belongs to Vāsudeva the wise, who, having assumed the form of Kapila, bears her unceasingly.
The breaking asunder of the earth and likewise the destruction of the short-lived sons of Sagara -- both are indeed already seen to be the eternal decree.
Hearing the Pitāmaha's words, the thirty-three gods, the subduers of foes, were exceedingly gladdened and returned the way they had come.
As the earth was being cloven, there arose among the great-souled sons of Sagara a sound like the crash of a thunderbolt.
Then, having cleft through the entire earth and performed the circumambulation, all the sons of Sagara together spoke these words to their father.
The entire earth has been traversed, and beings of power have been slain -- gods, dānavas, rākṣasas, piśācas, serpents, and kiṃnaras.
Yet we see neither that horse nor the one who stole it. What shall we do? May it be well with you -- let your wisdom be deliberated upon in this matter.
O delight of the Raghus, hearing those words of his sons, Sagara, the best of kings, spoke with anger.
Dig further -- may it be well with you -- cleaving through the floor of the earth; having found the thief of the horse, return having accomplished your purpose.
Abiding by the command of their father, the great-souled Sagara, the sixty thousand sons rushed down into Rasātala.
As the digging continued there, they then beheld Virūpākṣa, the directional elephant, mountain-like, bearing up the surface of the earth.
O delight of the Raghus, that great elephant Virūpākṣa bore upon his head the entire earth with all its mountains and forests.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
O Kākutstha, whenever at a sacred juncture that great elephant, wearied, shakes his head for the sake of rest, an earthquake then occurs.
O Rāma, circumambulating him and honouring that great elephant, guardian of the direction, they went onward cleaving through Rasātala.
Then, having cleft through the eastern direction, they again cleft through the southern; in the southern direction too they beheld a great elephant.
They gazed with the utmost wonder at Mahāpadma, the great-souled one, like unto a very great mountain, bearing the earth upon his head.
Then, having made the circumambulation, the sixty thousand sons of the great-souled Sagara cleft through the western direction.
In the western direction too those mighty ones beheld a great directional elephant named Saumanasa, like unto a great immovable mountain.
Circumambulating him and also enquiring after his well-being, they then, continuing to dig, advanced towards the direction of Somavatī.
In the northern direction, O best of the Raghus, they beheld Bhadra -- white as snow, bearing this earth with an auspicious form.
Then touching him and circumambulating him, all sixty thousand sons cleaved through the floor of the earth.
Then, going to the renowned north-eastern direction, all the sons of Sagara, in fury dug through the earth.
There they beheld Kapila, the eternal Vāsudeva, and the horse of that divine one wandering not far away.
Knowing him to be the destroyer of their sacrifice, with eyes distraught with rage, they rushed upon him in fury, crying out: Stand, stand!
You it is who has stolen our sacrificial horse, O dull-witted one! Know that we, the sons of Sagara, have arrived to reckon with you.
O delight of the Raghus, hearing those words of theirs, Kapila, seized by great wrath, then uttered the syllable hum.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then by that immeasurable great-souled Kapila, O Kākutstha, all the sons of Sagara were reduced to heaps of ash.
Knowing that his sons had been gone a long time, O delight of the Raghu line, king Sagara addressed his grandson, who blazed with his own brilliance.
"You are both a hero and a man of learning, equal in splendour to your forebears. Search out the fate of your fathers and find the one by whom the sacrificial horse was stolen."
"There are mighty and powerful creatures dwelling underground. To counter them, take up your sword and bow."
"Pay homage to those worthy of homage, but also slay the obstructors. Return with your purpose accomplished, having brought my sacrifice to completion."
Thus properly addressed by the great-souled Sagara, Aṃśumān took up his bow and sword and set forth with swift strides.
Urged on by the king, O best of men, he entered the underground passage that had been dug by those great-souled fathers.
The greatly radiant one beheld the elephant of the quarter, worshipped by Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, birds, and serpents.
He circumambulated it reverently, inquired of its well-being, and then asked after his fathers and the one who had stolen the horse.
The elephant of the quarter, hearing his words, replied to Aṃśumān with gladness: "You will soon return together with the horse, having fulfilled the purpose of Asamañja."
Hearing those words, he proceeded in due order, according to proper custom, to question all the elephants of the quarters.
Honoured by all those guardians of the quarters, skilled in speech and expert in discourse, he was assured: "You will depart with the horse."
Hearing their words, swift-striding Aṃśumān went to the place where his paternal uncles, the sons of Sagara, had been reduced to heaps of ash.
Overcome with grief, the son of Asamañja cried out in utter anguish, deeply distressed at their destruction.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That tiger among men, filled with grief and sorrow, also saw the sacrificial horse wandering not far away.
That tiger among men, the greatly radiant one, wishing to perform the water-oblation for them, sought water but found no body of water nearby.
Casting his gaze carefully in all directions, O Rāma, he then saw Suparṇa — Garuḍa, the lord of birds, the maternal uncle of his forefathers — matchless and without blemish.
The mighty Vainateya, Garuḍa, spoke these words to him: "Do not grieve, O tiger among men. This slaying was sanctioned by the world."
"These mighty ones were burned by the immeasurable Kapila. You should not, O wise one, offer them ordinary water — that mundane rite is not appropriate for them."
"Gaṅgā, the elder daughter of Himavat, O bull among men — she who purifies all worlds — can sanctify these who have been reduced to heaps of ash."
"When this ash is moistened by Gaṅgā, the beloved of all worlds, she will carry those sixty thousand sons to the heavenly realm."
"Go now, O greatly fortunate bull among men, take the horse, and complete your grandfather's sacrifice — that is what you must do, O hero."
Hearing Suparṇa's words, the exceedingly valiant and greatly glorious Aṃśumān swiftly took the horse and returned.
Then, reaching the king who was consecrated for the sacrifice, O delight of the Raghu line, he reported in full what had happened and likewise Suparṇa's words.
Hearing those dreadful tidings from Aṃśumān, the king completed the sacrifice in full accordance with ritual injunction and prescribed rule.
The glorious king of the earth, having completed his desired sacrifice, returned to his own city, yet the king could not arrive at any resolution concerning the bringing of Gaṅgā.
Without reaching a resolution, the great king, after a long passage of time — thirty thousand years of ruling — ascended to heaven.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When Sagara had gone the way of time, O Rāma, the subjects acclaimed the greatly righteous Aṃśumān as king.
That great king Aṃśumān reigned magnificently, O delight of the Raghu line, and his great son was known as Dilīpa.
Entrusting the kingdom to Dilīpa, O delight of the Raghu line, he performed extremely severe austerities on a beautiful peak of Himavat.
For thirty-two thousand years that greatly glorious king, dwelling in the austerity-grove and rich in the wealth of penance, won heaven.
But Dilīpa of great splendour, upon hearing of his great-grandfathers' destruction, could arrive at no resolution, his mind afflicted with grief.
"How is Gaṅgā to descend? How are the water-rites for them to be performed? How can I liberate these ancestors?" — thus was he wholly absorbed in anxiety.
While he was constantly pondering thus — he who had known the self through righteousness — a son was born to him named Bhagīratha, supremely virtuous.
Dilīpa of great splendour, having performed many sacrifices and worshipped the gods, ruled his kingdom for thirty thousand years.
Without reaching a resolution concerning the rescue of those ancestors, the king, O tiger among men, succumbed to illness and met the law of time.
That bull among men, the king, having anointed his son Bhagīratha on the throne, went to Indra's realm by virtue of his own accumulated merit.
Bhagīratha, the royal sage, righteous and of great splendour, O delight of the Raghu line, was childless; though he longed for offspring, he had none.
He undertook prolonged austerities at Gokarṇa, O delight of the Raghu line — arms raised, surrounded by five fires, eating only once a month, his senses fully subdued.
As he continued in that fierce austerity for thousands of years, the blessed Brahmā, the lord and master of all creatures, was greatly pleased.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the Grandfather, approaching together with the hosts of gods, spoke thus to the great-souled Bhagīratha who was practising his austerities.
"O greatly fortunate Bhagīratha, lord of the people, I am pleased with you and with your intensely performed austerities. Choose a boon, O man of excellent vows."
The greatly splendid and greatly fortunate Bhagīratha, standing with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus to him, the grandfather of all worlds.
"If you, O blessed one, are pleased with me, and if my austerities have borne fruit, then may all the sons of Sagara receive water-oblations from my hand."
"May the ashes of these great-souled ones be moistened by the waters of Gaṅgā, and may all of my great-grandfathers thereby attain the highest heaven."
"And may offspring be granted, O god, so that our lineage does not perish — let the line of the Ikṣvākus not decline, O god. Let this be the paramount boon for me."
To the king who had thus spoken, the grandfather of all worlds replied with a gentle, sweet speech, sweet in every syllable.
"This is a great desire of the heart, O Bhagīratha, great chariot-warrior. Let it be so. May it be auspicious for you, O increaser of the Ikṣvāku line."
"This Gaṅgā, daughter of Himavat, born of the snows, the eldest daughter of Himavat — in order to bear her descent, O king, Hara must be engaged for that purpose."
"The earth will not be able to bear Gaṅgā's fall, O king. To bear her, O hero, I see no one other than the wielder of the trident, Śūlin — Śiva."
Having spoken thus to the king, and having addressed Gaṅgā as well, the creator of worlds, the god, departed to the three heavens together with all the hosts of Maruts.
When that god of gods had departed, O Rāma, Bhagīratha stood on the tip of his big toe pressing the earth, and in that posture he worshipped for a full year.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, when the year was complete, Umāpati, Paśupati, the lord saluted by all worlds, spoke these words to the king.
"I am pleased with you, O best of men, and I will do what is dear to you. I will bear upon my head the daughter of the mountain-king."
Then the eldest daughter of the snowy mountain, saluted by all the worlds, assumed a form of immense size and unbearable velocity, and fell from the sky, O Rāma — fell indeed upon the auspicious head of the auspicious Śiva.
She found no way out, bewildered within the tangle of matted locks, and the goddess wandered there for many years.
Bhagīratha had greatly pleased Hara by this act, O delight of the Raghu line, and so Hara released Gaṅgā in the direction of Bindu Lake.
From Śaṃkara's head, descending from the sky to the earth, the water spread out there, preceded by a tremendous roar.
Then gods, sages, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and hosts of Siddhas all gazed upon her as she passed from the sky down to the earth.
The divinities were stationed there in aerial chariots shaped like cities, on horses and on magnificent elephants, and some hovered aloft, darting to and fro.
That most wonderful and supreme descent of Gaṅgā — the assembled hosts of gods of immeasurable might gathered to behold it.
With the hosts of gods rushing through it and the lustre of their ornaments blazing, the sky — drained of its clouds — shone as if lit by a hundred suns.
With Śiṃśumāra sea-creatures, hosts of serpents, and flashing fish darting about like scattered bolts of lightning, the sky blazed brilliantly at that moment.
With white surging sprays of water scattered in a thousand streams, the sky was covered as if with autumn clouds, or as if carpeted by flocks of swans in flight.
Somewhere she rushed very swiftly; somewhere she wound in curves; somewhere she stretched out long; somewhere she dipped low; somewhere she was tossed up high; somewhere she moved very slowly.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Somewhere water struck water and bounced back; repeatedly going upward and then falling again to the earth.
That water, having fallen from Śaṃkara's head, and then having fallen to the surface of the earth, then shone brilliantly — pure, its impurities gone.
There the hosts of sages and Gandharvas dwelling on the surface of the earth touched that water which had fallen from the body of Bhava — Śiva — knowing it to be holy.
Those who had fallen from the sky to the surface of the earth through a curse — bathing in those waters, they became free of all impurity.
Their sins washed away and purified by those brilliantly shining waters, they re-entered the sky and regained their own celestial realms.
The world rejoiced, rejoiced in those shining waters; whoever bathed in Gaṅgā became free from fatigue and weariness.
And the royal sage Bhagīratha, of great splendour, mounted his divine chariot and drove forward, while Gaṅgā followed behind him.
All the gods together with their hosts of sages, Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, the foremost of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kiṃnaras, and the great serpents —
— and all the Apsarasas, O Rāma, following in the wake of Bhagīratha's chariot, joyfully followed Gaṅgā, as did all the creatures that live in water.
Wherever king Bhagīratha went, thither went the glorious Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, the destroyer of all sins.
That king, accompanied by Gaṅgā, went to the ocean and descended to the floor of the earth where those sons had been reduced to ashes.
When the ashes had been bathed in Gaṅgā's waters, O Rāma, Brahmā, lord of all the worlds, spoke these words to the king.
"O tiger among men, the sixty thousand sons of the great-souled Sagara have been ferried across and have gone to heaven like gods."
"For as long as the waters of the ocean remain in this world, O king, the sons of Sagara shall dwell in heaven like gods."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"And this Gaṅgā shall be your eldest daughter; by the name you have bestowed she shall be renowned throughout the world."
"The divine Gaṅgā is called Tripathagā — she who moves by three paths — and Bhāgīrathī; because she sustains the three paths, she is thus remembered as Tripathagā."
"Perform the water-offering here for all your forebears, O lord of men; fulfill your vow, O king."
"Your forefather of surpassing glory, the foremost among the righteous, did not attain this cherished wish."
"Likewise Aṃśumat, O dear one, of matchless splendor in the world, who sought to bring Gaṅgā, was unable to fulfill his vow."
"The royal sage endowed with virtues, of splendor equal to a great ṛṣi, of austerity equal to mine, and steadfast in the dharma of the kṣatriya —"
"— Dilīpa, O greatly fortunate one, your father of surpassing brilliance, who desired to bring Gaṅgā, also could not achieve it, O sinless one."
"That vow has been fulfilled by you, O bull among men; you have attained the highest fame in the world, held in supreme esteem."
"And by this descent of Gaṅgā that you have accomplished, O subduer of foes, you have attained a great abode of dharma."
"Bathe yourself in these auspicious waters, O best of men, O tiger among men; become purified and reap the fruit of merit."
"Perform the water-rite for all your forebears. May you fare well; I shall depart to my own realm — let the king also go."
Having spoken thus, the lord of the gods, the grandsire of all worlds, of great glory, departed to the divine realm by the way he had come.
The royal sage Bhagīratha too, of great glory, having performed the highest water-rites for the Sāgaras in proper order and due form, the king — his rites completed and purified — entered his own city.
His purpose fulfilled, O best of men, he ruled his kingdom; and the people rejoiced on receiving that king, O Rāghava, — free from grief, their purposes fulfilled, rid of affliction.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
