This account of Gaṅgā in full has been told to you by me, O Rāma. May you prosper; may all be well with you. The hour of twilight is passing.
Meritorious, fame-bestowing, life-prolonging, heavenly, and conducive to offspring — such is this tale of the descent of Gaṅgā that I have narrated.
Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra, Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa was filled with the greatest wonder and spoke to Viśvāmitra.
"This is utterly wondrous, O brahman — this supreme account narrated by you: the auspicious descent of Gaṅgā and the filling of the ocean."
That entire night passed for him — together with Saumitri — as he pondered the auspicious tale of Viśvāmitra.
Then at the clear dawn, Rāghava, the subduer of foes, having performed his morning rites, spoke these words to the great sage Viśvāmitra.
"The blessed night has passed; what was most worthy of hearing has been heard. That night passed as if it were but a moment, O great ascetic, for me as I pondered your entire tale from beginning to end."
"Let us cross the foremost of rivers, the holy Tripathagā stream; this boat, comfortably spread out, belonging to the ṛṣis of meritorious deeds, has come here quickly knowing that the reverend one has arrived."
Having heard those words of the great-souled Rāghava, the sage together with the assembly of ṛṣis caused them all — with Rāghava — to be ferried across.
Having reached the northern bank and duly honored the company of ṛṣis, they encamped on the bank of the Gaṅgā and beheld the city of Viśālā.
Then the chief of sages quickly proceeded with Rāghava to the charming city of Viśālā, divine, resembling heaven.
Then Rāma of great wisdom, with joined palms, asked the great sage Viśvāmitra about that excellent city of Viśālā.
"What is this royal lineage in Viśālā, O great sage? I wish to hear; may all be well with you — I have the greatest curiosity."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having heard those words of Rāma, the bull among sages began to recount the ancient [history] of Viśālā.
"Hear, O Rāma, this auspicious tale as I tell it of Śakra. What transpired in this region — hear it in truth, O Rāghava."
"In the Kṛta age of old, O Rāma, the sons of Diti were of great strength, and the sons of Aditi were of great fortune, possessed of valor, and supremely righteous."
"Then a thought arose among those great-souled ones, O best of men: 'How may we become immortal, free from aging and free from disease?'"
"As those wise ones deliberated, O Rāma, a thought arose among them: 'By churning the ocean of milk, we shall obtain the nectar therein.'"
"Having resolved to churn, using Vāsuki as the churning rope and Mount Mandara as the churning staff, those of boundless might churned."
"Then one named Dhanvantari arose, and also the radiant Apsarases — from that churning of the waters, from that nectar, O best of men, those excellent women arose; hence they came to be called Apsarases."
"There were sixty crores of those radiant Apsarases, O Kākutstha, and their attendants were beyond counting."
"None of the gods or dānavas accepted them; and because none accepted them, they are remembered as 'common to all' (sādhāraṇāḥ)."
"Then the daughter of Varuṇa, Vāruṇī of great fortune, O delight of the Raghu line, arose seeking someone to accept her."
"The sons of Diti, O Rāma, did not accept that daughter of Varuṇa; but the sons of Aditi, O hero, accepted that blameless one."
"Thus the sons of Diti became asuras, and the sons of Aditi became suras; the suras were joyful and delighted at the acceptance of Vāruṇī."
"Uccaiḥśravā the chief of horses, the jewel-gem Kaustubha, and likewise the supreme amṛta arose, O best of men."
"Then, O Rāma, on account of this there was a great destruction of clans; the sons of Aditi thereafter slew the sons of Diti."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The heroic sons of Aditi slaughtered the sons of Diti in that terrible great battle between the Daiteyas and the Ādityas, which was exceedingly fierce."
"Having slain the sons of Diti and obtained the kingdom, Purandara joyfully ruled the worlds together with the assemblies of ṛṣis and Cāraṇas."
When those sons had been slain, Diti, overcome with the deepest grief, spoke these words to her husband, Mārīca Kāśyapa, O Rāma.
"My sons have been slain, O reverend one, by your great and mighty sons. I desire a son who will slay Śakra — a son won by long austerity."
"I shall perform austerities; you must grant me an embryo; grant your permission for one such as this — a slayer of Śakra."
Having heard her words, the greatly resplendent Mārīca Kāśyapa then replied to Diti, who was overcome with the deepest grief.
"So be it — may all be well with you, O one rich in austerity. Be pure; you shall bring forth a son who will be Śakra's slayer in battle."
"But if you remain pure throughout the full thousand years, you shall beget from me a son who will be the destroyer of the three worlds."
Having spoken thus, the greatly resplendent one stroked her with his hand; and having thus touched her and said "fare well," he departed for austerities.
When he had departed, O best of men, Diti was overwhelmed with joy; reaching the grove of Kuśaplava, she performed the most severe austerities.
While she was performing those austerities, O best of men, the thousand-eyed one attended upon her with the greatest excellence of virtuous service.
The thousand-eyed one presented her with fire, kuśa grass, firewood, water, fruits, and roots, and likewise whatever else was desired.
With massages of her limbs and the removal of her fatigue, Śakra attended upon Diti at all times.
Then, when ten years remained of the thousand, O delight of the Raghu line, Diti, filled with the utmost joy, spoke to the thousand-eyed one.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Ten years remain as I perform austerities, O best of the mighty; then, may it be well with you, you shall see a brother."
"Him, O son, I shall set to the task of conquest for your sake; you shall enjoy, O son, the conquest of the three worlds together, free from affliction."
Having spoken thus to Śakra, when midday had come, the goddess Diti was overcome by sleep, having placed her feet where her head should be.
Seeing her impure — her hair on the feet's side, her feet placed where the head should be — Śakra laughed and was delighted.
Purandara entered an opening of her body, O Rāma, and the supremely self-controlled one split the embryo into seven parts.
As the embryo was thus being pierced by the hundred-jointed thunderbolt, it wept with a clear voice, O Rāma; thereupon Diti awoke.
"Do not weep, do not weep" — thus Śakra addressed the embryo; yet the greatly resplendent Vāsava continued to split it even as it wept.
"It must not be slain, it must not be slain" — thus Diti cried out; thereupon Śakra emerged out of respect for his mother's words.
With joined palms and thunderbolt in hand, Śakra addressed Diti: "O goddess, you slept in an impure posture — your hair on the side of the feet, your feet placed where the head should be."
"Seizing that opportunity, I split into seven parts the one who would have been Śakra's slayer in battle, O goddess; you must forgive me for this."
When her womb had been split into seven parts, Diti, deeply grieved, spoke words of supplication to the thousand-eyed Indra, that invincible one.
Through my own transgression this embryo has been destroyed and split into seven; there is no fault in you in this matter, O lord of the gods, O slayer of Bala.
Yet I desire that something favorable be done for me in the ruin of my womb: let these seven become the guardians of seven regions as the Maruts.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Let these seven, bearers of the wind, roam heaven as my sons — known as the Mārutas, of divine form, my own children.
Let one roam the world of Brahmā, and another the world of Indra; let a third, of great renown, be known in heaven as Vāyu.
And may four, O foremost of gods, roam the four directions by your command — may all be well with you; my sons, become divine beings, shall be renowned as the Mārutas by the very name you have bestowed.
Having heard her words, the thousand-eyed Indra, the destroyer of citadels, the slayer of Bala, spoke these words to Diti with joined palms.
All that you have said shall come to pass — there is no doubt. May it be well with you; your sons, having become divine beings, shall roam as you wish.
Having thus come to this resolution, O Rāma, the mother and son, their purpose accomplished, departed from that ascetic forest to the three heavens — so we have heard.
This is the very region, O descendant of Kākutstha, once inhabited by Mahendra, where he thus attended upon Diti who had achieved the fruit of her austerity.
Of Ikṣvāku, O tiger among men, there was born a most righteous son, born of Alambuṣā, renowned by the name Viśālā.
By him was the city named Viśālā established here in this very place.
The son of Viśālā, O Rāma, was Hemacandra, of great might; Sucandra, next after Hemacandra, was renowned by that name.
The son of Sucandra, O Rāma, was known as Dhūmrāśva; and from Dhūmrāśva there arose a son called Sṛñjaya.
The glorious and valiant son of Sṛñjaya was Sahadeva; and Kuśāśva, most devoted to righteousness, was the son of Sahadeva.
Of Kuśāśva was born Somadatta, of great splendor and valor; and the son of Somadatta, O descendant of Kākutstha, is renowned as such.
His son, of great splendor, resembling an immortal, named Sumati, the unconquerable, now inhabits this city.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
By the grace of Ikṣvāku, all the kings of Viśālā are long-lived, great-souled, heroic, and deeply righteous.
Here today, O Rāma, let us pass the night in comfort; at tomorrow's dawn, O best of men, you should visit King Janaka.
The greatly splendid Sumati, foremost among excellent men, of great renown, having heard of Viśvāmitra's arrival, went forth to meet him.
Having offered the highest honor together with his teachers and kinsmen, with joined palms, inquiring after his welfare, he then spoke to Viśvāmitra.
I am blessed, I am honored, O sage, that you have arrived in my domain and that I have your audience — there is none more blessed than I.
Having inquired after each other's welfare at that mutual meeting, Sumati, at the conclusion of their conversation, addressed the great sage.
May all be well with you — these two princes, whose valor equals that of the gods, who move like elephant and lion, who are compared to a tiger and a bull,
With wide eyes like lotus petals, bearing sword, quiver, and bow, like the twin Aśvins in form, their youth just come to fullness —
Who have come to earth as if by chance, like immortals descended from the world of gods — how have they come here on foot, O sage, for what purpose, and whose sons are they?
They adorn this region as the sun and moon adorn the sky, similar to each other in measure, bearing, and conduct.
For what purpose have these two foremost of men arrived by so difficult a road, bearing the finest of weapons, these two heroes? I desire to hear the truth of it.
Having heard his words, Viśvāmitra reported to him what had happened: their stay at Siddhāśrama, and the slaying of the Rākṣasas.
Hearing Viśvāmitra's account, the king was filled with the greatest joy; those two most excellent guests who had arrived — the sons of Daśaratha, those two of great strength worthy of honor — he honored according to due rite.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the two Rāghavas, having received the highest hospitality from Sumati and having spent one night there, departed for Mithilā.
Seeing the beautiful city of King Janaka, all the sages praised it, exclaiming "Excellent! Excellent!" and honored Mithilā.
In the grove of Mithilā, Rāghava, seeing an ancient hermitage, deserted yet lovely, asked the foremost of sages about it.
What is this that has the appearance of a splendid hermitage yet is abandoned by sages? I wish to hear, O blessed one, whose former āśrama this was.
Having heard the words spoken by Rāghava, the great sage Viśvāmitra, eloquent in speech and of great splendor, replied.
Come, I shall tell you — listen to the truth, O Rāghava: this hermitage site was cursed in wrath by that great-souled one to whom it belonged.
O best of men, this was formerly the hermitage of the great-souled Gautama, divine in its appearance, worshipped even by the gods.
Here he dwelt performing austerities together with Ahalyā in former times, for many accumulations of years, O prince, that one of great renown.
Discerning an opportunity when Gautama was absent, the thousand-eyed Indra, lord of Śacī, disguised in the sage's form, spoke these words to Ahalyā.
Those who desire do not wait for the proper season, O composed one — I desire union with you, O slender-waisted one.
Recognizing the thousand-eyed Indra in the sage's disguise, O delight of the Raghu line, the foolish-minded Ahalyā resolved to do it out of curiosity about the king of the gods.
Then, her inner self satisfied and her purpose fulfilled, she spoke to that foremost of gods: "Your purpose is accomplished, O foremost of gods — depart quickly from here, O lord; protect both yourself and me always, O lord of the gods, O giver of honor."
Smiling, Indra spoke these words to Ahalyā: "O fair-hipped one, I am fully satisfied; I shall depart as I came."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having thus lain with her, he departed from the cottage, O Rāma, hurrying in agitation and fearing Gautama.
He then saw the great sage Gautama entering — that foremost of sages who was irresistible to gods and demons alike, endowed with the strength of austerity, wet from the waters of a sacred ford, blazing like a fire, holding sacrificial faggots and kuśa grass.
Seeing him, the lord of the gods was terrified and his face fell.
Then the sage, seeing the thousand-eyed Indra disguised as a sage — himself of upright conduct seeing this one of evil conduct — spoke in anger.
"Having assumed my form, O evil-minded one, you have done what ought not to be done — therefore you shall become bereft of your testicles."
The very instant that the great-souled Gautama spoke thus in anger, the two testicles of the thousand-eyed Indra fell to the ground.
Having thus cursed Indra, he also cursed his wife: "Here you shall dwell for many thousands of years."
"Living on air, without food, mortifying yourself, lying in ashes, invisible to all beings, you shall dwell in this hermitage."
"When Rāma, the invincible son of Daśaratha, comes to this dreadful forest, then you shall be purified."
"Offering hospitality to him, O sinful woman, freed from greed and delusion, joyful in my presence, you shall resume your own form."
Having spoken thus to her who had behaved wickedly, the greatly splendid Gautama, that great ascetic, abandoned this hermitage and performed austerities on a beautiful peak of the Himālayas, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Then Indra, now bereft of his testicles, with a frightened face, spoke to the gods led by Agni, together with the hosts of sages and Cāraṇas.
"By creating an obstacle to the austerities of the great-souled Gautama, by provoking his anger, I have accomplished this deed for the benefit of the gods."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"By him in his fury I have been rendered without testicles, and she has been repudiated; by my great curse she has been set free from it — her accumulated austerity I have taken from her."
"Therefore, O best of gods, all of you together with the hosts of sages and Cāraṇas, who perform deeds helpful to the gods — you all ought to restore me to wholeness."
Hearing the words of Śatakratu, the gods led by Agni, together with all the hosts of Maruts, approached the deity of the ancestors and said:
"This ram here has its testicles, while Indra has been rendered without his — take the ram's testicles and quickly give them to Indra."
"The ram, rendered without its testicles, shall bestow the highest satisfaction upon you; and those humans who will offer it to you for your delight shall also be benefited."
Hearing the words of Agni, the ancestors assembled, and having extracted the ram's testicles, presented them to the thousand-eyed Indra.
From that time onward, O descendant of Kākutstha, the ancestors when assembled partake of rams without their testicles — and they ordained that those animals' testicles be the fruit offered to them.
And Indra, from that time onward, O Rāghava, has had the testicles of a ram — by the power of the great-souled Gautama's austerity.
Therefore now come, O one of great splendor, to the hermitage of that one of holy deeds — liberate this illustrious Ahalyā, who is like a goddess in form.
Hearing the words of Viśvāmitra, Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa, placing Viśvāmitra at their head, entered the hermitage.
And he beheld the illustrious Ahalyā, her radiance blazing with austerity, impossible to gaze upon even for gods and demons assembled together.
She was like one fashioned with care by the Creator as a divine illusion, her body enveloped in smoke yet shining like the full moon.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
She was veiled in frost and clouds, like the splendor of the full moon, difficult to approach in the midst of waters, blazing like the brilliance of the sun.
For by Gautama's words she had become impossible to behold by the three worlds, until Rāma's sight should fall upon her.
Then the two Rāghavas clasped her feet; remembering Gautama's words, she received them.
Composed in mind, she performed the rites of water for the feet, the water of honor, and the guest-offering; the descendant of Kākutstha received them according to the prescribed rites.
There was a great shower of flowers accompanied by the sound of divine drums, and there was a great gathering of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Crying "Excellent! Excellent!", the gods honored Ahalyā, whose body had been purified by the power of austerity, who was now devoted to Gautama's will.
And the greatly splendid Gautama, that great ascetic, happy with Ahalyā, duly honored Rāma and resumed his austerities.
And Rāma, having duly received the highest honor from the great sage Gautama, then departed for Mithilā.
Then Rāma, together with Saumitri [Lakṣmaṇa], having gone toward the northeast and placing Viśvāmitra at their head, came to the sacrificial enclosure.
Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, said to that tiger among sages: 'Indeed the sacrificial prosperity of the great-souled Janaka is remarkable.'
'Here there are many thousands of brāhmaṇas, O greatly fortunate one, dwelling from various regions, distinguished by their study of the Vedas.'
'And the hermitages of seers are visible, thronged with hundreds of carts. O brāhmaṇa, kindly designate a place where we may lodge.'
Hearing Rāma's words, the great sage Viśvāmitra arranged their lodging in a secluded spot well supplied with water.
When the king heard of Viśvāmitra, that foremost among sages, he then came forward, placing at his head Śatānanda, his blameless royal chaplain.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The great-souled officiating priests too, swiftly taking the arghya [honorific offering of water], presented it to Viśvāmitra with due rite, accompanied by Vedic mantras.
Having received that honor from the great-souled Janaka, [Viśvāmitra] enquired after the king's welfare and the unimpeded progress of the sacrifice.
He, having inquired after the welfare of those sages together with the preceptors and priests, then met with all of them according to proper custom, filled with delight.
Then the king, with joined palms, addressed that foremost sage: 'Let the Blessed One be seated, along with these eminent sages.'
Hearing Janaka's words, the great sage sat down, as did the chaplain, the officiating priests, and the king together with his ministers.
Seeing them seated all around in their proper places, the king there then spoke to Viśvāmitra.
'Today the prosperity of my sacrifice has been made fruitful by the gods; today I have attained the fruit of the sacrifice by virtue of your blessed presence.'
'I am blessed, I am favored, O bull among sages, in that you, O brāhmaṇa, have come to my sacrifice together with the sages.'
'The wise declare that twelve days remain, O brahmarṣi; thereafter, O Kauśika, you shall behold the gods who come to receive their share [of the offerings].'
Having spoken thus to that tiger among sages, the king, with joyful countenance and joined palms, reverently questioned him again.
'Be it well with you — these two princes, whose valor equals the gods', heroes who move with the gait of elephant and lion, comparable to a tiger and a bull —'
'— with eyes wide as lotus petals, bearing sword, quiver, and bow, like the two Aśvins in beauty, arrived at the fullness of youth —'
'— having reached the earth as if by chance, like immortals from the world of gods — how have they arrived here on foot, O sage, and for what purpose, and whose [sons] are they?'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'Bearing excellent weapons, valiant heroes — whose sons are they, O great sage? They adorn this region as the moon and sun adorn the sky.'
'Resembling each other in stature, bearing, and conduct, these two heroes wearing their hair in the kakapakṣa style — I desire to learn the truth about them.'
Hearing those words of the great-souled Janaka, the two great-souled ones announced themselves as the sons of Daśaratha.
[Viśvāmitra narrated] their dwelling at Siddhāśrama, the slaying of the rākṣasas, their unhindered journey hither, and the sight of Viśālā.
And the beholding of Ahalyā, the meeting with Gautama, and their arrival here in order to see the great bow.
Having reported all this to the great-souled Janaka, the great sage Viśvāmitra of mighty splendor then fell silent.
Hearing those words of the wise Viśvāmitra, Śatānanda of great splendor and mighty austerities had the hair on his body stand erect with joy.
The eldest son of Gautama, whose luster blazed forth through his austerities, was overcome with the highest wonder at the very sight of Rāma.
Gazing at those two princes seated at ease, Śatānanda then spoke to Viśvāmitra, that foremost among sages.
'O tiger among sages, was my illustrious mother, who had practised long austerities, shown to the prince?'
'O you of great splendor, did my illustrious mother offer worship to Rāma with forest [gifts], to him who is worthy of worship by all embodied beings?'
'O you of great splendor, was the ancient event relating to my mother, that which the god [Indra] caused to be carried out wrongfully, narrated to Rāma?'
'O Kauśika, may it be well with you — was my mother reunited with my guru [Gautama] here, after the sight of Rāma, O foremost among sages?'
'O son of Kuśika, was Rāma of great splendor honored by my guru, having come here and received worship from that great soul?'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'O son of Kuśika, was my guru, with tranquil mind, reverently saluted by Rāma who had come here with pure devotion?'
Hearing his words, the great sage Viśvāmitra, skilled in speech, replied to Śatānanda, who was himself versed in eloquent speech.
'O foremost among sages, nothing beyond what was proper has been transgressed by me; the wife [Ahalyā] has been reunited with the sage [Gautama], even as Reṇukā [was reunited] with Bhārgava [Jamadagni].'
Hearing those words of the wise Viśvāmitra, the great-splendored Śatānanda addressed Rāma with these words.
'Welcome to you, O foremost among men; by good fortune have you arrived, O Rāghava, placing at your head the unconquered great sage Viśvāmitra.'
'Viśvāmitra of mighty splendor, a brahmarṣi of inconceivable deeds and boundless radiance through his austerities — know him to be the highest refuge.'
'There is none more blessed on earth than you, O Rāma; the son of Kuśika is your guardian, he who has practised great austerity.'
'And do listen — I shall recount the history of the great-souled Kauśika as best I can; hear it from me as I narrate it in full.'
'This one [Viśvāmitra] was a king for a long time, a subduer of enemies, righteous in soul, knowing dharma, accomplished in learning, and devoted to the welfare of his subjects.'
'There was a lord of the earth, son of Prajāpati, named Kuśa; Kuśa's son was the powerful and highly righteous Kuśanābha.'
'Kuśanābha's son was celebrated by the name Gādhi; Gādhi's son is the mighty and splendorous great sage Viśvāmitra.'
'The mighty Viśvāmitra governed the earth; as king he ruled the kingdom for many thousands of years.'
'At a certain time the mighty one, having marshaled his army, surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī [a full military division], roamed the earth.'
'Wandering through cities, kingdoms, rivers, mountains, and hermitages in succession, the king came [at last] —'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'— to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, adorned with trees bearing various flowers and fruits, filled with many herds of deer, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.'
'Beautified by gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras; filled with tranquil deer; frequented by throngs of twice-born ones.'
'Crowded with hosts of brahmarṣis, served by bands of divine sages, and by great souls perfected through the practice of austerities, who were like fires [in their splendor].'
'Ever thronged with resplendent great souls equal to Brahmā — those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, and those who eat only fallen leaves.'
'[And by seers] who subsist on fruit and roots, who are self-restrained, who have conquered anger, who have conquered the senses, and by the Vālakhilya sages devoted to japa and homa.'
'Vasiṣṭha's hermitage, like another realm of Brahmā — this the mighty Viśvāmitra, foremost among the victorious, beheld.'
Beholding it, the mighty Viśvāmitra was exceedingly pleased; the hero, bowing with humility, [approached] Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who recite [the Vedas].
Addressed with 'welcome' by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, the blessed Vasiṣṭha also indicated a seat for him.
And when the wise Viśvāmitra had taken his seat, that foremost sage offered him fruits and roots in accordance with proper custom.
Having accepted that honor from Vasiṣṭha, the foremost among kings [Viśvāmitra] enquired after the welfare of [his] pupils in austerities, the agnihotra, and [the sacred fires].
The greatly splendorous Viśvāmitra likewise [enquired] about the trees of the forest; and Vasiṣṭha declared to that foremost among kings that all was well in every respect.
Vasiṣṭha, son of Brahmā, the foremost among those who recite [the Vedas] and of mighty austerities, then questioned the king Viśvāmitra, who was seated comfortably.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'Is all well with you, O king? Do you, O righteous king, cherish and protect your subjects with righteousness and with the conduct befitting a king?'
'Are your servants well provided for? Do they abide by your commands? Have all your enemies been subdued, O slayer of foes?'
'Is all well with your army, treasury, and allies, O scorcher of enemies? Is all well with your sons and grandsons, O tiger among men, O blameless one?'
The king Viśvāmitra of great splendor, filled with humility, declared to Vasiṣṭha that all was well in every respect.
Both of them, most righteous in conduct, having exchanged those auspicious pleasantries for a long time, filled with the highest joy, delighted in each other's company.
Then at the end of their conversation, O delight of the Raghu line, the blessed Vasiṣṭha spoke this word to Viśvāmitra with a smile.
'I wish to offer hospitality, O mighty one, to this army of yours and to you yourself, who are beyond measure; please accept what is fitting from me.'
'Let Your Honor accept this honor prepared by me; O king, you are the most excellent of guests and are worthy of being honored with care.'
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, the great-minded Viśvāmitra, king, said: 'It has been done — you have honored me with words of respect.'
'With whatever fruit and roots there are in your hermitage, O blessed one, and with water for the feet and for sipping, and with the sight of your blessed self —'
'— in every way, O greatly wise one, honored by one worthy of honor, I shall depart. Let my obeisance be unto you; look upon me with a friendly eye.'
As the king spoke thus, Vasiṣṭha, righteous in soul and noble in mind, pressed his invitation upon him again and again.
The son of Gādhi [Viśvāmitra] replied to Vasiṣṭha simply: 'So be it — let it be as the Blessed One desires, O foremost among sages.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed, the great-splendored Vasiṣṭha, best among those who recite [the Vedas], free from all impurity, then joyfully summoned Kalmāṣī [Śabalā, the speckled cow].
'Come, come quickly, O Śabalā, and hear my words too; I am resolved to honor this royal sage together with his army — prepare for me a most worthy feast.'
'Whatever and whichever [food], as desired, honored in the six flavors — all of that, O divine wish-granting cow, rain down for me [now].'
'Create for me, O Śabalā, the complete store of foods combined with savory dishes, drink, lickables, and suckables — make haste!'
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, O slayer of enemies, Śabalā the wish-fulfilling cow granted the desires of each and every one exactly as they wished.
Sugar canes and honeys, as well as parched grain, choice maireyā liquors and fine wines, costly drinks, and eatables of every variety—all these she produced.
Mountain-like heaps of steaming cooked rice, fine prepared foods and soups, and streams of curds as well.
Vessels filled to the brim with sweet-tasting confections of various kinds, and thousands of molasses-based sweets as well.
Everything was abundantly satisfied; O Rāma, Viśvāmitra's entire army was gratified by Vasiṣṭha, crowded with men joyful and well-fed.
Viśvāmitra too, the royal sage, became glad and well-pleased at that time, as did the king of the foremost city together with his brāhmaṇas and chief priest.
Honored together with his ministers and counselors and his attendants, filled with the greatest joy, he spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha.
"I have been honored by you, O brāhmaṇa, who are worthy of honor; I have been well-received. O master of speech, hear the words I am about to speak.
"Let Śabalā be given to me in exchange for a hundred thousand cows; for, O venerable one, this is a jewel, and a king carries off jewels. Therefore give Śabalā to me, O twice-born—by right she is mine."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by Viśvāmitra, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, the foremost of sages and righteous-souled, replied to the king of the earth.
"I will not give Śabalā for a hundred thousand cows, nor for hundreds of crores of cows, O king, nor for masses of silver.
"She ought never to be abandoned from my side, O crusher of foes; Śabalā is eternally mine, as glory is to one possessed of a noble self.
"On her depend the oblations to the gods and to the ancestors, as well as my daily sustenance; on her depend the agnihotra fire-sacrifice, the bali offering, and the homa ritual as well.
"The invocations svāhā and vaṣaṭ, as well as the various branches of sacred knowledge—all these depend on her here, O royal sage; there is no doubt of this.
"All of this is truly my own; she always brings me contentment. For many reasons, O king, I will not give Śabalā to you."
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra then spoke words exceedingly more agitated, he who was so skilled in speech.
"I give you fourteen thousand elephants adorned with golden girths and neck-ornaments, decorated with golden goads.
"I give you eight hundred golden chariots yoked with four white horses each, adorned with little bells.
"I give you eleven thousand horses, born in good lands, of noble breed, and of great vigor, O steadfast one.
"I give you a full crore of cows distinguished by various colors and all in their prime; let Śabalā be given to me."
Thus addressed by the wise Viśvāmitra, the venerable Vasiṣṭha declared: "I will not give Śabalā under any circumstances whatsoever, O king."
"She alone is my jewel; she alone is my wealth; she alone is my all; she alone is my very life.
"The new-moon sacrifice and the full-moon sacrifice, and the great sacrifices yielding abundant sacrificial fees—all these rest on her alone, O king, as do my various ritual observances.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"All my rites are rooted in her, O king—there is no doubt. Why speak at length? I will not give away the wish-granting cow."
When the sage Vasiṣṭha would not surrender the wish-fulfilling cow, O Rāma, Viśvāmitra then dragged Śabalā away by force.
But as Śabalā was being taken away, O Rāma, by that great-souled king, she was distressed; weeping and wasted by grief, she reflected.
"Why have I been abandoned by Vasiṣṭha, that most great-souled one? Why am I, wretched and deeply afflicted, being carried off by the king's servants?
"What wrong have I done to that great sage of cultivated soul, that the righteous one abandons me who am guiltless, devoted, and dear to him?"
Having reflected thus and sighing again and again, she then swiftly went back to Vasiṣṭha, who was of supreme power.
Shaking off those hundreds of servants, O slayer of enemies, she went with the speed of the wind to the feet of the great-souled one.
Standing before Vasiṣṭha, that Śabalā, weeping and crying out, spoke these words with a voice resounding like a thunder-drum of clouds.
"O venerable one, O son of Brahmā, why have I been abandoned by you? Why are the king's servants taking me away from your side?"
Addressed thus, the brahmarṣi spoke these words to her whose heart was burning with grief, as one would speak to a sorrowful sister.
"I am not abandoning you, O Śabalā; nor have you done any wrong to me. This king of great might is taking you from me by force.
"My strength is simply not equal to his; the king today is particularly powerful—he is mighty, a kṣatriya, and lord of the earth.
"This full akṣauhiṇī division of his, teeming with horses and chariots and thronged with elephants and banners—by reason of this he is the stronger."
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, she who was skilled in speech replied humbly to the brahmarṣi of boundless splendor.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The strength of a kṣatriya is not reckoned as strength; a brāhmaṇa is the stronger. O brāhmaṇa, brahmic power is divine and mightier than kṣatra-power.
"Your power is immeasurable; none is stronger than you. The mighty Viśvāmitra is no match for the splendor that is yours and difficult to approach.
"O great-splendored one, employ me, filled as I am with your brahmic power; I shall destroy all the arrogance and strength of that wicked-souled one."
Thus addressed by her, O Rāma, Vasiṣṭha of great renown then said to her: "Create a force that shall break the power of the enemy."
From her hum-bellowing, hundreds of Pahlavas were released, O king, and they destroyed Viśvāmitra's entire army even as he watched.
The king, exceedingly enraged, his eyes wide with fury, destroyed those Pahlavas with weapons of various kinds.
Seeing the hundreds of Pahlavas being crushed by Viśvāmitra, she again created fearsome Śakas mixed with Yavanas.
The earth was covered by those Śakas mixed with Yavanas, mighty and powerful, resembling the golden filaments of a lotus.
Bearing long swords and battle-axes, clad in garments of golden hue, they burned down that entire army like blazing fires.
Thereupon the great-splendored Viśvāmitra discharged his weapons.
Then, seeing them thrown into confusion and bewildered by Viśvāmitra's weapons, Vasiṣṭha urged the wish-fulfilling cow: "Create with your yogic power."
From her hum-bellow were born Kāmbojas bright as the sun; from her udder were then born Pahlavas bearing weapons in their hands.
From her womb-region Yavanas, from her dung-region Śakas; from her pores barbarian Mlecchas, Harītas, and Kirātas together.
By them Viśvāmitra's army was slaughtered that very instant—infantry, elephants, horses, and chariots—O delight of the Raghu line.
Seeing the army destroyed by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, a hundred of Viśvāmitra's sons bearing weapons of every kind

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
rushed furiously against Vasiṣṭha, the foremost of those who recite sacred texts; with a mere huṃkāra the great sage reduced them all to ashes.
Those sons of Viśvāmitra, along with their horses, chariots, and infantry, were reduced to ashes in a moment by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Seeing his sons and his army destroyed, the greatly renowned Viśvāmitra became filled with shame and was plunged into despondency.
Like a river that has lost its current, like a serpent with broken fangs, like the sun at the moment of an eclipse—he instantly lost his radiance.
With his sons and army slain, wretched like a bird with clipped wings, his arrogance destroyed, his energy extinguished, he fell into dejection.
He appointed one son to the kingdom with the charge "rule it," to govern the earth according to kṣatriya duty, and then he departed to the forest.
Going to the slopes of the Himavat, frequented by Kiṃnaras and serpents, he of great austerities performed tapas in order to propitiate Mahādeva.
After some time had passed, the lord of the gods, he whose banner bears a bull, the granter of boons, appeared before the great sage Viśvāmitra.
"For what purpose do you practice austerities, O king? Speak what you wish to say. I am a granter of boons; declare whatever boon you desire."
Thus addressed by the god, Viśvāmitra of great austerities bowed down to Mahādeva and spoke these words.
"If you are pleased with me, O Mahādeva, O sinless one, let the Dhanurveda be given to me in its entirety—with all its subsidiary texts, upāṅgas, upaniṣads, and its secret doctrine."
"And let all the weapons that are among the gods, the Dānavas, the great sages, the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas—let all of these manifest themselves to me, O sinless one."
"By your grace let my desire be fulfilled, O god of gods." Having spoken the words "so be it," the lord of the gods departed to heaven.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having obtained the weapons, the royal sage Viśvāmitra of great might became filled with arrogance and swelled with immense pride.
Growing in his might like the ocean at the full moon, he then considered the foremost of sages, Vasiṣṭha, as already slain.
Then the king went to the hermitage and discharged his weapons, by which that entire grove of austerities was burned down by the power of those weapons.
Seeing that weapon of the wise Viśvāmitra blazing forth, hundreds of sages fled in terror in all directions.
And the disciples of Vasiṣṭha, as well as the deer and birds, fled in fear by the thousands in many directions.
The hermitage of the great-souled Vasiṣṭha became deserted; for a moment it was silent, resembling a barren wasteland.
Vasiṣṭha called out repeatedly: "Fear not! I shall destroy Gādheya today as the sun dispels the mist."
Having spoken thus, the great-splendored Vasiṣṭha, the foremost among those who recite sacred texts, then addressed Viśvāmitra in these angry words.
"Because you have destroyed this hermitage nurtured for so long, you are a man of wicked conduct; because of this, O fool, you shall be no more."
Having spoken thus, supremely enraged, he swiftly raised his staff—like the smokeless fire of universal dissolution, like another rod of Yama.
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, the mighty Viśvāmitra raised his fire-weapon and cried out, "Stand! Stand!"
The venerable Vasiṣṭha, in his anger, spoke these words:
"O wretch of a kṣatriya, here I stand — show whatever strength you possess! I shall destroy your pride in weapons, O son of Gādhi."
"Where is your kṣatriya strength, and where is the great power of brahman? Behold my divine power of brahman, O disgrace to the kṣatriyas!"
That dreadful, supreme fire-weapon of the son of Gādhi was quenched by the brahma-staff, as the force of fire is quenched by water.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
In fury, the son of Gādhi then hurled the vāruṇa weapon, the raudra weapon, the āindra weapon, the pāśupata weapon, and also the aiṣīka weapon.
He also discharged the mānava weapon, the mohana (bewildering) weapon, the gāndharvā weapon, the svāpana (stupefying) weapon, the jṛmbhaṇa (yawning) weapon, another mohana weapon, the saṃtāpana (tormenting) weapon, and the vilāpana (lamenting) weapon.
He hurled the śoṣaṇa (desiccating) weapon, the dāraṇa (rending) weapon, the vajra weapon most difficult to withstand, the brahma-noose, the kāla-noose, and the varuṇa-noose.
He hurled the beloved pinākāstra, the two thunderbolts — the dry and the wet — the daṇḍa weapon, the paiśāca weapon, and likewise the krauñca weapon.
He discharged the dharma-disc, the kāla-disc, and likewise the Viṣṇu-disc; the vāyavya (wind) weapon, the mathana (churning) weapon, and the hayaśiras (horse-head) weapon.
He also hurled a pair of śakti missiles, the kaṅkāla (skeleton) weapon, the musala (mace) weapon, the great vaidyādhara weapon, and the terrible kāla weapon.
He hurled the dreadful triśūla (trident) weapon, the kāpāla weapon, and the kaṅkaṇa weapon — all these weapons did he discharge, O joy of the Raghu line.
Against Vasiṣṭha, foremost among those who recite mantras, it was as though a marvel had occurred: the son of Brahman swallowed all those weapons with his staff.
When all those were quelled, the son of Gādhi released the brahmāstra. Seeing that weapon raised, the gods led by Agni,
the divine seers in agitation, and the gandharvas together with the great serpents — all three worlds were seized with terror when the brahmāstra was discharged.
That also — that most dreadful brahma weapon — Vasiṣṭha swallowed entirely with his brahma-staff by the power of brahman, O Rāghava.
As the great-souled Vasiṣṭha swallowed the brahmāstra, his form became exceedingly dreadful — bewildering to all three worlds and ferocious.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
From all the pores of the great-souled Vasiṣṭha's body there burst forth flames like rays of fire, dense with smoke.
The brahma-staff raised in Vasiṣṭha's hand blazed like the smokeless fire of universal dissolution, or like a second staff of Yama.
Then the assemblies of sages praised Vasiṣṭha, foremost among the reciters: "Your power is unfailing, O brahman — sustain your splendour with your splendour."
"The great ascetic Viśvāmitra has been subdued by you, O brahman. Be gracious, O foremost among chanters, and let the worlds be freed of their anguish."
Thus addressed, the great-splendoured and great-ascetic Vasiṣṭha became calm. And Viśvāmitra, humiliated, breathed a deep sigh and spoke these words:
"Shame upon kṣatriya strength — the power of brahman's splendour is the true strength! All my weapons have been struck down by a single brahma-staff."
"Having thus reflected, with senses and mind at peace, I shall undertake great austerity — that which indeed brings about the state of brahmanhood."
Then, with a burning heart, remembering his own defeat, sighing again and again, and bearing enmity toward the great-souled one,
Viśvāmitra, that great ascetic, went to the southern quarter along with his chief wife, O Rāghava, and performed the most intense and dreadful austerity; subsisting on fruits and roots, self-restrained, he practised supreme tapas.
Then there were born to him sons devoted to truth and righteousness: Haviṣpanda, Madhuṣpanda, Dṛḍhanetra, and Mahāratha.
When a full thousand years had elapsed, Brahmā, the grandsire of the worlds, spoke sweetly to Viśvāmitra, the treasury of austerity:
"The worlds of the royal seers have been won by you through your austerity, O son of Kuśika. By this austerity we recognise you as a royal seer (rājarṣi)."
Having spoken thus, that great-splendoured supreme lord of the worlds departed with the gods to the triple heaven, the world of Brahmā.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Viśvāmitra, hearing this, hung his head slightly in shame, overcome by great sorrow, and spoke with indignation:
"I have undergone very great austerity, yet the gods with all the assemblies of sages know me only as a royal seer. I think the fruit of my austerity is nothing."
Having thus resolved in his mind, the great ascetic, of supreme self-mastery, once more performed supreme austerity, O scion of Kākutstha.
At this very time, a truth-speaking, sense-conquering descendant of the Ikṣvāku lineage, known by the name Triśaṅku,
had a resolve arise in his mind, O Rāghava: "I shall perform a sacrifice and reach the highest abode of the gods in my own body."
He summoned Vasiṣṭha and told him his thought; but the great-souled Vasiṣṭha told him it was impossible.
Refused by Vasiṣṭha, he went to the southern quarter, to the place where the sons of Vasiṣṭha were performing their long austerities.
The greatly splendoured Triśaṅku beheld the hundred glorious sons of Vasiṣṭha, resplendent in the highest degree, engaged in their austerities.
Approaching them, those great-souled sons of his teacher, he saluted them in proper order and, hanging his head somewhat in shame, the greatly splendoured one addressed them all with joined palms.
"I take refuge in you, O worthy refuge, as one who has come for shelter. Good fortune to you — I have been refused by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha."
"Wishing to perform a great sacrifice, I seek your permission for that. Bowing to all of you, sons of my teacher, I entreat your grace."
"Bowing with my head, I beseech the brāhmaṇas established in austerity: let your honours, with concentration, officiate my sacrifice for its fulfillment, so that I may attain the world of the gods in my own body."
"Refused by Vasiṣṭha, O treasuries of austerity, I see no other recourse whatsoever except all of you, the sons of my teacher."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The family priest is the highest resort for all the Ikṣvākus; therefore, next after him, all of you are my divinities."
Then, having heard Triśaṅku's speech filled with anger, the hundred sons of the sage, O Rāma, spoke thus to the king:
"You have been refused, O foolish one, by the teacher who speaks only truth — how can you, having bypassed him, have come to a different branch?"
"The family priest is the highest resort for all the Ikṣvākus; it is not possible to transgress the word of the truth-speaker."
"The venerable sage Vasiṣṭha has declared it impossible — how then are we capable of performing that sacrifice for you?"
"You are foolish, O best of men — return to your own city. The venerable one is capable of officiating for even the three worlds, O king."
Hearing their speech, agitated by anger, the king spoke again to them these words:
"I have been refused by my teacher and likewise by the sons of my teacher; I shall seek another recourse. Good fortune be with you, O treasuries of austerity."
But the sons of the sage, hearing that speech laden with dreadful intent, cursed him in supreme wrath: "You shall become a caṇḍāla!" Having spoken thus, those great-souled ones entered their own hermitage.
Then, when the night had passed, the king had become a caṇḍāla: wearing dark garments, dark in complexion, rough, with hair dishevelled, wearing garlands and unguents from funeral pyres, and adorned with iron ornaments.
Seeing him transformed into the form of a caṇḍāla, all his ministers and the townspeople who were his followers fled together, O Rāma.
Alone, that king of supreme self-possession, O scion of Kākutstha, burning day and night in anguish, went to Viśvāmitra, the treasury of austerity.
Viśvāmitra, seeing that king reduced to failure, in the form of a caṇḍāla, O Rāma, was moved to compassion.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Out of compassion, that greatly splendoured and supremely righteous one spoke these words, wishing him well, to the king of dreadful appearance:
"What is the purpose of your coming, O prince, O mighty one, O hero, lord of Ayodhyā — you who have been reduced to caṇḍāla-hood by a curse?"
Then, hearing those words, the king who had attained caṇḍāla-hood, skilled in speech, spoke with joined palms to the one expert in speech:
"I have been refused by my teacher and likewise by the sons of my teacher; without having attained that desire of mine, I have met with this calamity."
"It was my gentle-visaged wish to ascend to heaven in my own body; I have striven with a hundred sacrifices, yet that fruit is not obtained."
"I have never spoken untruth in the past, nor shall I ever speak it — even gone into hardships, O gentle one, I swear to you by the dharma of the kṣatriya."
"I have made offerings with many and various sacrifices; my subjects have been protected by righteousness; the great-souled teachers have been gratified by conduct and good character."
"Though I strive in righteousness and wish to perform sacrifice, the teachers are not pleased — O foremost of sages."
"I hold fate alone to be supreme; human effort is futile. Everything is overridden by fate, for fate is the highest resort."
"For me, thus deeply afflicted and seeking your grace, O one of good fortune, whose actions have been undone by fate — you should show your favour."
"I shall seek no other recourse; there is no other refuge for me. You should turn back fate by the power of human effort."
Having heard the king's words, the son of Kuśika, moved by compassion, spoke sweetly to the one who stood before him in the very form of a caṇḍāla.
"Welcome, dear child of the Ikṣvāku line — I know you to be one of true righteousness. I shall be your refuge; fear not, O bull among kings."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I shall invite all the great seers of meritorious deeds who can assist in the sacrifice; then, O king, you shall perform the rite in peace."
"This form that rests upon you, wrought by your guru's curse — in this very form, with this very body, you shall go to heaven."
"I deem heaven to be already in the palm of your hand, O lord of men — for you have come to Kauśika, who is worthy of refuge, and taken shelter with him."
Having spoken thus, the greatly resplendent one gave instructions to his sons, who were supremely righteous and exceedingly wise, for the gathering of all that was needed for the sacrifice.
Summoning all his disciples together, he spoke these words to them.
"Bring hither, dear ones, all the foremost seers, by my command — along with their disciples, friends, and officiating priests who are versed in the sacred texts."
"Whatever any one of them may say when urged by the force of my words — all of it, whatever is spoken disparagingly, is to be reported to me in full."
Hearing those words of his, the disciples set out in all directions by his command; and from every region came the knowers of Brahman.
Those disciples, having assembled, all reported to the sage, who blazed with splendour, the words of all the Brahman-speakers.
Having heard the message, all the twice-born come — they arrived from every region, all excepting Mahodaya.
"Hear, O bull among sages, all that which the entire hundred of the Vasiṣṭhas said — every word they spoke, their eyes agitated with anger."
"The officiating priest of this man is a kṣatriya — and more particularly, he is a caṇḍāla. How then can the divine seers be partakers of the oblations at that assembly?"
"Or how shall the great-souled brāhmaṇas, having eaten the food of a caṇḍāla under the superintendence of Viśvāmitra, attain heaven?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
These harsh words were spoken, their eyes red with passion, by all the Vasiṣṭhas together with Mahodaya, O tiger among sages.
Having heard those words of all of them, the bull among sages, his eyes flushed red with wrath, spoke in great anger.
"These evil-souled ones who revile me, blameless as I am and engaged in fierce austerity — they shall be reduced to ashes, of this there is no doubt."
"This very day, led away by the noose of Kāla to the realm of Vaivasvata, may they all drink of the bitter cup through seven hundred births in every form of existence."
"Subsisting always on dog's flesh, pitiless ones known by the name Muṣṭika, disfigured and misshapen — may they wander through these worlds."
"And Mahodaya, that evil-minded one, has reviled me though I am beyond reproach; fallen from esteem in all the worlds, he shall attain the state of a Niṣāda."
"Devoted to the taking of life, having abandoned all compassion, he shall, by my wrath, dwell in misfortune for a very long time."
Having spoken this much, Viśvāmitra, the great ascetic, of mighty splendour, that great sage, fell silent in the midst of the seers.
Having struck down the Vasiṣṭhas together with Mahodaya by the force of his austerity, the greatly resplendent Viśvāmitra then addressed the assembly of seers.
"This descendant of the Ikṣvāku line, celebrated as Triśaṅku, is most righteous and most generous; he has come to me as his refuge, desiring to win the world of the gods in this very body."
"In such a manner that this man may ascend to the divine world in his own body — let the sacrifice be conducted by you together with me."
Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra, all the great seers, gathered together, those who knew the dharma, spoke what was in accord with dharma.
"This descendant of Kuśika is a sage of supreme wrathfulness; what he has said is right — this must be done, without doubt."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For the venerable one, resembling fire, will give a curse when provoked. Therefore let the sacrifice be conducted, so that the descendant of the Ikṣvāku line may ascend to heaven in his own body by the might of Viśvāmitra."
"Therefore let the sacrifice proceed; let all take up their respective offices."
Having spoken thus, the great seers took up all the rites, and the greatly resplendent Viśvāmitra himself became the chief officiant at the sacrifice.
And the officiating priests, one after another, all versed in sacred formulas, performed all the rites with mantras, according to prescription and proper procedure.
Then, after a great stretch of time, Viśvāmitra of great austerity invoked all the gods to come there for their shares of the oblation.
But though thus invoked, none of the gods came to receive their portions. Then the great sage Viśvāmitra was seized by anger.
Raising the sacrificial ladle in wrath, he spoke thus to Triśaṅku: "Behold the power of the austerity earned by myself, O lord of men."
"Now I shall bear you to heaven in your own body by my own might. Go to the sky in your own body, O ruler of men — that which is hard to attain in one's own body."
"Whatever fruit of austerity earned by myself there is — by the might of that fruit, O king, ascend to heaven in this very body."
When the sage had so spoken, the lord of men ascended to heaven in his own body, O Kākutstha, while the assembled sages looked on.
Seeing Triśaṅku arrived at the divine world, Pākaśāsana — Indra — along with all the hosts of gods, spoke these words.
"Triśaṅku, go back — you have no right to abode in heaven. You fool, struck down by your guru's curse, fall headlong to the earth."
Thus addressed by Mahendra, Triśaṅku fell back down, crying out "Save me! Save me!" to Viśvāmitra, that treasury of austerity.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing the cry of that falling man, Kauśika gathered fierce wrath and called out, "Stop! Stop!"
That resplendent one, like a second Prajāpati, in the midst of the seers, began creating a new set of seven sages established along the southern path.
Inflamed by anger, the greatly renowned one created a new garland of stars, taking the southern direction as his orientation, in the midst of the seers.
Having created the stellar lineage, darkened by wrath, he declared: "I shall create another Indra — or let the world exist without one." And in his anger he began to create the very gods as well.
Then the bulls among gods, the hosts of seers, all exceedingly agitated, spoke words of supplication to the great-souled Viśvāmitra.
"This king, O greatly fortunate one, O treasury of austerity, struck down by his guru's curse, is indeed not fit to go to heaven in his own body."
Having heard those words of the gods, Kauśika, the bull among sages, spoke very great words to all the deities.
"I have given my pledge that this lord of the earth, Triśaṅku, would ascend in his own body — I am not able to make that pledge false. May it be well with you all."
"Let there be a realm for this Triśaṅku in his own body, and let it be eternal; and let all my stars remain fixed and firm."
"For as long as the worlds shall endure, let all these creations of mine stand firm throughout. O gods, all of you ought to sanction this."
Thus addressed, all the gods replied to the bull among sages.
"So be it. May it be well with you. Let all these many creations stand firm in the sky, beyond the path of Vaiśvānara — the fire."
"O foremost of sages, let the stars stand, and among those luminaries blazing with light, let Triśaṅku too stand — head downward — resembling an immortal."
Then Viśvāmitra, righteous in soul, praised by all the gods and by the seers, the greatly resplendent one, said to the deities: "So be it."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then all the great-souled gods and the sages, those treasuries of austerity, departed just as they had come, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, O best of men.
Then the great-souled Viśvāmitra, watching those seers depart, spoke to all those forest-dwelling sages, O tiger among men.
"A great obstruction has arisen, stationed in the southern direction; let us set out for another direction — there we shall practise austerity."
"In the vast western region, in the sacred tīrthas of Puṣkara, we shall comfortably practise great austerity — for that is the supreme grove of penance."
Having spoken thus, the greatly resplendent great sage betook himself to Puṣkara and performed fierce, unapproachable austerity, subsisting on roots and fruits.
At this very time the king who ruled Ayodhyā, known as Ambarīṣa, set about performing a sacrifice.
But from that sacrificer Indra stole the sacrificial animal. When the animal had disappeared, the brāhmaṇa priest spoke these words to the king.
"O king, the sacrificial animal has been stolen and lost today through your lack of vigilance. Sins strike a king who does not protect what is entrusted to him, O lord of men."
"This requires a great expiation. O bull among men, bring either a man or an animal quickly, before the rite proceeds further."
Hearing the preceptor's words, that king, a bull among men, of great wisdom, sought after the sacrificial victim, offering thousands of cows in exchange.
The lord of the earth, searching, visited region after region, settlements, cities, forests, and sacred hermitages.
He then found, O dear one, O delight of the Raghu line, Ṛcīka seated on the hill Bhṛgutuṅga together with his sons and wife.
The royal seer of immeasurable splendour, having reverentially saluted and propitiated that brahmarṣi blazing with austerity, and having enquired after his welfare in every respect, spoke these words to Ṛcīka.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"If you would sell a son for a hundred thousand cows for the purpose of the sacrificial animal, O greatly fortunate one, O descendant of Bhṛgu, I shall have fulfilled my purpose."
"All regions have been traversed and I have not obtained the required sacrificial animal. You should give one son from among yours here, for the price stated."
Thus addressed, the greatly resplendent Ṛcīka spoke: "I would never sell the eldest under any circumstances, O best of men."
Hearing the words of Ṛcīka, the mother of those great-souled sons, the ascetic woman, spoke to Ambarīṣa, that tiger among men.
"Know also that the youngest, Śunaka, is dear to me, O king."
"For generally, O best of men, the eldest sons are dear to fathers, and the youngest to mothers; therefore I protect the youngest."
When the sage had spoken thus and the sage's wife likewise, the middle son, Śunaḥśepa himself, O Rāma, spoke these words.
"My father says the eldest is not to be sold; my mother says the youngest. I consider the middle son sold — O king, take me away."
The lord of men, taking Śunaḥśepa for a hundred thousand cows, departed in great joy, O delight of the Raghu line.
The royal seer Ambarīṣa, the greatly resplendent one of great renown, having placed Śunaḥśepa on the chariot, departed swiftly.
Having taken Śunaḥśepa, O best of men, that greatly renowned king rested at Puṣkara at midday, O joy of the Raghu line.
While he was resting, the greatly renowned Śunaḥśepa came to the foremost of holy places, Puṣkara, and beheld Viśvāmitra.
With a dejected face, wretched with thirst and exhaustion, he fell upon the sage's lap, O Rāma, and spoke these words.
I have no mother, no father — where then are kinsmen or relatives? O gentle one, O bull among sages, you ought to protect me through righteousness.
For you are the protector of all, O best of sages; you are the sustainer of all. The king would have his purpose fulfilled, and I would live long and imperishably.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
I would attain the heavenly world, having practised the highest austerity. Be my protector, for I am without a protector — with a gracious heart, O soul of righteousness, you ought to rescue me from sin as a father rescues a son.
Having heard those words of his, the great ascetic Viśvāmitra consoled him in many ways and then spoke these words to his sons.
The time has now come for that purpose for which fathers who seek the good beget sons — for the benefit of the next world.
This young son of a sage seeks shelter from me; do something dear for him at the mere cost of your own life, my sons.
All of you are doers of good deeds, all of you are devoted to righteousness — become the sacrificial animal of the king and grant satisfaction to the fire.
Then Śunaḥśepa would have a protector, the sacrifice would proceed without hindrance, the gods would be satisfied, and my word too would be fulfilled.
Hearing the sage's words, O best of men, his sons — Madhuṣyanda and the others — spoke these words with arrogance and disdain.
How, O lord, do you abandon your own sons to rescue another's son? We regard this as improper, like eating dog-flesh at a meal.
Hearing those words of his sons, the bull among sages, with eyes reddened by anger, began to speak.
This speech was uttered shamelessly, censured even by the law of righteousness — cruel and hair-raising, it transgresses my command.
All of you shall wander the earth for a full thousand years in your clans as eaters of dog-flesh, like the Vasiṣṭhas.
Having thus afflicted his sons with the curse, that best of sages then spoke to the distressed Śunaḥśepa, granting him a wholesome protection.
Bound with sacred cords, adorned with red garlands and unguents, approach the sacrificial post of Viṣṇu and invoke the fire with these hymns.
Chant these two divine hymns, O son of a sage, at this sacrifice of Ambarīṣa — thereby you shall attain fulfilment.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Śunaḥśepa, having received those two hymns with concentrated mind, quickly spoke to Ambarīṣa, that lion among kings.
O lion among kings, O great-spirited one, let us go quickly to the assembly hall; resume the rite, O lord of kings, and bring forward the consecration.
Hearing those words of the sage's son, the king, filled with eager joy, went swiftly and without delay to the sacrificial enclosure.
With the assent of the officiants, the king dressed Śunaḥśepa with sacred marks and a red garment and bound him to the sacrificial post.
Bound to the post, that son of a sage duly propitiated the two gods — Indra and the younger brother of Indra — with the foremost hymns.
Then Sahasrākṣa (Indra), pleased and satisfied by the esoteric hymns of praise, granted long life to Śunaḥśepa, O Rāghava.
And that king, O best of men, O Rāma, obtained the manifold fruit of the sacrifice, born of the grace of Sahasrākṣa.
And Viśvāmitra, the righteous-souled one of great austerity, practised severe penance once more at Puṣkara for a full thousand years, O best of men.
When the thousand years were complete, all the gods came to the great sage who had bathed upon completion of his vow, wishing to bestow the fruit of his austerity.
Brahmā of great splendour spoke pleasant words: 'You are a ṛṣi — good fortune to you — by the meritorious deeds you yourself have earned.'
Having thus spoken to him, the lord of gods departed once more to the three heavens; Viśvāmitra of great splendour then practised great austerity again.
Then after a great length of time, Menakā, the foremost among the apsarases, O best of men, came to Puṣkara to bathe.
The son of Kuśika of great splendour beheld Menakā there — unrivalled in beauty, like lightning amid a rain-cloud.
Seeing her, the sage, fallen under the power of Kandarpa (Kāma), spoke to her: 'Welcome to you, O apsaras; dwell here in my hermitage and bless me — good fortune to you — who am utterly bewildered by Madana.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed, that lady of noble hips made her abode there — for a great obstacle to austerity had come upon Viśvāmitra.
While she was dwelling there, O Rāghava, O gentle one, ten years (five and five) passed happily in Viśvāmitra's hermitage.
Then, when that time had passed, the great sage Viśvāmitra became as if filled with shame, overcome with anxiety and grief.
The thought arose in the sage's mind, indignant, O joy of the Raghu line: 'All this is the work of the gods — this great plundering of my austerity.'
Under the guise of days and nights, ten years have passed; overwhelmed by the delusion of desire, this obstacle has befallen me.
Heaving a deep sigh, that best of sages, afflicted with remorse.
Seeing the apsaras Menakā standing frightened and trembling with joined palms, the son of Kuśika dismissed her with gentle words and, O Rāma, Viśvāmitra departed to the northern mountain.
Having resolved upon unswerving resolve and desiring to conquer himself, that greatly renowned sage went to the bank of the river Kauśikī and practised most severe austerity.
As he practised that terrible austerity for a thousand years on the northern mountain, O Rāma, fear arose among the gods.
All the gods, assembled together along with the host of sages, took counsel: 'Let this son of Kuśika rightly obtain the title of maharṣi.'
Hearing the words of the gods, the Pitāmaha of all worlds spoke sweet words to Viśvāmitra, that treasury of austerity.
O Maharṣi, welcome, my child — I am pleased by your severe austerity; I grant you greatness and the foremost rank among the sages, O Kauśika.
Hearing those words of Brahmā, Viśvāmitra the treasury of austerity, bowing with joined palms, replied to the Pitāmaha.
If the Blessed One says that I have earned by my own meritorious deeds the incomparable title of brahmarṣi, then I am one who has conquered the senses.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Brahmā said to him: 'You have not yet conquered the senses; strive on, O tiger among sages,' — and having said so, departed to the three heavens.
When the gods had departed, the great sage Viśvāmitra continued his austerity with arms raised, without support, subsisting on air alone.
Abiding in righteousness, he subjected himself to the five fires (pañcatapa) in summer; in the rains he sheltered under the open sky; in winter he stood in water — day and night, that treasury of austerity.
Thus he pursued terrible austerity for a thousand years.
While that great sage Viśvāmitra was burning in austerity, great alarm arose among the gods and Vāsava (Indra).
Śakra (Indra), together with all the hosts of Maruts, spoke to the apsaras Rambhā words that were beneficial to himself and harmful to Kauśika.
O Rambhā, this great service to the gods must be performed by you — the alluring of Kauśika here, accompanied by the delusion of desire.
Thus addressed, O Rāma, that apsaras, by the wise Sahasrākṣa, stood ashamed with joined palms and replied to the lord of gods.
O lord of gods, this terrible great sage Viśvāmitra will surely release terrible wrath upon me, O god — there is no doubt. That is why I am afraid, O god; you ought to show your grace to me.
Sahasrākṣa spoke to her as she trembled with joined palms: 'Fear not, O Rambhā — good fortune to you; carry out my command.'
A cuckoo, captivating the heart, will be perched in a lovely tree in the spring season — I myself, together with Kandarpa (Kāma), will stand at your side.
You must assume a form of manifold excellence and supreme radiance, O Rambhā, and break the resolve of that ascetic sage Kauśika.
She, having heard his words, assumed an incomparable form and, graceful and bright-smiled, began to allure Viśvāmitra.
He heard the sweet sound of the cuckoo singing, and with a gladdened mind he then looked upon her.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, from that sound, the incomparable song, and the sight of Rambhā, the sage became filled with suspicion.
Recognising that deed as the work of Sahasrākṣa, the son of Kuśika, that bull among sages, possessed by rage, cursed Rambhā.
Because you, O Rambhā, seek to allure me who strive to conquer desire and anger, you shall stand as a stone for ten thousand years, O wretched one.
A brāhmaṇa of great splendour, endowed with the power of austerity, shall release you, O Rambhā, who have been polluted by my wrath.
Having spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra of great splendour, unable to restrain his anger, was overcome with anguish.
By his great curse, Rambhā became a stone at that moment; and Kandarpa, having heard the words of the great sage, also departed.
That one of great splendour, his austerity having been carried off by unmastered senses, O Rāma, found no peace within himself on account of his anger.
Then, O Rāma, having abandoned the Himālayan direction, the great sage reached the eastern quarter and performed exceedingly fierce austerities.
Having undertaken the supreme vow of silence for a thousand years, O Rāma, he performed incomparable and supremely difficult austerities.
When the thousand years were complete, though the great sage had become like a piece of wood and was shaken by many obstacles, anger did not enter within him.
Then the gods together with the Gandharvas, the Pannagas, the Asuras, and the Rākṣasas, bewildered by his brilliant energy, their radiance dimmed by his austerities, afflicted with distress, all spoke to Pitāmaha.
"O god, the great sage Viśvāmitra, having been tempted and provoked to anger by many means, continues to grow in austerities.
Not even the slightest fault is seen in him. And if what he desires in his heart is not granted, he will destroy all three worlds with their moving and unmoving beings through his austerities; all the directions are thrown into confusion and nothing shines forth.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
All the oceans are agitated, the mountains are crumbling apart, the earth trembles, and the wind blows in extreme turmoil.
O god, so long as the great sage, blazing like fire and of great splendour, does not turn his mind toward destruction, the blessed one must be appeased.
Just as the fire of dissolution formerly burns all three worlds entirely — if he desires sovereignty over the gods, let what he wishes be granted to him."
Then all the hosts of gods, led by Pitāmaha, spoke sweet words to the high-souled Viśvāmitra.
"O Brahmarṣi, be welcomed! We are thoroughly pleased by your austerities. By your fierce tapas you have attained Brahmanhood, O Kauśika.
And long life to you, O Brahman, I along with the Marut hosts grant — may you attain well-being, blessings upon you; go, O gentle one, as you please."
Having heard the words of Pitāmaha and all the celestials, the great sage bowed in obeisance and joyfully spoke.
"If Brahmanhood has been attained by me, and likewise long life — then may the Oṃkāra, the Vaṣaṭkāra, and the Vedas acknowledge me.
May Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, foremost among those who know the Vedas of the Kṣatriyas as well as the Vedas of the Brāhmaṇas, say this to me — O gods, if this supreme wish has been fulfilled, then let the foremost among gods depart."
Then Vasiṣṭha, best among those who recite sacred texts, appeased by the gods, entered into friendship with him and spoke, saying "So be it."
"There is no doubt: the state of Brahmarṣi — all of it shall be yours." Having spoken thus, all the divinities departed as they had come.
And Viśvāmitra, righteous in soul, having obtained the supreme Brahmanhood, paid homage to the Brahmarṣi Vasiṣṭha, best among those who recite sacred texts.
His desire fulfilled, he roamed the whole earth, abiding in austerity. Thus indeed was Brahmanhood attained by this high-souled one, O Rāma.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
This is the foremost of sages, O Rāma; this one is austerity in embodied form; this is the supreme eternal dharma; this is the ultimate resort of heroic power.
Having heard the words of Śatānanda in the presence of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, Janaka, with palms folded, spoke to the son of Kuśika.
"I am blessed, I am favoured, O foremost of sages — for you, O righteous one of Kākutstha's line, have arrived together to attend my sacrifice.
I have been purified by you, O Brahman, by your very sight, O great sage; manifold virtues have been obtained by me through beholding you.
And your great austerity narrated in full, O Brahman of mighty splendour, has been heard by me and by the high-souled Rāma.
And having reached this assembly along with the assembly members, your many virtues have been heard.
Immeasurable is your austerity, immeasurable your strength, and your virtues too are immeasurable and ever-constant, O son of Kuśika.
I have no satiety, O lord, with these wondrous tales; but the time for ritual acts is at hand, O foremost of sages — the solar disc hangs low.
Tomorrow at dawn, O one of great splendour, please deign to see me again. You are welcome, O foremost among ascetics; now please grant me leave."
Having spoken thus to the foremost of sages, the Vaideha, lord of Mithilā, together with his preceptors and kinsmen, quickly performed the circumambulation.
And Viśvāmitra, righteous in soul, along with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, honoured by the great sages, returned to his own encampment.
Then, at the pure dawn, after completing his morning rites, the lord of men summoned the high-souled Viśvāmitra along with Rāghava.
Having worshipped him, the righteous-souled king, with rites prescribed by the scriptures, then spoke these words to both the high-souled Rāghavas.
"O blessed one, be welcome. What shall I do for you, O sinless one? You must command me; I am indeed one who is to be commanded by you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by the high-souled Janaka, that righteous-souled sage, eloquent in speech, replied to the hero with these words.
"These two sons of Daśaratha, Kṣatriyas famed throughout the world, are desirous of seeing the supreme bow that stands in your keeping.
Show it to them — good fortune to you! Once the wishes of these two princes are fulfilled by sight of this bow, they shall depart as they desire."
Thus addressed, Janaka replied to the great sage: "Hear the purpose for which this bow stands here.
There was a renowned king called Devarāta, the sixth descendant of Nimi — this bow, O blessed one, was a trust deposited by that high-souled one into his keeping.
Formerly, at the destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice, the mighty Rudra, having strung this bow, sportively and in anger spoke thus to the thirty gods.
"Since the gods, though desiring their shares, did not apportion a share to me, I shall cut off your most excellent and precious limbs with this bow."
Then all the gods, O foremost of sages, being downcast, propitiated the Lord of Gods; and Bhava became pleased with them.
Filled with satisfaction, he gave it to all those high-souled ones.
This very jewel of a bow belonging to the great-souled God of gods was then deposited as a trust in the keeping of our ancestors, O lord.
Then, as I was ploughing the field, one was born who rose from the furrow — obtained by me while purifying the field, she became known by the name Sītā.
She who arose from the surface of the earth grew up as my daughter; this girl not born of a womb was established by me as one whose bride-price is valour.
And as she grew, this daughter of mine who rose from the earth — kings came, O foremost of sages, to sue for her hand.
To all those rulers of the earth who sought my daughter's hand, I answered: O blessed one, I do not give my daughter — her bride-price is valour.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then all the kings, O foremost of sages, assembled and came to Mithilā at that time, wishing to test their valour.
For them who wished to prove their valour, the bow was brought out; but they were unable even to lift or to take hold of that bow.
Knowing the valour of those valiant ones to be insufficient, O great sage, the kings were rejected — hear that, O wealth of austerity.
Then, O foremost of sages, in extreme anger and with their valour in doubt, all the kings besieged Mithilā.
Perceiving themselves to have been spurned, O foremost of sages, those kings, seized by great rage, afflicted the city of Mithilā.
Then, when a full year had passed, all resources were utterly exhausted, O most revered of sages, and I was deeply distressed.
Then I propitiated all the hosts of gods through austerity, and the gods, most graciously pleased, gave me a fourfold army.
Then the kings, broken and slain, fled in all directions — those evildoers devoid of valour, their boasted valour now in doubt, along with their ministers.
That supremely radiant bow, O tiger among sages, I shall show also to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, O one of excellent vows.
If Rāma should string this bow, O sage, I would give my daughter Sītā, not born of a womb, to the son of Daśaratha."
Having heard the words of Janaka, the great sage Viśvāmitra said to the king: "Show the bow to Rāma."
Then King Janaka commanded his ministers: "Let the divine bow, adorned with garlands of fragrant flowers, be brought."
Commanded by Janaka, the ministers entered the city; placing that bow at their head, they emerged by the king's command.
Five hundred men, tall and strong of great spirit, with great difficulty drew along that chest mounted on eight wheels.
Taking that great chest in which the bow lay, divine in its appearance, the royal ministers addressed Janaka.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This supreme bow, O king, honoured by all kings — O lord of Mithilā, O best of kings, it may now be displayed if you so desire."
The king, having heard their words, with palms folded, spoke to the high-souled Viśvāmitra and to those two — Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
"This supreme bow, O Brahman, has been worshipped by the Janakas and by kings of great valour; even then it could not be strung.
Not all the hosts of gods, nor Asuras, nor Rākṣasas, nor the foremost Gandharvas and Yakṣas, nor Kiṃnaras and great serpents —
— what then is the recourse of human beings in stringing, drawing, fastening the bowstring to, bending, or even merely lifting this bow?
This best of bows has been brought, O foremost of sages; O most blessed one, show it to these two princes."
And Viśvāmitra, righteous in soul, having heard what Janaka said, spoke to the Rāghava: "Child Rāma, behold the bow."
At the great sage's word, Rāma went to where the bow stood, and having opened that chest and looked at the bow, he then spoke.
"O Brahman, I shall touch this supreme bow with my hand, and I shall make effort in lifting and stringing it as well."
"Certainly!" — thus the king and the sage both replied to him. At the sage's word, he took hold of the bow in the middle, as if in play.
Before the gaze of many thousands of men, the delight of the Raghu clan, righteous in soul, strung that bow as if in sport.
And having strung the bowstring, the valiant one drew it to the full; then the foremost of men, of great glory, broke the bow in the middle.
