Its sound was tremendous, like the roar of a thunderclap; and there was a very great trembling of the earth, as if a mountain were splitting asunder.
And all the people fell to the ground, bewildered by that sound — all except the foremost sage, the king, and those two Rāghavas.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When the people had recovered, the king, his fear gone, with palms folded and skilled in speech, spoke these words to the foremost of sages.
"O blessed one, the valour of Rāma, son of Daśaratha, has been seen by me; this is utterly wondrous and inconceivable, unimagined by me.
My daughter Sītā will bring glory to the lineage of the Janakas, having obtained as husband Rāma, son of Daśaratha.
And my pledge stands true — valour is the bride-price, O Kauśika; Sītā, held by me dearer than life itself, must be given to Rāma.
With your permission, O Brahman, let my ministers go quickly — O Kauśika, blessings upon you — to Ayodhyā swiftly by chariots.
Let them bring the king here to my city with respectful words, and let them recount everything about the gift of one whose bride-price was valour.
Let them also tell the king of the two Kākutsthas under the sage's protection, and let those swift messengers bring the delighted king here.
Kauśika said "So be it"; and the king, righteous in soul, addressing his ministers, dispatched them to Ayodhyā as commanded.
Those messengers, dispatched by Janaka, with their mounts wearied, having rested three nights on the road, entered the city of Ayodhyā.
Those messengers, at the king's command, having been admitted into the royal palace, beheld the aged king Daśaratha, resplendent as a god.
All the messengers, with palms joined together, free from fear, composed, addressed the king in words of sweet syllables.
"King Janaka of Mithilā, accompanied by the agnihotra rite, inquires after your health and well-being, along with your preceptors and priests—"
"—again and again with sweet and affectionate words, O great king, Janaka asks after you and all your retinue."
"Having inquired calmly after your welfare, Vaideha, the lord of Mithilā, with Kauśika's approval, spoke these words to you:"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'My daughter's bride-price of valor was proclaimed long ago, and many kings, made angry and found lacking in valor, were turned away in disappointment.'
"'That daughter of mine, O king, has now been won by your sons—those heroes who came here led by Viśvāmitra, as if by fortune's own design.'
"'And that divine bow, O king, was broken in the midst of the great assembly by the noble Rāma, O great king, before the gathered multitude.'
"'Sītā, whose bride-price is valor, should be given by me to this great-souled one; I wish to fulfill my vow—you should grant your permission for this.'
"'Come quickly, O great king, together with your preceptors, with your priests at the fore—may it be well with you—you should see the two Rāghavas.'
"'You should fulfill my joy, O king of kings; and you yourself will also gain the joy of both your sons.'"
Thus the lord of Videha spoke his sweet words, acting with Viśvāmitra's sanction and in accordance with Śatānanda's counsel.
Having heard those words of the messengers, the king was supremely delighted; he addressed Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, his ministers, and others.
"He who delights Kausalyā, protected by the son of Kuśika, dwells in Videha together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa."
"The Kākutstha whose valor has been witnessed—the great-souled Janaka now wishes to bestow his daughter upon that Rāghava."
"If this action of the great-souled Janaka pleases you, let us proceed to the city quickly—let there be no lapse of time."
The ministers said "So be it" together with all the great sages; and the king, greatly pleased, told his ministers: "We depart tomorrow."
The ministers of the lord of men, most excellently honored, passed that night in joy, all endowed with every virtue.
Then, when the night had passed, king Daśaratha, delighted, together with his preceptors and kinsmen, spoke thus to Sumantra:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Today let all the treasurers, taking abundant wealth and adorned with various jewels, proceed well-arranged at the fore."
"Let the fourfold army also march out quickly in full, and let the finest carriages and teams be readied simultaneously with my command."
"Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, Kāśyapa, the long-lived sage Mārkaṇḍeya, and Kātyāyana likewise—"
"—let these twice-born ones proceed at the fore; yoke my chariot, so that no time may be lost, for the messengers press me to hasten."
At the command of the lord of men, that fourfold army followed behind as the king proceeded together with the sages.
Having traveled four days on the road and arrived in Videha, the glorious king Janaka, upon hearing of his coming, made arrangements to honor him.
Then king Janaka, approaching the aged king Daśaratha, was filled with joy and felt supreme delight; and that best of men, filled with gladness, spoke to that best of men.
"Welcome to you, O great king! By good fortune you have arrived, O Rāghava; you shall gain the joy of both your sons, won by their valor."
"By good fortune the greatly resplendent venerable sage Vasiṣṭha has arrived, together with all the foremost twice-born, like Śatakratu with the gods."
"By good fortune my obstacles are overcome; by good fortune my lineage is honored, through alliance with the Rāghavas—those great-souled ones supreme in valor."
"Tomorrow at dawn, O lord of lords of men, you should perform the marriage approved by the sages, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, O best of men."
Having heard those words of his, the lord of men, the foremost among those skilled in speech, spoke in return to that lord of the earth in the midst of the sages.
"The acceptance of a gift lies in the giver's power—so I have heard from of old; whatever you, O knower of dharma, shall say, that we will do."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having heard that speech—so righteous, so glorious—from one who speaks only truth, the lord of Videha was filled with supreme wonder.
Then all the bands of sages, gathered together with one another, filled with great joy, passed that night in happiness.
The king too, having beheld his two Rāghava sons, was overjoyed; he passed the night in supreme delight, honored magnificently by Janaka.
The greatly resplendent Janaka too, a true knower of dharma and ritual, having performed the rites both for the sacrifice and for his daughters, passed the night.
Then at dawn Janaka, having performed his duties along with the great sages, skilled in speech, addressed his priest Śatānanda.
"My younger brother, greatly resplendent and supremely righteous, known as Kuśadhvaja, dwells in a beautiful city—"
"—extending to the shores enclosed by water, drinking from the river Ikṣumatī, the city of Sāṃkāśyā, lovely as a sacred site, like the Puṣpaka aerial car."
"I wish to see him; he is the guardian of my sacrifice in my view; that greatly resplendent one shall also share in this joy together with me."
At the lord of men's command, they went forth with swift horses to bring that tiger among men, as if to summon Viṣṇu at Indra's bidding.
By the command of the lord of men, Kuśadhvaja came.
He beheld the great-souled Janaka, devoted to dharma; having paid his respects to Śatānanda and to the righteous king as well,
he ascended the supreme and radiant seat befitting a king. Both brothers, of unbounded splendor, then sat together.
The two heroes sent forth their foremost minister Sudāmana: "Go quickly, O lord of ministers; bring here the Ikṣvāku, of boundless splendor, who is difficult to assail—bring him with his sons and his ministers."
Going to the encampment, he found the increaser of Raghu's lineage; bowing his head in salutation, he spoke these words:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"O hero, lord of Ayodhyā, the Vaideha, lord of Mithilā, is resolved to see you together with your preceptors and priests."
Having heard the words of the foremost minister, the king, together with the groups of sages and his kinsmen, went to where Janaka was.
That king, accompanied by his ministers, with his preceptors and kinsmen, the foremost among those skilled in speech, spoke these words to the Vaideha:
"You know, O great king, that the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, the divinity of the Ikṣvāku lineage, is the spokesman in all matters."
"This righteous-souled Vasiṣṭha, with Viśvāmitra's sanction and together with all the great sages, will speak on my behalf in proper order."
When Daśaratha fell silent, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, skilled in speech, addressed the Vaideha together with his priest.
"Brahmā, whose origin is unmanifest, is eternal, ever-present, and imperishable; from him was born Marīci; from Marīci, Kaśyapa is the son."
"From Kaśyapa was born Vivasvān; Manu is known as Vaivasvata; Manu was the primeval Prajāpati; and Ikṣvāku is Manu's son."
"Know that Ikṣvāku was the first king in Ayodhyā; from Ikṣvāku the glorious Vikukṣi was born."
"From Vikukṣi, the greatly resplendent and mighty Bāṇa was born as son; from Bāṇa, the greatly resplendent and mighty Anaraṇya."
"From Anaraṇya Pṛthu was born; Triśaṅku is Pṛthu's son; from Triśaṅku was born the greatly renowned Dhundhumāra."
"From Dhundhumāra, the greatly resplendent great warrior Yuvanāśva; Yuvanāśva's son, the glorious Māndhātā, lord of the earth."
"From Māndhātā the glorious son Susaṃdhi was born; and Susaṃdhi had two sons: Dhruvasaṃdhi and Prasenajit."
"From the renowned Dhruvasaṃdhi was born one named Bharata; from Bharata the greatly resplendent one named Asita was born."
"Born together with that poison itself, he became Sagara; from Sagara came Asamañjas; from Asamañjas then Aṃśumān."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Dilīpa is Aṃśumān's son; from Dilīpa, Bhagīratha; from Bhagīratha, Kākutstha; and from Kākutstha, Raghu likewise."
"Raghu's son, the fierce and grown mighty man-eater, became Kalmāṣapāda; from him was born Śaṅkhaṇa."
"Sudarśana is from Śaṅkhaṇa; Agnivarṇa from Sudarśana; Śīghraga from Agnivarṇa; and Maru is the son of Śīghraga."
"From Maru came Praśuśruka; from Praśuśruka, Ambarīṣa; Ambarīṣa's son was Nahuṣa, lord of the earth."
"From Nahuṣa, Yayāti; from Yayāti, Nābhāga; from Nābhāga, Aja was born; from Aja, Daśaratha came to be; and from that Daśaratha were born the two brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."
"Of kings pure in their primordial lineage, supremely righteous, born in the Ikṣvāku line, heroes, speakers of truth—"
"—for the sake of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa I ask for your daughters, O king; O best of men, for these two who are their equals in worth, you should give those who are their equals in worth."
To him who had spoken thus, Janaka replied with joined palms: 'May it be well with you — you deserve to hear our lineage recited in full.'
For at the time of giving in marriage, O foremost of sages, one born of a noble line must declare that lineage without remainder. Hear it, O great sage.
There was a king named Nimi, renowned through all three worlds by his own deeds, supremely righteous in soul, the foremost among all beings of steadfast character.
His son was named Mithi; Mithi's son was Janaka — the first of that name. From that Janaka was born Udāvasu.
From Udāvasu was born Nandivardhana, righteous in soul; and Nandivardhana's son was named Suketu.
From Suketu too was born Devarāta, righteous in soul and of great might. From that royal sage Devarāta was known Bṛhadratha.
Bṛhadratha's son was the hero Mahāvīra, of great valor and blazing energy. From Mahāvīra was born Sudhṛti, steady of resolve and true in valor.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
From Sudhṛti too was born Dhṛṣṭaketu, righteous in soul and of excellent virtue. From that royal sage Dhṛṣṭaketu became known Haryaśva.
Haryaśva's son was Maru; Maru's son was Pratīndhaka; and the son of Pratīndhaka, righteous in soul, was King Kīrtiratha.
The son of Kīrtiratha too is remembered as Devamīḍha; from Devamīḍha came Vibudha, and from Vibudha came Mahīdhraka.
Mahīdhraka's son was King Kīrtirāta, of great might. From that royal sage Kīrtirāta was born Mahāromā.
From Mahāromā, righteous in soul, was born Svarṇaromā; and from that royal sage Svarṇaromā was born Hrasvaromā.
To him, that great-souled knower of righteousness, two sons were born: I am the elder, and the younger, my heroic brother, is Kuśadhvaja.
My father, lord of men, anointed me, the elder, to the kingdom; entrusting the burden to me with Kuśadhvaja in my care, he went to the forest.
When my aged father departed to heaven, I carried the yoke of duty righteously, watching over my brother Kuśadhvaja — radiant as a god — with affection.
Then after some time, the mighty King Sudhanvā came from the city of Sāṃkāśya and laid siege to Mithilā.
And he sent word to me: 'Give me the incomparable bow of Śiva, and the lotus-eyed maiden Sītā — let them be given to me.'
Because I did not give them, O brahmarṣi, battle ensued between us, and King Sudhanvā, pressing forward, was slain by me in combat.
Having slain that lord of men, Sudhanvā, O foremost of sages, I installed my heroic brother Kuśadhvaja at Sāṃkāśya.
This one is my younger brother and I am the elder, O great sage. With the greatest joy I give you two daughters-in-law, O foremost of sages.
Sītā to Rāma — may it be well with you — and Ūrmilā to Lakṣmaṇa; my daughter Sītā, whose bride-price is valor and who is like the daughter of the gods.
And Ūrmilā as the second — I say this three times, without doubt. With the greatest delight I give these two daughters-in-law to you, O joy of the Raghu line.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
O king, have the gift of cows performed for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, and the ancestral rites as well — may it be auspicious for you — and then conduct the wedding.
For today is the Maghā asterism, O mighty-armed one, and on the third day hence, O lord, is Uttara Phalgunī, O king — on that day perform the wedding. For the sake of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa let the auspicious gift-giving be performed.
To Vaideha who had thus spoken, the great sage Viśvāmitra, together with Vasiṣṭha, addressed these brave words to the king.
The lineages of the Ikṣvākus and the Videhas are beyond reckoning and beyond measure, O bull among men — there is no one equal to them.
The union is well-matched in righteousness, well-matched in the wealth of beauty — O king, Sītā and Ūrmilā with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
And there is something more to be said, O foremost of men — hear my words.
This younger brother of yours, O knower of righteousness, is King Kuśadhvaja. His two daughters, O king, whose beauty on earth is unrivalled — we seek them, O foremost of men, as wives.
For the young prince Bharata and the wise Śatrughna, O king, we seek those two daughters for those great-souled ones.
These sons of Daśaratha are all endowed with beauty and youth, comparable to the guardians of the world, equal to the gods in valor.
By this alliance with both, O lord of kings, let the Ikṣvāku line be unshakably bound to you of meritorious deeds.
Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra and concurring with the view of Vasiṣṭha, Janaka spoke with joined palms to those two foremost of sages.
'The alliance of lineages you yourselves have ordained is well-matched — so let it be; may it be auspicious for you. Let these two daughters of Kuśadhvaja become wives; let Śatrughna and Bharata, together, receive them both.'
On one and the same day, O great sage, let the four mighty princes grasp the hands of the four princesses.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
On the following day, O brahman, under the Phalgunī asterisms, the wise commend the wedding rite — there where Bhaga the Prajāpati presides.
Having spoken these gentle words, King Janaka rose and, with joined palms, addressed both those foremost of sages.
'The highest dharma has been conferred upon me; I am ever your pupil. Let the foremost of sages be seated on these principal seats.'
'As this city is Daśaratha's, so too is mine. There is no doubt about your lordship over it — you are fit to act here as befits you.'
While Vaideha Janaka spoke thus, King Daśaratha, joy of the Raghu line, joyfully replied to that lord of the earth.
'You two brothers, lords of Mithilā, are of immeasurable virtues. Sages and assemblies of kings alike are honored by you.'
'May you prosper; may it be well with you. I shall go to my own dwelling, having performed all the śrāddha rites.' So he also said.
Having taken leave of that lord of men, the illustrious King Daśaratha then departed quickly, placing those two lords of sages at the fore.
Having gone to his quarters, the king performed the śrāddha according to rule, and rising early at dawn he performed the noble gift of cows.
The king, lord of men, gave hundreds of thousands of cows to the brāhmaṇas, each lot dedicated individually to each of his sons, in accordance with dharma.
Four hundred thousand cows with gilded horns, in fine condition, each with her calf, with bronze-fitted milking vessels — so gave that bull among men.
And much other wealth besides, the Raghu-joy gave to the twice-born. Dedicated as the gift-of-cows for his sons, he who cherished his sons gave lavishly.
And that king, surrounded by his sons for whom the gift-of-cows had been performed, shone at that moment like the gentle Prajāpati surrounded by the guardians of the world.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
On that very day on which the king performed the noble gift of cows, the hero Yudhājit arrived.
The son of the Kekaya king, the actual maternal uncle of Bharata — having seen and enquired after the welfare of the king, he spoke thus.
'The lord king of Kekaya sends his loving regards and asks after your welfare. Those for whose well-being you are concerned — may they be free of illness now.'
'O lord of kings, O lord of the earth, desiring to see my nephew, O joy of the Raghu line, I came to Ayodhyā for that purpose.'
'Having heard, however, that your sons had set out for Mithilā for the wedding — together with you, O lord of the earth — I came hastening here, eager to see my sister's son.'
Then King Daśaratha, having received that welcome guest, honored him who was worthy of honor with the highest marks of respect.
Then, having spent that night together with his great-souled sons, he went to the sacrificial enclosure, placing the seers at the fore.
At the auspicious hour of Vijaya, Rāma, adorned with all ornaments and invested with the sacred marriage threads, accompanied by his brothers and placing Vasiṣṭha and other great seers at the fore —
— the venerable Vasiṣṭha came forward and spoke thus to Vaideha:
'King Daśaratha, O king, with his sons invested with the auspicious marriage threads, O foremost of the best of men, awaits the giver of the brides.'
'For all purposes are accomplished through the giver and the receiver together. Fulfil your own dharma by performing the supreme wedding rite.'
Thus addressed by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, the supremely generous one, blazing with great splendor, knower of the highest dharma, replied with these words:
'What doorkeeper stands blocking me? Whose command am I waiting upon? What deliberation is there in one's own home? This kingdom is yours even as it is mine.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'My daughters, O foremost of sages, have come to the foot of the altar, adorned with all the wedding ornaments, radiant as the flames of fire.'
'I am ready and wait for you, standing established at this altar. Let the king proceed without obstruction — why indeed is there delay?'
Hearing those words spoken by Janaka, Daśaratha then led in all his sons and also the company of seers.
King Janaka spoke to him who increases the joy of Kausalyā: 'This Sītā, my daughter, shall be your partner in dharma. Receive her — may it be auspicious for you — grasp her hand with your hand.'
'Lakṣmaṇa, come — may it be auspicious for you. Receive Ūrmilā, whom I have raised up for you; grasp her hand. Let not the auspicious moment pass.'
Having spoken thus, Janaka also addressed Bharata: 'Take the hand of Māṇḍavī with your hand, O joy of the Raghu line.'
And the righteous lord Janakeśvara also said to Śatrughna: 'O mighty-armed one, grasp the hand of Śrutakīrti with your hand.'
'You are all disciplined and all of excellent vows. Let the Kākutsthas be together with their wives — let not the auspicious moment pass.'
Hearing the words of Janaka, the four of them touched the four pairs of hands, standing in accordance with the direction of Vasiṣṭha.
Circumambulating the fire, the altar, and the king himself, and also the great-souled seers, the foremost of the Raghus, accompanied by their wives, performed the wedding in accordance with the prescribed rites, exactly as had been ordained.
A great shower of flowers fell from the sky, brilliant and auspicious, accompanied by the resounding of divine kettledrums and the sounds of song and instrumental music.
Hosts of apsarases danced and gandharvas sang melodiously at the wedding of the foremost of the Raghus — it was as though a wonder had come to pass.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
While all this was taking place, with the uproar of instruments resounding, those ones of great might circumambulated the fire three times, carrying their wives.
Then those joys of the Raghu line, together with their wives, went to the bridal chamber; and the king too followed, beholding all, with the company of seers and kinsmen.
Then, when the night had passed, the great sage Viśvāmitra took leave of both kings and departed toward the northern mountain.
After Viśvāmitra had departed, king Daśaratha quickly took leave of the Videha king, the lord of Mithilā, and returned to his own city.
Then the king of the Videhas, the lord of Mithilā, bestowed lavish bridal gifts — many hundreds of thousands of cows.
Foremost blankets and tens of millions of silk garments; elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers of divine appearance, richly adorned.
The father of the brides gave unsurpassed female and male attendants, as well as silver, gold, pearls, and coral.
With supreme delight the king gave these peerless bridal gifts; having bestowed abundant wealth, he duly took leave of the king.
The lord of Mithilā re-entered his own abode, Mithilā; and the king, the lord of Ayodhyā, departed together with his noble sons.
Placing all the sages at the fore, he set out with his army and retinue; and as that tiger among men, Rāghava, marched with the host of sages—
— dreadful birds uttered cries here and there, and all the earthly beasts moved in a clockwise direction around him.
Seeing these omens, the tiger among kings questioned Vasiṣṭha: "The birds are ominous and terrible, the beasts too go clockwise — what is this? My heart trembles and my mind is troubled."
Having heard these words of king Daśaratha, the great sage spoke in a sweet voice: "Hear what fruit these omens portend."
"A terrible, celestial danger has been declared by the birds; these beasts are propitious and allay it — let this anxiety be abandoned."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
While they were conversing there, a fierce wind arose, shaking the entire earth and toppling the stately trees.
The sun was shrouded in darkness, the directions could not be discerned, everything was covered with ash, and the whole army seemed bewildered.
Vasiṣṭha, the other sages, and the king with his sons retained their senses, while all else present seemed to lose consciousness.
In that terrible darkness, with the army as though smothered in ash, they beheld a figure of fearsome aspect wearing a crown of matted locks—
— as unconquerable as mount Kailāsa, as unbearable as the fire at the end of time, blazing with such splendour that common folk could scarce behold him.
With an axe slung upon his shoulder, a bow resembling a mass of lightning in his hands, and bearing the foremost arrow — like Hara who destroyed the three cities.
Beholding him of terrifying aspect, blazing as if he were fire, the brāhmaṇas headed by Vasiṣṭha — all the sages devoted to prayer and oblation — gathered and began to murmur to one another.
"Can it be that this one, still wrathful over his father's slaying, intends to annihilate the kṣatriyas? Having once massacred the kṣatriyas, his rage and fever were spent — surely he does not now intend their destruction again?"
Having spoken thus, the sages took the ceremonial offering and, approaching that fearsome son of Bhṛgu's line, addressed him in gentle words: "Rāma, Rāma!"
Accepting that homage offered by the sages, the mighty Rāma, son of Jamadagni, then addressed Rāma, son of Daśaratha.
"O heroic Rāma, son of Daśaratha, your wondrous valour has come to my ears; the breaking of the bow also I have heard in full detail."
"That breaking of the bow by you is wondrous and inconceivable; having heard of it, I have come, bringing yet another auspicious bow."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This great bow of Jamadagni's race, of terrifying aspect — string it with an arrow, and reveal your own strength."
"When I have seen your strength in stringing this bow, I shall offer you single combat — this is the true test of your valour."
Hearing those words of his, king Daśaratha, his face downcast and wretched, spoke with folded hands.
"You, of great renown among brāhmaṇas, have calmed the wrath born of the kṣatriya quarrel — you ought to grant safety to my young sons."
"Born in the lineage of the Bhārgavas, distinguished for their vows of sacred study, you made a promise to the thousand-eyed Indra and laid down your weapons."
"You, being devoted to dharma, gave the earth to Kaśyapa and retired to the forest — you whose dwelling was established by Mahendra."
"You have come, O great sage, for my total ruin; for if but one Rāma is slain, we cannot all of us survive."
While Daśaratha was speaking thus, the mighty son of Jamadagni disregarded those words entirely and spoke only to Rāma.
"These two are the foremost of bows — divine, renowned throughout the worlds, firm, powerful, supreme, and well crafted by Viśvakarman."
"One was bestowed by the gods upon the three-eyed Tryambaka, eager for battle — that Tripura-slaying bow which you, best of men, O Kākutstha, have broken."
"This second bow, O Kākutstha, unconquerable, was given to Viṣṇu by the greatest of gods — it is of equal substance to the bow of Rudra."
"At that time all the gods questioned the Grandfather Brahmā, wishing to assess the comparative strength of Śitikaṇṭha and Viṣṇu."
"Understanding the intention of the gods, the Grandfather, best among those who hold to truth, caused a conflict to arise between the two."
"In that conflict a great battle occurred, causing the hair to stand on end, as Śitikaṇṭha and Viṣṇu each strove to vanquish the other."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then the bow of Śiva, of terrible might, was made to yawn open; and by Viṣṇu's humkāra Mahādeva, the three-eyed one, was paralysed."
"Then the gods, assembling together with the hosts of sages and the Cāraṇas, besought them; thereupon those two best of gods desisted and came to peace."
"Seeing that Śaiva bow made to yawn by the might of Viṣṇu, the gods and the hosts of sages then deemed Viṣṇu to be the greater."
"But Rudra, greatly angered, of immense glory, placed that bow together with its arrow into the hands of the royal sage Devarāta among the Videhas."
"And this Vaiṣṇava bow, O Rāma, conqueror of enemy cities — Viṣṇu gave it as a most honoured trust to Ṛcīka of the Bhārgava line."
"And Ṛcīka, of great splendour, gave that divine bow to the great-souled Jamadagni, my father, as a gift of inestimable service."
"While my father had laid aside his weapons and was endowed with the strength of asceticism, Arjuna, acting from a base mind, brought about his death."
"Hearing of my father's wholly undeserved and terrible slaying, in wrath I exterminated the kṣatriyas time and again, generation after generation."
"Having conquered the entire earth, O Rāma, at the conclusion of the sacrifice I then gave it as the sacrificial fee to the great-souled Kaśyapa, as the fruit of that pious act."
"Having given the earth, I took up abode on mount Mahendra, endowed with the power of asceticism; then I heard of the breaking of the bow, and I came here swiftly."
"Therefore take this great Vaiṣṇava bow, O Rāma, which descended from father to grandfather — honouring the dharma of the kṣatriya, take this foremost of bows."
"Fit to this foremost bow the arrow that conquers enemy cities; if you are able, O Kākutstha, I shall then give you single combat."
Hearing those words of the son of Jamadagni, Daśaratha's son Rāma, his speech restrained out of deference to his father, then spoke.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I have heard of the deeds you have performed, O Bhārgava; I acknowledge them, O brahman — I stand here honouring my debt to my father."
"You treat me as though I were devoid of valour and incapable, O Bhārgava, by the code of the kṣatriya — witness my splendour today; behold my prowess!"
Having spoken thus, the swift and mighty Rāghava in anger took from the hand of the Bhārgava both his supreme weapon and the arrow,
and Rāma strung the bow and fitted the arrow to the string; then Rāma, enraged, spoke these words to Jāmadagnya Rāma.
"Because you are a brāhmaṇa you are venerable to me, and because of what Viśvāmitra has done for me — therefore, O Rāma, I am unable to release this life-taking arrow at you."
"I shall destroy either this your freedom of movement, O Rāma, or those incomparable worlds accumulated by the power of your asceticism — whichever you wish."
"For this divine Vaiṣṇava arrow, conqueror of enemy cities, does not fall in vain by virtue of its might — it is the destroyer of the arrogance of strength."
To behold Rāma bearing the supreme weapon, the hosts of sages and the gods, with Brahmā the Grandfather at their head, assembled there in multitudes.
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Kiṃnaras, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas — all came to witness that great wonder.
When the world had become stupefied, as Rāma held the bow of boons, that Jāmadagnya Rāma, now drained of valour, looked upon Rāma.
Stupefied, his power of valour struck down by Rāma's splendour, the son of Jamadagni slowly and softly spoke to Rāma of lotus-petal eyes.
"When I previously gave the earth to Kaśyapa, Kaśyapa told me: 'You must not dwell within my domain.'"
"Honouring the word of my guru, this is the vow I made to Kaśyapa, O Kākutstha: 'I shall not spend even a single night upon the earth.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Therefore, O hero Rāghava, you should not destroy this my freedom of movement; swift as thought I shall depart to Mahendra, the greatest of mountains."
"But those incomparable worlds I have conquered through asceticism, O Rāma — destroy those with the foremost arrow; let there be no delay of time."
"I know you to be the eternal slayer of Madhu, the lord of the gods — by your very touch of this bow it is proven; may good befall you, O scorcher of foes."
"All these hosts of gods have assembled and behold you, whose deeds are without equal and who has no rival in battle."
"Nor should this be a source of shame for me, O Kākutstha, that I have been turned back by you — you who are the lord of the three worlds."
"You should release this peerless arrow, O Rāma of noble vow; once the arrow is released I shall depart to mount Mahendra, the greatest of mountains."
While Jāmadagnya Rāma was speaking thus, the glorious and mighty Rāma, son of Daśaratha, released that supreme arrow.
Then all the directions and intermediate quarters became free of darkness; the gods and hosts of sages praised Rāma as he held his weapon aloft.
And Rāma the son of Jamadagni, having praised Rāma the son of Daśaratha, then circumambulated him clockwise and departed, that lord, to his own abode.
When that Rāma had departed, the tranquil-souled Rāma Dāśarathi handed the bow together with its arrow into the hand of immeasurable Varuṇa.
Then Rāma, the joy of the Raghu line, having saluted Vasiṣṭha and the other sages at their head, saw his father overcome with emotion and spoke to him.
"Rāma the son of Jamadagni has departed. Let the four-limbed army now march, facing Ayodhyā — that army which has been protected with you as its lord."
Hearing Rāma's words, King Daśaratha embraced his son with both arms and inhaled the fragrance of the head of that scion of Raghu.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing that that Rāma had gone, the king, thrilled and overjoyed, set the army in motion and quickly departed thence for the city.
The city was beautiful with its rows of banners and pennants, resounding with the proclamation of musical instruments, its royal roads sprinkled with water and strewn with heaped flowers —
— adorned with throngs of people, filled with citizens whose faces were bright with joy at the king's entry and with chanters of auspicious words: into this city the king entered.
Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and the slender-waisted Kaikeyī, together with the other royal ladies, were engaged in welcoming the daughters-in-law.
Then the queens received the supremely blessed Sītā, the illustrious Ūrmilā, and both daughters of Kuśadhvaja.
Adorned with auspicious utterances and robed in silk garments, all those women swiftly worshipped at the shrines of the gods.
After saluting those who deserved salutation and receiving the salutations of others, all the princes' wives rejoiced, each delighted and in private together with her husband.
Having taken wives, having mastered weapons, possessed of wealth and friends, those bulls among men passed their days serving their father obediently.
Among them, Rāma, whose glory surpassed all in the world and whose valour was true, stood foremost in virtues, even as the Self-born Brahmā stands among all beings.
And Rāma, that high-minded one, sported with Sītā through many seasons; his thoughts fixed entirely upon her, he was ever surrendered in her heart.
Sītā was dear to Rāma as "the wife given by my father," and beyond that, his love grew ever greater on account of her virtues and the excellence of her beauty.
And her husband moved doubly within her heart; even what arose within was made known, for heart speaks to heart.
And all the more conspicuously did Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka — Sītā, who equalled the goddesses in beauty, a very embodiment of Śrī herself — distinguish herself in his eyes.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
United with her, that enchanting daughter of the greatest of kings, exceedingly lovely and desired beyond measure, Rāma the all-pervading shone surpassingly — even as Viṣṇu, lord of immortals, shines in the company of Śrī.
Now, after some time had passed, king Daśaratha, that joy of the Raghu line, spoke to his son Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī.
"My son, this man who is staying here is the son of the king of the Kekayas — your maternal uncle Yudhājit has come, O hero, to take you away."
Having heard this from Daśaratha, Bharata, son of Kaikeyī, prepared to depart, accompanied by Śatrughna.
Taking leave of his father, and of Rāma who never wearied in action, and of his mothers as well, that best of men, the valiant Bharata, departed together with Śatrughna.
Yudhājit, overjoyed at receiving Bharata along with Śatrughna, that hero entered his own city, and his father was greatly pleased.
There Bharata dwelt together with his brother, honoured with great hospitality, and fondly indulged by his maternal uncle Aśvapati with a father's affection.
Even while dwelling there and being satisfied in every desire, the two heroic brothers kept remembering the aged king Daśaratha.
The king too, of great majesty, remembered his two sons who were away — both Bharata and Śatrughna, comparable to Mahendra and Varuṇa.
Yet all four of his sons, those bulls among men, were dear to him alike, as though they were four arms issuing from his own body.
Yet among them all, the great-spirited Rāma, who gave delight to his father, excelled in virtues, as the Self-born Brahmā excels among all beings.
After Bharata had departed, Rāma and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa honoured their father, who was like unto a god.
Placing his father's command foremost, Rāma, whose soul was set on righteousness, carried out all the duties toward the citizens — whatever was pleasing and whatever was beneficial.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
With the utmost self-restraint he performed the duties owed to his mothers, and at each proper time he attended to the duties owed to his teachers.
By Rāma's character and conduct, Daśaratha was pleased, as were the brāhmaṇas, the townspeople, and all the inhabitants of the kingdom.
For he was ever tranquil of soul and spoke with gentle words first; even when addressed harshly, he returned no harsh reply.
He was pleased by even a single service however slight, and through the mastery of his own self he did not remember even a hundred injuries done to him.
He was ever in conversation with good men who were advanced in conduct, knowledge, and age, even in the intervals between his exercises in archery.
He was of noble birth, virtuous, undepressed in spirit, truthful in speech, upright, and well-trained by elder twice-born men who understood righteousness and expediency.
He understood the true nature of dharma, artha, and kāma; he was endowed with memory and swift wit; he was well-versed and expert in worldly convention and social conduct.
He was learned in the śāstras and grateful for benefits received; he was skilled in reading the characters of men, and discerning in the proper exercise of restraint and favour.
He understood the means for raising revenue, and was knowledgeable about the workings of expenditure; he had attained eminence among the whole body of sciences, including the mixed branches of learning.
He grasped both artha and dharma together, was devoted to his own ease yet never indolent; he understood the principles and divisions of the practical arts.
He was accomplished in the mounting and training of elephants and horses; he was the foremost among those learned in the science of archery, and acknowledged as an atiratha — a supreme chariot warrior — in the world.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He was a bold attacker and a powerful striker, skilled in the movement of armies, and unconquerable in battle even by the wrath of gods and asuras alike.
He was free from envy, had conquered anger, was not arrogant, not jealous, did not belittle any being, and was not enslaved by the force of circumstance.
Thus endowed with the highest virtues, this son of the king was honoured among the people, respected in all three worlds for his earth-like quality of forbearance, equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom, and equal to the lord of Śacī in valour.
And so Rāma shone forth with virtues that were dear to all people and that inspired the father's love, blazing like the sun in his rays.
The earth itself desired him as her lord — him who was endowed with such conduct and character, whose valour was irresistible, who was comparable to the guardians of the worlds.
Beholding his son endowed with these many incomparable virtues, king Daśaratha, that scorcher of foes, fell to pondering deeply.
"This supreme joy that revolves within my heart — when indeed shall I behold my beloved son anointed as crown prince?"
"For he desires the welfare of the world, he has compassion for all beings, and he is dearer to the world than I am — like rain-bearing Parjanya is dearer than those who receive his rain."
"Equal to Yama and Śakra in valour, equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom, equal to a mountain in steadfastness — and yet surpassing even me in virtue."
"Having seen my own son governing this entire earth, and at this age, may I thereby attain to heaven."
Considering him to be endowed with all these gathered virtues, the great king deliberated with his ministers and resolved to appoint him crown prince.
The lord of the earth summoned the chief men dwelling in many different cities and separate provinces of the land.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then upon the various seats distributed by the king's command, the assembled kings took their places, facing toward the king himself.
The king shone forth, surrounded by those honoured and humble kings, the dwellers in cities, and the men from the provinces seated nearby — even as the blessed thousand-eyed Indra shines surrounded by the immortals.
Then the lord of the earth addressed the entire assembly and spoke this unequalled speech, beneficial and heartening.
With his great voice, deep and reverberating like the sound of a kettledrum, the king thundered like a rain-cloud.
"I, who have guarded this world that was protected by the former kings of the Ikṣvāku line, now desire to yoke it to greater prosperity — this entire world that is worthy of happiness."
"By me also, following the path walked by those of old, the subjects have been protected constantly, without fatigue, to the full extent of my power."
"This body of mine has grown old in the shade of this white royal umbrella, while I wandered about for the welfare of the whole world."
"Having lived many thousands of years of life, I now desire rest for this aged body of mine."
"I am weary from bearing this heavy burden of dharma for the world — a burden invested with royal dignity, difficult to carry for those who have not conquered their senses."
"Thus I desire rest, having set my son in care of the people, and with the assent of all these eminent twice-born men assembled here."
"For my eldest son has been born with all my virtues — Rāma, equal to Purandara in valour, the conqueror of enemy citadels."
"With joy I intend to invest that best of those who uphold dharma, that bull among men, with the dignity of crown prince — even as the moon is joined with the asterism Puṣya."
"That lord of fortune, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, is a fitting master for you — one by whose lordship even the three worlds would be better governed."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Having forthwith yoked this earth to this greater good, and having entrusted it to that son, I shall be free of toil."
The assembled kings, joyful, applauded the king as he spoke thus — like peacocks crying out in acclaim of a great rain-bearing cloud that thunders.
Having understood in full the intent of that king who was learned in dharma and artha, and having known the aged king Daśaratha's mind, they said:
"O king, you are aged, having lived many thousands of years; therefore anoint Rāma as crown prince, O lord of the earth."
Having heard those words pleasing to their hearts, the king, as if wishing to enquire further and not yet knowing their full mind, spoke these words.
"How is it that while I am righteously governing the earth, you all wish to see my son as crown prince?"
They, along with the citizens and the people of the provinces, addressed that great-souled king: "O king, your son possesses many auspicious virtues."
"Rāma, equal to Śakra in divine qualities and true in his valour, surpasses indeed all the Ikṣvākus, O lord of the people."
"Rāma is a good man in the world, devoted to true dharma, knowing righteousness, true to his word, of excellent character, and free from envy."
"He is forbearing, a conciliator, gentle, grateful, master of his senses, soft-spoken, firm of mind, ever auspicious, and without envy."
"That Rāghava speaks kindly to all beings and speaks the truth; he is an attendant upon brāhmaṇas who are greatly learned and advanced in age."
"By reason of this, his incomparable glory, fame, and splendour grow here; and he is proficient in all the weapons of gods, asuras, and men."
"Whenever he goes into battle for the sake of a village or the city, going along with Saumitri (Lakṣmaṇa), he never returns without victory."
"Returning from battle, whether on elephant or chariot, he always enquires after the welfare of the townspeople as though they were his own kin."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Regarding their sons, sacred fires, wives, servants and pupils — fully, in proper order, like a father with his own born sons."
"'Are your pupils diligently attending you, equipped for their duties?' — thus that tiger among men, Rāma, always addresses us."
"In the misfortunes of men he is greatly grieved, and at all their festivals he rejoices like a father."
"A speaker of truth, a great bowman, a servant of elders, master of his senses — by good fortune this Rāghava has been born as your son in a good hour; by good fortune you, endowed with the virtues of your son, are like Kaśyapa blessed with Mārīca."
"All the people in the kingdom and in the royal city pray for the strength, health, and long life of Rāma, that self-knowing one."
"The people of the inner and outer city, the town-dwellers and villagers, women old and young, morning and evening with concentrated mind —"
"— they bow in reverence to all the gods for the sake of the glorious Rāma; O lord, may their prayers be fulfilled by your grace."
"We wish to see Rāma, dark-complexioned as the blue lotus, the vanquisher of all enemies, your best of sons, established as crown prince."
"That son of yours, who is like unto the god of gods, who is devoted to the welfare of all the world — you, O granter of boons, should swiftly and joyfully anoint him who is endowed with nobility, for our own welfare."
Having received from all of them their lotus-like folded hands raised in salutation, the king spoke words both pleasing and beneficial to them.
"Ah, I am supremely delighted, and my majesty is unequalled, in that you desire my dear eldest son to be installed as crown prince."
Having thus honoured them in return, the king spoke these words to the brāhmaṇas, to Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, while those same men listened.
"This auspicious month of Caitra, sacred and with forests in full bloom — let everything be made ready for the installation of Rāma as crown prince."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"It shall be done" — so said those two foremost of twice-born men, Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, approaching the lord of the world, pleased and filled with joy, in accordance with his spoken command.
Then the radiant king spoke to Sumantra: "Let Rāma, that pure-souled one, be brought here by you swiftly."
Sumantra, having promised "So be it" and acting on the king's command, brought Rāma, the best of chariot-warriors, there by chariot.
Then the kings from the east, north, west, and south who were seated there around king Daśaratha —
— and the Mlecchas and the Āryas and all others who dwelt in forests and mountain borders — all waited upon him as the gods wait upon Vāsava (Indra).
That royal seer, standing in his palace among them like Vāsava among the Maruts, saw his son coming on the chariot.
— like unto the king of the Gandharvas, of renowned valour in the world, long-armed, of great being, walking with the gait of a rutting elephant —
— Rāma, whose face was fair as the moon, exceedingly pleasing to behold, whose beauty, nobility, and virtues stole away the eyes and minds of men —
— like rain-bearing Parjanya gladdening people scorched by summer heat — the lord of men, gazing upon him as he approached, was not satiated.
Sumantra, having helped that Rāghava down from the excellent chariot, followed him with joined palms as he walked toward his father's presence.
That bull among men, that Rāghava, ascended the palace that gleamed like the peak of Kailāsa to see his father, accompanied by the charioteer.
Approaching with joined palms, bowing low near his father, causing his own name to be announced, Rāma reverenced his father's feet.
Seeing him bowed at his side with joined palms, the king took his hands, drew him close, and embraced his beloved son.
And the glorious king directed Rāma to that excellent seat of honour which had been brought forward, adorned with gems and gold.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having taken that best of seats, Rāghava illumined it by his own radiance, as the pure sun at its rising illumines Mount Meru.
Illumined by him, the assembly hall shone forth splendidly — like the autumnal sky, clear of planets and stars, shining by the moon.
Gazing upon his beloved son, the king was pleased, as if beholding his own adorned self placed in the surface of a mirror.
Addressing his son with a smile, the king, best of those who have sons, spoke these words — like Kaśyapa addressing the lord of the gods.
"You are a fitting son born of my foremost wife who is fit for you; you have arisen as my dearest son Rāma, excelling in virtue, born of my own self."
"Since these subjects are won over by your own virtues, therefore you shall receive the dignity of crown prince under the asterism Puṣya."
"By your very nature you are disciplined and virtuous of your own accord; yet even to one already virtuous, I shall speak what is beneficial for you, out of affection, my son."
"Cultivating humility still more, be always master of your senses; and abandon the vices that arise from desire and anger."
"Whether acting in matters seen or unseen, win the affection of all the constituents of the state, beginning with the ministers."
"He who governs the earth with satisfied and devoted subjects — his allies rejoice as the immortals rejoice on obtaining ambrosia. Therefore, my son, conduct yourself only after restraining your own self."
Having heard this, the friends of Rāma who loved to do him service hastened swiftly and went to announce the news to Kausalyā.
That best of women, Kausalyā, distributed gold, cows, and various jewels to those who had brought her the glad tidings.
Then, having paid his respects to the king, Rāghava mounted the chariot and departed to his own radiant dwelling, honoured by the throngs of people.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And the townspeople too, having heard that word of the king, as if obtaining a cherished gain, took leave of the lord of men and went to their homes, and worshipped the gods with exceeding joy.
Then, after the citizens had departed, the king once more deliberated together with his ministers; and he who was wise in firm resolve made a firm resolve.
"Tomorrow is the Puṣya asterism; tomorrow let my son Rāma — his eyes red as lotus — be consecrated to the office of crown prince." So declared the lord.
Then king Daśaratha entered his private apartments and commanded his charioteer: "Bring Rāma back here again."
Receiving that command, the charioteer once more went swiftly to Rāma's dwelling to bring Rāma back again.
The doorkeepers announced to Rāma the charioteer's renewed arrival; and even as Rāma heard of his coming, he was filled with apprehension.
Having quickly admitted him, Rāma spoke these words: "Tell me fully and completely the purpose that brings you here again."
Then the charioteer said to him: "The king desires to see you; having heard his word, you may decide whether to go or not."
Hearing the charioteer's words, Rāma then set out in haste to the royal palace to see the lord of men once more.
King Daśaratha, upon hearing that Rāma had arrived, caused his beloved and most excellent son to be ushered into the inner chamber.
The glorious Rāghava, even as he entered his father's dwelling, saw his father from afar, bowed down before him with hands cupped in reverence.
The lord of the earth raised him as he bowed, embraced him, directed a splendid seat to be given him, and then spoke again.
"Rāma, I am old and have lived a long life; I have enjoyed all the pleasures I desired; I have performed hundreds of sacrifices with lavish food and generous dakṣiṇā-offerings.
You, O best of men, have been born to me as the beloved and peerless offspring on this earth; I have made the desired gifts and have pursued the desired learning.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
O hero, I have also experienced the desired pleasures; I am free from debt to the gods, to the sages, to the ancestors, to the Brāhmaṇas, and to my own self.
There is nothing left for me to accomplish other than your consecration; therefore whatever I tell you, you ought to carry it out for my sake.
Today all the ministers of state desire you as their sovereign; therefore, my son, I shall consecrate you as crown prince."
"Moreover, Rāma, today I see inauspicious and terrible dreams: great meteors accompanied by thunderbolts fall here with a mighty roar.
And the astrologers report to me, Rāma, that my birth star is beset by terrible planets — the Sun, Mars, and Rāhu.
For when such omens as these appear, a king generally meets with death or encounters a dreadful calamity.
Therefore, Rāghava, while my mind is still unconfused, let the consecration be performed without delay, for the minds of living beings are ever unstable.
Today the moon has come to Punarvasu, one asterism before Puṣya; tomorrow the astrologers will certainly announce the conjunction with Puṣya.
Under that Puṣya asterism let the consecration take place — my mind urges me toward haste. O scorcher of foes, tomorrow I shall consecrate you to the office of crown prince.
Therefore tonight you must observe a religious vow, with your mind disciplined and controlled, lying upon a bed of darbha-grass together with your wife, fasting the night.
And let your trusted friends guard you on all sides without negligence today, for undertakings of this kind are attended by many obstacles.
And since Bharata is absent from the city, this is precisely the opportune moment for your consecration — such is my considered view.
To be sure, your brother Bharata stands firm in the conduct of the virtuous — he is obedient to his elder, righteous in spirit, compassionate, and master of his senses.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Yet the human mind is fickle — such is my conviction; and even of the virtuous who are ever steadfast in righteousness, the character can be enhanced by what is already accomplished, O Rāghava.
Thus addressed and granted leave regarding the consecration to take place on the morrow with the word "Go," Rāma paid obeisance to his father and proceeded to his own dwelling.
Having entered his own dwelling, and learning of the consecration appointed by the king, he departed that very instant and went to his mother's inner apartments.
There he found his mother, clad in silk garments, engrossed in silent prayer in the household shrine, beseeching the goddess of prosperity.
Sumitrā had already arrived there, as had Lakṣmaṇa; and Sītā too had been summoned upon hearing the glad news of Rāma's consecration.
At that time Kausalyā stood with half-closed eyes in meditation, attended by Sumitrā, by Sītā, and by Lakṣmaṇa.
Having heard of her son's consecration as crown prince under the Puṣya asterism, she was engaged in breath-control exercises while meditating upon the divine Janārdana.
Approaching his mother who was thus absorbed in her religious observances and paying reverence to her, Rāma then spoke these words, gladdening her heart.
"Mother, I have been appointed by my father to the task of protecting the subjects; my consecration will take place tomorrow — such is my father's command to me.
Tonight Sītā and I must keep a fast together — so has my father commanded me, in the presence of the officiating priests and the preceptors."
"Whatever auspicious rites are appropriate here for the consecration tomorrow — arrange them today for me and for the Vaidehī as well."
Hearing this long-cherished news, Kausalyā spoke these words to Rāma, her voice broken with tears of joy.
"My son Rāma, live long; may your enemies be slain. Endowed with royal splendour, bring joy to me and to Sumitrā and to all our kinsmen.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Truly you were born to me under an auspicious star, my son — for by your virtues you have won the deepest affection of your father Daśaratha.
"Surely my patient endurance in bearing you, O man with eyes like lotus-petals, has not been in vain — for the royal splendour of the Ikṣvāku line shall now, my son, find its refuge in you."
Thus addressed by his mother, Rāma spoke these worthy words, glancing with a smile at Lakṣmaṇa who sat with folded hands and bowed head.
"Lakṣmaṇa, rule this earth together with me — you who are as my second self, my inner soul; this royal fortune has come to you as much as to me."
"Son of Sumitrā, enjoy the pleasures you desire and all the fruits of kingship; for it is for your sake that I long for both my life and the kingdom."
Having thus spoken to Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma paid obeisance to both mothers, obtained the permission of Sītā, and departed to his own dwelling.
Having given instructions to Rāma regarding the consecration on the morrow, the king summoned his family priest Vasiṣṭha and spoke these words.
"Go, O wealth of austerity, and cause the descendant of Kākutstha today to observe a fast, keeping his vow diligently together with his wife, for the attainment of royal glory, fame, and sovereignty."
Replying "So be it" to the king, the venerable Vasiṣṭha — best among those learned in the Veda — himself went to Rāma's dwelling.
That best of sages, reaching Rāma's dwelling which shone like a dense white cloud, entered three successive courtyards in his chariot itself.
Rāma, eager to honour him who was worthy of honour, went out of his dwelling to receive the arriving sage, hastening with a manner of respectful agitation.
Approaching quickly to the proximity of the sage's chariot, he then helped the wise one down from the chariot, taking hold of him himself.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing him humble and reverent, the family priest addressed him with pleased and gracious words, gladdening Rāma who was so deserving of joy, and spoke thus.
"Rāma, your father is pleased; you shall attain the office of crown prince. Let Your Honour today observe a fast together with Sītā."
"For in the morning your father, King Daśaratha, will consecrate you to the office of crown prince with loving delight, even as Nahuṣa once consecrated Yayāti."
Having spoken thus, the sage then caused Rāma, diligently keeping his vow, to observe the fast together with the Vaidehī, in accordance with the prescribed Vedic rites.
Then, having been duly worshipped by Rāma according to proper custom, the royal preceptor took his leave of the descendant of Kākutstha and departed from Rāma's dwelling.
Rāma too, having been honoured there by his well-wishers, took leave of them all and entered his dwelling, dismissing them all with his blessing.
Rāma's dwelling, thronged with rejoicing women and men, shone at that time like a lake filled with fully bloomed lotuses and joyful flocks of birds.
Vasiṣṭha, departing from that Rāma's dwelling which rivalled the royal palace, beheld the roads filled with crowds of people.
In Ayodhyā the royal highways in every direction were completely crowded and thronged with people eager with curiosity, gathered in groups upon groups.
At that time the noise of the royal highway, resounding with the joyful sounds of human waves and surging crowds, was like the roar of the ocean.
That day the city of Ayodhyā, adorned with garlands of forest-flowers and with banners raised above its houses, had its streets sprinkled and swept clean.
For then all the inhabitants of Ayodhyā — women, children, the aged, and the strong alike — yearning for Rāma's consecration, longed for the rising of the sun.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The people became eager to behold that great festival of Ayodhyā which was the very ornament of the subjects and the increaser of the people's joy.
Thus the family priest, as if cleaving through that mass of people, made his way slowly through the crowd-thronged royal highway toward the royal palace.
Ascending the palace whose pinnacles resembled white clouds, he came before the king of men, even as Bṛhaspati comes before Śakra, lord of the gods.
Beholding him as he arrived, the king rose from his royal seat and inquired; and Vasiṣṭha duly reported to him that the matter had been accomplished.
Dismissed by his preceptor, the king, having dispersed those throngs of men, entered his inner apartments like a lion entering a mountain cave.
That dwelling, thronged with women adorned in finest attire and rivalling the palace of the great Indra, the king made to radiate with his glorious entry, even as the moon illumines the sky crowded with multitudes of stars.
After the departure of the family priest, Rāma, having bathed and with mind controlled and composed, approached Nārāyaṇa together with his wide-eyed wife.
Taking on his head the vessel of the oblation offering, he then, in accordance with the prescribed rites, poured the clarified butter as a libation into the blazing fire for the great divinity.
And having consumed the remainder of the oblation, invoking blessings upon himself, meditating upon the divine Nārāyaṇa, he lay upon a well-spread bed of kuśa-grass.
Maintaining silence, with controlled mind, the son of the best of men lay in the beautiful shrine of Viṣṇu, together with the Vaidehī.
When but one watch of the night remained, he awoke and caused the entire prescribed arrangement of decorations to be prepared throughout the dwelling.
There, listening to the pleasant words of the panegyrists — bards, heralds, and eulogists — he attended to the rites of the early morning twilight and performed his silent prayers with concentrated mind.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He also hymned and bowed with his head before the slayer of Madhu, clad in spotless silken garments, and caused the Brāhmaṇas to recite sacred texts.
Then their holy-day proclamations — deep, melodious, and resonant — filled all of Ayodhyā, re-echoing with the sound of musical instruments.
All the inhabitants of Ayodhyā, upon hearing that the Rāghava had kept his fast together with the Vaidehī, were exceedingly joyful.
Then all the citizens of the city, having heard of Rāma's consecration and seeing the night give way to dawn, made the city resplendent once more with supreme adornment.
In the temples of the gods whose pinnacles were like white clouds, at the crossroads, on the thoroughfares, at the sacred shrines, and on the turrets and towers —
— in the merchants' stalls stocked with various wares, and in the prosperous and beautiful houses of householders —
— in all the assembly halls and even on the visible trees, decorated banners were raised and colourful flags were displayed at that time.
And from here and there were heard the words — pleasing to both the mind and the ear — of troupes of actors and dancers and of singers as they sang.
People conversed among themselves about matters relating to Rāma's consecration; at the crossroads and in their homes, with Rāma's consecration having arrived, they talked of nothing else.
Even children at play, gathered in groups at the doorways of houses, spoke among themselves of nothing else but what pertained to Rāma's consecration.
The royal highway was made magnificent by the citizens on the occasion of Rāma's consecration, adorned with flower offerings and pervaded with the fragrance of incense.
And fearing the coming of night — wishing to keep it illuminated — they also erected lamp-trees all along the streets in every direction.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having thus adorned the city in this manner, all the inhabitants of the city, longing for the consecration of Rāma to the office of crown prince —
— assembled together in groups at the crossroads and in the assembly halls, speaking to one another and praising the lord of men.
"Ah, how magnanimous is this king, this joy of the Ikṣvāku line — who, recognizing himself as old, will consecrate Rāma to the kingship!"
"We are all truly blessed, in that Rāma — a seer of all worlds, high and low — will be our protector and lord of the earth for a long time to come."
"A man of humble mind, learned, righteous in spirit, devoted to his brothers — as the Rāghava is affectionate to his brothers, so is he to us as well."
"Long may the blameless and righteous king Daśaratha live — by whose grace we shall behold the consecrated Rāma!"
While the city-dwellers were conversing in this manner, people from the rural districts arrived — those who had already heard the news — coming from all the quarters.
These rural folk, arriving at the city from all the quarters to witness Rāma's consecration, filled Rāma's city to overflowing.
From those spreading surges of human multitudes a roar was heard there, like the roar of the ocean whose currents surge and swell during the days of the full and new moon.
Then that city, resembling the abode of Indra, became on all sides noisy and crowded with the rural people who had come to behold it, even as the waters of the ocean are crowded and teeming with the creatures of the sea.
A servant-maid born of Kaikeyī's kinsmen, who had lived there alongside her, happened to climb the palace that shone like the moon.
From that palace Mantharā gazed out over the whole of Ayodhyā — its royal roads sprinkled with water and strewn with lotus blossoms and blue water-lilies.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The city was adorned with precious banners and pennants, sprinkled with sandalwood water, and thronged with people who had bathed and washed their hair.
Seeing a nurse standing nearby, Mantharā — filled with great curiosity and intent on learning the reason — questioned her.
"Why is Rāma's mother distributing wealth to the people? Tell me what is the reason for this extraordinary rejoicing. And what is the king so delighted about that he is about to do?"
Bursting with joy and with supreme delight, the nurse then disclosed to the hunchback all the great glory that was about to come upon Rāghava.
"Tomorrow, under the Puṣya constellation, King Daśaratha will consecrate the sinless Rāma, conqueror of anger, as crown prince."
Upon hearing the nurse's words, the hunchback was immediately seized with indignation and descended swiftly from the palace, which had the appearance of a Kailāsa peak.
Burning with rage, Mantharā, that one of evil vision, went to Kaikeyī as she lay resting and spoke these words to her.
"Arise, fool! Why do you lie there? Fear is fast approaching you. Submerged in a great flood, do you not understand your own situation?"
"You boast of your good fortune though its form is ill-omened. Your prosperity is as fleeting as the current of a river in summer."
Addressed thus with harsh words by the evil-sighted hunchback in her anger, Kaikeyī fell into the deepest distress.
Kaikeyī then said to the hunchback: "Is everything not well with you, Mantharā? I see your face is downcast and you seem deeply distressed."
Having heard Kaikeyī's sweet words, Mantharā — that one skilled in speech — replied with words filled with rage.
Becoming ever more despondent, the hunchback — claiming to act in Kaikeyī's interest — spoke to grieve her and to drive a wedge against Rāghava.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"A great misfortune has come about, O queen — your ruin is at hand. King Daśaratha will consecrate Rāma as crown prince."
"I am plunged into a bottomless fear, overcome with grief and sorrow, burning as if in fire — and yet I have come here for your sake."
"Your grief becomes my great grief, Kaikeyī, and your prosperity becomes my prosperity — of this there is no doubt."
"Born into a royal lineage, you are the chief queen of the king. How is it, O goddess, that you do not understand the harsh realities of royal duty?"
"Your husband, though he speaks of righteousness, is a deceiver; though he speaks gently, he is cruel. In your pure-hearted state you do not know this, and so he has outwitted you."
"Your husband deploys soothing words toward you as a mere pretense — when it comes to actual benefit, today he will endow Kausalyā."
"That evil-souled king, having sent Bharata away among your kinsmen, will tomorrow establish Rāma in the kingdom with all obstacles removed."
"An enemy under the guise of a husband, who appears to wish you well as a mother would — like a venomous serpent clasped to one's bosom — that is who you have taken to heart, dear girl."
"Just as a serpent or an enemy left unheeded would act, King Daśaratha has treated you together with your son today."
"By the wicked man's false soothing words, O young one, ever accustomed to comfort — by his installing Rāma in the kingdom — you together with your kin are truly ruined."
"Therefore, Kaikeyī, act at once while there is still time — do what is for your good. Save your son, save yourself, and save me too, O you of wondrous appearance."
Having heard Mantharā's words, the lovely-faced Kaikeyī rose from her couch and gave a fine ornament to that hunchback.
Having given the ornament to the hunchback, Kaikeyī, most excellent of women, joyfully said this again to Mantharā:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This that you have told me, Mantharā, is most pleasing to me. What more can I do for you who have brought me such welcome news?"
"I see no difference between Rāma and Bharata. Therefore I am pleased that the king will consecrate Rāma in the kingdom."
"There is nothing you could tell me that would please me more, O worthy one, well-spoken and excellent. Since you have spoken words that are all the more dear, I offer you a choice boon — choose it."
But Mantharā, envying her, flung back that ornament and spoke these words then filled with anger and sorrow:
"Why are you rejoicing so foolishly at the wrong moment, childish woman? Do you not understand that you stand in the midst of an ocean of grief?"
"How fortunate indeed is Kausalyā, whose son will be consecrated tomorrow under the Puṣya star with the great ceremony of crown prince by the foremost of brahmins."
"That Kausalyā, triumphant and her enemies destroyed, will have attained supreme delight — and you will wait upon her with hands folded like a servant girl."
"The chief wives of Rāma will indeed be joyful. But your daughters-in-law will be joyless at Bharata's ruin."
Seeing Mantharā speaking thus, filled with great grief, Queen Kaikeyī praised Rāma's virtues.
"Rāma knows dharma, is restrained by his elders, is grateful, truth-speaking, and pure. As the king's eldest son, he rightly deserves the position of crown prince."
"Long-lived, he will care for his brothers and servants as a father does. How can you grieve, hunchback, upon hearing of Rāma's consecration?"
"Bharata too, that bull among men, will certainly obtain the ancestral kingdom — his father's and grandfather's — after a hundred years in succession to Rāma."
"When prosperity has arrived, and is present, and good fortune is yet to come, why do you grieve, Mantharā? And moreover, Rāma serves me more than he does Kausalyā."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having heard Kaikeyī's words, Mantharā, deeply grieved, sighed a long, hot sigh and said this to Kaikeyī:
"Blind to your own ruin through foolishness, you do not perceive your own situation — you who are sinking into an ocean of grief, wide with sorrow and calamity."
"Rāghava will be king, and then whoever is Rāghava's son — but Bharata, Kaikeyī, will be excluded from the royal line."
"Not all sons of a king remain in the kingdom, O passionate one — for if all were to be installed, the transgression would be very great."
"Therefore, Kaikeyī, kings establish the mechanisms of rule in the eldest son — O you of faultless limbs — even when the others too are possessed of virtues."
"Your son will be utterly destitute, like one without a protector, cut off from comforts and from the royal line, dear one."
"I have come for your sake, yet you do not understand me — you who wish to give me a gift meant to celebrate a co-wife's advancement."
"Once Rāma has obtained an uncontested kingdom, he will certainly send Bharata away to another land — or even to another world."
"Bharata was sent to his maternal uncle's house while still a child and was not brought back by you — for affection grows even in stationary beings through proximity."
"Saumitri Lakṣmaṇa is Rāma's protector, and Rāghava is Lakṣmaṇa's — their fraternal bond is renowned in the worlds, like that of the twin Aśvins."
"Therefore Rāma will do no harm to Lakṣmaṇa — but that Rāma will do harm to Bharata, of this there is no doubt."
"Therefore let your son depart to the forest directly from the king's house. This is what I strongly favor, and it is greatly for your benefit."
"Thus it will be well for your kinsmen's side too, if Bharata obtains by right the paternal kingdom."
"Your boy, accustomed to comfort, is Rāma's natural enemy — deprived of wealth while the other is prosperous, how will he live in subjection?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Like the lord of an elephant herd in a forest attacked by a lion, Bharata being overwhelmed by Rāma — you ought to save him."
"Rāma's mother, your co-wife, was formerly humiliated by you in your pride and good fortune — how would she not now take revenge?"
"When Rāma obtains the earth, Bharata will certainly be destroyed. Therefore think at once of securing the kingdom for your own son — and of a cause for banishing the other's."
Thus addressed, Kaikeyī — her face blazing with anger — breathed a long, hot breath and said this to Mantharā:
"Today I will send Rāma away from here quickly to the forest, and will swiftly consecrate Bharata as crown prince."
"Now look at this: by what means, Mantharā, will Bharata obtain the kingdom and Rāma in no way obtain it?"
Thus addressed by the queen, Mantharā, evil-visioned, eager to harm Rāma's cause, said this to Kaikeyī:
"Very well — I shall tell you now, Kaikeyī; listen to me and hear how your son Bharata alone will obtain the kingdom."
Having heard those words of Mantharā's, Kaikeyī rose somewhat from her well-spread couch and spoke thus:
"Tell me the means — by what means, Mantharā, will Bharata obtain the kingdom and Rāma in no way obtain it?"
Thus addressed by the queen, Mantharā, evil-visioned, eager to harm Rāma's cause, the hunchback spoke these words:
"In the war between the gods and asuras, your husband went, taking you with him along with royal sages, to render aid to the king of gods."
"Heading toward the southern direction, toward the Daṇḍaka region, toward the city known as Vaijayanta, where dwelt Timidhvaja —"
"— that one known as Śambara, the great asura of a hundred illusions, who had not been defeated by the hosts of gods, gave battle to Śakra."
"In that great battle, King Daśaratha, having lost his senses, was carried away from the fighting by you, O queen."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"There too, your husband was wounded by weapons and was protected by you. Delighted with you, he granted you two boons, O beautiful one."
"You said to your husband then, O queen: 'Whenever I wish, I shall receive those two boons' — and that great-souled one said 'So be it.' I am not unaware of this, for you yourself told me long ago."
"Ask those two boons of your husband: the consecration of Bharata, and the banishment of Rāma for fourteen years."
"Enter the chamber of wrath today as though enraged, O daughter of Aśvapati; lie on the ground without your bed, dressed in soiled garments. Do not look at him nor speak to him."
"You are always dear to your husband — of this I have no doubt. For your sake the great king would even enter fire."
"He cannot bear to make you angry, nor to face you when you are angry. Indeed, the king would give up his very life for what pleases you."
"The lord of the earth is not capable of transgressing your word. Know your own power of good fortune, you who are slow to understand your own nature."
"King Daśaratha would give gems, pearls, gold, and various jewels — do not set your mind on those."
"Those two boons that Daśaratha granted in the war between the gods and asuras — remind him of them, O illustrious one. Do not let that matter pass you by."
"When Rāghava himself rises to grant you a boon, having settled the great king, then ask for this boon."
"Send Rāma to wander in the forest for fourteen years; let Bharata be made king over the earth — that bull among kings."
"Thus banished, Rāma will be without Rāma's estate, and Bharata, with his enemies destroyed, will become king for you."
"By the time Rāma returns from the forest, your son will have taken root and will have gathered his men, standing firm with his allies, self-possessed."
"I consider this the right moment — without hesitation, hold back the king and turn him from his resolve to consecrate Rāma."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Made to embrace disaster in the form of benefit by her, Kaikeyī — now elated and convinced — said this to Mantharā:
"Hunchback, I did not know you — the best of those who speak of the best! Among all hunchbacks on earth you are the greatest in the resolution of intelligence."
"You alone are ever engaged in my interests and wish me well. I would not have understood what the king intends, O hunchback."
"There are hunchbacks ill-formed, crooked, supremely wicked — but you, bent by the wind like a lotus, are pleasing to behold."
"Your chest curves inward, rising up to your shoulders, while your belly below is quiet, as though ashamed of its own navel."
"Your hips are well-formed, adorned with the girdle's cord; your calves are well-placed, and both your feet are long."
"You, Mantharā, clad in silk, going before me on your long thighs, shine like a regal swan."
"That hump of yours, which is long and extends like the front of a chariot — in it dwell your counsels, your knowledge of statecraft, and your stratagems."
"On it I will fasten a golden garland for you, hunchback, when Bharata has been consecrated and Rāghava has gone to the forest."
"With genuine gold, well-refined, O beautiful one — when your purpose is achieved and you are content — I will anoint your hump."
"I will have a bright auspicious tilaka mark made of gold applied to your face, and fair ornaments adorned on you, hunchback."
"Clad in beautiful garments you will move about like a deity among deities; with a face that rivals the moon, unmatched in beauty, you will go your way as chief among all, making your enemies proud."
"Even other hunchbacks, adorned with all ornaments, will attend upon your feet as you always attend upon mine."
Thus praised, she — Mantharā — said this to Kaikeyī as she lay upon her bright couch, like a flame of fire upon an altar:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"A dam is not built, dear one, after the waters have gone. Arise, do what is auspicious — show yourself to the king."
Thus encouraged, the queen — large-eyed, proud in the intoxication of her good fortune — went together with Mantharā and entered the chamber of wrath.
The beautiful woman removed her pearl garland worth many hundreds of thousands, and also her fine and worthy ornaments.
Then Kaikeyī, golden in complexion, brought under the spell of the hunchback's words, lay down upon the ground there and said this to Mantharā:
"Either, hunchback, you will report me dead here — or, when Rāghava has gone to the forest, Bharata will obtain the earth."
Having spoken those most terrible words, the passionate woman laid aside all her ornaments and lay down upon the bare earth without a covering, like a fallen kinnarī.
Her face veiled in the darkness of surging rage, her finest garlands and ornaments thus cast off, the wife of the lord of men became despondent — like the sky obscured by darkness, its stars submerged.
Having ordered the consecration of Rāghava, the great king — self-controlled and desirous of bearing glad tidings to one who deserved gladness — entered the inner apartments.
There the lord of the earth saw her fallen to the floor, lying prostrate in a manner wholly unbecoming her — he, who was himself as though scorched with grief.
That aged king — himself without guilt — beheld upon the ground his young wife, dearer to him than life itself, yet harbouring wicked intent.
As a great elephant in the forest tenderly touches a she-elephant pierced by a hunter's poisoned arrow, so did he, in affection, stroke her.
Having touched her with his hands, his heart greatly alarmed, the passion-bound king spoke thus to the lotus-eyed woman.
