"I do not perceive what anger has taken hold in your heart, O queen. By whom have you been aggrieved? By whom have you been dishonoured?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"O auspicious one, why do you lie thus in the dust for my grief? Why do you lie upon the ground, tormenting my heart — you whose heart is auspicious — as though possessed by an evil spirit?"
"I have skilled physicians, all of them entirely devoted. They shall bring you comfort — tell me your ailment, O lovely one."
"Whose favour shall I do for you? Who has done you displeasure? Who shall today receive great benefit, or who shall receive great harm?"
"Shall one who is not to be slain be slain, or shall one condemned to death be freed? Shall a poor man be made wealthy, or a wealthy man be stripped of all?"
"I myself and all that is mine are under your command. I dare not thwart any purpose of yours."
"Speak, even at the cost of my own life, whatever your heart desires — the entire earth over which the wheel of sovereignty turns is mine."
Thus reassured, she, intending to speak that which was hateful, set about further tormenting her husband.
"I have not been wronged by anyone, O lord, nor dishonoured. But there is a certain desire of mine — I wish it to be fulfilled by you."
"Make me a promise — swear that you will do it — and then I shall speak what it is that I desire."
Thus spoken to by his beloved, the king — fallen under a woman's sway — replied to Kaikeyī with a slight smile, the great-spirited one.
"O proud one, do you not know — there is no person dearer to me than you, save that tiger among men, Rāma?"
"O gentle one, search even this heart of mine and draw it forth — having considered this, Kaikeyī, say what you think right."
"Knowing your own power, you ought not to be doubtful of me. I will bring you joy — I swear to you by my good deeds."
Elated by those words, she disclosed her inner intention — dreadful as Death himself approaching.
"As you swear in due order and grant me the boon — let the thirty-three gods headed by Indra hear that!"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Let the moon and sun, the sky and planets, night and day and the directions, the whole world and the earth itself, along with Gandharvas and Rākṣasas —"
"— the night-roaming creatures, the household deities dwelling in houses, and whatever other beings there are — let them all know your spoken word."
"This great-splendoured one, true to his word, knowing dharma, and well-composed — he grants me a boon. Let the gods hear this for me."
Thus the queen, having embraced and adjured the great archer, then spoke further to that boon-granting one bewildered by desire.
"The two boons that were given to me by you at that time, O lord of the earth — I shall now state them this very day. Listen to my words."
"The consecration that has been prepared for Rāghava — with this very consecration let my Bharata be anointed."
"And let Rāma, wearing bark garments, deerskin, and matted locks, dwell as an ascetic in the Daṇḍaka forest for nine and five years."
"Let Bharata today assume the undisputed rank of crown prince — and this very day let me see Rāghava setting out for the forest."
Then the great king, having heard Kaikeyī's terrible words, was distressed and agitated, like a deer that has seen a tigress.
Seated upon the uncovered ground, breathing long and deep, crying out "Alas! Shame!" in anguish, the lord of men fell once more into a swoon, his consciousness overwhelmed by grief.
After a long while the king regained his senses, deeply distressed; in fury he spoke to Kaikeyī, as though burning her with his gaze.
"O cruel one, O evil in conduct, O destroyer of this family — what wrong has Rāma done you, O sinful woman? What wrong have I done you?"
"Rāghava always behaves toward you as he would toward his own mother — for what reason are you roused to work his ruin?"
"You were brought by me into my own house for my own destruction — a princess, not properly known, like a venomous serpent."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"When all the living world here sings the praises of Rāma's virtues, pointing to what offence shall I abandon my beloved son?"
"I could abandon Kausalyā, or Sumitrā, or royal fortune, or even my own life — but never Rāma, who is devoted to his father."
"My joy is supreme when I behold my eldest son; but when I do not see Rāma, consciousness itself forsakes me."
"The world might endure without the sun, or crops without water — but my life could not remain in this body without Rāma."
"Therefore, abandon this resolve, O you who are resolved on sin. With my head I touch your feet — be gracious to me."
That lord of the earth, lamenting like one helpless, seized by the woman in her exceeding firmness, fell — and, like one sick, could not quite reach the two extended feet of the queen.
That great king — lying prostrate in a manner wholly unbefitting him, like Yayāti fallen from the world of the gods at the exhaustion of his merit —
— that woman, herself the embodiment of calamity yet successful in her purpose, fearless though she showed fear, demanded once again that very same boon.
"You boast, O great king, of being truthful and firm in your vow — why then do you wish to withhold this boon of mine?"
Thus addressed by Kaikeyī, King Daśaratha replied in anger, reeling for a moment as though bewildered.
"When I am dead and Rāma — that foremost of men — has gone to the forest: alas, O ignoble woman, O my enemy, Rāma has been banished to the forest!"
"If I speak truly in this, then may it be untrue — for surely boundless infamy and dishonour will be mine in this world."
As he lamented thus, his mind whirling in confusion, the sun set and night drew on.
That night of three watches, adorned by the orb of the moon, did not shine beautifully for the king as he lamented in such affliction.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
So too the aged king Daśaratha, breathing hot sighs, lamented his sorrow like one in anguish, his eyes fixed upon the sky.
"I do not wish for a dawn to come through you — this folded salutation I now make. Or rather, go away quickly — I do not wish to see the merciless and cruel Kaikeyī, on whose account this great calamity has befallen."
Having spoken thus, the king then, with hands folded in supplication, sought once more to propitiate Kaikeyī, and spoke to her again.
"Let grace be shown — especially to this king of upright conduct, now wretched, dependent upon you, and with life nearly spent. O queen, O gentle one."
"This was spoken by me in utter desolation, O lovely-hipped one. Show me proper grace — you are, after all, a woman of feeling."
Yet she who harboured a wicked heart, though he was pure of heart — she, merciless, made no reply to her husband even after hearing that wondrous and piteous lamentation of the king, whose eyes were red and brimming with tears.
Then the king, looking once more upon his beloved who was unsatisfied and speaking contrary words regarding the banishment of his son, fell insensible to the ground, stricken with grief.
That sinful woman, gazing upon the descendant of Ikṣvāku — tormented by grief for his son, fallen unconscious to the ground and writhing — spoke thus.
"As though having committed a sin, why do you lie collapsed on the floor after having heard my promise? You ought to stand firm in your resolve."
"Those who know dharma declare that truth is the highest dharma. Relying on truth, I have urged you toward dharma as well."
"Śaibya the lord of the earth, O king, having pledged and then given his own body to the hawk, attained the highest destiny."
"Similarly the splendid Alarka, when a brahmin learned in the Vedas begged of him, plucked out his own eyes and gave them without hesitation."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The lord of rivers, bound to truth, does not, by its truth-compact, transgress the appointed shoreline at the proper season, however narrow that boundary."
"And if you will not honour this noble compact of mine, then, before your very eyes, having been abandoned, I shall abandon my life."
Thus pressed by the fearless Kaikeyī, the king was unable to free himself from the snare — like Bali from the bond fashioned by Indra.
Bewildered in his heart, he became pale and voiceless — like a draught-ox struggling between the yoke and the wheel.
The lord of the earth, his eyes unsteady and as though unseeing, summoning his composure with great difficulty through his fortitude, spoke thus to Kaikeyī.
"The hand of yours which I clasped in fire at the sacred rite, O sinful woman — that I renounce, and your son who is my own kin, and you along with him."
Then Kaikeyī — wicked in her conduct, yet skilled in speech — overcome with rage, spoke harsh words to the king once more.
"What is this you say, O king — words like a poison's sting? You should have Rāma, your son, brought here without delay."
"Having established my son in the kingdom, having sent Rāma to dwell in the forest, and having left me without a rival — you will then be one whose purpose is accomplished."
Goaded repeatedly like a noble horse urged by a sharp goad, the king spoke thus to Kaikeyī.
"I am bound by the bond of dharma and my understanding has forsaken me. I wish to see Rāma, my beloved eldest son, that righteous one."
Hearing the king's words, Kaikeyī thereupon herself spoke to the charioteer: "Go, bring Rāma here."
Then that majestic and righteous king, his joy extinguished in regard to his son, his eyes red with grief, looked up at the charioteer and spoke.
Sumantra, having heard the piteous words and seen the wretched state of the king, withdrew a little from that spot with hands folded in reverence.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When the lord of the earth was unable out of misery to speak himself, then Kaikeyī — well-versed in counsel — spoke to Sumantra.
"Sumantra, I wish to see Rāma — bring the handsome one quickly." He, thinking this to be auspicious, rejoiced in his heart.
Sumantra reflected, hastened on by her: "Clearly Rāma, who knows dharma, will come here for the consecration."
Having so resolved, the charioteer of great splendour went forth once more, with great joy, eager to behold Rāghava.
Then, having gone forth suddenly from the front, looking about at those standing at the gateway of the lords of the earth, he saw various townspeople of great wealth who had come and stood assembled at the door.
Having spent that night, the Brāhmaṇas who were masters of the Vedas presented themselves for the morning audience together with the royal chaplain.
Ministers, commanders of the army, and the leading men of the guilds — all delighted — assembled together for the consecration of Rāghava.
When the pure sun had risen and the day of the Puṣya asterism had arrived, the foremost twice-born had prepared everything for the consecration of Rāma.
Golden water-jars were arrayed, an auspicious throne was richly adorned, and a resplendent tiger-skin had been properly spread upon it for Rāma.
Water had been brought from the sacred confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, and from other holy rivers, lakes, wells, and ponds.
From streams flowing eastward, northward, and laterally, water had been carefully gathered, and likewise from all the oceans.
Honey, curds, clarified butter, parched grain, darbha-grass, flowers, and milk — golden and silver jars covered with milk-plants, adorned with lotuses and blue water-lilies, gleamed, filled to the brim with the finest water.
A splendid white yak-tail fan, bright as moonbeams, adorned with jewels, stood ready for Rāma.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And a white parasol resembling the orb of the moon — radiant, magnificent, and placed in readiness for the consecration — stood waiting.
A white bull stood ready, a white horse was properly stationed, and a majestic rutting elephant — fit for a king to ride — waited in attendance.
Eight auspicious maidens adorned with all their ornaments, all manner of musical instruments, and likewise bards and panegyrists — all were assembled.
In the manner customary within the kingdom of the Ikṣvākus for a royal consecration, all the prescribed requisites for the anointing of a prince had been assembled.
Those who had assembled there by the king's command, not seeing the lord of the earth, said among themselves: "Who now will announce us to the king?"
"We do not see the king, yet the sun has risen, and all is prepared for the consecration of wise Rāma as heir-apparent."
While they were speaking thus, Sumantra — honoured by the king — addressed all those sovereign lords of the earth with these words.
"On the king's command I shall inquire after the well-being of these long-lived lords, and also after the reason for their coming, once the king has been awakened."
Having said this, the knower of ancient lore went to the inner-palace gate and praised Rāghava with auspicious benedictions full of virtuous import.
"The blessed night has passed, an auspicious day has come. Awaken, O tiger among kings, and proceed to your duty without delay."
"Brāhmaṇas, commanders of the army, and the guild-leaders have all come, O king, awaiting your audience. Awaken, O Rāghava."
Having awakened while that charioteer Sumantra, skilled in counsel, was thus praising him, the king then spoke these words.
"I have not yet slept — bring Rāghava quickly." With these words king Daśaratha once more commanded the charioteer.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing the king's command and honouring it by bowing his head, Sumantra departed from the royal dwelling, thinking this a great favour.
Setting out along the royal road adorned with pennants and banners, that charioteer heard conversations all concerning Rāma.
Then Sumantra beheld Rāma's beautiful dwelling — radiant as Mount Kailāsa, in splendour equal to the abode of Indra.
It was closed by great doors, beautiful with hundreds of terraced pavilions, adorned with golden statues throughout, with arched gateways of gems and coral.
White as the thick clouds of autumn, blazing with light, resembling the caverns of Mount Meru, it was adorned with very long garlands of the finest flowers.
That charioteer, arriving with his horse-yoked chariot and beholding the vast, opulent royal palace crowded with people, was filled with delight — his hair standing on end with joy.
That charioteer entered unimpeded into the palace — resembling mountain-peaks, massive rocks, and clouds, like a great assemblage of the finest mansions, abounding in treasures — as a sea-creature enters the ocean.
Having passed through the inner-palace gate thronged with people, the knower of ancient lore reached a secluded inner courtyard.
It was guarded by young men bearing javelins and bows, wearing polished earrings, vigilant, single-minded, and deeply devoted.
There at the door he saw elderly women superintendents of the inner apartments, wearing ochre robes, holding cane-staffs, richly ornamented, and deeply composed.
Seeing him approach and wishing to please Rāma, they immediately announced Sumantra to Rāma together with his wife.
Learning that the charioteer had been announced as coming from his father within, Rāghava had him brought in at once, out of a desire to do what was pleasing.
The charioteer saw him — resembling Vaiśravaṇa himself, richly adorned — seated on a couch covered with a golden spread and upper cloth.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The scorcher of foes was anointed with the most exquisite sandal-paste — pure, fragrant, and the hue of boar's blood.
With Sītā standing at his side, yak-tail fan in hand, he was further graced, like the moon attended by the splendid star Citrā.
Sumantra, like a trained panegyrist observant of protocol, reverently saluted him — the granter of boons, blazing like the sun in his own radiance.
With hands joined in reverence, after inquiring about his comfort in recreation, sleep, and rest, Sumantra — honoured by the king — said this to the prince.
"O lord, the auspicious Kausalyā and your father wish to see you, together with the queen Kaikeyī. Go there without delay."
Thus addressed, that lion among men of great radiance was filled with joy; he then honoured Sītā and spoke to her thus.
"O lady, the king and the queen — consulting together in my presence — are surely deliberating something connected with my consecration."
"For she — gracious and fair-handed, intoxicating-eyed — having perceived the king's intention and being eager to please me, is urging the king on my behalf."
"Such is the assembly gathered there, and such is the messenger who has come — the king will certainly consecrate me as heir-apparent this very day."
"Come now, I shall go quickly hence and see the lord of the earth. You remain here comfortably with your retinue and rejoice."
Sītā, honoured by her husband, the dark-eyed lady, followed her lord as far as the door, silently invoking auspicious blessings upon him.
He saw all the petitioners who had gathered, greeted them affectionately, and then mounted his splendid chariot that blazed like fire.
That chariot seemed to steal away all eyes with its dazzling golden radiance, and was yoked with the finest horses swift as young elephants.
Like thousand-eyed Indra mounting a tawny-horsed chariot, Rāghava blazing with royal splendour swiftly set forth, having taken his seat.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Resounding like a rain-cloud in the sky, the illustrious Rāma emerged from his dwelling as the moon issues from a great cloud.
Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāghava, parasol and yak-tail fan in hand, mounted the chariot and guarded his brother from behind.
Then a great tumultuous roar arose on all sides from the multitude of people as he came forth.
Rāghava heard there the conversations and talk of the assembled people, and the varied utterances — extolling him — of the joyful citizens of the city.
"Today Rāghava, by the king's favour, is going to receive immense prosperity. We — whose ruler this one will be — are all our desires fulfilled. It is the gain of these people that he will obtain this entire kingdom for a long time."
Accompanied by resonant-sounding horses and elephants preceding him, honoured by svastika-reciters, bards, and panegyrists, praised by the finest musicians, he proceeded like Vaiśravaṇa himself.
Rāma beheld the beautiful great highway — teeming with she-elephants, bull-elephants, chariots, and horses, with its open spaces filled by great crowds of people, abounding in treasures and extensive stores of merchandise.
Illustrious Rāma, having mounted his chariot, with friends and well-wishers delighted around him, gazed upon the city thronged with multitudes of various people.
Rāma proceeded along the royal road, beautiful with white houses resembling clouds, and perfumed throughout with the smoke of burning agaru wood.
That excellent royal road was brilliant and unobstructed, filled with various wares and with foods of every kind, both fine and coarse.
Hearing many benedictions voiced by his well-wishers, and honouring all men as befitted them, he rode on.
"The path that was walked by your grandfathers and great-grandfathers — take it up from this day forward, once consecrated, and guard it well."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"As we were cherished by your father, as by the grandfathers of old — even more happily shall we all dwell under Rāma as our king."
"Enough today with eating, enough with all our other concerns — so long as we can see Rāma riding forth, established in his kingdom."
"For nothing shall be dearer to us, nor shall any other thing equal it, than the consecration of Rāma of boundless glory to his kingdom."
Hearing these and other such auspicious words from well-wishers — words that honoured him personally — Rāma rode with equanimity along the great highway.
For no person could turn either mind or eyes away from that best of men, even after Rāghava had passed by.
For that righteous-souled one shows compassion to all the four varṇas and to all four stages of life; therefore they were all devoted to him.
Reaching the royal palace — comparable to the abode of great Indra — that prince, blazing with royal splendour, entered his father's dwelling.
Having passed through all the courtyards, that son of Daśaratha dismissed all his attendants and proceeded to the pure inner apartments.
Then, after the prince had entered his father's presence, all that joyful multitude waited for his re-emergence, as the ocean awaits the rising of the moon.
Rāma saw his father seated on the auspicious throne, desolate, accompanied by Kaikeyī, his face withered and parched.
He first reverently saluted his father's feet in the customary humble manner, then composed, he also paid obeisance to the feet of Kaikeyī.
Having uttered only the word "Rāma," with eyes overwhelmed by tears, the wretched king was unable either to look at him or to speak to him.
Seeing that unprecedented, terrifying aspect of the lord of men, Rāma too was seized with fear, as though he had touched a serpent with his foot.
With senses joyless, he beheld the great king, emaciated by grief and anguish, sighing heavily, his mind troubled and distraught.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He was like the ocean, ordinarily unshakeable yet now agitated with waves; like the sun eclipsed; like a sage made to utter an untruth.
Perceiving the inconceivable, extraordinary grief of his father, Rāma became more agitated, like the ocean at the full moon.
Then Rāma, ever devoted to his father's welfare, began to reflect: "Why does the king today not welcome me as he usually does?"
"At other times, even when angry, my father grows pleased upon seeing me — what distress has come upon him today when he looks at me?"
Rāma, looking as though wretched, stricken with sorrow, the radiance of his face dimmed, saluted Kaikeyī and then spoke these words.
"Have I unknowingly committed some offense because of which my father is angry? Tell me that, and do you yourself appease him."
"Wretched, with face drained of colour, he does not speak to me — is there no bodily or mental affliction, no grief or burning anguish troubling him? For happiness is always hard to attain."
"Has nothing inauspicious befallen prince Bharata of lovely form, or mighty Śatrughna, or any of my mothers?"
"If I have failed to please the great king or have not acted on my father's words, I would not wish to live even for a moment while the king is angry."
"How should one not honor him through whom a person sees the origin of his own existence here in this world — he being a visible divinity before one's eyes?"
"Has my father perhaps been addressed by you with harsh words born of pride, spoken in anger, words that have agitated his mind?"
"Tell me truthfully, O queen, as I earnestly ask — what is the cause of this unprecedented change in the lord of men?"
"At the king's command I would leap into fire, drink sharp poison, or plunge into the sea — when directed to do so by my revered father, the king who wishes my good."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Therefore speak, O queen, whatever the king desires — I shall do it, and I swear to it: Rāma does not speak twice."
To Rāma, who was thus full of sincerity and truthful in speech, the ignoble Kaikeyī spoke words that were exceedingly cruel.
"Long ago, O Rāghava, in the war between gods and demons, your father, having protected me when I was wounded in that great battle, granted me two boons.
"From those boons I have asked the king: the consecration of Bharata as crown prince, and your departure, this very day, O Rāghava, to the Daṇḍaka forest."
"If you wish to keep your father true to his pledge, and to maintain your own honor, O foremost of men, then hear these words of mine."
"Abide by your father's command as he has promised on your behalf: you are to enter the forest for nine years and five years — fourteen years in all."
"Seven and seven years dwelling in the Daṇḍaka wilderness, abandoning this consecration, you shall live clad in matted locks and bark garments."
"Let Bharata rule this earth, rich in diverse gems and furnished with horses, chariots, and elephants, from the city of Kosala."
Hearing those unpleasant words, words equivalent to death, Rāma, slayer of enemies, was not disturbed, and he said this to Kaikeyī.
"So be it. I shall go from here to dwell in the forest, wearing matted locks and bark garments, upholding the king's pledge."
"But this I wish to know: why does the lord of the earth, the invincible subduer of enemies, not welcome me as before?"
"Do not feel anger, O queen. Speak before you. I shall go — be well pleased — to the forest wearing bark garments and matted locks."
"What pleasing act would I not confidently perform when directed by my beneficent elder, my grateful father the king?"
"Yet one false thing in my heart burns me as with fire: that the king did not himself tell me of Bharata's consecration."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For I would gladly give of my own accord — without being prompted — Sītā, the kingdom, my cherished life, and my wealth to my brother Bharata."
"How much more so when directed by the lord of men, my own father, and when upholding a pledge for the sake of fulfilling your desire?"
"So console him — why does the lord of the earth keep his gaze fixed on the ground and weep these slow tears?"
"Let messengers go this very day, by the king's command, on swift horses, to bring Bharata from his maternal uncle's home."
"As for me, I depart swiftly from here to the Daṇḍaka forest, without deliberating over my father's words, to dwell there for fourteen years."
Kaikeyī, delighted upon hearing those words of Rāma, believing his departure certain, urged Rāghava to set out without delay.
"So be it: men shall go on swift horses to bring Bharata back from his maternal uncle's family."
"But for you, who are not eager to linger, I think delay is not proper, Rāma — therefore you ought to depart swiftly to the forest from here."
"And that the king, filled with shame, does not speak to you himself — this is nothing at all, O foremost of men; let this anger be set aside."
"As long as you have not departed swiftly to the forest from this city, Rāma, your father will neither bathe nor eat."
Sighing, "Alas, what misery!" the king, overwhelmed with grief, fell unconscious on that gold-adorned couch.
Rāma, urged on by Kaikeyī, raised the king up, and like a horse struck by a whip, made haste to depart to the forest.
Having heard that cruel, deeply unpleasant speech of the ignoble woman, Rāma, free from distress, spoke these words to Kaikeyī.
"I am not devoted to material gain, O queen, nor do I aspire to inhabit the world for that — know me as equal to the sages, standing solely by dharma."
"Whatever agreeable thing it is possible for me to do for his honored self, even at the cost of giving up my life, that is in every way already done."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For there is no practice of dharma greater than service to one's father and the fulfillment of his command."
"Even uninstructed by his honored self, at your word I shall dwell in the lonely forest here for fourteen years."
"You truly expect no virtue in me at all, O Kaikeyī, that you — being more powerful than I — spoke to the king in this way on my behalf."
"As soon as I take leave of my mother and comfort Sītā, I shall depart this very day to the great Daṇḍaka forest."
"Let Bharata rule the kingdom and serve his father as befits him — this too must be arranged by you, for that is eternal dharma."
On hearing Rāma's words, the father, deeply stricken with pain, unable to hold back his tears from grief, wept aloud with a great cry.
Having saluted the feet of his father who had lost consciousness, and the feet also of the ignoble Kaikeyī, the great-resplendent Rāma departed.
Rāma, having circumambulated his father and Kaikeyī, stepped out of the inner apartments and saw his own circle of dear friends.
Eyes brimming with tears, utterly furious, Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of Sumitrā's joy, followed behind him.
Rāma circumambulated the consecration materials and walked slowly away, his gaze lingering, turning back with a longing look.
The loss of the kingdom did not diminish his great splendor, just as the night does not diminish the loveliness of the cool-rayed moon that is beloved of the world.
In one wishing to go to the forest and relinquishing the earth, no perturbation of mind was apparent — as in one who has transcended all the worlds.
Bearing the sorrow inwardly, restraining his senses, that self-possessed one entered his mother's dwelling, bearing the bearer of unwelcome tidings for her.
Having entered and seeing the dwelling filled with great joy, and having become aware of the calamity that had come to pass, even there Rāma showed no perturbation, out of concern lest his dear ones be alarmed at his own misfortune.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāma, greatly fatigued, sighing like an elephant, the self-restrained one went with his brother to his mother's inner apartments.
There he saw an elderly man of great honor seated at the doorway of the house, and many others standing there as well.
Entering the first courtyard, in the second he saw aged Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas, honored by the king.
Rāma bowed to those elders, and in the third courtyard he saw women — both old and young — intent on guarding the door.
Those delighted women greeted him and then swiftly entered the house and announced to Rāma's mother the joy of his arrival.
Queen Kausalyā too, having kept vigil through the night in concentrated prayer, at dawn performed worship of Viṣṇu, she who desired her son's welfare.
She, clad in a silk garment, joyful, ever devoted to vows, performed oblations into the sacred fire with mantras, having made all auspicious rites.
Then Rāma, entering his mother's auspicious inner apartments, saw his mother there engaged in making offerings to the sacred fire.
She, seeing her son who had long been awaited, the delight of his mother, now arrived, rushed forward overjoyed, as a mare rushes toward her young colt.
Kausalyā, out of maternal love for her son, spoke to that Rāghava, her invincible child, these words that were both affectionate and beneficial.
"May you attain the long life, glory, and dharma proper to the lineage of the noble, dharma-disciplined, great-souled royal sages."
"Behold, O Rāghava, your father the king, true to his pledges — this very day the righteous-souled one shall consecrate you as crown prince."
Rāghava, extending his joined palms toward his mother, spoke to her — he who was naturally humble and now bent down in reverence.
"O queen, you surely do not know that a great peril is at hand — one that will bring sorrow to you, to Vaidehī, and to Lakṣmaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For fourteen years I shall dwell in the lonely forest, living on honey, roots, and fruits, having forsaken meat in the manner of a sage."
"The great king grants the crown-princeship to Bharata, and banishes me — as an ascetic — to the Daṇḍaka forest."
Seeing her — unaccustomed to sorrow — fallen like a plantain tree, insensible, Rāma raised his mother up.
Having turned and raised her up — wretched as an overburdened mare — her every limb covered with dust, he stroked her with his hand.
She, afflicted with sorrow, she who was accustomed to happiness, spoke to Rāghava who sat beside her — that tiger among men — while Lakṣmaṇa listened.
"O Rāghava, my son, if you had not been born for my grief, then I, being childless, would have seen no greater sorrow than that."
"For a barren woman has only one human sorrow — the grief of 'I am without a child' — truly there is no other sorrow, my son."
"It was with the hope that I might behold good fortune or happiness through a husband's valor or through a son that I persevered, placing my faith in Rāma."
"I, though the chief among co-wives, shall be forced to hear many unpleasant, heart-piercing words from those junior co-wives — what greater sorrow can there be for any woman?"
"Even with you present near me, I was thus rejected and ignored — what then when you are gone, my dear? Death alone is certain for me."
"Whoever serves me or follows my wishes, upon looking toward Kaikeyī's son, that person does not address me."
"Seventeen years since your birth have passed, O Rāghava, while I waited in expectation for the end of my sorrows."
"Through fastings, austerities, and many hardships — reared with difficulty you have been raised in vain by me in my misfortune."
"Firm indeed I deem my heart, that it does not break apart, like the bank of a great river touched by the new flood-waters of the rains."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Surely death does not exist for me, nor is there room for me in Yama's realm, since Death does not this very day carry me off by force, as a lion carries off a weeping doe."
"My heart is surely firm as iron, that it does not shatter, that upon this earth it does not split asunder with this body given over to such grief — for truly, untimely death does not exist."
"This is my sorrow: that my vows, gifts, self-restraints, and austerities practiced for the sake of offspring are utterly fruitless — like good seed sown in barren soil."
"If one could attain untimely death by one's own will when worn away by great sorrow, I would have gone this very day to the assembly of the dead, like a cow bereft of her own calf."
Deeply unhappy, overcome with indignation, she lamented much, gazing upon Rāghava, perceiving that great calamity — like a kiṃnarī looking upon her son bound in chains.
To Kausalyā, Rāma's mother, lamenting thus, Lakṣmaṇa, stricken with sorrow, spoke words befitting that moment.
"It does not please me either, O noble lady, that Rāghava should go to the forest, abandoning royal splendor, having been subjected to the words of a woman."
"A king who has changed in character, who is old, and who has been overpowered by the senses — what might such a one not say when provoked while in the grip of passion?"
"I see no offense in him, nor any fault of that kind, on account of which Rāghava should be banished from the kingdom to dwell in the forest."
"I see no one in the world — not even speaking behind his back — no man, enemy or estranged, who would name a fault in him."
"Who, bearing in mind dharma, would abandon without cause a son who is godlike, upright, self-restrained, tender even toward his enemies?"
"What son, keeping in mind the conduct proper to kings, would take to heart this word of a king who has reverted to childhood?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"As long as no person knows of this matter, until then, establish your authority while it rests in yourself — act jointly with me."
"With me standing at your side bearing my bow, protecting you, O Rāghava, who is capable of doing you harm — as if standing against Death himself?"
"I shall empty this entire Ayodhyā of men with sharp arrows if she persists in this wrong, O bull among men."
"Whoever sides with Bharata or wishes his good — all of them I shall slay; for the gentle are always overpowered."
"With both you and me as his unsurpassed enemies, who has the power to give sovereignty to Bharata, O chastiser of foes?"
"I am genuinely devoted with my whole being to my brother, O queen — I swear to you by truth, by my bow, and by the sacrificial offerings I have made."
"If Rāma enters a blazing fire or the wilderness, know me, O queen, as having already entered there before him."
"I shall remove your sorrow by my valor, as the risen sun disperses darkness — let the queen behold my prowess, and let Rāghava behold it."
Having heard these words of the great-souled Lakṣmaṇa, Kausalyā, weeping and distracted with grief, spoke to Rāma.
"My son, you have heard what your brother Lakṣmaṇa has said — do accordingly whatever follows from that, if it pleases you."
"And you ought not to depart from here, leaving me scorched with grief, after hearing the unrighteous words spoken by my co-wife."
"O knower of dharma, if you are righteous and wish to practice dharma, then serve me, remaining here — practice the highest dharma."
"Serving his mother, my son, Kaśyapa, dwelling restrained in his own home, endowed with the highest austerity, attained the three heavens."
"Just as the king is to be honored by you with reverence, so too am I — I do not give you permission; you must not go to the forest from here."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Without you, life holds no purpose for me, nor happiness — with you beside me, even eating grass is my greater good."
"If you go to the forest leaving me here consumed with grief, I shall sit here in a fast unto death — I shall not be able to live."
"Then you, my son, shall attain the hell renowned in the world, just as the lord of rivers, the ocean, receives the sin of brahminicide through unrighteousness."
Then the righteous-souled Rāma spoke words suffused with dharma to his mother Kausalyā, lamenting thus in her misery.
"I have no power to transgress my father's word — I bow my head and beseech you: I wish to go to the forest."
"Even the learned sage Kaṇḍu, practitioner of vows, while carrying out his father's command — knowing dharma — slew a cow."
"And in our own lineage of old, by the Sāgaras who dug at their father Sagara's command, a most great destruction was accomplished."
"By Rāma Jāmadagnya, carrying out his father's command, his own mother Reṇukā was herself slain with an axe in the forest."
"This adherence to a father's command is not being done by me alone — this path, intended by the ancients, is being followed in their footsteps."
"This therefore must be done by me on earth, and no otherwise — for one who carries out his father's word never comes to diminishment."
Having thus addressed his mother, he spoke again to Lakṣmaṇa: "I know, Lakṣmaṇa, your unsurpassed love for me, though the purport of truth and of tranquility has not been understood."
"For dharma is supreme in the world; truth is grounded in dharma; and this highest word of my father rests upon dharma."
"Having pledged to a father's word, or a mother's, or a Brāhmaṇa's, one standing firm in dharma must not make it vain, O hero."
"I am not able to transgress my father's command — for it is by my father's word, O hero, that Kaikeyī has sent me forth."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Therefore abandon this ignoble resolve rooted in the dharma of warriors, take refuge in dharma, set aside harshness — let my counsel be followed."
Having thus spoken out of affection to his brother, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa spoke again to Kausalyā, with joined palms and bowed head.
"Grant me permission, O queen, as I go to the forest from here — I swear to you by my life: perform the auspicious rites for me; having fulfilled my vow, I shall return again from the forest to the city."
"For I am not able to bring about great prosperity behind the back of renown merely for the sake of the kingdom in a short while — nor, O queen, do I today choose a lesser earth through unrighteousness over life."
That bull among men, still intent on going to the Daṇḍaka forest by his own valor, propitiating his mother, and then firmly instructing his younger brother, made a final appearance, circumambulated his mother in his heart, and took his leave.
Then, seeing him afflicted with anguish, intensely indignant, breathing like a mighty serpent, his eyes dilated with fury —
— Rāma, self-possessed, steadying his composure with fortitude, approached Saumitri, that dear friend and beloved brother, and spoke these words:
"O Saumitri, let the bustle of preparations that was made for my consecration now serve instead for the reversal of that consecration.
She whose heart is being tormented on account of my consecration — that mother of ours — act in such a way that she may have no further cause for anxiety.
I cannot bear, O Saumitri, to disregard even for a moment the grief born of apprehension that has arisen in her heart.
I do not recall having ever done, intentionally or unwittingly, even the slightest thing displeasing to my mothers or to my father.
My father, who is truthful, steadfast in his truth-pledges, ever of true valor — may he who fears the sin of falsehood in the next world be freed from fear.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
For if this act is not carried through, his heart would burn with the torment that his pledge of truth was not honored — and his torment would in turn torment me.
Therefore, O Lakṣmaṇa, having set aside the rite of consecration, I wish straightaway to depart to the forest from this very place.
Once I am banished today, that king's daughter will have achieved her purpose, and then she will consecrate her son Bharata without impediment.
When I have gone to the forest clad in bark garments and deerskin, wearing matted locks, Kaikeyī's heart will be at peace.
That by which this resolve has been directed and the mind fully composed — that I ought not to trouble; I shall go forth without delay.
In my banishment and in the return of the kingdom that was granted to me — fate alone, O Saumitri, is to be seen at work.
For how could Kaikeyī have come to act in such a way as to cause me harm, were this not the disposition of fate, ordained by the god of death?
For you know, O gentle one, that there was never any distinction in my regard for my mothers, nor any special difference in hers toward me, her child.
Therefore, that she should have spoken to me those harsh, bitter words aimed at annulling the consecration and at banishment — I attribute this to nothing other than fate.
How could a princess of such natural nobility, possessed of such qualities, have spoken in the presence of her husband of my humiliation, as though she were a common woman?
That fate which is inscrutable cannot be prevented even among living beings — clearly, a reversal has befallen both her and me.
Who, O Saumitri, can venture to fight against fate, whose workings in any action can be grasped by nothing other than itself?
Pleasure and pain, fear and anger, gain and loss, existence and non-existence — whatever is thus constituted, is that not indeed the work of fate?

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Even though my consecration has been thwarted, I feel no grief. Therefore, free from grief yourself and following my lead, quickly withdraw the preparations for the consecration rite.
O Lakṣmaṇa, in this obstruction of my kingship, the younger mother is not to be overly blamed — for those overtaken by fate speak of unwished things; and you know well the power of fate to work thus.
While Rāma was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa repeatedly hung his head low; hearing these words, he felt himself pulled between grief and fierce resolve.
Then, O bull among men, he knitted his brows together, and breathed hard — like a great serpent coiled in its den, enraged.
His face, set with that fearsome frown, was then unbearable to behold — resembling the visage of a lion roused to wrath.
He who was unconstrained, shaking like an elephant shaking its own trunk, let his neck drop sideways and upward across his body —
— and looking at his brother askance from the corners of his eyes, he said: "This very great agitation of yours has arisen in the wrong place.
How could a man of your stature speak such things composedly, when the world would not so readily suspect fault in dharma?
Why do you, a bold bull among kṣatriyas, praise fate as though it were cowardly? Why do you invoke pitiful, impotent fate?
O righteous one, how is it that you harbor no suspicion of those two sinful ones? There are subtle tests of dharma — do you not perceive them?
The consecration of another in your place — which the world would hate — is what has led your mind to this confusion, O lord of the earth. That very dharma by whose invocation you are bewildered is hateful to me.
Even if your resolve is of divine origin and their opinion carries weight, still, the fact that you would overlook this — that does not please me either.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
One who is faint-hearted and bereft of valor submits to fate; heroes who hold their souls in high esteem do not merely worship fate.
A man who has the power to overcome fate by his own exertion does not sink down when his purpose is ruined by fate.
Today they shall see the power of fate and the power of a man; today the distinction between the divine and the human will be made manifest.
Today people shall see fate struck down by my valor, just as today we have seen your royal consecration struck down by fate.
Just as a maddened elephant running rampant beyond the goad is turned back, so I shall turn back fate by my own exertion.
Not all the guardians of the worlds together could obstruct Rāma's consecration today — nor could all three worlds — much less a father alone.
Those who have secretly conspired for your exile to the forest, O king — they shall dwell in the forest likewise for fourteen years.
I shall cut off that hope of your father and of her — the hope that works through obstructing your consecration so that a son may become king.
Faced with my power in opposition, the force of fate shall not be able to prevail to cause harm in the way my own fierce exertion shall.
After a thousand years, once the duty of ruling over the people is fulfilled, the noble-born sons shall perform the forest-dwelling themselves — after you have already gone.
For according to the way of former royal seers, forest-dwelling is prescribed — entrusting the people to one's sons to be cared for as children.
O king, if out of fear that the kingship might be disrupted by a divided mind you do not wish to hold the kingdom in yourself, O Rāma, O righteous one —
— then I pledge to you, O hero — may I forfeit my place in the world of heroes — I shall guard your kingdom as the shore guards the ocean.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Be consecrated with auspicious rites; be engaged in that alone. I alone am capable of holding back by force all the kings of the earth.
These two arms of mine are not for adornment; the bow is not worn by me for decoration; the sword is not bound on for show; the arrows are not for display.
All these four — arms, bow, sword, and arrows — serve me for the crushing of enemies; nor do I have excessive desire for what I regard as hostile.
With my sharp-edged sword, blazing like leaping lightning, I count as no foe even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself.
The ground before me, dense and hard to traverse, shall be strewn with the trunks, thighs, and heads of elephants, horses, and men — crushed and pressed by my sword's blows.
Today, struck by my sword's edge, elephants shall fall to earth blazing like mountains — like clouds falling with their lightning.
With my leather finger-guard strapped on and my bow taken up, how could anyone count himself a true man among men while I yet stand?
Surpassing many enemies as one, and many as if they were one, I shall release my arrows into the vital points of men, horses, and elephants.
Today the power of my weapons shall make itself felt — to strip the king of his sovereignty and to establish your sovereignty, O master.
Today — for the sake of sandalwood paste and the loosening of armlets, for the bestowal of wealth, and for the protection of friends —
— these two arms of mine shall do fitting work, O Rāma, in warding off those who are responsible for the obstruction of your consecration.
Tell me — who is your enemy, that he may this very day be separated from me, from life and glory? Command me as you see fit so that this earth may come under your sway; I am your servant.
Wiping away his tears and consoling Lakṣmaṇa again and again, he who was the enhancer of the Rāghava line said: "Know me as one firmly set in our father's command — this, O gentle Saumitri, is the true path."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing him steadfastly intent on fulfilling his father's decree, Kausalyā, choking with tears, spoke righteous words.
"One who has never known sorrow, righteous in soul, beloved in speech to all living beings — born of Daśaratha and of me — how shall he live by gleaning?
He whose own servants and slaves eat the finest prepared food — how shall that lord subsist in the forest on roots and fruits?
Who would believe this, hearing it? And for whom would fear not arise — that Rāghava, virtuous and beloved of the king, is being banished?
Bereft of you, the immeasurable great fire of grief shall consume me, as the bright-flamed fire consumes dry grass at the end of winter.
For how could a cow not follow her own calf when it departs? I shall follow you, O son, wherever you go.
Having heard those words spoken thus by his mother, Rāma, that bull among men, spoke in reply to his deeply grieved mother:
"Deceived by Kaikeyī, and with me gone to the forest, and abandoned by you as well, the king surely will not survive.
The abandonment of one's husband is said to be a cruelty peculiar to a woman — that you must not do, condemned even in thought.
As long as my father, the Kākutstha, lord of the earth, still lives — serve him; that is the eternal dharma.
Thus addressed by Rāma, the fair-visaged Kausalyā replied "So be it" with full willingness to Rāma the tireless in action.
Thus addressed, Rāma, foremost among the upholders of dharma, once more spoke these words to his deeply grieved mother:
"Both you and I must do our father's bidding — the king is husband, teacher, most excellent, the lord and master of all.
Having passed these fourteen years in the great forest, I shall return in supreme gladness and shall abide by your word.
Thus addressed, her face filled with tears, her heart consumed with anguish, Kausalyā, that devoted mother, then spoke to her beloved son:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"It is not possible for me to dwell among these co-wives, O Rāma. Take me too, O Kākutstha, to the forest, like a doe of the wild — if your mind is resolved on going, in deference to your father.
To her weeping thus, Rāma, himself in tears, replied: "For a living woman, her husband is the deity and the master — today the king is master, lord over both you and me.
And Bharata too, righteous in soul, dear in speech to all creatures, will attend to you — for he is always devoted to dharma.
Act vigilantly so that, after my departure, the king may not suffer even the slightest affliction through grief for his son.
A woman, however supremely excellent, who is devoted to vows and fasts but does not follow her husband's path — even she incurs a sinful fate.
She should render service alone, devoted to the beloved welfare of her husband — this is the dharma seen of old in the world, heard in the Veda, and remembered in the Smṛtis.
O queen, on my account you should honor the brāhmaṇas and those of excellent vows — and thus wait out the time, longing for my return.
You shall attain your supreme wish when I return — if the foremost of those who uphold dharma, the king, shall hold on to life.
Thus addressed by Rāma, her eyes clouded with a rush of tears, Kausalyā, afflicted by the sorrow for her son, spoke to Rāma: "Go, my son, single-minded; may you ever be blessed, O lord."
Thus indeed, seeing Rāma resolved upon forest-dwelling, the queen with her highest mind spoke words to Rāma of auspicious marks, and she became one who longed to perform rites of benediction over him.
Having performed her ablutions and touched the pure water, putting aside that distress, Rāma's wise and noble mother performed the auspicious rites.
May the Sādhyas, the Viśvas, the Maruts, and the great seers bestow well-being; may Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Aryaman bestow well-being.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
May the seasons, the fortnights, the months, the years, the nights, the days, and the hours always bring you well-being.
May Memory, Fortitude, and Dharma protect you on all sides, my son; and may the divine lord Skanda, Soma, and Bṛhaspati protect you.
May the Seven Seers and Nārada protect you on all sides; may all the lunar mansions and the planets together with their presiding deities protect you, the wise one clad in an ascetic's garb as you roam the great forests.
May jumping creatures, scorpions, biting insects, mosquitoes, reptiles, and all manner of bugs in the dense forest cause you no harm.
May the great elephants, lions, tigers, bears with their fangs, and the fierce horned buffalo do you no harm, my dear son.
May the terrible beings who feed on human flesh, and whatever other kinds of creatures there may be, do you no injury, my son — for I have duly propitiated them here.
May your journeys be auspicious; may your feats of valor be accomplished; may all prosperity attend you, Rāma. Go in safety, my son.
May there be well-being for you again and again from the celestial regions and from the earthly regions; from all the gods, and from those who obstruct your path.
May Brahmā, the lord of all worlds, the sustainer of all beings, along with the sages and the remaining gods, protect you as you dwell in the forest.
With these words, that illustrious wide-eyed woman honored the hosts of gods with garlands, perfumes, and fitting hymns of praise.
Whatever auspiciousness arose for the thousand-eyed Indra, saluted by all gods, at the slaying of Vṛtra — may that same auspiciousness be yours.
Whatever auspiciousness Vinatā fashioned long ago for Suparṇa — Garuḍa — when he was seeking the nectar of immortality, may that auspiciousness be yours.
Kausalyā also fashioned a protective charm using the efficacious and auspicious herb Viśalyakaraṇī, and muttered the appropriate sacred formulas over it.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Bowing, smelling his head, and embracing him, that illustrious woman said: "Go comfortably, Rāma, my son, your purposes fulfilled."
"May I see you again, my dear child, returned to Ayodhyā healthy, all your aims accomplished, dwelling happily and well established in the royal palace."
"The bands of gods headed by Śiva, the great seers, the beings, great asuras, and serpents that I have honored — may they and all the directions long desire your welfare, O Rāghava, as you depart for the forest."
Having spoken thus with eyes brimming with tears, and having duly completed the benedictory rites, she circumambulated the Rāghava and again and again pressed him tightly in her embrace.
Having thus been circumambulated by the queen, and having pressed his mother's feet again and again, that great-glorious Rāghava, blazing with his own splendor, departed for the dwelling of Sītā.
Having reverenced Kausalyā, Rāma set out for the forest, blessed with the auspicious rites performed by his mother, steadfast on the path of righteousness.
The prince, illuminating the royal road crowded with people, seemed to churn the hearts of the assembled folk by the sheer power of his virtues.
The afflicted Vaidehī had heard none of all this, for in her heart there was only the expectation of Rāma's consecration as crown prince.
Having performed her worship of the gods, that grateful and joyful woman, well versed in the duties of royalty, awaited the prince.
Then Rāma entered his own beautifully adorned dwelling, filled with joyful attendants, his face cast slightly downward out of shame.
Then Sītā sprang up and beheld her husband trembling — scorched by grief, his senses disturbed by anxious thoughts.
Seeing his face pale and streaming with perspiration, beside himself with agitation, and herself scorched by grief, she said: "What is this now, my lord?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Today, O Rāghava, the auspicious Puṣya asterism is in conjunction with Bṛhaspati — so declare the learned Brāhmaṇas. Why then are you downcast?"
"Your lovely face is not graced, as it should be, by the royal parasol with its hundred ribs, white as the foam of water, held above it."
"Your face, whose eyes resemble the lotus, is not being fanned by the two principal fly-whisks, white as the moon and the swan."
"O bull among men, the eloquent bards and panegyrists — the Sūtas and the Māgadhas — are not seen today joyfully singing your praises with auspicious hymns."
"The Brāhmaṇas who are masters of the Veda are not placing honey and curds upon your head in the prescribed manner, as upon one who has had the consecration poured over him."
"All the ministers of state, adorned with ornaments, and the heads of the guilds, together with the townspeople and the country folk, do not seem to wish to accompany you."
"Why does the chief ceremonial chariot, yoked to four swift horses adorned with golden ornaments, not go before you?"
"Nor is the auspicious, mark-honored elephant, dark as a rain cloud or a mountain, seen going before you in the procession, O hero."
"Nor do I see the golden, ornately decorated throne being carried ahead of you, O fair to behold, with heroes marching before it."
"When the consecration was ready, what has now happened to you? Your complexion is unprecedented, and no exhilaration is visible in you."
To her lamenting thus, the delight of the Raghu clan spoke: "Sītā, the revered lord — my father — is sending me into exile in the forest."
"O Jānakī, born of a great lineage, one who knows righteousness and walks in its ways, listen to how this has come about step by step."
"My father King Daśaratha, a man of true vows, once gladly granted two great boons to Kaikeyī."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Now, today, when the king had made ready my consecration, she has called in that old debt; that appointed time has been invoked and compelled by dharma."
"I must dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest for fourteen years; my father has also installed Bharata as crown prince. I have come to see you before I depart for the uninhabited forest."
"You should never speak of me in Bharata's presence. Men who have attained power cannot endure praise of a rival; therefore my virtues should not be spoken of before Bharata."
"Nor should you ever be treated by him as a special charge; you can comport yourself near him only with compliance and agreeableness."
"I too, honoring that promise made to my elder, shall depart for the forest this very day. Be steadfast, O wise one."
"And when I have gone to the forest frequented by sages, O auspicious one, O sinless one, you must be devoted to vows and fasts."
"Rising early in the morning and performing the worship of the gods in the prescribed manner, you must pay reverence to Daśaratha, my father, the lord of men."
"And my mother Kausalyā, aged and worn thin by grief, deserves your respect, placing dharma above all else."
"You must always revere my other mothers as well, for in terms of affection, tenderness, and the enjoyment of my company, they are all equal to my mother."
"And Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, who are dearer to me than my own life, are to be regarded by you especially as sons and brothers alike."
"And you must never do anything disagreeable to Bharata, for he is now the king and lord both of the realm and of the family."
"Kings who are gratified by good conduct and attended upon with effort become gracious; in the contrary case they grow wrathful."
"Kings abandon even their own natural sons if they act against their interests, and embrace even ordinary people who serve them capably."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I shall depart for the great forest, my dear; you must remain here, O beautiful one. So that you do no wrong to anyone, act in accordance with these words of mine."
Thus addressed, Vaidehī — who deserved only tender words and spoke only tender words — became indignant out of deep love, and spoke these words to her husband.
"O noble son, a father, a mother, a brother, a son — and likewise a daughter-in-law — each enjoys the fruits of their own merit and tends to their own separate destiny."
"But a wife, O bull among men, partakes solely of her husband's fortune. Thus it is I who have been destined to dwell in the forest as well."
"Neither a father, nor a son, nor one's own self, nor a mother, nor a circle of friends — in this world and after death, the husband is ever the sole refuge of women."
"If you depart today for that inaccessible forest, O Rāghava, I shall go before you, crushing underfoot the sharp kuśa grass and thorns."
"Setting aside jealousy and anger as one sets aside water left over after a meal, take me with you without apprehension, O hero — no sin resides in me."
"Whatever the condition — whether in palace towers, or aerial mansions, or traveling through the sky — the shadow of a husband's feet excels them all."
"I have been instructed by my mother and my father in conduct befitting all manner of circumstances; I need not now be told how I should comport myself."
"I shall dwell happily in the forest just as in my father's house, giving no thought to the three worlds, but thinking only of my vow to my husband."
"Ever attending upon you, self-disciplined, and observing the vow of chastity, I shall take delight with you, O hero, in the honey-fragrant forests."
"For you, Rāma, are able to protect in the forest the people of others — how much more so me, O giver of honor."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I shall subsist always on fruits and roots, without doubt. Living with you, I shall cause you no hardship."
"I long to see the rivers, the mountains, the lakes, and the forests everywhere, fearless in every place, with you, my wise lord, as my protector."
"I would wish, made happy by union with you, O hero, to behold the lotus pools thronged with geese and kāraṇḍava ducks, their lotuses in full and beautiful bloom."
"With you, O large-eyed one, I shall take the greatest delight — and thus I could dwell with you for a hundred thousand years."
"And if my abode, O Rāghava, O tiger among men, were to be even in heaven but without you, I should not desire that either."
"I shall go to the forest most difficult to traverse, filled with deer, inhabited by monkeys and elephants; I shall dwell in the forest as in my father's house, clasping your very feet, honored by you."
"Take me — whose mind is set on none other, whose heart cleaves to you alone, who am resolved on death if separated from you. Do this kindness, grant my entreaty; no burden shall thereby fall upon you from me."
Yet even as she spoke thus, that best of men, attached to righteousness, did not intend to take Sītā; and he spoke to her at length, on the subject of dissuasion, and concerning the hardships of dwelling in the forest, addressing her in her distress.
As Sītā spoke thus, that knower of dharma, devoted to righteousness, that righteous soul, spoke these words to turn her back.
"Sītā, you are born of a great lineage and are ever devoted to dharma. Practise your own duty here — do not act merely as your heart desires."
"Sītā, you must act as I shall tell you, O gentle one. The forest holds many hardships; hear me speak of them."
"Sītā, abandon this resolve to dwell in the forest. What is called the wilderness is full of many dangers."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I say this out of concern for your welfare: the forest knows no happiness — it is nothing but misery at every turn."
"The roars of lions dwelling in mountain caves, rising from mountain torrents — these are dreadful to hear. For this reason, the forest is suffering."
"One must sleep on leaf-beds, broken and spread on the bare ground, weary from exertion through the nights. For this reason, the forest is yet harder to bear."
"Fasts must be kept, O Maithilī, as one's strength allows; matted locks must be worn, and garments of bark must be borne."
"There the wind is fierce, the darkness deep, and hunger constant; great terrors abound — for this reason, the forest is harder still."
"Many reptiles of many forms, O passionate one, crawl boldly over the ground. For this reason, the forest is very hard to endure."
"Serpents that dwell in rivers, winding through their bends, lie coiled across the paths. For this reason, the forest is harder to bear."
"Locusts, scorpions, worms, horse-flies and mosquitoes together torment one ceaselessly, O gentle one. All of it is suffering — therefore the forest is misery."
"Thorny trees, and kusa grass and kāśa reeds, with their branch-tips tangled in the forest, O passionate one — for this reason the forest is harder to endure."
"Therefore, enough of going to the forest. The forest is not fit for you. Considering it carefully, I see the forest as full of many faults indeed."
But even after the great-souled Rāma resolved not to take her to the forest, Sītā paid no heed to his words. Then, deeply distressed, she spoke to Rāma thus.
Hearing Rāma's words, Sītā, stricken with grief, her face streaming with tears, spoke these words slowly.
"The hardships you have named regarding life in the forest — know that I regard all of them as virtues, offered forth by your love for me."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I must go with you — such is the command of my elders. Without you, Rāma, I must give up this life here."
"Standing at your side, O Rāghava, not even Śakra, lord of the gods, could overpower me by his might."
"A woman bereft of her husband cannot live — such is the very truth, Rāma, that you have yourself shown me."
"And besides, O greatly wise one, I once heard from brāhmaṇas, truly, in my father's house, that I am destined to dwell in the forest."
"Hearing the words of those auspicious twice-born sages at home, O mighty one, I have ever since felt a keenness for living in the forest."
"That sojourn in the forest, so foretold, must come to me — and there, beloved, I shall go with you alone, no other way."
"The prophecy shall be fulfilled — I shall go with you. Now the time has come; let the brāhmaṇa's word prove true."
"I know well that in forest-life, many kinds of suffering are surely encountered by men of undisciplined spirit, O hero."
"And as a girl in my father's house, I heard of forest-dwelling from a wandering ascetic woman of virtuous conduct, here in the presence of my mother."
"You have been entreated in many ways before, O lord — for the journey of forest-dwelling together with you is what I have longed for."
"I am ready and resolved for the journey, O Rāghava — bless you! The wandering life of the forest, proper to a hero, is pleasing to me."
"O pure-souled one, following my husband out of love, I shall be free of all sin — for a husband is my very deity."
"Even in the life after death, union with you is auspicious for me — so runs the holy scripture that is heard from the illustrious brāhmaṇas."
"O greatly wise one, a woman who has been given by her parents to a man here in this world with the rite of water and in accord with dharma — she belongs to him even in the afterlife."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Given all this, for what reason do you not wish to take me — your own wife, of good conduct and devoted to her husband?"
"You ought to take me, O Kākutstha — devoted, faithful to my vow, helpless, equal in joy and in sorrow — one who shares equally in happiness and grief."
"If you do not wish to take me, thus wretched, to the forest, then I shall resort to poison, fire, or water as the cause of my death."
Even as she pleaded with him in many ways for permission to go, the mighty-armed Rāma did not consent to taking her into the desolate forest.
Spoken to in this way, Maithilī fell into deep anguish, and the hot tears flowing from her eyes seemed to drench the earth.
As she brooded thus, the self-composed Kākutstha consoled Vaidehī at length, even as she was overcome with anger, trying to turn her away from her resolve.
But even while being consoled by Rāma, Maithilī, daughter of Janaka, spoke these words to her husband in order to go to the forest.
Deeply agitated, Sītā embraced broad-chested Rāghava out of both affection and wounded pride.
"What must my father, Vaideha, lord of Mithilā, have thought of you, Rāma — a son-in-law who has a woman's form in the shape of a man?"
"False and ignorant is what the world will say — that there is no supreme valour in Rāma — when he blazes like the sun in the sky."
"What have you done to make you downcast? Or whence comes the fear that makes you wish to abandon me who have no refuge but you?"
"Know me, O hero, to be like Sāvitrī who was devoted to Satyavat, son of Dyumatsena — wholly devoted to you, under your authority alone."
"I have never looked upon another man, even in my mind, O sinless one. How could I go without you, O Rāghava, like a woman who dishonours her family?"
"And yet, Rāma, you yourself wish to hand me over to others — your wife, taken in youth, long cohabited with, chaste — as a stage-dancer might his own."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Without taking me, you should not set out for the forest. Whether it be penance, wilderness, or heaven — all is to be with you."
"There will not be any hardship for me on the path, following behind you, whether in the places of wandering or in sleeping."
"The kuśa grass, kāśa reeds, śara rushes, and thorny trees along the way — to me, travelling with you, their touch will be as soft as cotton or hide."
"The dust that a great wind will scatter upon me, O beloved, I shall regard as the most precious sandalwood paste."
"Resting on the grassy meadows at the forest's edge, familiar with the forest, on beds spread with kuthā grass — what could be more pleasant than that?"
"Whatever leaf, root, or fruit you yourself gather and give me — whether little or much — that will be like the taste of nectar to me."
"There I shall not think of my mother, nor my father, nor the house, as I enjoy the seasonal flowers and fruits."
"There you shall not see anything unpleasant on my account; there will be no sorrow for you because of me, nor shall I be a burden to you."
"Where you are is heaven; where you are not is hell — knowing this supreme love of mine, go, Rāma, with me."
"But if you will not take me — thus calm and resolved — to the forest, I shall this very day drink poison. I will not fall under the power of your enemies."
"Even thereafter, life abandoned by you in sorrow is no life at all, O lord — death at that very moment is better."
"This grief I cannot bear even for a moment — how much less, wretched, for thirteen years?"
Thus she, scorched by grief, having lamented piteously and at length, clung tightly to her husband, weeping aloud in her anguish.
Pierced by many sharp words as a she-elephant by poisoned arrows, she released the tears long suppressed, like fire released from the araṇi wood.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Water clear as crystal, born of her anguish, flowed from her two eyes as water flows from two lotuses.
Embracing her in his arms — she who was grief-stricken and as if unconscious — Rāma then spoke words of reassurance.
"O goddess, I do not desire even heaven purchased by your suffering. I have no fear from any quarter, like Svayambhū himself."
"Without knowing your full mind, O fair-faced one, I did not wish to dwell in the forest — even though I am capable of protecting you."
"Since you were created to share forest-dwelling with me, O Maithilī, you cannot be forsaken by me — as a self-respecting man cannot forsake his honour."
"The dharma practised of old by the good — that I follow today, O elephant-gaited one, as Suvarcalā follows the sun."
"This is dharma, O fair-hipped one — to be subject to one's father and mother. Having transgressed their command, I cannot bear to live."
"I wish to conduct myself as my father instructs me, he who stands firm on the path of truth and righteousness — for that is eternal dharma. Follow me, O timid one; be my companion in dharma."
"Give jewels to the brāhmaṇas and food to the mendicants; give to those who seek — and make haste, do not delay."
Learning that her husband's departure and her own journey were now agreed, the goddess Sītā, joyful, swiftly set about giving gifts.
Then she, elated and with heart full of joy, the illustrious and noble-minded woman, heeding her husband's words, set about giving wealth and jewels to those who uphold dharma.
Then the great-spirited Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who stood before him ready to go forward, a hero entreating with palms joined together.
"O Saumitri, when you depart with me today into that forest, who will support the illustrious Kausalyā and Sumitrā?"
"The great-spirited king, who showered upon them their desires even as rain-clouds shower upon the earth, is now bound fast in the noose of passion."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For she, the daughter of King Aśvapati, having now obtained this kingdom, will not deal kindly with her co-wives who are in distress."
Having been addressed thus by Rāma with gentle words, Lakṣmaṇa — skilled in speech — then replied to that master of eloquence.
"By your very glory alone, O hero, Bharata will with devotion honour both Kausalyā and Sumitrā — of this there is no doubt."
"The noble Kausalyā could sustain even a thousand men like me, for she has the revenue of a thousand villages to live upon."
"Bearing bow and arrows, carrying a spade and a basket, I shall go ahead of you, pointing out the path."
"I shall constantly gather for you roots and fruits, and whatever other forest foods are the natural sustenance of ascetics."
"While you take delight with the Vaidehī on mountain slopes, I shall do everything for you, whether you are awake or asleep."
Rāma, greatly pleased by these words, replied to him: "Go take leave, O Saumitri, of all our dear friends."
"And the two divine bows of fearful aspect which the great-souled Varuṇa himself gave to King Janaka at the great sacrifice —"
"— the two divine, impenetrable coats of armour, two quivers with inexhaustible arrows, and two swords pure as the sun and adorned with gold —"
"— all this was reverently deposited in the preceptor's house. Go quickly, Lakṣmaṇa, and bring those weapons here."
He, resolute for forest life, took leave of his dear ones and of the preceptor of the Ikṣvāku line, and then took up those supreme weapons.
Saumitri, the tiger among princes, displayed all those divine, duly honoured, garland-adorned weapons to Rāma.
The self-controlled Rāma, with affection, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa who had arrived: "You have come at the right time, O gentle Lakṣmaṇa, when I was longing for you."
"O scorcher of foes, I wish to distribute this wealth of mine — together with you — to the brāhmaṇas and ascetics."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The most excellent twice-born who dwell here with steadfast devotion serving the elders — and especially to all who depend on me for their livelihood."
"Quickly bring here the noble Suyajña, son of Vasiṣṭha, foremost among the twice-born; for I shall depart to the forest after honouring all the other venerable brāhmaṇas as well."
Then, having learned his brother's most auspicious and beloved command, he went quickly and entered the dwelling of Suyajña.
Saluting that brāhmaṇa who was standing by the sacred fire, Lakṣmaṇa said: "Come, dear friend; behold the home of him who performs difficult deeds."
Then, after quickly completing the twilight devotions, he went together with Saumitri and entered that charming abode of Rāma, graced with prosperity.
With palms joined together, Rāghava, together with Sītā, approached the arrived Suyajña — knower of the Vedas — as one approaches a consecrated fire.
With splendid bracelets and earrings of pure gold, together with golden thread-necklaces, jewels, armlets, and bangles,
— and with many other gems — the Kākutstha honoured Suyajña; and then Rāma, prompted by Sītā, spoke to him.
"Convey, O gentle one, this necklace and golden thread to your wife; and now Sītā wishes to give you, dear friend, this girdle as well."
"The Vaidehī also desires to bestow upon you this couch with its excellent coverlet adorned with manifold gems."
"The elephant named Śatruṃjaya which my maternal uncle gave me — that elephant, worth a thousand common elephants, I give to you, O bull among the twice-born."
Thus addressed by Rāma, Suyajña accepted all that and pronounced auspicious blessings upon Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā.
Then Rāma, sweet of speech, spoke these words to his dear and composed brother Saumitri, even as Brahmā might address Indra, lord of the thirty gods.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Invite both Agastya and Kauśika, those two most excellent brāhmaṇas, O Saumitri, and honour them with jewels as rain bestows blessings on crops."
"And the one who devotedly attends on Kausalyā with blessings — the teacher of the Taittirīyas, handsome and learned in the Vedas —"
"— give to him, O Saumitri, a carriage, female servants, and silk garments — as much as may satisfy that brāhmaṇa."
"The noble charioteer Citraratha, a trusted minister of long standing — gratify him too with precious gems, garments, and wealth."
"And prepare also, O Saumitri, a thousand loads of fine rice, two hundred auspicious ones, and a thousand cows to be used for relish."
Then that tiger among men, Lakṣmaṇa, himself distributed that wealth to the foremost of brāhmaṇas just as instructed, even as Kubera the wealth-giver.
Then, after bestowing abundant goods upon each of his dependants who stood there with tears in their eyes, he spoke to them.
"Both Lakṣmaṇa's house and this house of mine are to be kept each one occupied and not left empty, until my return."
Having spoken thus to all those grieving dependants, he said to the treasurer: "Let the wealth be brought here." Thereupon all his dependants brought all his wealth.
Then that tiger among men, together with Lakṣmaṇa, caused that wealth to be distributed to the twice-born, to children and the aged, and to the destitute.
There was among them a tawny-eyed brāhmaṇa of the Gārgya lineage named Trijaṭa; no one barred him up to the fifth enclosure.
Approaching the prince, Trijaṭa spoke these words: "O prince of great renown, I am without wealth and have many sons; I live by gleaning grain in the forest — please look after me."
Then Rāma spoke to him with gentle humour: "Not even one of a thousand cows has yet been distributed by me; however far you throw your staff, that far shall you receive."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He hastily and excitedly wrapped his cloth tightly round his waist, then whirling his staff hurled it with all the force of his might.
Then Rāma spoke, reassuring that scion of the Gārgyas: "Do not be angry — for this was but a jest of mine."
Then the great sage Trijaṭa, together with his wife, joyfully received the herd of cattle and in return offered to the great-souled one blessings that swelled with fame, strength, joy, and happiness.
Having distributed abundant wealth to the brāhmaṇas together with the Vaidehī, the two Rāghavas set out together with Sītā to see their father.
Then, with those terrible-to-behold weapons taken up and adorned by Sītā with garlands and strings of flowers, the two shone resplendent.
Then the prosperous people, climbing the palaces, mansions, and the pinnacles of towers, looked on with sorrowful detachment.
For the streets thronged with so many people that it was impossible to pass through them; hence they climbed the palaces and in grief watched Rāghava.
Seeing Rāma proceeding on foot without his royal umbrella, the people, their hearts stricken with grief, uttered many diverse words.
"He whom a great four-division army used to follow when he went forth — now only Lakṣmaṇa follows that one alone, together with Sītā."
"He who knows the taste of sovereignty and who is the fulfiller of desires for those who desire, yet he does not wish to render his father's word false, out of reverence for dharma."
"Sītā, who could not be seen even by beings moving through the sky, is today seen by the people who have come into the royal road."
"Sītā, accustomed to body-unguents and to the use of red sandalwood paste, will quickly be discoloured by rain, heat, and cold."
"Surely today Daśaratha speaks under the sway of some other force — for a king ought not to banish a beloved son."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"How could there be banishment even of a son without virtues? — and how much more of him who has won the entire world by his conduct alone?"
