"Non-cruelty, compassion, learning, good character, self-control, and tranquillity — these six virtues adorn Rāghava, the most excellent of men."
"Therefore, by the affliction done to him, the subjects are sorely tormented, like water-creatures in summer when the waters dry up."
"The entire world is afflicted by the affliction of this lord of the world, just as a fruit- and flower-bearing tree is afflicted by the striking of its root."
"Let us quickly follow, together with our kin, even as Lakṣmaṇa does — following where Rāghava goes."
"Abandoning our gardens, our fields, and our houses, sharing in one sorrow and one joy, let us follow the righteous Rāma."
"Our treasuries dug up and emptied, our courtyards ruined, our grain and wealth taken, stripped of all substance —"
"— our houses covered with dust, abandoned by the gods, deserted by us — let Kaikeyī have them."
"Let the forest where Rāghava goes become the city; and let this city, abandoned by us, become a forest."
"Let all the fanged beasts take to the lairs and the mountain slopes to the deer and birds; and what we abandon — let them inhabit what was frequented, and abandon what was abandoned."
Rāma heard all these diverse words uttered by people of every kind; and having heard them, his mind was not shaken.
Waiting for those kinsfolk who were suffering, yet himself appearing without distress and almost smiling, Rāma went forward, wishing to see his father and to fulfil his father's command in due order.
Before that, the great-souled son of the Ikṣvāku line, Rāma, about to depart for the forest, paused on seeing Sumantra there, intending to use him as an intermediary to his father.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The Rāghava, devoted to dharma and with his resolve firmly fixed on entering the forest in accordance with his father's command, looked at Sumantra and said: "Announce my arrival to the king."
Sent swiftly by Rāma, his senses clouded with grief, the charioteer entered and found the king sighing deeply.
Seeing the king's mind utterly distraught and lamenting for Rāma alone, the greatly wise charioteer sat down with folded hands.
"This son of yours, tiger among men, stands at the door, having distributed wealth to the brāhmaṇas and to all who depend upon him."
"May Rāma of true valor see you — may it be well with you; having taken leave of all his friends, he now desires to behold you."
"He is about to depart for the great forest — behold him, O lord of the earth, encircled by all the qualities of a king, as the sun is encircled by its rays."
That king — truthful, righteous in soul, deep as the ocean, spotless as the sky — answered him.
"Sumantra, bring me all my wives who are here; surrounded by all my consorts I wish to behold Rāghava."
Passing into the inner apartments, he spoke to those women: "The noble king summons you — go there without delay."
Thus addressed by Sumantra on the king's command, all the women set out for that dwelling, heeding their lord's decree.
Those seven hundred and fifty women of copper-red eyes, firm in their vows, surrounding Kausalyā, moved forward slowly.
When his wives had arrived, the lord of the earth surveyed them and said to the charioteer: "Sumantra, bring me my son."
The charioteer then swiftly led Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Maithilī before the lord of the earth.
The king, seeing his son approaching from afar with joined hands, leapt swiftly from his seat in anguish, surrounded by the women.
The lord of the people rushed toward Rāma with speed; before he could reach him, stricken with sorrow, he fell to the ground in a swoon.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāma rushed quickly to him, and so did the great warrior Lakṣmaṇa — to the king who lay as though senseless, overwhelmed with grief.
A wail arose from a thousand women throughout the royal palace — the cry "Alas, Rāma!" suddenly overwhelmed by the clamor of their ornaments.
Both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa embraced him with their arms and, weeping, laid him together with Sītā upon his couch.
Then, after a moment, when the lord of the earth had regained consciousness — inundated in an ocean of grief — Rāma spoke to him with joined hands.
"I take leave of you, great king — you are the lord of us all; behold me, who am about to depart for the Daṇḍaka forest, and send me off with your blessing."
"Grant leave also to Lakṣmaṇa, and to Sītā who follows me into the forest — though dissuaded with many true reasons, neither of them is willing to desist."
"Grant leave to all of us — Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, and me — setting aside your grief, O giver of honor, as Prajāpati gives leave to his creatures."
As Rāghava waited patiently for the leave-granting of the lord of the earth, the king gazed upon him and spoke of the forest-dwelling.
"I, O Rāghava, have been deluded by the boon-gift of Kaikeyī; restrain me now and yourself become king of Ayodhyā this very day."
Thus addressed by the king, Rāma — best among upholders of dharma, skilled in speech — replied to his father with joined hands.
"You are lord of the earth for a thousand years, O king; I shall dwell in the forest. No falsehood need be done by you on my account."
"For your welfare and prosperity, dear father, and for my return hereafter — go in peace, undisturbed, by a path free from all danger."
"But do not go this very night at all, my son; seeing your mother and me, spend this night here; gratified in all your desires, you may set out at dawn."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Rāma, having heard thus the words of his grief-stricken father, spoke sorrowfully to his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
"Whatever merits I may acquire today, who will grant me those same ones tomorrow? Therefore I choose departure itself over all pleasures."
"Let this earth — with its kingdoms, its people, abundant in wealth and grain, relinquished by me — be given over to Bharata."
"Let your grief depart; do not be overwhelmed with tears; for the invincible ocean, lord of rivers, is not disturbed."
"I desire neither kingship, nor comfort, nor even Maithilī — I desire only your truth, not untruth, O bull among men."
"The city, the kingdom, and the whole earth — relinquished by me — let them be given to Bharata; I, honoring your command, shall go to the forest to serve it for a long time."
"Let Bharata govern this earth — relinquished by me — with its mountain ranges, its cities, and its forests, auspicious and well-bounded; only let what you have said, O king, stand as it is."
"My mind is not so fixed on great pleasures, O king, nor even on what is dear to myself, as it is on fulfilling your command approved by the righteous — let your sorrow on my account depart, O sinless one."
"Therefore today I would choose neither the imperishable kingdom, nor all pleasures, nor comfort, nor Maithilī, nor even life itself, so as to involve you in falsehood — let your vow of truth remain so."
"Eating fruits and roots in the forest, beholding mountains, rivers, and lakes, entering the forest with its manifold trees, I shall be content — may you find peace."
Then the scion of Ikṣvāku, tormented by this pledge, breathing in deep sighs with tears, spoke again and again.
"Charioteer, let an army of the fourfold force, richly furnished with gems, be swiftly prepared to escort Rāghava."
"Let graceful courtesans of excellence, and merchants of great wealth, spread out and adorn the prince's retinue."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Those who depend upon him and those with whom he delights to display his valor — assign them here too, after giving them manifold gifts."
"Hunting deer and elephants, drinking the wild honey of the forest, beholding the various rivers, he will not remember the kingdom."
"Whatever treasury of grain and treasury of wealth I possess — let both follow Rāma as he dwells in the desolate forest."
"Performing sacrifices at sacred places, distributing gifts with fitting fees, and meeting with sages, he will dwell happily in the forest."
"Long-armed Bharata shall protect Ayodhyā; may glorious Rāma be fully provided with all that he desires and then return."
As the scion of Kākutstha spoke thus, fear came upon Kaikeyī; her face grew parched and her voice choked.
Dejected and fearful, Kaikeyī spoke: "O virtuous one, a kingdom emptied of its people, like wine from which the cream has been drunk, utterly tasteless and barren — Bharata will not accept such."
When Kaikeyī spoke thus, utterly shameless, in the most cruel manner, King Daśaratha said to her of the wide eyes: "Why do you torment me, harnessing me to a yoke not fit to bear?"
Kaikeyī, doubly enraged, said this to the king: "In your own lineage, Sagara obstructed his eldest son — known as Asamañja — and so this one also deserves to go."
Thus addressed, King Daśaratha only exclaimed "Shame!" and all the assembled people were mortified — but she took no heed of this.
There an aged chief minister, Siddhārtha by name, pure in conduct and highly regarded by the king, said this to Kaikeyī.
"Asamañja, seizing children to play with along the path and flinging them into the waters of the Sarayū — this wicked-minded one amused himself thus."
"Seeing this, all the citizens, enraged, said to the king: choose between Asamañja alone and us, O increaser of the realm."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The king then said to them: what is the cause of this fear? And the subjects, questioned by the king, spoke their grievance."
"'This one, out of his senses, snatches our young children to play with and out of folly casts them into the Sarayū, enjoying incomparable delight.'"
"Hearing the words of his subjects, O lord of men, Sagara abandoned that harmful son, wishing to do what was dear to them."
"Thus the most righteous king Sagara indeed abandoned his son. What sin has Rāma committed, that he should be obstructed in this manner?"
Hearing the words of Siddhārtha, the king — his voice still more exhausted — spoke thus to Kaikeyī in a voice afflicted by grief.
"I shall follow Rāma today, abandoning the kingdom, comfort, and wealth; together with King Bharata, enjoy the kingdom at leisure for a long time as you please."
Having heard the words of the minister, Rāma then addressed Daśaratha, versed in courtesy, speaking in a courteous manner.
"For me who have renounced enjoyments, O king, living in the forest on forest fare, who have relinquished all attachments — what need is there of an escort?"
"For one who has given away the finest elephant and then sets his mind upon the halter-rope — what use is that rope's attachment to one who has relinquished the finest elephant?"
"So for me likewise, O best among the righteous, O lord of the earth — what use is an army? I renounce everything; let only bark-cloth garments be brought for me."
"Bring also a spade and a basket for me as I depart; I shall dwell in the forest for fourteen years."
Then Kaikeyī herself fetched bark-cloth garments and, shamelessly, before the multitude, said to Rāghava: "Put these on."
That tiger among men accepted the bark-cloth from Kaikeyī, laid aside his fine garment, and put on the ascetic's dress.
Lakṣmaṇa too, right there, setting aside his auspicious garments, took on the hermit's covering before his father.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Sītā — clad in silk — gazed at the bark-cloth meant for her own wearing, trembling like a doe caught in a snare.
Receiving it as if with shame, downcast in heart, she said to her husband — who was like the king of gandharvas: "How do the sages who dwell in the forest tie the bark-cloth?"
She, the daughter of Janaka, unskilled in this and ashamed, draped one strip of bark-cloth around her neck and held another in her hand, and stood there not knowing how to proceed.
Coming quickly to her, Rāma — best among upholders of dharma — himself tied the bark-cloth over Sītā's silk garment.
As she who had a protector was being dressed in bark-cloth as if she had none, all the people cried out: "Shame upon you, Daśaratha!"
Sighing a hot breath, the scion of Ikṣvāku said to that wife: "Kaikeyī, Sītā does not deserve to go clad in kusa-bark."
"Is not the banishment of Rāma itself enough of a sin for you, wicked woman? What need of these further wretched transgressions committed by you?"
Even as his father spoke thus, Rāma — already setting out for the forest — spoke these words to him who sat with his head bowed down.
"This Kausalyā — righteous, illustrious, my mother, aged and of noble character — let her not be held in contempt by you in an act censured by the gods."
"O giver of boons, you must take thought once more for her — bereft of me, plunged into an ocean of grief, facing a misfortune such as she has never known before."
"You must so provide for this my mother — who bore within her a child comparable to great Indra — that, wasting away in grief while I abide in the forest, she does not lay down her life and depart to the realm of Yama."
Having heard Rāma's words and having seen him clad in the garb of an ascetic, the king, together with his wives, lost all consciousness.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Tormented by grief, he could not look upon that Rāghava, nor, gazing at him, could he bring himself to speak — so wretched was he in his mind.
For a moment that lord of the earth, afflicted and senseless, lamented, his great arms hanging limp, his thoughts fixed on Rāma alone.
"Surely in a former life I must have separated many creatures from their young, or else slain living beings — and therefore this calamity has come upon me."
"Yet the life-breath does not depart the body before its appointed hour; even as I am tormented by Kaikeyī, death does not find me."
"I who look upon my own son standing before me, radiant as fire, having set aside his fine garments for the dress of an ascetic —"
"For the sake of one woman alone — Kaikeyī — who strives for her own ends and has resorted to this base deception, all this people suffers."
Having spoken these words, his eyes sealed shut with tears, he uttered once only the name "Rāma" and could speak no more.
After a moment that king of the earth recovered his senses and, with eyes brimming with tears, spoke these words to Sumantra:
"Harness the royal chariot with the finest horses and come; convey this most fortunate one beyond the boundaries of this kingdom."
"Such, I believe, is said to be the fruit of virtue for the virtuous — that a righteous hero is banished to the forest by both his father and his mother."
Understanding the king's command, Sumantra, swift of movement, harnessed the chariot adorned with horses and drove it there.
The charioteer, joining his palms together, announced to the prince that chariot adorned with gold and yoked with the finest steeds.
The king, knowing time and place, quickly summoned the treasurer who was engaged in the management of the treasury and spoke to him clearly, with full resolution.
"Count out the years of her exile and bring quickly the most precious garments and the finest ornaments befitting Vaidehī."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by the king, the treasurer went to the treasury and, having brought everything, gave it all immediately to Sītā.
She who was born of noble lineage, Vaidehī, setting forth for the forest, adorned her graceful limbs with those many-coloured ornaments.
Vaidehī, thus richly adorned, illumined that palace as the radiance of the rising sun illumines the sky at the hour of dawn.
Her mother-in-law embraced her in both arms, kissed her on the crown of the head, and spoke, even as Maithilī showed no sign of despair:
"In this entire world, women who are constantly honoured and pampered by their dear ones do not follow their husbands when they fall upon misfortune — such women are false."
"My son who has been sent into exile must not be slighted by you; whether he be penniless or wealthy, let him be your deity."
Understanding her mother-in-law's words, which were rooted in righteousness and truth, Sītā stood before her, folded her palms, and replied:
"I shall do all that the noble lady instructs me. I know well how one ought to conduct oneself toward one's husband — this I have heard and learnt."
"The noble lady need not count me among ignoble women. I am no more capable of straying from dharma than moonlight is of straying from the moon."
"A vīṇā without its strings does not sound; a chariot without its wheel does not move; a wife does not flourish in happiness without her husband, even if she has a hundred sons."
"A father gives in measure; a mother gives in measure; a son gives in measure — but a husband gives without measure. What woman would not revere such a giver?"
"Being thus, I am the best, well-versed in the highest and lowest teachings of dharma. Noble lady, why should I dishonour my husband? For a husband is indeed the deity of women."
Having heard Sītā's words, which touched the heart, Kausalyā — pure of nature — suddenly shed tears born at once of sorrow and of joy.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Rāma, supremely versed in dharma, drew near with joined palms to his mother who was honoured above all among the mothers, and addressed her:
"Mother, do not grieve. Attend to my father. The period of forest exile will come to an end swiftly."
"The fourteen years will pass for you as if in sleep, and you shall see me returned here, complete, surrounded by friends."
Having spoken these words of well-measured meaning to his mother, he looked and beheld the three hundred and fifty mothers gathered there.
To those mothers, equally distressed, the son of Daśaratha spoke this righteous word with palms joined together:
"Whatever harsh thing has been done by me from living together in close quarters, or from ignorance, please forgive me all of it — and I take leave of you all."
Then, as Rāghava spoke thus, a wail arose from those wives of the lord of men — like the cry of krauñca cranes.
The mansion of Daśaratha, which had once resounded like the rumble of murajas and paṇavas and thunder-clouds, now became utterly wretched, filled with lament and wailing, plunged into calamity.
Then Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa, with joined palms, embraced the king and, pitifully, performed the rite of circumambulation around him.
Having obtained the king's leave, Rāghava, the knower of dharma, dazed with grief, then paid obeisance to his mother together with Sītā.
After his brother, Lakṣmaṇa paid obeisance to Kausalyā, and then in turn clasped the feet of his own mother Sumitrā.
His mother, weeping, wishing his good, kissed Lakṣmaṇa of the mighty arms on the crown of the head as he bowed, and spoke to the son of Sumitrā:
"You were born for this forest sojourn, deeply devoted to those dear to you. Son, be not heedless toward Rāma as your elder brother proceeds on his way."
"Whether he be in adversity or in prosperity, he is your refuge, O sinless one. This is the dharma of the good in this world — to be obedient to one's elder brother."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This is the eternal, fitting conduct of this lineage: giving, consecration in sacrifices, and the offering of one's body in battle."
"Know Rāma as Daśaratha, know me as Janaka's daughter, know the forest as Ayodhyā — go, dear child, at your ease."
Then Sumantra, humble and well-versed in courtesy — as Mātali addresses Vāsava — spoke to that scion of the Kākutstha line with joined palms:
"Mount the chariot — good fortune to you, O prince of great renown. I shall swiftly convey you, Rāma, wherever you direct me."
"For fourteen years are to be spent by you in the forest; those years must now be entered upon, as the queen has urged upon you."
Sītā, that noble lady, adorned herself and then, with a joyful heart, mounted that chariot resplendent as the sun.
Likewise the two brothers placed in the body of the chariot all manner of weapons, their armour, and the leather quivers with their hard casings.
Having seen the three — Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa — mounted, Sumantra boldly urged on the chosen horses, swift as the wind in their speed.
But as Rāghava set out for the great forest for so many long nights, a swoon fell over the city, a swoon fell over the army and the people alike.
That city, thrown into confusion and agitation, resounded with great noise — the trumpeting of frenzied elephants and the jingling of horses.
Then that city — young and old together — stricken with extreme anguish, rushed after Rāma alone, as the heat-parched earth rushes toward water.
Clinging to the sides and the rear of the chariot, all faces turned toward him, their faces filled with tears, all spoke to him in deep distress:
"Hold back the reins of the horses, charioteer — drive slowly, slowly! I would behold Rāma's face, which shall be hard for us to see again."
"Surely the heart of Rāma's mother must be made of iron, since it does not break even as one who is like the offspring of a god goes to the forest."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Vaidehī has truly accomplished her life's purpose — like a shadow she follows her husband, she who is devoted to dharma forsakes him not, as the sun's radiance does not forsake Mount Meru."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, you have achieved your purpose, you who shall attend upon your brother who is ever kind in speech and radiant as a god."
"This indeed is a great achievement for you; this is a great rise of fortune; this is the very path to heaven — that you follow him." So saying, those people could not hold back the tears that had come upon them.
Then the king, his spirit utterly desolate, surrounded by wretched women, came forth from the palace, saying "I will see my dear son."
And ahead of him was heard the great wailing of the women weeping — like the cry of she-elephants when a great bull elephant is bound in chains.
And the father, that glorious king of the Kākutstha line, appeared at that moment stricken and diminished — like the full moon at the appointed time swallowed by a eclipse.
Then a great tumult of wailing arose behind Rāma as the people looked upon the king sinking under his terrible grief.
Some among the people cried "Ah, Rāma!" and others cried "Ah, Rāma's mother!" — and the prosperous inner palace lamented and wept all around.
As Rāma looked back he saw the king — dejected, his mind reeling — and his mother both following along the road; bound by the bonds of dharma, he could not openly look upon them.
Seeing those two who deserved to ride in a vehicle, who deserved no sorrow and were accustomed to happiness, now proceeding on foot, he urged the charioteer: "Drive swiftly!"
For that tiger among men could not endure that painful sight of his father and mother — as an elephant cannot endure the goad.
Again and again he looked back at Kausalyā weeping and running after that chariot, crying "Rāma! Rāma!" and "Ah, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!" — his mother then appeared to him as though she were dancing.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The king cried out "Stop!" while Rāghava called out "Drive on! Drive on!" — and Sumantra's spirit was caught between the two, as between the two wheels of a chariot.
"Even if you are reproached, you can say to the king: 'I did not hear' — for this deception, long the cause of suffering, is the least sinful course," so Rāma spoke to him.
Acting on Rāma's word and taking leave of those people, the charioteer urged on the horses to speed, even as they were already in motion.
The people of the king turned back after circumambulating Rāma — yet in their hearts, and in the rush of their tears, no human being turned back.
"One who wishes him to return should not follow him far" — thus the ministers spoke their word to the great king Daśaratha.
Hearing their words, endowed with every quality, the wretched king — his body bathed in sweat, his appearance sunken — stood still together with his wife, his eyes fixed upon his son.
When that tiger among men departed with his palms joined, a great cry of anguish arose from the women in the inner apartments.
"He who was the resort and refuge of this helpless, weak, and afflicted people — where now does that protector go?"
"He who does not grow angry even when falsely accused, who avoids all occasions of wrath, who appeases those who are wrathful, who regards the suffering of others as his own — where does he go?"
"He of great splendour, that great-souled one, who conducts himself toward us exactly as he conducts himself toward his mother Kausalyā — where does he now go?"
"Urged to the forest by a king tormented by Kaikeyī — he who was the protector of these people and of the world — where does he now go?"
"Alas, the king is without wisdom — Rāma, beloved of all the living world, devoted to dharma and to the vow of truth, will now dwell in forest exile!"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus all those great queens, afflicted with sorrow, wept and wailed aloud, like cows that have lost their calves.
The lord of the earth, already scorched by grief for his son, heard that terrible cry of anguish from the inner apartments and was plunged into yet deeper sorrow.
The sacred agnihotra fires were not kindled; the sun seemed to disappear; elephants dropped their mouthfuls of food; cows did not suckle their calves.
Triśaṅku, the red-limbed one (Mars), Bṛhaspati, and Budha too — all the planets, malefic, drew close to the Moon and stood there in dreadful conjunction.
The nakṣatras lost their radiance and the planets lost their lustre; Viśākhā herself appeared in the sky shrouded in smoke.
Suddenly all the townspeople fell into a state of dejection; no one applied his mind either to eating or to recreation.
The people moving along the royal road had faces clouded with tears; not one person was to be seen with joy — all were given over entirely to grief.
The cool wind did not blow; the moon did not show its gentle face; the sun gave no warmth to the world — the entire universe was thrown into confusion.
Sons indifferent to their mothers, husbands indifferent to their wives, brothers indifferent to their brothers — all, abandoning everything, thought only of Rāma.
Those who were friends of Rāma had all become bewildered in mind; overwhelmed by the weight of grief, they did not then resort to their beds.
Then Ayodhyā, bereft of that great-souled one — as the earth bereft of Indra — shook terribly, oppressed by the weight of fear; her elephants, warriors, and troops of horses all cried out.
As long as the dust-cloud raised by his departure was visible, the lord of the Ikṣvākus kept his own eyes fixed upon it, unable to withdraw them.
As long as the king gazed upon his beloved and supremely righteous son, the earth seemed to swell and rise before him in the sight of that son.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When the lord of the earth could no longer see even the dust of Rāma's chariot, stricken with grief and utterly desolate, he fell to the ground.
Kausalyā, that noble lady, supported his right arm, while Kaikeyī, dear to Bharata, supported his left side.
The king, endowed with statecraft, righteousness, and propriety, looked at Kaikeyī and, his every sense tormented, spoke to her thus.
"Touch not my limbs, O Kaikeyī, you of wicked conduct! I have no wish to see you — you are neither wife nor kin to me."
"Those who depend upon you — I am not theirs, nor are they mine. You who have abandoned dharma in pursuit of mere self-interest — I renounce you."
"Whatever vows I made when I took your hand, whatever acts I performed when we circled the sacred fire — I hereby release all of that, both in this world and the next."
"If Bharata takes pleasure in this indestructible kingdom once he obtains it, let whatever he might offer on my behalf for my funerary rites never come to me."
Then Queen Kausalyā, wasted by grief, lifted up the lord of men who had been cast down and covered in dust, and turned back.
The righteous-souled king burned with remorse — as one who has slain a brahmin out of passion, as one who has touched sacred fire with bare hands — reflecting upon his ascetic son.
Turning back again and again, sinking into despondency on the chariot-path, the king's form shone not at all — like the sun when it is swallowed up in eclipse.
Tormented by sorrow, recalling his beloved son, the king lamented; and understanding that his son had reached the outskirts of the city, he cried out.
"The hoofprints of the finest steeds that bore my son are still visible on the road, yet that great-souled one himself is nowhere to be seen."
"Surely he will take shelter at the root of some tree this very night, and rest his head upon a log or a stone."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"And he will rise pitifully from the earth, smeared with dust, sighing deeply — like a great bull elephant rising from a stream."
"The forest-dwellers will surely behold long-armed Rāma, the lord of the world, rising and walking as though he were lordless and without refuge."
"Rejoice in your desire, O Kaikeyī! Rule the kingdom as a widow — for without that tiger among men, I cannot bring myself to live."
Thus lamenting, the king, surrounded by a throng of people, entered that finest of cities — like one who has bathed without performing the obligatory rites after an ill omen.
Its crossroads and inner courts were deserted; its shops and shrines were shuttered; its people were weary, weak, and grief-stricken; its great thoroughfares were no longer crowded.
Surveying the entire city and thinking only of Rāma, the lamenting king entered his palace as the sun enters a cloud.
The palace, bereft of Rāma, of Vaidehī, and of Lakṣmaṇa, was like a great deep lake, once unagitated, whose serpent has been carried off by Suparṇa.
"Take me quickly to the home of Kausalyā, Rāma's mother" — so saying, the king was led by the doorkeeper to her dwelling.
Having entered Kausalyā's apartments and even having mounted his couch there, his mind remained utterly distraught.
Seeing that, the great king, valiant though he was, raised his arm and cried aloud in a loud voice: "Ah, Rāghava! You have abandoned me!"
"Blessed indeed will those best of men be at that time — they shall live in happiness, embracing Rāma upon his return!"
"I do not see you, Kausalyā — touch me kindly with your hand. My eyes have followed after Rāma and even now will not come back."
Seeing the lord of men lying on the couch thinking only of Rāma, the queen sat beside him, her form utterly overcome with anguish, and she lamented with sighs and great difficulty.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Kausalyā, herself tormented by grief for her son, looked at the lord of the earth who had sunk upon his couch in sorrow, and spoke to the great king.
"O tiger among men, Kaikeyī, having sown her poison like a two-tongued serpent, will now roam freely — like a serpent that has shed its skin."
"Having exiled Rāma, that fortunate woman has achieved her desire and, composed, will continue to terrify me again and again — like a vicious serpent within the house."
"Better it would have been for Rāma to remain in the city begging for alms and living in our home than to grant his stepmother's wish — even if it meant his becoming her servant."
"Having toppled Rāma from his rightful place as she desired, Kaikeyī has assigned the share — as it were — to the rākṣasas, like sacrificial oblations cast into fire at a lunar rite."
"That hero with the gait of a lordly elephant, long-armed, bearing his bow — surely he has entered the forest now, accompanied by his wife and together with Lakṣmaṇa."
"By your consent to Kaikeyī's command, you have abandoned to forest-exile those who have never known hardship — what will become of them in the forest?"
"Those tender ones, stripped of every gem and jewel, banished in the fruiting season — how will they live pitifully, subsisting on fruit and roots?"
"Will that auspicious time ever come — the end of my grief — when I may behold Rāghava here once more, together with his wife and his brother?"
"On the very news of those two heroes' arrival — when will Ayodhyā again be glorious, its people rejoicing, adorned with tall raised banners?"
"When, beholding those two tigers among men returned from the forest, will the city rejoice with delight — as the ocean rejoices at the full moon?"
"When will that long-armed hero enter the city of Ayodhyā, placing Sītā before him on the chariot — as a bull leads the cow at his side?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"When will thousands of living beings strew parched grain upon those two tamers of enemies, my sons, as they enter along the royal road?"
"When will the maidens, bearing flowers and the fruits of the twice-born, cheerfully circumambulate the city in their joy?"
"When will he — matured in wisdom and in years, radiant as the cāmara white yak-tail fan — he who knows dharma, approach me playfully as if he were a child of three?"
"Doubtless, O hero, I believe that in a former life I must have cruelly severed, out of wretched selfishness, the breasts of mother animals from their suckling young."
"And now I, loving and devoted, have been made childless — like a cow bereft of her calf by a lion, O tiger among men — as Kaikeyī has forcibly taken my young calf."
"For I, who have but one son — one so endowed with virtues and learned in all the śāstras — I cannot bring myself to live without my son."
"For me, not seeing my beloved son — long-armed and of great strength — there is no reason for this life to continue."
"This fire of grief for my son, having arisen, consumes me — as the blessed sun in the hot season scorches this earth with his blazing rays."
But as that foremost of noble women Kausalyā lamented thus, Sumitrā — herself steadfast in dharma — spoke to her these words befitting dharma.
"O noble lady, your son is endowed with all good qualities — that best of men. What purpose is served by your lamenting thus, by your pitiful weeping?"
"O noble lady, your son of great might has gone — having renounced the kingdom — doing right by his great-souled father who had given his word in truth."
"Rāma stands firm in that dharma which the virtuous have ever rightly practiced, which yields its fruit in the life beyond — he is the foremost of men and is never to be mourned."
"And Lakṣmaṇa, ever sinless and compassionate toward all beings, serves that great-souled one in the noblest manner — he has gained great good fortune through this."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Vaidehī, though accustomed to comfort and well aware of the hardships of forest life, follows your son, the soul of righteousness — this too speaks of his greatness."
"The lord who waves as his banner throughout the world the flag that is his very glory, who is devoted to self-restraint, truth, and sacred vows — what has your son not already attained?"
"Knowing Rāma's purity and his supreme greatness, the sun himself surely would not dare to scorch his body with his rays."
"Auspicious at all times, blowing forth from the forest groves, the gentle wind — pleasantly cool, neither too cold nor too warm — will attend upon Rāghava."
"As Rāma sleeps at night, the moon — embracing the sinless one as a father would — will refresh him, touching him with its cool rays."
"And Brahmā himself bestowed divine weapons upon him of great might, having seen him slay in battle Timi's banner-son, the lord of the Dānavas."
"That bull among men, Rāma, will soon be consecrated together with these three — the earth, Vaidehī, and royal Śrī — as his companions."
"The tears of sorrow you now shed gazing upon him as he departed — from those same eyes you will quickly shed tears of joy."
"Seeing your son bow to you in greeting, surrounded by his beloved companions, you will quickly shed tears of gladness — like a rain-cloud of the monsoon season."
"Your boon-granting son will swiftly return to Ayodhyā and press your feet with his own soft and full hands."
Hearing those words of Lakṣmaṇa's mother, spoken to the mother of Rāma, the queen consort of the lord of men — immediately the grief in her body dissolved, like an autumn cloud diminished of its water.
The people, deeply devoted to that great-souled Rāma of true valour, followed him as he set out for his forest sojourn.
Even when the king and the circle of his friends were forcibly turned back, those who had followed Rāma's chariot would not themselves return.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
For to the men dwelling in Ayodhyā, that one of great fame, endowed with every virtue, was as dear as the full moon.
That descendant of Kākutstha, though entreated by his own subjects, held true his word to his father and went on into the forest.
Gazing upon them with affection, drinking them in as it were with his eyes, Rāma addressed those subjects with the tenderness one shows one's own children.
"The love and high regard that you, the residents of Ayodhyā, bear toward me — let that be especially directed to Bharata for my sake.
He is of auspicious conduct, the increaser of Kaikeyī's joy, and he will duly accomplish all that is pleasing and beneficial to you.
Though young in years, he is mature in wisdom, gentle in nature, endowed with the virtue of valour — he will be a worthy lord for you and a remover of all fear.
He has been recognized as a crown prince furnished with every royal virtue. And moreover, it is your duty, as men of good conduct, to follow the command of your lord.
And the great king must not grieve when I have gone into the forest — see to it so, I pray you, out of your desire to please me."
The more that son of Daśaratha stood firm in righteousness, the more his subjects desired him as their lord.
Rāma, together with Saumitri, seemed to draw back that wretched, tear-veiled populace by the bonds of his virtues, as if drawing them again to their seats.
Those brāhmaṇas, aged in the threefold manner — by knowledge, by years, and by vigour — their heads trembling with age, called out from a distance these words:
"Ho, ho, O swift horses of noble breed that carry Rāma — turn back, you must not go on! Be loyal to your lord: your lord is one to be borne forward, not to be borne away from the city to the forest!"
Beholding those aged brāhmaṇas lamenting in such anguished cries, Rāma suddenly descended from the chariot.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He then went on foot, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma placing his steps close to the ground, his course set upon the forest.
That Rāma, devoted to righteous conduct, compassionate of eye, could not bear to pass those brāhmaṇas who went on foot by riding ahead in his chariot.
Seeing him walking on nonetheless, their minds overwhelmed with distress, those brāhmaṇas, utterly anguished, addressed this speech to Rāma:
"All this entire brāhmaṇa community, devoted to brāhmaṇical conduct, follows you; even these sacred fires, borne upon the shoulders of brāhmaṇas, follow you.
Behold these parasols, earned through the Vājapeya sacrifice, following behind us like a flock of geese at the season of floods.
For you who have no parasol of your own and are scorched by the sun's rays, we shall make shade with these our Vājapeya-won parasols.
The mind of ours that was ever devoted to following the Vedic hymns — for your sake, dear child, that mind has now made itself devoted to following you into the forest.
The Vedas, which are our highest wealth, abide within our hearts; and our wives, guarded by their own virtue, will remain in our houses.
We shall make no further calculation about your going — our minds are nobly resolved. And when you yourself disregard dharma, what value is there in attending to dharma?
O man of self-restrained conduct, we implore you — turn back — by these our heads with hair white as swans, bowed down and grey with the dust of prostrations upon the earth.
The many sacrifices of the brāhmaṇas who have come here are spread out and begun; their completion, dear child, depends upon your return.
All creatures, both moving and unmoving, are filled with devotion to you. When these devotees implore you, show your devotion to your devotees.
These trees, unable to follow you, raised high by the force of their roots, are crying out as it were, driven by the rush of the wind.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Even the birds, motionless, having ceased eating and moving, fixed each upon a single tree, are beseeching you, O compassionate one to all beings."
As those brāhmaṇas cried out thus imploring him to return, the river Tamasā appeared there as if blocking the way of Rāghava.
Then Rāghava, having reached the beautiful bank of the Tamasā, looked up at Sītā and spoke these words to Saumitri:
"This is the first night, O Saumitri, since we set out for the forest. Good fortune in this forest sojourn — you must not be sorrowful.
See how the forests seem to weep on every side, as the deer and birds draw near to their respective shelters and settle there.
Today the city of Ayodhyā, my father's royal capital, will grieve for our departure, men and women alike — of that there is no doubt.
Bharata, who is truly righteous of soul, will comfort my father and my mother with words encompassing dharma, artha, and kāma.
Reflecting again and again upon Bharata's compassionate nature, I do not grieve for either my father or my mother, O Lakṣmaṇa.
You, O tiger among men, have done what had to be done by following me; for the sake of protecting Vaidehī, help must be sought.
But I shall pass this night, O Saumitri, on water alone — this pleases me, even though a variety of forest food is available.
Having spoken thus to Saumitri, Rāghava also addressed Sumantra: "Be vigilant, O gentle one, in attending to the horses," he said.
Sumantra, having attended to the horses, and when the sun had set, having given them abundant fodder, stood close by in readiness.
After the auspicious twilight had been duly observed and night had come, the charioteer, together with Saumitri, prepared Rāma's bed.
Seeing that bed made of tree-leaves on the bank of the Tamasā, Rāma lay down upon it together with his wife and with Saumitri.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing his brother thus fallen fast asleep with his wife, Lakṣmaṇa recounted to the charioteer the manifold virtues of Rāma.
For Saumitri, keeping vigil through that entire night and recounting the virtues of Rāma to the charioteer on the bank of the Tamasā, the sun rose.
At a distance from the Tamasā whose banks were crowded with herds of cattle, Rāma passed that night there together with his people.
Rising up, that one of great splendour, having observed those subjects, spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, he of auspicious marks:
"See, O Saumitri, these people who have abandoned all concern for us and even for their own homes are now fast asleep at the roots of the trees, O Lakṣmaṇa.
The manner in which these citizens are making a vow to prevent our return — they will forfeit their very lives rather than abandon their resolve.
While they are yet asleep, let us swiftly mount the chariot and depart upon the road where no fear comes from any quarter.
Hereafter again let these devoted residents of the Ikṣvāku city not sleep at the roots of trees on my account.
For it is the duty of princes to free their citizens from self-incurred suffering; certainly the people of the city must not be made to suffer through one's own actions."
Lakṣmaṇa replied to Rāma, who stood there like righteousness personified: "This pleases me, O greatly wise one — let us mount at once."
The charioteer then quickly harnessed the chariot with those finest of horses and, with joined palms, reported to Rāma that it was ready.
For the purpose of confusing the citizens, Rāma spoke these words to the charioteer: "Mount the chariot and drive northward, O charioteer.
Drive swiftly for a moment, then turn the chariot about and return; do this attentively so that the citizens do not discover me."
The charioteer, having heard Rāma's command, did exactly so, and having returned, reported the chariot to Rāma.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāghava, with all his equipment, mounted that chariot and crossed the swift-flowing river Tamasā with its eddying whirlpools.
Having crossed over, that long-armed and glorious one reached the great road — auspicious, thornless, and without fear for those who fear.
But when night had brightened into dawn, those citizens, without Rāghava, were stunned by grief, motionless, their minds stricken.
Their faces wasted with tears born of grief, looking here and there, those wretched ones could not catch even a glimpse of Rāma.
Then, having followed the road for a little while, overwhelmed by great despondency at the loss of the trail,
those nobly-minded men turned back at the loss of the chariot's tracks, saying: "What is this? What shall we do, struck down as we are by fate?"
Then, by the very same road by which they had come, with exhausted hearts, they all went back to Ayodhyā, the city whose good people were afflicted with grief.
For the city-dwellers who had followed Rāma and now turned back, their inner beings seemed to have departed, leaving them spiritless.
Each arriving at his own dwelling, surrounded by his children and wife, all shed tears with faces veiled by weeping.
Merchants neither rejoiced nor conducted their trade; their wares held no lustre; householders did not cook.
A man who had lost his wealth felt no grief upon seeing a great windfall of riches; a mother who had obtained her first-born son felt no joy.
In house after house women wept and, in their anguished grief, reproached their husbands who had come home, goading them with words as one goads elephants.
"What use are their houses to those who do not see Rāghava? What use are wives, or wealth, or sons, or even pleasures?
There is but one true man in this world — Lakṣmaṇa — who together with Sītā follows Kākutstha Rāma, serving him in the forest.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Blessed are those rivers, those lotus ponds and lakes, in whose pure waters Kākutstha will immerse himself and bathe.
The lovely forest glades, the great marshy rivers, and the mountains with their peaks will make Kākutstha radiant.
Whatever forest or mountain Rāma approaches, none of them will be able to receive him without honouring him, as though a beloved guest had arrived.
The mountains, adorned with garlands of varied flowers and bearing abundant clusters of blossoms, will out of compassion display to Rāma as he comes even the finest flowers and fruits out of season.
The trees on the mountain peaks, revealing manifold and wondrous waterfalls again and again, will delight Rāghava.
Where Rāma is there is no fear; there is no defeat there — for he is a hero, long-armed, and the son of Daśaratha.
"Before he has gone too far, let us follow Rāghava — the shade of the feet of such a great-souled lord is a sweet comfort; for he is this people's lord, their refuge, and their final resort."
"We women shall attend upon Sītā; you men shall attend upon Rāghava" — thus the women of the city, consumed by grief, spoke various such words to their husbands.
"Rāghava will provide your welfare and security in the forest; Sītā will provide welfare and security for the women folk."
Who could find contentment in this disagreeable, joyless habitation, with its people pining and longing, their minds stolen away?
If the kingdom should be under Kaikeyī's sway — unrighteous and without a true protector — then we have no use for life, let alone for sons or wealth.
She who has abandoned both her son and her husband for the sake of power — that Kaikeyī, the disgrace of her lineage — whom else would she spare?
We shall never dwell in the kingdom as hirelings of Kaikeyī — we swear this by our very lives and by the lives of our children!

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
She who mercilessly sends the son of the king of kings into exile — that unrighteous, wickedly acting woman — who could live happily under her sway?
For the lord of the earth will not survive when Rāma has gone into exile; when Daśaratha dies, clearly devastation will follow.
"Those of you whose merit is exhausted and who are truly wretched — drink poison mixed and prepared, or follow Rāghava, or go where you will never hear of him again."
Rāma has been wrongfully sent into exile, together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa; we have been handed over to Bharata like animals to a butcher.
The women of the city, lamenting thus, cried out in fierce anguish as though at the approach of death.
Those women, afflicted on Rāma's account, wept and lamented helplessly as though their own son or brother had been sent away — for he had become dearer to them than their own sons.
Rāma too, that tiger among men, keeping his father's command ever in mind, covered a great distance through the remaining hours of the night.
As he journeyed on in this way, the auspicious night passed away; having duly observed the auspicious twilight rite, he pressed onward to the border of the realm.
Beholding villages with their far-flung boundaries and flowering forests, he sped swiftly past, as if borne by arrows, on those excellent horses.
He heard the words of the people dwelling in the villages along the way: "Shame on King Daśaratha, who has fallen under the sway of desire!"
"Alas, how cruel is Kaikeyī today — wicked, ever trailing wickedness, harsh, one who has shattered all propriety and pursues a terrible deed!"
"She who sends away into forest exile such a son of the king — righteous, supremely wise, compassionate, and ever diligent!"
Hearing these words of the people who dwelt in the villages, that hero, the lord of the Kosalas, passed beyond the land of Kosala.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, having crossed the river named Vedaśruti, whose waters are auspicious and wholesome, he set out toward the quarter once inhabited by the sage Agastya.
Having traveled for a long while, he then crossed the river Gomatī, whose waters are cool, whose banks are rich with cattle and meadows, and which flows down to the ocean.
And having passed beyond the Gomatī, Rāghava, with his swift-footed horses, crossed the river Syandikā, which resounds with the cries of peacocks and geese.
Rāma pointed out to Vaidehī that prosperous land, encircled by the kingdom, which was once granted to Ikṣvāku by King Manu in the days of old.
Repeatedly addressing the charioteer as "sūta," that glorious bull among men, his voice deep and resonant as a swan in rut, spoke thus:
"When shall I come back again and roam in sport through the flowering forest along the Sarayū, reunited with my mother and my father?"
"I do not overly crave the hunt in the forest of the Sarayū — yet this pleasure is peerless in the world and is esteemed by the assemblies of royal sages."
Thus that scion of Ikṣvāku journeyed on, addressing his charioteer in a sweet voice, speaking one thought after another as each came to his mind.
Having traversed the wide and lovely lands of Kosala, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, that mighty-armed one, drew near to the city of Śṛṅgaverapura.
There Rāghava beheld the divine Gaṅgā, flowing across three paths, her waters auspicious and free of algae, holy and frequented by sages.
She was filled with the clamor of swans and sāras cranes, the cooing of cakravāka birds; she was frequented by śiṃśumāra dolphins, crocodiles, and serpents.
Gazing upon her, swirling with eddies set in motion by her waves, that great warrior spoke to the charioteer Sumantra: "Here we shall encamp today."
"Not far from the river stands this great iṅgudī tree, laden with many blossoms and tender shoots — let us stay right here, O charioteer."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Both Lakṣmaṇa and Sumantra replied "So be it" to Rāghava, and thereupon drove the horses up to that iṅgudī tree.
Rāma, that joy of the Ikṣvāku line, approached that lovely tree and descended from the chariot together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa.
Sumantra too alighted, and having unharnessed those excellent horses, stood before Rāma who had seated himself at the foot of the tree, with hands joined in reverence.
There lived a king named Guha, a dear friend of Rāma and equal to him in spirit, born of the Niṣāda people, powerful, and renowned as the lord of that territory.
Hearing that Rāma, that tiger among men, had arrived in his territory, he came forward surrounded by his elders, ministers, and kinsmen.
Seeing the lord of the Niṣādas standing at a distance, Rāma together with Saumitri went forward and met with Guha.
Guha, filled with grief, embraced Rāghava and said: "Rāma, this land is as Ayodhyā to you — what may I do for you?"
Then, having gathered food and eatables of excellent quality in great variety, he quickly brought the honorific offering of arghya as well, and spoke these words:
"Welcome, O mighty-armed one! This whole earth is yours; we are your servants and you are our lord — graciously rule over our kingdom."
"Food to chew, food to eat, drink, and things to lick — all stand ready; and the finest beds are prepared, and fodder for your horses."
To Guha as he was still speaking, Rāghava replied: "We are honored and gladdened by you in every way."
Squeezing him with both his well-formed arms — both on account of his coming on foot and as a display of affection — he spoke these words:
"It is my good fortune to see you, Guha, in good health together with your kinsmen. Is all well with you in your kingdom, among your friends and in your wealth?"
"As for all that you have prepared out of affection, I accept it — yet I do not stand in need of receiving gifts."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Know me to be one who wears kuśa grass and bark-cloth garments, who subsists on fruits and roots, devoted to dharma, an ascetic whose range is the forest."
"I desire nothing but fodder for the horses — by this much alone shall I be well honored by your good self."
"For these horses are beloved to the king, to my father Daśaratha — by having these horses well cared for shall I be truly honored."
Guha then straightway commanded his men right there: "Let both water and fodder for the horses be brought at once!"
Then, with his upper garment of bark-cloth, having duly attended the evening twilight rite, he took only water as his meal — the food was fetched by Lakṣmaṇa himself.
As he lay upon the ground together with his wife, Lakṣmaṇa washed his feet, and then, drawing near, stood leaning against the tree.
Guha too, together with the charioteer, conversing with Saumitri, kept vigilant watch over Rāma through the night, bow in hand and alert.
Thus, as that wise and glorious great-souled son of Daśaratha lay resting — he who had never known suffering, accustomed to comfort — that night passed slowly away.
Guha, burning with anguish, spoke to Rāghava — addressing Lakṣmaṇa, who kept watch without pretense for the sake of his brother:
"Dear friend, this comfortable bed has been prepared for your sake — rest well upon it, O prince, at your ease."
"All these people are accustomed to hardship; it is you who are accustomed to comfort. We shall keep watch through the night for the protection of Kākutstha."
"There is no one on earth dearer to me than Rāma — I speak this truth, and by truth itself I swear it to you."
"By his grace I hope for supreme fame in this world, for abundant attainment of dharma and for the sole attainment of wealth."
"Therefore I shall guard my dear friend Rāma as he sleeps with Sītā, bow in hand, together with my kinsmen on all sides."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Nothing in this forest is unknown to me, who roam here constantly — indeed we could withstand even a very great fourfold army."
Lakṣmaṇa then replied to him: "Being guarded by you, O sinless one, who ever have dharma in view, we have nothing here to fear."
"How could I obtain sleep, or life, or pleasures, when the son of Daśaratha lies upon the bare ground together with Sītā?"
"Behold him who could not be overpowered in battle by all the gods and asuras together — now lying comfortably on the grass with Sītā."
"This one son of Daśaratha, who was obtained by sacred rites, austerities, and various efforts, possessing every auspicious mark — he alone."
"With him gone into exile, the king will not live long — the earth will surely become widowed very soon."
"The women, exhausted with weeping, having cried out with a great lament, have fallen silent — I believe the king's palace has grown quiet, dear friend."
"Kausalyā, and the king, and likewise my own mother — I do not hope that all of them will survive this night."
"My mother might yet live, sustained by care from Śatrughna — yet it is grief that Kausalyā, the mother of this hero, shall perish."
"That city, filled with devoted people, offering delight and joy to those who behold it, now touched by the calamity of the king, shall perish."
"Gone, utterly gone — without having fulfilled his heart's desire, without having installed Rāma in the kingdom, my father shall perish."
"Those whose purpose is accomplished — when that hour arrives and the king has passed — shall perform all the funerary rites and consecrate the lord of the earth."
"With its lovely squares and intersections, its great highways well laid out, adorned with palaces and mansions, graced by the finest of courtesans —"
"— thronged with chariots, horses, and elephants, resounding with the music of instruments, filled with every prosperity, and crowded with cheerful and well-fed people —"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"— rich with pleasure groves and gardens, distinguished by assemblies and festivals — may the happy ones roam through my father's royal capital."
"May we too, safe and sound, enter Ayodhyā together with him of true vow, when this forest sojourn has come to its end."
As the great-souled prince stood there, lamenting and stricken with grief, the night passed fully away.
For as that prince, devoted to the welfare of his people, spoke thus truthfully, Guha, oppressed by calamity and burning with grief out of his deep affection for his master, shed tears — like an elephant tormented by pain.
When the night had brightened into dawn, the great-famed Rāma, standing by the broad trees, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, that one bearing auspicious marks.
"The hour of the sun's rising is come; the blessed night has departed. There, dear one, that dark-plumaged bird, the kokila, calls out."
"The cry of peacocks is heard calling in the forest. Let us cross the Jāhnavī, dear friend — swift-flowing, bound for the ocean."
Understanding Rāma's words, Sumitrā's son, the joy of his friends, took leave of Guha and the charioteer and stood before his brother.
Then, fastening their quivers and girding on their swords, the two Rāghavas, bearing bows, went together with Sītā toward the Gaṅgā.
The charioteer, approaching Rāma — that knower of dharma — humbly with palms joined, said: "What shall I do for you?"
"Turn back" — so he told him — "this much has been done for me. Leaving the chariot behind, we shall go on foot into the great forest."
Then the charioteer Sumantra, distressed to see himself thus dismissed, spoke these words to the tiger among men, the Aikṣvāka prince.
"No one in this world has ever surpassed this — that you, together with your brother and wife, should dwell in the forest like a common man."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I do not think there is any fruit in celibacy, in sacred study, or in gentleness and uprightness, if such misfortune has come upon you."
"Dwelling in the forest with the Vaidehī and your brother, you shall attain a station, O hero, as if conquering the three worlds."
"We are truly ruined, O Rāma, we who have been deceived by her — we shall come under the sway of that sinful Kaikeyī, sharers in sorrow."
Speaking thus, the charioteer Sumantra — so dear to himself as Rāma was — seeing Rāma gone far away, wept long in his grief.
Then, when his tears had subsided, Rāma spoke sweet words again and again to the charioteer, who had touched water and was ritually pure.
"I see no friend equal to you among the Ikṣvākus. Do what must be done so that King Daśaratha does not grieve for me."
"The lord of the earth is stricken in mind by grief, he is old, and he is weighed down by the burden of desire — it is for that reason I say this to you."
"Whatever the great-souled lord of the earth may command, whatever must be done for the sake of gratifying Kaikeyī's wish, do that without hesitation."
"For this purpose do kings rule their kingdoms — that their minds are not thwarted in any of their undertakings."
"So do what must be done, Sumantra, that the great king does not suffer reproach, nor does he faint from sorrow."
"Having saluted him, you should speak these words to the king on my behalf — to that king who has not known such sorrow before, who is old, noble, and master of his senses."
"Neither I grieve, nor Lakṣmaṇa, nor the Maithilī — neither at having been cast out from Ayodhyā, nor at dwelling in the forest."
"Once the fourteen years have passed, you will soon see Lakṣmaṇa, me, and Sītā returned again."
Having thus addressed the king, greet my mother, and the other queens together, including Kaikeyī, again and again.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Convey wishes of good health to Kausalyā and the salutation at her feet — from Sītā, from me, and at the word of the noble Lakṣmaṇa."
"Tell the great king: 'Bring Bharata quickly.' And when Bharata has come, he must be established in the royal office according to the king's wish."
"Having embraced Bharata and consecrated him as crown prince, the sorrow born of grief for us will no longer overpower you."
"Bharata too must be told: 'As you conduct yourself toward the king, so you must conduct yourself toward all the mothers without distinction.'"
"Just as Kaikeyī and Sumitrā are for you without distinction, so too must Queen Kausalyā be honored — she is my mother especially."
Being dismissed by Rāma and emaciated by grief, Sumantra, having heard all those words, spoke out of affection to the Kākutstha.
"Whatever I might say out of devotion and unguarded love — without ceremony, without distress — you must forgive those words of a loyal servant."
"How shall I, bereft of you, return to that city which, dear one, is like one overwhelmed by the grief of losing a son, on account of your separation?"
"When the people saw the chariot with Rāma on it, how will the city bear seeing the chariot now without Rāma — it would shatter at the sight."
"The city will sink into anguish seeing this empty chariot with only the charioteer remaining — like an army that has lost its hero in battle."
"The people, thinking of you dwelling afar yet standing before them in their minds, have surely gone without food today."
"The cry of anguish that the citizens raised at the time of your exile — on seeing me seated in the chariot, they will raise it a hundredfold."
"And what shall I say to the queen — 'Your son has been taken by me to his maternal uncle's house; do not grieve'? How could I say even this?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I would not speak even a falsehood of that kind. And how shall I speak this truth, which is so painful?"
"These excellent horses that serve at my command, that have carried your kinsmen — how will they draw the chariot bereft of you?"
"If you resolve to abandon even me though I beg you, then the moment you forsake me here, I shall enter fire together with the chariot."
"Whatever creatures in the forest might disturb your austerities, I will ward them off with the chariot, O Rāghava."
"The comfort I have gained from the service of the chariot — I aspire now to the comfort of forest-dwelling, done for your sake."
"Be pleased to let me be next to you in the forest. I wish to be told with affection: 'Be next to my lord.'"
"I will with bowed head render service to you, dwelling in the forest. Ayodhyā and the world of the gods — I abandon them both entirely."
"I cannot enter that Ayodhyā without you — just as an evildoer cannot enter the capital of great Indra."
"These horses too, O hero — if they serve you while you dwell in the forest, they will attain the highest state."
"When the period of forest-dwelling has come to an end, this is my heart's desire: to carry you back to the city in this very chariot."
"The fourteen years spent in the forest in your company will pass like a moment; whereas otherwise they would stretch like hundreds of years."
"O lord who loves your servants — one who is devoted, who stands steadfast in his duty, who stands in the path that follows the master's son — you should not abandon me."
When Sumantra begged thus piteously in many ways again and again, Rāma, who was compassionate toward his servants, spoke these words to him.
"I know your supreme devotion toward me, O one devoted to your master. Listen also to the reason why I am sending you back to the city from here."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"When she sees you returned to the city, my younger mother Kaikeyī will gain confidence that Rāma has indeed gone to the forest."
"For when I have gone to dwell in the forest, that queen, being satisfied, would not unduly suspect the righteous king of speaking falsely."
"This is my foremost consideration: that my younger mother should obtain the prosperous kingdom safe under the rule of her son Bharata."
"For my sake and for the king's sake, go to the city with the chariot. And convey the various messages you have been charged with, just as I have told you."
Having spoken thus and comforted the charioteer again and again, Rāma spoke firm and reasoned words to Guha: "I shall make matted locks and go — bring me the sap of the nyagrodha tree."
Guha quickly brought that sap to the prince. With it, Rāma made matted locks for Lakṣmaṇa and for himself.
Then the two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, clad in bark garments and bearing coils of matted hair, shone like sages.
Then, having entered the path of the forest-ascetics together with Lakṣmaṇa and enjoined his vow, Rāma spoke to his companion Guha.
"Be ever vigilant, Guha, in matters of army, treasury, the fort, and the countryside — for a kingdom is held to be the most difficult thing to guard."
Then, having taken leave of Guha, the delight of the Ikṣvākus departed swiftly and undistracted, with his wife and together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing a boat on the bank of the river, the delight of the Ikṣvākus, wishing to cross the swift-flowing Gaṅgā, spoke thus to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Board this waiting boat gently, O tiger among men, and help the noble-minded Sītā on board, holding her close to you."
Hearing his brother's instruction and not opposing any of it, he first helped the Maithilī on board, and then the self-controlled one climbed up himself.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the radiant one, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, himself boarded; after that the lord of the Niṣādas, Guha, urged his kinsmen on.
Having bidden farewell to Sumantra and to Guha along with his forces, Rāma boarded the boat and urged on the boatmen.
Then, urged by them, the boat, steered by the helmsman and driven by the swift strokes of well-crafted oars, quickly crossed the waters.
Reaching the middle of the Bhāgīrathī, the blameless Vaidehī, joining her palms in reverence, spoke these words to that river.
"This son of the wise great king Daśaratha — may he fulfill the command, O Gaṅgā, protected by you."
"Having dwelt in the forest for a full fourteen years with his brother and with me, he will return again."
"Then, O auspicious goddess, having returned safely, I shall joyfully worship you, O Gaṅgā, for the fulfillment of all desires."
"For you, O goddess, flow in three worlds and behold the realm of Brahmā; you are known in this world as the wife of the lord of the ocean."
"I salute you, O goddess, and praise you, O beautiful one, when the tiger among men has returned safely after regaining his kingdom."
"Hundreds of thousands of cows, fine garments, and food — I shall give these to Brāhmaṇas out of my desire to please you."
Speaking thus, the blameless Sītā, turning to the right, quickly reached the right bank.
Having reached the far bank and leaving the boat behind, the bull among men, the scorcher of foes, set forth together with his brother and the Vaidehī.
Then the mighty-armed one spoke to the joy-increaser of Sumitrā: "Go ahead, O Saumitri; let Sītā follow you."
"I shall go behind, guarding both you and Sītā. Today the Vaidehī will come to know the hardship of forest life."
But Sumantra, that wretched one, gazing steadily at Rāma who had quickly crossed to the far bank of the Gaṅgā, with his gaze finally turned back by the distance of the road, shed tears in his anguish.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Those two, having slain four great forest animals there — a boar, a ṛśya antelope, a spotted deer, and a large deer — took the pure meat and, being hungry, quickly went at the proper time to a tree for shelter.
Having reached that tree and performed the evening twilight rite, Rāma, best among those who bring delight, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"This is the first night spent outside the inhabited land, away from Sumantra — you should not be anxious about it."
"From this day forward we must both keep vigil through the nights without slackness, for the safety and well-being of Sītā rests on us."
"Somehow, Saumitri, we shall pass this night, lying down on the ground on what we have gathered ourselves."
Lying down on the earth — he who was accustomed to beds of the highest worth — Rāma spoke these auspicious words to Saumitri.
"Surely the great king sleeps in sorrow tonight, Lakṣmaṇa. But Kaikeyī, having achieved her desire, is fit to be satisfied."
"For that queen Kaikeyī, for the sake of the kingdom, would not even spare the life of the great king — not even when she sees Bharata arrived."
"Helpless, old, bereft of me, and enslaved to desire, come under Kaikeyī's control — what will the king do?"
"Looking at this calamity and at the king's confusion of mind, I think desire is greater than both wealth and dharma."
"For what man, even an ignorant one, would for the sake of a woman abandon a son who follows his wishes — as our father has abandoned me, Lakṣmaṇa?"
"How fortunate Bharata, son of Kaikeyī, must be — with his wife beside him, he alone will enjoy the joyful Kosalas like an overlord."
"For he will be the sole master of the whole kingdom, when our father has passed beyond his years and I have taken refuge in the forest."
"One who abandons wealth and dharma and follows desire alone quickly meets such ruin as King Daśaratha has met."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I believe that Kaikeyī has come to bring about the end of Daśaratha, my banishment, and the kingdom for Bharata, O gentle one."
"I only hope that Kaikeyī, intoxicated by the pride of her good fortune, does not now oppress Kausalyā and Sumitrā on my account."
"Let not Queen Sumitrā suffer grief on my account. You should enter Ayodhyā from here when the time comes, Lakṣmaṇa."
"I alone will go to the Daṇḍakas with Sītā. For you will be the protector of Kausalyā, who would otherwise be without protector."
"For Kaikeyī, given to petty acts, might out of hatred do what is unjust. You must entrust my mother to the dharma-knowing Bharata."
"Surely in some past life women were separated from their sons — and now that same fate has come upon my mother, Saumitri."
"Kausalyā, who nurtured me for so long and raised me through suffering, is now separated from me at the time of bearing fruit — shame on me!"
"Let no woman, Saumitri, ever give birth to a son like me, who brings endless grief to his mother."
"I think that myna bird of Lakṣmaṇa is more blessed than I am — the one from whom those words are heard: 'Parrot, bite the foot of the enemy.'"
"What use is a son to one who is without son's benefit — to my grieving, ill-fortuned mother, when I have done nothing to help her, O subduer of foes?"
"Ill-fated is my mother Kausalyā, bereft of me — she lies stricken with the deepest sorrow, fallen into an ocean of grief."
"I alone, were I angry, could overcome Ayodhyā and the whole earth with my arrows — though valor without cause is no virtue, Lakṣmaṇa."
"But I am afraid of unrighteousness and afraid for the other world, O sinless one — it is for that reason, Lakṣmaṇa, that I do not consecrate myself today."
Lamenting thus and in many other piteous ways in that lonely place, his face full of tears, Rāma sat down in silence in the night.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Lakṣmaṇa comforted Rāma when he had finished his lament — like a fire whose flames have died down, like an ocean whose waves have stilled.
"Surely today, O Rāma, O best among warriors, the city of Ayodhyā is without luster since your departure — like a night bereft of the moon."
"It is not fitting, O Rāma, that you should torment yourself thus and grieve both Sītā and me, O bull among men."
"Neither Sītā without you nor I without you, O Rāghava, could live even for a moment — like fish drawn out of water."
"I would not wish to see our father, nor Śatrughna, nor Sumitrā, O scorcher of foes, nor even heaven itself without you."
Hearing these noble and full words of Lakṣmaṇa, the Rāghava, that scorcher of foes, having embraced dharma for a long time, composed himself with reverence for all the years of forest life ahead.
Having spent the auspicious night at that great tree, when the pure sun had risen, they departed from that place.
They went toward the place where the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā approaches the Yamunā, penetrating deep into the great forest.
Those illustrious ones came upon the earth through various regions — charming places never seen before — beholding them here and there.
Proceeding at ease and observing various trees, when the day had just turned, Rāma spoke to Saumitri.
"Look around Prayāga, Saumitri, at the tall column of smoke — the banner of the sacred fire. I think the sage is nearby."
"Surely we have reached the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā — for the sound of water meeting water is heard."
"Wood cut by those who live off the forest, and these various trees are visible — this is the hermitage of Bharadvāja."
Those two bearing bows, traveling comfortably as the sun hung low, reached the abode of the sage at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Rāma, having approached the hermitage and startling the deer and birds, walked a moment's distance and came to Bharadvāja.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the two heroes, wishing to see the sage, having approached the hermitage with Sītā following them, stood at a respectful distance.
Seeing the great one who had offered his agnihotra oblation, Rāma, with joined palms, together with Saumitri and with Sītā, saluted him.
The elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa presented himself to him: "We two are the sons of Daśaratha, O venerable one — Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."
"This is my wife, the Vaidehī, the auspicious daughter of Janaka — blameless, she has followed me into this desolate forest hermitage."
"As I was being sent into exile by my father, this dear younger brother Saumitri, firm in his vow, followed me into the very forest."
"Commanded by our father, O venerable one, we shall enter the forest hermitage; there we shall practice dharma alone, subsisting on roots and fruits."
Hearing those words of the wise prince, the righteous-souled one then brought forth a cow, arghya water, and drinking water.
Surrounded on all sides by deer, birds, and sages, the sage honored Rāma on his arrival and welcomed him with the word of welcome.
Having received that honor, Bharadvāja then spoke these dharma-filled words to Rāma as he sat down together with his companions.
"At long last, O Kākutstha, I see you arrived here. I have heard of this causeless exile of yours."
"This spot is secluded, at the confluence of two great rivers — sacred and beautiful. May your honor dwell here in happiness."
Being thus spoken to by Bharadvāja, the Rāghava Rāma, devoted to the welfare of all, replied with auspicious words.
"O venerable one, the people of the city and countryside are close by here; crowds will come to gaze upon the Vaidehī and upon me. For this reason I am not pleased to dwell here."
"Look, O venerable one, for an excellent and solitary hermitage-place where the Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka who deserves happiness, may find delight."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing these auspicious words of the Rāghava, the great sage Bharadvāja then spoke words that grasped his meaning.
"Ten krośas from here, dear one, is a mountain where you shall dwell — sacred, frequented by great sages, pleasant to behold from every side."
"Roamed by golāṅgūla monkeys, frequented by monkeys and bears — known as Citrakūṭa, it resembles the Gandhamādana mountain."
"As long as a person looks upon the peaks of Citrakūṭa, his mind settles in what is auspicious and does not turn toward evil."
"Many sages there, having sported through hundreds of autumns, have ascended to heaven through austerity — together with Kapālaśiras."
"I think that secluded dwelling will be pleasant for you — or else dwell here for your forest sojourn with me, O Rāma."
That knower of dharma, Bharadvāja, received Rāma — that beloved guest — together with his wife and brother, with all manner of hospitalities.
For Rāma, having come to Prayāga and arrived at that great sage, the sacred night passed by as they told various tales.
When the night had brightened into dawn, the tiger among men came to Bharadvāja and spoke to the sage of blazing splendor.
"O one of truthful nature, this night just dawning — we have spent it here in your hermitage. May your honor grant us leave for our dwelling."
When that night had been passed, Bharadvāja spoke thus: "Go to Citrakūṭa, which abounds in honey, roots, and fruits."
"There herds of elephants and herds of deer roam on every side through the forest glades — you will see them, O Rāghava."
"Reaching that auspicious mountain, resounding with the cries of delighted koyaṣṭika birds and kokila cuckoos, filled with intoxicated deer and many elephants — most beautiful — set up your hermitage and dwell there."
Having spent the night there, the two princes, those tamers of foes, saluted the great sage and then set out toward that mountain.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Watching them depart, he followed after them as a father follows his sons; then that great sage began to speak these words.
"When you reach the Kālindī, the swiftly flowing river, there you must build a raft and cross the river Aṃśumatī."
"Then, having reached the great banyan tree with its green canopy, grown tall amid many trees, dark and frequented by siddhas —"
"— having gone just one krośa from there, O Rāma, you will see a dark forest, mixed with palāśa trees, badara shrubs, and the bamboo groves of the Yamunā."
"That is the path to Citrakūṭa, which I have traversed many times — pleasant, gentle underfoot, and free of forest fires." Having thus pointed out the road, that great sage turned back.
When that sage had turned back, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: "We are truly blessed, O son of Sumitrā, that the sage shows such compassion toward us."
Having thus taken counsel together, those two tiger-like men, steadfast in mind, placed Sītā ahead of them and proceeded to the river Kālindī.
Then the two of them assembled a very large raft from logs; Lakṣmaṇa, cutting the timber, fashioned it for Sītā's comfort and peace of mind.
There Rāma, son of Daśaratha, lifted his beloved — who was like an unimaginable Śrī, slightly bashful — onto the raft.
Then on the raft they crossed the Yamunā — swift-flowing Aṃśumatī, garlanded with waves, its banks lined with many trees.
Having crossed, they abandoned the raft and, setting forth from the Yamunā forest, they reached the dark banyan tree, cool and green-leafed.
"May I see Kausalyā, and glorious Sumitrā as well" — with these words Sītā, folding her hands in reverence, circumambulated the lord of the forest.
Having gone just one krośa from there, the two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, slew many pure deer and roamed about in the Yamunā forest.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
