And do adorn yourself now before my very eyes, O daughter of Mithilā — bring me joy, dear child, shining with the divine ornaments."
Then Sītā, having adorned herself, she who is like a daughter of the gods, bowed her head to Anasūyā and went toward Rāma.
The best among the eloquent, Rāghava, beheld Sītā thus adorned and rejoiced at the gift of affection from the female ascetic.
Then the daughter of Mithilā, Sītā, reported to Rāma all the gift of affection from the female ascetic — the garment, ornaments, and garlands.
Rāma and the great warrior Lakṣmaṇa were overjoyed upon seeing the honour rendered to the daughter of Mithilā — something exceedingly rare among humans.
Then, pleased, that moon-faced joy of the Raghu line passed that auspicious night there, honoured by the siddha ascetics.
When that night had passed and the sacred fires had been anointed and the offerings made, those two tigers among men took leave of the ascetics who ranged the forest.
Those forest-ranging ascetics, walkers in dharma, spoke to them of the passage through that forest, which was beset by rākṣasas.
"This is the path of the great sages who fetch fruits in the forest; by this path, O Rāghava, it is fitting for you to enter the difficult forest."
Thus, blessed by those ascetic brahmins with joined palms who had performed the rite of benediction, that scorcher of foes, Rāghava, with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa, entered the forest like the sun entering a mass of clouds.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Entering the great forest, the Daṇḍaka wilderness, the self-possessed and invincible Rāma beheld the precinct of the ascetics' hermitage.
Surrounded by kuśa grass and bark cloth, pervaded by the radiance of Brahmā, it blazed forth, difficult to behold — like the disk of the sun flaming in the sky.
It was a refuge for all beings, its courtyard always well-swept, perpetually honored and danced upon by troops of Apsarases.
It was adorned with broad fire-shelters, sacrificial ladles and vessels, antelope skins, kuśa grass, sacred fuel, water-pots, fruits and roots.
Ringed with great forest trees bearing auspicious sweet fruits, consecrated by bali offerings and fire-oblations, holy and resounding with the chanting of the Veda.
Encircled by wild flowers and a lotus-pond thick with blooms, inhabited by self-restrained ascetics subsisting on fruits and roots, clad in bark cloth and black antelope hides.
Surrounded by ancient sages effulgent as the sun and fire, adorned by great seers of controlled diet and holy conduct.
That place resembled the abode of Brahmā, reverberating with Vedic recitation, beautified by blessed brāhmaṇas who knew Brahman.
Beholding that precinct of the ascetics' hermitage, the glorious Rāghava of great splendor strung his great bow and advanced.
Those great seers, possessed of divine knowledge, seeing Rāma, came forward joyfully to meet him and the illustrious Vaidehī as well.
Those walkers of righteousness, firm in their vows, beholding him like the rising moon, pronouncing auspicious blessings, received him with honor.
The forest-dwelling ascetics gazed in wonder at Rāma's physical form, his noble bearing, his beauty, his delicacy, and the grace of his appearance.
All those forest wanderers beheld Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, and Rāma with eyes that seemed not to blink, as though gazing at marvels.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
There the blessed ones, devoted to the welfare of all beings, lodged Rāghava as a guest in the leaf-thatched hall.
Then those blessed sages, blazing like fire, walkers of righteousness, having duly honored Rāma with proper rites, brought water for him.
Having offered roots, flowers, forest fruits and the hermitage to the great-souled one, those knowers of dharma then spoke with joined palms.
"The king is protector of the dharma of his people, refuge of the greatly renowned, worthy of worship and of honor, the wielder of the rod of justice, the master."
"A king who protects his subjects receives a fourth share of Indra's merit, O Rāghava; therefore the king, honored by all the world, enjoys wealth even from forests."
"We dwell within your domain and must be protected by you; whether you reside in the city or the forest, you are our king and lord of the people."
"We who have laid down the rod, conquered anger, and mastered our senses — we ascetics whose wealth is austerity — must always be protected by you as though we were in the womb."
Having spoken thus, they honored Rāghava along with Lakṣmaṇa with fruits, roots, wild flowers, and various other foods.
Other accomplished ascetics, blazing like Vaiśvānara fire, righteous in conduct, likewise gratified the lordly Rāma in proper fashion.
Rāma, having been duly received as a guest, then, toward the rising of the sun, took leave of all the sages and plunged into the forest.
Crowded with herds of various animals, frequented by tigers and wolves, its trees, creepers and thickets fallen and broken, its pools of water hard to see.
Rāma, followed by Lakṣmaṇa, beheld the interior of that forest bereft of calling birds, but resounding with the cries of swarms of crickets.
In the midst of that forest filled with fearsome beasts, Kākutstha encountered a man-eater, tall as a mountain peak, roaring with a mighty voice.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Deep-eyed, vast-mouthed, misshapen, with a belly like a poison-pot — repulsive, uneven, towering, grotesque, and terrible to behold.
He was clad in a tiger skin soaked in fat and drenched in blood, his gaping mouth inspiring terror in all creatures — like Death itself with jaws flung wide.
Three lions, four tigers, two wolves, ten spotted deer, and the great head of an elephant with its tusks, all smeared with marrow and fat —
— were hung upon an iron spit. That one, roaring with a great voice, upon seeing Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā the daughter of Maithilī —
— rushed at them in violent fury like Death the Destroyer come for living creatures, uttering a fearsome roar as if shaking the very earth.
Seizing Vaidehī with one arm and withdrawing, he then spoke: "You two bear matted hair and bark cloth, yet travel with a wife — your lives are forfeit."
"You have entered the Daṇḍaka forest bearing arrows, bows and swords. How can two who pass as ascetics dwell here in the company of a woman?"
"Who are you two sinners, walkers of unrighteousness, defilers of sages? I am the Rākṣasa named Virādha, and this impenetrable forest is mine."
"I roam here always, armed, devouring the flesh of sages. This woman of beautiful form shall become my wife, and I shall drink the blood of you two sinners in battle."
Hearing the arrogant and boastful words thus spoken by the evil-souled Virādha, Sītā, daughter of Janaka, became distraught and trembled with anguish like a plantain tree in the wind.
Seeing the lovely Sītā clutched in Virādha's embrace, Rāghava spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, his face parched with grief.
"See, dear Saumya, the daughter of King Janaka, my wife, virtuous in conduct, the illustrious princess reared in the utmost comfort — now placed in Virādha's lap."
"Whatever was intended against us, whatever boon was sought and obtained — all of Kaikeyī's scheming has come to swift fruition this very day, O Lakṣmaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"She who was not satisfied with the kingdom, that far-sighted one who had me — declared a blessing to all beings — sent to the forest for the sake of her son: that middle mother of mine has now achieved her desire."
"O Saumitre, there is no grief deeper for me than the touch of another man upon Vaidehī — not the death of my father, not the seizure of my rightful kingdom."
As Kākutstha spoke thus, overwhelmed by tears and grief, Lakṣmaṇa, enraged, spoke — restrained, yet hissing like a great serpent.
"You who are like Vāsava, the lord of all beings, why do you grieve as though you had no protector, O Kākutstha, when I, your servant, stand here?"
"Struck down today by my arrow in fury, the Rākṣasa Virādha, bereft of life, shall have the earth drink his blood."
"The rage that was in me against Bharata, who coveted the kingdom — that I shall now release upon Virādha, as the wielder of the thunderbolt hurls his bolt upon a mountain."
"Driven by the force and speed of my arm's strength, let a great arrow fall upon his broad chest, let it strip the life from his body, and let him then fall spinning to the earth."
Then Virādha spoke again, filling the forest with his voice, asking the two about themselves: "Tell me who you two are, and where you intend to go."
Then Rāma of very great splendor addressed the Rākṣasa with his blazing countenance as he questioned them, declaring his own lineage of Ikṣvāku.
"Know us as two Kṣatriyas endowed with proper conduct, roaming the forest. We, in turn, wish to know you: who are you, roaming the Daṇḍaka forest?"
Virādha then addressed Rāma of true valor: "Very well, I shall tell you, O king — hear what is mine, O Rāghava."
"I am the son of Jaya; my mother is Śatahradā. All Rākṣasas in the world call me Virādha."
"By my austerities I have also obtained, by the grace of Brahmā, invulnerability to weapons in this world, and the quality of being neither cleavable nor pierceable."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Abandon this woman and flee the way you came, without a backward glance. I shall not take your lives — go, make haste and preserve yourselves."
Rāma, his eyes reddened with anger, replied to that Rākṣasa of misshapen form, Virādha of evil mind:
"Wretch! Shame on you, base creature — you seek death. You shall certainly find it in battle. Stand fast; you shall not leave me alive."
Then Rāma, stringing his bow, nocking razor-sharp arrows with great speed, struck the Rākṣasa.
He released seven arrows from his string-fitted bow — arrows with golden flights, of great velocity, swift as Suparṇa and the wind.
Piercing the body of Virādha, who was clad in peacock feathers, those arrows fell to the ground drenched in blood, blazing like fire.
He — uttering a mighty roar — raised a pike tall as Indra's banner, and stood blazing forth like Death with gaping jaws.
That pike, resembling a thunderbolt, blazing in the sky like fire — Rāma, foremost of weapon-bearers, split it asunder with two arrows.
Saumitre broke the left arm of that fearsome being, while Rāma swiftly broke the right arm of the Rākṣasa.
His arms broken, the agitated Rākṣasa fell swiftly to the earth — like a cloud-mass, like a mountain split by the thunderbolt. Then Virādha spoke to Kākutstha, bull among men:
"Kausalyā is indeed blessed in her son — I recognize you, dear one: you are Rāma, and the greatly blessed Vaidehī, and the greatly glorious Lakṣmaṇa."
"By a terrible curse I entered this Rākṣasa form — I am the Gandharva named Tumburu, cursed by Vaiśravaṇa."
"And when I sought to propitiate him, the greatly glorious one said to me: 'When Rāma, son of Daśaratha, slays you in battle —'"
"'— then you shall regain your true nature and go to heaven.' Thus spoke King Vaiśravaṇa to me, who had been attached to the Apsarā Rambhā."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"When I did not attend upon him he became enraged and pronounced the curse. By your grace I am freed from this most dreadful curse; I shall now go to my own abode. May you be well, O scorcher of enemies."
"Not far from here, a league and a half away, dwells the righteous and valiant great sage Śarabhaṅga, O dear one, blazing like the sun."
"Go to him swiftly; he will arrange what is best for you. And cast me into a pit, O Rāma, then depart in good health."
"This is the eternal law for Rākṣasas who have departed life: those who are interred in a pit attain eternal worlds."
Having thus addressed Kākutstha, Virādha, pierced by arrows, the mighty one, laid down his body and attained heaven.
Lifting up that open-throated, spike-eared one roaring with a dreadful sound, they cast Virādha bellowing into a pit.
Then those two, bearing bows adorned with gold, having slain the Rākṣasa and taking Maithilī between them, roamed joyfully through the great forest — like the moon and sun standing together in the sky.
Having slain Virādha, that demon of terrible strength, in the forest, the valiant Rāma then embraced Sītā, comforted her, and spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa of blazing splendour.
"This forest is terrible and difficult to traverse, and we are not accustomed to woodland living. Let us quickly go to Śarabhaṅga, that treasury of ascetic merit."
And so Rāghava proceeded to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Near Śarabhaṅga—that one whose soul had been purified by asceticism and who possessed the radiance of a god—Rāma beheld a great and wondrous sight.
He saw the lord of the gods, his form blazing like the sun and fire combined, not touching the earth.
The god was adorned with brilliant ornaments, wore spotless garments, and was being venerated by many great-souled beings of his own kind.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
From a distance Rāma beheld his chariot standing aloft in the sky, yoked with tawny horses, resembling the newly risen sun.
He saw a pure white parasol resembling a dense pale cloud or the orb of the moon, adorned with varied garlands.
Two foremost fly-whisks of yak-tail hair, fitted with golden handles of great worth, were held by forest women and waved above his head.
Many gandharvas, immortals, siddhas, and supreme sages were praising the god stationed in the sky with choice words of hymn.
Beholding the Performer of a Hundred Sacrifices there, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Those tawny horses moving through the sky—these are certainly the divine horses of Puruhūta, of Śakra, of whom we have heard tell."
"And these, O tiger among men, who stand around the chariot in hundreds upon hundreds—young, wearing earrings, swords in hand—"
"—on each one's chest gleam garlands like flames; they all bear the appearance, O son of Sumitrā, of twenty-five years of age."
"For such, they say, is the eternal age of the gods—just as these tiger-like men appear, so pleasing to behold."
"Stay here a moment with Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, while I find out clearly who this radiant one in the chariot is."
Having thus addressed Saumitri with the words "remain right here," Kākutstha advanced toward the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Then the lord of Śacī, seeing Rāma approaching, took leave of Śarabhaṅga and said this to the celestials:
"That Rāma is coming here. Until he has not yet spoken to me, lead on to the conclusion; thereafter he is worthy to behold me."
"I shall behold him ere long as one who has conquered and accomplished his purpose—for a great deed, exceedingly hard for others to perform, is yet to be done by him."
Thus speaking, the wielder of the thunderbolt took his leave of the ascetic, paid him honour, and with his chariot yoked to tawny horses, that subduer of foes ascended to the sky.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When the Thousand-Eyed one had departed, Rāghava with his companions approached Śarabhaṅga, who was tending his sacred fire.
Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa clasped his feet; then, having received his invitation and being granted a place to stay, they sat down at his bidding.
Then Rāghava asked about Śakra's visit, and Śarabhaṅga reported all of it to Rāghava.
"This granter of boons, O Rāma, wished to convey me to Brahmaloka—won by fierce austerity, hard to reach for those who have not disciplined their souls."
"Knowing you, O tiger among men, to be near at hand, I would not go to Brahmaloka without having seen you, my cherished guest."
"Having met with you, I shall depart to the triple heaven frequented by the gods. Accept from me, O tiger among men, the imperishable, auspicious worlds I have won—both those of Brahmā and those on the back of the firmament."
Thus addressed by the sage Śarabhaṅga, Rāghava, that tiger among men versed in all the scriptures, spoke his reply:
"I myself shall win all the worlds, O great sage. But now I desire a dwelling-place appointed for me here in this forest."
Thus addressed by Rāghava, who was equal in might to Śakra, the greatly wise Śarabhaṅga spoke again:
"Go to the ascetic Sutīkṣṇa in a pure spot, in a delightful region of the forest; he will arrange a dwelling for you."
"This is the path, O tiger among men. Behold me for a moment, dear one, while I shed these limbs as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin."
Then, having built up the fire and offered oblations of clarified butter with the proper mantras, the greatly resplendent Śarabhaṅga entered the sacrificial flames.
The fire consumed the great-souled one's body hair and head hair, then his withered skin, then his bones, his flesh, and his blood.
And he became like fire incarnate, a youth renewed; Śarabhaṅga rose up from that funeral pyre and blazed with light.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Transcending the worlds of those who maintain the sacred fires, of the great-souled sages, and of the gods, he ascended to Brahmaloka.
That doer of meritorious deeds, that bull among twice-borns in the world, beheld the Grandfather accompanied by his attendants; and the Grandfather too, beholding that twice-born, rejoiced and said, "Welcome, thou art truly welcome."
When Śarabhaṅga had attained heaven, assembled throngs of sages came forward to meet Kākutstha Rāma, blazing with splendour.
Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, Saṃprakṣālas, Marīcipas, many Aśmakuṭṭas, and ascetics who subsisted on leaves—
—those who used their teeth as mortar, and others who were Unmajjakas; sages who subsisted on water, and others who lived on air—
—those who dwelt in the open sky, those who slept on the bare ground, those who stood upright and had mastered their senses, and those who wore constantly wet garments—
—those ever engaged in muttering sacred syllables, those devoted to austerity, and those who practised the five-fire penance—all endowed with the glory of Brahmā and firmly steadied in yoga: these ascetics from the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga came to Rāma.
Having approached Rāma, the best among upholders of dharma, the assembled sages, knowing the highest dharma, composed of mind, spoke to him who was supremely learned in dharma:
"You are the great warrior foremost of this Ikṣvāku lineage, and the lord of the earth, as Maghavan is the lord of the gods."
"You are renowned in the three worlds for your glory and your valour; in you abide devotion to a father's vow, truthfulness, and dharma in full bloom."
"Having come to you, O lord, great-souled one, learned in dharma and fond of dharma, we shall speak as suppliants—and may you be pleased to pardon us this."
"Great adharma would befall that king, dear Rāma, who takes the sixth part of tribute yet does not protect his subjects as a father protects his sons."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"One who is ever engaged, protecting all dwellers of his realm as his own life-breath, as sons dear as life itself—"
"—such a one attains, O Rāma, eternal fame lasting many years; and having reached the realm of Brahmā, he is glorified even there."
"Whatever supreme dharma a sage subsisting on roots and fruits performs—a quarter share of that accrues to a king who protects his subjects with righteousness."
"This great assembly of forest-dwellers, composed mostly of brahmins, is being slaughtered grievously by rākṣasas, O Rāma, as though it had no lord, though you are its lord."
"Come and behold the bodies of the sages, those who had purified their souls, slain in manifold ways throughout the forest by the terrible rākṣasas—so many of them."
"A great carnage is being wrought upon those who dwell by the river Pampā, along the Mandākinī, and upon those who make their home on Citrakūṭa."
"Thus we can no longer endure the terrible injury being done to ascetics in the forest by the rākṣasas of fearful deeds."
"Therefore we have come to you, the refuge-giver, seeking refuge. Protect us, O Rāma—we who are being slain by the night-wanderers."
Having heard this from the ascetics—those men of tapas—the dharma-souled Kākutstha addressed all the ascetics: "You ought not speak to me in this fashion; I am one who takes orders from ascetics."
"I have come here by good fortune precisely to accomplish your purpose; this sojourn of mine in the forest shall bear great fruit. I desire to slay in battle the rākṣasas who are the enemies of the ascetics."
Having granted a boon to those whose wealth was tapas, the hero, steadfast in dharma, conducted himself nobly with those ascetics; and together with Lakṣmaṇa, accompanied by those ascetics, he proceeded onward to Sutīkṣṇa himself.
Rāma, that scorcher of foes, accompanied by his brother and by Sītā, went to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa together with those twice-born sages.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Travelling a long way, crossing rivers full of water, he beheld a vast mountain range towering like a great rain cloud.
Then those two best of the Ikṣvāku line, the two Rāghavas, entered that forest thick with diverse trees, together with Sītā.
Having entered the awesome forest with its many flowering and fruit-bearing trees, he saw in a secluded spot a hermitage adorned with garlands of bark-cloth strips.
There, seated, wearing matted locks caked with mud and grime, great in his asceticism—Rāma duly addressed the ascetic Sutīkṣṇa.
"I am Rāma, O Blessed One; I have come to behold you. So speak to me, O knower of dharma, O great sage of true valour."
He then gazed upon Rāma, that hero, the best among upholders of dharma, and embraced him with both arms, saying these words:
"Welcome indeed to you, O hero Rāma, best among upholders of dharma! This hermitage, now that you have entered it, is like one that has found a master."
"Waiting for you alone, O greatly renowned one, I have not ascended to the world of the gods from this place by abandoning my body upon the earth, O hero."
"From when you took up residence at Citrakūṭa, having been deprived of your kingdom, I heard of your coming here, O Kākutstha; and Indra, the king of the gods, the Performer of a Hundred Sacrifices, declared that all the worlds had been won by me through my meritorious deeds."
"In those worlds frequented by gods and sages, won by me through austerity—by my grace, roam freely together with your wife and with Lakṣmaṇa."
To that blazing great sage of fierce austerity and truthful speech, the self-possessed Rāma replied as Vāsava might reply to Brahmā:
"I myself shall win the worlds, O great sage. But I desire a dwelling-place appointed for me here in this forest."
"You have been described to me by Śarabhaṅga and by the great-souled Gautama as one skilled in all matters and devoted to the welfare of all beings."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by Rāma, the great sage, renowned through the worlds, flooded with great joy, spoke sweet words:
"This very hermitage, O Rāma, is endowed with good qualities; take your delight here. Frequented always by assemblies of sages, it abounds in roots and fruits."
"Herds of deer, O greatly renowned one, come to this hermitage, roam about fearlessly, tempting one to hunt, and depart again."
Hearing those words of the great sage, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa—the steadfast one—spoke, drawing his bow with arrow nocked:
"Those deer that come in herds, O greatly fortunate one, I would slay with a sharp-edged arrow blazing like a thunderbolt—"
"—but then you would be implicated in that act, and what could be more troublesome than that? Therefore I do not think a long stay in this hermitage advisable."
Having spoken thus to that granter of boons, Rāma went to perform the evening rites; and having observed the western twilight, he settled there for the night.
Then the great-souled Sutīkṣṇa himself, having duly honoured those two bulls among men, gave them wholesome food fit for an ascetic, as the twilight ended and night set in.
Rāma, together with Saumitri, having been honoured by Sutīkṣṇa, passed the night there and awoke at dawn.
Rising at the proper hour, the Rāghava, together with Sītā, performed his ritual ablution with cool water fragrant with lotuses.
Then Vaidehī, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa duly worshipped the fire and the gods at dawn, in that forest hermitage of ascetics.
Beholding the rising sun, freed from all impurity, they approached Sutīkṣṇa and spoke these gentle words.
"We have dwelt here in comfort, O reverend one, honoured by you who are yourself worthy of honour. We take our leave and must depart; the sages urge us on."
"We hasten to visit the entire circle of hermitages of those virtuous sages who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"We wish to take leave of you along with these foremost of sages — ever steadfast in dharma, restrained through austerity, blazing like arrows of fire."
"While the sun has not yet blazed with unbearable heat — like a prosperity obtained by a crooked path yet unattained by those without lineage."
"So long do we wish to go" — having spoken thus, the Rāghava, together with Saumitri and Sītā, bowed at the feet of the sage.
The foremost of sages raised the two as they touched his feet, embraced them firmly with affection, and spoke these words.
"Go your way without mishap, O Rāma, together with Saumitri and with this Sītā who follows you like your own shadow."
"Visit the delightful hermitages of these ascetics who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest, O hero — those whose souls have been purified by austerity."
"You shall see forests abundant with fruits and roots, in full flower, where herds of deer are tranquil and flocks of birds at peace."
"You shall see ponds and lakes with clusters of blooming lotuses, clear waters, scattered with kāraṇḍava ducks."
"You shall see mountain streams delightful to the eye, and charming forests resounding with the calls of peacocks."
"Go, my dear child; and you too, Saumitre, shall also go. After seeing all this, you must return again to my hermitage."
Thus addressed, the Kākutstha replied "So be it," and together with Lakṣmaṇa, having circumambulated the sage, began to depart.
Then Sītā of the large eyes handed the two brothers their auspicious quivers and bows, and thereafter the two bright swords.
Having strapped on the auspicious quivers and taken up the twanging bows, both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa issued forth from the hermitage to go.
As Raghunandana set out, having been given leave by Sutīkṣṇa, Vaidehī spoke these words to her husband in an affectionate voice.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This great dharma is attained by an exceedingly subtle discipline; it is achievable here by one who has turned away from the vices born of desire."
"There are precisely three vices arising from desire: false speech, which is the foremost; and graver than that, the other two — approaching another's wife, and violent cruelty without enmity."
"False speech has never been nor will ever be in you, O Rāghava; still less the desire for other men's wives, which destroys dharma."
"All of this, O mighty-armed one, can be borne by those who have mastered their senses; and I know that your senses are indeed under your control, O fair to behold."
"But this third vice, the terrible injury to the lives of others, done without enmity out of delusion — that is now upon you."
"You have pledged, O hero, to slay the rākṣasas in battle for the protection of the sages who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest."
"It is for this reason that you set out with your brother into the forest renowned as Daṇḍaka, bearing arrows and bow."
"Seeing you thus set out, my mind is filled with anxiety; pondering on what befits you, let me speak what may be for your highest good."
"I do not approve of your going into the Daṇḍaka, O hero; hear the reason I shall state as I speak."
"You have gone into the forest bearing arrows and bow in hand, with your brother; seeing all the forest-dwellers, might you not spend your arrows freely?"
"For warriors here, the bow and the fuel of fire standing near one another greatly inflame the power of that energy."
"Long ago, O mighty-armed one, there was, they say, an ascetic — truthful, pure — who delighted in deer and birds in a certain sacred forest."
"To create an obstacle to his austerity, Indra, the lord of Śacī, came to the hermitage in the guise of a soldier, sword in hand."
"That excellent sword was left in the hermitage grounds; it was given as a deposit in trust to him who persevered in his sacred austerity."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Having received that weapon, intent on guarding the deposit, he wandered through the forest carrying it, protecting the trust placed in him."
"Wherever he went to gather roots and fruits, he would not go without that sword, so intent was he on guarding the deposit."
"Constantly carrying the weapon, that ascetic, rich in austerity, gradually developed a fierce disposition, abandoning his resolve in austerity."
"Then that sage, addicted to violence, heedless, dragged down by adharma, went to hell through constant association with that weapon."
"Out of love and deep respect I remind you, not instruct you: that disposition should in no way be entertained by you who have taken up the bow."
"I do not wish, O hero, for the thought of slaying the rākṣasas sheltering in the Daṇḍaka without cause, or of slaying people without offence."
"For heroic warriors living in the forests with disciplined minds, the purpose of the bow is only this: to protect those in distress."
"What place has the weapon here? What place has the forest? What place the warrior's dharma, and what place austerity? These are discordant — let the duty of the place be honoured."
"That intellect becomes tainted of its nobility through resort to weapons; when you return to Ayodhyā you will practise the warrior's dharma again."
"The delight of my mothers-in-law and father-in-law would be undying if you were to renounce the kingdom and become a devoted sage."
"From dharma arises wealth; from dharma happiness arises; through dharma all is obtained — dharma is the essence of this world."
"Dharma is attained by the wise through diligent self-mortification by various restraints; happiness is not obtained from happiness alone."
"Ever of pure mind, O gentle one, practise dharma in this forest of austerity; for all the three worlds are truly known to you in their essence."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This has been spoken by me out of a woman's impulsiveness; who indeed is capable of instructing you in dharma? Reflecting with your brother, do what seems fit without delay."
Hearing these words thus spoken by Vaidehī who was devoted to her husband, Rāma, established in dharma, replied to the Maithilī.
"What is beneficial has been spoken by you, O queen, words befitting your affection and reflecting your noble lineage, O daughter of Janaka, knower of dharma."
"But I shall say, O queen, what you yourself have stated: warriors bear the bow so that the cry of distress shall not be heard."
"And those sages in the Daṇḍaka forest, O Sītā, afflicted and firm in their vows, have themselves come to me — those deserving refuge have sought my refuge."
"Dwelling in the forest devoted to dharma, subsisting on roots and fruits, they find no peace, frightened by the rākṣasas of cruel deeds."
"Though engaged season by season in various restraints in the forest, they are devoured by terrible rākṣasas who live upon human flesh."
"Those sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, being thus devoured, said to me — those best of twice-born: 'Come to our aid.'"
"I, having heard these words thus fallen from their lips, paid reverence at their feet and spoke this reply."
"'May your honours be gracious to me — this shame of mine is incomparable, that those such as you brāhmaṇas, whom I should approach, have had to approach me.' And I said in the assembly of twice-born: 'What shall I do?'"
"Then all of them together uttered this speech: 'We are greatly oppressed in the Daṇḍaka forest by the many rākṣasas who change form at will, O Rāma; you are worthy to protect us.'"
"When the time for the fire-oblation arrives and at the times of sacred rites, O sinless one, those unconquerable rākṣasas who feed on flesh assail us."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For us ascetics, those practitioners of austerity who are harassed by rākṣasas and seek a course of refuge, you are the highest refuge."
"By the power of austerity we are indeed capable of slaying the night-wanderers; but we do not wish to squander the austerity long accumulated."
"Austerity, O Rāghava, is beset with many obstacles and is hard to perform; therefore we do not release a curse even as we are being devoured by the rākṣasas."
"Therefore protect us as we are tormented by the rākṣasas who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest, you together with your brother — for we have no lord but you in the forest."
"And I, having heard these words, pledged the complete protection of the sages in the Daṇḍaka forest, O daughter of Janaka."
"Having pledged, I am not able, while living, to act otherwise than my promise to the sages — truth is ever dear to me."
"I would sooner abandon my life, or even you, O Sītā, along with Lakṣmaṇa, than a pledge once given — and especially one given to brāhmaṇas."
"Therefore the protection of the sages must necessarily be done by me, O Vaidehī — even if I had not spoken, and how much more having made a solemn pledge?"
"These words you have spoken to me out of love and affection; I am pleased, O Sītā — for one dear is not instructed against what is right. It is fitting and befitting your lineage, O beautiful one."
Having spoken these words, the great-souled Rāma, bearing his bow, together with Lakṣmaṇa, departed with his beloved Sītā, princess of Mithilā, into the beautiful hermitage-forests.
Rāma went in front, the slender-waisted Sītā in the middle, and Lakṣmaṇa, bow in hand, followed behind.
The two of them, beholding various mountain plateaus, forests, and lovely rivers of every kind, journeyed on together with Sītā.
They saw sārasa cranes and cakravāka birds roaming the sandy river banks, and lotus-covered lakes teeming with water-birds.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
They saw spotted deer moving in herds, rutting-mad horned animals, buffaloes, wild boars, and elephants that are the enemies of trees.
Traveling a long way, as the sun descended, they together beheld a beautiful lake extending a full yojana.
It was crowded with lotuses and blue water-lilies, graced by herds of elephants, and filled with sārasa cranes, haṃsas, kādamba ducks, and other water-fowl.
From that beautiful lake with its clear waters, the sounds of song and music were heard, yet nothing could be seen.
Then, out of curiosity, Rāma and the great warrior Lakṣmaṇa approached the sage named Dharmabhṛt to inquire.
"Having heard this most wondrous thing, great curiosity has arisen in all of us, O great sage. Please explain well what this is."
Thus addressed by the righteous Rāghava, that sage of virtuous soul then began to relate the full glory of the lake.
"This lake, O Rāma, is named Pañcāpsaras and is eternal; it was created through the austerities of the sage Māṇḍakarṇi."
"For the great sage Māṇḍakarṇi had practiced severe austerities for ten thousand years, subsisting on air alone, standing in water."
"Then all the gods, headed by Agni, were alarmed and, gathering together, said to one another: 'This sage is seeking the position of one among us.'"
"Then, commissioned by all the gods to obstruct his austerity, five chief apsarases, their splendor flickering like lightning, were sent."
"By those apsarases, the sage who knew past and future was then brought under the sway of Kāma, for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose."
"Those five apsarases became the sage's wives, and their hidden dwelling was built in this lake."
"There those five apsarases, dwelling at ease, delight the sage who, though devoted to austerity, retains the vigor of youth."
"As they sport, this sound of instruments mixed with the jingling of ornaments and the delightful sound of singing is heard."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Calling it wonderful, the illustrious Rāghava, along with his brother, accepted the account of that purified soul.
While he was thus narrating, they beheld a hermitage precinct enclosed by kuśa grass and bark-cloth garments and surrounded by various trees.
Kākutstha Rāghava then entered that beautiful hermitage precinct along with Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa.
Dwelling there in great comfort, honored by the great sages, he visited in turn the hermitages of those ascetics.
He, the master of great weapons, had previously stayed near those sages—sometimes for ten months, sometimes for a full year.
Somewhere for four months, elsewhere for five or six, in other places for more than that, and sometimes for more than a year and a half.
Rāghava dwelt happily for three months or eight months at a time; dwelling thus in the hermitages of the sages and enjoying himself in all manner of ways, ten years passed for him.
The illustrious Rāghava, the knower of dharma, after wandering about with Sītā, returned once more to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa.
Arriving at that hermitage, honored by the sages, Rāma the subduer of enemies dwelt there for some time.
Then, residing in the hermitage, on one occasion Kākutstha humbly approached that great sage, and seated beside Sutīkṣṇa, spoke thus:
"O venerable one, I have always heard from storytellers that the foremost of sages, Agastya, dwells in this forest."
"But on account of the vastness of this forest, I do not know in what place the holy hermitage of that wise great sage lies."
"By your grace, I would go with my brother and with Sītā to pay reverence to the sage Agastya."
"This great wish turns over in my heart—that I might myself serve that best of sages."
Hearing these words of the righteous Rāma, the sage Sutīkṣṇa, delighted, replied thus to the son of Daśaratha:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I too was wishing to tell you precisely this—go to Agastya, together with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, O Rāghava."
"By good fortune you yourself speak to me of this matter now. I shall tell you, dear one, where the great sage Agastya dwells."
"Go four yojanas from the hermitage, dear one; then to the south lies the great and beautiful hermitage of Agastya's brother."
"In a mostly dry forest region, beautiful with a grove of pippalī trees, abundant with flowers and fruits, lovely, resounding with various birds—
"—there are various lotus pools with clear, auspicious waters, thronged with haṃsas and kāraṇḍava ducks, graced by cakravāka birds."
"Having passed one night there, O Rāma, set out in the morning, taking the southern direction along the flank of the forest tract."
"Proceeding thence for one yojana, you will reach Agastya's hermitage in a delightful forest region thickly covered with trees; there Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa will delight in dwelling with you."
"For that forest region is charming and dense with many trees. If you have decided to see that great sage Agastya, resolve to depart this very day, O greatly illustrious one."
Hearing this from the sage, Rāma paid homage to him along with his brother, and set out toward Agastya with his younger brother and Sītā.
Beholding wondrous forests and mountain peaks resembling clouds, and lakes and rivers as they came along the path,
traveling comfortably by the path indicated by Sutīkṣṇa, greatly joyful, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"This must indeed be the hermitage of the holy-actioned brother of the great-souled sage Agastya, which is now visible."
"For behold—the trees of this forest, recognizable on the path in their thousands, are bent low with the weight of fruits and the load of blossoms."
"This fragrance wafted from this forest by the wind is the suddenly arising pungent scent of ripened pippalī fruits."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Here and there are visible neatly gathered piles of wood; and along the path one sees cut darbha grass with the luster of vaidūrya gems."
"And in the midst of the forest, resembling the peak of a dark cloud, the tip of smoke from the fire of the resident ascetics is clearly visible."
"At secluded tīrthas, twice-born ones who have bathed are making flower offerings with blossoms gathered by themselves."
"This must indeed be the hermitage of Agastya's brother, just as I heard it described in Sutīkṣṇa's words, O gentle one."
"This is the direction made safe and sheltering by that one's brother, who with great power suppressed death out of desire for the welfare of the worlds, through his holy deeds."
"Here, it is said, the cruel Vātāpi and also Ilvala, two great demons who were killers of brāhmaṇas, once dwelt together as brothers."
"Ilvala, assuming the form of a brāhmaṇa and speaking the refined language, would mercilessly invite brāhmaṇas under the pretext of a śrāddha."
"Then the brother, after transforming his brother into the form of a ram, would feed those twice-born guests with him according to the rite of the śrāddha."
"After those brāhmaṇas had eaten, Ilvala would call out in a loud voice: 'Vātāpi, come forth!'"
"Then Vātāpi, hearing his brother's call, bleating like a ram, would tear through the bodies of the brāhmaṇas and burst forth."
"By those two flesh-eating shape-shifters operating together in this way, thousands of brāhmaṇas were constantly destroyed."
"Then the great sage Agastya, implored by the gods, having partaken of the śrāddha, ate that great demon."
"Then, after saying 'The meal is complete' and performing the hand-rinsing rite, Ilvala spoke thus: 'Brother, come forth.'"
"But to that brother speaking thus—the slayer of brāhmaṇas—the wise Agastya, foremost of sages, replied with a smile:"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'How can your brother, now digested by me, have the power to come forth—the demon in the form of a ram who has gone to the abode of Yama?'"
"Then, hearing those words announcing his brother's death, the night-roving demon, in his rage, began to assail the sage."
"He charged at that foremost of twice-born ones, but was utterly consumed by the blazing-glorious sage with a glance like fire, and met his death."
"This is the hermitage of his brother, graced by a lake and forest—he by whose compassion for brāhmaṇas this difficult deed was done."
As Rāma thus narrated, together with the son of Sumitrā, the sun set and the hour of twilight came.
Having observed the western twilight rite with his brother according to the prescribed manner, he entered the hermitage and paid homage to that sage.
Properly received by that sage, Rāghava spent that one night there, having partaken of roots and fruits.
When that night had passed and the disk of the sun was bright, Rāghava addressed that brother of Agastya:
"I pay you reverence, O venerable one; I have dwelt here in comfort through the night. I take my leave of you; I go to see your elder brother, my preceptor."
Told 'You may go' by him, the delight of Raghu's line departed, beholding that forest as he went along the indicated path.
He saw nīvāra grasses, jackfruit trees, palms, timiśa, vañjula, dhava, ciribilva, madhūka, bilva, and tinduka trees—
—trees in bloom, wound about by creepers with flowering tips, Rāma beheld by the hundreds in that wilderness.
He saw trees uprooted by elephant trunks, graced by monkeys, and resounding in their hundreds with flocks of intoxicated birds.
Then the lotus-eyed Rāma spoke to the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, increaser of prosperity, who followed close behind:
"Just as the trees have glossy leaves, just as the deer and birds are tame—the hermitage of the great sage of cultivated soul is not far off."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Known in the world as 'Agastya's' by his own deeds alone, his hermitage is visible—the remover of fatigue for the weary."
"Its forest filled with abundant smoke, adorned with garlands of bark garments, with herds of deer at rest, and resounding with various birds—
"—this is the hermitage of him who with great power suppressed death for the welfare of the worlds, and by whose holy deeds the southern quarter was made a place of refuge."
"This is his hermitage precinct—by whose power this southern quarter, through fear of him, is not oppressed by rākṣasas."
"From the time this quarter was secured by his holy deeds, from that time the night-roaming demons have been without enmity and at peace."
"This southern quarter bears the venerable one's name as 'Agastya's quarter,' renowned in the three worlds as inviolable by those of cruel deeds."
"Obeying his command so as not to constantly obstruct the sun's path, the great Vindhya mountain does not grow."
"This is the beautiful hermitage of long-lived Agastya, famed for his deeds in the world, frequented by tame deer."
"This virtuous one, worshipped by the worlds, ever devoted to the welfare of the good—he will unite us, who have now arrived, with what is most beneficial."
"Here I shall propitiate that great sage Agastya, O gentle one, and I shall dwell here for the remainder of my forest exile, O lord."
"Here gods with gandharvas, siddhas, and supreme sages constantly attend upon Agastya who is disciplined in his diet."
"No liar, no cruel one, nor a rogue, nor a savage man, nor one given to sensual indulgence could live here—such is the power of this sage."
"Here gods, yakṣas, nāgas together with birds dwell with regulated diet, wishing to worship dharma."
"Here supreme sages, great-souled siddhas, having abandoned their bodies and taken new bodies, have gone to heaven in celestial vehicles resembling the sun."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Here gods, propitiated by auspicious beings, grant the state of yakṣa, immortality, and various kingdoms."
"We have arrived at the hermitage precinct; enter first, O son of Sumitrā, and announce to the sage that I have come here with Sītā."
Lakṣmaṇa, younger brother of Rāghava, entering the hermitage precinct, approached a disciple of Agastya and spoke these words:
"There was a king named Daśaratha; his eldest son, the mighty Rāma, has come to see the sage, together with his wife Sītā."
"I am his younger brother named Lakṣmaṇa, devoted and loyal to him, if you have heard of me."
"We have entered this most formidable forest by our father's command; we all wish to see the venerable one—please inform him."
Hearing those words of Lakṣmaṇa, the sage wealthy in austerities said 'So be it' and entered the fire-chamber to announce the news.
Entering and joining his palms, he straightforwardly announced to the foremost sage, invincible through his austerities, the arrival of Rāma:
"These two sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, have entered the hermitage precinct together with Sītā, his wife."
"They have come, those two subduer of enemies, to see you and to serve you; it is right that you command what should be done next."
Then, having heard from his disciple of the arrival of Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa and the highly blessed Vaidehī, he spoke these words:
"By good fortune Rāma has come after so long to see me today; for his coming was indeed longed for by me also in my heart."
"Let Rāma be honored and brought in with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa; let him be ushered into my presence. Why has he not already been brought in?"
Addressed thus by the sage, the great-souled knower of dharma, the disciple bowed and said 'Very well,' his hands joined in reverence.
Then the disciple emerged in haste and said to Lakṣmaṇa: 'Where is Rāma? Let him come to see the sage; let him enter himself.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Lakṣmaṇa went to the hermitage precinct along with the disciple and presented Kākutstha and Sītā, daughter of Janaka.
The disciple, speaking Agastya's words with due humility, ushered him in properly, with all honor, for the purpose of receiving hospitality.
Then Rāma entered with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, gazing at the hermitage thronged with peaceful deer.
There he saw the altar of Brahman, and likewise the altar of Agni, the altar of Viṣṇu, the altar of Mahendra, and the altar of Vivasvat;
the altar of Soma, the altar of Bhaga, the altar of Kubera, the altar of Dhātṛ, the altar of Vidhātṛ, and likewise the altar of Vāyu;
Then the sage himself came forth surrounded by his disciples; Rāma saw him ahead, blazing with the radiance of sages, and the hero spoke to the prosperity-increasing Lakṣmaṇa:
"This is the venerable sage Agastya who comes forth, O Lakṣmaṇa; by his majesty I recognize him as the treasury of austerities."
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed scorcher of foes, supremely delighted, grasped the feet of sun-radiant Agastya.
Having paid reverence, the righteous Rāma stood with joined palms, together with Vaidehī Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Receiving Kākutstha and honoring him with a seat and water, and asking after his welfare, Agastya said: 'Be seated.'
Having offered oblations to the fire, presented the arghya offering, and honored the guest, he gave them food according to the dharma of a forest-dweller.
Then the foremost sage, the knower of dharma, having first seated himself, spoke to Rāma who sat with joined palms, that expert in dharma:
"Truly, O Kākutstha, an ascetic who behaves otherwise—not properly receiving a guest—would in the next world eat his own flesh like a false witness."
"A king of all the worlds who walks in dharma, a great warrior—you are a beloved guest deserving of worship and honor who has arrived."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having spoken thus and honored Rāghava as desired with fruits, roots, flowers, and other things, he then spoke again:
"This divine and mighty bow, adorned with gold and diamond, belonging to Viṣṇu, O tiger among men, was fashioned by Viśvakarman—
"—this supreme arrow, infallible, bright as the sun, given by Brahman; and these two quivers of inexhaustible arrows were given to me by Mahendra—
"—filled with sharp arrows blazing like fire; and this great silver scabbard, and this sword adorned with gold—
"—with this bow, O Rāma, having slain great demons in battle, Viṣṇu in former times took the resplendent glory of the heaven-dwellers."
"Accept this bow, those two quivers, the arrow, and the sword for victory, O giver of honor, as the thunderbolt-holder accepts his bolt."
Having spoken thus, the greatly glorious venerable Agastya, after giving all those excellent weapons to Rāma, spoke again:
"O Rāma, I am pleased; good fortune to you; O Lakṣmaṇa, I am fully content that you have come to pay reverence to me together with Sītā."
"The fatigue of the road afflicts you two greatly; and evidently Maithilī, daughter of Janaka, also yearns for comfort."
"For she is delicate and not unaccustomed to hardships; yet she has reached the forest with its many adversities, impelled by her love for her husband."
"Arrange it so that Sītā may find delight here, O Rāma; she has done what is difficult, following you in the forest."
"For this is the nature of women, O delight of Raghu's line, innate since creation: they love a man when he is prosperous and abandon him when he is in adversity."
"Women follow the fickleness of lightning, the sharpness of weapons, and the swiftness of Garuḍa and the wind."
"But this wife of yours is free from these faults, praiseworthy and worthy of acclaim, just as the goddess Arundhatī herself."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"And this region will be adorned by the place where you, O subduer of foes, will dwell with the son of Sumitrā and with this Vaidehī."
Thus addressed by the sage, Rāghava, with joined palms, spoke humble words to the sage who blazed like a fire:
"I am blessed, I am favored—the foremost of sages, the granter of boons, is fully satisfied with the virtues of me together with my brother and wife."
"But do indicate to me a region with water and many forests, where I might establish a hermitage and dwell in contentment."
Then the foremost sage, hearing Rāma's words, reflecting for a moment, the righteous and resolute one spoke words yet more resolute:
"Two yojanas from here, dear one, is a region abounding in roots, fruits, and water, rich with many animals, beautiful, celebrated as Pañcavaṭī."
"Going there, establishing a hermitage with the son of Sumitrā, take your delight, keeping faithfully to your father's word as it was spoken."
"For this entire history of yours is known to me, O sinless one, both through the power of my austerities and through my affection for Daśaratha."
"And the wish dwelling in your heart has been discerned by me through austerity—the desire to reside here in this forest of austerities with me."
"Therefore I tell you: go to Pañcavaṭī; for that forest region is lovely, and Maithilī will delight there."
"That region is praiseworthy, not too far, O Rāghava, and near the Godāvarī; Maithilī will delight there."
"Abundant in roots and fruits, filled with various flocks of birds, secluded, O mighty-armed one, holy and lovely as well—
"—and you too, together with your wife and capable of protection, dwelling there, O Rāma, will protect the ascetics."
"This great grove of madhuka trees is visible, O hero; one must go to the north of it, heading toward the nyagrodha tree."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then ascending the high ground not far from the mountain, one reaches the forest perpetually in bloom, renowned as Pañcavaṭī itself."
Thus addressed by Agastya, Rāma together with the son of Sumitrā took proper leave of that truth-speaking sage.
The two of them, granted leave by him and having made obeisance at his feet, set out from that hermitage toward Pañcavaṭī together with Sītā.
The two sons of the lord of men, having taken up their bows, with quivers fastened on, fearless in battle, proceeded with collected minds toward Pañcavaṭī by the path indicated by the great sage.
Now, as the delight of Raghu's line was on his way to Pañcavaṭī, he encountered midway a vulture of enormous body and fearsome might.
Seeing that bird perched in the forest, the two illustrious ones, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, thought it a rākṣasa, and asked: "Who are you?"
He, as if gladdening them with a sweet and gentle voice, said: "Know me, my child, as a companion of your own father."
Recognising him as his father's friend, Rāghava honoured him; then he calmly inquired about his lineage and name.
Hearing Rāma's words, that twice-born one — for a bird too is twice-born — disclosed to him his lineage and his own origin, which traces back to the source of all living beings.
"O mighty-armed one, hear from the beginning as I recount all the Prajāpatis who existed in former times, O Rāghava."
"Kardama is the first among them; Vikṛta comes next; then Śeṣa, Saṃśraya, and the valiant Bahuputra."
"Sthāṇu, Marīci, Atri, and the greatly powerful Kratu; Pulastya, Aṅgiras, Pracetas, and likewise Pulaha."
"Dakṣa, Vivasvān, and then Ariṣṭanemi, O Rāghava; and the greatly resplendent Kaśyapa was the last among them."
"The Prajāpati Dakṣa had sixty daughters — so we have heard — all renowned, O Rāma of great glory."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Kaśyapa took eight of those slender-waisted women: Aditi and Diti, Danu, and also Kālakā,"
"Tāmrā, Krodhavaśa, Manu, and also Analā. Then Kaśyapa, well pleased, spoke again to those maidens:"
"'You shall bear sons equal to me, lords of the three worlds.' Aditi agreed with that intent, O Rāma — as did Diti and Danu."
"Kālakā too agreed, O mighty-armed one; the remaining ones were not of that mind. From Aditi were born the thirty-three gods, O subduer of foes."
"The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Aśvins, O scorcher of foes. Diti bore sons, the illustrious Daityas, my child."
"This earth was formerly theirs alone, a sea of divine rites. Danu bore a son named Aśvagrīva, O subduer of foes."
"Naraka and Kālaka were born of Kālakā. And Tāmrā gave birth to five daughters: Krauñcī, Bhāsī, Śyenī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Śukī."
"These five daughters of Tāmrā are famed throughout the worlds. Krauñcī gave birth to owls; Bhāsī bore the bhāsa birds."
"Śyenī bore hawks and vultures, all of great brilliance. Dhṛtarāṣṭrī bore all manner of geese and bar-headed geese,"
"and cakravāka birds too did that fair lady produce. Śukī gave birth to Natā, and from Natā was born Vinatā."
"Krodhavaśa, O Rāma, bore ten daughters of her own: Mṛgī, Mṛgamandā, Hari, and Bhadramadā,"
"Mātaṅgī, Śārdūlī, Śvetā, and Surabhī, and also Surasā endowed with all auspicious marks, and Kadrukā."
"All deer are the offspring of Mṛgī, O best of men. From Mṛgamandā come bears, as well as sṛmaras and cāmaras."
"Then Bhadramadā bore a daughter named Irāvatī; and Irāvatī's son is Airāvata, the great elephant who is lord of the worlds."
"From Hari come the haras and also the ascetic monkeys. Śārdūlī bore golāṅgūlas and tigers as her sons."
"From Mātaṅgī come elephants as her offspring, O bull among men. And Śvetā bore as her son the white-eyed directional elephant."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then, O Rāma, the goddess Surabhī bore two daughters — well be it with you — one named Rohiṇī, and the illustrious Gandharvī."
"Rohiṇī bore cows; Gandharvī bore horses as her sons. Surasā bore the nāgas, O Rāma, and Kadrukā bore the serpents."
"Manu bore humankind for the great-souled Kaśyapa — brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, O bull among men."
"Brāhmaṇas were born from his mouth; kṣatriyas likewise from his chest; vaiśyas were born from his thighs; śūdras from his feet — so the Vedic tradition declares."
"Analā also bore all trees bearing sacred fruits. Vinatā is the granddaughter of Śukī, and Kadrukā is the sister of Surasā."
"Kadrukā bore a thousand nāgas who uphold the earth. Vinatā had two sons: Garuḍa and Aruṇa."
"From that Aruṇa I was born, and Saṃpāti is my elder brother. Know me as Jaṭāyus, son of Śyenī, O subduer of foes."
"I shall be a companion and protector for you, if you so wish. And I shall guard Sītā, my child, when you go out together with Lakṣmaṇa."
Honouring Jaṭāyus, Rāghava embraced him joyfully and bowed in reverence; for that self-possessed one heard again and again from Jaṭāyus of the old friendship with his father.
Entrusting Maithilī Sītā to that supremely powerful bird's care, he proceeded to that Pañcavaṭī together with Lakṣmaṇa, longing to burn his enemies as fire burns moths.
Then, having arrived at Pañcavaṭī — teeming with diverse serpents and wild beasts — Rāma addressed his brother, the blazing-splendoured Lakṣmaṇa.
"We have arrived at this place as directed by the great sage. This, dear Lakṣmaṇa, is the region of Pañcavaṭī, with its flowering groves."
"Let your gaze range all around; you are skilled in forest matters. In which spot shall our hermitage suitably be made?"
"Where Vaidehī may delight, and you and I as well, O Lakṣmaṇa — let such a place be found, one close to a body of water."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"A place where the forest is charming and the water is charming, and where firewood, flowers, kuśa grass, and water are close at hand."
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa — hands folded in reverence — spoke these words to Kākutstha in the presence of Sītā:
"I am subject to you, O Kākutstha — were you to stand thus a hundred years. Tell me yourself: 'Build it in this pleasing spot.'"
Greatly pleased by that speech of Lakṣmaṇa's, that one of great splendour, reflecting carefully, approved of a place endowed with every virtue.
Stepping onto that beautiful spot with the work of building the hermitage in mind, Rāma took the son of Sumitrā by the hand and said:
"This ground is level and beautiful, surrounded by flowering trees. Here, dear Lakṣmaṇa, you should build our hermitage properly."
"Not far away one can see this lovely lotus-pond, adorned with lotuses — fragrant lotuses that rival the sun — gleaming with lotus-blooms."
"Just as described by the sage Agastya of purified soul, here flows the lovely Godāvarī, lined with flowering trees."
"Thronged with geese and kāraṇḍava ducks, adorned with cakravāka birds, neither too far nor too close, frequented by herds of deer."
"Resonant with the cries of peacocks, lovely and lofty, riddled with many caves, the hills are visible, dear Lakṣmaṇa, clad in full-blossomed trees."
"With golden, silver, and copper minerals here and there across the slopes, the mountains gleam like elephants adorned with the most devout markings."
"Adorned with śāla trees, palmyras, tamāla, date-palms, jackfruit and mango trees, nīvāra grass, timiśa trees, and puṃnāga trees,"
"and covered with mango, aśoka, tilaka, campaka, and ketaka trees, as well as with flowering shrubs and creepers of every kind."
"With sandalwood, syandana, nīpa, jackfruit, and lakuca trees; dhava, aśvakarṇa, khadira, śamī, kiṃśuka, and pāṭala trees."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This place is sacred, this place is pure, this place abounds in animals and birds. Here we shall dwell, O son of Sumitrā, together with this bird."
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa — slayer of enemy heroes and supremely mighty — in no time built his brother's hermitage.
A leaf-hut, spacious and well-plastered with earth, firmly pillared, framed with long bamboo poles, and very beautiful.
The glorious Lakṣmaṇa then went to the river Godāvarī; having bathed and gathered lotuses, he returned having accomplished his errand.
Then, having offered a floral oblation and performed the pacificatory rites in the prescribed manner, he presented to Rāma the hermitage thus completed.
Seeing that hermitage built — gentle and fair — together with Sītā, Rāghava entered the leaf-hut and felt the utmost joy.
Greatly delighted, he then embraced Lakṣmaṇa with both arms, and spoke these words, tender and heartfelt:
"I am pleased with you, O lord; great is the deed you have done. For this reason the embrace I have given you is your due reward."
"With you as a son — one who knows feelings, one who is grateful, one who knows dharma, O Lakṣmaṇa — my father, that righteous soul, has not truly passed away."
Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava — that increaser of glory, self-controlled — dwelt happily in that fruit-abundant place.
For some time that righteous soul dwelt there, attended by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, like an immortal in the world of heaven.
As the great-souled Rāghava was dwelling there in contentment, with autumn's passing, the beloved season of hemanta — early winter — commenced.
One day, as night turned to dawn, the delight of Raghu's line set out to bathe at the lovely river Godāvarī.
The valiant son of Sumitrā, bowing respectfully, water-pot in hand, followed behind him along with Sītā, and spoke these words:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"That beloved season you hold dear has arrived, O sweet-spoken one — by which the auspicious year seems adorned, as if decked out in finery."
"The world grows rough with frost; the earth is garlanded with grain; the waters are no longer agreeable to touch; fire, the carrier of oblations, is most welcome."
"The virtuous, having worshipped the ancestors and the gods with offerings of the new first-fruits, complete the new-grain rite in due season, purged of all impurity."
"The kingdoms, rich in desire for plenty and blessed with abundant dairy produce; the earth's protectors rove about, eager for conquest, setting out on campaign."
"As the sun clings steadfastly to the direction frequented by Yama, the northern quarter shines no more brightly, like a woman deprived of her tilaka."
"Rich in frost by nature and now with the sun far away, the mountain Himavat lives up to its name — the snow-mountain — most manifestly."
"The days bring extreme ease for travel; at noon they are pleasant to the touch; the sun in them is pleasant — yet shade and water are unwelcome."
"The days now shine with a mild sun, veiled in mist, sharply cold, with steady breezes, the forests bare of creatures, blasted by frost."
"The nights now pass — their open-sky sleeping done, led onward by the Puṣya star, reddened by frost, cold, and grown longer still."
"His beauty transferred to the sun, the moon's orb reddened by frost — like a mirror clouded by breath — the moon no longer shines."
"The moonlight, soiled by frost, does not gleam even on a full-moon night; it appears, like Sītā darkened by the sun's glare, but does not shine with beauty."
"Cold to the touch by nature, and now pierced by frost, the western wind blows in this season twice as cold as before."
"The forests, wrapped in mist, filled with barley and wheat, grow beautiful at sunrise, resounding with the cries of krauñca birds and sārasa cranes."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Rice plants, golden in lustre, slightly drooping with heads full of grain shaped like date-palm blossoms, stand beautifully."
"With its rays drawing near yet veiled in frost and mist, the sun rising at a great distance appears like the moon."
"Lacking strength to warm in the morning, pleasant to the touch at noon, deep red and yet faintly pale, the sunlight shines beautifully upon the earth."
"Wet with the fall of dew, the grassy ground of the forests, bathed in the young morning sunlight, shines beautifully."
"Swathed in the darkness of dew, covered over by the darkness of mist, the rows of trees in the forest — flowerless — appear as though deep in slumber."
"Their waters covered with vapour, their sārasa cranes identifiable only by their cries, with banks of frost-wet sand — the rivers shine now in this season."
"From the fall of frost, from the mildness of the sun, and from the cold — even water not seized by fire is, for the most part, still savoured warm."
"Their leaves yellowed and withered with age, their stamens and pericarp shed, reduced to mere stalks, blasted by frost — the lotus pools no longer shine."
"In this very season, O tiger among men, Bharata, that righteous soul, is practising austerity in the city, afflicted with sorrow, out of devotion to you."
"Having renounced the kingdom, honour, and many varied pleasures, he sleeps — a man of austerity with regulated diet — on the cold bare ground."
"He too, at this very hour, no doubt rising for his ablutions, ever attended by the counsellors of the realm, proceeds to the river Sarayū."
"Raised in the utmost comfort, tender by nature, now tormented by the frost — how does he plunge into the Sarayū in the hours before dawn?"
"Lotus-petal-eyed, dark-complexioned, glorious, with a slender waist yet great in stature, knowing dharma, truthful, restrained by modesty, master of his senses —"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"— sweet of speech, gentle, long-armed, subduer of foes — having given up various pleasures entirely, he has taken refuge wholly in the noble path."
"Heaven has been conquered by your brother Bharata, that great-souled one, who, even though you are in the forest, follows your example in austerity."
"'Bipeds follow the father's nature, not the mother's' — so runs the world-famous saying; but Bharata has made it otherwise."
"She whose husband is Daśaratha and whose son is the virtuous Bharata — how, then, is that Kaikeyī, our own mother, so cruel in her designs?"
As the righteous Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words out of affection, Rāghava — unable to bear that reproach of his mother — replied:
"Your middle mother must not be reviled in any way, my child. Speak rather only of Bharata, the lord of the Ikṣvāku line."
"Even my mind — firm in its resolve to dwell in the forest, steadfast in its vow — is again made foolish, scorched as it is by longing for Bharata."
Lamenting thus, Kākutstha reached the river Godāvarī there, and together with his younger brother and with Sītā performed his ablutions.
Then, having offered water to the ancestors and the divinities, they praised the sun newly risen and the gods, composed and intent.
Having completed his ablutions, Rāma shone resplendent — with Sītā as his second and together with Lakṣmaṇa — as the blessed lord Rudra, ever joyful, shines with the daughter of the mountain king after his own ablutions.
Having performed the ablution ritual, Rāma together with Sītā and Saumitri departed from that bank of the Godāvarī and proceeded to their own hermitage.
Having reached that hermitage, Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa performed the morning religious rites and entered the leaf-hut.
That great-armed Rāma, seated in the leaf-hut with Sītā, shone like the moon adorned with stars; together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa he engaged in various conversations.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
While Rāma sat there with his mind absorbed in conversation, a certain rākṣasī came to that place by chance.
She was Śūrpaṇakhā by name, sister of the rākṣasa Daśagrīva; approaching Rāma, she beheld him who resembled a god.
He had the chest of a lion, great arms, and eyes resembling lotus petals; he was tender of form, of great essence, and bore the marks of a sovereign.
Beholding Rāma, dark as the blue lotus, radiant as the god of love, comparable to Indra himself, the rākṣasī was overpowered by passion.
He was fair-faced while she was ugly-faced; he had a trim waist while she was great-bellied; he had wide eyes while she had misshapen eyes; he had beautiful hair while her locks were copper-red.
He was lovely in form while she was disfigured; he had a beautiful voice while she had a terrifying voice; he was young while she was old and fearsome; he was gentle while she spoke ill.
He was righteous in conduct while she was deeply wicked; he was pleasing while she was unpleasant to behold. Possessed by passion born of the body, the rākṣasī addressed Rāma:
"You have come to this region which is frequented by rākṣasas, wearing matted locks in the guise of an ascetic, accompanied by a wife, bearing a bow and arrows — how so?"
Thus addressed by the rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhā, the scorcher of foes, with his straightforward nature, began to tell her everything.
"There was a king named Daśaratha, of the valor of the gods; I am his eldest son, known among men by the name Rāma."
"This is my younger brother named Lakṣmaṇa, devoted to following me; and this is my wife, the Vaidehī, celebrated by the name Sītā."
"By the command of the king my father, and constrained by my mother as well, desiring righteousness and seeking the good of dharma, I have come here to dwell in the forest."
"But I wish to know about you — tell me, who are you, whose are you? And what is the reason for your coming here? Tell me the truth."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The rākṣasī, tormented by passion, having heard his words, said: "Listen, O Rāma — I shall speak to you words that are true in meaning."
"I am a rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā, able to take any form at will; I roam this forest alone, instilling terror in all."
"I have a brother named Rāvaṇa, a rākṣasa, lord of the rākṣasas; and Kumbhakarṇa, ever deep in slumber, of great strength."
"Then there is Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous of soul, not given to rākṣasa ways; and my brothers Khara and Dūṣaṇa, both renowned for their valor in battle."
"Surpassing all of them, O Rāma, upon seeing you for the first time I have come with my heart set on you as my husband, O best of men. Be my husband at last — what will you do with Sītā?"
"She is deformed and disfigured — she is not a fitting match for you; I alone am a proper match for you. Regard me in the form of a wife."
"I shall devour this deformed, wicked, hideous, shrunken-bellied human woman together with your brother here."
"Then, beholding mountain peaks and various forests, you shall wander through the Daṇḍakas with me, O beloved."
Thus addressed, Kākutstha, skilled in speech, laughed at the intoxicated-eyed one and began to speak these words.
Then Rāma, with a smile and smooth words at his pleasure, addressed Śūrpaṇakhā who was ensnared in the noose of passion:
"I am already married, dear lady; this is my beloved wife. For women of your kind, the condition of co-wifehood is very difficult to bear."
"This younger brother of mine, virtuous, handsome, endowed with prosperity, and not yet married, is named Lakṣmaṇa, a man of valor."
"Without a wife as yet and seeking one, young and handsome — this one would make a fitting husband for a beauty such as yours."
"Seek this brother of mine as your husband, O wide-eyed one, O fine-hipped one — without a rival co-wife, like the sun's radiance on Mount Meru."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by Rāma, the rākṣasī bewildered by passion suddenly turned away from Rāma and spoke to Lakṣmaṇa:
"I, of excellent complexion, am a fitting wife for your beauty; with me you shall wander through all the Daṇḍakas in happiness."
Thus addressed by the rākṣasī, Saumitri, skilled in speech, smiled at Śūrpaṇakhā and replied with fitting words:
"How would you wish to become the wife of a servant like me? I am subject to my noble elder brother, O lotus-complexioned one."
"Become the junior wife of that noble one who has accomplished his purpose and is rich in attainment; rejoice in your spotless beauty, O wide-eyed one."
"Abandoning this deformed, wicked, utterly infatuated, great-bellied, old wife, he will surely take you as his own."
"For what wise man, O fine-complexioned one, O fine-hipped one, would direct his affection toward a human woman, forsaking this exquisite beauty of yours?"
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, that hideous shrunken-bellied one, inexperienced in mockery, took his words to be true.
She, bewildered by passion, then addressed Rāma, the scorcher of foes, who sat in the leaf-hut — formidable even alongside Sītā:
"Clinging to this deformed, wicked, hideous, shrunken-bellied, old wife, you do not regard me highly."
"Today I shall devour this human woman before your eyes; then I shall roam with you without a rival, at perfect ease."
Having spoken thus, with eyes blazing like firebrands, she rushed in great fury at the deer-eyed Sītā, like a great meteor rushing at the star Rohiṇī.
The mighty Rāma, enraged, seized her as she charged like the noose of Death, and then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa:
"With cruel and ignoble beings, O Saumitri, one must never jest. See how the Vaidehī barely escapes with her life, O gentle one."
"This disfigured, wicked, utterly infatuated, great-bellied rākṣasī — you must disfigure her further, O tiger among men."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus commanded, Lakṣmaṇa, filled with fury, in the sight of Rāma drew his sword and the mighty one cut off her ears and nose.
With her ears and nose cut off, the dreadful Śūrpaṇakhā let out a discordant shriek and fled into the forest in the direction from which she had come.
That disfigured, most dreadful rākṣasī, drenched in blood, let out various cries like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
Streaming blood on all sides, terrible to behold, she flung up her arms, roaring, and plunged into the great forest.
Then, disfigured as she was, she approached Khara who was stationed at Janasthāna surrounded by troops of rākṣasas — that brother of fierce energy — and fell to the ground before him like a thunderbolt falling from the sky.
Then, faint with fear and confusion, drenched in blood, that sister of Khara recounted everything to him — the arrival of Rāghava in the forest together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa, and the mutilation done to her own person.
Seeing his sister fallen thus, disfigured and drenched in blood, the rākṣasa Khara, scorched by wrath, questioned her:
"You who are endowed with strength and valor, who go where you will, who take any form at will — by whom have you been reduced to this condition, brought to a state equal to death?"
"Among gods, gandharvas, spirits, and great-souled sages — who is this one of such great valor who has disfigured you in this way?"
"For I see no one in the world who would do harm to me, save for the thousand-eyed Mahendra, the chastiser of Pāka himself."
"Today I shall drain his life-breaths with arrows that put an end to life, as a crane sucks up milk clinging to water."
"When he has been slain by me in battle, his vital points severed by arrows, whose frothy red blood shall the earth drink?"
"Whose flesh will the birds, gathering joyfully, tear from the body and devour, of him who has been slain by me in battle?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Neither gods nor gandharvas, neither piśācas nor rākṣasas will be able to rescue him from my grasp in the great battle, wretched as he will be."
"Recovering your senses gradually, you must tell me about the one by whom you, arrogant in the forest, were overpowered and defeated."
Having heard her brother's words, especially his rage, Śūrpaṇakhā then spoke these tearful words:
"They were two young men endowed with beauty, tender of form yet of great strength, with eyes as wide as white lotuses, wearing bark garments and black antelope skins."
"Resembling the king of the gandharvas, bearing the marks of sovereignty — whether they be gods or humans, I cannot determine."
"I saw there a young woman endowed with beauty, adorned with all ornaments, slender-waisted, standing between the two of them."
"Those two, acting together on account of that woman, have reduced me to this condition, like a wretched masterless creature."
"In the forefront of battle I wish to drink the frothy blood of that one of crooked conduct, and of those two as well, slain there."
"This would be my first wish fulfilled by you, dear brother — that I might drink their blood in battle, hers and those two men's alike."
While she was still speaking thus, enraged Khara dispatched fourteen rākṣasas of great strength, resembling Death itself:
"Two humans, well-armed, wearing bark garments and black antelope skins, have entered the dreadful Daṇḍaka forest together with a woman."
"Having slain those two and that wicked woman, you must return; and my sister here shall drink their blood."
"This desired wish of my sister — let it be accomplished swiftly, O rākṣasas; go and crush those two by your own might."
Thus commanded, those fourteen rākṣasas set out thither together with her, like storm-clouds driven by the wind.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the terrible Śūrpaṇakhā, having come to Rāghava's hermitage, described to the rākṣasas those two brothers together with Sītā.
They saw Rāma, of mighty strength, seated in the leaf-hut together with Vaidehī Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing them — and the rākṣasī who had come — the glorious Rāghava spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, blazing with energy.
"For a moment, O Saumitri, stand guard close beside Sītā — I shall slay these ones who have come here following her track."
Having heard this word of Rāma, who knows the self, Lakṣmaṇa honored Rāma's command with the reply: "So be it."
And Rāghava, the righteous one, strung his great bow adorned with gold, and then addressed those rākṣasas.
"We two are sons of Daśaratha, brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa; we have entered the difficult Daṇḍaka forest together with Sītā."
"Living on fruits and roots, self-restrained, ascetics who walk in dharma, dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest — why do you harm us?"
"I have come, bow in hand, by the command of the sages, to slay you wicked ones who commit outrages in the great forest."
"Stay right here, contented, and do not advance — if you value your lives, turn back, O night-roamers."
Having heard his words, those fourteen rākṣasas — slayers of brāhmaṇas, tridents in hand — replied in great fury.
With reddened eyes, those fierce ones addressed Rāma, whose eyes are red at the corners, who speaks sweetly though he addresses harsh things, whose prowess is gladly witnessed.
"You have provoked the anger of our master, the great-souled Khara — you yourself shall lose your life today, slain by us in battle."
"What power does one lone man have to stand before many of us at the forefront of battle — much less to fight us in combat?"
"By our iron clubs, tridents, and battle-axes, hurled by our arms, you shall forfeit your life, your valor, and the bow clutched in your hand."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having spoken thus in fury, those fourteen rākṣasas, weapons and swords upraised, charged at Rāma alone — and hurled their spears at Rāghava, the unconquerable.
Kākutstha cut all those fourteen spears to pieces with exactly as many arrows adorned with gold.
Then, blazing with great energy and utterly enraged, he took up fourteen iron-shafted arrows, sun-bright and whetted on stone.
Taking up his bow and drawing it to its full extent, aiming at his rākṣasa targets, Rāghava released those arrows like thunderbolts hurled by Śatakratu.
