Those sharp shafts with golden nocks, blazing and adorned with gold, blazed in the sky with the brilliance of great meteors.
Those arrows, drenched in blood, swiftly pierced through the rākṣasas' chests and drove into the ground with the sound of thunderbolts.
With their hearts split open, they fell to the ground like trees severed at the root — their limbs wet with blood, disfigured, their lives extinguished.
Seeing them fallen on the ground, the rākṣasī, overcome with rage and terror, let out a dreadful cry.
Śūrpaṇakhā, shrieking a great cry, swiftly went to Khara and, her blood somewhat dried, fell down again in anguish before him, like a creeper weeping its sap.
Having seen the rākṣasas laid low in battle, Śūrpaṇakhā fled; the sister of Khara then reported fully and entirely the slaughter of all those rākṣasas.
Seeing Śūrpaṇakhā fallen again, Khara spoke in anger with measured words to her who had come bringing news of calamity.
"I have just now dispatched those valiant rākṣasas, feeders on blood, for your sake — why do you weep again?"
"Devoted and loyal, ever well-disposed to me — even while slaying enemies they are not to be slain, for they would not disobey my word."
"I wish to hear this — what is the cause for which you writhe on the ground again, crying out like a serpent, 'Ah, my master!'?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Why do you lament as though without a protector when I, your protector, stand here? Rise up, rise up — do not fear; let this helplessness be abandoned."
Thus addressed and fully consoled by the formidable Khara, she wiped her tear-filled eyes and spoke to her brother Khara.
"Those fourteen fierce and valiant rākṣasas were sent by you to slay Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa, for my sake."
"But all of them — furious, tridents and battle-axes in hand — were slain in battle by Rāma with arrows that pierced their vital points."
"Seeing those mighty ones fallen to the ground in an instant, and witnessing Rāma's great feat, a tremendous terror seized me."
"I am afraid, deeply agitated, and dejected, O night-roamer — I have come again to you for refuge, seeing danger on every side."
"Why do you not rescue me, sinking in the vast ocean of grief — haunted by crocodiles of despair, its waves a garland of terror?"
"And these flesh-eating rākṣasas who came following my track have been slain on the ground by Rāma with sharpened arrows."
"If you have compassion for me and for those rākṣasas, if you have power and energy against Rāma, O night-roamer — then destroy this thorn of the rākṣasas who dwells in the Daṇḍaka forest."
"If you will not slay today this enemy of mine, Rāma, then I shall cast away my life right before your eyes, without shame."
"I consider with my mind and see that you are not capable of standing face to face in battle against bow-armed Rāma in great combat."
"You think yourself a hero but are no hero, your prowess is falsely claimed — for you cannot slay those two men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."
"Leave Janasthāna quickly with your kinsmen — for one without substance and of little valor, what kind of dwelling is this place?"
"Overwhelmed by the blazing power of Rāma, you will swiftly perish — for Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is endowed with blazing power, as is his brother of mighty valor, by whom I was disfigured."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus provoked by Śūrpaṇakhā, the valiant Khara then spoke, among the rākṣasas, words that were harsher than his name implied.
"This boundless wrath of mine born from your dishonor cannot be held back — like salt water risen in a flood."
"I do not count Rāma as formidable by his valor — he is a mere mortal whose life is exhausted; he has destroyed himself by his wicked deeds and today shall relinquish his life."
"Let these tears be checked and this agitation abandoned — I shall send Rāma together with his brother to the abode of Yama."
"Today, O rākṣasī, you shall drink the warm blood of Rāma as he lies on the ground, his life barely remaining, struck down by my battle-axe."
She, delighted upon hearing the words that issued from Khara's mouth, foolishly praised her brother again as the best among rākṣasas.
First rebuked by her and then praised again, Khara at that moment spoke to the army commander named Dūṣaṇa.
"Fourteen thousand rākṣasas who follow my will, of terrible swiftness, who never retreat in battles —"
"— dark as storm clouds in color, fierce, cruel in their deeds, who roam like lions among men, mighty, of terrible power —"
"— of these rākṣasas, proud as tigers, with great gaping mouths, of mighty splendor, fully roused for every effort — have them marshaled, dear Dūṣaṇa."
"Bring quickly for me, dear Dūṣaṇa, my chariot, bows, bright-colored arrows, swords, and diverse, sharpened lances."
"I, skilled in battle, wish to march out at the fore, for the slaughter of that insolent Rāma on behalf of the great-souled descendants of Pulastya."
While he was yet speaking, Dūṣaṇa announced the great chariot, bright as the sun, yoked with excellent dappled horses.
That chariot was shaped like the peak of Mount Meru, adorned with burnished gold, with golden wheels, unobstructed, with a pole inlaid with vaidūrya gems.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
It was adorned all over with auspicious images in gold: fish, flowers, trees, the moon and sun, flocks of birds, and stars.
Fitted with standards and swords, adorned with tinkling bells, yoked with fine horses — upon this chariot Khara mounted in fury.
Seeing him mounted on the chariot, the rākṣasas of terrible valor stood surrounding him, and surrounded the mighty Dūṣaṇa as well.
Standing on his chariot, Khara looked upon all the rākṣasas — those great bowmen with their dreadful shields, weapons, and standards — and commanded: "March out!"
Then that rākṣasa army — with dreadful shields, weapons, and standards — marched out from Janasthāna with a great roar and tremendous speed.
With clubs, battle-axes, very sharp tridents and hatchets, swords, and discuses held in hand, and gleaming javelins —
— with lances, dreadful spiked clubs, oversized bows, maces, iron hammers, and thunderbolt-weapons grasped in their hands, terrible to behold —
— fourteen thousand of those most dreadful rākṣasas, followers of Khara's will, marched forth from Janasthāna.
Seeing those rākṣasas of terrible valor advancing, Khara's own chariot followed close behind them.
Then the charioteer, knowing Khara's intent, urged on those dappled horses adorned with burnished gold.
Urged on, that swift chariot of Khara — the slayer of foes — filled all the cardinal and intermediate directions with its sound.
The mighty Khara, whose voice is harsh, his fury grown great, roaring like a cloud raining hailstones, urged the charioteer on again, hastening like Death itself to slay his enemy.
As that dreadful army, inauspicious as a river of blood, set out, a great roaring cloud, dark as a donkey's hide, rained down upon it.
His swift horses, yoked to the chariot, stumbled and fell on their own on the royal road in a flower-strewn level place.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
A dark halo edged with blood appeared, resembling a wheel of firebrands, encircling the sun.
Then a huge and terrible vulture alighted on the tall golden-shafted standard, clutching and perching upon it.
Near Janasthāna, flesh-eating beasts and birds, braying with harsh voices, made various discordant cries.
In the blazing quarter of the sky, dreadful jackals uttered terrifying, inauspicious howls, portending ill for the living.
Fearsome storm-clouds, resembling cleaved mountains, carrying rain dried within, made the sky no sky—obscuring it utterly.
A terrible, oppressive darkness arose that made the hair stand on end; neither the cardinal directions nor the intermediate ones could be clearly discerned.
A glow the color of wet blood appeared though it was not twilight, and dreadful beasts and birds cried out facing toward Khara.
Jackals, ever portending ill in battle, terrible in their appearance, howled before the army with mouths belching flames.
A headless torso (kabandha), resembling an iron bar, was seen near the sun; and the great planet Svarbhānu seized the sun though it was not an eclipse-node.
A fierce wind blew; the sun became devoid of luster; and stars with the faint glow of fireflies rose though it was not night.
Lotus-pools saw their fish and birds withdraw and their lotuses close; and at that moment trees stood bare of flowers and fruit.
Dust of a cloud-red hue was stirred up with no wind, and mynahs (sārikā) there called out in mournful, broken cries.
Fiery meteors fell with terrible sounds; and the earth itself trembled along with its mountains, forests, and groves.
Even as the wise Khara stood in his chariot roaring, his left arm trembled involuntarily, and his voice faltered.
His gaze, looking all about, became tearful; a pain arose in his forehead; yet from delusion he did not turn back.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Beholding those great portents, hair-raising as they were, Khara laughed and addressed all the rākṣasas:
"All these terrible great portents that have arisen—I heed them not. In my valor I am the strong one; I regard them as I would the weak."
"Even the stars I could bring down from the vault of heaven with my sharp arrows. Enraged, I visit death upon all who are subject to death."
"Without slaying that Rāghava—intoxicated with his strength—and his brother Lakṣmaṇa with my sharp arrows, I have no desire to turn back."
"Let my sister have her desire fulfilled by drinking the blood of those two—for whose sake the destruction of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa has come about."
"Never anywhere have I suffered defeat in battle—this is plain to you all; I speak no untruth."
"Enraged, I could slay even the king of the gods riding his intoxicated Airāvata with thunderbolt in hand—what then of these two mere mortals?"
Hearing that rākṣasa's roar, the great army felt incomparable exultation—though it was already ensnared in the noose of death.
And noble sages, gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and cāraṇas assembled, eager to witness the battle.
Gathering together, those of meritorious deeds spoke among themselves: "May there be welfare for the cows, the brāhmaṇas, and all beings held in esteem."
"May Rāghava be victorious in battle over the night-roaming descendants of Pulastya, just as Cakra-handed Indra was victorious over all the foremost asuras."
Saying this and much else besides, the great seers beheld that army of rākṣasas whose lives were already spent.
Khara swiftly drove his chariot out ahead of the army; seeing that rākṣasa advance, the other rākṣasas also sallied forth.
Śyenagāmī, Pṛthugrīva, Yajñaśatru, Vihaṃgama, Durjaya, Karavīrākṣa, Paruṣa, and Kālakārmuka—
Meghamālī, Mahāmālī, Sarpāsya, and Rudhirāśana—these twelve of great valor set forth surrounding Khara on all sides.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And four foremost commanders—Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, Pramāthī, and Triśiras—followed behind Dūṣaṇa.
That fearsome, battle-hungry, utterly terrible army of rākṣasa warriors suddenly descended upon those two princes as clouds descend upon the sun and moon at eclipse-time.
When Khara of fierce valor marched toward the hermitage, Rāma along with his brother witnessed those very portents.
Seeing those great and terrible portents arise—hair-raising and harmful to all creatures—he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O mighty-armed one, behold these great portents that have arisen to sweep away all living beings—portending the destruction of all the rākṣasas."
"Those harsh, donkey-hued clouds rolling in the sky, raining down streams of blood and uttering braying sounds—"
"And all my arrows, Lakṣmaṇa—they who delight in battle—smoke; and my gold-backed bows tremble."
"The manner in which these forest-roaming birds cry out here foretells that danger has come upon us and that our lives hang in uncertainty."
"A great clash of battle will surely occur—of this there is no doubt; this arm of mine, throbbing again and again, proclaims it."
"O hero, your face appearing bright and serene at this juncture portends our victory and the enemy's defeat."
"For those about to engage in battle whose faces, O Lakṣmaṇa, appear lustreless—their lives dwindle away."
"One who desires good fortune and who suspects danger must make provision against what is yet to come—so must a wise man act."
"Therefore, taking Vaidehī, bearing arrows in hand and bow strung, take shelter in the difficult cave of the mountain, dense with trees—"
"I wish to encounter them head-on. Do not oppose this word of mine. By my feet I adjure you—go, my dear, and without delay."
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, taking his arrows and bow along with Sītā, took shelter in the difficult cave.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When Lakṣmaṇa had entered the cave together with Sītā, Rāma said "Good, the duty is assigned," and donned his armor.
Adorned with that armor blazing like fire, Rāma appeared in the darkness like a smokeless fire leaping up.
The valiant one, raising his great bow and taking up his arrows, stood there filling all the directions with the twang of his bowstring.
Then the gods along with gandharvas, siddhas, cāraṇas, and guhyakas, greatly alarmed, spoke among themselves:
"Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds—and Rāma alone, righteous of soul. How will this battle unfold?"
Then the army of the yātudhānas appeared on all sides with deep reverberating sounds, with fearsome armor, weapons, and banners.
Uttering lion-roars, bellowing at one another, twanging their bows, and yawning again and again—
—and beating kettledrums with resounding noise, their tumultuous clamor filled that forest completely.
Terrified by that sound, the beasts of prey roaming the forest fled to wherever it was silent, not looking back.
That army of great momentum, holding various weapons aloft, deep and ocean-like, advanced toward Rāma.
Rāma too, skilled in battle, casting his eyes in all directions, beheld Khara's army drawn up and advancing with battle intent.
Drawing his terrible bow and pulling arrows from his quiver, he summoned fierce wrath for the slaughter of all the rākṣasas.
Enraged, he became difficult to look upon, blazing like the fire at the end of an eon; seeing him possessed by that radiance, the forest deities trembled.
The form of Rāma enraged was seen then as that of Piṇākin Śiva ready to strike down the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
Khara, arriving at the hermitage along with his vanguard, beheld Rāma gripping his bow, enraged and the slayer of foes.
Seeing him, Khara raised his bow with its string in place, and roaring like a donkey, urged his charioteer: "Drive forward toward Rāma."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
At Khara's command the charioteer drove the horses toward where the mighty-armed Rāma stood alone, wielding his bow.
Seeing him charge forward, all those night-roaming companions shouted with great cries and surrounded him.
Khara, having plunged into the midst of those yātudhānas, appeared like the red-limbed Mars risen in the midst of stars.
Then all those night-roamers, enraged, rained various weapons upon that invincible Rāma of the terrible bow.
The rākṣasas, intent on fury, struck Rāma in battle with iron clubs, spears, javelins, swords, and battle-axes.
Those mighty ones, resembling storm-clouds, roaring loudly, charged at Kākutstha Rāma in battle, intent on killing him.
Those mighty rākṣasas discharged showers of arrows upon Rāma, like great rainclouds drenching the king of mountains with their torrents.
Surrounded by those terrible hosts of rākṣasas, Rāghava appeared like Mahādeva surrounded by his host of attendants on festival days.
Those weapons hurled by the yātudhānas, Rāghava received with his own shafts, as the ocean receives the floods of rivers.
Though his body was pierced by those terrible weapons, Rāma did not waver—like a great mountain struck by many blazing thunderbolts.
Rāghava, pierced and drenched in blood over all his limbs, appeared like the sun enveloped by twilight clouds.
The gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and great seers were filled with dismay seeing him—one man—surrounded by many thousands.
Then Rāma, greatly enraged, drew his bow to a full circle and released sharp arrows by the hundreds and then thousands.
Rāma released with ease in battle those straight-flying, heron-feathered arrows—difficult to ward off, difficult to endure, resembling the noose of Time.
Those arrows released so effortlessly by Rāma into the enemy's army bore away the lives of the rākṣasas like the nooses fashioned by Time.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Piercing through the bodies of the rākṣasas, those arrows, soaked in blood and blazing with the radiance of kindled fire, shone as they passed through the sky.
Innumerable, exceedingly fierce arrows of Rāma—life-takers of rākṣasas—poured forth from the orb of his bow.
With those arrows he shattered bows, the tops of standards, and coats of armor; he struck off heads and the many thighs adorned with bracelets—thighs resembling elephant trunks.
Then, pierced by nālīka and nārāca arrows with their sharp points and by vikarṇi shafts, the night-roamers emitted terrible cries of anguish.
That army, tormented by Rāma's sharp arrows that pierced the vital points, found no ease—like a dry forest in fire.
Some of the night-roaming heroes of tremendous strength, exceedingly enraged, hurled spears, swords, and battle-axes at Rāma.
The mighty-armed Rāghava, intercepting those weapons with his arrows, robbed them of their lives in battle and severed their necks.
And the night-roamers who remained there, despondent and tormented by arrows, fled toward Khara himself seeking refuge.
Dūṣaṇa, taking all of them back and reassuring them, charged at Kākutstha—enraged as Yama before Rudra.
All of them, having turned back and now fearless under Dūṣaṇa's shelter, once more charged at Rāma, armed with śāla trees, palmyra palms, and rocks.
That battle—between Rāma and those rākṣasas—became wondrous, tumultuous, hair-raising, and supremely terrible.
That deadly shower of trees and boulders, the righteous Rāghava received and intercepted with his sharp arrows.
Having received that onslaught, like a bull with eyes half-closed, Rāma gathered his supreme wrath for the purpose of slaying all the rākṣasas.
Then, seized by fury and blazing as though with inner fire, he rained arrows upon the entire host together with Dūṣaṇa from all sides.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the enraged general Dūṣaṇa, destroyer of enemies, seized a bar-mace resembling a mountain peak, terrible enough to make one's hair stand on end.
It was wrapped in bands of gold, a crusher of divine armies, bristling with sharp iron spikes, and drenched with the fat of enemies.
Terrifying to the touch like the vajra and the thunderbolt, a splitter of enemy citadels, resembling a great serpent — seizing that bar-mace, the cruel-actioned night-roamer Dūṣaṇa flew at Rāma in battle.
As Dūṣaṇa came rushing upon him, Rāghava severed both his arms — ornaments and all — with two arrows.
The mace fell from the hands of the severed-armed one and crashed to the forefront of the battlefield, enormous, like Indra's banner toppled.
His arms scattered wide, Dūṣaṇa fell to the earth like a great spirited elephant whose tusks have been broken off.
Seeing Dūṣaṇa fallen slain on the battlefield, all living beings cried out "Well done! Well done!" and honoured Kākutstha.
At that moment three enraged vanguard commanders, ensnared by the noose of death, joined forces and charged at Rāma: Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, and the mighty Pramāthin.
The rākṣasa Mahākapāla raised a huge spear, Sthūlākṣa seized a broad sword, and Pramāthin took up a battle-axe.
Seeing those three rushing at him, Rāghava received them with sharp, keen-tipped arrows as one receives guests who have arrived.
The scion of Raghu severed Mahākapāla's head and crushed Pramāthin with countless floods of arrows.
He filled Sthūlākṣa's eyes with sharp arrows; Sthūlākṣa fell slain to the ground like a great branching tree cut down.
Then, with arrows blazing like fire and adorned with gold and iron, the radiant Rāma slew the remainder of that army.
Those gold-fletched, smoke-trailing shafts blazing like fires struck down those rākṣasas as thunderbolts strike down great trees.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
In the vanguard of battle, Rāma slew a hundred rākṣasas with a single hundred of his arrow-swift shafts, and a thousand with a thousand.
Their armour and ornaments shattered, their bows cut and broken, smeared with blood, those night-roaming rākṣasas fell to the ground.
The entire earth, spread with those fallen in battle, their hair loose, drenched in blood, looked like a great sacrificial altar strewn with kuśa grass.
In an instant that great dreadful forest, its rākṣasas slain, became a hell-like swamp of flesh and blood.
Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds were slain by the single human Rāma, fighting on foot.
Of that entire host, only the great warrior Khara remained, and the rākṣasa Triśiras — and Rāma, the destroyer of foes.
Then, seeing that fearsome force destroyed in the great battle by the mighty Rāma, Khara mounted his great chariot and advanced on Rāma, like Indra with his thunderbolt upraised.
As Khara advanced toward Rāma, the rākṣasa army-commander named Triśiras intercepted him and spoke these words.
"Appoint me instead, O valiant one; withdraw yourself from this rash act. Watch the mighty-armed Rāma laid low in battle."
"I swear truly to you and I touch my weapons: I will kill Rāma, who deserves death at the hands of all rākṣasas."
"Either I am death to him in battle, or he is death to me in battle. Restrain your own eagerness to fight; be a spectator for a moment."
"If Rāma is slain, you may return to Janasthāna rejoicing; or if I am slain, you may then come forward to fight Rāma."
Khara, gratified by Triśiras' eagerness for death, gave him permission: "Go, fight!" and Triśiras proceeded toward Rāghava.
And Triśiras, mounted on his splendid chariot drawn by swift horses, charged at Rāma in battle like a three-peaked mountain in motion.
Like a great thundercloud releasing masses of rain-streams, he loosed torrents of arrows and gave forth a sound like a water-drenched war-drum.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing the rākṣasa Triśiras coming at him, Rāghava received him with his bow, shaking out sharp arrows.
That tumultuous and great clash between Rāma and Triśiras, both exceedingly powerful, was like the clash between a lion and an elephant.
Then, struck on the forehead by three of Triśiras' arrows, Rāma — impatient, angered, greatly provoked — spoke these words.
"Ah, such is the strength of this brave rākṣasa warrior — I am grazed on the forehead by arrows that feel like flowers! Now receive my arrows too, discharged from the bowstring."
So saying, in great fury, enraged, he shot fourteen arrows resembling venomous serpents into Triśiras' chest.
With four well-jointed arrows, the radiant Rāma brought down Triśiras' four horses.
With eight arrows he struck down the charioteer onto the floor of the chariot, and with an arrow Rāma also severed Triśiras' upraised banner.
Then, as the night-roaming rākṣasa leaped from his destroyed chariot, Rāma pierced him in the heart with arrows; he became senseless.
And the immeasurably great-souled Rāma, with wrath, struck off that rākṣasa's three heads with three swift, powerful arrows.
That night-roamer, pressed by Rāma's arrows and vomiting blood, fell to the ground, his own three heads having fallen before him.
Then the surviving remnant of the rākṣasas who had taken shelter with Khara broke and fled; they did not stand firm, like deer terrified by a tiger.
Seeing them flee, Khara turned them back in fury, then himself rushed directly at Rāma, as Rāhu rushes at the moon.
Seeing Dūṣaṇa slain in battle together with Triśiras, and witnessing Rāma's prowess, even Khara felt fear.
Seeing the irresistible, mighty rākṣasa army — and even Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras — slain by the single Rāma,
that army mostly destroyed — disheartened as he surveyed it, the rākṣasa Khara advanced upon Rāma, as Namuci once advanced upon Vāsava.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Drawing his powerful bow mightily, Khara hurled iron-headed arrows that feed on blood at Rāma, like enraged venomous serpents.
Snapping his bowstring repeatedly, displaying his mastery of missile-science, Khara on his chariot traced tactical paths across the battlefield with his arrows.
The great warrior filled all the cardinal and intermediate directions with arrows; seeing him, Rāma also took up his great bow.
With arrows irresistible as spark-shooting fires, he made the sky without gaps, like a rain-cloud with its downpour.
The surrounding sky became void of voids — everywhere dense with arrows — from the sharp shafts loosed by Khara and Rāma together.
The sun did not shine then, enveloped in a net of arrows, as both warriors fought in their mutual fury to kill the other.
Then with nālikā-arrows, iron shafts, and keen-tipped flanged arrows, he struck Rāma in battle as if goading a great elephant with prods.
All living beings beheld that rākṣasa standing in his chariot, bow in hand, looming over the field, like Death himself with his noose in hand.
Yet seeing him — mighty as a lion, moving with a lion's gait — Rāma felt no alarm, as a lion does not tremble before a lesser beast.
Then on his great chariot blazing like the sun, Khara drew up to Rāma in battle, as a moth draws near to fire.
Then Khara cut Rāma's bow along with its arrow at the grip, displaying his swiftness of hand against the great-souled Rāma.
And then taking up seven more arrows blazing like Indra's thunderbolt, he struck Rāma on his armour in battle, in his fury.
Then that armour of Rāma, radiant as the sun, struck by Khara's well-jointed arrows, fell to the ground.
Thus pierced by arrows in all his limbs and incensed with anger, Rāghava blazed in battle like a smokeless fire burning.
Then Rāma, crusher of enemies, strung another great bow with a deep resounding twang, for the annihilation of his foe.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Taking up that supremely great Vaiṣṇava bow which had been bestowed as a gift by the great sage, he rushed against Khara.
Then with gold-fletched, well-jointed arrows, the greatly enraged Rāma cut down Khara's battle standard in the fight.
That beautiful golden banner, severed in many pieces, fell to the earth like the sun descending at the gods' command.
Enraged, Khara, knowing the vital points, pierced Rāma in the limbs with four arrows and in the heart — as one might goad a great elephant with lances.
Rāma, pierced by many arrows discharged from Khara's bow, his limbs drenched with blood, became exceedingly incensed.
He, the foremost of archers and supreme bowman, gripping his bow in the great battle, released six well-aimed arrows.
With one arrow he struck Khara on the head; with two he struck him on both arms; and with three crescent-faced arrows he smote him on the chest.
Then afterwards, the great-splendoured Rāma, desirous of killing the rākṣasa and enraged, took up thirteen iron arrows whetted on stone, blazing like the sun.
Then with one arrow he cut the yoke, with four he felled the four horses, and with the sixth in battle he severed the head of Khara's charioteer.
With three he destroyed the triple-bamboo chariot-pole, the mighty one with two cut the axle, with the twelfth arrow he severed Khara's bow together with its arrow; and then, smiling as it were, with the thirteenth — blazing like the vajra — Rāghava, equal to Indra, pierced Khara in battle.
His bow shattered, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, his charioteer killed, Khara then leaped down and stood on the ground, mace in hand.
At that feat of the great warrior Rāma, the gods and the great sages gathered there, stationed at the prows of their celestial vehicles, rejoiced and honoured him with joined palms.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Rāma, of great radiance, first gently and then harshly addressed Khara, who stood dismounted from his chariot, mace in hand.
Standing amid a great force of elephants, horses, and chariots, you have performed a most terrible deed that all the worlds condemn.
One who is cruel, a doer of evil deeds, and a cause of terror to all beings cannot endure even if he be lord of the three worlds.
One who acts against the world's order, O night-roaming demon, all people destroy sharply, as one destroys a venomous snake that approaches.
He who, out of greed or passion, commits sins and does not understand, ruined, he sees his own end — as a Brahmin woman watches a hailstone melt away.
What fruit do you think you will obtain, O demon, by slaying the noble ascetics, those who walk in righteousness, dwelling here in the Daṇḍaka forest?
Those who do evil deeds, the cruel and those condemned by the world, do not long retain their lordship once gained — like trees whose roots have rotted.
The doer inevitably reaps the terrible fruit of evil action when the time comes around, as a tree blooms in its season.
The fruit of evil actions is swiftly obtained in this world, O night-wandering demon, like food laced with poison once it has been eaten.
I am a king appointed to slay those who commit terrible sin and who seek what is harmful to the world — I have come to take your life, O night-prowler.
Today the gold-adorned arrows I release will tear through you and fall upon you as serpents descend upon an anthill.
Those righteous ones whom you devoured in the Daṇḍaka forest — today, slain in battle along with your army, you shall follow them.
May the great sages whom you once harmed, now seated in their celestial cars, look down today and behold you laid low by arrows, fallen into hell.
Strike as you wish, make your utmost effort, O disgrace to your lineage — today I shall strike off your head as one strikes down a palm fruit.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by Rāma, Khara, enraged with blood-red eyes, laughed and replied to Rāma, overcome with fury.
Having slain mere common rākṣasas in battle, O son of Daśaratha, how do you praise yourself — though self-praise is ignoble?
Truly valiant and mighty men, the bulls among men, say nothing of themselves, even when filled with their own blazing splendour.
Only the ignoble, the undisciplined, the stains upon the Kṣatriya order in this world boast uselessly, as you, O Rāma, boast.
What hero in battle would invoke his lineage and sing his own praises unprompted, when the hour of death has arrived?
In every way your smallness has been revealed by your boasting, like fool's gold revealed by the fire of a touchstone.
Do you not see me standing here, mace in hand, immovable as a mountain bearing the earth, streaked with its veins of ore?
I am fully capable, mace in hand, of taking your life in battle — even as Yama with noose in hand rules the three worlds.
There is much indeed I could say to you, yet I will not — for should the sun set, battle would thereby be hindered.
Fourteen thousand rākṣasas have been slain — by destroying you today I shall wipe away their tears.
Having spoken thus, in supreme fury Khara hurled that great mace, blazing like a thunderbolt, at Rāma.
That great blazing mace, released from Khara's arm, reduced trees and shrubs to ash as it flew toward Rāma.
As that blazing mace, like death's own noose, flew through the air toward him, Rāma shattered it into many pieces with his arrows.
Shattered and pierced by those arrows, it fell to the ground, like a great serpent brought down by the power of mantras and herbs.
Having split that mace with his arrows, Rāghava, devoted to righteousness, smiled and spoke these fierce words to Khara.
You have shown the full extent of your strength, O vilest of rākṣasas — you are more feeble than I, and your roaring was in vain.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
This mace, pierced by my arrows, has gone to the ground — a refutation of your arrogant boasting.
As for what you said — "I shall wipe away the tears of the slain rākṣasas" — that too was a false boast.
From this base, mean-natured, false-living demon I shall take his life as Garuḍa seizes the amṛta.
Today the earth shall drink your blood, foaming and bubbling, as my arrows split open your throat and rend your body.
With every limb smeared in dust, your two arms fallen and outstretched, you shall sleep embracing the earth as if she were a rare and beloved woman.
When you lie sunk in the deepest sleep, O disgrace of the rākṣasas, these Daṇḍaka forests shall become a refuge for those who now have no refuge.
With Janasthāna become a place of slaughter for your rākṣasas by my arrows, the sages shall roam fearlessly in every part of the forest.
Today the rākṣasī women, their kinsmen slain, faces drenched with tears, wretched and themselves a terror to others, shall scatter in flight.
Today, O night-prowler, those wives who belong to a lineage fitted for such a lord as you shall come to taste the full flavour of grief.
O cruel-natured one, petty of soul, ever a thorn to Brāhmaṇas — because of you the sages cast their oblations into the fire with trembling hands.
As Rāghava spoke thus in fierce passion in battle, Khara, his voice even harsher in rage, reviled him harshly.
You are thoroughly puffed up with pride and fearless even in the face of peril — that is why you do not discern what should and should not be said, for you are already in the grip of death.
Those men who are ensnared in the noose of Death know not what should or should not be done — their six senses are utterly swept away.
Having spoken thus to Rāma, furrowing his brow in fury, the night-roaming demon then caught sight of a great śāla tree nearby.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Looking all around for a weapon to use in battle, he fixed his gaze upon that tree and baring his teeth uprooted it.
Lifting it aloft with both arms and roaring mightily, that one of great power hurled it at Rāma, crying out: "You are slain!"
Rāma, of blazing valour, cut down that oncoming tree with a shower of arrows, then drew up fierce fury within himself to slay Khara in battle.
Then Rāma, perspiring, his eyes red at their corners with rage, pierced Khara in battle with a thousand arrows.
From the gaps between the arrows blood flowed forth in great foaming streams, like the rushing flow of water cascading from a mountain spring.
Though made frantic by the arrows in combat with Rāma, Khara, intoxicated by the smell of blood, rushed swiftly at him.
As he charged in frenzied fury, drenched in blood, Rāma — skilled in weaponry — with swift, measured steps yielded ground slightly before him.
Then Rāma took up an arrow blazing like fire for the killing of Khara in battle — a second rod of Brahmā, as it were.
That arrow — given formerly by the wise king of the gods, Maghavat (Indra) — the righteous-souled Rāma nocked and released it toward Khara.
Released with the bow raised, that mighty arrow, thundering like a thunderclap, struck Khara square in the chest.
Khara fell to the ground, consumed by the fire of that arrow, even as Andhaka was burned up by Rudra himself in the Śveta forest.
Khara fell slain — as Vṛtra fell by the thunderbolt, as Namuci fell by the foam, as Bali fell struck by Indra's thunderbolt.
Then all the royal sages and the great seers assembled together, honoured Rāma with joyful hearts, and spoke these words.
For this very purpose did the great and resplendent Mahendra, the chastiser of Pāka, the destroyer of cities, come to the sacred hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
You were brought to this region by the device of the great sages, for the purpose of slaying these cruel rākṣasas of evil deeds.
This task of ours has been accomplished by you, O son of Daśaratha — the great sages shall now live and follow righteousness in the Daṇḍaka forests in peace.
In the meantime, the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sītā, emerged from the mountain fortress and happily entered their hermitage.
Then the victorious hero Rāma, honoured by the great sages, entered the hermitage, greeted with reverence by Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing him — the destroyer of enemies, the bringer of joy to the great sages — Vaidehī was filled with delight and embraced her husband.
Then Śūrpaṇakhā, having seen fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds slain single-handedly by Rāma,
and Dūṣaṇa, Khara, and Triśiras slain in battle, let out once more a great cry, like a cloud bursting.
Having witnessed this deed of Rāma's, impossible for others to accomplish, she went in extreme agitation to Laṅkā, the realm protected by Rāvaṇa.
She saw Rāvaṇa at the fore of his palace, blazing with splendour, seated in the company of his ministers as Vāsava sits surrounded by the Maruts.
Seated upon a splendid golden throne brilliant as the sun, placed upon a golden dais, blazing like fire.
Unconquerable in battle by gods, gandharvas, spirits, and great-souled sages alike — a hero with gaping mouth like Death himself.
His body bearing scars made by Indra's thunderbolt in battles between gods and asuras, his chest scarred and furrowed by the tusks of Airāvata.
Twenty-armed, ten-headed, with splendid attire, broad-chested, heroic, bearing the marks of royalty.
His complexion like polished vaidūrya gem, wearing earrings of burnished gold, with handsome arms, white teeth, a vast mouth, and a form like a mountain.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
His body struck hundreds of times by Viṣṇu's discus in battles with the gods, and likewise by all the weapons of the devas.
Who stirs the unstirrable oceans, swift in action, who hurls the peaks of mountains and crushes the gods.
Destroyer of righteousness, violator of others' wives, wielder of all divine weapons, ever a disrupter of sacrifices.
Who went to the city of Bhogavatī, defeated Vāsuki, and then overpowering Takṣaka, carried off his beloved wife.
Who went to Mount Kailāsa, defeated Kubera who rides men as his vehicle, and seized his wish-fulfilling aerial chariot, the Puṣpaka.
Who, mighty in valour, out of rage devastates the celestial garden of Caitraratha, and the lotus pond, and the grove of Nandana, and the parks of the gods.
Who, standing like a mountain peak, holds back with his own arms the mighty Sun and Moon when they rise — those two of great splendour who afflict their foes.
Who, resolute, in ancient times performed asceticism for ten thousand years in the great forest, and then offered his own heads to Svayambhū (Brahmā).
Whom gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, birds, and serpents cannot threaten with death in battle — save only a mortal man.
He of great might who seizes the soma from the sacrificial vessels — the holy and gratifying offerings — when the twice-born perform their sacred rites.
That pillager of duly performed sacrifices, cruel, slayer of Brāhmaṇas, of corrupt conduct, harsh, without compassion, intent on harming subjects — Rāvaṇa, a terror to all beings and to all the worlds.
The rākṣasī saw her cruel and mighty brother — adorned with divine garments and ornaments, beautified with divine garlands — the lord of the rākṣasas, the illustrious delight of the Paulastya lineage.
Displaying her blazing, wide eyes, overcome with fear, confusion, and anguish, Śūrpaṇakhā — who had walked fearlessly before but was now disfigured by the great-souled Rāma — spoke these most terrible words to him.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Śūrpaṇakhā, wretched and enraged, spoke harsh words to Rāvaṇa, the terror of the world, in the midst of his ministers.
"You are intoxicated with sensual pleasures, wandering at will, unchecked — you do not perceive the terrible danger that has arisen, which ought to be understood."
"A lord of the earth who is addicted to vulgar pleasures, ruled by desire, and greedy — his subjects do not hold him in esteem, just as they regard a cremation-ground fire."
"A king who does not himself attend to affairs at the proper time perishes together with his kingdom and those very affairs."
"Men shun from afar a lord of men who has no proper intelligence-network, who is hard to approach, and who has lost self-mastery — as elephants shun the mire of a river."
"Those lords of men who have lost self-mastery and do not protect their realm do not shine with prosperity, just as mountains do not shine within the ocean."
"Having made enemies of those with composure — gods, gandharvas, and dānavas — lacking intelligence-service and being fickle, how will you remain a king?"
"O best among conquerors, those lords of men whose intelligence-network, treasury, and statecraft are not under their own control are equal to common people."
"Because lords of men see through their spies all matters even from afar, kings are therefore called 'those of far-reaching sight.'"
"I consider you to be without proper intelligence-service, surrounded by ordinary ministers — for you did not perceive the slaughter of your own people in Janasthāna."
"Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds have been slain by Rāma alone, and Khara together with Dūṣaṇa as well."
"Safety has been granted to the sages, the Daṇḍaka forest has been made secure, and Janasthāna has been overrun by Rāma, whose deeds are effortless."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"But you, Rāvaṇa, are greedy, heedless, and dependent on others — you who do not perceive the danger that has arisen in your own domain."
"All creatures do not rush to the aid of a king in misfortune who is harsh, gives little, is heedless, arrogant, and deceitful."
"Even his own people slay a lord of men in his misfortune who is excessively proud, unapproachable, self-conceited, and irascible."
"He who does not attend to affairs and does not fear dangers will swiftly be cast from his kingdom and become wretched, equal to a blade of grass."
"One may find use in dry wood, in clods of earth, even in dust — but there is no use in lords of the earth who have fallen from their station."
"Just as a garment already worn, or a garland already crushed, so one fallen from kingship is without value even if capable."
"A king who is vigilant, omniscient, who has conquered his senses, is grateful, and is devoted to righteousness — such a king endures long."
"Though asleep with his eyes, he is awake with the eye of statecraft; and whose anger and favor are clearly manifest — such a king is honored by the people."
"But you, Rāvaṇa of wicked intellect, are devoid of these virtues — you by whose spies the great slaughter of your rākṣasas was not made known to you."
"One who despises others, addicted to sense-pleasures, ignorant of the true nature of distinctions of place and time, of disordered intellect in judging merits and faults — such a ruined king will soon come to total destruction."
Thus having considered with his intellect those own faults enumerated by her, Rāvaṇa — the lord of those who move in the night, endowed with wealth, pride, and power — reflected for a long while.
Then Rāvaṇa, himself aroused to anger, questioned Śūrpaṇakhā who was speaking harsh words in anger, in the midst of his ministers.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Who is this Rāma? What is his valor? What is his form, and what his prowess? And for what reason has he entered the Daṇḍaka forest, which is so very hard to penetrate?"
"What is Rāma's weapon, with which the rākṣasas were slain, and Khara was killed in battle along with Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras?"
Thus addressed by the lord of rākṣasas, the rākṣasī, overcome with rage, then began to describe Rāma in proper order.
"Rāma, son of Daśaratha, is long-armed, broad-eyed, clad in barkcloth and black antelope skin, and equal in beauty to the god of love."
"Drawing his bow that resembles Indra's rainbow, with his golden armlets, he releases blazing iron arrows like mighty venomous serpents."
"In the battle I could not see Rāma, that great warrior, taking up his terrible arrows, releasing them, or drawing his bow — so swift was he."
"Yet I saw that army being slain by showers of arrows, as the finest crop is struck down by Indra's hailstorms."
"Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible valor have been slain by sharp arrows by that one man fighting on foot."
"In somewhat more than half a muhūrta, Khara together with Dūṣaṇa was slain; safety was granted to the sages, and the Daṇḍaka forest was made secure."
"I alone escaped somehow, scorned by that great-souled Rāma, that knower of the self, who was reluctant to slay a woman."
"His brother too is of great splendor, equal in valor by virtue of his qualities, devoted and loyal — the mighty one named Lakṣmaṇa."
"Intolerant of insult, unconquerable, a victor, valiant, wise, and powerful — he is the right arm of Rāma, always like his life-breath moving outside him."
"Rāma's lawful wife is the renowned Vaidehī, named Sītā, broad-eyed, of excellent hips, slender-waisted."
"Neither goddess, nor gandharvī, nor yakṣī, nor kiṃnarī — no woman of such beauty have I ever seen before on this earth."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"He whose wife Sītā might be, whom she might joyfully embrace — that one would surpass even Indra the destroyer of citadels in all the worlds."
"She is of good character, praiseworthy of form, without peer in beauty on earth — she is the fitting wife for you, and you would be the fitting husband for her."
"Her of the broad hips and full, high breasts, of lovely face — I set out to bring her to you for your wife."
"When you behold that Vaidehī today, whose face is like the full moon, you will fall under the command of the arrows of Manmatha, the god of love."
"If the desire for her as your wife arises in you, then quickly raise your right foot here for the march to victory."
"Do what is dear to those rākṣasas likewise, O lord of rākṣasas, by slaying that cruel Rāma who dwells in the hermitage."
"Having slain him with sharp arrows, and Lakṣmaṇa the great chariot-warrior, you will enjoy Sītā, deprived of her lord, easily and as you please."
"If this my speech pleases you, O lord of rākṣasas, then let my words be carried out without hesitation, O Rāghava."
"Having heard of the night-wanderers stationed in Janasthāna slain by Rāma's straight-flying arrows, and knowing that Khara and Dūṣaṇa have been killed, you ought today to undertake the proper course of action."
Then Śūrpaṇakhā, having heard that hair-raising speech, took leave of the ministers, and having determined upon her course of action, departed.
And having pursued that matter, having properly comprehended it, and having weighed the strengths and weaknesses of faults and merits,
Having thus made his own firm resolve — "this is what must be done" — he, of steadfast mind, then went to the charming vehicle-hall.
Having gone to the vehicle-hall, the lord of rākṣasas then secretly commanded the charioteer: "Let the chariot be yoked."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus commanded, the charioteer of swift movements yoked in an instant that excellent chariot which was his master's favorite.
Mounting the golden chariot that could go wherever desired, adorned with jewels, yoked with mules of piśāca-faces, ornamented with gold,
With a roar resembling that of a thundercloud, the glorious lord of rākṣasas, younger brother of Kubera the lord of wealth, set forth to the lord of rivers and streams — the ocean.
He with the white fly-whisk and white parasol, the ten-faced one, gleaming like polished vaidūrya gemstone, adorned with refined gold ornaments —
Ten-mouthed, twenty-armed, of magnificent attire, enemy of the gods, slayer of the lords of sages — like the king of mountains himself with ten peaks.
Mounted on his wish-moving chariot, the lord of rākṣasas shone resplendent like a cloud wreathed with lightning, accompanied by cranes in the sky.
The mighty one gazed upon the landscape with its mountains and ocean shores, strewn with thousands of trees bearing manifold flowers and fruits,
Surrounded on all sides by lotus-pools with cool and auspicious waters, covered with vast hermitage sites possessing sacrificial altars,
Thronged with plantain and āḍhakī plants, adorned with coconut palms, with śāla, palm, tamāla and other trees in full bloom,
Beautified by great sages of most rigorously regulated diet, and by thousands of nāgas, suparṇas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras,
Adorned with siddhas who have conquered desire, and with cāmaṇas, Ājas, Vaikhānasas, Māṣas, Vālakhilyas, and Marīcipas,
Enveloped by thousands of apsarases bearing divine ornaments and garlands, of divine beauty, versed in the arts of sport and love,
Frequented by the radiant wives of gods, invested with beauty, and traversed by throngs of gods and dānavas who subsist on ambrosia,

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Filled with haṃsas, krauñcas, and plavas, resounding with the calls of sārasas, its vaidūrya-gem floor charming and gleaming with the ocean's luminosity,
White and vast celestial vehicles adorned with divine garlands, resounding with musical instruments and song, on every side —
Wish-moving vehicles of those who had won worlds through austerities, flying about — thus did the younger brother of Kubera behold gandharvas and apsarases.
He saw thousands of gentle, fragrance-satisfying sandalwood groves with their resinous sap at their roots,
And forests and garden-groves of the finest agaru trees, and of takkola, jātī, and fragrant fruit trees,
And flowers of the tamāla tree, thickets of pepper plants, and heaps of pearls drying along the shore,
And beds of conch-shells and heaps of coral, and mountains of gold and silver everywhere,
And charming springs and pellucid lakes endowed with treasure and grain, surrounded by gem-like women,
He looked upon cities dense with elephants, horses, and chariots, and that even, uniformly pleasant land with its gentle-to-the-touch breezes,
He saw the riverine land of the lord of rivers, resembling heaven. There he beheld a cloud-like banyan tree surrounded by sages.
That tree whose branches extended a hundred yojanas in all directions — to one of whose branches the mighty Garuḍa came, carrying an elephant and a great-bodied tortoise for his meal.
That best of birds, the mighty Suparṇa, suddenly broke that leafy branch of it with the weight, the great-powered one.
There were assembled Vaikhānasas, Māṣas, Vālakhilyas, Marīcipas, Ajas, and Dhūmras — great sages gathered together.
Out of compassion for them, Garuḍa swiftly took up that branch of a hundred yojanas, together with both the elephant and the tortoise,
And that righteous-souled best of birds, having consumed that meat with one foot, having struck the Niṣāda country with the branch, gained incomparable joy, having freed the great sages.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And with that very joy, his power doubled, the wise one formed the resolve to fetch the ambrosia.
Having churned through the iron nets and broken open the finest jeweled chamber, he then fetched the ambrosia that was guarded in Mahendra's abode.
That banyan tree frequented by hosts of great sages, bearing the mark made by Suparṇa, named Subhadrā — this the younger brother of Kubera beheld.
Having gone to the far shore of the ocean, the lord of rivers, he saw a hermitage set apart in a holy, charming forest-grove.
There he saw the rākṣasa named Mārīca, wearing a black antelope skin, bearing matted locks and barkcloth, of regulated diet.
Rāvaṇa met with that rākṣasa according to proper courtesy, and thereafter, skilled in speech, spoke these words.
"O Mārīca, dear one, hear the words I now speak to you. I am in distress, and for me in distress you are indeed the highest refuge."
"You know Janasthāna, where my brother Khara dwells, and the mighty-armed Dūṣaṇa, and my sister Śūrpaṇakhā as well."
"And the greatly resplendent flesh-eating rākṣasa Triśiras, and many other valiant night-roving rākṣasas of unerring aim."
"Those rākṣasas dwell there under my command and as my appointed garrison, oppressing in that great forest the sages who walk in righteousness."
"Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds, valiant and unerring in aim, following the will of Khara —"
"— those great-powered ones now dwelling in Janasthāna met in total dependence upon one another in battle with Rāma."
"By that Rāma, inflamed with wrath, without speaking a single harsh word, his bow was set to work with arrows at the forefront of battle."
"Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds were slain with sharp arrows by that human fighting on foot."
"Khara was slain in battle and Dūṣaṇa was felled; having also killed Triśiras, he made the Daṇḍaka forest free from fear."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This Rāma, disgrace of the kṣatriyas, banished by his angry father along with his wife as one whose life-force is spent — he is the slayer of that army."
"He is without virtue, harsh, cruel, foolish, greedy, with unmastered senses, one who has abandoned dharma — a soul of adharma, devoted to the harm of all beings."
"By him, without cause in the forest, relying solely on his own courage, my sister was disfigured by the cutting off of her ears and nose."
"His wife Sītā, who resembles the daughter of a god, I shall carry away by force from Janasthāna. Be my helper in this."
"With you, O great-powered one, standing at my side as my helper, and with my brothers, I do not give thought even to all the gods in battle."
"Therefore be my helper — you are capable, O rākṣasa; in valour, in battle, and in pride there is none equal to you."
"For this purpose I have come to your presence, O night-rover. Hear the act of assistance to be performed at my word."
"Becoming a golden deer dappled with silver spots, roam before Sītā at the hermitage of that Rāma."
"Sītā, upon seeing you in the form of a deer, will without doubt urge her husband and Lakṣmaṇa saying: 'Catch it!'"
"Then, once those two have gone away and the place is empty, I shall carry off Sītā at my ease without hindrance, as Rāhu seizes the moon's radiance."
"Afterwards, when Rāma is wasted by the abduction of his wife, I shall strike him at ease, assured and satisfied in my inmost heart."
Upon hearing Rāvaṇa's words, the great-souled Mārīca's mouth became dry and he was seized with terror.
He, with mind terrified and downcast, knowing the might of Rāma, addressed Rāvaṇa in that great forest with joined palms, speaking words that were truthful and salutary both for him and for himself.
Having heard the words of the lord of rākṣasas, the highly wise Mārīca, skilled in speech, replied to the lord of rākṣasas:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Men who ever speak pleasing words, O king, are easily found; but one who speaks and one who hears what is unpleasant yet salutary — both are rare."
"Surely you do not perceive Rāma — of great valour and exalted in virtues, comparable to Mahendra and Varuṇa — for you are of wayward conduct and restless mind."
"I hope, dear one, that all the rākṣasas on earth may be well; I hope that Rāma, when angered, may not make the world free of rākṣasas."
"I hope that the daughter of Janaka has not arisen to be the end of your life; I hope that Sītā may not become the cause of a great calamity."
"I hope that the city of Laṅkā, having obtained you as its lord — unrestrained and acting on desire — may not perish along with all its rākṣasas and with you."
"For a king of your kind — acting on desire, of evil character, taking wicked counsel — that foolish one destroys himself, his own people, and his kingdom."
"Rāma was not abandoned by his father, nor is he in any way transgressor of decorum; he is not greedy, nor of evil character, nor a disgrace to the kṣatriyas."
"The increaser of Kausalyā's joy is not devoid of the virtues of dharma; he is not cruel — indeed he is devoted to the welfare of all beings."
"Seeing his father, a man of truthful speech, deceived by Kaikeyī, the dharma-souled one said 'I shall do it,' and thereupon went forth to the forest."
"For the sake of Kaikeyī's desired happiness and his father Daśaratha's, he abandoned his kingdom and pleasures and entered the Daṇḍaka forest."
"Rāma is not harsh, dear one, nor ignorant, nor of unmastered senses; what is untrue has never been heard of him — you ought not speak so."
"Rāma is dharma embodied, a righteous man of true valour, king of all the world as Vāsava is king of the gods."
"How do you wish to forcibly carry away his Vaidehī, protected by his own blazing energy, as though stealing the radiance of the sun?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You ought not rashly enter that Rāma-fire blazing in battle, unapproachable, fed by bow and sword, with arrows as its flames."
"That hero, bearing bow and arrows, whose blazing mouth is spread wide with his bow, whose flames are arrows, intolerant, the destroyer of enemy armies —"
"— having abandoned kingdom, ease, and your own dear life, you ought not, dear one, rush up to Rāma here, who is the very end of you."
"Immeasurable is the blazing energy of him whose Janakātmajā she is; you are not able to carry her away in the forest, for she takes refuge in Rāma's bow."
"The slender-waisted Sītā, ever devoted, more dear to him than his own life, is like the flame of a blazing sacrificial fire — to touch her is to be consumed."
"Why undertake this futile effort, O lord of rākṣasas? Should you be seen by him in battle, that is the end of your life — your life, your happiness, and your kingdom, all so difficult to obtain."
"Together with all your ministers, with the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa placed foremost among them, having deliberated and resolved upon your own course of action —"
"— having weighed well the strengths and weaknesses of faults and virtues, and knowing truly your own strength and that of Rāghava, you ought to determine what is beneficial for you and act accordingly."
"But I think it is not fitting for you to meet the son of the king of Kosala in battle. Hear again this excellent, fitting, and appropriate word, O lord of night-rovers."
"Once upon a time, roaming this earth out of my own valour, bearing the strength of a thousand elephants, mountain-like in form —"
"— dark as a rain-cloud, with earrings of refined gold, causing fear to the world, crowned, armed with a club, I roamed the Daṇḍaka forest eating the flesh of sages."
"Then the great sage Viśvāmitra, dharma-souled and terrified of me, went himself to Daśaratha, lord of men, and said this:"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'Let this Rāma, with concentrated mind, protect me during the ritual observance period; a terrible fear from Mārīca has arisen for me, O lord of men.'"
"Thus addressed, the dharma-souled king Daśaratha at that time replied to the greatly blessed great sage Viśvāmitra:"
"'This Rāghava is not yet sixteen years old and has not mastered weapons; but whatever army of mine will march with me — I shall slay your enemy, O best of sages, as you desire.'"
"Thus addressed, the sage replied again to the king: 'Other than Rāma, no force in the world is sufficient against that rākṣasa.'"
"'Even though a boy, this one of great blazing energy is capable of subduing him. I shall go taking Rāma — may you be well, O scorcher of foes.'"
"Having spoken thus, the sage Viśvāmitra, exceedingly pleased, took that son of the king and went to his own hermitage."
"Then Rāma, consecrated for the sacrifice in the Daṇḍaka forest, stood there wondrously bending his bow."
"A beautiful youth whose secondary marks had not yet appeared, dark-complexioned, of auspicious eyes, wearing a single garment, bearing his bow, with a topknot adorned by a golden garland —"
"— illuminating the Daṇḍaka forest with his own blazing energy, Rāma appeared at that time like a new moon rising."
"Then I, resembling a rain-cloud, with earrings of refined gold, powerful, having obtained a boon, came to that hermitage out of pride."
"Seen by him as I entered, he instantly raised his weapon. But upon seeing me, without any agitation, he strung his bow."
"Despising Rāghava out of delusion — thinking 'this is just a boy' — I rushed with great haste toward Viśvāmitra's sacrificial altar."
"Then a sharp arrow was released by him, the destroyer of enemies; struck by it, I was hurled into the sea a hundred yojanas away."
"Driven away by the velocity of Rāma's arrow, my wits reeling, I was cast down by him into the deep ocean waters. After a long time regaining my senses, dear one, I made my way back to the city of Laṅkā."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Thus was I merely released at that time, while your helpers were slain — by that Rāma who had not yet mastered all weapons, a boy of effortless deeds."
"Therefore, if you, though warned by me, enter into conflict with Rāma, you will swiftly meet a terrible calamity and perish."
"You will bring grief and calamity upon the rākṣasas who delight in sport and the arts of pleasure, who are distinguished by their gatherings and festivals."
"You will see the city of Laṅkā, crowded with mansions and palaces, adorned with jewels of every kind, ruined on account of the Maithilī."
"Even those who do no evil themselves, innocent ones, are destroyed by another's sin through association with sin — as fish perish in a lake infested with a serpent."
"You will see rākṣasas whose bodies are anointed with divine sandal-paste and adorned with divine ornaments, struck down upon the ground — through your fault."
"You will see night-rovers fleeing in all ten directions, their wives stolen, with wives, survivors of slaughter, shelterless."
"You will see Laṅkā — surrounded by a net of arrows, enveloped in tongues of fire, its dwellings burnt to ash — this is without doubt."
"Thousands of women are your household, O king. Be devoted to your own wives; protect your own lineage, O rākṣasa."
"Honour, prosperity, kingdom, and your own dear life — if you wish to enjoy these long, do not do what is displeasing to Rāma."
"If, though earnestly restrained by me your friend, you persist by force and violate Sītā, you will go — with your strength exhausted, your life taken by Rāma's arrow, together with your kinsmen — to the realm of Yama."
In this way I was barely freed from him in that combat. Now hear what further occurred even after that.
Undeterred even after being so dealt with by those two rākṣasas, I entered the Daṇḍaka forest together with them, both of them having taken the form of deer.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
With blazing tongue, a great body, sharp horns, and immense strength, I roamed the Daṇḍaka forest as a mighty beast, feeding on flesh.
O Rāvaṇa, utterly terrible, I roamed about at sacrificial fires, at sacred fords, at holy trees — harassing the ascetics there.
Slaying the pious ascetics in the Daṇḍaka forest, I drank their blood and devoured their flesh.
Eating the flesh of sages, cruel and intoxicated with blood, I wandered through the Daṇḍaka forest, terrifying all who dwelt there.
While I was thus ranging through the Daṇḍaka forest as a transgressor of righteousness, I then encountered Rāma — an ascetic abiding in dharma.
And the illustrious Vaidehī, and Lakṣmaṇa the great warrior — an ascetic of regulated diet, devoted to the welfare of all creatures.
I — recalling old enmity and thinking him merely an ascetic — showed contempt for the mighty Rāma dwelling in the forest.
In a form of a deer with sharp horns, full of rage, mindless, remembering his previous blow against me, I rushed at him with intent to kill.
He drew his great bow with force and released three sharp arrows, destroyers of enemies, swift as Garuḍa or the wind.
Those three arrows, thunderbolt-like, utterly terrible, feeding on blood, and straight-jointed, came flying together and struck.
I, the cheat, knowing Rāma's prowess and having felt his power before, sprang up and fled — and both those rākṣasas were slain.
Barely escaping Rāma's arrow alive, I was banished here, and now I live as a composed ascetic, disciplined and intent.
In every tree I see Rāma wearing bark-cloth and black antelope skin, bearing his bow, like Death himself with a noose in hand.
In my fear I see thousands of Rāmas, O Rāvaṇa — this entire forest appears to me as if it were Rāma himself.
Even in solitude, O lord of rākṣasas, I see only Rāma — seeing Rāma even in my dreams, I start up senseless.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
O Rāvaṇa, every name beginning with the syllable 'ra' — and even jewels and chariots — causes terror in me, so frightened am I of Rāma.
I know his power well — battle with him is not fitting for you. Either fight Rāma in battle, or make peace, O rākṣasa. If you wish to see me again, speak no further of Rāma.
This counsel, spoken by me for the good of your kinsmen — if you do not heed it as spoken, you and your kinsmen shall lose your lives, slain today in battle by Rāma's straight-flying arrows.
Rāvaṇa, thus addressed by Mārīca with words appropriate and fitting, did not accept them — as one who desires death refuses medicine.
The lord of rākṣasas, driven by fate, spoke harsh and unsuitable words to Mārīca, who had spoken what was wholesome and beneficial.
"What is told to me by you, O Mārīca, is altogether improper in meaning — utterly fruitless speech, like seed sown in barren ground.
By your words you cannot shake my resolve in battle against Rāma — especially not against that sinful, foolish mortal.
He who abandoned friends, kingdom, mother, and father alike — and at the ordinary words of a woman departed to the forest at one step.
Sītā, more dear to him than life, must certainly be taken from that slayer of Khara in combat — before your very eyes.
Such, O Mārīca, is the firm resolve that abides in my heart — it cannot be turned back even by the gods and asuras with Indra at their head.
When asked, you ought to speak of fault or virtue, of risk or remedy — in determining what is to be done in this matter.
A wise minister who desires his own welfare, when questioned, should speak to the king with hands raised in reverence.
The lord of the earth should be addressed with speech that is not contrary, beginning with gentleness, auspicious, beneficial, and delivered with proper courtesy.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
But the beneficial counsel that is spoken condescendingly, O Mārīca — a king worthy of honour does not rejoice in such words, stripped as they are of respect.
Kings of immeasurable might bear five natures: those of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Varuṇa — heat and valour, graciousness, punishment, and serenity.
Therefore kings are to be honoured and revered in all circumstances. But you, not understanding dharma, have resorted to mere delusion.
You address me, your guest, with such harsh words out of malice. I do not question merits and faults, nor what is appropriate for myself, O rākṣasa — in this matter, you ought to render me assistance.
Becoming a golden deer, dappled with silver spots, you shall entice Vaidehī and then go where you please.
Seeing you, a magical golden deer, Maithilī — full of wonder — will quickly say to Rāma: 'Bring me this creature.'
And when Kākutstha has gone away, and Lakṣmaṇa too, I shall carry off Vaidehī at ease, just as the thousand-eyed Indra carried off Śacī.
Having accomplished this task, go where you please, O rākṣasa. I shall give you half the kingdom, O Mārīca of good vows."
"Go, dear one, travel a safe path for the accomplishment of this task. Having obtained Sītā and deceived Rāghava without battle, I shall return to Laṅkā with you, my purpose fulfilled."
"You shall carry out this task for me, even by compulsion — for one who opposes a king never prospers in any way."
"Should you encounter him, your life will be in peril — death is certain if you oppose me today. Having considered this properly with your mind, do that which is best for you here."
Thus commanded, the night-wanderer Mārīca, though the order was contrary to his counsel, spoke harsh words to the lord of rākṣasas.
"By what evil-doer has this destruction been counselled to you, O night-wanderer — destruction of you with your sons, your kingdom, and your ministers?

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"What sinful one, O king, does not rejoice in your happiness? By whom has this gateway to death been pointed out to you as a course of action?
"Clearly your enemies, O night-wanderer — weak in valour — desire to see you destroyed, restrained by one mightier than yourself.
"By what base and malicious counsellor has this been advised to you — one who desires to see you perish by your own deed, O night-wanderer?
"Your ministers, O Rāvaṇa, deserve death and yet are not slain — those who do not restrain you in every way when you have strayed onto a wrong path.
"Indeed, a king swayed by passion who has taken a wicked path must be restrained in every way by virtuous men — yet you, who ought to be restrained, are not being restrained.
"Dharma, wealth, pleasure, and glory — ministers attain all these through the favour of their lord, O best of conquerors, O night-wanderer.
"But in the reverse case, all that becomes worthless, O Rāvaṇa — and other people too suffer calamity on account of a flawed master.
"For dharma and victory both have the king as their root, O best of conquerors. Therefore the lord of men must be protected in all circumstances.
"A kingdom cannot be governed by one who is harsh, O night-wanderer, nor by one who is contrary, nor by one who is ill-bred, O rākṣasa.
"Ministers who give harsh counsel are broken along with their king in adversity — just as swift chariots with poor drivers come to ruin on rough terrain.
"Many virtuous men in the world, who practised dharma fittingly, have been ruined together with their households because of the transgressions of others.
"Subjects guarded by a harsh and perverse master do not flourish, O Rāvaṇa — just as sheep do not thrive when guarded by a jackal.
"All the rākṣasas will surely perish, O Rāvaṇa — those whose king you are: harsh, evil-minded, with unmastered senses.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You have brought about this terrible crow-and-palm coincidence upon yourself. What is auspicious in this — that you shall perish together with your army?
"After killing me, that Rāma will swiftly slay you as well. By this I consider my purpose fulfilled — that I die slain by an enemy.
"At the very sight of Rāma, consider me already slain. And know yourself slain too, along with all your kinsmen, once you have abducted Sītā.
"If you bring Sītā from her hermitage, with me as your accomplice — neither you shall exist, nor I, nor Laṅkā, nor the rākṣasas.
"Though restrained by me who wish you well, you do not endure this counsel, O night-wanderer — for men whose lives are spent, resembling the dead, do not accept the benefit spoken by friends."
Having spoken thus harshly, Mārīca then said to Rāvaṇa, "Let us go," reduced to submission by fear of the lord of night-wanderers.
"I have again come face to face with him who bears bow, arrows, and sword, and whose weapon was raised for my slaying — my life is already as good as destroyed."
"Yet what can I do when you, O wicked one, are like this? I shall go. May it be well with you, O night-wanderer."
That rākṣasa was overjoyed by those words; embracing him tightly, he spoke as follows.
"This speech of yours, full of courage, sounds as if it were said at my own bidding. Now you are truly Mārīca; formerly you were a different night-wanderer."
"Mount quickly this sky-ranging chariot adorned with jewels, yoked with donkeys bearing the faces of piśācas, together with me."
Thereupon Rāvaṇa and Mārīca mounted that chariot, which resembled an aerial vehicle, and departed swiftly from that hermitage-region.
As they traveled they observed towns and forests, mountains and all rivers, kingdoms and cities below.
Arriving at the Daṇḍaka forest, the lord of rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa, together with Mārīca, then saw the hermitage of Rāghava.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Descending from that golden-ornamented chariot and taking Mārīca by the hand, Rāvaṇa spoke these words.
"That hermitage-site of Rāma, encircled by banana trees, is visible yonder. Friend, do swiftly that for the sake of which we have come."
Hearing those words of Rāvaṇa, the rākṣasa Mārīca thereupon transformed himself into a deer and began to roam about at the entrance of Rāma's hermitage.
His horn-tips were of finest gems; his face was of mingled white and black hues, like a red lotus and a blue water-lily; his ears were like indranīla-blue lotuses.
His neck was somewhat arched, his belly resembled the indranīla gem in hue, his flanks were like the madhūka flower, and his body was like the filaments of a lotus.
His hooves resembled vaidūrya gems; his shanks were slender and well-knit; his tail, held aloft, gleamed with the colors of Indra's rainbow.
With a mind-entrancing, glossy complexion and covered all over with gems of many kinds, in an instant the rākṣasa became a deer of supreme beauty.
Illuminating the lovely forest and that hermitage-site of Rāma, the rākṣasa, having assumed that mind-enchanting, wondrous form—
—variegated with minerals of many kinds, for the purpose of enticing Vaidehī, moved about properly among the green meadows on all sides.
Adorned with hundreds of silver spots and having become pleasing to behold, he wandered about, snapping off and nibbling the tender shoots of trees.
Going toward the banana grove, resting now here now there among the karṇikāra trees, moving at a slow pace, he sought at that time to be seen by Sītā.
That great deer, his back dappled like a lotus, shone brilliantly as he wandered at ease in the vicinity of Rāma's hermitage.
That foremost of deer would go forward and then return, roaming about; having gone away for a moment with speed, he would come back again.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He would play again, then seat himself on the ground once more; approaching the hermitage gate, he would move off toward herds of deer.
Followed by herds of deer, he would return once more — the rākṣasa, having assumed deer-form, yearning to be seen by Sītā.
He wheeled about in varied circles, bounding through them; and all the other deer that roamed the forest looked up and saw him—
—approached him, sniffed him, and then fled in all ten directions. That rākṣasa, intent on the slaughter of deer, also pursued those wild deer—
—yet for the purpose of concealing his true nature he did not devour them even when he touched them. At that very time Vaidehī of lovely eyes—
—intent on gathering flowers, was moving among the trees — karṇikāras, aśokas, and mango trees — she of intoxicating eyes.
Plucking flowers and roaming about with her lovely face — she who was undeserving of forest-life — that foremost of women beheld that gem-jeweled deer, its limbs variegated with pearls and precious stones.
That deer with beautiful teeth and lips, its body-hair like silver mineral, she gazed upon with eyes wide open in wonder, and with affection.
And that deer, made of illusion, looking back at her — Rāma's beloved — roamed about there as if setting the forest ablaze with its brilliance.
Never before having seen such a deer, all made of varied gems, Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, was seized by the greatest astonishment.
She of beautiful hips, while gathering flowers, gazed intently at that deer adorned on both flanks with hues of gold and silver—
—and, filled with delight, that woman of flawless limbs and the color of refined gold called out to her husband and also to Lakṣmaṇa bearing his weapons.
Those two tigers among men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, called by Vaidehī, scanning that spot, then both saw the deer.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
But Lakṣmaṇa, suspicious upon seeing it, said to Rāma: "This deer — I take it to be none other than the rākṣasa Mārīca."
"O Rāma, kings who roamed the forest on the hunt, rejoicing, have been slain in the forest by this wicked deceiver who changes form at will."
"This form of an illusory deer has been fashioned by this master of māyā — O tiger among men of brilliant valor, it is like a city of the Gandharvas."
"For a deer of this kind, variegated with gems, does not exist anywhere in the world, O Rāghava, O lord of the earth — this is undoubtedly illusion."
Interrupting Kākutstha who was speaking thus, Sītā of the pure smile spoke, thrilled with delight, her mind stolen away by the ruse.
"O noble son, that deer ravishes my mind with its beauty. Bring it here, O mighty-armed one — it shall be our plaything."
"Here at our hermitage-site many auspicious-looking deer wander together — camaras, sṛmaras, and others—"
"—bears, herds of spotted deer, monkeys, and kiṃnaras too roam here, O mighty-armed one, most beautiful in form and of great strength—"
"—yet no deer equal to this one has ever been seen before, O king, in radiance, grace, and brilliance, as this foremost of deer."
"With limbs variegated in many colors, studded all over with gem-spots, illuminating the forest serenely, it shines like the moon."
"Ah, what beauty! Ah, what splendor! And what a lovely richness of voice! That wondrous, marvelous deer steals away my heart, it seems."
"If this deer comes to be captured alive by you, it would become a wonder and shall cause amazement."
"When our forest-exile is complete and we return to dwelling in the kingdom, this deer shall serve as an ornament for the inner apartments."
"This divine deer-form shall cause amazement to noble Bharata, to my lord, to my mothers-in-law, and to myself, O lord."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"If this foremost of deer does not come to be taken alive by you, O tiger among men, its beautiful hide shall be mine."
"When this creature has been slain, I wish to sit upon its skin, which is made of jāmbūnada gold, spread out on a grass mat."
"This excessive desire may be considered dreadful and unlike what is fitting for women — yet it is the wondrous beauty of this creature that has aroused it in me."
By that deer with golden hair, with horns of finest gems, with the color of the newly risen sun, with the luminosity of the path of the stars — Rāghava's mind too was seized by wonder.
Having heard Sītā's words thus and having seen that wondrous deer, Rāghava, filled with delight, spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
"See, Lakṣmaṇa, this yearning of Vaidehī directed toward the deer. By reason of its supreme beauty this deer shall not escape today."
"Neither in Nandana forest nor in the domain of Caitraratha — where then in the whole earth, O son of Sumitrā, is there any deer equal to this one?"
"Lovely rows of hair, running both against and with the grain, adorned with golden spots of varied hues, shine beautifully upon this deer."
"See its tongue as it yawns — blazing, like a flame of fire, issuing from its mouth like lightning from a cloud."
"With a face of masāra and galvarka gems, a belly resembling conch-shells and pearls — whose mind, tell me, would that deer of indescribable form not entice?"
"Upon seeing this form with the radiance of jāmbūnada gold, divine and made of gems of many kinds, whose mind would not be overcome by wonder?"
"Kings who are bowmen slay deer in the great forest during the hunt, O Lakṣmaṇa, for the sake of both their flesh and sport."
"Wealth is also sought through enterprise in the great forest, as are various minerals, along with gems, precious stones, and gold."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"All that which is the wealth-essence of men — wealth that increases accumulation — is found here in the forest, just as it was conceived in the mind of Śukra, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"The purpose for which a man in need of wealth roams without hesitation — that very wealth the knowers of artha-śāstra and wealthy men praise, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"On the supremely precious golden hide of this jewel among deer, the slender-waisted Vaidehī will sit with me."
"Neither the kādalī, nor the priyakī, nor a rug, nor wool would be comparable to this in softness of touch — such is my judgment."
"This glorious deer here, and that divine one who roams the sky — both are divine deer: the deer of the stars and the deer of the earth."
"Even if this is as you say to me, Lakṣmaṇa — that it is the māyā of a rākṣasa — then slaying him is all the more necessary for me."
