"For it was by this cruel, unrestrained Mārīca, roaming the forest previously, that foremost sages were harmed."
"By him many kings, supreme archers, were slain after setting out on the hunt — therefore this deer must be killed."
"In former times Vātāpi here, having subdued ascetics and entered their bellies, slew brāhmaṇas from within, as a foetus destroys a mule."
"Once, after a long time, he encountered in the world the great sage Agastya, endowed with spiritual power, and became his food."
"Seeing him about to rise up and resume that form, the blessed one smiled and spoke these words to Vātāpi."
"'O Vātāpi, you have disregarded and by your power oppressed the foremost of brāhmaṇas in the world of the living — therefore you are now reduced to old age.'"
"Therefore, O Lakṣmaṇa, that rākṣasa would not fare otherwise than Vātāpi did — whoever disrespects one like me, constantly devoted to dharma and with conquered senses."
"This one shall be slain as Vātāpi was by Agastya — may his fate be no different. Here you remain armed and disciplined, and guard Maithilī."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"O delight of the Raghu line, the task that must be done by us depends on her safety. I shall either kill this one or take the deer alive."
"Until I go swiftly, O son of Sumitrā, to bring the deer — watch over Vaidehī, O Lakṣmaṇa, whose longing is set upon the deer-hide."
"For today this deer shall not escape, its hide being the chief prize. You must be vigilant, remaining at the hermitage with Sītā."
"I shall slay the spotted deer with a single arrow; having slain it and taken its hide, I will return quickly, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"With the auspicious, exceedingly mighty bird Jaṭāyu, wise as he is, present on the right hand, O Lakṣmaṇa, be vigilant — guard Maithilī every moment, alert in every direction."
Having instructed his brother thus, the delight of the Raghu line, of great splendor, girded on his sword with a hilt of jāmbūnada gold.
Then taking up his triple-bent bow, the ornament of his person, and fastening on two quivers, he set out, striding with bold steps.
Deceiving him — having looked at the approaching king of kings — the deer vanished from sight out of fear; then it reappeared once more.
With sword girded and bow in hand, he ran in the direction of the deer; he beheld it shining before him, as if ablaze with its own radiance.
Again and again glancing back, the bow-bearing deer fled through the great forest, sometimes advancing beyond arrow's range, then luring him on.
Alarmed and agitated, leaping as if into the sky, now visible and now invisible in certain new spots—
—like the autumn moon's disk veiled by scattered clouds, it appeared only for a moment, then shone out repeatedly from afar.
By this repeated appearing and disappearing he drew Rāghava far away; Kākutstha grew angry, yet was helpless, deluded by him.
Then the deer halted, exhausted, taking refuge in the shade in a green meadow, and was seen from not far away, surrounded by wild deer.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing it, Rāma of great splendor, resolute in his intention to slay it, notched an arrow to his firm bow and drew it back with great force, he of mighty strength—
—and aiming at that very deer, let fly a blazing, flaming arrow, bright as a glowing serpent, fashioned by the divine weapons-lore of Brahman.
That foremost arrow, piercing violently through the deer-form, cleaved the very heart of Mārīca like a thunderbolt.
Leaping up the height of a tāla tree, he fell wounded by the arrow, crying out a dreadful cry as he fell to the earth, his life almost gone; dying, Mārīca abandoned that artificial body.
Knowing the appointed moment had come, he then uttered a voice exactly like Rāghava's own, crying: "Ah, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!"
Pierced to the vital core by that incomparable arrow, abandoning the deer-form, Mārīca, that immense-bodied one, took on his own rākṣasa form as he gave up his life.
Thereupon, struck by the arrow, the rākṣasa appeared with variegated armlets, adorned with all his ornaments, wearing a golden garland, with great fangs.
Seeing that rākṣasa of dreadful appearance fallen to the ground, Rāma went in mind to Sītā, remembering the words of Lakṣmaṇa.
"Having cried out thus, 'Ah, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!' with a great voice, this rākṣasa has died — upon hearing that, what will become of Sītā?"
"And to what state will the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa be driven?" — reflecting thus, the righteous Rāma felt his body hair bristle with apprehension.
There, having slain that rākṣasa in deer-form and having heard that cry, a sharp fear born of anguish entered Rāma.
Having slain another spotted deer and taken its flesh, Rāghava ran in haste, making his way back toward Janasthāna.
Recognizing that cry of anguish as matching her husband's voice in the forest, Sītā said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Go — find Rāghava."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"My life finds no steady ground, nor does my heart hold still, for I have heard with intensity that cry of one in utmost agony."
"You must save your brother who is crying out in the forest — run swiftly to that brother who is seeking refuge."
Thus addressed, Lakṣmaṇa did not go, for he knew his brother's command — just as a bull fallen under the power of lions cannot move.
Then the daughter of Janaka, enraged, spoke to him there: "O Saumitri, you are your brother's enemy disguised as a friend."
"You who in this situation do not go to your brother — you desire Rāma's destruction, O Lakṣmaṇa, for my sake."
"I think calamity is dear to you; there is no affection in you for your brother — that is why you stand at ease without even looking for that one of great splendor."
"For what purpose have you come here as the chief one, while I remain here — what could I do for him if he is in peril?"
So speaking, the Vaidehī was overwhelmed with tears of grief; Lakṣmaṇa then addressed Sītā who trembled like a doe.
"O goddess, among gods, humans, gandharvas, birds, rākṣasas, piśācas, kiṃnaras, and beasts —
— and even among terrible dānavas, O beautiful one, there exists none who could oppose Rāma in battle, who is the equal of Indra."
"Rāma cannot be slain in battle; you ought not to speak thus. I do not dare to abandon you in this forest without Rāghava."
"His strength is irresistible even by the forces of the mighty, even by all three worlds arrayed together with their lords and with the Maruts."
"Let your heart be at peace; abandon this anguish. Your husband will return swiftly, having slain that excellent deer."
"That was not clearly his voice, nor could any deity be harmed. It is the illusion of that demon, resembling a phantom city of the gandharvas."
"You are a deposit, O Vaidehī, entrusted to me by the great-souled Rāma, O one of lovely limbs; I do not dare to forsake you here."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"We have made enemies of these night-roaming demons, O auspicious one, O goddess, on account of the slaying of Khara and the destruction of the forces at Janasthāna."
"Rākṣasas emit voices by their craft in the great forest, O Vaidehī — those whose sport is violence; you ought not to be troubled by this."
So addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, she grew furious, her eyes reddened, and she spoke harsh words to the truthful Lakṣmaṇa.
"O ignoble one, O pretender of compassion, O cruel one, O stain upon your lineage — I think this is what you desire, and that is why you speak thus."
"It is no wonder that wickedness of this sort should arise among rivals, O Lakṣmaṇa — among cruel men like you who always move in secret."
"You are utterly corrupt — you follow Rāma alone into the forest, concealing yourself for my sake, or perhaps sent by Bharata."
"How could I, who have as my husband Rāma — dark as the blue lotus, with eyes like lotus petals — desire another man?"
"Right before your eyes, O Saumitri, I will cast off my life — of this there is no doubt; without Rāma I cannot live on this earth even for a moment."
Thus spoken to harshly by Sītā with words that made the moon shudder, Lakṣmaṇa — who had mastered his senses — joined his palms and said to Sītā:
"I do not dare to give a reply, for you are a deity to me. But words unbecoming — that is no wonder among women, O Maithilī."
"For this is the nature of women as seen in these worlds: they are lawless, fickle, sharp-tongued, and sowers of discord."
"Let all the forest-dwellers hear me as witnesses: harsh words have been spoken to me by you — I who speak only what is right."
"Shame on you — perish! — for thus suspecting me, who stands firm in the word of my elder, owing to your corrupt womanly nature."
"I will go where Kākutstha is. May you fare well, O fair-faced one; may all the forest deities protect you, O large-eyed one."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Yet the terrible omens that are appearing before me — may I, upon returning, still see you together with Rāma."
So addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, the daughter of Janaka, weeping, then replied with sharp words, overwhelmed with tears.
"I shall enter the Godāvarī without Rāma, O Lakṣmaṇa, or else I will hang myself — or I will cast off my body from a precipice."
"Or I will drink sharp poison, or I will enter fire — but I will never touch, even with a footstep, any man other than Rāghava."
Having thus reviled Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, filled with grief, beat her own belly with her hands while weeping in her sorrow.
Saumitri, looking upon her who appeared in anguish, downcast, weeping, with wide eyes, tried to reassure her — yet Sītā said not a word more to that brother of her husband.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, saluting Sītā with joined palms, bowing slightly, and casting many a backward glance at Maithilī, the self-possessed one departed toward Rāma.
Spoken to harshly by her, the younger brother of Rāghava, though angered, yearning intensely for Rāma, set out quickly.
At that very moment Daśagrīva, having quickly seized upon the opportunity, approached the Vaidehī bearing the form of a wandering ascetic.
Clad in a smooth saffron robe, wearing a topknot, carrying an umbrella and sandals, and hanging upon his left shoulder the staff and water-pot, he approached the Vaidehī in the guise of a wandering ascetic.
That one of tremendous strength approached her in the forest, bereft of her two protectors, as a great darkness approaches a twilight bereft of the sun and moon.
He then beheld that youthful, illustrious princess — as a fierce planet regards Rohiṇī deprived of the Moon.
Seeing that fierce, evil-deeded one, the trees rooted in Janasthāna did not tremble, and the wind did not blow.
And the swift-flowing Godāvarī river, seeing him with blood-red eyes gazing about, out of fear began to flow sluggishly.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāvaṇa, the ten-headed one, seeking to exploit the gap left by Rāma's absence, during that interval approached the Vaidehī in the form of a mendicant.
The inauspicious one in an auspicious form drew near to the Vaidehī who was lamenting for her husband — as Saturn approaches Citrā.
That evil one, in his auspicious form, covered as a well is covered with grass, stood watching the illustrious Vaidehī, the wife of Rāma.
Auspicious, with beautiful teeth and lips, with a face like the full moon, seated in the leaf-hut, oppressed by tears and grief —
— her with lotus-petal eyes and garbed in yellow silk, that Vaidehī was approached by the night-roaming demon of evil mind.
Pierced by the arrows of the god of love, uttering sacred Vedic sounds, the lord of rākṣasas spoke courteous words in that secluded place.
Rāvaṇa praised her who was the foremost among the three worlds, blazing with her beauty like Śrī without her lotus.
"Who are you, glowing like gold, robed in yellow silk, wearing a lovely garland of lotuses like a lotus-pool?"
"Are you Modesty, Prosperity, Fame, the auspicious Lakṣmī, or an apsaras, O fair-faced one? Are you Fortune, O one of lovely limbs, or Rati who roams at will?"
"Your teeth are even, peaked, glossy, and white; your eyes are wide, clear, reddened at the corners, with dark irises."
"Your hips are wide and full, your thighs are like the trunks of an elephant — firm, round, well-matched, and bold."
"Your two breasts are full and high-nippled, lovely, smooth like palm fruits, adorned with choice jewels, beautiful."
"O beautiful-smiled, beautiful-toothed, beautiful-eyed, graceful one — you steal my mind as a river-bank is taken by water."
"Your waist is measured by a hand's span, your hair is lovely, your breasts are firm — you are neither goddess, nor gandharva woman, nor yakṣī, nor kiṃnarī."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Never before have I seen a woman of such beauty on the face of this earth; and your dwelling in this thicket stirs my mind."
"Turn back — may you fare well; you ought not to dwell here. This is the abode of terrible rākṣasas who take on any form they wish."
"Lofty and delightful palaces, city-gardens — prosperous, fragrant — are fitting for you to inhabit."
"The finest garlands, the finest drink, the finest garments, O beautiful one — and a husband who is the finest — I consider these fitting for you, O dark-eyed one."
"Who are you among the Rudras, or among the Maruts, O pure-smiling one? Among the Vasus, O one of lovely limbs, you appear to me as a deity."
"The gandharvas do not come here, nor the gods, nor the kiṃnaras — this is the abode of rākṣasas. How then have you come here?"
"Here there are monkeys, lions, leopards, tigers, deer, bears, hyenas, and vultures — how are you not afraid of them?"
"Of terrible, swift-moving elephants in rut — how do you not fear them, alone in this great wilderness, O forest-faced one?"
"Who are you, whose are you, and whence do you come? For what reason do you wander alone in the dreadful Daṇḍaka forest, O auspicious one, haunted by rākṣasas?"
Thus praised by the evil-souled Rāvaṇa — and seeing him as a brahmin guest who had arrived — Maithilī honored that Rāvaṇa who had come with all the courtesies due to a guest.
First bringing a seat and welcoming him with water for the feet, she then said to that one of pleasant appearance: "Everything is ready."
Seeing him who had arrived in the garb of a twice-born, bearing bowl and staff — one impossible to dismiss given the appearance he showed — Maithilī invited him in the manner of a brahmin, as he had come.
"Here is a seat, brahmin, please be seated; and receive this water for the feet. Here too is excellent food of the forest, prepared for you — partake of it here at your leisure."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Being thus invited, Rāvaṇa looked at Maithilī, the wife of a king, who spoke with full courtesy, and laughing, he fixed his mind upon her abduction — and thereby upon his own destruction.
Then, waiting for her well-attired husband gone hunting, she looked out and saw only that great, green forest — but not Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Then the Vaidehī, questioned by Rāvaṇa — who desired to abduct her — in the form of a wandering ascetic, declared herself.
Reflecting "This is a brahmin and a guest — if left unaddressed he might curse me," Sītā reflected for a moment and then spoke.
"I am the daughter of the great-souled Janaka, king of Mithilā; Sītā is my name — may you fare well — the wife of Rāma, O foremost of twice-born."
"For a year I dwelt in the household of Rāghava, enjoying human pleasures, fulfilled in every desire."
"Then, after a year, my husband, together with the royal ministers, resolved to consecrate Rāma as king."
"But while the consecration of Rāghava was being prepared, the noble Kaikeyī — so she is named — asked a boon of my father-in-law."
"Kaikeyī, having bound my father-in-law with a former boon, asked of that husband of hers — bound to truth, foremost among kings — two things: my exile and the consecration of Bharata."
"'I will not eat today, nor sleep, nor drink at any time — this is the end of my life, if Rāma is consecrated' —
— so spoke Kaikeyī; my honorable father-in-law implored her with gifts upon gifts, but she did not withdraw her demand."
"My husband is of great splendor, twenty-five years of age, renowned in the world as Rāma — virtuous, truthful in speech, pure, wide-eyed, long-armed, devoted to the welfare of all beings."
"When Rāma came to his father's presence for the consecration, Kaikeyī quickly spoke these words to my husband:"
"'Hear this that has been decreed by your father for me, O Rāghava: this kingdom, free of thorns, is to be given to Bharata.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'And you indeed must dwell in the forest for fourteen years — go forth into exile, O Kākutstha, and free your father from falsehood.'"
"'So be it,' said Rāma to Kaikeyī without any fear; and my husband of firm vows carried out her words."
"To give but never receive, to speak truth and never falsehood — this, O brahmin, is Rāma's vow, certain and supreme."
"His half-brother, named Lakṣmaṇa, is powerful — a tiger among men, Rāma's companion, a slayer of enemies in battle."
"That brother named Lakṣmaṇa, a walker of the path of dharma, of firm vow, followed him with bow in hand as he went into exile with me."
"We three, deprived of the kingdom on account of Kaikeyī, wander this deep forest with vigor, O foremost of twice-born."
"Rest here awhile; you may stay here. My husband will come bringing an abundance of forest-produce."
"And you — tell me truly your name, lineage, and family; and for what purpose do you wander alone in the Daṇḍaka forest, O twice-born?"
While Sītā, the wife of Rāma, was speaking thus, the mightily powerful Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas, replied sharply.
"I am the one by whom the worlds have been terrified — gods, asuras, and serpents together; I am that one called Rāvaṇa, O Sītā, the lord of the host of rākṣasas."
"Having seen you, golden-hued, clad in silk, I find no pleasure in my own wives, O blameless one."
"Among the many excellent women brought from here and there — may you fare well — become the chief queen of all of them for me."
"There is a great city of mine called Laṅkā in the middle of the ocean, surrounded by the sea, situated upon a mountain-peak."
"There, O Sītā, you will roam the forests with me; you will no longer long for this life in the wilderness, O passionate one."
"Five thousand female attendants, adorned with all ornaments, will serve you, O Sītā, if you become my wife."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, the daughter of Janaka, enraged, her limbs without blemish, disregarding the demon, replied:
"I am devoted to Rāma — my husband immovable as a great mountain, resembling Mahendra, unperturbable as the great ocean."
"I am devoted to Rāma — long-armed, broad-chested, striding with a lion's prowess, a man-lion, resembling a lion."
"I am devoted to Rāma — his face like the full moon, heroic, princely in bearing, master of his senses, of wide fame, long-armed."
"And you — a jackal desires me here, a lioness beyond reach. I cannot be touched by you, as the sun's radiance cannot be grasped."
"You surely see many golden trees, O dull-witted Rāvaṇa — you who desire the beloved wife of Rāghava."
"You desire to extract a fang from the mouth of a hungry lion — that swift foe of deer, that venomous serpent."
"You desire to carry off Mandara, the foremost of mountains, with your bare hand; you desire to drink the Kālakūṭa poison and walk away unharmed."
"You rub your eye with a needle, you lick a razor with your tongue — you who desire to possess the beloved wife of Rāghava."
"You desire to swim the ocean with a boulder hung about your neck; you desire to snatch both the sun and the moon with your hands — you who desire to violate the beloved wife of Rāma."
"You desire to carry off a blazing fire with a cloth — you who desire to abduct the virtuous wife of Rāma, O so-called auspicious one."
"You desire to walk upon the points of iron-tipped spears — you who desire to possess a wife worthy of Rāma."
"As great as the difference between a lion and a jackal in the forest; as great as the difference between a rivulet and the ocean; as great as the difference between the finest wine and sour rice-beer — so great is the difference between Daśaratha's son and you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"As great as the difference between gold and lead; as great as the difference between sandalwood and muddy water; as great as the difference between an elephant and a cat in the forest — so great is the difference between the son of Daśaratha and you."
"As great as the difference between a crow and Garuḍa, son of Vinatā; as great as the difference between a grebe and a peacock; as great as the difference between a sāras crane and a vulture in the forest — so great is the difference between the son of Daśaratha and you."
"Even if I were taken by you — while Rāma, equal in might to the thousand-eyed Indra, stands with bow and arrow in hand — I would not decay, as a thunderbolt swallowed by a fly would not decay."
Having spoken that word with pure heart and clear sight to that night-roaming demon, she — the slender one — trembled from a shuddering of her limbs, like a plantain tree shaken by the wind.
Observing Sītā trembling, that Rāvaṇa — equal in power to Death — declared his lineage, his strength, his name, and his deeds, in order to cause her fear.
As Sītā spoke thus, Rāvaṇa, enraged and harsh of speech, drew his brows together on his forehead and replied.
"I am the half-brother of Vaiśravaṇa, O fair-complexioned one — Rāvaṇa by name, be it known to you, the ten-necked one, mighty in valor."
"Before whom gods together with gandharvas, piśācas, birds, and serpents flee in terror, just as creatures flee always before Death."
"By whom Vaiśravaṇa, his half-brother, was on some occasion brought to single combat out of wrath, and was defeated in battle through valor."
"Tormented by fear of me, he abandoned his own prosperous abode and now dwells on Kailāsa, the best of mountains — he whose vehicle is men."
"Whose celestial chariot named Puṣpaka, lovely and going wherever one wills, was seized by force — O fair one — in which I travel through the sky."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"When my anger arises, the gods headed by Śakra flee in all directions, terrified, merely upon beholding my face, O Maithilī."
"Wherever I stand, the wind blows there with apprehension; the sun with his fierce rays becomes cool out of fear."
"Wherever I stand or move, the trees stand with their leaves motionless and the rivers with their waters stilled."
"Beyond the ocean lies my beautiful city named Laṅkā, full of terrible rākṣasas, even as Amarāvatī is full of Indra's hosts."
"That lovely city is encircled by a gleaming white rampart, its inner courtyards of gold and its gateways of vaidūrya gems."
"Thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, resounding with the music of instruments, adorned with gardens teeming with trees that yield every desired fruit."
"Living there with me, O Sītā, O princess, you will not tire of the pleasures of human women, O noble-minded one."
"Enjoying both human and divine pleasures, O fair-complexioned one, you will not remember Rāma — a mere mortal whose life is spent."
"The eldest son, feeble in valor, who was sent to the forest by King Daśaratha after establishing his beloved other son on the throne —"
"What will you do with that Rāma who has lost his kingdom, whose wits have gone astray, O wide-eyed one, that wretched ascetic of a hermit?"
"You ought not to reject me, the lord of all rākṣasas, who has come here of his own desire, who is pierced by the arrows of the love-god."
"For having rejected me, O timid one, you will come to grief, as Urvaśī did when she struck away Purūravas with her foot."
Thus addressed, the daughter of Videha, angry and red-eyed, spoke harsh words to the lord of rākṣasas in that solitary place.
"How do you desire to do evil, invoking as your own the divine Vaiśravaṇa, worshipped by all beings, as your brother?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"All the rākṣasas will surely perish, O Rāvaṇa, whose king you are — harsh, evil-minded, with senses uncontrolled."
"One might carry off Śacī, Indra's wife, and still survive; but there is no life for anyone who carries me away, Rāma's wife."
"One might long survive having violated Śacī — of incomparable beauty — from the hand of the Vajra-bearer; but for one who has violated a woman like me, there is no escape, even if you have drunk the nectar of immortality."
Hearing Sītā's words, the mighty ten-necked one slapped one hand against the other and assumed a very great bodily form.
He then spoke again insistently to the Maithilī: "I think you have not heard of my valor and might — you are surely mad."
"Standing in the sky, I could lift the earth with these arms; I could drink the ocean dry, and standing in battle I could slay Death himself."
"I could block out the sun with sharp arrows; I could split the very earth asunder. O madwoman, see me, who take whatever form I will — I am a husband who grants every desire."
As Rāvaṇa thus spoke, his two eyes — edged with yellow, blazing like fire — became red with rage.
Instantly casting off the gentle form of a mendicant, Rāvaṇa — the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa — assumed his own form, resembling the form of Death.
With blood-red eyes, resplendent, wearing earrings of molten gold, ten-faced, bearing bow and arrows — thus did the ranger of the night appear.
Abandoning the disguise of a wandering mendicant, that great-bodied Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas, resumed his own true form.
With eyes reddened by anger, blazing like a mass of storm-clouds, clad in crimson garments, he stood gazing upon the Maithilī, that jewel among women.
Then Rāvaṇa spoke to that Maithilī, whose hair-ends were dark, who shone like the sun's radiance, adorned with garments and ornaments.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"If you desire a husband renowned in the three worlds, take refuge in me, O fair-hipped one — I am a fitting husband for you."
"Give yourself to me for all time — I am worthy of praise, I shall be your beloved; O fair one, never shall I do you any displeasure. Abandon your attachment to a mortal; direct your heart toward me."
"What virtues could make you attached to Rāma — fallen from his kingdom, his purpose unaccomplished, of limited lifespan — you fool, who consider yourself wise?"
"That one of evil mind who, at a woman's word, abandoned his kingdom and his companions and now lives in this forest haunted by serpents —"
Having spoken thus to the Maithilī — who deserved only kind treatment, who spoke sweet words — Rāvaṇa seized Sītā as the planet Mercury seizes Rohiṇī in the sky.
With his left hand he grasped lotus-eyed Sītā by her hair, and with his right hand he clasped her about the thighs.
Beholding him — towering like a mountain peak, sharp-fanged, long-armed, resembling Death — the forest deities fled away in terror.
And there appeared Rāvaṇa's great chariot — wrought of illusion, divine, yoked with braying asses, its body of gold, resounding with a harsh din.
Then that great-voiced one, having terrified her with harsh words, lifted the daughter of Videha into his lap and placed her upon the chariot.
Seized thus, the glorious Sītā cried out with a great shriek in her distress: "Rāma!" — to Rāma who was far away in the forest.
Then Rāvaṇa, consumed by desire, lifted her who was unwilling — struggling and twisting like the wife of the king of serpents — and soared upward.
Then she, being carried away through the sky by the lord of rākṣasas, cried out loudly, like one maddened, her mind bewildered, as though stricken by illness.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, O great-armed one, who bring joy to the heart of your elder — you do not know that I am being carried away by a rākṣasa who takes any form he wills!"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"O Rāghava, you who have abandoned life, happiness, and wealth for the sake of righteousness — do you not see me being carried away in unrighteousness?"
"Are you not the subduer of the arrogant, O scorcher of foes? How is it you do not chastise Rāvaṇa for this wicked deed?"
"Surely the fruit of an arrogant man's deed is seen quickly; even Time here becomes a participant, as in the ripening of a harvest."
"He has committed this deed with a mind struck by doom — he will suffer from Rāma a terrible calamity that brings his life to an end."
"Alas, now Kaikeyī together with her kinsmen will be gratified, for I — the lawful and glorious wife of the righteous and desiring-of-virtue Rāma — am being carried away."
"I take my leave of Janasthāna and of the blooming karṇikāra trees — quickly announce to Rāma: Rāvaṇa is carrying Sītā away!"
"I salute Mālyavān, Śikharī, and the mountain Prasravaṇa — quickly announce to Rāma: Rāvaṇa is carrying Sītā away!"
"I salute the Godāvarī river resounding with swans and sārasa cranes — quickly announce to Rāma: Rāvaṇa is carrying Sītā away!"
"And the divinities that reside in the various trees of this forest — I bow to them all: announce to my husband that I have been abducted."
"Whatever beings live here as well — I take refuge in all of them, even in the herds of deer and the flocks of birds."
"Tell him: 'Sītā, dearer to her husband than life itself, has been carried away helpless by Rāvaṇa — she has been abducted.'"
"Knowing of me, the great-armed and mighty one will retrieve me by his valor even from the beyond — even from one taken by Vaivasvata himself."
"O Jaṭāyu, you must faithfully report the whole account of my abduction to Rāma and to Lakṣmaṇa, completely and without remainder."
Jaṭāyu, who had been asleep, heard that cry and quickly beheld Rāvaṇa and saw the daughter of Videha.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then that best of birds, resplendent as a mountain peak, with a sharp beak, perched upon a forest tree, uttered a clear and noble speech.
"O ten-necked one, I stand in ancient dharma, grounded in truth — I am named Jaṭāyu, king of vultures, and I am mighty."
"Rāma, son of Daśaratha, comparable to Mahendra and Varuṇa, is king of all the worlds and is devoted to the welfare of those worlds."
"This glorious and fair-hipped woman named Sītā, the lawful wife of that lord of the world — it is she whom you desire to carry off."
"How could a king who abides in dharma lay hands upon another's wife? The wife of a king must especially be protected, O great one. Turn back your base intent of violating another's wife."
"A wise man should not do what others would condemn in him; upon reflection, the wives of others must be protected as one's own."
"The learned, in matters of artha or kāma not explicitly covered in the śāstras, determine dharma by following the example of the king, O delight of the eastern people."
"The king is dharma, and kāma, and the supreme treasury of wealth; whether dharma issues in good or evil — it proceeds with the king as its root."
"Evil by nature and fickle — how have you, O best of rākṣasas, come to possess sovereignty, like a sinner who has somehow boarded a celestial chariot?"
"A man's inherent nature cannot be wiped away; O noble one — nay, do not pursue this — prosperity does not dwell long in the house of those with corrupt souls."
"When the mighty Rāma, righteous of soul, has committed no offense against your realm or city, how do you transgress against him?"
"If Khara, stationed at Janasthāna, transgressed and was formerly slain by Rāma of effortless action — that was on account of Śūrpaṇakhā's instigation."
"Tell the truth here: what transgression of Rāma's is it — on account of which you would carry off the wife of that lord of the world?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Release the daughter of Videha at once, lest his terrible gaze burn you — blazing like fire — as Indra's thunderbolt burned Vṛtra."
"Binding a venomous serpent in the hem of your garment, you do not perceive it; nor do you see the noose of Death fastened about your neck."
"That burden alone is worth bearing, O gentle one, which does not weigh a man down; that food alone is worth eating which, when digested, causes no illness."
"An act that produces no dharma, no fame, no glory in this world, but only distress for the body — who would undertake such a deed?"
"For sixty thousand years since my birth, O Rāvaṇa, have I been duly following the ancestral and grandfatherly path of kingship."
"Old as I am, and young as you are — an archer mounted on a chariot, armored and bearing arrows — even so you will not depart safely with the daughter of Videha."
"You are not capable of forcibly carrying away the daughter of Videha before my eyes — no more than one can remove a firmly grounded Vedic truth by means of clever arguments."
"Fight if you are a hero — stand your ground a moment, Rāvaṇa — you will lie slain upon the earth, just as Khara did before."
"By whom daityas and dānavas have been slain again and again in battle — that bark-clad Rāma will slay you in combat before long."
"What can I do, when those two princes are gone so far away? You surely flee quickly, O base one — you are without doubt afraid of them."
"While I yet live, you shall not carry away this beautiful one — lotus-eyed Sītā, the beloved great wife of Rāma."
"I must assuredly do what is dear to that great-souled Rāma — even at the cost of my life — and likewise what is dear to Daśaratha."
"Stop, stop, O ten-necked one — wait a moment, behold, Rāvaṇa — I shall offer you the hospitality of battle to the full measure of my life, O ranger of the night; I shall bring you down from your magnificent chariot like a fruit from its stalk."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When Rāvaṇa was thus rightly addressed by Jaṭāyu, all twenty eyes of that enraged one blazed like fire.
His eyes crimson with rage, his earrings of heated gold swinging, the lord of rākṣasas, overcome with fury, rushed at the king of birds.
The collision between those two in that great forest was tumultuous, like that of two storm-driven clouds clashing in the sky.
That battle between the vulture and the rākṣasa was wondrous, like that of two mighty winged mountains, the Mālyavat peaks.
Then the mighty one rained upon the king of vultures arrows — nālīkas, nārācas, and vikarṇis with sharp tips — all exceedingly fearsome.
Jaṭāyu, the lord of birds that ride on wings, intercepted those showers of arrows, those weapons of Rāvaṇa, in the battle.
With his two feet armed with sharp talons, that most excellent of birds, immensely powerful, slashed many wounds all over Rāvaṇa's body.
Then Daśagrīva, burning with anger and longing to crush his foe, seized ten terrible arrows resembling the staff of Death.
With those arrows — drawn to the full, flying straight, sharp-tipped, and terrifying — that exceedingly mighty one pierced the vulture.
Seeing Jānakī on the rākṣasa's chariot, her eyes filled with tears, he gave no thought to those arrows and charged straight at the rākṣasa.
Then with his two feet, that most radiant lord of birds shattered his arrow-set bow, adorned with pearls and gems.
And with his wings, that most radiant lord of birds scattered Rāvaṇa's quiver of arrows that blazed like fire.
The mighty one also slew in battle his fleet mules — those divine, swift animals with golden trappings and demon-like faces.
He also smashed the magnificent chariot — fitted with its triple shaft, going at will, blazing like fire, beautifully adorned with gems and gold — and likewise the parasol resembling the full moon, together with the fly-whisks.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
His bow shattered, his chariot wrecked, his horses slain, his charioteer killed, Rāvaṇa fell to the ground, clutching Vaidehī in his lap.
Seeing Rāvaṇa fallen on the ground with his vehicle destroyed, all beings praised the king of vultures, crying "Bravo! Bravo!"
But seeing that leader of the bird host exhausted by old age, Rāvaṇa leaped up again with renewed vigour, seizing Maithilī.
Seeing him joyfully bearing the daughter of Janaka away in his lap, the king of vultures, Jaṭāyu, soared up and spoke these words.
"O Rāvaṇa, O dim-witted one, you carry off the wife of Rāma, whose arrows strike like the thunderbolt — this is truly for the destruction of the rākṣasas."
"Together with your allies and kinsmen, your ministers, your army, and your retinue, you drink this poison as a thirsty man drinks water."
"Those who are heedless and do not perceive the consequence of their actions quickly perish — just as you shall perish."
"You are bound in the noose of Time — wherever you go, how will you escape it? Like a water-creature that swallows a baited hook and is caught for slaughter."
"The two Kākutsthas are never to be assailed, O Rāvaṇa; the Rāghavas will never tolerate this violation of their hermitage."
"The deed you have done, O coward, is censured by the world. This is the path of a thief — it is not the way trodden by heroes."
"Fight if you are a hero — stand a moment, O Rāvaṇa! You shall lie slain on the ground just as your brother Khara did."
"The deed that a man embarks on at the hour of his doom is one leading to his own destruction, one contrary to dharma — and that is the deed you have undertaken."
"Who then would carry out that action whose consequence is sin? Not even the lord of the worlds, the blessed Svayambhū, would do it."
Having spoken those righteous words to that rākṣasa, the valiant Jaṭāyu fell with great force upon the back of Daśagrīva.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seizing him and raking him all over with sharp talons, he mounted him as a mahout mounts a rogue elephant.
He tore at him with his talons, burying his beak into his back, and tore out his hair — Jaṭāyu, who fights with talons, wings, and beak as weapons.
Tormented again and again by the king of vultures in this way, that rākṣasa trembled, his lips quivering with indignation.
Rāvaṇa, clasping Vaidehī in his left arm, overwhelmed by pain and overcome with rage, struck Jaṭāyu with his open palm.
Jaṭāyu, that subduer of foes and master of harsh deeds, turning on him with his beak, then severed all ten of his left arms.
Then Daśagrīva, enraged and powerful, releasing Sītā, pounded the king of vultures with fists and feet.
For a moment a battle raged between those two of incomparable might — the foremost of rākṣasas and the greatest of birds.
As he strained himself on Rāma's behalf, Rāvaṇa drew his sword and cut off his wings, his feet, and his flanks.
His wings severed by that rākṣasa of terrible deeds, the vulture suddenly fell slain to the earth, barely alive.
Seeing Jaṭāyu fallen on the ground soaked in blood, Vaidehī ran toward him in grief, as toward her own kinsman.
The lord of Laṅkā beheld Jaṭāyu lying on the earth — dark as a blue storm-cloud in form, his breast very pale, his valour noble, quiescent as a forest-fire that has burned out.
Then Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, whose face shone like the moon, embraced once more that bird who rides on wings, lying struck down on the ground and crushed by Rāvaṇa's violence, and wept.
The lord of rākṣasas saw the vulture fallen on the ground, barely alive and quivering, near the hermitage of the Rāghavas.
She whose face was like the lord of stars, looking upon that king of vultures slain by Rāvaṇa, lamented in the deepest grief.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Omens, knowledge of portents, and the sound and sight of birds are invariably manifest for men in matters of happiness and sorrow."
"Surely, O Rāma, you do not know of the great calamity, O son. Surely, O Kākutstha, the beasts and birds are running on my behalf."
"Save me today, O Kākutstha! O Lakṣmaṇa!" — the most excellent of women cried out in uttermost terror, so that those nearby could hear.
Rāvaṇa, the lord of rākṣasas, rushed at Vaidehī, her garlands and ornaments dishevelled, lamenting like one without a protector.
As she clung like a creeper winding around the great trees, the lord of rākṣasas repeatedly called out "Let go, let go!"
As she cried out "Rāma! Rāma!" — bereft of Rāma in the forest — he who resembled Death seized her by the hair to end her life.
When Vaidehī was thus violated, the entire world, moving and unmoving, became lawless and was shrouded in blinding darkness.
Seeing Sītā seized and wretched with his divine eye, the illustrious Pitāmaha declared: "The purpose is accomplished."
All the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, beholding Sītā thus seized, were simultaneously filled with joy and anguish.
And Rāvaṇa, the lord of rākṣasas, carrying her away into the sky as she wept calling "Rāma! Rāma! Lakṣmaṇa!", departed.
The princess, all her limbs adorned with burnished ornaments and clad in a yellow silk garment, shone like a flash of lightning named Saudāmanī.
With her yellow garment streaming in the wind, Rāvaṇa shone all the more gloriously, like a mountain lit by a lamp of fire.
The coppery, fragrant lotus petals of that most auspicious Vaidehī scattered and fell upon Rāvaṇa all around.
Her silk garment, streaming in the sky with the radiance of gold, glowed copper-red in the sun's rays, like a cloud at sunset.
Her spotless face, borne in Rāvaṇa's lap in the sky, did not shine without Rāma — like a lotus without its stalk.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
It was as though the moon had risen cleaving a dark cloud: her face with its beautiful brow, lovely hair-line, the splendour of a lotus interior, unblemished, adorned with white, very pure, lustrous teeth.
Tear-streaked, her mascara smeared, yet lovely to behold like the moon, with a beautiful nose and charming copper-red lips, she blazed in the sky with a radiance like gold.
Her auspicious speech, shaken by the lord of rākṣasas, did not shine without Rāma, like the moon risen by day.
Maithilī, golden in complexion, shone against the dark-limbed lord of rākṣasas as a golden girdle resting against a sapphire.
The daughter of Janaka, lotus-fair and radiant as gold, adorned with burnished ornaments, shone against Rāvaṇa as lightning shining within a dark cloud.
With the jingling of Vaidehī's ornaments, the lord of rākṣasas became like a dark, pure storm-cloud sounding with thunder.
The shower of flowers fallen from her hair scattered all around and fell to the ground as Sītā was being carried off.
But that shower of flowers, scattered all around by the speed of Rāvaṇa's flight, returned and fell again upon Daśagrīva.
A stream of flowers fell back upon the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa, pure as a garland of stars, as upon the most excellent of mountains, Meru.
An anklet set with jewels slipped from Vaidehī's foot — resembling a circle of lightning and tinkling sweetly — and fell to earth.
Red as the new shoot of a tree, Vaidehī adorned the dark-limbed lord of rākṣasas as a golden girth-strap adorns an elephant.
The younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa carried Sītā away through the sky, blazing with her own radiance like a great meteor in the heavens.
Her ornaments, fire-coloured and jingling, fell scattered to the earth like waning stars dropping from the sky.
The pearl necklace, bright as the lord of stars, that slipped from between Vaidehī's breasts and fell shone like the Gaṅgā fallen from heaven.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Struck by the blast of Rāvaṇa's passage, the trees teeming with flocks of various birds, their tops shaken, seemed to cry out "Fear not!"
The lotus ponds with their blossoms battered, their fish frightened and darting through the water, seemed to mourn for Maithilī as for a friend who had lost all hope.
Lions, tigers, deer, and birds, rushing together from all sides and then following the shadow of Sītā below, pursued her out of fury.
Their waterfalls like weeping eyes, their peaks like upraised arms, the mountains seemed to cry out aloud as Sītā was being carried off.
Seeing Vaidehī being carried off, the sun himself grew faint, his radiance shattered, the glorious one's disc turning pale.
"There is no dharma, where then is truth? There is no uprightness, no compassion — in a world where Rāvaṇa carries off Rāma's wife Vaidehī."
Thus all beings lamented in groups; the young deer, frightened and their faces pitiable, wept.
Looking up again and again with eyes clouded by falling tears, their bodies trembling greatly, the forest goddesses were overcome with grief.
Seeing Sītā crying out so loudly and sunk in such grief, crying out "Lakṣmaṇa! Rāma!" in a sweet voice —
— Vaidehī, who looked back again and again at the ground below, her hair dishevelled at the ends, her cosmetic marks smeared, was carried off by Daśagrīva to his own destruction, that noble-minded woman.
Then she, the beautiful-toothed, pure-smiling Maithilī, bereft of her kinsmen, not seeing Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, her face drained of colour, tormented by the weight of fear —
Seeing him soaring into the sky, Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, grieved and utterly terrified, standing in the midst of great fear —
— her eyes copper-red with anger and weeping, Sītā, being carried off, addressed the fearsome-eyed lord of rākṣasas in piteous weeping with these words.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You feel no shame, O vile Rāvaṇa, for this deed — you who, knowing me to be alone and unprotected, have stolen me and flee."
"Surely it was you yourself, O wicked-souled coward, who, wishing to abduct me, lured away my husband through the illusion of a deer-form; and even this one who rose to protect me has been struck down."
"Truly your valour is paramount, O most wretched of rākṣasas — you proclaim your name but in battle there is none whom you have conquered!"
"How do you feel no shame having done this most censurable deed — the abduction of another's wife, O vile one, in secret and when she is alone?"
"Men in the world will proclaim your despicable, most cruel, most unrighteous deed — you who fancy yourself a hero."
"Shame on your heroism and your character as you then proclaimed it — a disgrace to your lineage in the world! And shame on conduct such as yours!"
"What can be done if you flee only with speed! Stand even for a moment — you will not return alive!"
"Were you to come within sight of those two sons of kings, you would not be capable of living even a moment, even with your whole army."
"You are no more capable of enduring the touch of their arrows than a bird is capable of enduring the touch of a blazing fire in the forest."
"Do what is beneficial for yourself — release me, O Rāvaṇa. For my husband, angered by the violation done to me, together with his brother, will bring about your destruction if you do not release me."
"The purpose with which you wish to carry me off by force, O vile one, that purpose of yours will prove fruitless."
"Not seeing that husband of mine who is like a god, I, fallen into the enemy's power, cannot bear to sustain my life for long."
"Surely you do not consider what is good or beneficial for yourself, just as a mortal at the hour of death pursues what is contrary to his welfare."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Indeed, for all those who are about to die, what is beneficial does not please them. I seem to see the noose of Time already fastened around your throat."
"That you feel no fear in this place of danger, O ten-faced one, evidently you are seeing only trees of gold before your eyes."
"You are beholding, O Rāvaṇa, the terrible river Vaitaraṇī flowing with streams of blood, and the dreadful forest whose leaves are swords."
"You shall behold the śālmalī tree, dreadful, studded with sharp iron thorns, its flowers of heated gold, its finest leaves of vaidūrya gem."
"Having done such a wrong to that great-souled one, you will not be able to sustain yourself for long — like a merciless one who has drunk poison."
"You are bound by the irresistible noose of Time, O Rāvaṇa — wherever you go, how will you find safety from my husband, that great-souled one?"
"He who in the mere twinkling of an eye slew fourteen thousand rākṣasas in battle without even his brother —"
"— how would that Rāghava, the hero, skilled in all weapons and mighty, not slay you with sharp arrows for stealing his beloved wife?"
This and much else that was harsh did Vaidehī, sitting in Rāvaṇa's lap, seized by fear and grief, lament pitifully.
Thus deeply afflicted and speaking many words, having first lamented pitifully, that sinful one carried off the high-spirited young princess, daughter of a king, writhing in his grasp, her body trembling all over.
As Vaidehī was being carried off, seeing no protector anywhere, she beheld five foremost monkeys stationed on a mountain peak.
The wide-eyed Maithilī, of beautiful form, dropped among them her upper garment of silk, bright as gold, and her auspicious ornaments — thinking they might report to Rāma.
She cast down that garment together with the ornaments into their midst; but Daśagrīva, bewildered and dull of wit, did not perceive her act.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The tawny-eyed bull-monkeys gazed with unblinking eyes at wide-eyed Sītā as she cried out pitifully.
Crossing beyond the Pampā lake, the lord of rākṣasas went, holding weeping Maithilī, with his face turned toward the city of Laṅkā.
Rāvaṇa, greatly exultant, seized her — his own death — even as one clasps in one's lap a sharp-fanged serpent of great venom.
Swiftly he traversed through the sky forests, rivers, mountains, and lakes, like an arrow released from a bow.
He came to the ocean — the home of Varuṇa, inexhaustible, the abode of timi-fish and crocodiles, the refuge of rivers — and crossed it.
As Vaidehī was being carried off, the ocean — Varuṇa's domain — became agitated with turbulent waves, its fish and great serpents restrained.
Then the Cāraṇas moving through the sky called out; the Siddhas too declared at that moment: "This, O Daśagrīva, is your end."
Taking on his lap Sītā as she writhed and struggled, Rāvaṇa entered the city of Laṅkā — his own death incarnate.
Reaching the city of Laṅkā with its great roads well laid out, he entered his own inner apartments, richly furnished with fully grown enclosures.
There Rāvaṇa placed dark-eyed Sītā, wholly overcome with grief and stupor, as Maya placed his demonic māyā.
Daśagrīva then spoke to the dreadful-looking demonesses: let no man or woman look upon Sītā without his sanction.
"Whatever she desires — pearls, gems, gold, garments, ornaments — all that shall be given to her in accordance with my wish."
"And she who speaks any unpleasant word to Vaidehī, whether from ignorance or knowingly — her life shall be forfeit."
Having spoken thus to those demonesses, the powerful lord of rākṣasas departed from the inner apartments and, pondering what was to be done, he beheld eight mighty flesh-eating rākṣasas.
That most mighty one, intoxicated by boons granted to him, beholding them, praised their strength and valor and spoke these words to them.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Armed with various weapons, go from here swiftly and quickly to Janasthāna, the ruined place, the former abode of Khara."
"Stay there in Janasthāna, now empty with its rākṣasas slain, relying on your manly valor, casting fear far away."
"For the great force I had stationed in Janasthāna — along with Dūṣaṇa and Khara — has been slain in battle by Rāma's arrows."
"Hence an unprecedented rage mounts over my composure, and a great, dreadful enmity toward Rāma has arisen within me."
"I wish to repay that enmity to my enemy; truly I shall not find sleep without slaying my foe in battle."
"Slaying him now — Rāma the killer of Khara and Dūṣaṇa — I shall attain peace, as a pauper attains ease upon gaining wealth."
"While dwelling in Janasthāna, you must bring me true intelligence of all that concerns Rāma — what he is doing and how."
"All night-wanderers must go there without carelessness, and effort must ever be made toward the slaying of Rāghava."
"For I know your strength well from many a battle-front; and it is for that reason I have assigned you to this Janasthāna."
Then those eight rākṣasas, receiving these pleasing and weighty words, saluted Rāvaṇa and together departed from Laṅkā toward Janasthāna, vanishing from sight.
Having thus secured Sītā and taken possession of Maithilī, Rāvaṇa was greatly exultant; and having now committed himself to supreme enmity with Rāma, that rākṣasa was delighted through his own delusion.
Having dispatched the eight terrible, mighty rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa, through the confusion of his intellect, considered himself as having accomplished his purpose.
Thinking of Vaidehī, pierced through by the arrows of love, he hastily entered his beautiful dwelling, eager to see Sītā.
Rāvaṇa, the lord of rākṣasas, entering that dwelling, saw Sītā in the midst of the demonesses, wholly given over to grief.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Her face filled with tears, wretched, crushed by the weight of sorrow, like a boat assailed by fierce winds sinking in the ocean.
Strayed from her herd of deer, like a doe surrounded by dogs, her face cast downward, wretched — the night-stalker approached her.
The lord of rākṣasas then forcefully showed that wretched, helpless one, overcome by grief, his palace comparable to the abode of the gods.
It was filled with mansions and palaces, frequented by thousands of women, thronged with diverse flocks of birds, adorned with gems of every kind.
With pillars of gold and refined gold, of crystal and silver, inlaid with diamond and vaidūrya, captivating to the eye.
Resounding with divine kettledrums, with archways of refined gold, he ascended with her the splendid golden stairway.
There were rows of palaces with latticed windows of ivory and silver, pleasing to behold, covered with golden nets.
The floors everywhere were variously decorated with plaster and gems; Daśagrīva showed all these to Maithilī in his own dwelling.
Rāvaṇa showed grief-stricken Sītā the long ponds and lotus pools covered with diverse flowers.
Having shown Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka, all of that magnificent dwelling, the wicked-souled Rāvaṇa spoke these words to her.
"One hundred and twenty million night-wandering rākṣasas, excluding the old, the aged, and the young —
"Of all those — terrible in deed, O Sītā — I am the lord; one thousand of them stand ready, each one, to execute my commands."
"This entire realm and sovereignty of mine rests in you; my life too, O wide-eyed one — you are dearer to me than my own breath."
"Of the many thousands of women who are in my household, you, Sītā, shall be sovereign over them all — become my wife, my beloved."
"Come, what use is this contrary mind of yours? Find my words pleasing; I am consumed with longing — you ought to bestow your grace upon me."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This Laṅkā, encircled by the ocean, spanning a hundred yojanas, cannot be assailed even by gods and asuras with Indra at their head."
"Neither among gods, nor yakṣas, nor gandharvas, nor among human sages — I see none in all the worlds who might equal me in valor."
"What will you do with Rāma — a mere mortal, wretched, bereft of his kingdom, a wandering ascetic, of little splendor, whose life is as good as gone?"
"Cherish me alone, O Sītā — I am a husband worthy of you; youth is impermanent, O timid one; enjoy yourself here with me."
"Direct not your mind to the sight of Rāghava, O most beautiful-faced one; who has the power to come here, O Sītā, even in imagination?"
"The mighty swift wind cannot be fettered in the sky with snares, nor the pure flame of blazing fire be grasped."
"In all three worlds I see none, O beautiful one, who by valor could take you away from the shelter of my arms."
"Rule with me this vast kingdom of Laṅkā; anointed with consecration waters, be content and give me delight."
"Whatever evil karma you have from former deeds has been expiated by your forest sojourn; now enjoy here the fruit of whatever good merit you have accumulated."
"Here all garlands, divine fragrances, O Maithilī, and the finest ornaments — enjoy all these with me."
"There is a chariot called Puṣpaka, O beautiful-hipped one, my brother Vaiśravaṇa's; that chariot is delightful and swift as thought."
"In it, O Sītā, sport with me to your heart's content; your face, lotus-like, pure, lovely to behold —
"Tormented by grief, O beautiful-formed one, it does not shine, O most lovely-faced one; enough of this shame on account of the transgression of dharma ascribed to you, O Vaidehī."
"This coming to you is a divine dispensation ordained by fate; these my feet, with affection, I press to my head before you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Grant me your favor swiftly; I am your devoted servant — let not these words spoken by me, as I wither with longing, be uttered in vain."
"Never indeed has Rāvaṇa bowed his head to any woman." Having thus spoken, Daśagrīva addressed Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka —
— thinking to himself: "She has fallen into the power of Fate; she is mine."
Thus addressed, Vaidehī, fearless though worn by grief, placing a blade of grass between herself and Rāvaṇa as a barrier, spoke in reply.
"There is a king named Daśaratha, immovable as a dyke of righteousness, known to all as true to his vows — whose son is that Rāghava."
"He is named Rāma, righteous-souled, renowned in all three worlds, long-armed, wide-eyed — he is my god, my husband."
"Born in the line of the Ikṣvākus, lion-shouldered, of great splendor — together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, he will take your life."
"Were I, who am directly his, to be violated by you by force, you would lie slain in battle just as Khara was slain at Janasthāna."
"Those rākṣasas you have described as terrible in form and mighty — before Rāghava they are all venom-less, like serpents before Garuḍa."
"His arrows, adorned with gold, released from the bowstring, will tear through your body as waves batter the banks of the Gaṅgā."
"Even if you be invulnerable to asuras and gods, O Rāvaṇa, having provoked this great enmity, you will not escape him alive."
"That mighty Rāghava will be the destroyer of what remains of your life; your survival is as uncertain as that of a sacrificial beast bound to the post."
"Should Rāma look upon you with eyes ablaze with fury, you would be burnt to ash that very instant, O demon, and meet immediate destruction."
"He who could hurl the moon down from the sky or destroy it, who could dry up the ocean — such a one could liberate Sītā from here."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Your life is spent, your fortune gone, your vitality gone, your senses gone; Laṅkā through your deed will be plunged into widowhood."
"This sinful act of yours — carrying me away from the forest, from my husband's side, against my will — will not yield happy results for you."
"For my husband, of great splendor, supported by the gods, dwells fearlessly in the desolate Daṇḍaka, relying on his valor."
"He will strip your pride, strength, valor, and arrogance from your limbs with a rain of arrows in battle."
"When the destruction of beings is seen, urged on by Time, then men fallen under Time's power grow heedless in their deeds."
"By violating me, that Time has arrived for you, O vilest of demons — for the slaughter of yourself, your rākṣasas, and your inner household."
"An altar set in the midst of a sacrifice, adorned with ladles and vessels, consecrated by the mantras of twice-born priests, cannot be defiled by a caṇḍāla."
"This body, now insensible — bind it or slay it; I hold neither this body nor my life dear, O demon; for I cannot bring upon myself disgrace in this world."
Having thus spoken these exceedingly harsh words out of anger to Rāvaṇa, Maithilī Vaidehī said nothing further to him there.
Having heard Sītā's harsh, hair-raising words, he then replied to Sītā with words designed to inspire terror.
"Hear my words, O Maithilī, O passionate one: if within twelve months' time you do not come to me, O lovely-smiling one, the cooks will then cut you to pieces for my morning meal."
Having spoken these harsh words, Rāvaṇa — the terror of his enemies — then in fury spoke these words to the demonesses.
"Swiftly, you demonesses of hideous and terrible appearance, eaters of flesh and blood, must break her pride."
At his mere word, those hideous and terrible demonesses, joining their palms in obeisance, surrounded Maithilī.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That king, Rāvaṇa of dreadful appearance, spoke to them, stamping his feet with such force it seemed to split the earth.
"Let Maithilī be taken to the Aśoka grove; let her be guarded there in secret, surrounded by her warders."
"There, with terrible threats and again with gentle words, bring Maithilī fully under control — as one tames a wild elephant cow."
Thus instructed by Rāvaṇa, those demonesses took hold of Maithilī and went to the Aśoka grove.
It was surrounded by trees bearing every desired fruit, covered with diverse flowers and fruits, frequented by birds intoxicated at every season.
And Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, her limbs overcome by grief, having fallen into the power of the demonesses, was like a doe in the power of tigresses.
Maithilī found no comfort there, excessively threatened by those demonesses of disfigured eyes; remembering her beloved husband and dear brother-in-law, she fell into a state of unconsciousness, tormented by fear and grief.
Having slain Mārīca — the rākṣasa who roamed in the form of a deer, a shape-shifter at will — Rāma quickly turned back upon the path.
As he hurried along, eager to see Maithilī, a jackal behind him cried out with a harsh, ominous shriek.
Recognising that dreadful, hair-raising cry and deeply troubled by the jackal's omen, he fell into anxious reflection.
"Inauspicious indeed, I fear, is this howling of the jackal. May Vaidehī be safe and undevoured by the rākṣasas!"
"If Lakṣmaṇa were to hear that cry uttered in the form of a deer by Mārīca — who mimicked my voice as he discerned it — [he would come to me]."
"That son of Sumitrā, on hearing that voice and being urged by her — abandoning Maithilī — will quickly come here to my side."
"Surely the rākṣasas in concert have plotted the killing of Sītā, and by taking the form of a golden deer they have lured me away from the hermitage."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Having drawn me far away, that rākṣasa Mārīca was struck by an arrow and cried out 'Ah, Lakṣmaṇa, I am slain!' — such were the words he uttered."
"May those two, left alone by me in the forest, be safe! For it is on account of Janasthāna that I have made enemies of the rākṣasas. And today many terrible omens appear."
Reflecting thus, having heard the jackal's cry and realising how he had been lured away by the rākṣasa in a deer's form, the Rāghava came to Janasthāna filled with deep misgiving.
Beasts and birds approached that great soul who was wretched and downcast of mind, circling him on his left side and uttering dreadful cries.
After seeing those exceedingly dreadful omens, the Rāghava then beheld Lakṣmaṇa approaching, his lustre gone.
Not far off, Lakṣmaṇa — despondent — met with Rāma — despondent; the grief-stricken one met with his grief-sharing companion.
Then the elder brother upbraided Lakṣmaṇa who had come [back], having abandoned Sītā alone in the desolate forest haunted by rākṣasas.
Taking Lakṣmaṇa by the left hand, the joy of the Raghu clan spoke these harsh words — grievous yet with a gentle resonance underneath.
"Ah, Lakṣmaṇa, what you have done is blameworthy — that you have come here abandoning Sītā, my good kinsman. May she yet be well!"
"I have no doubt, O hero, that the daughter of Janaka has in every way been destroyed or devoured by the forest-roaming rākṣasas."
"Yet even as these inauspicious signs multiply before me, may we still find Sītā whole, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"This rākṣasa who resembled a deer — having lured me and led me far away — was killed only with great effort; and even as he died, he revealed his true rākṣasa nature."
"My mind here is wretched and joyless, and my left eye throbs with ill omen. Without doubt, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā is no more — she has been carried off, or slain, or lies somewhere on the road."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing the dejected Lakṣmaṇa returned alone, the son of Daśaratha — righteous in soul — questioned him anxiously about Vaidehī.
"Where is that Vaidehī who followed me when I departed into the Daṇḍaka forest, O Lakṣmaṇa — she whom you have abandoned and come here?"
"Where is that slender-waisted Vaidehī, my companion in sorrow, as I — fallen from my kingdom and miserable — wander through the Daṇḍaka wilds?"
"Without whom, O hero, I cannot endure to live even a moment — where is that Sītā, the companion of my very breath, like unto the daughter of the gods?"
"Sovereignty over the immortals or over the very earth itself — without that golden-hued daughter of Janaka I should not desire it, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"Does Vaidehī still live — she who is dearer to me than life itself? Will this exile of mine, O gentle one, not prove to have been in vain?"
"On account of Sītā, O son of Sumitrā, if both you and I perish, will that Kaikeyī then be content and happy with her desire fulfilled?"
"The wretched Kausalyā, her son dead, will attend upon Kaikeyī — Kaikeyī who has her own son and her kingdom and her purpose fulfilled. May this not be so, O gentle one."
"If Vaidehī lives, I shall return to the hermitage; if she has met her end — however blameless her conduct — I shall give up my life, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"If Vaidehī does not speak to me when I arrive at the hermitage — if Sītā no longer greets me with her smile — I shall perish, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"Tell me, Lakṣmaṇa — does Vaidehī live or not? Has that hapless woman been devoured by the rākṣasas while you were heedless?"
"Tender and young, she who has never before known sorrow — Vaidehī is surely grieving now, her heart in anguish, separated from me."
"By that treacherous, utterly wicked rākṣasa — crying out 'Lakṣmaṇa!' in a loud voice — fear was surely instilled even in you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I suspect that voice, resembling mine, was heard by Vaidehī; frightened, she sent you off, and you came quickly to find me."
"In every way it was a dreadful thing to abandon Sītā alone in the forest — an opportunity given to those merciless rākṣasas to act against her."
"Those flesh-eating rākṣasas, aggrieved by the slaughter of Khara, will surely have killed Sītā — those dreadful ones. Of this there is no doubt."
"Alas, I am plunged into calamity in every way, O destroyer of foes! Yet what can I do now? Such, I believe, was the fate destined to befall."
Thus brooding on Sītā of noble bearing, the Rāghava arrived hastily at Janasthāna together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Reproaching his younger brother who looked stricken with grief, heaving sighs, his mouth parched with hunger, exhaustion and thirst, despondent — upon reaching the dwelling and seeing it empty,
— the hero entered his hermitage, searched through the various places she had frequented, murmuring 'here — there,' and throughout the dwelling place his body-hair stood erect in anguish.
Then, as he turned back from the hermitage on the way, the joy of the Raghu clan — Rāma, tormented by grief — questioned the son of Sumitrā once more.
He said to him: "Why have you come back having abandoned Maithilī, when she was wandering in the forest entrusted by me to your care?"
"On seeing you come back having left Maithilī, O Lakṣmaṇa, I suspect some great evil has occurred — truly my heart is anguished."
"My left eye throbs, and so does my arm and my heart, O Lakṣmaṇa, seeing you from afar on the road, separated from Sītā."
Thus addressed, the son of Sumitrā — Lakṣmaṇa of auspicious marks — himself overwhelmed with grief, spoke to the grieving Rāma.
"I did not come here of my own accord, wilfully abandoning her; I was urged by her herself with harsh and vehement words to come to your side."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Maithilī heard those words — as if your noble cry: 'Ah, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa! Save me!' — and it entered her ears."
"She, Maithilī, hearing that voice of distress and moved by her love for you, said to me 'Go, go!' — weeping, overcome with fear."
"As I repeatedly urged 'Go!' upon her, Maithilī answered back to me with these words directed at you in full confidence:"
"'I see no rākṣasa that could bring danger to him. Be calm; this is nothing — it has been spoken so by no one of consequence.'"
"'How could that noble one — who could protect even the thirty gods — utter words of supplication, "Save me!"? Such words are base and unworthy of him, O Sītā.'"
"'For what reason has someone, borrowing my brother's voice, cried out discordantly: "Lakṣmaṇa, save me"? You need not be distressed by this — it is the way of foolish, base women.'"
"'Enough of this faintheartedness — be composed, free of anxiety. There is no man in the three worlds, born or yet to be born, who could defeat the Rāghava in battle.'"
"Thus addressed, Vaidehī — her mind utterly bewildered — wept and then spoke these harsh words to me:"
"'Your feelings toward me are utterly base and sinful! With your elder brother dead or in peril, you think you will obtain me — but you shall not!'"
"'By prior arrangement with Bharata you accompany Rāma — yet although he now cries out in great anguish, you do not go to him!'"
"'You are a secret enemy moving covertly, following along for my sake, seeking an opportunity against the Rāghava — that is why you do not go to him!'"
"Thus spoken to by Vaidehī, I became enraged, my eyes reddened, my lips quivering with fury, and I departed from the hermitage."
To Lakṣmaṇa speaking thus, Rāma — deluded by anguish — said: "You have done ill, gentle one, in coming here without her."
"Though knowing full well that I am capable of repelling rākṣasas, you departed at the angry word of Maithilī."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I am not at all pleased with you for abandoning Maithilī and coming here, having heeded the harsh words of an angry woman."
"In every way it was an unwise act on your part: urged on by Sītā, you fell under the sway of anger and did not observe my command."
"That rākṣasa who lured me away from the hermitage in the form of a deer — he now lies slain, struck down by my arrow."
"Drawing the bow and fitting the arrow, with ease I struck him; and that rākṣasa — he who wore bracelets on his upper arms — abandoned his deer-form and cried out in a distorted voice."
"Even as he was struck by the arrow, in his agonised voice he mimicked my voice and cried out from afar that dreadfully cruel utterance — it is on account of that cry that you came here, abandoning Maithilī."
As Rāma was hurrying back, his lower left eye twitched and throbbed, and a trembling came over him.
Observing these ill omens again and again, he could only say, "May Sītā at least be well."
He hastened forward, longing to see Sītā, but upon finding the dwelling empty his heart was seized with anguish.
The joy of the Raghus, as though frantic with urgency, roamed about searching everywhere around the site of the leaf hut.
He beheld the leaf cottage empty of Sītā, stripped of its beauty and in ruin, like a lotus pond in winter bereft of its glory.
The trees seemed to weep, the flowers were withered, the deer and birds were still; the grove was desolate, stripped of its splendour, abandoned by its forest deities.
Seeing the site of the hut empty, with the antelope-skin and kuśa grass scattered about and the woven mat tossed aside, he lamented again and again.
"Has she been abducted, or is she dead, or has she disappeared? Has she been devoured? Or perhaps the timid one is hiding somewhere, or has gone deep into the forest?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Has she gone to gather flowers or fruits? Or has she gone to a lotus pond, or gone to the river for water?"
Though he searched diligently, he could not find his beloved in the forest; his eyes reddened with grief, he appeared as one driven mad by sorrow.
Running from tree to tree, from hill to hill, from river to river, Rāma lamented, plunged deep in the swamp-like ocean of grief.
"O Kadamba tree, have you seen her who loves the kadamba? If you know, tell me — tell me of Sītā of the fair face."
"O Bilva tree, if you have seen her whose breasts resemble the bilva fruit, who is clad in yellow silk and whose complexion is like tender fresh shoots, then tell me."
"Or you, O Arjuna tree, tell me of her who loves the arjuna — whether Janaka's timid daughter lives or not."
"The kakubha tree surely knows that Maithilī whose thighs are like the kakubha — for it gleams rich with creeping shoots and blossoms."
"Surely this tilaka tree, best of trees hummed over by bees, knows her who loves the tilaka."
"O Aśoka, remover of sorrow — quickly make me worthy of your name by showing me my beloved, for my heart is crushed by grief."
"O Tāla tree, if you have seen her whose breasts are like ripe tāla fruit, if you have any compassion for me, then tell me of that fair-limbed one."
"O Jambū tree, if you have seen Sītā whose radiance is like gold from the Jāmbūnada river, if you know my beloved, speak to me without hesitation."
"O deer, do you know Maithilī with eyes like a fawn? She who gazes like a doe — perhaps she is among your does."
"O elephant, if you have seen her whose thighs are like an elephant's trunk, I believe she is known to you — tell me, O noble bull elephant."
"O tiger, if you have seen my beloved Maithilī whose face is like the moon, tell me freely — you have nothing to fear."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Why do you run, my beloved? Surely I see you, O lotus-eyed one — why do you hide yourself behind that tree and not speak to me?"
"Stop, stop, O fair-hipped one — have you no compassion for me? You are not given to excessive jesting — why then do you disregard me?"
"You are revealed by your yellow silk garment, O fair-complexioned one — even as you run I have seen you. Stop, if there is any affection between us."
"No, it is not she — or else that lovely-smiling one has been slain; for surely the calamity that has befallen me warrants such utter disregard."
"Evidently the young one has been devoured by flesh-eating rākṣasas, her every limb dismembered — my beloved, bereft of me."
"Surely that face with its fair teeth and lips has lost its lustre; and that neck, radiant as the campaka flower and adorned with a necklace — gone."
"Surely those two tender arms, soft as young shoots, of my lamenting beloved — those lovely arms as she was being tossed about — have been devoured."
"Those arms with their quivering fingertips, adorned with bracelets and armlets, have been devoured — the young one, separated from me, given over as food for rākṣasas."
"Abandoned as though by a merchant's caravan and devoured, she who had so many kinsmen — Ah, Lakṣmaṇa, O mighty-armed one, do you see my beloved anywhere?"
"Ah, beloved, where have you gone? Ah, fortunate one! Ah, Sītā!" — thus lamenting again and again, Rāma ran from forest to forest.
Somewhere he rushed forward with frantic speed, somewhere he staggered uncontrollably, and somewhere he appeared like a madman, intent on searching for his beloved.
Unstable and unsettled, he wandered swiftly through forests, rivers, mountains, mountain torrents, and groves.
Having gone thus through the vast great forest and searched it all, yet finding no certainty regarding Maithilī, he made the utmost effort in searching for his beloved once again.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, had seen the āśrama site empty, the leaf hut deserted, and the seats scattered in disarray.
Not seeing the Vaidehī there and having surveyed everything carefully, Rāma cried out and raised his beautiful arms in lamentation, and spoke.
"Where has the Vaidehī gone, Lakṣmaṇa? To what place has she departed from here? By whom has she been carried off, O Saumitri, or by whom has my beloved been devoured?"
"Sītā, if you wish to laugh at me by hiding behind that tree, enough with laughter — come to me now, for I am overwhelmed with grief."
"Sītā, the trusting fawns with whom you used to play — these, left behind by you, O gentle one, now stand lost in thought with tear-filled eyes."
"My father the great king will surely see me in the next world, slain by this immense grief born of Sītā's abduction."
"How is it that you, having accepted a promise from me, have come back to my presence without fulfilling the appointed time?"
"'Shame on you,' my father will surely say to me in the next world, 'you who acted from mere desire, who are ignoble, who are a speaker of false words.'"
"Fame has abandoned me here — helpless, scorched by grief, wretched, and broken in spirit — as if I were a dishonest man abandoned by glory."
"Where are you going, O fair-hipped, slender-waisted one, leaving me behind? Separated from you, I shall give up my very life."
Thus lamenting, and longing to see Sītā, Rāma the Rāghava, afflicted by the most severe grief, could not find the daughter of Janaka.
Seeing Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, unable to find Sītā and sinking like a great elephant that has reached deep mire, Lakṣmaṇa spoke to him with exceeding earnestness, out of a desire for his welfare.
"Do not despair, O mighty-armed one — make effort together with me. This forest, O hero, is adorned with many mountain caverns."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Maithilī, who loves to roam the forest and becomes intoxicated by it, may have entered the forest or gone to a well-flowering lotus grove."
"Or she may have reached a river frequented by fish and cranes; or the Vaidehī, wishing to startle us, O bull among men, may be hiding somewhere in the forest, curious to know where you and I are."
"Let us swiftly make effort, O glorious one, to search for her — let us two search the entire forest where the daughter of Janaka might be. If you agree, O Kākutstha, do not let your mind dwell in sorrow."
Thus spoken to with affection by Lakṣmaṇa and steadied by it, Rāma set out together with Saumitri to search; the two of them began to search through forests, mountains, rivers, and lakes.
The two sons of Daśaratha searched thoroughly for Sītā — the slopes of that mountain, its caves and its peaks.
Though they searched thoroughly, they did not find her. Having searched the mountain in every direction, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"I do not see the Vaidehī here on this lovely mountain, O Saumitri." Then Lakṣmaṇa, overcome with grief, spoke these words.
"Wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest, O greatly wise one, you will find Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka — that blazing-spirited brother of yours awaits."
"Just as mighty-armed Viṣṇu having bound Bali recovered this earth" — thus spoken to by the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, that Rāghava —
— spoke in a piteous voice, his mind crushed by sorrow: "The entire forest has been well searched, the lotus ponds with their blooming lotuses —"
"— and this mountain, O greatly wise one, with its many caves and cascades; yet I do not see the Vaidehī who is dearer to me than life."
Thus lamenting, Rāma, emaciated by the abduction of Sītā, wretched and utterly consumed by grief, became bewildered for a moment.
With every limb trembling, his intellect gone, his senses absent, he sank down in distress, miserable, heaving long and cold sighs.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Sighing deeply many times, lotus-eyed Rāma cried out many times, "Ah, my beloved!" his voice choked with tears.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, the dear kinsman, versed in dharma, with humility and folded hands, consoled him in many ways.
But disregarding those words that had fallen from Lakṣmaṇa's lips, not seeing his beloved Sītā, he cried out again and again.
Wretched, in a wretched voice he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa: "Go quickly, Lakṣmaṇa, and find out what has become of the river Godāvarī — perhaps Sītā has gone to the Godāvarī to bring back lotuses."
Thus spoken to by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, swift in his movements, went once again to the lovely river Godāvarī.
Having searched that river with its many fords, Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Rāma: "I do not see her at the fords; she does not hear me even when I call out."
"What place has the Vaidehī, the destroyer of sorrow, reached? I do not know, O Rāma, where that slender-waisted one has gone."
Hearing Lakṣmaṇa's words, wretched and bewildered by anguish, Rāma himself proceeded to the river Godāvarī.
