Approaching her, Rāma spoke thus: "Where is Sītā?"
Neither the beings dwelling there, nor the river Godāvarī, revealed to Rāma that she had been carried off by the lord of rākṣasas who deserves to be slain.
Then, though the beings urged her, "Tell him about his beloved," yet she, when questioned by Rāma, did not disclose Sītā's whereabouts, being filled with grief.
Reflecting on the form and the deeds of that wicked-souled Rāvaṇa, the river, out of fear, did not reveal the Vaidehī's fate.
Made hopeless by that river of ever seeing Sītā, Rāma, emaciated by his longing to see Sītā, spoke to Saumitri.
"What words shall I say, O Lakṣmaṇa, when I meet Janaka and the mother of the Vaidehī, without her — what unpleasant news shall I bring?"
"She who removed all my grief as I lived in the forest on forest fare, deprived of my kingdom — where now has that Vaidehī gone?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For me, bereft of my kinsmen's side and not seeing the princess, the nights will be long indeed, I think, as I lie awake."
"I shall roam through the Godāvarī, this Janasthāna, and this mountain with its cascades — all of them — if only Sītā might be found."
As the two brothers were thus conversing with one another, they noticed on the ground a trail of scattered flowers.
Seeing that shower of flowers fallen on the earth, the heroic Rāma, grieving, spoke these grievous words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"I recognize these flowers here, Lakṣmaṇa — the ones that had been worn upon the Vaidehī's body, given by me in the forest."
Having said this, the mighty-armed one, that bull among men, spoke in fury to the mountain there, like a lion addressing a small deer.
"Show me Sītā, O mountain, she of golden hue and golden radiance — before I shatter all your slopes to ruin."
"Scorched by the fire of my arrows, you will be reduced to ash, forever inaccessible, stripped of grass, trees, and foliage."
"Or today I shall dry up this river as well, Lakṣmaṇa, if she does not reveal to me today Sītā of the moon-like face."
Thus enraged, with eyes blazing as though to set fire to everything, Rāma saw on the ground a great footprint left by the rākṣasa.
Seeing the tracks of Sītā and the rākṣasa, Rāma, his heart seized with agitation, told his dear brother.
"Look, Lakṣmaṇa — the scattered gold droplets from the Vaidehī's ornaments, O Saumitri, and various garlands as well."
"Look, O Saumitri — the ground everywhere is covered with bright drops of blood like glowing molten metal."
"I think, Lakṣmaṇa, that the Vaidehī has been torn limb from limb and dismembered, or devoured, by the shape-shifting rākṣasas."
"For the sake of the Vaidehī, there must have been a terrible battle here between two rākṣasas who were quarreling, O Saumitri."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Whose great bow is this, inlaid with pearls and gems, adorned with refined gold, lying broken on the ground, O gentle one?"
"Whose is this golden armour, radiant as the young sun, set with beryl globes, shattered and fallen to the earth?"
"Whose royal parasol, with its hundred ribs, adorned with divine garlands, its handle broken, has been cast down to the earth, O gentle one?"
"And these donkeys with golden chest-coverings, with the faces of piśācas, of fearsome form and massive bodies — whose are they, slain in battle?"
"Whose war chariot, brilliant as blazing fire, resplendent with its battle-standard, has been hurled away and broken?"
"Whose are these terrible arrows, as long as a chariot axle, adorned with refined gold, that lie scattered about after striking their mark?"
"Look at this enmity against me, a hundredfold, lethal to my very life, O gentle one — wrought by those shape-shifting rākṣasas of utterly vile hearts."
"Sītā the ascetic has been abducted, or killed, or devoured — dharma did not protect Sītā as she was being carried off in this great forest."
"With the Vaidehī devoured or even abducted, O Lakṣmaṇa, O gentle one — what lords in this world are capable of doing something dear to me?"
"All beings, O Lakṣmaṇa, shall disrespect out of ignorance even the creator of worlds, even one who is heroic and compassionate."
"Surely the lords of the thirty gods consider me, who am gentle, devoted to the welfare of the world, self-restrained, and compassionate, to be devoid of heroism."
"A virtue has turned into a fault upon meeting with me — look, Lakṣmaṇa: today, withdrawing the moonlight as a great sun rises, I shall arise for the destruction of all beings and rākṣasas alike."
"Neither yakṣas, nor gandharvas, nor piśācas, nor rākṣasas, nor kiṃnaras, nor human beings shall find happiness, O Lakṣmaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Look, Lakṣmaṇa — today I shall fill the sky with my weapons and arrows, making it impassable for those who travel through the three worlds."
"With the host of planets blocked off, the moon obstructed, the light of fire, wind, and sun extinguished and covered over —"
"— with mountain peaks shattered, water-bodies drying up, trees, creepers and shrubs destroyed, the oceans obliterated —"
"If the lords do not restore to me Sītā safe and well, this very moment, O Saumitri, they shall witness my might."
"No creature shall fly through the sky, O Lakṣmaṇa, under the unceasing torrents of arrows released from my bowstring."
"Look today, O Lakṣmaṇa, at the universe tormented by my iron arrows, its roaming deer and birds destroyed, thrown into chaos and stripped of all bounds."
"With arrows drawn to the ear, arrows that are hard to resist, I shall reduce the world of the living, for Maithilī's sake, to one without piśācas and without rākṣasas."
"Today the gods shall witness the power of my arrows, loosed by my fury, discharged in wrath, flying far."
"Neither gods, nor daityas, nor piśācas, nor rākṣasas shall exist once the three worlds are annihilated by my wrath."
"The worlds of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas alike shall fall down in many pieces, ripped apart by floods of arrows; today with my shafts I shall make these worlds lawless."
"Just as old age, death, time, and fate are never obstructed among all beings, O Lakṣmaṇa — so I, filled with fury, am beyond all restraint, without doubt."
"If they do not restore to me today Maithilī, that blameless one of lovely teeth, as they did before, I shall overturn the entire world with its gods, gandharvas, humans, serpents, and mountains."
Rāma, tormented and emaciated by Sītā's abduction, blazed like the doomsday fire fit for the destruction of all worlds.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He gazed upon his strung bow and breathed repeatedly in fury, like Rudra enraged and desiring to slay the sacrificial beast at Dakṣa's sacrifice.
Seeing Rāma enraged as never before, Lakṣmaṇa spoke words with folded hands and a parched mouth.
"You who were formerly gentle, self-restrained, and devoted to the welfare of all beings — you should not abandon your nature by falling under the sway of anger.
Splendour belongs to the moon, radiance to the sun, speed to the wind, patience to the earth — all these are fixed qualities — and in you, unsurpassed glory.
I do not know to whom this shattered war-chariot belongs, armed and fully equipped as it is, nor by whom or for what reason it was destroyed.
This place is scarred by hooves and wheel-rims, sprinkled with drops of blood — a very dreadful spot where battle was joined and then ended, O son of a king.
The marks of combat here are those of a single fighter, not two — I see no trace, O best of speakers, of a large army having passed this way.
You should not destroy the worlds on account of a single person. Lords of the earth who are gentle and tranquil apply punishment in due measure.
You are ever the refuge and supreme resort of all beings, O Rāghava — who then would consider it good that you should lose your wife?
Rivers, oceans, mountains, gods, gandharvas, and dānavas are not capable of doing what is displeasing to you, as the virtuous are not capable of wronging one who has taken a sacred vow.
O king, you should seek out the one by whom Sītā was abducted — with me at your side, bow in hand, and with the great sages as allies.
We shall search the ocean, the mountains, the forests, the many dreadful caves, the lotus-ponds, and the highland lakes.
We shall search the worlds of gods and gandharvas as well, with concentrated minds, until we find the abductor of your wife.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
If even the lords of the thirty gods do not return your wife through conciliation, O lord of Kosala, you will then act as the occasion demands.
If through good conduct, conciliation, humility, and policy you cannot recover Sītā, O lord of men, then annihilate them with showers of arrows gold-feathered and equal to Mahendra's thunderbolt."
Rāma was thus tormented by grief, lamenting like one without a protector, seized by great delusion, utterly dispirited and bereft of consciousness.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, after consoling him for what seemed like a moment, began to rouse Rāma, pressing his feet.
"You were obtained, O Rāma, by king Daśaratha through great austerity and great deeds, as the immortals obtained amṛta.
Bound by your qualities and unable to bear separation from you, that lord of the earth, the king, has attained divine status — so it is heard from Bharata.
If you, O Kākutstha, cannot endure this grief that has befallen you, what other ordinary man of little strength shall endure it?
If in your distress you were to scorch the worlds with your energy, O tiger among men, where would the afflicted subjects go to find peace?
This is the very nature of the world: Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, had attained the same realm as Śakra, and yet calamity touched him as well.
The great seer Vasiṣṭha, who was the household priest of our father, begat a hundred sons in a single day — and those same sons were slain.
And the goddess who is the mother of the world and revered by all — even the trembling of the earth, her quaking, is seen, O you to whom truth is a vow.
And these two eyes of the world, the sun and moon — in whom all things are established — even they, mighty as they are, are seized by eclipses.
Even the mightiest beings and the gods, O bull among men — no embodied creature in all existence is released from the power of fate.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Even among the gods headed by Śakra, both good fortune and misfortune are heard to occur, O tiger among men — you should not be distressed.
Even though Vaidehī is lost, even though she has been abducted, O sinless one, you should not grieve as another ordinary man would, O hero.
Those like you who constantly behold truth and who, like Rāma, are never despondent, do not grieve even in the greatest of adversities.
Reflect carefully upon reality with your intellect, O best of men. The greatly wise, endowed with discernment, know the auspicious from the inauspicious.
For actions whose merits and faults are unseen and which are not firmly undertaken, the desired fruit does not come to pass without effort.
O hero, it was you yourself who instructed me repeatedly in the past. Who indeed could teach you now — even Bṛhaspati himself in person?
Your wisdom, O greatly wise one, is unsurpassed even by the gods. I am awakening your knowledge that has fallen asleep under grief.
Considering your own divine and human prowess, O bull of the Ikṣvāku line, strive for the destruction of your enemies.
What is the use of destroying everything, O bull among men? You should identify that one wicked enemy and root him out."
Though Rāma was the elder, upon hearing Lakṣmaṇa's excellent speech, Rāghava, being one who grasps the essence, accepted the great substance of what was said.
The mighty-armed Rāma, suppressing his swollen anger and firmly gripping his splendid bow, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa:
"What shall we do, dear one? Where shall we go, Lakṣmaṇa? By what means might I see Sītā? Think on this."
Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Rāma, who was thus afflicted with burning anguish: "This very Janasthāna you should search."
"Swarming with many rākṣasas and filled with diverse trees and creepers, there are here mountain fastnesses, cliffs, and ravines,

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And many dreadful caves teeming with various herds of animals, the abodes of kiṃnaras, and the dwelling-places of gandharvas.
Those places you, accompanied by me, should search. Great-souled ones endowed with intellect such as yours, O bull among men,
Are not shaken in adversities, like mountains in the gusts of the wind." So addressed, Rāma ranged through that entire forest together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Rāma, enraged, fitting a dreadful razor-headed arrow to his bow, then saw the most noble bird, that foremost among twice-born creatures, like a mountain peak,
Jaṭāyu, lying fallen on the ground, drenched in blood. Seeing him who resembled a mountain summit, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Sītā Vaidehī has been devoured by this one — there is no doubt."
"Clearly this rākṣasa in the form of a vulture wanders the forest; having devoured Sītā of the wide eyes, it rests at ease. I shall slay it with my blazing-tipped, dreadful, straight-flying arrows."
Having spoken thus, the enraged Rāma rushed toward the vulture, fitting the razor-headed arrow to his bow, as if shaking the earth to its ocean-bounded ends.
But the bird, vomiting frothy blood, addressed Rāma, son of Daśaratha, in a voice pitifully feeble:
"That goddess whom you seek in the great forest, O long-lived one, like a healing herb — she and my very life-breath have both been carried off by Rāvaṇa.
The goddess separated from you and Lakṣmaṇa, O Rāghava, being carried away by the mighty Rāvaṇa — she was seen by me.
I fell upon Sītā's abductor and upon Rāvaṇa in battle; by me his chariot and parasol were shattered and he was brought down to the ground.
This is his shattered bow, this is his quiver of arrows, and this, O Rāma, is his war-chariot broken in battle.
When I was exhausted, Rāvaṇa cut off my wings with his sword; having seized Sītā Vaidehī, he soared into the sky. I was struck down first by the rākṣasa — you should not slay me."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāma, understanding that the beloved tale was bound up with Sītā, embraced the king of vultures and wept together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing the solitary one lying alone on that impassable ground, barely breathing, grief-stricken Rāma spoke these words to the son of Sumitrā:
"Expulsion from the kingdom, dwelling in the forest, Sītā lost, and now a twice-born creature slain — such is my misfortune; it would burn even fire.
Were I even today to cross the full expanse of the great ocean, the lord of rivers would surely dry up from my ill-luck.
There is none more unfortunate than I in this world of moving and unmoving things, for this great snare of calamity has ensnared me.
This king of vultures, who was like a father to me, aged and venerable, lies slain on the ground by reason of my misfortune."
Having spoken thus many times, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, touched Jaṭāyu, showing the affection of a father.
Embracing that king of vultures whose wings had been cut off and who was drenched in blood, Rāma released from his lips the words — "Where are you, O Maithilī, you who are equal to my very life?" — and fell to the ground.
Seeing that vulture struck down to the ground by the terrible demon, Rāma spoke these words to Saumitri, who was possessed of every friendly virtue.
"This bird was surely striving for my welfare; struck down in battle by the demon, he is now giving up his life — that life so hard to surrender."
"There is still life in this body of his, Lakṣmaṇa; though deprived of voice, he gazes about him with bewilderment."
"Jaṭāyu, if you are able to speak once more, tell me of Sītā — may it go well with you — and tell me also of your own wounding."
"For what reason did Rāvaṇa carry off Sītā? What wrong had I done him, seeing which Rāvaṇa abducted my beloved?"
"How was that moon-like, heart-ravishing face of hers? And what words did Sītā speak at that time, O foremost of birds?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"What is the might, what the form, and what the deeds of that demon? And where is his dwelling? Tell me, dear one, as I ask you these things."
Looking up at him lamenting thus, Jaṭāyu then spoke these words to Rāma in a voice that had grown extremely faint.
"She was carried off through the sky by Rāvaṇa, the lord of rākṣasas, who had assumed a great illusion filled with wind and storm-cloud."
"Having cut off my wings, dear one, while I was utterly exhausted, that night-roamer took Vaidehī Sītā and departed facing southward."
"My life is being arrested, my sight grows dim, O Rāghava; I see golden trees with shoots of uśīra grass for their crests."
"In that same auspicious moment in which Rāvaṇa departed carrying Sītā, lost wealth swiftly returns to its owner."
"That moment is called Vinda, but he, O scion of Kākutstha, did not understand it; like a fish that seizes the hook, he will quickly perish."
"And you should feel no anguish regarding the daughter of Janaka; you will quickly rejoice with Vaidehī after slaying that demon in battle."
Even as that clear-minded vulture spoke these words back to Rāma, blood mixed with flesh flowed from the mouth of the dying bird.
"He is the direct son of Viśravas and the brother of Vaiśravaṇa" — having uttered these words, the lord of birds relinquished his life, so hard to surrender.
As Rāma stood with palms joined, saying "Speak, speak!", the vital breaths of the vulture departed from his body into the sky.
Then, lowering his head to the ground, stretching out his feet, and convulsing his own body, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
Beholding that red-eyed vulture, his life departed, motionless as a mountain, Rāma — overcome with many sorrows — said to Saumitri:
"Many years were happily passed by this bird dwelling here in the Daṇḍaka forest, which is under the sway of demons."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"He who had risen up and lived for so many years, for such a long time — he lies slain today; for time is indeed impossible to transgress."
"Look, Lakṣmaṇa — this vulture who was my benefactor has been slain; he rushed to shield Sītā against the all-powerful Rāvaṇa."
"Forsaking his great ancestral realm — the kingship of the vultures inherited from his fathers and forefathers — this lord of birds gave up his life for my sake."
"Indeed, virtuous men — those who walk in dharma, heroes who offer refuge — are seen everywhere, Saumitri, even among those born as animals."
"The grief born of Sītā's abduction has not struck me so hard, O gentle one, O scorcher of foes, as the death of this vulture for my sake."
"Just as the illustrious King Daśaratha, so glorious, is to be worshipped and honored by me, so too is this lord of birds."
"Saumitri, bring wood; I shall kindle fire. I wish to cremate the king of vultures who has met his death for my sake."
"I shall place upon the funeral pyre the lord of the bird-world and cremate him, O Saumitri — this one slain by the terrible demon."
"Whatever the way gone by those devoted to sacrifice, whatever the way of those who have established the sacred fire, whatever the way of those who do not turn back in battle, and of those who give away the earth —"
"— granted permission by me, go to those highest realms, O king of vultures, O great being! Duly consecrated by me, depart."
Having spoken thus and placed the lord of birds upon the blazing pyre, the righteous-souled Rāma cremated him with grief, as though he were his own kinsman.
Then valiant Rāma, together with Saumitri, went into the forest; after slaying large rohiṇī deer, he spread them out as an offering over the bird.
Taking out the deer-flesh and shaping it into portions, the greatly glorious Rāma offered it to the bird upon a lovely green lawn.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That which the twice-born declare concerning the passage of a mortal soul to heaven — that rite of passage — Rāma quickly recited for his sake.
Then the two sons of that best of men went to the Godāvarī river and both of them offered water oblations to the king of vultures.
That king of vultures, who had performed a glorious and exceedingly difficult deed, who had been felled in battle, who was then consecrated in accordance with the rites fitting a great sage — he attained the pure and auspicious state befitting his own soul.
Having thus offered the water oblation to him, the two Rāghavas set out, searching for Sītā in the forest, and proceeded toward the western quarter.
Going toward the southern quarter, bearing arrows, bows, and swords, the two sons of Ikṣvāku found an unobstructed path.
It was entangled with many shrubs, trees, and creepers; hemmed in on all sides, difficult of access, dense, and fearsome to behold.
Swiftly passing through, taking the southern direction, the two mighty heroes traversed that vast and formidable great forest.
Then, proceeding three krośas beyond Janasthāna, the two Rāghavas of great splendor entered the dense Krauñca forest.
It resembled a mass of various storm-clouds; it appeared joyful on all sides, adorned with flowers of many beautiful colors, and filled with herds of deer and flocks of birds.
Desiring to see Vaidehī, the two searched through that forest, pausing here and there, worn thin by the abduction of Sītā.
Then the greatly resplendent Lakṣmaṇa — possessed of courage, good conduct, and purity — spoke with joined palms to his brother of blazing splendor:
"My arm throbs strongly; my mind seems agitated; and for the most part I perceive ill omens all around."
"Therefore, noble one, be ready and heed my beneficial counsel, for the omens on my own body proclaim imminent confusion."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This bird called the vañculaka, most dreadful, cries out as if proclaiming victory for us in battle."
While the two of them searched thus throughout that forest with their combined might, a tremendous sound arose, as if it would shatter that very forest.
The sound of that dense forest, as if excessively tossed about by the wind, arose filling heaven itself.
Hearkening to that sound with his brother in the brushwood, Rāma saw a demon of immense body and broad chest.
Then both of them approached him as he stood before them — that monstrous Kabandha, who had neither head nor neck, with his mouth set in his belly.
He was bristling with thick, sharp hairs; tall as a great mountain; resembling a dark cloud; terrible; his voice like the thunder of storm-clouds.
He had a single eye on his chest — tawny, with great lashes, wide and elongated, terrible, keen-sighted.
Furnished with great fangs, licking his enormous mouth, he was devouring the most dreadful bears, lions, deer, and elephants.
Extending his two terrible arms, each a yojana in length, he was seizing with his hands various bears, flocks of birds, and animals.
Drawing in and dragging out many leaders of animal herds, he stood blocking the path of those two brothers who had fallen into his reach.
Then, as the two pressed forward, at the distance of a krośa they saw the great, dreadful, and fearsome Kabandha, enveloped by his own arms.
He of the great arms extended his two vast arms to the utmost and seized both Rāghavas together, squeezing them forcibly.
Those two brothers — bearing swords, clutching their firm bows, blazing with fierce energy, great-armed — fell helpless into his power and were being dragged along by the mighty one.
Kabandha, the foremost of dānavas, great-armed, spoke to the two: "Who are you, bull-shouldered ones, bearing great swords and bows?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Having reached this dreadful region, you have come as food for me. Speak of your business here — for what purpose have the two of you come?"
"Having arrived in this region where I stand tormented by hunger, bearing arrows, bows, and swords, like two bulls with sharp horns, you have approached my mouth; life will be hard to regain."
Having heard those words of evil-souled Kabandha, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa with face grown parched:
"Having encountered calamity upon calamity, O truly valiant one, we have arrived at this dreadful misfortune that brings life to an end — and still without finding my beloved."
"The power of Time is exceedingly great over all beings, Lakṣmaṇa; behold both you and me, O tiger among men, bewildered by misfortune. The burden of fate is not too heavy upon all creatures, Lakṣmaṇa."
"Heroes, the mighty, those skilled in arms on the battlefield — when overtaken by Time they sink down like embankments of sand."
Speaking thus, the son of Daśaratha — of firm and true valor, greatly glorious, of high majesty — looking upon Saumitri of lofty valor, then made his own resolve steadfast within himself.
Seeing those two brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa standing there, ensnared in the coils of his arms, Kabandha spoke:
"Why do you two stand here looking at me, O bulls among kṣatriyas, tormented by hunger? Surely fate has ordained you as my food, your minds now lost."
Having heard those words, Lakṣmaṇa — overwhelmed with pain yet resolved upon a course of action — then spoke words that were timely and beneficial:
"This lowest of demons is quickly swallowing both you and me; therefore let us swiftly cut off his two great arms with our swords."
Then those two Rāghavas, knowing time and place, with their swords and with great exhilaration severed both his arms at the shoulder joints.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāma on the right cut the right arm cleanly with his sword in one swift stroke, while heroic Lakṣmaṇa cut the left.
He of the great arms fell, his arms severed, making a tremendous sound, filling the sky, the earth, and all the quarters, like a storm cloud.
Seeing his arms cut off, drenched in a flood of blood, that dānava pitiably asked those two heroes: "Who are you?"
As he spoke thus, the auspiciously marked and mighty Lakṣmaṇa proclaimed Kākutstha to Kabandha.
"This is the heir of the Ikṣvāku lineage, known among men by the name Rāma; and know me, Lakṣmaṇa, as his younger brother."
"This one of divine might has been dwelling in the desolate forest; his wife has been carried off by a demon, and it is in search of her that the two of us have come here."
"But who are you, and for what reason do you writhe in the forest in this form resembling a Kabandha, with a blazing mouth in your chest and your legs broken?"
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, Kabandha spoke his reply, supremely delighted, recalling the words of Indra.
"Welcome, O tigers among men! By good fortune I behold you, and by good fortune these arms of mine that have been my bondage have now been severed by the two of you."
"And this disfigured form of mine — how it was obtained through insolence — hear that from me, O tiger among men, as I tell you the truth of it."
In former times, O Rāma, great-armed one of mighty strength and valor, my form was inconceivable and renowned throughout the three worlds — even as the form of Soma, of Śakra, and of Sūrya.
That same I, having assumed this form so terrifying to the worlds, went here and there frightening the sages dwelling in the forest, O Rāma.
Thereupon a great sage named Sthūlaśiras, while gathering various forest produce, was affronted by me in this form and roused to wrath.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He, the utterer of a terrible curse, looked upon me and said: "Let this very cruel and censured form be thine forever."
I besought him in his fury asking when the curse might end. He who had laid the curse upon me then spoke these words:
"When Rāma shall cut off your arms and burn you in a lonely forest, then shall you regain your own expansive and beautiful form."
"Know me, O Lakṣmaṇa, to be the radiant and glorious son of Danu — this form was obtained through Indra's wrath on the field of battle, even as I shall relate."
By fierce austerity I had gratified the Grandfather, and he granted me long life; thereafter a delusion took hold of me.
"Long life has been granted to me — what can Śakra do to me?" — resting on this thought, I defied Śakra in battle.
By the hundred-jointed thunderbolt released from his arm, both my thighs and my head were driven into my body.
As I implored him, he brought word from the abode of Yama: "Let the word of the Grandfather be true" — thus he spoke to me.
"Without food, with thighs, head, and mouth smashed and struck by the thunderbolt, how can one live for such a very long time?"
Addressed thus by me, Śakra granted arms each a yojana in length, and fashioned a mouth with sharp fangs in my belly.
Thus I, with those two great arms, drag in from all sides forest-wandering creatures — lions, elephants, deer, and tigers — and devour them.
And Indra told me: "When Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa shall sever your arms in battle, then shall you depart for heaven."
You are that Rāma — good fortune to you! I cannot be slain by any other, O Rāghava, as the great sage truly declared.
I shall indeed render counsel to your intelligence, O bull among men, and I shall direct you to a friend — once I am purified by fire at your hands.
Addressed thus by that son of Danu, the righteous Rāghava spoke this reply while Lakṣmaṇa listened nearby:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Sītā, my illustrious wife, has been carried off by Rāvaṇa, freely and at ease, while I had departed from Janasthāna together with my brother.
I know only the name of that rākṣasa, not his form; we know nothing of his dwelling or his power.
For us who are grief-stricken and helpless and thus wandering about, it befits one who is compassionate and disposed to render aid.
Having gathered dry logs broken in their season by elephants, we shall burn you, O hero, in a great pit that we shall dig.
You then — tell us of Sītā, by whom or to where she was taken; do us this supreme kindness, if you know the truth."
Addressed thus by Rāma, the son of Danu spoke a most excellent reply — he who was skilled in speech, even to Rāghava who is himself a master of eloquence:
"I have no supernatural knowledge, nor do I know of Maithilī. But once I am burned and have regained my own form, I shall tell you of one who will know her.
In my unburned state I have no power to discern that rākṣasa of mighty valor, O lord, by whom your Sītā was taken.
My great knowledge was lost through the fault of the curse, O Rāghava, and this form censured by the world was obtained through my own doing.
But before Savitṛ with his weary steeds sets into the west, cast me into the pit and burn me duly, O Rāma.
Burned by you in the pit according to the rite, O delight of the Raghu line, I shall tell you, O hero, of the one who will know that rākṣasa.
And friendship must be made with him — one of righteous conduct, O Rāghava; he of swift valor, being pleased, will render you assistance.
There is nothing unknown to him in the three worlds, O Rāghava; in former times, for another reason, he ranged through all the worlds."
Addressed thus by Kabandha, those two heroes and lords of men, having reached a mountain ravine, kindled fire.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Lakṣmaṇa, with blazing firebrands on every side, ignited the pyre, and it flared up all around.
That great body of Kabandha, like a lump of clarified butter, sizzled slowly as the fire consumed it, rendered down by its own fat.
He quickly shook off the pyre and rose up, like a smokeless fire, wearing spotless garments and a divine garland — that one of great strength.
Then swiftly from the pyre that radiant one, clad in stainless raiment, leaped up with great joy, adorned with ornaments on every limb.
Standing in a luminous celestial chariot yoked with swans and celebrated for glory, that one of great splendor illumined the ten directions with his radiance.
Kabandha, risen to the sky, spoke to Rāma: "Hear, O Rāghava, truly how you shall reach the boundary of your goal.
O Rāma, there are six expedients in the world by which all is deliberated; one who has been tested by adversity is to be sought in a tenth part of that adversity.
You, O Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, are in that diminished tenth-part condition — the calamity of your wife being violated has been brought upon you.
Therefore you must certainly make that ally yours, O best of friends; reflecting on it, I do not see your success without doing so.
Hear, O Rāma, I shall tell you: there is a monkey named Sugrīva, who has been expelled by his angry brother Vālin, son of Śakra.
That self-possessed hero dwells on the excellent mountain Ṛśyamūka, beautiful with its borders of Pampā, together with four monkeys.
Go from here this very day and quickly make him your companion, O Rāghava; meet with him without treachery before the blazing fire.
Nor should Sugrīva, lord of monkeys, be disregarded by you; he is grateful, capable of assuming any form at will, desirous of allies, and valiant.
For you two are now able to accomplish what he desires to do; and whether his own purpose is fulfilled or not, he will accomplish your task.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He, son of Ṛkṣaraja and natural son of Bhāskara, wanders about Pampā in fear, wronged by Vālin.
Having set aside your weapons, quickly make the monkey who dwells on Ṛśyamūka your sworn companion in truth, O Rāghava, that forest-wanderer.
For that elephant among monkeys in his entirety, by his skill, reaches all the haunts in the world of those who eat human flesh.
Nothing whatsoever in the world is unknown to him, O Rāghava, as far as the thousand-rayed Sūrya blazes, O subduer of enemies.
He, searching great rivers, mountains, mountain-strongholds, and caves together with his monkeys, will discover your wife.
And he will send out mighty-bodied monkeys in every direction, O Rāghava, to search for that Sītā who grieves in separation from you.
That foremost of leaping ones will restore your beloved to you — even if she has gone to the peak of Meru, or taken refuge at the floor of the netherworld — entering even there and slaying the rākṣasas.
Having thus shown Rāma the way to recover Sītā in words pregnant with meaning, Kabandha, knower of purposes, spoke again:
"This, O Rāma, is the auspicious path where these flowering trees, stretching toward the western direction, shine forth in delightful beauty.
Jambū, priyāla, panasa, plakṣa, nyagrodha, tinduka, aśvattha, karṇikāra, cūta, and other trees as well —
climbing them or felling them to the ground by force, you two shall go on eating fruits that rival ambrosia.
Roaming through fine regions, from mountain to mountain, from forest to forest, you two heroes shall then reach the lake and pool called Pampā.
O Rāma, it is without pebbles, without slipperiness, with even banks, free from algae, with sandy shores newly formed, beautified with lotuses and water-lilies.
There, O Rāghava, swans, waterbirds, cranes, and osprey — dwelling in the waters of Pampā — cry out melodiously.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Those beautiful birds, unversed in slaughter and untroubled at the sight of men, you two shall feast upon — those plump birds resembling lumps of clarified butter.
Rohita fish, crooked-mouthed fish, and reed-fish, O Rāghava — choice fish struck with arrows there in Pampā, O Rāma —
— those skinned, scaled, iron-roasted, plump, single-boned ones, Lakṣmaṇa, joined in devotion to you, shall offer you.
As you eagerly eat the fish amid the cluster of blooms of Pampā, Lakṣmaṇa shall give you to drink the auspicious water fragrant with lotuses, pleasantly cool and wholesome.
Drawing it up fresh and unstained, resembling silver and crystal, Lakṣmaṇa shall then give you to drink using a lotus leaf.
Plump boars sleeping in mountain caves, forest-wanderers returning out of greed for water, roaring like bulls, handsome in form — these you shall see at Pampā, O best of men.
At evening, roaming about, O Rāma, seeing the flowering trees adorned with garlands and the cool water of Pampā, you shall cast off your grief.
There the tilaka and naktamāla trees are painted with blossoms, and the utpala and paṅkaja lotus-flowers are in full bloom, O Rāghava.
No man will have strung those garlands there; the sages who were disciples of Mataṅga dwelt there, supremely concentrated.
From those who were wearied by their burdens and brought forest produce for their teacher, the beads of sweat that fell swiftly to the earth from their bodies —
— from those have these garlands been born, arising from the beads of sweat, through the austerity of the sages in that time; they perish not, O Rāghava.
Even to this day there is seen serving them in that very place an ascetic woman named Śabarī, O descendant of Kākutstha, long-lived.
Steadfast ever in righteousness, revered by all beings, she, upon seeing you, O Rāma, who are like a god, shall depart for the heavenly world.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, O Rāma, taking shelter on the western bank of Pampā, you shall see that hermitage, incomparable and secret, O descendant of Kākutstha.
Not even elephants are able to enter that hermitage, by the ordinance of that sage Mataṅga, nor can they enter that forest grove.
In that forest resembling Nandana, like the divine grove, filled with diverse birds, you shall delight, O Rāma, at peace.
To the east of Pampā stands Ṛśyamūka, covered with flowering trees, very difficult to ascend, guarded by young elephants, and magnanimously fashioned by Brahmā in ancient time.
O Rāma, a man sleeping on the summit of that mountain — whatever wealth he obtains in a dream, that he obtains upon waking.
But a man of crooked conduct and evil deeds cannot ascend it; the rākṣasas there seize him as he sleeps and strike him down.
From there too a great cry of young elephants is heard, O Rāma — those who sport in Pampā, dwelling in the Mataṅga forest.
Wetted with streams of blood from fighting together, those supreme elephants, cloud-colored and swift, roam about scattered in different directions.
Having drunk the pure, cool, and inexhaustible water there, those forest-dwelling ones turn back and plunge into the forests.
O Rāma, there shines on that mountain a great cave, sealed by a boulder, O descendant of Kākutstha, and entry into it is difficult.
Before the eastern entrance of that cave lies a great pool of cool water, delightful, rich in roots and fruits, surrounded by diverse trees.
In that cave dwells Sugrīva together with four monkeys; at times he stands upon the peak of that mountain.
Having thus instructed both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, Kabandha — wearing a garland, radiant as the color of the sun, full of valor — shone in the sky.
Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, about to depart, addressed that illustrious Kabandha standing in the sky from nearby: "Go now."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"May you go for the accomplishment of your purpose" — thus he spoke to those two; and having given leave to those two who were supremely pleased, Kabandha departed then.
That Kabandha, having recovered his form, endowed with splendor, his body equal to the sun, standing in the sky and showing himself, looked upon Rāma and then spoke: "Make alliance."
Those two sons of the best of kings, having received from Kabandha the path to Pampā shown in the forest, set out taking the western direction.
Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, beholding the many trees on the hills laden with honey-like fruits, proceeded in order to meet Sugrīva.
Having spent the night on the ridge of a mountain, the two descendants of Raghu approached the western bank of Pampā.
Reaching the western bank of the lotus-filled Pampā, those two then saw there the lovely hermitage of Śabarī.
Approaching that hermitage, surrounded by many trees, and gazing upon its great beauty, the two went up to Śabarī.
Upon seeing those two, that accomplished female ascetic rose up with palms joined in reverence and clasped the feet of Rāma and of the wise Lakṣmaṇa.
Rāma then spoke to that female ascetic, firm in her vows: "Have your obstacles been overcome? Does your austerity grow?
Have your anger and diet been subdued, O treasure of austerity? Have your religious observances been fulfilled? Is your mind at peace? Has your devoted service to your teacher borne fruit, O fair-spoken one?"
Thus questioned by Rāma, that ascetic, accomplished and honored by the accomplished, the aged Śabarī, presented herself before Rāma and spoke.
"When you reached Citrakūṭa, those whom I used to serve ascended from here to heaven in celestial chariots of incomparable splendor.
And those great seers, knowers of dharma and of great fortune, told me: 'Rāma will come to this most holy hermitage of yours.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
He, together with the son of Sumitrā, is to be received by you as a guest, and upon seeing him you will depart to the highest and imperishable worlds.'
By me, O bull among men, O tiger among men, various forest fruits growing on the banks of Pampā have been gathered for your sake."
Thus addressed by Śabarī, the righteous Rāghava spoke these words to Śabarī, who was ever excluded from no understanding:
"The power of your great-souled teacher, truly as heard from Danu's source — I wish to witness it directly, if you think fit."
Hearing these words issued from Rāma's mouth, Śabarī showed those two that great forest.
"Behold, O joy of the Raghus, this forest renowned as the Mataṅga grove, dense as a mass of clouds and teeming with deer and birds.
Here, O greatly resplendent one, my teachers, whose souls were purified, performing fire-offerings, created a sacred ford, sanctified with sacred hymns just as the sacred hymns sanctify.
This is the western altar where those well-honored teachers of mine offered flowers with hands trembling from the effort of austerity.
By the power of their austerities, behold even now, O best of the Raghus, that the altars illumine all directions with radiance of incomparable splendor.
When they, wearied by fasting and austerity and unable to travel, merely thought of them, behold — the seven oceans came together and arrived here.
The bark-garments shed by them after they had bathed — even to this day they do not dry out in this spot, O joy of the Raghus.
This entire forest has been seen by you, and what was to be heard has been heard. I therefore wish, with your permission, to abandon this body.
I wish to go to the presence of those sages of purified souls, whose hermitage I served as an attendant."
Hearing these most righteous words, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, said with a joyful countenance: "I give you leave; go."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Given leave by Rāma, she offered herself into the sacrificial fire and, brilliant as blazing flame, departed to heaven itself.
To that holy abode where those great seers of virtuous souls roam in delight, Śabarī departed in the absorption of her own self.
When Śabarī had gone to heaven through her own deeds, Rāghava reflected with his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
Having reflected upon that power of the great-souled ones, the righteous Rāghava spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who was single-minded and ever devoted to his welfare:
"This hermitage of those who have perfected their souls has been seen, O gentle one — full of great wonders, where deer and tigers live in trust, frequented by birds of many kinds.
And at these sacred fords of the seven oceans, O Lakṣmaṇa, the ritual bath has been taken and the ancestors have been duly propitiated.
Whatever inauspiciousness there was has vanished, and good fortune is now at hand. Because of that, O Lakṣmaṇa, my mind is now greatly gladdened.
For auspiciousness will manifest itself in my heart, O tiger among men. Come then — let us go to that Pampā, lovely to behold.
Near there, not too far away, the mountain Ṛśyamūka gleams, on which the righteous-souled Sugrīva, son of Aṃśumat, dwells — ever terrified by fear of Vālin, together with four monkeys.
Hasten to meet that bull among monkeys, Sugrīva; for the search for Sītā, O gentle one, depends upon him.
To Rāma speaking thus, the son of Sumitrā replied: "Let us go there quickly — my mind too hastens."
That lord of men then departed from the hermitage and came to Pampā, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, the subduer of foes.
Gazing upon it, rich with blossoms, filled everywhere with great trees, that vast forest resonant with herons, arjuna birds, śatapatra cranes, kīcaka reeds, and many other varied creatures.
Rāma, duly observing the trees and the various lakes, tormented by longing, proceeded toward the supreme lake.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Approaching from afar the water-bearing river, Rāma plunged into the lake known as the Mataṅga pool.
That son of Daśaratha, Rāma, overcome with grief, entered the lotus-filled Pampā, covered with water-lilies.
— adorned with tilaka, aśoka, puṃnāga, bakula, and uddāla trees, gleaming with kāśī blossoms, crowded with beautiful groves, its waters pressed thick with lotuses —
— filled with water resembling crystal, spread with fine sand, teeming with fish and tortoises, adorned by trees standing on its banks —
— entwined by creepers as if by dear companions, frequented by kiṃnaras, serpents, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, strewn with trees and creepers of every kind, that auspicious repository of cool waters —
— copper-red with fragrant lotuses, white with clusters of kumuda lilies, blue with the mass of kuvalaya flowers — many-hued like a decorated carpet —
— abounding in aravinda and utpala lotuses, rich with fragrant padma blossoms, flanked by forests of flowering mango trees, resounding with the cries of peacocks —
Beholding that Pampā, Rāma — that splendid son of Daśaratha — together with the son of Sumitrā, broke into lamentation out of longing.
— with tilaka trees, citron trees, vaṭa figs, śukladruma trees, blossoming karavīra shrubs, and abundantly flowering puṃnāga trees —
— with clusters of mālatī and kunda blossoms, bhaṇḍīra figs, niculas, aśokas, saptaparṇas, ketaka reeds, atimukta vines, and many other varied trees — embellished like a woman in her prime —
On the bank of this lake stands the mountain spoken of before, adorned with mineral ores, known as Ṛśyamūka, with its grove of varied blossoms.
The son of that great-souled Ṛkṣarajas, mighty in valor, known as Sugrīva, dwells upon that mountain.
"Go to Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, O bull among men" — so Rāma again spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa, whose valor was true.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, proceeding gradually along the great road and the distant crossing, and gazing out over the forest, he beheld Pampā — beautiful to behold, its groves crowded with many birds of diverse and varied kinds.
Having reached that lotus-pond teeming with blue lotuses and fish, Rāma, accompanied by Saumitri, lamented with distraught senses.
At the very sight of it his senses trembled with delight; overpowered by longing, he spoke thus to Saumitri.
"O Saumitri, behold the beautiful forest of Pampā, where trees that resemble mountains stand splendid, as if with crests."
"Yet anguishes torment me, scorched as I am by grief — by the sorrow of Bharata and by the abduction of Vaidehī."
"This meadow of blue and yellow gleams all the more richly, spread as if with garlands of the many-coloured blossoms of the trees."
"O Saumitri, this season's breeze is pleasant; Kāma reigns abundantly; the month is fragrant and sweet-scented, the trees laden with flowers and fruit."
"See, O Saumitri, the beauty of these flower-bearing forests as they shed showers of blossoms, like rain-clouds releasing rain."
"On the charming rocky ledges, diverse forest trees, shaken by the rush of the wind, scatter flowers upon the earth."
"The wind blows with a pleasant touch, cool as sandalwood, in the honey-scented forests that hum with swarms of bees."
"On the charming hillslopes, the mountains blaze with glory, their peaks interlocked with great trees full of blossoms."
"See these karṇikāra trees in full bloom all around, covered with golden flowers — like men robed in yellow garments."
"This spring, O Saumitri, resounding with many birds, fans the flames of my grief for one who is parted from Sītā."
"Manmatha scorches me, overwhelmed by grief, while the joyful cuckoo calls and seems to challenge me."
"This water-cock, joyful in the lovely forest waterfall, will make me grieve still more, O Lakṣmaṇa, stricken as I am with desire."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Birds of mingled kinds, gladdened by their own flocking together, rejoicing with the king-bee, sing in sweet voices, O Saumitri."
"The cruel wind of Caitra's forest scorches me, O Saumitri, overwhelmed by anguished grief for that doe-eyed one."
"Peacocks attended by peahens on the mountain ridges intensify the longing of one — me — already consumed by longing."
"See, Lakṣmaṇa, the peacock dancing — the peahen, filled with desire, dances beside her lord on the mountain ridge."
"Surely the beloved of the peacock has not been stolen by a rākṣasa in the forest; but my dwelling without her in the month of flowers is utterly unbearable."
"See, Lakṣmaṇa, the flowers become fruitless for me, even though the forests are rich with burdens of blossoms at winter's end."
"Birds in joyful flocks cry out their melodies, calling to one another as if challenging — driving me mad with desire."
"Surely Sītā, fallen into another's power, grieves even as I do — that dark-complexioned one, lotus-petal-eyed, gentle in speech, my beloved."
"This flower-laden wind, pleasant to the touch and carrying coolness, is like fire to me as I think longingly of that beloved."
"Without her, that bird — a crow perched in a tree — cries out joyfully, calling in its delight."
"Surely this very bird shall be the herald of Vaidehī there; the bird will lead me to the side of the wide-eyed one."
"See, Lakṣmaṇa, the chorus in the forest — heightening intoxication — of birds calling among the flower-crowned trees."
"O Saumitri, see how in the variegated groves of Pampā the lotuses shine in the water like the newly-risen sun."
"Here is Pampā with her clear waters, stretching with lotuses and blue water-lilies, swarming with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, rich with white saugandhika flowers."
"She is ever graced with cakravāka birds, her variegated banks enclosed by groves, and she gleams with herds of elephants and deer that seek the water."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The eye, on beholding the petals of lotus buds, imagines they resemble the eye-cups of Sītā, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"Mingled with lotus pollen, issuing from among the trees, the enchanting breeze blows like the breath of Sītā."
"O Saumitri, see on the southern ridge of Pampā the supremely beautiful flowering stalk of the karṇikāra tree."
"This king of mountains, adorned yet more by its mineral veins, sheds a many-coloured dust driven loose by the force of the wind."
"O Saumitri, the hillslopes everywhere seem like lamps with the kiṃśuka trees in full bloom on all sides, leafless and charming."
"These clustered, honey-fragrant trees growing on the bank of Pampā — thickets of mālatī and mallikā — and the karavīra trees are in bloom."
"Ketakī, sinduvāra, and vāsantī are beautifully flowered; the mādhavī vines are full of fragrance, and kunda shrubs bloom everywhere."
"Ciribilvā, madhūka, vañjula, bakula, campaka, tilaka, and nāgavṛkṣa trees are all in bloom."
"Nīpa, varaṇa, and kharjūra trees are beautifully blossoming; aṅkola, kuraṇṭa, cūrṇaka, and pāribhadraka bloom as well."
"Mango, pāṭalā, and kovidāra trees are in flower; mucukunda and arjuna too are visible on the mountain ridges."
"Ketaka, uddālaka, śirīṣa, śiṃśapā, dhava, śālmalī, kiṃśuka — red and blooming — kurabaka, tiniśa, naktamālā, sandal, and syandana trees as well."
"The rocky ledges on the mountain ridges, O Saumitri, are made golden and red by the varied blossoms of those diverse trees scattered upon them."
"See, O Saumitri, the flowering of trees at winter's end; in the month of flowers the trees bloom as if through mutual friction."
"See this cool-watered lake, O Saumitri, filled with lotuses, attended by cakravāka birds, frequented by kāraṇḍava ducks, teeming with plavas and cranes, and visited by boars and deer."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Pampā shines all the more with its calling birds."
"Various joyful birds seem to kindle my desire as I remember my beloved — dark-complexioned, moon-faced, lotus-eyed."
"See the deer accompanied by does on the variegated ridges — and me, bereft of Vaidehī of the doe-like eyes."
Thus lamenting there, his mind stricken by grief, he gazed upon the auspicious Pampā, her lovely waters flowing, fair and beautiful.
The great-souled one, gazing suddenly at the whole forest with its waterfalls and ravines, agitated of heart, deliberated together with Lakṣmaṇa, and then set forth, stricken by sorrow.
Those two set forth together toward Ṛśyamūka, frequented by Sugrīva and his band of monkeys. On seeing those two — the mighty Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa — the monkeys were struck with fear.
On seeing those two great-souled brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, those heroes bearing excellent weapons, Sugrīva became suspicious.
With an anxious heart, scanning all directions, that foremost of monkeys could not stay in any one place.
His mind would not settle in one spot as he watched those two of great strength; the mind of the monkey, utterly terrified, faltered.
Having pondered and weighed what was grave and what was slight, Sugrīva, greatly agitated, together with all his attendants —
— then that lord of leaping monkeys, Sugrīva, spoke to his counsellors, utterly alarmed, watching those two — Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
"These two, surely, have been sent here by Vālin into this impenetrable forest — moving about in disguise, clad in bark garments, they have come here."
Then the counsellors of Sugrīva, seeing those two supreme archers, left that mountain-ledge and went to another excellent peak.
Those horde-leaders quickly approached and surrounded that bull among herds, that best of monkeys, and stood in attendance.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Going one by one on a single path, leaping from mountain to mountain, with their speed they shook the peaks of the mountains.
Then all those powerful branch-animals, leaping, broke down the flowering trees that grew in those difficult places.
Those foremost of tawny monkeys, leaping around that great mountain on all sides, went forth frightening the deer, wildcats, and tigers.
Then the counsellors of Sugrīva, having taken refuge on the king of mountains, gathered before that foremost of monkeys and all stood with hands folded in reverence.
Then Hanūmān, skilled in speech, spoke to Sugrīva who was trembling with fear and suspected the sin of Vālin.
"The one on account of whom you flee with agitated heart, O foremost of monkeys — that cruel-looking, cruel Vālin — I do not see him here."
"The one from whom you fear, dear friend — your elder brother of wicked deeds — that evil-souled Vālin is not here; I see no danger for you."
"Ah, your monkey-nature is evident indeed, O leaping one — through such fickleness of mind you cannot steady yourself in thought."
"Act in everything by signs, endowed with intelligence and discernment; for a king without wisdom cannot rule all beings."
Sugrīva, having heard all of Hanūmān's fair words, then spoke an even fairer speech to Hanūmān.
"Long-armed, broad-eyed, bearing arrows, bows, and swords — who would not feel fear on seeing these two who resemble sons of the gods?"
"I suspect these two foremost of men have been sent by Vālin; kings have many friends, and trust is not appropriate here."
"Enemies must be recognised by a man though they move in disguise; the untrustworthy, after gaining trust, strike at vulnerabilities."
"Vālin is clever in his undertakings; kings of wide vision are destroyers of enemies — ordinary men must be alert to that."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Go to them yourself in an ordinary guise, O leaping one, and learn who they are through the means used with those who are suspected — by form and by speaking with them."
"Observe the disposition of those two; if their minds are joyful, reassure them again and again with praise and with signs."
"Standing in my very presence, ask them, O foremost of monkeys, what is the purpose of those bow-bearers' entry into this forest."
"If these two have pure souls, so learn, O leaping one; their wickedness, if any, will be discerned through their speech or through their forms."
Thus directed by the king of monkeys, the son of the Wind God resolved to go where those two — Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa — were.
Having honoured the words of that greatly fearful, unapproachable monkey with "so be it," the great-spirited Hanūmān then went to where Rāma of surpassing strength and Lakṣmaṇa were.
Hanūmān, having understood the words of the great-souled Sugrīva, leaped from the mountain Ṛśyamūka to where the two Rāghavas were.
Having gone there, the powerful Hanūmān, foremost of monkeys, of true valour, approached those two with gentle words.
Abandoning his own form, the monkey approached in the guise of a mendicant and spoke to those two heroes and praised them as was fitting.
"You two ascetics, resembling royal sages or gods, firm in vows and of excellent complexion — how have you arrived in this place?"
"Frightening the herds of deer and other forest-dwellers, gazing in all directions at the trees that grow on the banks of Pampā —"
"— you who adorn this river of auspicious waters, you who are swift, steadfast, golden in lustre — who are you two, clad in bark garments?"
"Heroes with the side-glance of lions, with the surpassing might and gait of lions, holding bows resembling Indra's bow in your wide arms —"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"— endowed with majesty and beauty, with the gait of the foremost of bulls, with arms like an elephant's trunk, radiant, O bulls among men —"
"— by whose radiance this king of mountains is illumined, you two worthy of kingship, resembling immortals — how have you come to this place?"
"Lotus-petal-eyed heroes, wearing circles of matted locks, heroes alike to one another — you seem to have come from the world of the gods."
"As if by chance arrived on this earth — like the moon and the sun — broad-chested heroes, human in form but divine in appearance."
"With lion shoulders, of great spirit, equal in pride like bull-oxen, your arms long and well-rounded, like the finest iron bars, worthy of all ornaments — why then are you not adorned?"
"I consider you both fit to protect this entire earth — with its oceans and forests, adorned with Vindhya and Meru."
"And these two bows, beautiful and smooth, adorned with wondrous decorations, shine like Indra's thunderbolt decked with gold."
"And the quivers, filled with sharp arrows and fair to behold, are terrible, life-ending — like blazing serpents."
"These two swords, of great size and broad, adorned with refined gold, blaze with glory like serpents that have shed their skins."
"Thus I address you — why do you not speak to me?"
"There is one named Sugrīva, a righteous-souled leader of a monkey troop, a hero wronged by his brother, who wanders the world in misery."
"I have come, sent by that great-souled Sugrīva, king among the foremost of monkeys — I am a monkey named Hanūmān."
"The righteous-souled Sugrīva desires friendship with you two; know me as his minister, a monkey, the son of the Wind God."
"Concealed in the guise of a mendicant, able to go wherever I will, able to take any form I wish, I have arrived here from Ṛśyamūka out of desire to please Sugrīva."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having thus spoken to those two heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who were versed in speech, the one skilled in speech said nothing more.
Having heard his words, the glorious Rāma, with a delighted face, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, his brother standing at his side.
"This is the minister of Sugrīva, the great-souled lord of monkeys, for whom I have been longing — he has come to my presence."
"Address him, O Saumitri — this monkey who is Sugrīva's minister, versed in speech — with sweet words full of affection, O subduer of foes."
Then Hanūmān, greatly delighted, on hearing those sweet-spoken words — "one whose purpose is accomplished" — went in his mind to Sugrīva.
"The return of the kingdom is fitting for that great-souled Sugrīva, since one whose purpose is accomplished has arrived, and this very purpose has come to meet him."
Then Hanūmān, the foremost of monkeys, supremely delighted and skilled in speech, replied with these words to Rāma.
"For what purpose have you come, along with your younger brother, to this dreadful and inaccessible forest adorned by the Pampā woodland and filled with all manner of serpents and wild beasts?"
Hearing those words of his, Lakṣmaṇa, prompted by Rāma, described the great-souled Rāma, son of Daśaratha.
"There was a king named Daśaratha, resplendent and devoted to righteousness; this man is his elder son, known among people by the name of Rāma."
"A refuge for all living beings, one who has perfectly fulfilled his father's command, this hero is the most virtuous among the sons of Daśaratha."
"Fallen from his kingdom, he came here to dwell in the forest together with me; self-controlled and of great splendour, he was followed by his wife Sītā — like the sun at the close of day attended by its radiance."
"I am his younger brother, who by reason of his virtues have taken upon myself the condition of a servant; my name is Lakṣmaṇa — of one who is grateful and widely knowledgeable."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Of one worthy of happiness, worthy of greatness, whose soul is devoted to the welfare of all beings — now stripped of sovereignty and resorting to forest-dwelling."
"His wife has been carried off by a rākṣasa who assumed any form at will, seizing his moment when they were alone; nor is it known which rākṣasa it was that abducted his wife."
"Danu by name, the son of Śrī, who had become a rākṣasa through a curse, informed him of Sugrīva, the capable lord of monkeys."
"'That mighty hero will know the abductor of your wife' — having said thus, Danu departed radiant to heaven in peace."
"All this has been truthfully told to you as you inquired; both Rāma and I have come to Sugrīva for refuge."
"This man, having formerly been lord of the world and having bestowed wealth and attained unsurpassed renown, now desires Sugrīva as his master."
"With Rāma overwhelmed by grief, afflicted by sorrow and seeking refuge, it is fitting that Sugrīva, together with his troop-leaders, show him his favour."
To Lakṣmaṇa, who was speaking thus in a pitiful manner with tears falling, Hanūmān, skilled in speech, replied with these words.
"Such men as these — endowed with wisdom, who have conquered anger and mastered their senses — are indeed to be met by the lord of monkeys; by good fortune they have come into view."
"For he too has been driven from his kingdom, has been made an enemy by Vālin, his wife has been taken, he wanders in the forest in fear, and has been grievously wronged by his brother."
"Sugrīva, son of the Sun-god, together with us, will render assistance to you both in the search for Sītā."
Having said thus, Hanūmān spoke smoothly and with sweet speech to Rāghava: "Let us go to Sugrīva."
The righteous-souled Lakṣmaṇa, having duly honoured Hanūmān who had spoken thus, said this to Rāghava.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"As this son of the Wind-god, the monkey, reports with delight — one whose purpose is accomplished has also arrived here; your purpose too is as good as accomplished, O Rāghava."
"His countenance is serene and bright, and he speaks with evident gladness; the heroic Hanūmān, son of Vāyu, will not speak anything untrue."
Thereupon the greatly wise Hanūmān, son of the Wind-god, took the two heroes, the Rāghava princes, and went to the king of the monkeys.
That foremost of monkeys, the son of the Wind, of vast renown and great valour, with auspicious mind, as though his task were already accomplished, set forth in great delight along with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa toward that best of mountains.
And Hanūmān, going from Ṛśyamūka to that Malaya mountain, then announced the two heroes, the Rāghava princes, to the king of monkeys.
"This is Rāma, of great wisdom and firm valour, who has arrived along with his brother Lakṣmaṇa — this Rāma of true heroism."
"Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, the son of Daśaratha, Rāma is renowned for righteousness and has honoured his father's command."
"While this great-souled, disciplined man was dwelling in the forest, his wife was carried off by a rākṣasa; he has come to you for refuge."
"He is one by whom the sacrificial fire has been gratified with Rājasūya and Aśvamedha rites, and by whom gifts of cows numbering hundreds of thousands have been distributed as sacrificial fees."
"He by whose ascetic power and truthful speech the earth was governed — for the sake of a woman, that son, this Rāma, has come to you for refuge."
"These two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who desire friendship with you — receive them and honour them; both are most worthy of honour."
Having heard the words of Hanūmān, Sugrīva was glad at heart; the dreadful fear he had felt on account of the Rāghava princes left him, and his anxiety was gone.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, assuming human form and having become most handsome in appearance, addressed Rāghava with affection.
"You are disciplined in righteousness, valiant, and affectionate toward all; your virtues have been truthfully described to me by the son of Vāyu."
"Therefore this is indeed my honour and the highest gain for me, O lord, that you desire friendship with me, a mere monkey."
"If friendship pleases you, here is my arm extended; let hand take hand, and let the bond of that compact be made firm."
Hearing those well-spoken words of Sugrīva, Rāma, with a joyful heart, clasped that hand in his own hand and embraced him tightly, taking that heartfelt friendship to himself.
Then Hanūmān, the subduer of enemies, casting aside his mendicant's form, kindled fire in his own true form from two sticks of wood.
Having then worshipped and honoured the blazing fire with flowers, he, greatly pleased and with full concentration, placed it between those two.
Then Sugrīva and Rāghava both circumambulated the blazing fire and thus entered into the state of friendship.
Then those two — the monkey and the Rāghava — both with greatly gladdened hearts, gazed at each other without finding satiation.
Then the spirited Sugrīva, with one-pointed mind, spoke these words to Rāma, son of Daśaratha, who is versed in all matters.
"O Rāma, this counsellor of mine, that best of ministers Hanūmān, has told me the reason for which you have come to this desolate forest."
"While you were dwelling in the forest together with your brother Lakṣmaṇa, your wife Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, was carried off by a rākṣasa."
"She was crying, separated from you and from the wise Lakṣmaṇa; that one, seeking his opportunity, after slaying the vulture Jaṭāyus —"
"The sorrow born of separation from your wife — you shall be freed from it before long; I will bring her back, as a lost Vedic text is recovered."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Whether she abides in the netherworld or in the sky above, O subduer of foes, I will bring your wife back and give her to you."
"Know this to be the truth of my word, O Rāghava; cast aside grief, O mighty-armed one — I will bring that beloved wife to you."
"By inference I know — there is no doubt — it is that Maithilī; I saw her being carried away by a rākṣasa of cruel deeds."
"She was crying out 'Rāma! Rāma!' and 'Lakṣmaṇa!' loudly, writhing in the arms of Rāvaṇa like the wife of the king of serpents in his coils."
"Having seen me standing on the mountain slope as the fifth among my companions, she cast down her upper garment and her bright ornaments."
"Those were gathered up and stored away by us, O Rāghava; I will bring them — you should identify them."
Then Rāma said to Sugrīva, who had spoken such pleasing words: "Bring them quickly, my friend — why do you delay?"
Thus addressed, Sugrīva quickly entered the deep cave of the mountain, out of desire to please the Rāghava.
And taking the upper garment and the bright ornaments, the monkey showed them to Rāma saying, "Look at these."
Then, having taken that garment and those bright ornaments, he was choked with tears — like the moon obscured by mist.
Overwhelmed by the flood of tears welling up from his love for Sītā, crying out "Ah, my beloved!" he abandoned his composure and fell to the ground.
Pressing those finest ornaments again and again to his heart, he heaved deep sighs — like an angered serpent in its burrow.
With an unbroken stream of tears, Rāma looked to Lakṣmaṇa at his side and, in his wretchedness, began to lament.
"Look, Lakṣmaṇa — this upper garment cast away upon the ground by the daughter of Videha as she was being carried off, and these ornaments from her body."
"On the grassy ground it was surely cast by Sītā as she was carried away; this ornament is seen here, of just such an appearance as hers."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Tell me, Sugrīva — in what direction was she seen by you as she was being carried off by the fearsome-formed rākṣasa — she who is as dear to me as my own life?"
"Or where does that rākṣasa dwell — that great affliction of mine — on whose account I shall destroy all the rākṣasas?"
"By the one who carried off Maithilī and who has grievously enraged me, the door of death has been opened for the end of his own life."
"She who is dearest to me has been seized and carried off from the forest by a night-wanderer who overpowered her — tell me who that enemy of mine is, O lord of monkeys; today I will send him to the presence of Yama."
Thus addressed by the grief-stricken Rāma, the monkey Sugrīva spoke with hands folded in reverence, his voice choked with tears and his speech broken by weeping.
"I do not know the abode of that wicked demon in any way, nor his power, his prowess, nor indeed the lineage or family of that base-born one.
Yet I truly promise you: abandon your grief, O subduer of enemies — I shall make such effort that you will recover the daughter of Mithilā.
Having slain Rāvaṇa together with his retinue and having satisfied my own valor, I shall act in such a way that before long you will be pleased.
Enough of clinging to this despondency — recall the inner fortitude natural to you. Such mental feebleness does not befit one of your kind.
I too have suffered a great calamity born of the abduction of my wife, yet I do not grieve in this manner, nor do I abandon my fortitude.
I, a mere common monkey, do not mourn her — you who are high-souled and well-disciplined, how much less should you who are so resolute grieve!
You ought to restrain these tears that have come upon you through lack of fortitude; you ought not to abandon the steadfastness that is the mark of those endowed with true courage.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
In calamity, or in hardship, or in fear, even when life itself is at stake — one who reflects with his own reason and remains steadfast does not sink into despair.
But the man who perpetually follows after despondency is a fool — helplessly he sinks into grief, like a ship in water overwhelmed by its cargo.
With these hands folded in supplication, I entreat you out of affection: take refuge in your valor — you ought not to give room to grief.
Those who follow grief find no happiness, and their energy diminishes. You should not grieve thus.
I speak to you as your well-wisher, with a friend's regard — I do not presume to instruct you. Honoring our friendship, you should not grieve, I say."
Sweetly consoled by Sugrīva in this manner, that scion of the Raghu clan wiped his face, wet with tears, with the hem of his garment.
Restored to his natural composure by Sugrīva's words, that mighty Kākutstha embraced Sugrīva and spoke these words:
"What ought to be done by a friend who is affectionate and well-meaning, what is fitting and proper — all that you have done, Sugrīva.
And indeed I have been restored to my natural state by your entreaties, O friend. Such a kinsman as this is rare to find, especially in a time like this.
Yet effort must be made by you to search for the daughter of Mithilā, and against that fierce demon, the evil-souled Rāvaṇa.
And let what I must do be told to me in confidence — as rain on good soil, all shall come to fruition for you.
And this speech uttered by me in pride — let it be taken by you, O tiger among monkeys, as the truth.
I have never spoken a falsehood before, nor shall I ever speak one — this I promise you, and by truth itself I swear to you."
Then Sugrīva was delighted, along with his monkey ministers, having heard the words of the scion of the Raghu clan — above all, the vow that was made.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having heard the words of that great-spirited one, the bull among men, that foremost hero among monkeys — knowing in his heart that his own purpose was as good as accomplished — considered it done.
Thoroughly pleased by those words, the monkey Sugrīva spoke these words to Rāma, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa:
"I am, without doubt, blessed by the gods in every way — I, whose friend is you, endowed with qualities both natural and acquired.
Truly, O Rāma, O sinless one, with you as ally it would be possible to win even the kingdom of the gods — how much more my own kingdom, O lord?
I am to be honored by kinsmen and friends alike, O scion of the Raghu clan, for I have gained as a friend, with fire as witness, one born of the Raghu lineage.
I too am a fitting companion for you — you shall come to know this gradually. Yet I am not capable of proclaiming my own inner qualities myself.
For great-souled ones like you, those who have mastered themselves, the affection that arises is steadfast — like the fortitude of those who possess true self-possession.
Silver or gold, garments or ornaments — the good regard these as undivided and held in common: such is the understanding of the good.
Whether wealthy or poor, whether in sorrow or in happiness, whether blameless or at fault — a true companion is the highest refuge.
Giving up wealth, giving up comfort, and even giving up one's body — men act thus for the sake of a friend, when they have seen affection of such a kind.
To Sugrīva who spoke such agreeable words, Rāma said "so be it" — in the presence of Lakṣmaṇa, as Indra the wise might reply to his glorious companion.
Then, seeing Rāma standing there and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa beside him, Sugrīva let his gaze wander restlessly in all directions through the forest.
Then that lord of monkeys saw, not far away, a śāla tree in full bloom, with somewhat sparse foliage but adorned by humming bees.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Breaking off one leafy, well-flowering branch of that śāla tree, Sugrīva spread it out and sat down together with Rāma.
Then seeing the two seated, Hanūmān too pulled off a śāla branch and had Lakṣmaṇa seated upon it with due courtesy.
Then the delighted Sugrīva, with smooth and sweet speech, spoke to Rāma out of affection, his words faltering with joy:
"I, wronged by my brother, wander here tormented by fear, on the excellent mountain Ṛśyamūka, my wife stolen away, in great misery.
Thus I dwell in fear, immersed in dread, my mind distracted, wronged by my brother Vālin, with enmity made between us, O scion of the Raghu clan.
O you who dispel the fear of all the worlds — I, tormented by fear of Vālin, masterless as I am, you ought to show grace to me as well."
Thus addressed, that splendid one, the knower of dharma, the lover of dharma — that Kākutstha replied to Sugrīva almost with a smile:
"A friend is one whose fruit is helpfulness; harm is the mark of an enemy. This very day I shall slay him who has stolen your wife.
For these arrows of mine are swift as wind, feathered, of sharp brilliance, golden-adorned, born of the groves sacred to Kārttikeya.
Covered with heron feathers, resembling the thunderbolt of Mahendra, well-jointed, with very sharp tips, they are like angry serpents.
See your enemy who bears the name of brother — Vālin who has committed this offense — struck down by my arrows, like a mountain shattered."
Hearing the words of the scion of the Raghu clan, Sugrīva, lord of the host, was filled with incomparable joy and cried out "Well said! Well said!"
"I, overwhelmed by grief just as Rāma is, pour out my lament to you — for you are the refuge of those afflicted by grief — counting you as my companion.
For you are the friend made by the joining of hands, witnessed by fire — held dear as life itself — I swear by truth itself.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And so, counting you as my companion, I speak freely — the grief that lies within, that ever burns my heart.
Having spoken these many words, his eyes clouded with tears, his voice stricken by weeping, he could no longer speak loudly.
But Sugrīva restrained by his fortitude, in the presence of Rāma, that sudden surge of tears which had come upon him like the current of a river.
Having suppressed those tears, having wiped his beautiful eyes and drawn a deep breath, that splendid one again addressed the scion of the Raghu clan:
"Long ago, O Rāma, I was deposed from my own kingdom by Vālin — having caused me to hear harsh words, the mighty one cast me out.
My wife was stolen by him — she who is dearer to me than life itself — and those who were my friends were bound in imprisonment by him.
And that most corrupt soul made repeated efforts for my destruction, O scion of the Raghu clan, and the many monkeys sent by him I have slain.
Yet out of this same suspicion, even upon seeing you, O scion of the Raghu clan, I did not approach — I was afraid, for all fear when there is reason to fear.
For these alone are my allies, Hanūmān foremost among them — it is because of them that I maintain my life even now, fallen into such hardship as I have.
These affectionate monkeys protect me on all sides — they go with me when I go, and they always remain with me when I remain still.
In brief, this is my situation, O Rāma — why should I say more at length to you? That brother of mine, Vālin of celebrated prowess, is my elder and my enemy.
By his destruction my misery would immediately vanish; my happiness and my very life are bound up in his destruction.
This, O Rāma, is the end of my grief as reported by one afflicted by grief — whether in sorrow or not, a friend is ever the refuge of a friend.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing this speech, Rāma spoke to Sugrīva: "What was the cause from which the enmity arose? I wish to hear it truly and in detail.
For having heard the reason for your enmity easily, O monkey, I shall arrange for what follows, having weighed the relative strength and weakness.
For my indignation upon hearing of your humiliation is powerful and grows, making my heart throb — like the rushing surge of water in the rainy season.
Tell me gladly and with confidence — before the bow is strung, my arrow loosed, and your enemy dispatched."
Thus addressed by the great-souled Kākutstha, Sugrīva was filled with incomparable delight, together with his four monkey companions.
Then Sugrīva, his face radiant with joy, began to recount to the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa the true cause of the enmity.
"My brother named Vālin, the destroyer of enemies, is my elder — always held in high esteem by our father, and so too by me in former times.
When our father passed away, the ministers, saying 'this one is the elder,' installed him, with the highest approbation, as lord of the monkeys over the kingdom.
While he ruled over that great ancestral kingdom, I remained always bowing to him in humility, standing like a servant.
There was a powerful demon named Māyāvī, the firstborn son of Dundubhi — between him and Vālin there arose a great enmity, over a woman, as is well known of old.
He came to the gate of Kiṣkindhā at night while the people slept, roaring with great fury, challenging Vālin to battle.
My brother Vālin, asleep, heard that terrifying roar and could not endure it — he leapt forth instantly.
