Going out in wrath to slay that greatest of demons, he was restrained by the women of the household and by me, who bowed humbly before him.
But he, the mighty one, shaking off all of us, went out. Then I too, out of brotherly affection, went forth together with Vālin.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
But that demon, on seeing my brother and seeing me standing at a distance, was seized with terror and fled with great speed.
As he fled in terror, the two of us pursued him at even greater speed — and the rising moon made the path bright at that time.
That demon, with great speed, entered a large difficult cave in the earth covered over with grass, while we two stood there having reached the place.
Seeing the enemy enter the cave, Vālin, overcome with anger, his senses agitated, spoke these words to me:
"Wait here, Sugrīva, at the mouth of the cave, attentive — until I enter within and slay the enemy in combat."
Having heard these words, I besought him, O scorcher of foes — but he made me swear by his feet, and then entered the cave.
More than a full year passed after his entering the cave — and that time elapsed while I stood at the entrance.
I, considering him lost and filled with the agitation that comes from affection — for I could not see my brother — and my mind suspected something terrible.
Then, after that long time, seeing blood — red and foaming — flowing out from that cave, I was overcome with deep sorrow.
And the sound of demons roaring reached my ears, and the outcry of my elder being overwhelmed in battle and crying out.
Concluding by those signs that my brother had been slain, and blocking the mouth of the cave with a rock as large as a mountain, I performed the water-rites in grief and returned to Kiṣkindhā, O friend.
The truth I was concealing was diligently ascertained by the ministers — and then, meeting together with them all assembled, I was consecrated as king.
While I was ruling the kingdom rightfully, O scion of the Raghu clan, Vālin returned, having slain that greatest of demons.
Seeing me consecrated, his eyes reddened with anger, he bound my ministers and spoke harsh words to me.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Though capable of restraining him, against that wicked one, O scion of the Raghu clan, my mind did not stir to action — constrained by reverence for my brother.
Honoring that great-souled one duly, I greeted him with proper salutation — and blessings were spoken by him, his inner self apparently satisfied."
Then, out of desire for his good will, I sought to placate my brother who had come upon me seized with anger and agitation.
"By good fortune you have returned safe, and the enemy has been slain by you; for me who was without a protector, you alone are my protector — the joy of one who had none."
"Receive this royal parasol, raised aloft by me, adorned with many ribs, risen like a full moon, together with the yak-tail fans."
"You alone are the king worthy of honour, and I am ever as before — I restore to you this kingdom that was held in trust."
"Do not be angry with me, gentle one, O destroyer of enemies; I beseech you, O king, with my head — these joined palms are folded by me."
"I was forcibly brought together with the ministers and the citizens of the capital and installed in the royal office out of a desire to keep the kingdom from becoming masterless."
But that monkey, despite my speaking to him with affection, reviled me and, saying "Shame on you," said many reproachful things.
Having gathered the subjects together and the respected ministers as well, he spoke to me in the midst of friends words that were most shameful.
"You know how that great demon, that trickster, that cruel and utterly wicked one who longed for battle, challenged me one night."
"Hearing that roar of his, I issued forth from the royal palace, and this harsh brother of mine followed swiftly behind me."
"That mighty one, seeing me accompanied by another in the night, fled in fear; we two gave chase, and he, being pursued, swiftly entered into the great cave."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Knowing he had entered that most dreadful and vast cavern, I then addressed this brother of mine, fierce in aspect:"
"'I have not the power to return to the city without slaying him — wait at the mouth of the cave until I have killed him.'"
"Believing he would remain there, I entered that difficult lair; and while I was searching for him, a full year passed."
"That fearsome enemy was finally found by me without despairing, and there he was slain by me along with his kinsmen."
"That cave became filled with a flood of blood flowing from his mouth, impassable, while he rumbled upon the ground."
"Having slain that valiant enemy, the son of Dundubhi, I saw even as I was coming out that the mouth of the cave was sealed shut."
"As I called out again and again 'Sugrīva!' and there was no answer at all, I became exceedingly sorrowful."
"I broke it open again and again with blows of my feet, then made my way out through it and returned home."
"There, by this cruel Sugrīva, who sought the kingdom for himself and forgot the bond of brotherhood, I was barred from entry."
"Having spoken thus against me there, Vālī the monkey banished me, stripped of fear, with but a single garment."
"Cast out by him and robbed of my wife, O Rāghava, I have traversed this entire earth with its forests and oceans in fear of him."
"Anguished by the abduction of my wife, I entered the foremost of mountains, Ṛśyamūka, which is impregnable, by reason of another circumstance concerning Vālī."
"All this great tale of the enmity has been told to you — behold, O Rāghava, the calamity that has befallen me though I am innocent."
"O hero who brings safety to all the worlds, you should grant me your grace, who am stricken with fear of Vālī, through his suppression."
When thus addressed, that splendid one, the knower of dharma, began to speak words consonant with righteousness to Sugrīva, smiling gently.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"These sharp arrows of mine, bright as the sun, unfailing, will fall upon that wicked Vālī filled with my wrath."
"Only until I set eyes upon him who stole your wife does that vile-souled Vālī, that defiler of conduct, continue to live."
"Judging by my own experience, I see you plunged in an ocean of grief; I will carry you across, and you shall attain every abundance."
Hearing Rāma's words, which heightened both joy and valour, Sugrīva honoured the Rāghava and praised him.
"Without doubt, with your blazing, sharp arrows that pierce vital spots, you could, when angered, burn the worlds, like the sun at the end of an age."
"Having heard with one-pointed mind what prowess, what valour, and what resolve Vālī possesses, decide thereafter what is to be done."
"Before the sun has risen, Vālī strides — from the western ocean to the eastern, from the southern to the northern — without weariness."
"Having ascended the peaks and great summits of mountains, that valiant one hurls them upward with force and catches them again."
"Many sturdy trees of various kinds in the forests have been snapped by Vālī with force as he displays his strength."
"There was a buffalo named Dundubhi, brilliant as the peak of Kailāsa, who possessed the strength of a thousand elephants, so valiant was he."
"Intoxicated by excess of might and deluded by the boon he had received, that great-bodied, evil-souled one went to the ocean, lord of rivers."
"Surpassing the wave-crested ocean, treasure-laden, he addressed the great sea: 'Give me battle!'"
"Then the ocean, righteous-souled and mighty, rising up, spoke these words to that demon driven on by fate, O king:"
"'I am not capable of giving you battle, O master of warfare; hear, I shall tell you who will give you battle.'"
"'There is the king of mountains in the great forest, the supreme refuge of ascetics, the father-in-law of Śaṃkara, renowned by the name Himavān.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'Possessed of caverns and springs, full of many gorges and cascades — he is capable of giving you matchless satisfaction in combat.'"
"Recognising that the ocean was afraid, that foremost of demons rushed to the Himālayan forest like an arrow discharged from a bow."
"Then Dundubhi hurled many white boulders, as vast as great elephants, of that mountain to the ground and roared loudly."
"Then Himavān, white as a rain-cloud, gentle, of pleasant form, standing upon his own peak, spoke:"
"'You ought not to harass me, O Dundubhi, O devotee of dharma — I am unskilled in the deeds of battle, for I am the refuge of ascetics.'"
"Hearing those words of the wise king of mountains, Dundubhi spoke, his eyes reddened with anger:"
"'If you are incapable of battle, or if you have no inclination out of fear of me, then name to me one who would today give battle to me who am eager to fight.'"
"Himavān, master of speech, righteous-souled, hearing him, spoke words never spoken before to that foremost of demons in his anger:"
"'There is a monkey of great wisdom named Vālī, glorious and of valour equal to Indra's, who resides in Kiṣkindhā of incomparable splendour.'"
"'That greatly wise one, skilled in warfare, is capable of giving you great single combat, as Vāsava gave to Namuci.'"
"'Go to him quickly, if you desire battle here — for he is ever irresistible, a hero in the deeds of war.'"
"Hearing the words of Himavān, Dundubhi, overcome with anger, went to that city of Vālī — Kiṣkindhā."
"Wearing the form of a buffalo, with sharp horns, terrifying, he was like a great rain-cloud full of water in the sky at the onset of the monsoon."
"Then that mighty Dundubhi, arriving at the gate of Kiṣkindhā, roared, shaking the earth like a kettledrum."
"Breaking the nearby trees, tearing the earth with his hooves, scratching at that gate with his horns in arrogance, like an elephant."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Vālī, who had entered the inner chambers, hearing the noise and being intolerant, burst forth with his women, like the moon with the Tārā stars."
"Vālī, lord of all the forest-ranging monkeys, spoke to that Dundubhi in measured, clear words:"
"'For what reason do you roar here blocking this city gate? You are known to me, O Dundubhi, O mighty one — protect your life.'"
"Hearing those words of the wise lord of monkeys, Dundubhi spoke, his eyes reddened with anger:"
"'You ought not to speak in the presence of women, O hero — give me battle; then I shall know your strength.'"
"'Or else I shall restrain my anger for this one night — take your pleasure freely in the enjoyment of desires, O monkey.'"
"'For whoever would slay one who is intoxicated, heedless, asleep, or utterly alone — such a one would be a slayer of an embryo in this world, one deluded by pride, like you.'"
"He laughed and spoke gently with anger to that foremost of demons, having sent away all those women beginning with Tārā."
"'Do not think of me as drunk — if you are fearless in battle, let this intoxication in this combat be reckoned as the warrior's drink.'"
"Having spoken thus and being greatly angered, he threw up the golden garland given him by his father the great Indra and stood ready for battle."
"Seizing that Dundubhi, who resembled a mountain, by the horns, Vālī threw him down and roared with a great sound."
"In that life-taking battle, Dundubhi was crushed; blood then flowed from both his ears as he fell, and that great-bodied one crashed to earth, reduced to the five elements."
"Having lifted that lifeless, unconscious body with both arms, swift Vālī hurled it a full league with a single burst of speed."
"From the mouth of him thus hurled with force, drops of blood were carried by the wind and fell toward the hermitage of Mataṅga."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Seeing those drops of blood fallen there, the sage discharged a great curse against Vālī, the thrower: 'This place must not be entered by him; if he enters, he will meet his death.'"
"He went to the great sage and besought him with joined palms."
"Then, afraid and fearful of the curse, that monkey will not enter, nor even approach, the great mountain Ṛśyamūka, O lord of men."
"Knowing his prohibition from entry, O Rāma, I roam this great forest with my minister, free from despair."
"Here the heap of bones of that Dundubhi, hurled away in excess of valour, is visible — great, resembling a mountain peak."
"And here are these seven great śāla trees, their branches hanging down — to strip a single one of its leaves is Vālī's feat of strength."
"This incomparable valour of his has been set forth by me, O Rāma; how, O king, will you be able to slay that Vālī in battle?"
"If you, O mighty-armed one, were to split these śāla trees with a single arrow, then I would know you capable of slaying Vālī."
Hearing those words of the great-souled Sugrīva, the mighty-armed Rāghava effortlessly lifted the body of Dundubhi with his big toe and hurled it ten leagues.
Seeing the body thus hurled, Sugrīva then spoke these meaningful words to Rāma in the presence of Lakṣmaṇa:
"When it was hurled before, O friend, the body was fresh, moist and full of flesh; now, O Rāghava, it is light, desiccated, and reduced to straw — hence your strength or his, which is greater, cannot be judged from this."
Hearing these well-spoken words of Sugrīva, the greatly resplendent Rāma took up his bow to give proof of his power.
He, the honoured one, taking up the terrible bow and a single arrow, let fly at the śāla trees, filling the directions with the sound of the bowstring.
That arrow, adorned with gold, released by the powerful one, pierced all seven śāla trees on the mountain slope and entered the earth.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having entered the earth, that swift arrow, piercing through to the netherworld, swiftly leapt back out and returned to its own quiver.
Seeing those seven śāla trees pierced through by the speed of Rāma's arrow, the foremost of monkeys was filled with the utmost amazement.
Sugrīva, exceedingly delighted, his ornaments hanging loose, fell to the ground with his head and joined his palms to the Rāghava.
Gladdened by that feat, he spoke these words to Rāma, knower of dharma, best among all who know weapons, the steadfast hero:
"You, O bull among men, are capable of slaying in battle all the gods together with Indra by your arrows — how much more then Vālī, O lord."
"By whom seven great śāla trees, the mountain, and the earth have been cloven by a single arrow, O Kākutstha — who could stand before you in the van of battle?"
"Today my grief has departed, today my joy is supreme, having encountered you as my friend — you who are comparable to Mahendra and Varuṇa."
"Today itself, for my dear sake, slay Vālī — who is my enemy wearing the guise of a brother, O Kākutstha; these palms are joined by me in supplication."
Then Rāma, the greatly wise one, embracing the pleasing-looking Sugrīva, replied with words approved by Lakṣmaṇa:
"Let us go from here to Kiṣkindhā — go quickly in front; and upon arriving, O Sugrīva, challenge Vālī who has only the semblance of a brother."
All of them went quickly to Kiṣkindhā, the city of Vālī, and concealed themselves with trees, standing in the dense forest.
Sugrīva roared terribly for the purpose of challenging Vālī, clothed in a tight garment, splitting the sky, as it were, with his cries in his swiftness.
Hearing that roar of his brother, the mighty Vālī, enraged, burst forth in great fury, like the sun from the rim of the sunset mountain.
Then there arose a most tumultuous and terrible battle between Vālī and Sugrīva in the sky, like that of the planets Mercury and Mars.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Those two brothers, overcome with rage, struck each other in combat with palms like thunderbolts and fists like vajras.
Then Rāma, bow in hand, observing both of them — those two heroes who resembled each other mutually, like two divine Aśvins —
— since the Rāghava could not distinguish Sugrīva from Vālī, he did not then resolve to release the death-dealing arrow.
In this interval, Sugrīva was broken by Vālī and, not seeing the Rāghava as his protector, fled headlong to Ṛśyamūka.
Exhausted, his body drenched in blood, shattered by blows, pursued by Vālī in wrath, he entered the great forest.
Seeing him enter the forest, the mighty Vālī, out of fear of the curse, said 'You are freed' and turned back.
The Rāghava too, together with his brother and also with Hanūmat, came to that very forest where the monkey Sugrīva was.
Seeing Rāma arrive with Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, ashamed and dejected, looking down at the earth, spoke these words:
"Having told me 'Challenge him,' and having displayed your prowess, and then having had me struck down by my enemy — what is this that you have now done?"
"At that very moment you should have told me truly, O Rāghava, 'I will not slay Vālī' — then I would not have departed from here."
As the great-souled Sugrīva spoke thus with pitiable and mournful voice, the Rāghava again replied:
"Hear me, dear Sugrīva, and let your anger be dispelled — hear the reason why that arrow was not released by me."
"In ornaments, dress, build, and gait, you and Vālī, O Sugrīva, are alike to each other."
"In voice, in lustre, in glance, O monkey, in manner of movement, and in speech — I could not discern any mark of distinction between you two."
"Thus, O foremost of monkeys, confounded by the similarity of form, I did not release that swift, enemy-destroying arrow."
"But see now — this very moment I shall fell Vālī in battle with a single arrow, writhing on the ground."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Make some distinguishing mark upon yourself, O lord of monkeys, by which I may recognise you as you come to single combat."
"Uprooting this blossoming gajapuṣpī creeper of auspicious marks, place it, O Lakṣmaṇa, around the neck of this great-souled Sugrīva."
Then, having uprooted from the mountain slope that gajapuṣpī laden with blossoms, Lakṣmaṇa placed it around his neck.
He, the glorious one, thus adorned with the creeper clinging to his neck, shone like a rain-cloud with the Saṃdhyā glow, like a garland of cranes.
Shining brilliantly in form, confirmed by Rāma's words, he went together with Rāma to Kiṣkindhā, governed by Vālī.
That righteous-souled elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa departed from Ṛśyamūka together with Sugrīva toward Kiṣkindhā, which was guarded by the might of Vālī.
Rāma took up his great bow adorned with gold, and grasped his battle-winning arrows, blazing like the sun.
In front of that great-souled Rāghava went Sugrīva with his powerful neck, and mighty Lakṣmaṇa.
Behind came the heroic Hanūmān, the monkey Nala, Nīla, and the great-splendored Tāra—leaders of the monkey troops.
They gazed upon trees bending under the weight of blossoms, and upon rivers bearing clear waters flowing toward the ocean.
They looked upon caves and mountain ranges, cascading waterfalls, caverns, prominent peaks, and lovely rocky clefts.
Along the way they beheld ponds full of water, beautified by leaves clear as vaidūrya gems and by lotuses with sky-reaching buds.
Those ponds resounded with kāraṇḍava ducks, sārasa cranes, haṃsa geese, vañjūla birds, water-hens, cakravāka pairs, and many other birds.
On all sides they saw deer standing on open ground, ranging the forest fearlessly, feeding on tender shoots of fresh grass.
They also saw fearsome wild elephants adorned with white tusks, lone wanderers, enemies of embankments, striding alone through the forest.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Beholding yet other forest-dwelling creatures and sky-roaming birds, those who were subject to Sugrīva's command advanced quickly.
As they hastened along, Rāma the delight of the Raghu lineage, catching sight of a grove of trees, spoke to Sugrīva.
"This cluster of trees gleams in the sky like a cloud—vast as a mass of storm-clouds, its borders ringed with plantain trees."
"I wish to know what this is, my friend—I am curious. I want you to relieve my curiosity."
Hearing those words of the great-souled Rāghava, Sugrīva, even as he walked on, described that great forest.
"O Rāghava, this is a vast hermitage, a destroyer of fatigue, endowed with gardens and woodland, rich in sweet roots, fruits, and water."
"Here dwell sages known as the Seven Persons, of sharpened vows—seven in number, who remain with heads downward, ever lying in the water."
"They eat once every seven nights, they subsist on air, dwelling in the forest; over seven centuries they have ascended to heaven, still embodied."
"By their power this hermitage, encircled by a wall of trees, has become utterly unconquerable—even by gods and demons together with Indra."
"Birds avoid this place, as do other forest-wanderers; those who enter it through delusion do not return."
"From here, O Rāghava, are heard the distinct sounds of ornaments, and strains of music and song, and a divine fragrance."
"The three sacred fires still blaze here; that smoke is visible, a dense pigeon-gray-red column, wrapping itself around the treetops."
"O righteous-souled Rāghava, offer obeisance to them—reverently, with your brother Lakṣmaṇa, with palms joined."
"For those who bow to these enlightened sages, O Rāma, no misfortune whatsoever is seen to afflict their bodies."
Thereupon Rāma, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, with palms joined, directed his obeisance toward those great-souled sages and reverently saluted them.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having paid their salutations, the righteous-souled Rāma, his brother Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, and the monkeys proceeded with joyful hearts.
Having traveled a great distance from that hermitage of the Seven Persons, they beheld Kiṣkindhā, that impregnable city, ruled by Vālī.
All of them, having swiftly reached Kiṣkindhā ruled by Vālī, concealed themselves among trees and stood in the dense forest.
Casting his glance all around the forest, Sugrīva who delighted in the forest—broad-necked—roused his anger fiercely.
Then, surrounded by his retinue, he let out a terrible roar, as if splitting the sky with his cries, challenging Vālī to battle.
Then Sugrīva, radiant as the morning sun, with the gait of a proud lion, seeing Rāma skilled in action, spoke these words.
"We have arrived at the city of Kiṣkindhā belonging to Vālī—filled with monkey nets, with portals of burnished gold, abundant with flagstaffs and devices."
"The pledge you made earlier, O hero, regarding the slaying of Vālī—now fulfill it swiftly, like the season of fruiting come for the vine."
Thus addressed by Sugrīva, that righteous-souled Rāghava, destroyer of enemies, then spoke these words to Sugrīva.
"You must bear a distinguishing mark, by means of this garland of gaja flowers, so that I may know you—as the sun in the sky is distinct from the garland of stars."
"Today, O monkey, I shall free you in a single stroke—releasing one arrow in battle—from both the fear and the enmity arising from Vālī."
"Show me Vālī, the enemy of Sugrīva who wears the form of a brother—so that he may writhe in the forest dust when struck down."
"If he comes within range of my sight and yet retreats alive, then let that fault not fall on me—and you must not blame me then."
"Before your eyes I pierced seven śāla trees with a single arrow—know by that power that Vālī is today already slain by me."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I have never spoken an untruth, O hero, even in the most difficult circumstances, overwhelmed though I may be by desire for righteousness—nor shall I ever speak one."
"I shall fulfill my pledge—abandon your agitation. As Indra of a hundred sacrifices brings rain to make the sown grain sprout in the field, so shall it be."
"Therefore, for the purpose of that challenge, O Sugrīva, make that sound which will cause the golden-garlanded Vālī, that monkey, to rush forth."
"That Vālī who glories in victory, who boasts of conquest, who loves combat—having been challenged and provoked by you, he will spring forth from the city without hesitation."
"Heroes do not endure provocation by enemies in battle, especially when they know their own valor—and all the more so before the eyes of women."
Then Sugrīva, tawny as gold, hearing Rāma's words, roared with a fierce and terrible cry, as if cleaving the sky asunder.
Terrified by his sound, cows scattered, their brightness dimmed, distraught like noblewomen afflicted by the vice of a king.
Deer fled swiftly, like horses broken and routed in battle; birds fell to the ground, like planets whose merit is exhausted.
Then that son of the Sun, with valor-enhanced splendor, confident and swift, sent forth a roar like the thunder of gathered storm-clouds—like the lord of rivers whose waves are stirred by the wind.
Then Vālī, intolerant of his brother, who was within the inner apartments, heard that roar of the great-souled Sugrīva.
Hearing that roar which made all creatures tremble, in an instant his intoxication vanished and great fury descended upon him.
Vālī, his body suffused with rage, blazed like the reddened sun at twilight—and instantly became as it were stripped of his calm radiance.
Vālī with his fearsome fangs, resembling blazing fire in his wrath, shone like a pond whose lotuses have sprung up together with their stalks.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing that unbearable sound, the monkey lord sprang forth with such speed that the stamp of his feet seemed to split the earth.
But Tārā, embracing him and showing her affection from love, frightened and agitated, spoke to him these words bearing beneficial consequences.
"It is well, O hero—restrain this anger that has swept in like a river in spate; having just risen from your bed at daybreak, put it away like a garland already enjoyed."
"Your sudden sally does not please me. Hear me—I shall tell you the reason why you are being restrained."
"Before, he came upon you in anger and challenged you to combat; but when he was repulsed by you and lay nearly slain, he fled in all directions."
"That he returns here now to challenge you again, after having been so utterly routed and afflicted by you—this arouses my suspicion."
"The pride and resolve that can be read in his roaring, and the fierce urgency of that cry—this is no small cause for concern."
"I do not think Sugrīva has come here without allies; he roars here relying on some powerful support."
"That monkey is by nature shrewd and wise; Sugrīva would not go to combat alongside one whose valor he has not tested."
"Even before now, O hero, I heard words from Prince Aṅgada's account; I shall now speak to you words that are for your good."
"Your brother's ally is the renowned and battle-hardened Rāma, crusher of enemy armies, arisen like the fire of the world's end."
"He is the sheltering tree of the virtuous, the ultimate refuge of those who are distressed, the support of the afflicted, and the sole vessel of glory."
"Endowed with knowledge and realized wisdom, devoted to his father's command—like the king of mountains is to minerals, he is a great mine of virtues."
"Therefore it is not fitting that you enter into conflict with that great-souled Rāma, who is unconquerable and immeasurable in the deeds of battle."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"O hero, I will tell you something—I do not wish to be censured for it. Listen, and do as I counsel; I shall tell you what is for your welfare."
"Quickly and properly install Sugrīva as crown prince; do not, O hero and king, enter into conflict with a brother who is backed by a mightier power."
"I truly believe what befits you is friendship with Rāma and reconciliation with Sugrīva—casting enmity far away."
"This younger monkey is your brother who deserves to be cherished; whether he is there or here, he is in every way still your kinsman."
"If my good is dear to you, and if you consider me well-wishing, then, earnestly entreated, heed my words well."
To Tārā who spoke thus — she whose face resembles the lord of stars — Vālī spoke words of rebuke and said this:
"For what reason should I endure the fury and roaring of him who is both my brother and my enemy? Tell me, O lovely-faced one.
For heroes who have never been humbled, who never turn back in battle — to endure insult, O timid one, is worse than death.
I am incapable of enduring in combat the fury and roaring of Sugrīva, that wretched-necked one who thirsts for battle.
You should not grieve on my account concerning Rāghava; how would one who knows dharma and is grateful commit sin?
Turn back with the women — why do you follow me further? O Tārā, your friendship toward me has been shown; your devotion has been rendered.
I shall go and fight Sugrīva — abandon your agitation. I will crush his arrogance; he shall not escape with his life.
I swear by my own life — turn back. I shall return victorious after defeating that brother of mine in battle."
Then Tārā, that sweet-spoken one, embraced Vālī and, weeping softly, performed the auspicious circumambulation of him.
Then, having performed the benedictory rites as prescribed by injunction, she who desired his victory entered the inner apartments together with the women, overcome with grief.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When Tārā had entered her dwelling together with the women, the angry Vālī went forth from the city, hissing like a great serpent.
That swift Vālī, utterly furious, cast his gaze in all directions, eager for the sight of his enemy.
Then that glorious one beheld Sugrīva — tawny as gold, well-girded, steadfast, blazing like a fire.
Seeing Sugrīva of great might standing ready for battle, the utterly furious Vālī girded his garment tightly.
That valiant Vālī, firmly girded, raised his fist and advanced straight toward Sugrīva, resolved to do battle.
Sugrīva too, raising his tightly-clenched fist and coming forward with even greater fury, aimed himself at Vālī who wore a golden garland.
To Sugrīva the battle-expert, who came rushing with great speed, Vālī — his eyes red with rage — spoke these words:
"This fist of mine, tightly closed with fingers firmly set — when I hurl it with full force, it will depart taking your life with it."
Thus addressed, Sugrīva in anger replied to Vālī: "Let my fist fall upon your head, bearing away your very life."
Struck by him, Vālī in great fury rushed forward with speed and began to pour forth blood, like a mountain gushing with a spring.
By Sugrīva, who with his might uprooted a sāla tree and struck Vālī across the limbs, Vālī was shaken like a great mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Vālī, assaulted and reeling from the blow of the sāla tree, became like a vessel in the ocean weighed down by a heavy load.
Those two, of fearsome strength and prowess, with the speed of Suparṇa, towering and terrible in form, were like the sun and moon in the sky.
Sugrīva, his pride shattered by Vālī and his strength failing, yet showing his agility in anger, displayed his nimbleness before Vālī.
Then Rāghava, fitting to his bow an arrow like a venomous serpent, loosed that mighty shaft and drove it into the chest of Vālī.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Struck with great force, Vālī fell to the earth.
Then, drenched with streams of blood-water, like a blossoming aśoka tree tossed by the wind, the son of Indra — his senses fled — fell to the ground in battle like the banner of Indra cast down.
Then Vālī, that hardened warrior, struck by Rāma's arrow, fell suddenly like a felled tree.
His whole body laid upon the earth, adorned with ornaments of refined gold, he fell like the banner of the king of gods when its ropes are loosed.
When that lord of the host of monkeys fell to the ground, the earth ceased to shine, like the sky when the moon is lost.
Even as that great-souled one lay fallen on the earth, neither glory, nor life, nor splendour, nor heroic power departed from his body.
The excellent garland given by Śakra — golden, adorned with gems — upheld the life, the radiance, and the glory of that foremost among monkeys.
That hero, lord of the monkey hosts, wreathed in that golden garland, its borders fringed as if with twilight hues, resembled a rain-cloud.
His garland, his body, and the arrow that had pierced his vitals — as though the glory were fashioned in three parts — shone even in his fallen state.
That weapon, hurled from Rāma's bow, lighting the path to heaven for that hero, conveyed him toward the highest destiny.
Him thus fallen in battle — like a fire whose flames have departed, like Yayāti fallen from the celestial world when his merit was exhausted —
like the sun cast down to earth by time at the end of an age, like Mahendra himself impossible to assail, like Mahendra himself impossible to endure —
— Vālī, son of Mahendra, fallen, wearing his golden garland, lion-chested, mighty-armed, blazing-faced, with tawny eyes — Rāma, followed by Lakṣmaṇa, beheld and approached him.
Seeing Rāghava and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, Vālī spoke words that were at once respectful and harsh, yet in accord with dharma:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"What virtue have you gained by slaying one turned away from you? For it is because of you that I, inflamed for battle, have met my death.
'Rāma is of noble lineage, endowed with virtue, radiant, faithful to his vows, compassionate, and devoted to the welfare of his subjects' —
'He is merciful, of great energy, knowing the appointed times, firm in his vows' — thus all beings speak of your fame upon this earth.
Weighing those virtues and your high lineage — though restrained by Tārā — I came forth to meet Sugrīva.
'He should not strike me — enraged and unwary as I am — from the side of another' — such was the thought that arose in me at not seeing you openly.
I did not know you to be this — a man of destroyed soul, bearing the banner of dharma yet unrighteous, of evil conduct, like a well covered with grass.
Bearing the guise of the virtuous yet evil, like a fire concealed — I did not recognize you, wrapped in the disguise of dharma.
When I have done you no harm in your domain or in your city, and I do not even know you, why do you slay the innocent?
I, a monkey who always subsists on fruits and roots, who roams the forest — who was here engaged in combat with another, not with you —
You are known as the son of a king of men, pleasing in appearance; even the mark of dharma can be seen upon you, O king.
Who, born in a kṣatriya family, learned, with doubts resolved, wearing the mark of dharma as a guise, would commit such a cruel act?
Rāma — born in a royal lineage, renowned as righteous — why do you roam about, unworthy yet wearing a worthy form?
Conciliation, gift, forbearance, dharma, truth, steadfastness, and heroism — these are the qualities of kings, O king; and punishment too, for those who transgress.
We, O Rāma, are forest-dwellers, animals who eat roots and fruits — that is our nature. You are a man, a lord of men.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Land, gold, and silver — these are reasons for punishment. What greed of yours in the forest, or for my fruits, is there?
Both policy and propriety, both punishment and favour — the conduct of kings is unsullied. Kings do not act by the rule of passion.
But you are governed by passion, irascible, unstable, your royal conduct muddled, and devoted only to the bow.
You have no reverence for dharma, your mind is not fixed on what is right; enslaved by passion through the senses, you are dragged about, O lord of men.
Having slain me here with an arrow — me, the guiltless one — O Kākutstha, what will you say in the assembly of the virtuous, having committed this censurable deed?
Slayer of a king, slayer of a brahmin, killer of cows, thief, one addicted to killing living beings, an atheist, one who marries before his elder brother — all these go to hell.
My hide is not to be worn by the virtuous; my hair and bones are to be avoided; my flesh is not to be eaten by those like you who practise dharma.
Five five-clawed animals are permitted as food for brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas, O Rāghava: the porcupine, the śvāvidha, the monitor lizard, the hare, and the tortoise as the fifth.
My hide and bones, O king, the wise do not touch, and my flesh is not to be eaten — such am I, a five-clawed animal, slain by you.
With you as its lord, O Kākutstha, the earth is truly without a worthy lord — like a virtuous woman fallen prey to a scoundrel.
Treacherous, deceitful, petty, false in your outward show of humility — how is it that you, a sinner, were born of the great-souled Daśaratha?
By the elephant that is Rāma — whose girths of good conduct are severed, who transgresses the dharma of the virtuous, who has cast off the goad of righteousness — I have been slain.
Had you fought openly against me in battle, O son of a king, today you would have met the god Vaivasvata, slain by my hand.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
But I, formidable as I am, have been slain in battle by you who remained unseen — like a man overpowered by drink, bitten by a snake while asleep.
Though you have slain me for the sake of pleasing Sugrīva, I could have bound Rāvaṇa by the neck and delivered him to you unslain in battle.
I would have found out for you, at your command, where Maithilī is hidden — whether in the ocean's waters or in the underworld — as one traces a white she-mule.
It would be fitting that Sugrīva obtain the kingdom on my death by natural causes — but it is unfitting that I have been slain by you through unrighteousness in battle.
Let the world be thus disposed by time as it will — if indeed you have a fitting response, let it be well considered."
Having spoken thus, his mouth parched, the great-souled son of the king of the immortals — tormented by the wound of the arrow — gazed upon Rāma who blazed like the sun, and fell silent.
Thus addressed with words at once respectful, grounded in dharma and good counsel, yet harsh — words spoken by the stricken and senseless Vālī — Rāma replied.
To that foremost of monkeys who had spoken his words — like the sun bereft of radiance, like a cloud that has released its water, like a fire that has subsided —
— endowed with the qualities of dharma and statecraft, that peerless lord of monkeys, by whom Rāma had been rebuked — Rāma then spoke to Vālī:
"Without understanding dharma, artha, kāma, and worldly convention, how do you in your childishness rebuke me here today?
Without consulting the wise elders honoured by teachers, O gentle one, you wish to speak against me here out of mere monkey frivolity.
This entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves — and the power of punishment and favour over animals, birds, and men alike — belongs to the Ikṣvākus.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That earth is governed by the righteous-souled Bharata — truthful, upright, knowing the true nature of dharma, kāma, and artha, devoted to punishment and favour alike.
In whom both policy and propriety, and truth too are well-established, and whose heroism has been witnessed — he is the king who knows place and time.
Acting on his orders established in dharma, we and the other kings roam the entire earth, desiring the perpetuation of righteousness.
While that tiger among kings, Bharata — devoted to dharma — governs the entire earth, who could transgress the bounds of righteous rule?
We, established in our highest dharma, placing Bharata's command foremost, restrain those who have strayed from the right path, according to due procedure.
But you, your dharma sullied, censured by your deeds, governed by the rule of passion — you have not stood on the path of kingship.
An elder brother, a father, and one who confers knowledge — these three are to be known as fathers; and they who walk the path of dharma.
A younger brother, one's own son, and a pupil endowed with virtues — these three are to be thought of as sons, if dharma is the governing principle here.
The dharma of the virtuous is subtle and supremely difficult to know, O leaper; dwelling in the heart, the ātman of all beings knows the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Fickle as you are, deliberating with fickle monkeys of unformed selves — like one born blind deliberating with the congenitally blind — what indeed can you see?
I shall make this matter clear to you. Surely you ought not to rebuke me from mere anger alone.
Observe then this reason for which you have been slain by me: you cohabit with your brother's wife, having abandoned the eternal law of dharma.
While the great-souled Sugrīva is still alive, you in your lust cohabit with Rumā — who is as a daughter-in-law to you — O perpetrator of evil deeds.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Therefore, this punishment has been meted out to you — who have transgressed dharma and acted by passion — for this violation of your brother's wife, O monkey.
For one who has acted contrary to dharma and strayed from worldly convention, I see no restraint other than punishment, O lord of monkey hosts.
A man who from lust makes advances upon his own natural sister, or upon the wife of his younger brother — for him death is prescribed as the punishment.
Bharata is the sovereign of the earth; we act on his command; and you have transgressed dharma — how could this be overlooked?
The wise Bharata, governing righteously those who transgress the dharma of their superiors, is established in the restraint of those who act by passion.
And we, O lord of monkeys, making Bharata's command our rule, are established in the restraint of those like you who have broken the boundaries of propriety.
My friendship with Sugrīva is the same as with Lakṣmaṇa; and he who is devoted to highest good — his cause concerning wife and kingdom is mine as well.
And a pledge was given by me then in the presence of the monkeys — how could one such as I leave a pledge unregarded?
Therefore, by all these reasons, great and in accord with dharma, let you accept that which is a fitting chastisement for you.
In every way, your restraint is to be seen as dharma itself; and to one who looks upon dharma as supreme, it is a service to a friend.
Men who have committed sins and been punished by kings come forth purified and reach heaven, like the virtuous who have performed meritorious deeds.
By the noble Māndhātṛ of mine, a grievous calamity was once sought — just as the sin was committed by an ascetic in that case, so the sin has been committed by you.
Even sins committed by other heedless sovereigns — they perform atonement for them, and by that the taint is quenched.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Therefore, enough of anguish — this death has been ordained according to dharma, O tiger among monkeys; we do not act by our own will.
With snares, nooses, and various traps, both hidden and visible, men take very many animals — whether running, frightened, calm, or standing still.
Men seeking meat strike animals forcefully whether they are heedless or heedful, and even those with their backs turned — and there is no fault in this.
Royal sages too skilled in dharma go hunting here. Therefore you, O monkey, have been slain in battle by me with an arrow — whether you fought back or not — for you are a tree-dwelling animal.
Of the rare gift of dharma and of auspicious life, O foremost of monkeys, kings are the givers — there is no doubt.
One should not injure them, nor revile them, nor offend them, nor speak unpleasant words to them — these kings walk the earth in human form as gods.
But you, not knowing dharma, clinging to mere rage, seek to sully me — who am established in the dharma inherited from my fathers and forefathers."
Thus addressed by Rāma, Vālī, greatly pained, then replied to Rāma with joined palms — that lord of monkeys:
"What you have said, O best of men — it is indeed so; there is no doubt in this. Against the exalted, the lowly is not capable of reply.
Whatever unbecoming and unpleasant word I spoke before through heedlessness — even for that you should not find fault with me, O Rāghava.
For you are the knower of the true nature of things that are seen, devoted to the welfare of your subjects; your imperishable intellect is clear in determining cause and effect.
Me too — who am recognized as one who has placed transgression of dharma foremost — protect with words in accord with dharma, O knower of dharma.
Then Vālī, his throat choked with tears, in a voice full of grief and sorrow, gazing at Rāma softly spoke — like an elephant mired in mud:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"It is not for myself that I grieve, nor for Tārā, nor for my kinsmen — but for my son Aṅgada, golden-limbed, foremost in virtues.
He who, cherished from his very childhood, will be wretched at not seeing me — like a pool whose waters have been drunk, he will wither away.
Bestow your highest regard upon both Sugrīva and Aṅgada — for you are the chastener and the protector, established in the rule of what should and should not be done.
The same conduct that you observe, O lord of men, toward Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa — that same conduct toward Sugrīva and Aṅgada, O king, you should think fit to show.
You should conduct yourself in such a way that Sugrīva does not despise that afflicted Tārā — blameless on her own account yet tainted by my fault.
For one favoured by you, walking under your sway and following your will, the kingdom can be enjoyed in peace."
Rāma then consoled Vālī, who was now clear of vision.
"Neither should you be anxious about us, nor about yourself, O best of monkeys — we have acted with special regard for you, our resolve established in dharma.
He who metes out punishment to one deserving punishment, and he who deserves it and is punished — both, their purpose of cause and effect accomplished, do not fall into disgrace.
Therefore you, through this contact with punishment, freed from taint, have returned to your own righteous nature, walking the path as seen by dharma.
Hearing those sweet, collected words of the great-souled Rāma — who treads the path of dharma, who crushes the arrogant in battle — those well-reasoned words, the monkey replied:
"O lord, whatever offensive words I, scorched by the arrow and out of my senses, not knowing, spoke against you — for this, O one comparable to Mahendra in fearsome prowess, be pleased and forgive me, O lord of the earth."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That great king of the monkeys, struck by the arrow and lying prostrate, though addressed with reasoned words, could find no reply.
His limbs shattered by rocks, grievously struck by trees, and now overwhelmed by Rāma's arrow, he fell into a swoon at the threshold of death.
Tārā heard that Vālin, that tiger among monkeys and her own lord, had been slain in battle by the arrow discharged by Rāma at a wife's behest.
Hearing that most terrible news of her husband's death — dreadful alike for her and for her son — she rushed out in great terror from the various mountain caves.
The mighty monkeys who formed Aṅgada's escort, catching sight of Rāma with his bow, fled in terror.
She then saw the terrified monkeys racing toward her in headlong flight — like deer scattered from a herd whose leader has been slain.
She, herself stricken with grief, approached those grief-stricken ones — all of them put to flight by Rāma as though pursued by his arrows — and spoke to them.
"O monkeys, you who were the vanguard of that lion among kings — why do you flee in such great terror, abandoning him, reduced to this miserable state?"
"If indeed that brother has felled this brother for the sake of a kingdom — by Rāma, with his far-flying shafts loosed from a distance — then flee!"
Hearing the words of the monkey-queen, the monkeys — those shape-shifters — spoke to her in timely and coherent words.
"Live for your son — turn back! Protect your son Aṅgada. Death, having taken the form of Rāma, has slain Vālin and carries him away."
"Vālin, who had hurled uprooted trees and massive boulders — that Vālin has been struck down by arrows like thunderbolts, as if by the thunderbolt itself."
"With this tiger among monkeys slain — he whose splendor was equal to Indra's — this entire army that had charged forward has now scattered and fled."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Let the city be guarded by the heroes, and let Aṅgada be consecrated as king. Standing firm in his father's place, the monkeys will rally to Vālin's son."
"Or else, O fair-faced one, this stronghold is a fitting refuge for you — the monkeys are quickly entering the fortresses even today."
"Among these forest-dwellers, some have wives and some do not; we face tremendous danger from our own folk — the greedy and the lawless."
Having heard the words of those who had drawn near within a short distance, that beautiful-smiling woman spoke what was fitting for herself.
"What need have I of a son, what of a kingdom, what of my own life, now that that most glorious lion among monkeys, my husband, has perished?"
"I shall go to the feet of that noble great-souled one himself, who has been struck down by the arrow set flying by Rāma."
Having spoken thus, she ran forward weeping, wasted by grief, beating her head and her breast with her arms in her anguish.
As she hurried forward she then saw her husband fallen upon the ground — he who in battles had never turned back, the slayer of lords of demons.
He who had hurled the kings of mountains like Vāsava his thunderbolts, who had been filled with the force of a great storm and roared like a mass of great thunder-clouds —
— whose valor equaled Indra's, terrible in his roaring among those who roar, like a cloud stilled after releasing its rain, that hero laid low by a hero.
As a tiger kills a lion for the sake of flesh — him who was honored by all the world with banners and ceremonial platforms.
As Garuḍa demolishes a sacred tree for the sake of a serpent — thus she saw him, still grasping and upholding his mighty bow, even as he lay fallen.
That beautiful woman passed by Rāma and Rāma's younger brother, and also her husband's younger brother, and drew near to her husband slain in battle.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Gazing upon him she fell to the ground, anguished and bewildered; then rising again as if from sleep, she cried aloud, "My noble lord!"
She wept, beholding her husband bound fast in the bonds of death. Sugrīva, watching her crying out like an osprey, —
— fell into deep despondency, and seeing Aṅgada also arrived, sorrow overwhelmed him.
Tārā — she whose face was like the lord of stars — seeing him struck down upon the ground by the death-dealing arrow loosed from Rāma's bow,
that passionate woman drew near to her husband and embraced him, seeing Vālin, who resembled a great elephant, struck down by the shaft.
Tārā lamented in anguish over the lord of monkeys, who resembled great Indra, her heart tormented by grief — as over a great tree torn up by the roots.
"O you of terrible valor in battle, O hero, O best among those who leap — why do you not speak today to me who am wretched and without good fortune?"
"Rise, O tiger among monkeys, and take your place on an excellent couch — for kings of your kind do not lie upon the bare earth."
"Truly the earth is exceedingly dear to you, O lord of the earth, that even having lost your breath of life you abandon me and lie embracing her with your limbs."
"It is clear, O hero, that another has been chosen by you, you who proceed according to your own dharma — a beautiful city like Kiṣkindhā has been fashioned for you on the path to heaven."
"Those pleasures we enjoyed together with you in the fragrant forests — you have in your time put an end to all of them."
"I am joyless, I am hopeless, plunged into an ocean of grief, now that you — the lord of great monkey-troops — have been reduced to the five elements."
"My heart is very firm indeed — that, seeing you struck down upon the ground, it does not burst today into a thousand pieces, scorched by grief."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You seized Sugrīva's wife and drove him into exile — and now, O lord of monkeys, this retribution from him has come upon you for that deed."
"And I too, who out of concern for the welfare of the lord of monkeys had spoken words of benefit to you, was censured by you in delusion as one fixated on mokṣa."
"Time, the ender of life, is doubtless irresistible — it is by Time's force that you have fallen helplessly under Sugrīva's power."
"Wretched that I am, a wretched woman, unaccustomed to sorrow before, I shall now live out widowhood, grief, and torment, like one without a protector."
"Aṅgada the hero, who was pampered, tender, accustomed to comfort — in what condition will he live now for me, with his uncle enraged and maddened?"
"Look well upon your father, my son — he who was devoted to dharma and virtuous. The sight of him, my dear child, will henceforth be hard to obtain."
"Comfort your son, and give him your final message; sniff his head in farewell, for you are departing on a long journey from which there is no return."
"Great indeed is the deed done by Rāma in slaying you — he has thereby discharged his debt in fulfillment of his pledge to Sugrīva."
"May you have your desire, Sugrīva — you shall recover Rumā; rule the kingdom without anxiety; your enemy, your brother, has been slain."
"Why do you not speak to me with affection as I lament so? Look upon these, your many excellent wives, O lord of monkeys."
Hearing her lament, the female monkeys all around, embracing the wretched Aṅgada, cried out in their anguish.
"O hero of powerful arms, why do you depart today on this long journey leaving Aṅgada behind? It is not fitting, O you who loved your son, to go thus, leaving behind a son so close to you in virtues."
"What wrong have I done you, O master of lovely and pleasing form, or what has your son done, that today, O hero, leaving me your companion, you go recklessly to the abode of Yama?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"If I have done anything displeasing to you without knowing it, forgive me for that, O long-armed one, O master of the monkey lineage — I go, O hero, touching your feet with my head."
And thus Tārā, of blameless complexion, weeping piteously together with the female monkeys near her husband, resolved upon the fast unto death, settling down beside Vālin where he lay upon the ground.
Then Hanūmān, the leader of the monkey troops, gently consoled Tārā where she had fallen — like a star fallen from the sky.
"A being, composed of virtues and faults, and conditioned by the fruits of its own actions, receives without fail all the good and ill that is due to it in the next world."
"You who are worthy of lamentation lament for whom? You who are pitiable take pity on whom who is pitiable? And who is there to mourn for whom, in this body that is like a bubble?"
"This prince Aṅgada must be looked after by you who have a son still living; think also of what is capable of being done for him in the future."
"You know that the coming and going of all beings is thus uncertain; therefore, O wise one, what is auspicious must be done — not what is merely of this world."
"He in whose service thousands, millions, and ten-hundreds-of-millions of monkeys performed their appointed portions — even he has come to his fated end."
"Because he was one who perceived things rightly, who was devoted to conciliation, generosity, and forbearance, he has gone to the realm won by dharma — you ought not to grieve for him."
"All the monkeys, and this your son Aṅgada, and the kingdom of the lords of monkeys and bears — all these, O blameless one, have you as their protector."
"Gently urge these two who are tormented by grief, O passionate one; let this Aṅgada, taken under your guardianship, rule the earth."
"And the line of succession as it has been established, and whatever is now the pressing duty for the king — let all of that be carried out; such is Time's decree."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Let the king of monkeys be duly cremated, and let Aṅgada be consecrated; beholding your son seated upon the lion-throne, you will find peace."
She, tormented by the calamity of losing her husband, heard his words and replied to Hanūmān as he stood before her.
"A hundred sons equal to Aṅgada placed on one side — the embrace of the body of this hero, even slain, is better."
"And I have no power over the kingdom of the monkey king, nor over Aṅgada — Sugrīva, his paternal uncle, is the next in authority in all matters."
"This resolve is not to be entertained regarding Aṅgada, O Hanūmān — for it is the father who is the kinsman of the son, not the mother, O best of monkeys."
"For there is nothing more fitting for me than to take refuge with the king of monkeys — in this world or the next; and it is fitting that I attend upon this couch attended by the hero who fell facing the foe."
Breathing faintly and gazing all around, Vālī, his life-breath now slow, saw Sugrīva standing there first of all, alert and watchful near his own son.
Vālī addressed Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, who had now attained victory, and spoke these words to him with a clear voice full of affection.
Do not go blaming Sugrīva's fault for my ruin; it was I who was dragged by force into this, my intellect bewildered by what fate had decreed.
Dear brother, I do not think prosperity was ordained for both of us simultaneously; the fraternal bond and affection between us has thus turned out otherwise.
Take up at once this very day the kingdom of these forest-dwellers; and know that I too am departing this very day to the abode of Vaivasvata, the god of death.
Life, kingdom, this vast royal glory, and great unblemished fame — I am quickly relinquishing all of them now.
O hero, O king, in this condition I shall speak words which, though difficult to carry out, you must nonetheless perform.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Look at this boy Aṅgada, fallen to the ground, his face filled with tears — he who deserves happiness and was reared in comfort, blameless though young.
Guard this son, dearer to me than my own life, as if he were your own born son; though bereft of me, let him lack nothing — protect him in every way.
You too shall be his provider, his protector in all things, and his deliverer from every fear — just as I was, O lord of the monkeys.
This glorious son of Tārā, equal to you in valor, shall march at the forefront of your forces in the slaying of those rākṣasas.
Young Aṅgada, Tārā's son, swift and mighty, shall perform deeds worthy of his lineage, displaying his prowess in battle.
And this daughter of Suṣeṇa — Tārā — is thoroughly versed in adjudicating subtle matters of policy, and is fully accomplished in interpreting all manner of omens and portents.
Whatever she pronounces as right and proper, let that be done without doubt; for nothing that Tārā deems wise ever turns out otherwise.
And you must carry out Rāghava's purpose without hesitation; for neglecting it would be unrighteous, and he, if slighted, would harm you.
And take this divine golden garland of Sugrīva's — great sovereignty resides in it; it would abandon this world on my death.
Thus spoken to by Vālī out of brotherly love, Sugrīva, abandoning all joy, became wretched again — like the moon seized by a planet.
Pacified by Vālī's words, acting rightly and without hesitation, he accepted — having been given leave — that golden garland.
Having given away that golden garland and seeing his son standing near, Vālī, readied now for departure from this life, spoke to Aṅgada with affection.
Attend now to place and time; bear with equanimity both the pleasant and the unpleasant; endure joy and sorrow alike; and in due season remain submissive to Sugrīva.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
O mighty-armed one, Sugrīva will not hold you in the same regard as I always did when I indulged you; behave accordingly.
Do not follow those who have gone over to enemies; do not go with your foes, O subduer of foes; be self-restrained, devoted to your lord's interests, and obedient to Sugrīva.
Neither excessive intimacy nor excessive aloofness should be practiced by you; both are great faults. Therefore be one who sees the middle path.
Having said these words, his eyes rolled back, tormented greatly by the arrow, his fearsome teeth bared — Vālī's life departed from him.
When that heroic lord of monkeys was slain, the forest-roaming monkeys found no peace — even as cows in a great forest find no peace when their bull has been killed by a lion.
Then Tārā, overwhelmed and drowned in an ocean of grief, gazed upon the face of her dead husband and fell to the ground embracing Vālī — like a creeper clinging to a great tree that has been felled.
Then Tārā, pressing her face close to inhale the scent of the monkey-king's face, her husband fallen from the living world, spoke these words to him as he lay dead.
You lie here, O hero, on this hard and painful earth strewn with crushed grass, without having heeded my words — and in great sorrow do I find myself.
The earth is surely dearer to you than I am, O lord of monkeys; for you lie there embracing her, and you do not speak a word to me.
O hero, O bold and beloved one — it is Sugrīva alone who has triumphed; yet the chieftains of bears and monkeys attend upon you, the mighty one.
Hearing the anguished lamentations of these, the grief of sorrowing Aṅgada, and this speech of mine — why do you not wake and reply?
This is that hero's resting place where you lie slain in battle — the very ground where in former times your enemies were laid low and slaughtered by you.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
O you of pure nature and noble lineage, O lover of battle, my beloved, O giver of honor — you have gone, leaving me alone, without a protector.
Truly the wise should not give a maiden in marriage to a hero; look at the wife of a hero now slain — see me, made a widow in an instant.
My pride is shattered; my eternal path is broken; I am sunk deep in a boundless, fathomless ocean of grief.
My heart must surely be made of the hardest iron, for upon seeing my husband slain it does not break into a hundred pieces this very moment.
He was my friend, my husband, by nature my beloved; and he was a hero who showed his valor in battle — and now he has merged into the five elements.
A woman bereft of her husband — let her have sons if she will, let her be filled with wealth and grain — is still called a widow by the wise.
O hero, you lie thus on a bed born of your own body — a pool of blood, covered with insects and reddish matter — as if resting on a couch.
Your body is smeared all over with dust and blood; I am unable to embrace it with my arms, O bull among monkeys.
Sugrīva has today accomplished his purpose in this most terrible enmity — his fear has been removed by a single arrow released by Rāma.
The arrow lodged in your heart prevents me from touching your body; I look at you and hold myself back — now that you have merged into the five elements.
Then Nīla drew out the arrow lodged in his body — as one draws out a blazing venomous serpent that has coiled itself deep in a mountain cave.
As that arrow was being drawn out, its radiance shone forth — like a ray of sunlight blocked by the summit of the setting mountain.
Streams of blood poured from his wounds on all sides — like streams tinged with red ochre flowing from a mountain.
Wiping the battle-dust that had settled on her husband, she bathed the hero — struck down by the weapon — with the tears flowing from her eyes.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing her husband slain, his entire body drenched in blood, Tārā spoke to her tawny-eyed son Aṅgada.
Son, look upon the dreadful final condition of your father — one who pursued enmity and met his end through sinful deeds.
Son, pay homage to the king your father — who gave honor to all — as he departs to Yama's abode, his body glowing like the rising morning sun.
Thus addressed, Aṅgada rose up and clasped his father's feet with his two stout rounded arms, saying "I am here, I am Aṅgada."
Why do you not speak to Aṅgada as he salutes you — as you used to do before — saying "May you live long, my son"?
I attend upon you, senseless as you are, together with your son — even as a cow with her calf attends upon a bull that a lion has just slain.
Having performed the sacrifice of battle with the waters of various weapons, how did you bathe in this concluding ablution without me, your wife?
The golden garland that the king of the gods, pleased with you in battle, once gave to you — why do I not see it on you here now?
The royal glory does not abandon you even in death, O giver of honor — like the light that does not leave the king of mountains even as the sun moves away.
You did not heed my wholesome words, nor was I able to restrain you. I am ruined — I and my son — by you who are ruined; along with you slain in battle, prosperity deserts me here.
Seeing Vālī now lifeless, Rāghava, the scorcher of enemies, thereupon addressed Sugrīva with gentle words.
The dead are not served by the torment of grief; you should now attend to what is to be done next in this matter.
The shedding of tears, which is the way of the world, has been done by you; no act can be carried out beyond its appointed time.
Fate is the cause in this world; fate is the instrument of action; fate is the cause that ordains all beings to their appointed tasks here.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
No one is the independent maker of anything, nor is anyone master of their own ordainment; the world moves according to its own nature, and time is its ultimate refuge.
Time does not transcend time; time is never diminished; and once one's nature is reached, no one can transgress it.
Time has no kinship, no motive, no heroic valor; neither friendship, nor relation, nor family ties are a cause for it; and one's own will is not the cause either.
Rather, the ripening of time must be observed by one who sees clearly; dharma, artha, and kāma are all gathered together through the orderly course of time.
From here Vālī has gone to his own elemental nature, having attained the fruit of his deeds; he is purified by the conjunction of dharma, artha, and kāma, O lord of monkeys.
Through his adherence to his own duty, that great soul has conquered and secured heaven — he who did not protect his life in battle.
This is indeed the highest destiny that this leader of monkey troops has attained; therefore enough with grief — let what is timely and appropriate now be attended to.
When Rāma had finished speaking, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, addressed Sugrīva, who was lost in grief, with gentle words.
Sugrīva, perform the funeral rites for him now without delay; together with Tārā and Aṅgada, proceed with the cremation of Vālī.
Give orders for many dry pieces of wood to be assembled, along with divine sandalwood — for the purpose of Vālī's obsequies.
Comfort Aṅgada whose heart is stricken; do not be foolish in your thinking — this city now depends upon you.
Let Aṅgada bring garlands, various garments, clarified butter, oil, perfumes, and whatever else is required next in this matter.
You, Tāra, quickly bring a palanquin with all haste; speed is especially meritorious at this particular time.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Let the monkeys who are fit to bear a palanquin make themselves ready — those who are capable and strong — they shall carry Vālī forth.
Having spoken thus to Sugrīva, Lakṣmaṇa — increaser of Sumitrā's joy, slayer of enemy heroes — stood by his brother's side.
Hearing Lakṣmaṇa's words, Tāra, his mind agitated and his thoughts fixed on the palanquin, quickly entered the cave.
Taking the palanquin, Tāra furnished it duly, to be borne by monkeys — those heroic ones trained to carry burdens.
Then Sugrīva, lifting Vālī and wailing aloud, placed him upon the palanquin — together with Aṅgada.
Having placed Vālī, bereft of life, upon the palanquin, he was adorned with various ornaments, garlands, and garments.
Then King Sugrīva, lord of monkeys, gave command: "Let the post-mortem rites befitting a noble one be performed duly."
"Let the monkeys go in front, distributing various gems in great numbers; the palanquin shall follow directly after."
Such special royal splendors as are seen among kings on earth — with such did they swiftly perform Vālī's post-mortem rites.
Quickly taking hold of Aṅgada, and together with Tāra and the others, all the monkeys, bereaved of their kinsman, went forward weeping aloud.
All the female monkeys, led by Tārā, whose troop-leader had been slain, followed their husband with piteous cries, wailing mournfully.
By the sound of those female monkeys weeping in the forest's depths, the forests and all the mountains seemed to cry out in every direction.
On a sandbar of a mountain river, in a secluded place surrounded by water, the many forest-roaming monkeys built the funeral pyre.
Then those trained to carry, lowering the palanquin from their shoulders, stood apart in a secluded spot, all overcome with grief.
Then Tārā, seeing her husband lying on the floor of the palanquin, placed his head in her lap and lamented in profound sorrow.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
You seem to look upon this grief-stricken people — your face appears almost joyful, O giver of honor; even in death it glows like the color of the setting sun, as though you still lived.
It is time itself, in the form of Rāma, that has dragged you away, O monkey — by whose single arrow all these women have been made widows in battle.
These beloved monkey-wives of yours, O king of kings, have come a long road trudging on foot — why do you not take notice of them?
Are these not your beloved wives with faces like the moon? Why do you not look at them now, and why not at Sugrīva, lord of monkeys?
O blameless king, these ministers of yours, led by Tāra, and all these citizens of your city sit gathered around you.
Dismiss these mighty ones fittingly, O subduer of foes, and then let us all sport in the forests, intoxicated with wine.
As Tārā lamented thus, overwhelmed with grief for her husband, the female monkeys, themselves wasted with sorrow, raised her up.
Then Aṅgada, together with Sugrīva, weeping for his father and his senses struck down by grief, placed Vālī upon the funeral pyre.
Then, having duly offered fire, he walked the circumambulation counter-clockwise around his father, who had set out on the long journey — his senses overwhelmed with grief.
Having performed the rites for Vālī according to prescribed custom, those monkeys went to a river of cool, auspicious waters to make the water-offering.
There, assembled together, they placed Aṅgada at the fore; and together with Sugrīva and Tārā, they poured the water-oblation for Vālī.
And Kākutstha — Rāma of great might — himself stricken, sharing the same grief together with the wretched Sugrīva, caused all the funeral rites to be performed.
Then the great ministers among the tree-dwelling monkeys gathered around Sugrīva, who was burning with grief and whose garments were still damp.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
All of them approached the mighty-armed Rāma, who acts without fatigue, and stood with folded hands, like sages before Brahmā the Grandfather.
Then Hanūmān, son of the Wind-god, who shines like a mountain of gold and whose face blazes like the rising sun, spoke these words with folded hands.
"By your grace, O lord, Sugrīva has obtained this great kingdom of the monkeys — the realm of his fathers and grandfathers — which was so very difficult to recover."
"With your permission he will enter the fair city and attend to all the affairs of state together with his friends and allies."
"Having bathed and been anointed with various perfumes and medicinal herbs according to prescribed rite, he will especially honour you with jewels and garlands."
"You should come from here to this lovely mountain cave, O master; establish your connection with us and delight the monkeys."
Thus addressed by Hanūmān, the wise Rāghava, slayer of enemy heroes, who was skilled in speech, replied to Hanūmān.
"For fourteen years, dear friend, I shall not enter any village or city — I who honour my father's command, O Hanūmān."
"Let the heroic Sugrīva, bull among monkeys, who has entered the richly furnished and splendid cave according to rite, be swiftly consecrated to the kingdom."
Having spoken thus to Hanūmān, Rāma said to Sugrīva: "O hero, consecrate this Aṅgada also as crown prince."
"This is the first month of the rainy season, Śrāvaṇa, that brings the coming of the waters; the four months known as the rainy season have now begun, dear friend."
"This is not the season for military exertion. Enter your fair city; I shall dwell on this mountain together with Lakṣmaṇa, dear friend."
"This mountain cave is lovely and spacious, well-ventilated, rich in water, and abundantly filled with lotuses and blue water-lilies, dear friend."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"When Kārtika arrives, devote yourself to the slaying of Rāvaṇa — this is our agreement, dear friend. Enter your own dwelling, get yourself consecrated to the kingdom, and gladden your friends."
Thus granted leave by Rāma, Sugrīva, bull among monkeys, entered the fair city of Kiṣkindhā, which had been governed by Vālin.
Thousands of monkeys, filled with joy, saluted that lord of monkeys as he entered and surrounded him on all sides.
Then all the subjects, upon seeing the lord of the monkey host, prostrated themselves with bowed heads to the ground with composed minds.
The valiant and mighty Sugrīva addressed all the subjects, raised them up, and then entered the fair inner apartments of his brother.
When Sugrīva, bull among monkeys, had entered and then came forth again, his friends consecrated him just as the immortals consecrated the Thousand-eyed Indra.
They brought for him a white parasol adorned with gold, and two white fly-whisks with golden handles that bestow glory.
Likewise all manner of jewels, all kinds of seed-bearing plants and medicinal herbs, and the sprouts and blossoms of milk-bearing trees.
And white garments, white unguent, fragrant garlands, and flowers both of land and water.
And divine sandalwood and many various fragrances, whole unhusked grain, gold, priyaṅgu grain, honey, and clarified butter.
And curd, a tiger-skin, and sandals made from the hide of a boar. Sixteen choice maidens arrived there with joy, bearing an anointing preparation, yellow orpiment, and manaḥśilā mineral.
Then they satisfied the best of the twice-born with jewels, garments, and food-offerings as befitting the time and proper rite, doing honour to that foremost of monkeys.
Then those versed in sacred formulas, having laid out a spread of kuśa grass and kindled the fire of Jātavedas, offered oblations into it with clarified butter consecrated by mantras.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, on the lovely summit of the palace that was furnished with a golden throne-platform covered with choice spreads and adorned with colourful garlands,
having placed him facing east on an excellent seat with various mantras, and having gathered water from all directions — from rivers, streams, and sacred fords —
— and having brought water from all the oceans and stored the pure and auspicious water in golden vessels, the bulls among monkeys —
— using auspicious bull-horns and golden vessels, according to the rite prescribed by the scriptures and established by the great sages —
— Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Śarabha, Gandhamādana, Mainda, Dvivida, Hanūmān, Jāmbavān, and Nala —
— consecrated Sugrīva with clear and fragrant water, just as the Vasus consecrated Vāsava, the Thousand-eyed Indra.
When Sugrīva had been consecrated, all those noble bulls among monkeys there raised a shout of joy in their thousands.
Acting upon Rāma's word, Sugrīva, the foremost among the tawny monkeys, embraced Aṅgada and consecrated him as crown prince.
When Aṅgada too had been consecrated, the noble and compassionate monkeys honoured Sugrīva, saying "Well done, well done!"
The fair city of Kiṣkindhā in its mountain gorge was filled with joyful and prosperous people and shone with banners and flags.
Having reported the great consecration to the noble Rāma, the valiant lord of the monkey army, having also recovered his wife Rumā, obtained the kingdom just as the lord of the thirty gods.
When Sugrīva had been consecrated and the monkey had entered the cave, Rāma came together with his brother to Mount Prasravaṇa.
That mountain resounded with tigers and deer, was thronged with lions of fearsome roar, was dense with various shrubs and creepers, and was thick with many trees.
Frequented by bears, monkeys, and langurs, and by wild cats, that mountain resembling a mass of clouds always sheltered pure water.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
On the summit of that mountain, Rāma together with Saumitri took up for dwelling a great and spacious cave.
The righteous Rāghava dwelt there together with Lakṣmaṇa on that Mount Prasravaṇa, full of ravines and glades offering many lovely views.
Even though that mountain was most pleasant and rich in many things, dwelling there afforded not the slightest joy to Rāma, who constantly thought of the wife who had been taken from him — she who was dearer than life itself.
Especially upon seeing the moon risen at its rising, sleep would not come to him at night even when he had lain down.
His brother Lakṣmaṇa, sharing in his pain, spoke consoling words to that scion of Kākutstha, whose mind was shattered by tears, who constantly lamented with grief arising from this sorrow, ever given over to grief.
"Enough, hero — do not surrender to anguish; you should not grieve. For you well know that all one's purposes sink when one grieves."
"You, Rāghava, are foremost in action in the world; you are devoted to the gods; you are a believer; you are of righteous disposition; and you are a man of resolution."
"For without firm resolve, you are not capable of slaying in battle that enemy, that Rākṣasa in particular — that one who acts crookedly — with your valour."
"Uproot your grief, make your resolve firm, and then extirpate that Rākṣasa together with his entire retinue."
"O scion of Kākutstha, you are capable of overturning the entire earth with its oceans, forests, and mountains — how much less, then, Rāvaṇa?"
"I, for my part, am awakening your heroic energy that has fallen asleep, as one revives with blazing oblations a fire covered in ashes at the right moment."
Having honoured Lakṣmaṇa's beneficial and auspicious words, Rāghava spoke this reply to his loving friend.
"What should be said by one who is devoted, affectionate, and well-wishing — by one endowed with true valour — that have you said, O Lakṣmaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This grief, which depresses all one's purposes, is hereby abandoned. I rouse my energy, which is unhindered in its valorous deeds."
"I await the season of autumn — this rainy season has now arrived. When it passes, I shall slay that Rākṣasa together with his kingdom and his entire host."
Hearing those words of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā and the joy of his friends, was delighted and spoke once more.
"This speech you have uttered is worthy of you, O destroyer of enemies. Now, O scion of Kākutstha, you have returned to your true nature."
"Having understood your own true heroic power, you ought to be as you really are. What you have said is befitting both your learning and your noble lineage."
"Therefore, O tiger among men, let the night of the rainy season that has arrived pass by while you contemplate the subduing of the enemy, O Rāghava."
"Restraining your anger, await the autumn season. Bear with these four months; dwell on this mountain with me — this mountain frequented by the king of beasts — growing ever more resolved for the slaughter of the enemy."
Then Rāma, having slain Vālin and consecrated Sugrīva and now dwelling on the slopes of Mount Mālyavat, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"This season has now arrived — the time of the coming of waters. Look now at the sky covered over with clouds like mountains."
"Having drunk up the essence of the oceans through the rays of the sun and held it as an embryo for nine months, the sky now gives birth to its elixir."
