"One could climb up into the sky by staircases formed of clouds and deck the sun himself with garlands of Kuṭaja and Arjuna blossoms."
"With its smooth cloud-coverings that are copper-coloured from the crimson of twilight at the edges and more pale in the middle, the sky looks as if a wound has been bound up."
"With its gentle-wind sighs, painted with the sandal-paste of twilight glow, bearing clouds that are somewhat pale, the sky shines like one smitten with longing."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This earth, afflicted by the law of nature, inundated with fresh water, and tormented by grief — like Sītā — sheds its tears."
"The breezes released from the bellies of clouds, cool and pleasant as the Kahlāra water-lily, fragrant with the scent of Ketaka — one could drink them up in cupped hands."
"This mountain with its Arjuna trees in full bloom, fragrant with Ketaka flowers, is consecrated by the streams of rain — like Sugrīva, his enemies now at peace."
"Wearing dark cloud-skins, with their sacred threads of downward streams, their caves filled with wind-sound, the mountains are like those who have thoroughly studied the Vedas."
"Struck as if by golden whips — by lightning bolts — with the rumble of thunder deep within, the sky seems to be in pain."
"The lightning flashing among the dark clouds appears to me like the suffering Vaidehī, writhing in Rāvaṇa's embrace."
"These directions, which were beneficial to those struck by the arrows of Manmatha, are now obscured — smeared over as it were by the clouds, with their stars and moon invisible."
"Look, O Saumitri, at the Kuṭaja shrubs in bloom here and there on the mountain slopes — pent up with moisture like tears, exuberant at the arrival of the rains — they stand there kindling desire in me who am already overwhelmed by grief."
"The dust is settled, the wind today carries moisture, the afflictions spreading from the summer heat have abated. Military campaigns of kings have halted; wanderers and travellers return to their own lands."
"The Cakravāka birds, eager to reach their beloved Mānasa lake, set out now together with their mates; but their vehicles do not run on the roads battered by the constant rain-water."
"The sky adorned with scattered clouds shines bright in some places and dark in others, its form obstructed here and there by mountains — like the great ocean when it has grown calm."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The mountain rivers carry swiftly water mingled with the blossoms of Sarja and Kadamba trees, copper-coloured from the mountain minerals, followed by the cries of peacocks."
"The Jambū fruit, full of juice and resembling a bee in colour, is being relished abundantly; and the mango fruit, ripened fully, is tossed down to the ground by the wind."
"The forms of the clouds adorned with lightning-banners, emitting deep and mighty sounds, shine like great war-elephants poised for battle."
"A row of cranes flying all about, eager toward the clouds and joyful, shaken by the wind, shines like a garland of choice white lotuses hung in the sky."
"Sleep approaches Keśava slowly; the river rushes swiftly to the ocean; the joyful crane approaches a cloud; the ardent beloved approaches her lover."
"Forest borders have come alive, with peacocks dancing beautifully; Kadamba trees have grown, with Kadamba-laden boughs; bulls have grown ardent among the cows, equally desirous; the earth has become lovely, adorned with fields of grain and groves."
"Rivers flow; clouds rain; rutting elephants trumpet; forest borders gleam; devoted-to-beloved women meditate; peacocks dance; monkeys take breath."
"Thrilled, having caught the fragrance of Ketaka blossoms, the great elephants in the forest waterfalls, disturbed by the thunderous sounds, cry out together with the maddened peacocks."
"Bees, beaten by the downpours of rain and hanging on Kadamba boughs, slowly relinquish the intoxication that was quickly gained from being immersed in the flowers' nectar."
"The boughs of the Jambū trees shine out with their fruits resembling heaped coal-powder, richly filled with abundant juice, as if settled upon by swarms of bees."
"The forms of the storm-clouds adorned with lightning-banners, emitting deep and mighty rising sounds, shine like elephants roused for battle."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"A maddened king elephant, walking the path and following the mountain forest, having set out and then heard the thunderclap of the clouds, eager for battle and suspecting it to be a rival bull, has turned back."
"Birds with ruffled plumage, joyful and thirsty, drink from the folds of leaves the water falling like pearls — pure and clear, gifted by the lord of the gods."
"Clouds — dark, filled with fresh water — shine clinging to dark clouds, and mountains scorched by forest-fire cling to mountains scorched by forest-fire, as if fixed in place by roots."
"The great elephants are in rut; the chief bulls are joyful; in the forests the lions rest at greater ease; the great trees are lovely; the great serpents are still; and Indra, lord of the gods, plays with the rain-bearing clouds."
"The military campaigns of kings have ceased; armies turn back; enmities and roads alike are levelled by water."
"In the month of Prauṣṭhapada, the sacred season has arrived — the time of study of the Brahman — for brāhmaṇas who wish to expound, and for those who chant the Sāmaveda."
"Bharata, the guardian of the royal treasury, having now finished his seasonal observances and accumulated his stores, has surely observed the Āṣāḍhī vow."
"Surely the current of the swelling Sarayū river rises stronger — like the sound of Ayodhyā seeing me come home."
"These rains, full of abundance, Sugrīva enjoys in happiness — his enemy defeated, his wife restored to him, established in a great kingdom."
"But I, my wife stolen and fallen from a great kingdom, sink down, O Lakṣmaṇa, like a waterlogged riverbank."
"My grief is vast, the rains make travel utterly impossible, and Rāvaṇa is a great enemy — the obstacle before me seems without end."
"Seeing this season unfit for marching and the roads utterly impassable, and since Sugrīva bows before me, I have said nothing at all to him."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Moreover, the monkey has been long distressed and has only recently been reunited with his wives; because my own need weighs heavily on me, I do not wish to press him."
"For Sugrīva will himself, having rested and knowing that the proper time has come, recognise the obligation of repaying a service — of this there is no doubt."
"Therefore I stand here awaiting the right moment, O auspicious one, watching for the clearing of Sugrīva and of the rivers."
"A hero is indeed bound by service rendered to return service; an ungrateful one who does not repay wounds the hearts of those who are virtuous."
Then, thus addressed, Lakṣmaṇa listened carefully, joined his palms in reverence, honoured that speech, and spoke to Rāma — displaying his own auspicious outlook to him whose very sight is beautiful.
"All that you have desired as you have spoken it, the lord of the monkeys will accomplish before long. Awaiting the autumn, may you, O king of men, bear this outpour of rain, firm in your resolve to subdue the enemy."
Having observed the clear sky, emptied of lightning and clouds, resounding with the calls of sārasas and āravas, smeared as it were with lovely moonlight,
and having observed Sugrīva, his object accomplished, but slack in the pursuit of duty and purpose, exceedingly gone the way of the ignoble, his mind wholly bent on pleasure,
his tasks discharged, his aims fulfilled, always delighting in women, having obtained all the desires of his heart,
sporting day and night with his own beloved wife and with Tārā whom he desired, having achieved his end, free from fever,
sporting like the lord of gods in Nandana with hosts of Apsarases, having delegated his affairs to his ministers, and not supervising those ministers—
having abandoned his royal commands, remaining under the sway of desire — Hanūmān, who had resolved on his purpose, who knew the true nature of things and the special significance of time and duty,

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
having propitiated with sweet, reasoned, and pleasing words the lord of the monkeys who was skilled in speech and knew the truth of language — the son of Māruta,
approaching the lord of the monkeys, spoke words that were beneficial, truthful, and wholesome, in accord with the polity of conciliation, duty and purpose, joined with affection and love, and designed to inspire confidence.
"Kingdom has been gained, glory as well, the ancestral prosperity has increased; what remains is the gathering in of friends — that, Your Lordship, it is right for you to do."
"For the one who is wise regarding timing and always behaves rightly toward friends — his kingdom, his fame, and his majesty continually increase."
"O lord of the earth, he whose treasury, power of punishment, allies, and self are all united — he enjoys great kingship."
"Therefore you, endowed with virtue, standing on the blameless path, ought properly to fulfill what is well-ordered and meant for the sake of your friend."
"But he who attends to a friend's affairs when the time has passed — even if he achieves great things, he will not be joined to the fruit of friendship."
"Let the search for Rāghava's Vaidehī be carried out. O hero, O subduer of foes, this task of yours has passed its proper time."
"A wise man who knows the right moment, though eager himself, does not report to you that the time has passed, O king — he who follows your command."
"Rāghava is the banner of his prosperous lineage, a friend for long ages, of immeasurable power, and himself without equal in virtues."
"Do his task — what was done for you first by him. O lord of monkeys, you should command the foremost of monkeys."
"For the time would not have passed without a prompting; but for a task already prompted, there could indeed be a transgression of time."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You, O lord of monkeys, are the doer even for one who has done nothing; how much more so for him who has repaid you with kingdom and wealth."
"You are capable and valiant, O lord of troops of monkeys and bears; why then do you hesitate at the command to bring joy to the son of Daśaratha?"
"Indeed, the son of Daśaratha is certainly capable with his arrows of bringing gods, demons, and great serpents under his sway; yet he waits upon your promise."
"Without hesitation in abandoning even life, he did what was dear to you; let us search for his Vaidehī — on earth or in the sky."
"Neither gods nor Gandharvas, neither Asuras nor hosts of Maruts, nor Yakṣas could cause him fear — let alone Rākṣasas."
"Since he is thus endowed with power, and since he had previously done what was dear to you, O lord of tawny monkeys, you ought with your whole soul to do what is dear to Rāma."
"By your command, O lord of monkeys, none of our movements is impeded — not below on the earth, not in the waters, not above in the sky."
"Therefore give the command — who shall dwell where and for what purpose; your monkeys, invincible, number crores upon crores, O sinless one."
Having heard his words, well-spoken at the right moment, Sugrīva, endowed with good judgment, formed a most excellent resolve.
He commanded the trusted Nīla, ever diligent, to gather together the armies from all directions.
"Arrange things so that my entire army and all the troop-leaders assemble without delay, together with their vanguards."
"And let those monkey border-guards who are swift and resolute quickly summon the troops by my command; and you yourself thereafter shall personally review the army."
"Whatever monkey fails to arrive here within fifteen days shall suffer the penalty of death — in this matter no deliberation need be made."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"And together with Aṅgada, let the elder monkeys approach with my command firmly established in view." Having thus arranged affairs, the mighty lord, chief among the foremost of monkeys, entered his palace.
When Sugrīva had entered his cave-palace and the sky was emptied of clouds, Rāma, who had spent the rainy nights waiting, tormented by desire and grief,
seeing the pale sky, the clear orb of the moon, and the autumnal night smeared as it were with moonlight,
and reflecting that Sugrīva was absorbed in pleasure, that the daughter of Janaka was lost, and that the time had passed — fell into a swoon, exceedingly afflicted.
But after a moment, regaining consciousness, the wise Rāghava began to think of Vaidehī who dwelt only in his mind.
Seated on the summit of the mountain adorned with golden minerals, gazing at the autumnal sky, he went in his mind to his beloved.
And seeing the clear sky, emptied of lightning and clouds, resounding with the cries of sārasas and āravas, he lamented with a voice full of pain.
"The young woman who used to delight in the hermitage, herself calling out like the sārasas and āravas — how does she delight today without me?"
"Seeing the flowering aśana trees, pure as gold — how does that young woman delight, beholding them yet not seeing me?"
"She who once awakened at the sweet speech of the kalahaṃsas, herself sweet-voiced, beautiful in every limb — how does she awaken today without me?"
"Having heard the cries of the cakravāka birds with their companions — she whose eyes are wide as a white lotus — how will she fare?"
"Wandering among lakes, rivers, pools, forests, and groves — without her, whose eyes are like a fawn's, I find no happiness today."
"Surely separation from me and her own delicateness must not long torment that passionate woman — love continuously accompanied by autumnal qualities."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus and in like vein the best of men, that prince, lamented — like a sāranga bird seeking water from the lord of the thirty gods.
Then, having roamed the lovely mountain slopes in search of fruit and turning back, the glorious Lakṣmaṇa saw his elder brother.
Seeing him overwhelmed by unbearable grief, barely conscious, alone in a deserted place, the high-souled son of Sumitrā, distressed and pained by his brother's despair, spoke to Rāma:
"Why, noble one, surrender to the power of desire? Why overpower your own manly strength? This steadiness of mind is always to be gathered in — what is accomplished here by abandoning such discipline?"
"Apply yourself to action, to the tranquility of mind, to the time suited to disciplined effort, to the capacity of your allies — O you of undaunted spirit, make the cause of your own deeds your motive."
"O lord of the human lineage, Jānakī is not easily gained by another while she has you as her protector; and approaching a blazing fire crowned with flame, no one, O you worthy of the foremost of heroes, goes unburned."
Then Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, spoke to the indomitable Lakṣmaṇa a natural word, both beneficial and wholesome, attached to prudent policy and composed with conciliation, duty, and purpose:
"The task must undoubtedly be attended to; indeed the particular undertaking must be pursued; surely for a difficult task once set in motion, the fruit need not be anxiously considered — it follows in course."
Then, brooding upon Maithilī whose eyes are like lotus petals, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa with a face that had grown parched:
"The thousand-eyed Indra, having satisfied the earth with water, having caused the crops to ripen, stands established having done his work.
"The clouds, their sound deep and resonant, with mountains and trees preceding them, having released their waters, are now exhausted, O prince.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Dark as petals of the blue lotus, having darkened all ten directions, the rain-clouds, like elephants out of rut, have quieted their rush.
"The rain-winds, laden with water, of great speed, fragrant with kuṭaja and arjuna blossoms, having coursed their way, have ceased, O gentle one, though they were fully roused.
"The sound of the clouds, of elephants, of peacocks, and of mountain torrents, O Lakṣmaṇa — O sinless one — has suddenly grown still.
"Drenched by the great clouds, the mountains with their varied slopes shine clear, gleaming as if anointed with the rays of the moon.
"The autumnal rivers slowly, slowly reveal their sandbanks — like women bashful at a new union revealing their hips.
"The bodies of water, O gentle Lakṣmaṇa, their waters clear, resounding with the cries of kurara birds, and filled with flocks of cakravākas, shine beautifully.
"For those kings who are bound together in mutual enmity and eager for victory, O prince, O gentle one, the season of enterprise has arrived.
"This is the foremost season of campaign for kings, O prince — yet I do not see Sugrīva, nor any such effort on his part.
"The four months of the rains have passed, each seeming like a hundred years to me, scorched by grief as I am, not seeing Sītā, O gentle Lakṣmaṇa.
"Bereft of my beloved, afflicted by sorrow, my kingdom taken, banished from home — yet king Sugrīva shows no compassion toward me, O Lakṣmaṇa.
"Without a protector, his kingdom stolen, humiliated by Rāvaṇa, wretched, far from home, maddened with desire — he came to me as his refuge.
"For all these reasons, O gentle scorcher of foes, I am being scorned by that evil-souled king of monkeys.
"He who, having reckoned the time for the search for Sītā and made a compact, now that his purpose is achieved, that evil-minded one does not remember.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You — enter Kiṣkindhā and speak to that foremost of monkeys, that fool attached to rustic pleasures: speak to Sugrīva on my behalf, this word:
"He who, having promised hope to supplicants who have come to him — and those who have also previously done him service — then destroys that hope, is the most wretched of men in the world.
"He who, whatever word is spoken — auspicious or inauspicious — grasps it with truthfulness: he is a hero, he is the best of men.
"Those who, having achieved their own ends, cease to be friends to those whose ends are not yet achieved — even flesh-eaters do not consume those ingrates when they die.
"Surely he wishes to see the form of my golden-backed bow, drawn in battle, like a cluster of lightning.
"He wishes to hear again the terrible sound of my bowstring when I am angry in combat — a sound like the crash of Indra's thunderbolt.
"Though things have come to such a pass, O hero, O prince, if his valor is well-known and I have you as my ally, I need have no worry.
"The purpose for which this undertaking was made — O conqueror of enemy cities — the lord of monkeys, having achieved his own aim, does not honor the compact.
"Having pledged the rainy season as the time, the lord of monkeys sports through the four months that have passed and takes no heed.
"Sporting with his ministers and assembly, he engages only in drinking; Sugrīva shows no compassion toward us who are wretched with grief.
"Go, and tell Sugrīva — O mighty son, let him be told what the nature of my wrath is; and speak this word to him:
"The path by which Vālin went when he was slain has not narrowed, O Sugrīva — stand by your compact; do not follow the path of Vālin."
"Vālin alone was slain by my arrow in battle; but you, who have transgressed truthfulness, I shall slay together with your kinsmen."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"With affairs having come to such a pass, speak whatever is beneficial, O bull among men, O best of men — make haste; time is being transgressed."
"Fulfill toward me, O lord of monkeys, what was promised, looking to the eternal law of duty; do not, after death, go to Yama's abode to behold Vālin there — struck down today by my arrows sent upon you."
He — the lord of monkeys and lord of the race of men, of fierce splendor — having observed his elder brother lamenting, his rage intensely grown, wretched, formed a resolute and fierce intention.
He — the son of the lord of men, Rāma's younger brother, of undaunted spirit — spoke thus to his elder, that son of the lord of gods, who was afflicted by desire, wretched, overwhelmed by grief, his anger surging:
"A monkey will not stand firm in righteous conduct, nor reflect on the fruits that follow from deeds, nor will he abandon the prosperity of the monkey-kingdom — for such is the bent of his mind.
"Through the decay of his mind, addicted to rustic pleasures, incapable of requiting your grace — let him, slain, behold his elder Vālin; kingship ought not to be given to one so lacking in virtue.
"I cannot contain the wrath of surging force — I shall slay that untruthful Sugrīva today; then let the son of Vālin, with the foremost heroes of the monkeys, carry out the search for the wife of the lord of men."
To him who had seized his bow and arrows and was about to spring forward, his fierce battle-rage declared, Rāma — slayer of enemy heroes — spoke a word of his own judgment, with gentle entreaty:
"Truly, one like you in the world would not act in such an evil manner; he who, though noble, destroys evil — he is a hero, he is the best of men.
"This course, O Lakṣmaṇa of righteous conduct, ought not to be taken by you today; pursue rather that affection, and the compact made at our previous association.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"With words employing conciliation, avoiding harshness, you ought to speak to Sugrīva — who has let time pass in the course of seasons."
Thus duly instructed in purpose by his elder, the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, that bull among men, entered the city.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, of auspicious mind and wisdom, devoted to the well-being and good of his brother, his anger fully roused, went toward the palace of the monkey.
Seizing his bow resembling the bow of Indra, his wrath like that of Death at the end of time, like Mount Mandara with its peaks —
the younger brother of Rāma, a doer of what was commanded, considering counter-word after counter-word, in wisdom equal to Bṛhaspati —
enveloped in the fire of his brother's wrath arising from desire and anger, Lakṣmaṇa went forth then like an angry tempest.
Swiftly felling many śāla, tāla, and aśvakarṇa trees, circling mountain peaks and other trees with speed,
shattering rocks with his feet like a swift elephant, covering great distances in a single stride, he moved quickly under the urgency of the task.
That tiger of the Ikṣvāku line beheld the great city of the monkey-king Kiṣkindhā, filled with hosts of monkeys, set in the mountain gorge, difficult to approach.
Lakṣmaṇa, his lips quivering with rage toward Sugrīva, saw the fearsome monkeys moving outside Kiṣkindhā.
The monkeys, resembling elephants, were seizing hundreds of mountain crags and full-grown great trees among the mountain hollows.
Seeing those monkeys who had taken up weapons, Lakṣmaṇa became doubly enraged, like a fire fed with much fuel.
Seeing him in fury, like Death at the end of time, those monkeys were seized with terror in all their limbs and fled in hundreds in every direction.
Then those foremost monkeys, entering the palace of Sugrīva, reported both the anger and the arrival of Lakṣmaṇa.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
But the bull of monkeys, filled with desire, was absorbed in private company with Tārā; at that moment he did not hear the words of those monkey-heroes.
Then, dispatched by the ministers, monkeys that made the hair stand on end, resembling mountain-elephants and clouds, issued forth from the city.
Armed with claws and fangs, all terrible, all of distorted appearance, all with the pride of tigers, all of monstrous aspect —
some having the strength of ten elephants, some ten times that and more, and some were equal in valor to a thousand elephants —
the angry Lakṣmaṇa saw all of Kiṣkindhā, that impregnable city, pervaded by those powerful monkeys who bore trees in their hands.
Then all those monkeys came forth from within the ramparts and moats and stood there displaying themselves, their spirits erect.
Reflecting on Sugrīva's negligence and his afflicted elder brother, the self-possessed hero, under the sway of wrath, went forward again.
He breathed long, hot, great sighs; his eyes reddened with fury; that tiger of men blazed like a fire with smoke.
His tongue darting like an arrow's point, his body the coil of bow and arrows, the accumulated venom of his own splendor — he was like a five-headed serpent.
Approaching him who blazed like the fire of Time, who was like an enraged lord of serpents, Aṅgada fell into deep despondency from fear.
Then Sugrīva, of great glory, his eyes copper-red with rage, commanded Aṅgada: "Go, dear son, and announce my coming."
"The subduer of foes, Lakṣmaṇa — the younger brother of Rāma — has come to your vicinity; scorched by his brother's misery, he stands at the gate."
Having heard Lakṣmaṇa's words, Aṅgada, overwhelmed with grief, came near his father and said: "The son of Sumitrā has arrived here."
Seeing him, whose roar was like a great flood, whose sound was like a thunderbolt, those monkeys together raised a lion's roar near Lakṣmaṇa.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Roused by that great sound, the monkey awoke — his eyes copper-red, dazed with intoxication, his garlands and ornaments in disarray.
Then, having heard Aṅgada's words and come together by the same impetus, two ministers of the monkey-king who were respected and of broad vision —
Plakṣa and Prabhāva, ministers versed in purpose and duty, both reported to him the arrival of Lakṣmaṇa, who had come to speak of matters high and low.
Having propitiated Sugrīva with words firmly set in conciliation, they sat in attendance upon him as he was seated — even as one attends upon Indra, lord of the Maruts.
"The two brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, true to their pledges, of great fortune, who have attained the status of friends, who are worthy of kingdoms and givers of kingdoms —
"— of those two, one, Lakṣmaṇa, stands at the gate with bow in hand; from fear of him the monkeys tremble and let out cries.
"He — this brother of Rāghava, Lakṣmaṇa, whose charioteer is speech, whose chariot is resolve — has arrived by the command of that Rāma.
"O king, bow your head to him and, together with your son and kinsmen, stand firm in your proper compact; be one who is true to his promise."
Having heard the words of Aṅgada, and having heard that Lakṣmaṇa was enraged, the self-possessed Sugrīva rose from his seat together with his counsellors.
Skilled in counsel and thoroughly versed in deliberation, he weighed the gravity and lightness of the matter and spoke these words to his ministers who were wise in counsel.
"I have spoken no ill word, nor have I done anything amiss. Why then is Lakṣmaṇa, the brother of Rāghava, angered? This I ponder."
"By my ill-wishers and enemies, who ever seek to sow discord, Rāghava's younger brother has been made to hear of faults in me that do not exist."
"In this matter, you must all carefully and methodically ascertain the true state of things, each according to his understanding and with due deliberation."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Indeed I have no fear of Lakṣmaṇa, nor of Rāghava; yet a friend angered without proper cause does indeed cause anxiety."
"In every way it is easy to acquire a friend but difficult to maintain that friendship; for because of the inconstancy of minds, affection is sundered even by a trifle."
"For this very reason I am afraid regarding the great-souled Rāma: that the benefit he has conferred upon me I am unable to repay."
When Sugrīva had spoken thus, Hanūmān, foremost among the monkeys, spoke his own reasoned counsel in the assembly of the monkey ministers.
"In every respect it is no wonder, O lord of the monkey host, that you do not forget the auspicious act of deep affection and service rendered to you."
"By the heroic Rāghava, casting fear far aside, Vālin — whose prowess equalled Indra's — was slain for your sake alone."
"Without any doubt Rāghava is angry out of affection; it is for that reason he has dispatched his brother Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of glory."
"You have been negligent and do not perceive the season, O best of those who know the proper time: the auspicious autumn has arrived, dark-green with flowering saptacchada trees."
"The sky is clear, its planets and stars unclouded; the storm-clouds have dispersed; all the quarters, the rivers and the lakes are bright and serene."
"Yet you do not recognise the season of effort that has arrived, O foremost of monkeys. It is manifest that you are heedless — and so Lakṣmaṇa has come here."
"The harsh words of the great-souled Rāghava — who is afflicted and whose wife has been stolen — spoken through an intermediary, must be endured by you."
"For one who has committed an offence such as yours, I see no other fitting course save joining your palms and propitiating Lakṣmaṇa."
"A king must inevitably be told what is for his benefit by the ministers he has appointed; and so it is that, setting fear aside, I speak these resolute words."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For Rāghava, when truly enraged and raising his bow, has the power to bring the entire world — gods, asuras, and gandharvas included — under his sway."
"He who must afterwards be propitiated again ought not to be provoked; especially so by one who is grateful and remembers the prior benefit received."
"Bowing your head before him, together with your son and your allies, O king, abide by your own covenant and remain under his command, as a wife obeys her husband."
"The command of Rāma and Rāma's younger brother, joined with the authority of the lord of monkeys, cannot be set aside even in thought; for your mind will come to know the human might of this Rāghava, who blazes with the splendour of Indra."
Then Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, having been duly announced, entered the fearsome cavern-city of Kiṣkindhā by the command of Rāma.
The great-bodied and mighty monkeys stationed at the gate, upon seeing Lakṣmaṇa, all stood with their palms joined in reverence.
Seeing the son of Daśaratha breathing heavily with rage, the monkeys became frightened and did not surround him.
The glorious Lakṣmaṇa beheld that vast and divine cavern, filled with jewels, adorned with flowering groves, charming, and strewn all about with gems.
It was crowded with mansions and palace-towers, beautified by merchandise of every kind, and adorned by flowering trees bearing all desired fruits.
It was graced by monkeys who were sons of gods and gandharvas, shapeshifters wearing divine garlands and garments, delightful to behold.
Its broad avenues were suffused with the fragrances of sandalwood, agaru, and lotuses, and with the sweet scents of maireyā liquors and honey.
Rāghava saw there multi-storeyed palaces resembling the slopes of Vindhya and Meru, and clear mountain streams as well.
He saw the charming mansions of Aṅgada and Mainda, of Dvivida, Gavaya, Gavākṣa, Gaja, and Śarabha;

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
of Vidyunmālin, Saṃpāti, Sūryākṣa, Hanūmat, Vīrabāhu, Subāhu, and the great-souled Nala;
of Kumuda, Suṣeṇa, Tāra, Jāmbavat, Dadhivaktra, Nīla, Supāṭala, and Sunetra.
Lakṣmaṇa saw the principal dwelling-places of these great-souled monkey chiefs, standing along the royal road, vast and of great substance.
They shone white as autumn clouds, adorned with divine garlands, filled with abundant wealth and grain, and beautified by women of surpassing excellence.
Surrounded by a white rocky hill and thus impregnable, the charming abode of the lord of monkeys resembled the dwelling of great Indra.
It was adorned with bright, towering palace-summits resembling the peaks of Kailāsa, and by well-nourished trees bearing all desired fruits.
Gifted by great Indra, the magnificent trees resembling dark rain-clouds bore divine flowers and fruits, gave cool shade, and were wondrously beautiful.
Its gateway was guarded by powerful monkeys armed with weapons, was bright and pure, wreathed in divine garlands, and its archway was of burnished gold.
The mighty son of Sumitrā entered the charming abode of Sugrīva, unhindered, like the sun entering a great cloud.
The righteous Lakṣmaṇa passed through seven inner courtyards filled with vehicles and seats, and then beheld the vast and well-guarded inner apartments.
It was adorned throughout with beds of gold and silver, with many excellent seats, and furnished with coverings of the highest quality.
As he continued to enter, he heard without pause a melodious sound — a song composed of well-formed syllables, mingled with lute music.
The mighty Lakṣmaṇa saw many women of varied forms in Sugrīva's palace, proud of their beauty and youth.
He observed them to be of noble birth, wearing garlands of many-hued flowers, occupied with making choice garlands, and adorned with the finest ornaments.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Lakṣmaṇa observed that Sugrīva's attendants too were neither unsatisfied nor overly agitated, and were attired in noble dress.
Then he saw Sugrīva seated on a supreme golden throne spread with the finest covering, blazing like the sun.
His body was adorned with divine ornaments, his form was divine, his fame resplendent; wearing divine garlands and garments, he was unconquerable as great Indra, and surrounded by women decked in divine ornaments and garlands.
The heroic Sugrīva, tawny as fine gold, seated on his splendid throne and holding Rumā in a close embrace, caught sight of the undaunted Lakṣmaṇa of wide eyes — he himself wide-eyed.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa, that bull among men, enter unimpeded and in a rage, Sugrīva was seized with distress in all his senses.
Seeing the son of Daśaratha — breathing in rage, blazing as it were with energy, scorched by anguish over his brother's misfortune —
the foremost of monkeys leapt up, abandoning his golden throne, like the great well-adorned banner of Mahendra rising aloft.
As Sugrīva leapt up, Rumā and the other women rose after him, as a cluster of stars follows the full moon across the sky.
The glorious Sugrīva, his eyes flushed red, approached with palms joined and stood there like a great wish-fulfilling tree.
Then the angry Lakṣmaṇa addressed Sugrīva, who stood in the midst of the women with Rumā at his side, as if addressing the moon ringed by its stars.
"A king endowed with valour and noble birth, compassionate, with his senses mastered, grateful, and truthful in speech — such a king is honoured in the world."
"But what king is more cruel than one who abides in unrighteousness and makes a false promise to friends who have rendered him service?"
"A falsehood concerning a horse destroys a hundred; a falsehood concerning a cow destroys a thousand; but a man who utters a falsehood concerning a man destroys himself and all his kindred."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"He who, his purpose having been served, does not requite his friends — that ingrate deserves to be slain by all beings, O lord of the leaping ones."
"This verse was sung by Brahmā himself, revered by all the worlds — uttered in wrath upon beholding an ingrate. Hear it, O monkey."
"For the slayer of a brahmin, for the drunkard, for the thief, for the one who has broken his vow — the righteous have prescribed expiation; but for an ingrate there is no expiation."
"You are ignoble, ungrateful, and a speaker of falsehood, O monkey — for having had your purpose served by Rāma, you do not requite him for it."
"Surely you, O monkey, having had your purpose served, ought — if you truly wish to act rightly — to exert yourself in the search for Sītā on Rāma's behalf."
"Yet you are absorbed in vulgar pleasures and have given a false promise. Rāma did not know you to be like a serpent that merely croaks like a frog."
"O sinful one, you of wicked soul were given sovereignty over the monkeys by the greatly blessed and compassionate Rāma, that great-souled one."
"If you do not acknowledge the deed done by Rāma, whose actions are tireless, you will this very moment, struck by his sharp arrows, behold Vālin."
"The path by which Vālin went after being slain has not grown narrow. Abide by your covenant, Sugrīva; do not follow the path of Vālin."
"Surely you do not see the arrows — thunderbolt-like — released from the bow of that foremost scion of the Ikṣvākus; it is only therefore that, at ease, you indulge in pleasures and do not attend even in mind to Rāma's cause."
As Saumitri spoke thus, blazing as it were with energy, Tārā — whose face resembled the lord of stars — addressed Lakṣmaṇa.
"Do not speak thus, Lakṣmaṇa; the lord of the monkeys does not deserve to hear harsh words, especially from your mouth.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Sugrīva is not ungrateful, nor is he deceitful or cruel; the lord of monkeys is not a speaker of falsehood, O hero, nor is he dishonest.
This brave monkey Sugrīva has not forgotten the service rendered by Rāma in battle — what others would find impossible to do.
By Rāma's grace, Sugrīva has here obtained glory, the eternal kingship of the monkeys, Rumā, and myself, O scorcher of foes.
Having lain previously in great misery and then attaining this supreme pleasure, he does not perceive the passing of time — just as the sage Viśvāmitra did not.
Absorbed in Ghṛtācī for ten years, O Lakṣmaṇa, the righteous great sage Viśvāmitra reckoned it as but a single day.
If even Viśvāmitra of great splendor, the foremost among knowers of time, did not perceive time thus passed, what then of an ordinary man?
For this one who has succumbed to the ways of the body, who is weary, O Lakṣmaṇa, and who is not yet sated in sensual pleasures — Rāma should bear with him here.
You should not, dear one, fall under the sway of anger, O Lakṣmaṇa, or act rashly without ascertaining the truth, like a common man.
Men of true virtue such as yourself, O bull among men, do not suddenly fall under the sway of anger without deliberation.
O knower of righteousness, I earnestly beseech you on Sugrīva's behalf — this great agitation born of anger should be relinquished.
It is my opinion that Sugrīva would give up Rumā, myself, the kingship of the monkeys, and all wealth, grain, and treasures for Rāma's sake.
Sugrīva will reunite Rāghava with Sītā — like the moon reunited with Rohiṇī — after slaying Rāvaṇa in battle.
In Laṅkā there are, it is said, hundreds of thousands of crores of rākṣasas, and thirty-six ten-thousands plus thousands and hundreds more.
Without slaying those invincible rākṣasas who change form at will, it is not possible to slay Rāvaṇa, by whom the Maithilī was abducted.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
They cannot be slain in battle without allies, O Lakṣmaṇa, and especially not Rāvaṇa of cruel deeds by Sugrīva alone.
Thus spoke Vālin, who was knowledgeable in these matters, the lord of monkeys. My information is not from direct knowledge — I speak from what I heard from him.
Indeed for the purpose of your assistance, foremost monkeys have been dispatched to bring back very many monkey troops — the leaders of monkey battalions for battle.
Awaiting those valiant and supremely powerful ones, the lord of monkeys does not depart — for the purpose of accomplishing Rāghava's goal.
Moreover, a time limit has been set by Sugrīva as before, O Saumitri — today all those mighty monkeys are to arrive.
Thousands of crores of bears and hundreds of golāṅgūlas will approach you today — abandon your anger, O subduer of foes! Many crores of brilliantly glowing monkeys will come to you, O scion of the Ikṣvāku line.
Beholding your face and gazing upon your eyes reddened with anger, O one born to wound foes, the wives of the foremost monkeys find no peace — indeed we are all alarmed by this initial dread."
Thus addressed by Tārā with words that were humble and imbued with righteousness, Saumitri — gentle by nature — accepted those words.
When that speech was accepted, the lord of the monkey host cast off his great fear of Lakṣmaṇa as one sheds a wet garment.
Then Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, removed the variegated, many-stringed, great garland from his neck and, free from intoxication, came to his senses.
Sugrīva, the best of all monkeys, addressed Lakṣmaṇa of fearsome might with humble words, gladdening him.
"Lost prosperity, glory, and the eternal kingship of the monkeys — all this has been regained by me through Rāma's grace, O Saumitri.
Who is capable of repaying such valor to that godlike hero, renowned by his own deeds, O warrior, O subduer of enemies?

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The righteous Rāghava will recover Sītā and will slay Rāvaṇa by his own might — with me serving only as an ally.
What need has he of allies — he by whom seven great trees, a mountain, and the very earth were pierced with a single arrow?
He at whose mere twanging of the bow the earth with its mountains trembled, O Lakṣmaṇa — what need does such a one truly have of allies?
I shall accompany the lord of men, O bull among men, as he goes to slay the enemy Rāvaṇa along with his entourage.
If I have transgressed at all out of trust or affection — as a servant — that should be forgiven me; there is no one who does not err.
As the great-souled Sugrīva spoke thus, Lakṣmaṇa became pleased and spoke to him with affection.
"In every way my brother has a protector, O lord of monkeys — especially with you, O Sugrīva, as his modest and devoted guardian.
Such is your power, O Sugrīva, and such is your supreme purity — you deserve to enjoy the unsurpassed glory of the kingship of the monkeys.
With you as his ally, O Sugrīva, the mighty Rāma will slay his enemies in battle before long — there is no doubt in this.
The words you have spoken, O Sugrīva, are fitting and proper, coming from one who knows righteousness, is grateful, and never turns back in battle.
Who else, being capable and knowing what is fitting, deserves to speak thus — save my elder brother and yourself, O best of monkeys?
You are a match for Rāma in valor and strength — you have been given by the gods as his ally for a long time, O foremost of monkeys.
But now, O hero, depart quickly from here with me and console your friend who is afflicted with grief over the abduction of his wife.
And the harsh words with which I addressed you, having heard Rāma's words spoken in his grief-stricken state — that too you should forgive."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by the great-souled Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva spoke these words to Hanūmān, his minister, who stood at his side.
"Those who dwell on the peaks of Mahendra, Himavat, Vindhya, and Kailāsa, on Mandara, on Pāṇḍuśikhara, and on the five mountains —
Those dwelling on mountains glowing with the color of the rising sun, shining in all directions, along the ocean's edge in the western direction —
And the foremost monkeys who inhabit the fearsome forest of lotuses and palmyra palms on the mountain that is the abode of Āditya, resembling clouds at twilight —
Those leaping monkeys who resemble the dark Añjanā cloud, who possess the strength of elephants, and who dwell on and beyond Mount Añjanā —
Those monkeys of golden radiance who dwell in caves of red arsenic ore, those ranging the slopes of Meru, and those who have taken refuge on the smoky mountain —
And those leaping monkeys of fearsome speed, colored like the young sun, who drink honey-wine on the great red mountain —
And those dwelling in very beautiful, fragrant, great forests, and in the pleasant forest margins of ascetics, on all sides —
Bring all those various monkeys throughout the earth quickly; dispatch the monkeys swiftly by means of conciliation, gifts, and such other expedients.
Those swift messengers who were previously dispatched by me — for the purpose of hastening them, send yet more monkeys additionally.
Those monkeys who are absorbed in pleasures or who are dilatory — bring all of them here quickly by my command.
Those wicked ones who do not come within ten days by my order — they are to be slain, for they are violators of the royal command.
Hundreds, thousands, and crores of lion-like monkeys, abiding by my will, are to set out in the various directions at my command.
Resembling clouds and mountains, seemingly covering the sky, the foremost monkeys of fearsome appearance are to depart from here at my command.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Knowing the ways and having traversed all routes, all those monkeys throughout the earth are to bring all the monkeys here swiftly, in accordance with my command."
Hearing the words of the monkey king, the son of Vāyu dispatched valiant monkeys in all directions.
Traversing the path measured by Viṣṇu's stride, following the route of birds and lightning, those monkeys sent forth by the king departed instantly.
Those monkeys spurred on all monkeys — in the oceans, on mountains, in forests, and along rivers — for the sake of Rāma.
Hearing the command of Sugrīva, king of kings, which was like the call of death, the monkeys came — having perceived the terror of Sugrīva's wrath.
Then three crores of leaping monkeys, resembling collyrium, of great speed, issued forth from that mountain to where Rāghava was.
From that excellent mountain where the sun sets, where they delight — those resembling refined gold in their brilliance — ten crores issued forth.
From the peaks of Kailāsa came thousands of crores of monkeys with the lustre of lion manes.
Those who live on fruits and roots and dwell on Himavat — from among them thousands of crores arrived, numbering a thousand.
From the Vindhya, resembling burning coals, fearsome and of fearsome deeds — thousands of crores of monkeys rushed forth swiftly.
Those dwelling on the shores of the milk ocean, inhabiting forests of tamāla trees, and feeding on coconuts — their number is beyond reckoning.
From forests, from caverns, and from rivers, the monkey army came at great speed — as if drinking up the sun.
Those valiant monkeys who had gone to hasten all the monkeys beheld the Himavat mountain with its great trees.
On that excellent, beautiful mountain a great sacrifice had once been performed by Maheśvara — divine, enchanting, and pleasing to the minds of all gods — and its glory still shone.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
There the monkeys saw roots and fruits born from the flowing of the sacrificial food — tasting like nectar in flavor.
That divine, enchanting fruit and root born of the sacrificial food — whoever eats even once becomes satisfied for a full month.
Those fruit-eating leaders of monkey troops gathered those divine roots, fruits, and divine herbs.
Going there, the monkeys also brought back fragrant flowers from that sacrificial ground — for the sake of pleasing Sugrīva.
And all those foremost monkeys, having swiftly urged on all the monkeys throughout the earth, marched at the head of the troops.
In that very hour, those swift-acting troop leaders swiftly reached Kiṣkindhā, where Sugrīva the monkey dwelt.
Those monkeys, having taken all the herbs, fruits, and roots, presented them to him and spoke these words.
"All the mountains, oceans, and forests have been traversed; all the monkeys of the earth are coming at your command."
Hearing this, Sugrīva, lord of the leaping monkeys, was overjoyed and gladly accepted all the gifts they had brought.
Having received all that had been brought and presented as tribute, and having consoled all the monkeys, he dismissed them all.
Having dismissed those heroic monkeys who had accomplished their task, he considered both himself and the mighty Rāghava to have attained their purpose.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, delighting Sugrīva, spoke deferential words to that best of all monkeys possessed of terrible strength: "Come forth from Kiṣkindhā, O gentle one, if it pleases you."
Hearing those well-spoken words of Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, supremely pleased, spoke these words in reply.
"So be it; let us go — I must abide by your command." Having spoken thus to the auspicious-marked Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva then...
...dismissed Tārā and the other women at that moment. Then Sugrīva called out loudly to the foremost of the monkeys, saying "Come!"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing his command, the monkeys — all of those who were fit to appear before women — came quickly with palms joined in reverence.
To those who had arrived, the king, whose radiance resembled the sun's, then said: "Monkeys, quickly bring my palanquin forward."
Hearing his words, the monkeys of swift step at once brought forward a beautiful palanquin pleasing to behold.
Seeing the palanquin brought forth, the lord of monkeys said to Saumitri: "Lakṣmaṇa, mount this quickly."
Having spoken thus, Sugrīva mounted together with Lakṣmaṇa the golden conveyance that resembled the sun, drawn by large monkeys.
A white royal parasol was held above his head, and white yak-tail fans were waved about him on all sides.
Acclaimed by bards and heralded by the sounds of conches and kettledrums, Sugrīva, having attained the unsurpassed glory of kingship, set forth.
Surrounded by many hundreds of fierce monkeys bearing weapons in hand, he proceeded to the place where Rāma was stationed.
Reaching that excellent place frequented by Rāma, the great-spirited one descended from the palanquin together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Approaching Rāma, he stood with palms joined in reverence; and as he stood thus with joined palms, the monkeys did likewise.
Seeing that vast army of monkeys — like a lake full of closed lotuses — Rāma was filled with affection for Sugrīva.
When the lord of monkeys fell at his feet, touching them with his head, Rāghava raised him up and embraced him with affection and deep regard.
Having embraced him, the righteous-souled one said: "Be seated." Then, seeing him seated upon the ground, Rāma spoke these words.
"O hero, O best of monkeys — the one who constantly pursues righteousness, wealth, and pleasure each in its proper time and measure, he is a true king.
But one who, abandoning righteousness and wealth alike, indulges only in pleasure, wakes to find himself fallen — like a man who fell asleep at the top of a tree.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
A king who is engaged in the destruction of enemies, devoted to the protection of allies, and who enjoys the fruit of the threefold human aims — he is joined to righteousness.
The time for exertion has now arrived, O destroyer of enemies. Take counsel, O tawny-eyed lord, together with the monkeys and your ministers."
Thus addressed, Sugrīva spoke these words to Rāma.
"Prosperity, fame, and the eternal kingdom of the monkeys — all of it had been lost to me, O mighty-armed one, and has been regained through your grace.
By the grace of you who art as a god, and of your brother, O best among the victorious — one who does not requite a good deed done is the blight of mankind.
These foremost of monkeys have arrived by hundreds, O slayer of enemies, bringing with them all the powerful monkeys of the earth.
Bears too are here, watchful and heroic, O Rāghava, and the golāṅgūlas — those fearsome in appearance who know the fastnesses of wildernesses and forests.
Monkeys who are sons of gods and gandharvas, who can assume any form at will, each surrounded by their own armies — they are on the march, O Rāghava.
Hundreds, hundreds of thousands, tens of millions — the leaping ones arrive; heroes encompassed by tens of thousands and by śaṅkus in number, O scorcher of foes.
By arbuda-multitudes and hundreds of arbudas, by madhyas and antas, by samudras and parārdhhas — the monkeys and monkey-troop-leaders come in such numbers.
They shall come to you, O king — those whose valor matches Mahendra's, who loom like Meru and Mandara, whose abodes are on the Vindhyas and Meru.
They will come to you — having slain Rāvaṇa together with his kinsmen in battle, they will bring back the Maithilī."
Then, beholding that readiness of the foremost monkey who stood obedient to his direction, the wise son of the earth's lord blazed with joy — his appearance equal to that of a blooming blue lotus.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
While Sugrīva spoke thus, Rāma, best among those who uphold righteousness, embraced him with both arms and replied to him who stood with palms joined.
"That Indra sends down rain upon the earth — that is no wonder; that Āditya of the thousand rays dispels darkness from the sky —
that the moon with its rays purifies the earth — O gentle one, O scorcher of foes, that one like you should requite friends — none of this is a marvel.
So also in you, whatever is noble and good is no wonder, O gentle one. I know you, Sugrīva, as one who always speaks with affection.
With you as my protector, O friend, I shall conquer all enemies in battle. You alone are my well-wisher and ally; it is fitting that you render me aid.
That vilest of rākṣasas abducted the Vaidehī to his own destruction, just as Anuhlāda carried off Śacī, daughter of Puloman, by deception.
Before long I shall slay Rāvaṇa with my keen arrows, as Śatakratu, the destroyer of enemies, slew the proud father of Paulomī."
Just then a great cloud of dust arose, hot and dense, obscuring the bright radiance of the thousand-rayed sun in the sky.
The directions became confused and thick with that dust; the whole earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
Then the entire earth was covered over by innumerable leaping monkeys resembling mountain-peaks, possessing sharp fangs and immense strength.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, it was covered by those monkey-troop-leaders, able to assume any form at will, each attended by hundreds of crores of followers.
By monkeys of the rivers, of the mountains, and of the oceans — all of great strength, thundering like clouds — and by others who roam the forests.
By monkeys of the color of the young sun, and by those as pale as the moon; by those of the hue of lotus stamens, and by the white ones who make their home on Meru.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then appeared the illustrious and heroic monkey named Śatabali, surrounded by ten thousand crores of monkeys.
Then appeared the valorous father of Tārā, resembling a mountain of gold, with many tens of thousands of crores.
Of the hue of lotus stamens, with a face like the young sun — wise, the foremost of monkeys, the best of all the monkey-host —
— attended by armies of many thousands of monkeys, the illustrious Kesarī, father of Hanūmān, appeared.
The great king of the golāṅgūlas, Gavākṣa of terrible valor, appeared surrounded by a thousand crores of monkeys.
Dhūmra, destroyer of enemies, lord of bears of terrible speed, advanced surrounded by two thousand crores.
The troop-leader named Panasa, of great valor, came attended by three crores of monkeys terrible as great mountains.
The troop-leader named Nīla appeared — of the hue of a mass of blue antimony, immense of body — attended by ten crores.
The powerful troop-leader Darīmukha came forth at that time, surrounded by a thousand crores, and presented himself to Sugrīva.
Mainda and Dvivida, both sons of the Aśvins, both of immense strength, appeared with a thousand crores of crores of monkeys.
Then Gandhamādana arrived, followed from behind by thousands of thousands of crores, along with hundreds of crores of monkeys.
Then came Aṅgada the crown prince, equal to his father in valor, surrounded by a thousand padmas and a hundred śaṅkus.
Then Tāra, the monkey of terrible valor and with the radiance of a star, was seen from afar, attended by five crores of monkeys.
The heroic monkey Indrajānu, a troop-leader, appeared as the lord of eleven crores, surrounded by them.
Then Rambha arrived, resembling the young sun, surrounded by ten thousand along with a thousand hundreds.
Then the heroic troop-leader, the powerful monkey named Durmukha, appeared surrounded by two crores.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hanūmān appeared, surrounded by a thousand crores of monkeys of terrible valor who resembled the peaks of Kailāsa.
Nala too, of great valor, surrounded by tree-dwellers, arrived with a hundred crores along with a hundred thousands.
Śarabha, Kumuda, Vahni, the monkey Rambha — these and many other monkeys who could assume any form at will —
— covering the whole earth, its mountains and its forests, leaping, bounding, and roaring, those leaping ones came toward Sugrīva as clouds come toward the sun.
Making great clamor, joyful and strong, they presented themselves to Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, bowing their heads.
Other foremost of monkeys, having met and saluted Sugrīva in the proper manner, stood before him with palms joined.
Swiftly Sugrīva, the righteous-minded one, introduced all those bull-like monkeys to Rāma, then stood with palms joined and spoke.
"Let the lords of monkeys quarter the forces at ease in the mountain streams and all the forests; then he who knows strength, having arrayed the army properly, is ready to march."
Then Sugrīva, lord of the leaping ones, his purpose fully achieved, spoke to Rāma, that tiger among men and crusher of enemy armies.
"The lords of monkeys who dwell in my domain — powerful, able to assume any form at will, and resembling Mahendra — have arrived and are encamped.
These terrible monkeys who have come, each attended by many thousands of monkeys of fearful valor, are like the Daityas and Dānavas in might.
Known for deeds and exploits, powerful, inured to fatigue, renowned for their valor and foremost in their undertakings —
— wanderers of the earth and waters, O Rāma, dwellers on many mountains — these monkeys have arrived by the crore as your servants.
All are obedient to command, all are devoted to the welfare of their lord; they are capable of carrying out your purpose, O subduer of enemies.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Whatever you deem timely, O tiger among men — let it be declared. This army is at your disposal; you ought to give the command."
"Though this task of theirs is truly known to me in its essence, even so, you ought to give the command in the proper way."
To Sugrīva speaking thus, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, embraced him with both arms and spoke these words.
"Let it be ascertained, O gentle one, whether the Vaidehī lives or does not live — and the place, O greatly wise one, where Rāvaṇa dwells.
Having found the Vaidehī and Rāvaṇa's dwelling, I shall do what is fitting in that time, together with you.
In this task, O lord of monkeys, I am not the master, nor is Lakṣmaṇa — you are both the cause and the master of this undertaking, O lord of leaping ones.
You yourself, O lord, must determine and direct my task; for you know what is to be done for me, O hero — of this there is no doubt.
You are valorous, accompanied by a friend, wise, knowing the distinctions of time — you are engaged in our welfare, accomplished in worthy deeds and foremost among those who understand purpose."
Thus addressed, Sugrīva spoke in the presence of Rāma and the wise Lakṣmaṇa to the troop-leader named Vinatā — that lord of leaping ones, mountain-like, thundering like a cloud, and mighty.
"O foremost of monkeys, accompanied by monkeys who are sons of Soma and Sūrya, guided by policy suited to place and time, adept at distinguishing what ought and ought not to be done —
— attended by one hundred thousand swift-moving monkeys, go and search the eastern direction with its mountains, forests, and groves.
There, search for Sītā the Vaidehī and for Rāvaṇa's dwelling in the mountain fastnesses, in the forests, and in the rivers.
The lovely Bhāgīrathī, the Sarayū, the Kauśikī, the Kālindī, the lovely Yamunā, and the great mountain Yamunā —

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
— the Sarasvatī and the Sindhu; the Śona with its gem-bright waters; the Mahī and the Kālamahī adorned with hills and forests —
— the Brahmamālas, the Videhas, the Mālavas, the Kāśi-Kosalas; the Māgadhas with their great towns; the Puṇḍras and the Vaṅgas as well —
— the city of the silk-worm workers and the land rich in silver mines — all this must be searched through, ranging here and there in your quest.
Search for Sītā, the dear wife of Rāma and daughter-in-law of Daśaratha — in the seas, on the mountains, and in the cities.
And those who inhabit the high ridge of Mandara — those who use their ears as coverings, and those with lip-ears too —
— the terrible iron-mouthed ones, the swift one-footed ones, the inexhaustible and powerful men-eaters —
— Kirātas with topknot-ears, golden-limbed, beautiful to behold; Kirātas who eat raw fish, dwelling there on islands —
— those terrible ones known as tiger-men who range beneath the waters — all the forest-dwellings of these must be searched.
And those places reached by mountains, or by swimming, or by boat — Yavadvīpa, rich in gems, adorned with seven kingdoms —
— rich in gold and silver, ornamented with mines of gold. Beyond Yavadvīpa is a mountain named Śiśira —
— whose peak touches the sky, frequented by gods and dānavas. In the fastnesses of these mountains, their sun-scorched heights, and their forests —
— Rāvaṇa with the Vaidehī must be searched for, here and there. Then you must look upon the ocean-islands, so dreadful to behold.
There, asuras of great body, who are perpetually hungry and have been so permitted by Brahmā, ever seize upon shadows.
Approaching the great ocean, which roars loudly and resembles a dark rain-cloud, by a proper ford — that sea frequented by great serpents —
— going onward, you shall see the dread Lohita ocean with its blood-red waters, and also the great Kūṭaśālmalī tree.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And there too is the dwelling of Vainateya, adorned with manifold jewels, white as Kailāsa, fashioned by Viśvakarman.
There, rākṣasas named Mandehas, terrible and mountain-like, of many forms and inspiring terror, hang from the mountain-peaks.
They fall into the water every day at the sun's rising, and, scorched by the sun, they hang again and again.
Then, advancing, you shall see the Kṣīroda ocean, resembling a pale-white cloud, whose waves make it like a garland — a formidable sight.
In its midst stands a great white mountain named Ṛṣabha, surrounded by silver trees in blossom with divine fragrances.
And there is a lake named Sudarśana, filled with silver lotuses blazing with golden stamens, thronged with royal swans.
The vibudhas, cāraṇas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and hosts of apsarases, joyful and desirous of sport, all frequent that lotus-lake.
Passing beyond the Kṣīroda, you will then see, O monkeys, the Jaloda, foremost of oceans and inspiring fear in all creatures.
There, they say, resides that great fire born of wrath, which has been given the form of a horse's mouth — that one of tremendous speed, which consumes all things moving and still.
There the cries of ocean-dwelling creatures are heard — of those unable to endure what they see — upon beholding that submarine mare-fire.
To the north of the sweet-water ocean, thirteen yojanas away, stands a great golden mountain named Jātarūpaśila.
Seated on the peak of that mountain, adored by all beings, is the god Ananta of a thousand heads, clothed in blue garments.
The three-headed golden banner in the form of a palmyra palm, planted atop that mountain by that great soul, shines with its altar.
That construction in the eastern direction was made by the lords of the thirty gods; beyond it stands the glorious Udaya mountain made of gold.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Its peak, touching the sky and extending a hundred yojanas, shines with a divine altar made of pure gold.
It is adorned with śāla, tāla, tamāla, and flowering karṇikāra trees — all made of pure gold, divine, and resembling the sun.
There stands a certain peak named Saumanasa, one yojana in breadth and ten yojanas in height, immovably made of pure gold.
There Viṣṇu, the supreme among persons, in the ancient act of his triple-stride, placed his first step; his second stride he placed on the peak of Meru.
The sun, moving northward to circuit Jambūdvīpa, is most fully visible from that towering peak.
There the great sages called Vaikhānasas and Vālakhilyas, of solar radiance, glowing with ascetic power, may be seen.
In front of it shines Sudarśana island — the very place which is the light and the sight of all living beings.
In the thickets, caves, and forests of that mountain, Rāvaṇa along with the Vaidehī must be searched for, here and there.
Pervaded by the energy of that golden mountain and of the great-souled sun, the eastern twilight shines red.
Beyond that, the eastern direction becomes impassable — encircled by the thirty gods, void of sun and moon, invisible, enveloped in darkness.
In all those mountains, caves, and forests, and in those regions not named by me, Jānakī must be searched for in all of them.
This far, O bull-like monkeys, is it possible for monkeys to go. What lies beyond — sunless and boundless — we do not know.
When you have found the Vaidehī and Rāvaṇa's dwelling, return when the month is full, having reached the Udaya mountain.
Beyond the month, none may remain — one who dwells beyond it shall be slain by my order. Having accomplished your purpose and found the Maithilī, return.
Monkeys, having searched that direction beloved of Mahendra, adorned with forest thickets, with skill and care — having found Sītā, the beloved of the scion of the Raghu lineage, and then returned, you shall be happy."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Sugrīva, having dispatched that great monkey army, sent to the south those monkeys distinguished by their marks.
Nīla, son of Agni, and the monkey Hanūmant, and the great ape Jāmbavant, son of Pitāmaha —
and Suhotra, Śarīra, and Śaragulma likewise, Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Suṣeṇa, and Ṛṣabha,
and Mainda and Dvivida, Vijaya and Gandhamādana, Ulkāmukha and Asaṅga — both sons of Hutāśana —
these heroes led by Aṅgada — swift and valiant — the heroic lord of the monkey troops, wise in distinctions, commanded.
Placing at their van a great and unimpeded force of monkey heroes, he directed them toward the southern quarter.
Whatever localities in that direction were most difficult of access, the lord of monkeys recounted them all to those foremost of monkeys.
The Vindhya with its thousand peaks, covered with diverse trees and creepers, and the river Narmadā, difficult of passage, haunted by great serpents —
then the lovely Godāvarī, the great river Kṛṣṇāveṇī, and the auspicious Varadā, that most blessed stream haunted by great serpents —
the Mekhala lands and the Utkala country, the cities of Daśārṇa, and Avanti and Abhravantī — search all of these.
The Vidarbhas, the lovely Ṛṣikas, the Māhiṣakas as well, and likewise the Vaṅgas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Kauśikas on all sides.
Having searched the Daṇḍaka forest with its mountains, rivers, and caves, and the river Godāvarī — inspect all of it.
Likewise the Āndhra country and the Puṇḍras, the Colas, Pāṇḍyas, and Keralas; and the mountain Ayomukha, adorned with mineral ores, must be visited.
That great mountain with its variegated peaks, its forests bright with flowering trees, its tracts of sandalwood groves — that splendid range must be searched.
Then you shall see the divine Kāverī, that auspicious river of clear waters, where bands of Apsarases disport themselves.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
There on the crest of mount Malaya you shall see Agastya, best of seers, of mighty power and radiance like the sun, seated there.
Then, granted leave by that great-souled one in his graciousness, you shall cross the great river Tāmraparṇī, frequented by crocodiles.
Shrouded in divine groves of sandal, adorned with islands, she enters the beloved sea like a young woman embracing her beloved.
Then, having gone there, you monkeys shall see the divine gate of the Pāṇḍyas, made of gold and adorned with pearls and gems.
Then, having reached the ocean and deliberated on your purpose, you will find there in the sea what was installed by Agastya.
The splendid Mahendra, foremost of mountains, bright with diverse trees, golden and glorious, plunges into the great ocean.
It is adorned with diverse kinds of flowering trees and creepers and is frequented by foremost gods, sages, yakṣas, and Apsarases.
It is scattered with throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas and is most enchanting; the thousand-eyed Indra always visits it on each sacred day.
On the further shore of it lies an island, a hundred yojanas in extent, blazing with light, inaccessible to humans — search it on all sides. There Sītā must be sought with all your might, above all.
For that region is the abode of the wicked Rāvaṇa, the lord of Rākṣasas deserving death, whose splendor equals that of the thousand-eyed Indra.
In the midst of that southern ocean there is a Rākṣasī known as Aṅgārakā, who feeds by seizing the shadow of her prey.
Having passed her, there is in the sea at a hundred yojanas a glorious mountain named Puṣpitaka, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Radiant as the rays of the sun and moon, surrounded by the waters of the ocean, it gleams with its broad peaks as if scratching the sky.
One of its peaks is golden — that one the sun frequents; one is white and silvery — that one the moon frequents.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The ungrateful do not see it, nor the cruel, nor the impious. Having bowed your heads to that mountain, search onward, O monkeys.
Having passed it, O irresistible ones, there is a mountain named Sūryavān, fourteen yojanas distant along a road difficult to traverse.
And having passed that too, there is the mountain named Vaidyuta, with trees bearing fruits of all desires, charming in every season.
There, having eaten the excellent roots and fruits and drunk the finest honeys, proceed onward, O monkeys.
There is a mountain named Kuñjara, delightful to eye and mind, where the dwelling of Agastya was built by Viśvakarman.
There stands a divine golden pavilion, one yojana wide and ten yojanas high, adorned with various jewels.
There is the city called Bhogavatī, abode of serpents, with broad thoroughfares, formidable, guarded on all sides, protected by dreadful serpents with sharp fangs and great venom.
In it dwells Vāsuki, the great and terrible king of serpents; venturing out, that city of Bhogavatī must be searched.
Having passed that region, there stands great Ṛṣabha, shaped like a bull, the glorious mountain called Ṛṣabha, composed of all manner of gems.
There the divine sandal varieties grow: Gośīrṣaka, Padmaka, and the dark-green Hariśyāma, as brilliant as fire.
Yet having seen those sandalwood trees they must never be touched, for fearsome Gandharvas named Rohitas guard that forest.
There the lords of Gandharvas dwell, each blazing like five suns: Śailūṣa, Grāmaṇī, Bhikṣu, Śubhra, and Babhru likewise.
At the very end of the earth, those irresistible ones stand who have conquered heaven. Beyond that, you must not enter the realm of the Pitṛs — most terrible, the capital of Yama, shrouded in dreadful darkness.
Only thus far, O heroes, O foremost of monkeys, is it possible for you to search and go — beyond this there is no path even for those who can move anywhere.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having surveyed all this and whatever else may be seen, and having discovered the whereabouts of the princess of Videha, you should return.
Whoever returns within a month and declares 'Sītā has been seen' — he shall enjoy pleasures equal to mine and live in happiness.
Furthermore, there is none dearer to me than he — above even my own life — and one who has wronged me many times shall become my kinsman.
You are of immeasurable strength and valor, born in lineages of great virtue; undertake this highest of human goals so that you may find the daughter of the king of men.
Then Sugrīva, having dispatched those monkeys endowed with intelligence and valor — swift as the wind — to the southern direction,
then summoned a troop-leader named Suṣeṇa, the mighty king, father of Tārā and his own formidably valiant father-in-law.
He approached him with joined palms, bowed, and said: "Render your assistance to Rāma in this task that has now presented itself."
"Attended by a hundred thousand swift monkeys, O gentle one, O lord, proceed to the western quarter, the quarter of Varuṇa."
"The Surāṣṭra lands together with the Bāhlīkas, the Śūrābhīras likewise, the prosperous Añjana territories, their lovely settlements and great cities —"
"thickets of puṃnāga trees, regions dense with uddalāka trees, and groves of ketaka — search all these, O leaders of monkey troops."
"Rivers flowing westward with cool and auspicious waters, the forests of ascetics, the wildlands, and whatever mountains there are —"
"Having searched the west, that difficult quarter enclosed by chains of mountains, then upon reaching the western ocean you shall behold its unagitated waters teeming with timi fish and crocodiles, O monkeys."
"Then the monkeys shall roam through groves of ketaka, through dense tamāla forests, and through coconut groves."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"There search for Sītā and for the dwelling of Rāvaṇa, and also the lovely city of Marīcipattana and Jaṭīpura."
"Avanti and Aṅgalopā, the unseen forest, and the broad kingdoms and towns here and there —"
"At the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean there is a great mountain named Hemagiri, with a hundred peaks and mighty trees."
"On its beautiful plateaus live winged lions who carry timi fish, ordinary fish, and elephants up to their nests."
"In those nests of the lions, and on the mountain peaks, proud and well-fed elephants, rumbling like thunder-clouds, roam about through that vast water-filled expanse on all sides."
"Its sky-touching golden peak, with its variegated trees — all of this must be swiftly searched by the shape-shifting monkeys."
"There in the ocean you shall see the golden cape of Pariyātra, a hundred yojanas in extent, difficult to behold, O monkeys."
"Twenty-four crores of swift Gandharvas dwell there, terrible shape-shifters blazing like fire."
"Those Gandharvas must not be approached too closely by even the formidably valiant monkeys, and no fruit whatsoever from that region must be taken by the leaping ones."
"For those heroes are unapproachable, possessed of great vitality and might; those ones of fearsome valor guard the fruits and roots there."
"Yet effort must be made there and Jānakī must be sought; there is no fear at all from them for those who follow the nature of monkeys."
"At the fourth quarter of the ocean stands the mountain named Cakravān; there the discus of a thousand spokes was fashioned by Viśvakarman."
"There, having slain Pañcajana and the demon Hayagrīva, the Supreme Person carried off the discus and the conch shell."
"On its variegated slopes and in its vast caves, Rāvaṇa together with the princess of Videha must be searched for here and there."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Sixty-four yojanas distant, in the fathomless realm of Varuṇa, stands the mountain named Varāha, with golden peaks, supremely splendid."
"There is the golden city called Prāgjyotiṣa, in which the evil-souled one named Naraka dwells, in caves as well."
"On its variegated slopes and in its vast caves, Rāvaṇa together with the princess of Videha must be searched for here and there."
"Having passed that king of mountains, there is a wholly golden mountain with rifts and caverns of gold within, filled with cascades and waterfalls."
"Elephants, boars, lions, and tigers continually roar all around it, made proud by that very sound."
"On that mountain named Meghavān, the splendid Mahendra with horse-colored steeds, Pākaśāsana Indra, was consecrated king by the gods."
"Having passed that king of mountains guarded by Mahendra, you shall travel through sixty thousand golden peaks."
"They are the color of the young sun, gleaming on all sides, beautified by golden trees in full bloom."
"In the midst of these stands the king Meru, the highest of mountains — the mountain to which a boon was granted of old by the gracious Āditya."
"Thus addressed by the sun, the lord of mountains was told: 'All those who take refuge in you shall become golden by my grace, both by day and by night.'"
"'And whatever gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas dwell upon you — they shall be suffused with golden radiance, blazing with that luster.'"
"The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and Maruts — all the celestial beings — come at the western twilight to Meru, the highest of mountains,"
"and attend upon the sun; and the sun, worshipped by them, becomes invisible to all creatures and goes to the western mountain."
"In half a muhūrta the day-maker swiftly traverses ten thousand yojanas to reach that rocky mass."
"On its peak stands a great divine palace radiant as the sun, filled with the excellence of palatial halls, fashioned by Viśvakarman."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Adorned with variegated trees and thronged with birds of all kinds, it is the abode of the great-souled Varuṇa, who holds the noose."
"Between Meru and the western mountain stands a great ten-headed palmyra tree, golden and splendid, blazing on its variegated altar-base."
"In all those fastnesses, and in the lakes and rivers as well, Rāvaṇa together with the princess of Videha must be searched for here and there."
"There dwells the righteous-souled sage Merusāvarṇi, perfected by his own austerities, renowned, equal to Brahmā himself."
"The great sage Merusāvarṇi, radiant as the sun, must be asked — bowing your heads to the ground — about any tidings concerning the daughter of Mithilā."
"This far the sun illuminates the world of the living, and at the end of night, having dispelled all darkness, sets behind the western mountain."
"Thus far, O foremost of monkeys, it is possible for monkeys to go; beyond this, sunless and boundless, we have no knowledge."
"But having found the princess of Videha and the dwelling of Rāvaṇa, and having reached the western mountain, return when the month is complete."
"No one may remain beyond a month — one who does so shall be condemned to death by me; together with you brave ones my father-in-law shall go."
"All of what this one says must be heeded by you, who do as ordained; this is my guru, my long-armed, mighty father-in-law."
"And you too are heroic — authorities in all endeavors; taking him as your guide, proceed to survey the western quarter."
"But once the wife of the king of immeasurable splendor has been found, we shall have accomplished our purpose by rendering this return service for what was done for us."
"Whatever else besides this might be beneficial to this task, weigh it well — bearing in mind the place, the time, and the purpose."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then those leaping ones led by Suṣeṇa, having carefully heard Sugrīva's words and taken leave of the lord of the monkeys, all went to that quarter protected by Varuṇa.
Then Sugrīva, that bull among monkeys, having dispatched his father-in-law to the western quarter, addressed the heroic monkey named Śatabali,
the king, learned in counsel, spoke words approved by all the monkeys, words that were for his own benefit and equally for Rāma's benefit.
"Attended by a hundred thousand forest-dwellers of your kind, along with the sons of Vaivasvata, set forth with your own counselors."
"Search the heroic northern quarter, crowned with the Himālayan range, on all sides for the blameless wife of Rāma."
"When this task is accomplished and the favor of the son of Daśaratha is fulfilled, we shall be freed from our debt — best of those who know the meaning of what is accomplished."
"For the great-souled Rāghava has done what is dear to us; if there is a return service for him, then life has borne fruit."
"Holding to this resolve, act in whatever way Jānakī may be found — you who seek what is dear and beneficial to us."
"For this Rāma, conqueror of enemy cities, is the most honored of all beings and came to us with affection."
"These forest fastnesses, rivers, and mountain gorges — search through them all with the fullness of your intelligence and valor."
"There search among the Mlecchas and Pulindas, likewise the Śūrasenas, the Prasthālas and Bharatas, the Kurus along with the Madras,"
"the Kāmbojas and Yavanas as well, the Śakas and the Āraṭṭakas, the Bāhlīkas and Ṛṣikas, and also the Pauravans and Ṭaṅkaṇas;"
