"the Cīnas and Paramacīnas, and the Nīhāras again and again, and having searched the Daradas as well, thoroughly comb the Himavat mountains."
"In the groves of lodhra and padmaka trees, and in the deodar forests, Rāvaṇa together with the princess of Videha must be sought here and there."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then, having gone to the hermitage of Soma frequented by gods and Gandharvas, you shall proceed to that great-plateaued mountain named Kāla."
"On its great peaks, in its rifts and caves, thoroughly search for the glorious, illustrious wife of Rāma."
"Having passed that king of mountains, the great golden Hemavarga range, you should then proceed to the mountain named Sudarśana."
"In its forest groves, rifts, and caves, Rāvaṇa together with the princess of Videha must be sought here and there."
"Having passed it, there is a void sky of a hundred yojanas on all sides, without mountain, river, or tree, devoid of all living beings."
"But having swiftly passed that hair-raising wilderness, upon reaching the white mountain Kailāsa you shall be filled with joy."
"There is the divine palace of Kubera, fashioned by Viśvakarman, white as a cloud, adorned with Jāmbūnada gold."
"There is the vast lotus pond, rich in lotuses and blue water-lilies, thronged with haṃsa and kāraṇḍava birds, frequented by bands of Apsarases."
"There the glorious Vaiśravaṇa, king of yakṣas, the lord of wealth honored by all beings, disports himself together with the Guhyakas."
"On those moonlit mountains and in their caves, Rāvaṇa together with the princess of Videha must be sought here and there."
"Upon reaching mount Krauñca, its cave most difficult of access must be entered with utmost vigilance, for that passage is known to be hard to enter."
"For there dwell great-souled great sages, radiant as the sun, duly worshipped even by the gods, divine in form."
"The other caves of Krauñca too, its plateaus, peaks, rifts, and slopes — all must be searched here and there."
"Having surveyed Krauñca's peak as well, here and there, then proceed to the treeless Kāmaśaila and to Mānasa, the abode of birds."
"No beings — gods, Dānavas, or Rākṣasas — have passage there; yet it must be searched by all of you, with its slopes, plateaus, and mountain heights."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Having passed mount Krauñca, there is a mountain named Maināka; there is the self-built dwelling of the Dānava Maya."
"Maināka must be searched along with its slopes, plateaus, and gorges; and there here and there are the abodes of horse-faced women."
"Having fully passed that region, there is a hermitage frequented by Siddhas; there the Siddhas, the Vaikhānasas, and the Vālakhilya ascetics dwell."
"Those ascetics perfected through austerities, free from all blemish, must be reverenced; and with all humility they must be asked for news of Sītā."
"There is the Vaikhānasa lake, covered with golden lotuses, roamed by auspicious haṃsas radiant as the young sun."
"Kubera's riding elephant, known as Sarvabhauma, continually roams that region together with the she-elephants."
"Having fully passed that lake, there is a sky where moon and sun are lost, without a host of stars, cloudless, without beginning."
"Yet that region is illuminated as if by the sun's own rays by the self-luminous ones, god-like beings perfected in austerity who rest there."
"Having passed that region, there is a river named Śailodā, on both banks of which grow bamboos called Kīcaka."
"Those bamboos carry the Siddhas to the far shore and bring them back again; the Uttara Kurus are there, dwelling in the reward of their accumulated merit."
"Then thousands of rivers there have their waters set with golden lotuses, their leaves rich in blue vaidūrya gems."
"And the water bodies there, adorned with groves of red water-lilies and made of gold, blaze like the young sun."
"With leaves of most precious gems, with filaments of golden luster, with varied groves of blue lotus — that region is enclosed on all sides."
"With incomparable pearls and gems of great worth, the rivers there have banks rising up, and golden sandbars."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Those best of mountains, made of all jewels and variegated, plunge deep into the waters, and golden ones blazing like fire as well."
"And here the trees always bear flowers and fruits, thronged with birds, divine in fragrance and taste and touch, and stream forth all desires."
"Other foremost trees yield garments of various kinds, and ornaments variegated with pearls and vaidūrya likewise."
"Other foremost trees yield what is fitting for women and for men alike — things pleasant to enjoy in every season."
"Other foremost trees produce beds of great worth, variegated and golden, with their variously spread coverings."
"Other trees here bear garlands delightful to the mind, and most precious drinks, and various foods as well."
"And women endowed with virtues, marked by beauty and youth — Gandharvas, Kiṃnaras, Siddhas, Nāgas, and Vidyādharas as well, blazing as the sun, disport themselves there together with those women."
"All of them have performed meritorious deeds, all are devoted to pleasure, all dwell with their women together with love and prosperity."
"The sound of song and music mingled with loud laughter is continually heard there, captivating the minds of all beings."
"There no one is joyless, no one has an unwelcome beloved; the charming virtues there increase day by day."
"Having fully passed that region, there is the northern treasury of waters; in its midst stands the great golden mountain named Somagiri."
"Both those gods who have gone to Indra's realm and those who have gone to Brahmā's realm gaze upon that king of mountains, which has reached the sky."
"That region, though sunless, is illuminated by its own radiance; it is recognizable by the splendor of the sun — as if by the austerity-light of the sun-god himself."
"There too dwells the blessed Śambhu, the soul of the universe, of eleven forms, Brahmā the lord of gods, surrounded by Brahmarṣis."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"In no way must you proceed to the north of the Kurus; the passage of other beings too does not transgress beyond."
"For Somagiri is difficult of access even to the gods; having beheld it, you should swiftly turn back from there."
"Thus far, O foremost of monkeys, it is possible for monkeys to go; beyond this, sunless and boundless, we have no knowledge."
"All that I have described must be searched; and what has not been mentioned — let your minds apply themselves to that as well."
"Then a great favor to the son of Daśaratha will have been accomplished, and a still greater one to me will have been done by that act of finding her — the daughter of Videha, unrivaled as the wind."
"Then, having accomplished your purpose, assembled with your kinsmen, honored by me, charming with all virtues, with your enemies pacified, with your beloved ones, O leaping ones who uphold existence, you shall roam the earth."
Sugrīva spoke in particular on behalf of Hanūmān, for he was resolved in his purpose upon that foremost of monkeys as the one to accomplish the task.
"I see no obstacle to your movement, O bull among monkeys — not on earth, nor in the atmosphere, nor in the sky, nor in the abode of the gods, nor in the waters."
"All the worlds are known to you — together with the asuras, the gandharvas, the nāgas, the humans, and the gods, along with the oceans and the mountains."
"Your speed of movement, your swiftness, your energy, and your agility are equal to those of your father, the mighty-vigoured Māruta, O great monkey, O hero."
"There exists no being on earth equal to you in splendour. Therefore, demonstrate in truth how Sītā may be found."
"In you alone, O Hanūmān, O learned in statecraft, reside strength, wisdom, valour, and the policy of conforming to the demands of place and time."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Rāghava, understanding the urgency of the task to be accomplished by Hanūmān, and knowing Hanūmān's nature, reflected within himself.
"The lord of the monkeys is wholly resolved upon Hanūmān for this purpose, and Hanūmān himself is even more firmly resolved in the accomplishment of the task."
"For one thus dispatched, thoroughly known by his deeds, and taken up by his lord — the fruit of the task is certain to arise."
Seeing that monkey of supreme determination, the great-splendoured one felt as if his purpose were already accomplished, his senses and mind filled with joy.
Then the scorcher of foes, filled with affection, gave him his signet ring adorned with his own name inscribed upon it, as a token of recognition for the princess.
"By this token, O foremost of monkeys, the daughter of Janaka will look upon you as come from my presence, and will be reassured."
"Your resolution, O hero, and your valour combined with fortitude, together with the message of Sugrīva, seem to declare success to me."
Taking that ring, the foremost of monkeys placed it upon his head, bowed with joined palms, paid reverence to Rāma's feet, and set forth — that best of leapers.
Urging onward the great army of monkeys, the heroic son of the Wind became like the moon with its clear disc in a sky cleared of clouds, adorned by the host of stars.
"Relying on your exceedingly mighty strength and the many feats of valour befitting the foremost of monkeys, O son of the Wind, do whatever is necessary so that the daughter of Janaka may be reached, O Hanūmān."
Understanding the stern command of their lord, those foremost of monkeys set forth, covering the earth like locusts.
Rāma resided there on mount Prasravaṇa together with Lakṣmaṇa, awaiting that month which had been appointed for the finding of Sītā.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The heroic monkey Śatabali then swiftly set out toward the northern quarter, beautiful and encompassed by the king of mountains.
Vinatā, the leader of the monkey troop, marched toward the eastern quarter.
The son of the Wind, that leaping monkey who leads the monkey host, set out toward the southern quarter — the region traversed by Agastya — accompanied by Tārā, Aṅgada, and others.
Suṣeṇa, the lord of leaping monkeys, that tiger among monkeys, set forth toward the formidable western quarter, guarded exceedingly by Varuṇa.
Then the king, having dispatched in due order the chief leaders of the monkey army to all the quarters, rejoiced in full contentment.
Thus urged by the king, all the leaders of the monkey bands set out swiftly, each heading toward his own assigned quarter.
Shouting and roaring and thundering, the leaping monkeys — those best of leapers — went on, bounding and running, crying: "We shall bring back Sītā and slay Rāvaṇa!"
"I alone will slay Rāvaṇa when I encounter him in battle, and then I shall swiftly seize and bring away the daughter of Janaka."
"Let those of you trembling with fatigue stay where you are — I alone shall bring back Jānakī even from Pātāla itself."
"I shall tear up trees, I shall split open mountains, I shall cleave the earth asunder, I shall churn the oceans into turmoil."
"I am capable of leaping a hundred yojanas in count — nay, more than a hundred yojanas — of this there is no doubt."
"Whether on the surface of the earth, in the ocean, upon the mountains, in the forests, or even in the depths of Pātāla — my movement cannot be arrested."
Thus each of them, one by one, spoke their boastful words in the presence of the king of monkeys, intoxicated with the pride of their strength.
When the monkey lords had departed, Rāma said to Sugrīva: "How did you, without any battle, come to know the entire orb of the earth?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Sugrīva then spoke to Rāma with a humble heart: "Hear, O bull among men — I shall recount everything in full detail."
"When Vālī was pursuing the dānava named Dundubhi, who had taken the form of a great buffalo, in the direction of Mount Malaya —"
"— then the buffalo entered a cave of Mount Malaya, and Vālī too entered there into Malaya, intent on killing him."
"I was left posted at that cave, like a water-vessel set at a gate, and Vālī did not emerge — a full year having passed."
"Then that cave became filled with a torrent of blood; seeing this I was overcome with amazement and tormented by grief for my brother."
"Then, having resolved that my elder brother had surely been slain, I placed at the mouth of the cave a boulder resembling a mountain, so that the buffalo, unable to emerge, would perish within."
"Then I came to Kiṣkindhā, despairing of his life. A great kingdom fell to me, and together with Tārā, with Rumā, and with allies, I dwelt there, freed from anxiety."
"Then Vālī returned, having slain that bull among dānavas, and I surrendered the kingdom to him out of deference, constrained by fear."
"That wicked-souled Vālī, his senses disturbed, wishing to slay me, pursued me in anger together with his ministers as I fled."
"Then I was chased by Vālī together with his retinue, beholding various rivers, forests, and cities as I fled."
"Then the earth appeared to me like the surface of a mirror, resembling a whirling firebrand, and in my speed it seemed no larger than a cow's hoofprint."
"Then I first went east, then took refuge in the south, and again turned to the west, trembling with fear; and as I was heading north, Hanūmān spoke to me."
"Now I recall, O king, how Vālī, that lord of monkeys, was formerly cursed by the sage Mataṅga within this hermitage precinct."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"If Vālī should enter here, his head would shatter into a hundred pieces; our dwelling there would be easy and free from fear."
"Then, reaching Mount Ṛśyamūka, O son of a king, Vālī did not enter it then — out of fear of the curse of Mataṅga."
"Thus, O king, the entire orb of the earth was directly observed by me at that time, and then I came to take refuge in this cave."
For the sake of finding Vaidehī, the leaders of the monkey troops, dispatched by the monkey-king as instructed, set forth swiftly in all directions.
They searched all around through lakes, rivers, thickets, the sky, and cities, through river-fastnesses and mountains on every side.
All the leaders of the monkey troops thoroughly searched the regions named by Sugrīva, along with their mountains, forests, and woodlands.
Having searched throughout the day, all the monkeys, resolute in finding Sītā, would return to the earth when night came.
In regions bearing fruit in every season, the monkeys would come to fruit-laden trees and make their nightly resting places, day after day.
Having completed the first appointed day, the leaders of the monkey troops returned to Prasravaṇa at the end of the month and met with the monkey-king, having found nothing.
Having searched the eastern direction as instructed, along with his ministers, mighty Vinatā returned without having seen Sītā.
And that great monkey, the valiant Śatabali, having searched the entire northern direction, returned together with his army.
Suṣeṇa, having searched the western quarter together with the monkeys, approached Sugrīva when the full month was spent.
Approaching Sugrīva, who was seated on the summit of Prasravaṇa together with Rāma, they saluted him and spoke these words.
"All the mountains have been searched, and all the forests and cities, the rivers reaching to the ocean, and all the inhabited lands.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
All the caves named by you have been searched, and the great thickets overgrown and interlaced with creepers have been searched as well.
In dense, inaccessible, and rugged regions, creatures of immense size have been searched out and slain; and those dense places have been searched again and again.
That great-souled foremost of monkeys, born of noble spirit, will behold Maithilī; for Hanūmān, son of the Wind, has taken the very direction in which Sītā went."
Then that monkey Hanūmān, going together with Tārā and Aṅgada, approached the region indicated by Sugrīva.
Having gone far, together with all those best of monkeys, he searched the caves and dense forests of the Vindhya range.
The summits of mountains, river-fastnesses, lakes, vast trees, diverse groves of trees, and mountains thick with foliage—
—all those valiant monkeys, searching in every direction, did not find Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, Maithilī.
Eating roots and various fruits as they searched, those formidable ones dwelt here and there; for that region was vast, hard to search, full of caves and dense forest.
Leaving that region then, all the leaders of the monkey troops, fearless and undaunted, entered another forbidding land.
Where the trees bore no fruit, were flowerless and stripped of leaves; where the rivers were waterless, and roots were extremely scarce—
—where there were no buffaloes, no deer, no elephants, no tigers, no birds, nor any other forest-dwelling creatures—
—where on dry land there were lotus-pools with gleaming, full-blown lotuses, beautiful and fragrant, yet forsaken even by bees—
—there lived a great sage named Kaṇḍu, most glorious, truth-speaking, rich in austerities, utterly intolerant, and unapproachable through his self-discipline—
—whose son, a boy of ten years, was lost to death in that very forest; the great sage, enraged, cursed that place—

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
—by that righteous-souled one the entire great forest was cursed: desolate, forbidding, devoid of beasts and birds.
The borders of that forest, the ravines of the mountains, and the headwaters of rivers they searched with careful attention.
And there too those great-souled ones, devoted to Sugrīva's good, did not see the daughter of Janaka, nor Rāvaṇa, her abductor.
Entering that terrible region overgrown with creepers and thickets, they saw a demon of cruel deeds, fearless even of the gods.
Seeing that terrible one standing there like another mountain, all the monkeys drew closely together upon beholding that mountain-like figure.
That powerful one said to all the monkeys, "You are finished!" and, raising his clenched fist, charged at them in great fury.
As he rushed forward, Aṅgada, son of Vālin, recognizing him as Rāvaṇa, struck him on the spot with the flat of his palm.
Struck by the son of Vālin and vomiting blood from his mouth, that demon fell to the ground like a mountain toppled over.
While he lay breathless, the monkeys, exulting in victory, searched most of that mountain-gorge region all around.
Having searched that forest, all of them then entered yet another terrible mountain-cavern.
Searching again, exhausted, they leapt out and came together, sitting down at the foot of a solitary tree with downcast hearts.
Then Aṅgada, most wise, exhausted, gently composing himself, spoke these words to all the monkeys.
"Forests, mountains, rivers, fastnesses, dense thickets, cliffs, and mountain-caves — all have been searched by us on every side.
Everywhere, even among us, Jānakī cannot be seen — Sītā, equal to the daughter of the gods, carried off by some demon.
A great time has already passed for us, and Sugrīva is fierce in his commands; therefore let all of you together continue to search on every side.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Abandoning sloth, grief, and the sleep that has come upon you, search so that we may find Sītā, the daughter of Janaka.
Perseverance, skill, and the unconquered spirit of the mind — these are said to bring success in one's tasks; therefore I say this to you.
Even today let the forest-dwellers search this inaccessible forest; abandoning weariness, let this entire forest be searched once more.
The fruit of an action diligently performed is surely seen; enough of despondency — for dejection is not fitting for us.
Sugrīva, O monkeys, is a wrathful king, swift to punish; one must always be wary of him, and of the great-souled Rāma as well.
This has been said for your own good; act on it if it pleases you, or else say, O monkeys, what is proper for all of us together."
Having heard Aṅgada's words, Gandhamādana spoke in a faint voice, weakened by thirst and fatigue.
"Indeed, what Aṅgada has said is worthy of you — it is both beneficial and agreeable; let what he has said be done."
"Let us search once more: mountains, ravines, and cliffs as well, the empty woodlands and the mountain-springs."
"Let all search everywhere through the forest and the mountain-fastnesses, exactly as all of them were indicated by great-souled Sugrīva."
Then those mighty monkeys rose up again and roamed the southern direction, which was interspersed with Vindhya forests.
Those monkeys climbed the glorious Silver Mountain, resembling an autumn cloud, full of peaks and caves.
There the best of monkeys, eager to behold Sītā, searched through the charming lodhra-forests and the saptaparṇa-groves.
Climbing to its summit, those great-striding ones, though exhausted, did not see Vaidehī, the beloved queen of Rāma.
Having surveyed that mountain of many caverns to the full extent of their sight, the monkeys descended, looking all around.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having descended to the ground, exhausted and dispirited, they rested for a moment and then took shelter at the foot of a tree.
Having recovered for a moment, somewhat relieved of exhaustion, they rose once more, determined to search the entire southern direction.
Those best of leaping monkeys, with Hanūmān at their head, set forth and ranged all around the Vindhya from its very beginning.
Together with Tārā and Aṅgada, Hanūmān the monkey searched through the caves and thickets of the Vindhya.
They searched all around through caves frequented by lions and tigers, and through the great cascading waterfalls in the rough terrain of that lord of mountains.
As they remained searching there, the allotted time passed away.
That region was hard to explore, vast and filled with caves and dense thickets; yet there Vāyu's son searched every part of the mountain.
Separated from one another yet not far from each other, Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Śarabha, and Gandhamādana searched.
Mainda and Dvivida, and likewise Hanūmān and Jāmbavān, and the crown prince Aṅgada, and Tāra who roams the forest.
Having searched the southern quarter through regions covered with mountain ranges, overcome by hunger and thirst, exhausted and in need of water, they caught sight of a great cave overgrown with creepers and trees.
Then cranes and geese and sārasas were flying out of it, and wet cakravākas with their limbs reddened by lotus pollen.
Then, having approached that cave which was fragrant and impassable, those bull-like monkeys became minds filled with wonder and eagerness.
Seized by curiosity, those foremost among the leaping monkeys, glowing with energy and possessed of great strength, approached that cave with great excitement.
Then Hanūmān, son of the Wind-god, resembling a mountain peak and skilled in wilderness and forests, addressed all the monkeys.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Having searched the southern quarter through regions covered with mountain ranges, we are all exhausted, and I do not see the Maithilī."
"And from this cave, geese and cranes together with sārasas, and water-wet cakravākas, fly out on all sides."
"Surely there is water here, whether a well or a pool; and likewise these trees standing at the cave entrance are fresh and lush."
Spoken to thus, all the monkeys entered that cave enveloped in darkness, without moon or sun, a sight that made the hair stand on end.
Then in that cave, difficult to traverse and filled with many kinds of trees, clasping one another mutually, they advanced a distance of a yojana.
Losing their senses, thirsty, bewildered, and desperately seeking water, they wandered about within that cave for some time without rest.
Those leaping ones, now gaunt, with wretched faces, thoroughly exhausted—those heroes then saw a light ahead, at that point despairing of their lives.
Then, arriving at that place, they saw a pleasant forest free from darkness—golden trees blazing with the radiance of the kindled fire Vaiśvānara.
Śala trees, palms, puṃnāgas, kakubhas, vañjulas, dhavas, campankas, nāga trees, and karṇikāras in full bloom.
Resembling the young sun in color, with altars made of vaidūrya gems, and lotus ponds the hue of blue vaidūrya, thronged with birds.
Encircled by great golden trees resembling the young sun, and with great fish made of pure gold and tortoises in the waters.
There they saw lotus ponds filled with clear water, and likewise aerial palaces of gold and of silver.
With windows of refined gold and covered with lattices of pearls, the floors laid with gold and silver and inset with vaidūrya gems.
The monkeys saw there on all sides the finest of dwellings, and trees with flowers and fruit, resembling coral and precious gems.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And golden bees on every side, and honeycombs, and beds and seats marvellous with gems and gold.
They saw on all sides vehicles of great worth, and accumulations of vessels made of gold, silver, and bronze.
And stores of divine aloe wood and sandalwood, and pure edible roots and fruits.
And precious drinks and rich honeys, and stores of divine garments of great worth, and heaps of variegated blankets and of skins.
Searching here and there in that cave, those radiant and heroic monkeys saw, not far away, a certain woman.
Seeing her, they were greatly startled—a female ascetic clad in bark garment and black antelope skin, of regulated diet, blazing as it were with her own splendor.
Then Hanūmān, resembling a mountain, with hands joined in reverence, greeted that venerable woman and asked: "Who are you? Tell us whose is this dwelling, this cave, and these treasures."
Having spoken thus, Hanūmān there again addressed that illustrious female ascetic clad in black antelope skin, that one devoted to dharma.
"We have entered suddenly into this cave enveloped in darkness, overcome by hunger and thirst, thoroughly exhausted and distressed in every way."
"Thirsty, we entered this great golden cavity; and having seen these various conditions of such astonishing kind, we are disturbed, bewildered, and have lost our wits."
"Whose are these golden trees resembling the young sun, and the pure edible roots and fruits?"
"Whose are these aerial palaces of gold and the houses of silver, with windows of refined gold and covered with lattices of gems?"
"These trees in flower and fruit, holy and fragrant—these trees made of jāmbūnada gold—by whose power do they exist?"
"And golden lotuses grown in the clear water—how is it that golden fish move about together with tortoises?"
"The self, the greatness, and the ascetic power—whose is all this? Since all of us do not know, you ought to explain everything to us."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Addressed thus by Hanūmān, the female ascetic devoted to dharma, delighting in the welfare of all beings, replied to Hanūmān.
"Maya by name—a great-spirited dānava of powerful illusion, the foremost among dānavas—by him all this golden forest was fashioned through māyā."
"Formerly, he was the Viśvakarman among the foremost of dānavas; by him this divine golden mansion of supreme excellence was fashioned."
"He performed austerities for thousands of years in the great forest and obtained from the Pitāmaha a boon—all the wealth of Uśanas."
"Having created everything, that powerful one, master of all desires, dwelt happily for some time in this great forest."
"That bull among dānavas, having become attached to the apsarā Hemā, was slain by the lord Purandara, who took up his thunderbolt and struck him by force."
"And this supreme forest was given by Brahmā to Hemā, along with the eternal enjoyment of desires and this golden dwelling."
"I am Svayaṃprabhā, the daughter of Merusāvarṇi, her attendant; I guard this dwelling of Hemā, O best of monkeys."
"Hemā is my dear friend, skilled in dance and song; given the boon by her, I guard this supreme dwelling."
"What is your purpose, and for what reason do you traverse the wildernesses? And how was this difficult-to-find forest discovered by you?"
"After eating these edible things, the roots and fruits, and drinking the water, you ought to tell me everything."
Then with single-pointed concentration, the female ascetic devoted to dharma spoke these words to all those troop-leaders among the monkeys who had rested.
"O monkeys, if your fatigue has passed from eating the fruits, and if this is something I should hear, I wish to hear it—let it be told."
Hearing those words of hers, Hanūmān, son of the Wind-god, began to relate truthfully and straightforwardly exactly what had occurred.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The glorious Rāma Dāśarathi, king of all the world, comparable to Mahendra and Varuṇa, entered the Daṇḍaka forest."
"Together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife the Vaidehī; his wife was carried off by force from Janasthāna by Rāvaṇa."
"That hero's friend, that king's companion, is a monkey named Sugrīva, king of the foremost monkeys; it is by him that we were dispatched."
"The southern quarter—traversed by Agastya, guarded by Yama—we, together with these foremost monkeys led by Aṅgada."
"Were charged altogether: 'Search for Rāvaṇa, that rākṣasa who can assume any form at will, together with Sītā the Vaidehī.'"
"Having searched the whole of the southern quarter, all of us, hungry and exhausted, took shelter at the foot of a tree."
"All with pallid faces, all absorbed in thought, we could find no end, sunken as we were in the great ocean of worry."
"Then casting our eyes about, we saw the great cave, covered over with creepers and trees, enveloped in darkness."
"Geese wet with water, their wings beaded with water droplets, ospreys and sārasas flying out from it—I said to the leaping ones, 'Come, let us enter here.'"
"And for all of them too the reasoning prevailed: 'Let us go in and enter'—urged on as they were by eagerness for their master's business."
"Then, having fallen into close formation, grasping one another's hands, we suddenly entered this cave enveloped in darkness."
"This is our situation; it is with this purpose that we came here; and it is to you that all of us have come, exhausted and famished."
"The roots and fruits given by the law of hospitality—these have been consumed by us, who were tormented by hunger."
"Since all of us were saved by you when dying of hunger, tell us—for the sake of return service—what the monkeys may do for you."
Thus addressed by those monkeys, the all-knowing Svayaṃprabhā then replied to all those leaders of monkey troops.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I am fully satisfied with all these swift monkeys; while I practise my dharma, there is no service here to be done for me by anyone."
Thus addressed by the auspicious, dharma-laden words of the female ascetic, Hanūmān spoke his words to that woman of blameless conduct.
"We have all taken refuge in you, O lady of righteous conduct. The time-limit set for us by the great-souled Sugrīva has passed, and we have been dwelling inside the cave."
"You yourself should rescue us from this dreadful cave."
"Therefore please save all of us, who have overstepped Sugrīva's command, whose lives are as good as forfeit, and who are filled with dread of Sugrīva."
"There is also a great task that must be accomplished by us, O righteous lady, and that task too has not been done by us who have been dwelling here."
Thus addressed by Hanūmān, the female ascetic spoke: "I think it is exceedingly difficult for any living being who has entered here to turn back."
"But by the power of my austerities and by virtue of the self-discipline I have acquired, I shall draw all these monkeys out of this cave."
"Close your eyes, all you bull-like monkeys. For it is not possible to emerge with eyes open."
Then all of them, eager and desirous of departing, instantly covered their eyes with their soft-fingered hands and shut them tight.
Those high-souled monkeys, their faces covered by their hands, were lifted out of the cave by her in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Then the virtuous female ascetic, having brought all those monkeys forth from that treacherous place, reassured them and spoke thus.
"This is the glorious Vindhya mountain, covered with many trees and creepers. This is the Prasavaṇa peak. And this is the ocean, the great sea."
"May good fortune attend you; I will return to my abode, O bull-like monkeys." Having said this, Svayaṃprabhā entered that beautiful cave once more.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then they beheld the dreadful ocean, abode of Varuṇa, boundless and roaring loudly, churned by terrible waves.
While they had been searching through that mountain stronghold fashioned by Maya's magic, the month set as the time-limit by the king had passed.
Sitting at the foot of the Vindhya mountain, beneath fully flowering trees, those great and fortunate ones then fell into anxious thought.
Then, seeing the springtime trees laden with blossoms at their crowns and encircled by hundreds of creepers, they became filled with fearful apprehension.
Informing one another that spring had arrived, and recognizing that the time and purpose of their mission were lost, they sank down upon the ground.
Then Aṅgada, the crown prince, that great wise monkey with the shoulders of a lion and bull, with broad long arms, spoke.
"We all set out under the command of the monkey-king; a full month has passed while we were dwelling in the cave — do the monkeys not perceive this?"
"Now that the time-limit set by Sugrīva himself has expired, it is fitting for all of us forest-dwellers to undertake a fast unto death."
"Sugrīva is by nature harsh, and he is firm in his role as master; he will not pardon all of us who have transgressed and return before him."
"And without news of Sītā, he will surely do evil. Therefore it is proper for us to undertake a fast unto death right here today."
"Before the king slaughters all of us who have returned from here — having abandoned sons, wives, wealth, and homes — with a punishment beyond fitting, death here itself is better for us."
"Moreover, I was not consecrated as crown prince by Sugrīva; it was by Rāma, the lord of men, whose deeds are effortless, that I was consecrated."
"That king who bore enmity toward me before, seeing my transgression, will put me to death with a sharp punishment, his resolve fixed."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"What use are my friends witnessing my calamity at the moment of death? I shall sit here in fast unto death on this sacred shore of the ocean."
Having heard these words spoken by the young crown prince, all those foremost monkeys spoke pitifully in reply.
"Sugrīva is by nature harsh, and Rāghava is ardently attached to his beloved; with Vaidehī not found, and seeing us return together —"
"— for Rāghava's sake and to please him, he will undoubtedly have us killed. And it is not proper for those who have transgressed to go before their master."
Then Tāra, hearing the words of the terror-stricken monkeys, spoke thus: "Enough of despair. Let us all enter the cave and dwell there, if you agree."
"For this cave wrought by Maya's magic is most inaccessible; it has abundant trees, water, food, and drink. Here we need fear neither Indra, nor Rāghava, nor the monkey-king."
Hearing even Aṅgada's favorable response, all the monkeys, encouraged, said: "Let a plan by which we shall not be slain be devised for us without delay, this very day."
While Tāra, who shone with the splendor of the lord of stars, spoke thus, Hanūmān perceived that the kingdom was being seized by Aṅgada.
Hanūmān judged Vālin's son to be endowed with the eight qualities of intellect, possessed of the fourfold strength, and graced with fourteen royal virtues.
He saw him ever increasing in splendor, strength, and valor, growing in royal majesty like the moon waxing from the first night of the bright fortnight.
He was Bṛhaspati's equal in intellect, his father's equal in valor, and was attending upon Tāra as Śukra attends upon Indra.
Then Hanūmān, perceiving him exhausted in his master's cause and skilled in all the sciences, began to address Aṅgada with persuasive words.
Describing the third of the four political means — dissension — he split apart all those monkeys with the excellence of his speech.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When all those monkeys had been thus divided, he then alarmed Aṅgada with many frightening words, employing the means of intimidation with anger.
"You, O son of Tārā, are more capable than your father in battle; you are able to bear the burden firmly and rule the monkey kingdom just as your father did."
"For monkeys are by nature fickle-minded, O bull among monkeys; without you they will not endure being commanded, apart from their sons and wives."
"These very ones — Jāmbavān, Nīla, and the great monkey Suhotra — would follow you; I tell you this plainly."
"Neither I nor all these others can be drawn away from Sugrīva by conciliation, gifts, or any other means — nor by force — except by you."
"They say that even taking a position in defiance of a stronger power is self-preserving for the weak; therefore the weak should not enter into conflict."
"And this cave that you regard as a protective refuge — it is said that Lakṣmaṇa's arrows would make short work of tearing it open."
"Indra once accomplished little by hurling his thunderbolt; Lakṣmaṇa would split it apart with his sharp arrows as though slicing a leaf-cup, and Lakṣmaṇa has many iron-shafted arrows of that kind."
"The very moment you, O afflictoer of enemies, sit down in the fast unto death, all the monkeys, their resolve firm, will abandon you."
"Remembering their sons and wives, ever anxious, hungry, worn out by uncomfortable beds, they will put you behind them."
"You, bereft of friends and of kinsmen who wish you well, will be fearful even of a trembling blade of grass."
"And Lakṣmaṇa's dreadful arrows, swift and irresistible, intent on killing the fugitive, will certainly pierce you."
"But if you come with us, presenting yourself humbly, Sugrīva will in due course establish you in the kingdom."
"Your uncle is devoted to dharma, steadfast in his vows, pure, and true to his promises; he will never seek to harm you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"He also desires your mother's well-being, and his very life exists for her sake; he has no other offspring. Therefore, Aṅgada, let us go."
Hearing Hanūmān's words — modest, filled with dharma, and accompanied by due honor to his master — Aṅgada replied.
"Steadfastness, complete purity of soul, compassion, uprightness, valor, and courage — none of these are to be found in Sugrīva."
"He who, while his elder brother yet lives, takes for himself that brother's cherished queen-wife — she who should rightfully be regarded as a mother — is contemptible."
"How can he know dharma — that evil-souled one who, while his brother was engaged in battle, blocked the mouth of the cave?"
"He who has forgotten Rāghava — who took his hand in truth, who has done him service, who is of great renown — whose good deed would such a one remember?"
"He who, not through fear of adharma but through fear of Lakṣmaṇa alone, commanded us to search for Sītā — how can there be dharma in such a one?"
"Who among the noble, who is well-born and desires to live, would ever trust that sinner, that ingrate, that forgetful and unstable soul?"
"Having established his own son in the kingdom — whether that son be virtuous or not — how will Sugrīva allow me to live, born of an enemy's line?"
"With my counsel betrayed, myself in transgression, and my power diminished, how could I reach Kiṣkindhā and live there, helpless and weak like an orphan?"
"That deceitful, cruel, and pitiless Sugrīva would have me punished in secret and put in bonds, for the sake of securing his kingdom."
"A fast unto death is better for me than imprisonment and degradation. Grant me leave, all of you; let the monkeys go to their homes."
"I declare to you: I will not go to the city. I shall sit here in fast unto death; death itself is better for me."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"And my younger uncle Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, should first be given my respectful salutation and then asked about his welfare."
"Ask about the good health and welfare of Rumā as well, my mother. And you should please console my mother Tārā."
"She is by nature devoted to her son, compassionate, a woman of many austerities; upon hearing that I have perished here, she will surely abandon her life."
Having said this much and having also bowed to the elders, Aṅgada lay down upon the ground on the darbha grass, weeping and downcast in spirit.
As he lay there, the bull-like monkeys, weeping, stricken with grief, shed hot tears from their eyes.
Blaming Sugrīva and extolling Vālin, they all surrounded Aṅgada and resolved to undertake the fast unto death.
Knowing the intention of Vālin's son, those bull-like monkeys — all having touched water, facing east, seated on southward-tipped darbha grass, on the bank of the ocean — settled down together.
That mountain, as many monkeys massive as great mountain peaks lay down upon it —
— resounded through its ravines and cascades, as though with the violent tumult of roaring rain-clouds.
While all those monkeys sat fasting at the mountain place prepared for death, the king of vultures approached that very spot.
That long-lived bird was named Saṃpāti, splendid and renowned for his strength and valor — the elder brother of Jaṭāyu.
Emerging from a cave of the great Vindhya mountain and seeing the monkeys seated there, he spoke with a delighted heart.
"Fate in this world surely follows its own ordinance — how fitting that this destined prey has come to me at last after so long."
"I shall devour these monkeys one by one as they die, each in turn" — so the bird spoke, gazing upon those leaping creatures.
Hearing the words of that bird hungry for prey, Aṅgada, greatly distressed, then spoke to Hanūmān.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Look — under the pretext of Sītā, Yama, the son of Vivasvān himself, has come to this place for the destruction of us monkeys."
"Rāma's task has not been accomplished, the king's command has not been fulfilled — this unforeseen calamity has suddenly come upon the monkeys."
"The deed done by Jaṭāyu, the king of vultures, out of love for Vaidehī — all of that you have already heard in full."
"Even so, all beings — even those born into animal wombs — do Rāma's bidding, abandoning their lives just as we ourselves do."
"Exhausted in the service of Rāghava, we have given up our lives; we entered the wilderness — yet we have not found the princess of Mithilā."
"That king of vultures is fortunate — slain in battle by Rāvaṇa, he was freed from all fear of Sugrīva and has attained the highest state."
"By the destruction of Jaṭāyu, by the death of King Daśaratha, and by the abduction of Vaidehī, the monkeys have fallen into peril."
"The forest-dwelling of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa together with Sītā, and likewise the slaying of Vālin by Rāghava's arrow —"
"And the total destruction of the rākṣasas through Rāma's wrath — all this calamity has been wrought by the boon granted to Kaikeyī."
Upon hearing those words uttered from Aṅgada's mouth, the vulture with his sharp beak spoke in a loud voice.
"Who is this who proclaims with his voice the slaying of my brother Jaṭāyu, dearer to me than life itself, making my heart tremble?"
"How did the battle between the rākṣasa and the vulture take place at Janasthāna? After so long, I hear today this name of my brother."
"I wish to hear the end of my younger brother — he who knew virtue and was praiseworthy for his valor. Tell me, O best of monkeys."
"My brother Jaṭāyu dwelt at Janasthāna, and Daśaratha was that very brother's dear friend — he whose beloved eldest son Rāma is devoted to his elders. How did this come to pass?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Since my wings were burned by the rays of the sun, I cannot spread them; I wish to descend from this mountain, O destroyers of enemies."
Though the leaders of the monkey troops heard those words — his voice broken by grief — they did not trust them at all, suspicious of his intentions.
Those monkeys, seated in their fast unto death, saw the vulture and formed this terrible thought: "He will devour all of us."
"If he eats us while we sit here fasting in any case, we shall have achieved our purpose — swiftly obtaining release from this place."
After all those foremost monkeys formed this resolve, Aṅgada then addressed the vulture who had descended from the mountain peak.
"There was a powerful lord of monkeys named Kṣaraja — he was my noble king, O bird, and righteous were both of his sons."
"Sugrīva and Vālin — both sons endowed with torrential strength. King Vālin, renowned throughout the world for his deeds, was my father."
"Rāma the son of Daśaratha, the great warrior and splendid king of the entire world among the Ikṣvākus, entered the Daṇḍaka forest."
"Together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife Vaidehī, devoted to his father's command and treading the righteous path — his wife was forcibly abducted from Janasthāna by Rāvaṇa."
"Jaṭāyu the vulture-lord, a friend of Rāma's father, saw Sītā Vaidehī being carried away through the sky."
"He made Rāvaṇa chariotless and caused Maithilī to be set down — but exhausted and old, he was slain in battle by Rāvaṇa."
"Thus that vulture, slain by the mighty Rāvaṇa, was duly cremated by Rāma and attained the highest destination."
"Then Rāghava formed a friendship with Sugrīva, my great-souled paternal uncle — and he slew my father Vālin."
"For Sugrīva, estranged from my father, together with his ministers — after slaying Vālin, Rāma then consecrated Sugrīva as king."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"That Sugrīva, lord of monkeys, was installed in the kingdom by Rāma as king of the foremost monkeys — and it is he who dispatched us."
"Thus sent forth by Rāma, searching here and there, we have not found Vaidehī — like seeking the sun's radiance in the night."
"We searched the Daṇḍaka forest carefully — and then, unknowingly, we entered a cave that had opened in the earth."
"That cave was fashioned by Maya's magic, and while we searched within it, the month that the king had fixed as our deadline passed."
"We, who are all subject to the monkey-king's command, have exceeded the appointed time — and so out of fear we undertake this fast unto death."
"With Kākutstha Rāma angry, and Sugrīva together with Lakṣmaṇa wrathful, there is no life for us even if we were to return — so we have resolved to die here."
Thus addressed with piteous words by the monkeys who had abandoned hope of life, the vulture, with tears in his eyes, replied to the monkeys in a great voice.
"That younger brother of mine named Jaṭāyu, whom you have told me was slain in battle by the powerful Rāvaṇa —"
"On account of old age and my winglessness, even hearing this I must endure it — for I have no strength today to avenge my brother's enemy."
"Long ago, when the slaying of Vṛtra had occurred, both he and I, eager for victory, flew up toward the blazing sun wreathed in rays."
"Covering the path through the sky with great speed we flew — but when the sun reached its zenith, Jaṭāyu began to sink."
"Seeing that brother of mine tormented by the sun's rays and utterly overwhelmed, out of affection I shielded him with my wings."
"My wings scorched and burned, I fell upon the Vindhya, O best of monkeys — and dwelling here, I have had no news of my brother."
When Saṃpāti had spoken thus of Jaṭāyu, the crown prince Aṅgada of great wisdom then replied.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"If you are truly the brother of Jaṭāyu, you have heard what I have told you — now tell us, if you know, the abode of that rākṣasa."
"That Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas, who is lacking in foresight — whether nearby or far, if you know, inform us."
Then the elder brother of Jaṭāyu, blazing with great energy, spoke words befitting his own nature, filling the monkeys with joy.
"Though I am a vulture with scorched wings and diminished strength, O leaping ones, I will render supreme aid to Rāma — at least by means of speech."
"I know the worlds of Varuṇa and the three strides of Viṣṇu as well; I know the battles of gods and asuras, and the churning of the nectar."
"As for this task of Rāma's, it should have been done first by me — but old age has stolen my vigor and my life-breath is weakened."
"I saw a young woman of perfect beauty, adorned with all ornaments, being carried off by Rāvaṇa, that wicked-souled one."
"She was crying out 'Rāma! Rāma!' and 'Lakṣmaṇa!' — that radiant woman, flinging off her ornaments and writhing her limbs."
"Her finest silk garment, like the sun's glow atop a mountain, shone against that dark rākṣasa as lightning blazes against a rain cloud."
"By the mention of Rāma's name, I believe that woman is Sītā. Now hear from me as I describe the dwelling of that rākṣasa."
"The rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa — the own son of Viśravas and brother of Vaiśravaṇa — dwells in the city of Laṅkā."
"From here, a full hundred yojanas across the ocean on an island, the lovely city of Laṅkā was built by Viśvakarman."
"In that city dwells Vaidehī, wretched, wearing silk, confined in Rāvaṇa's inner quarters and closely guarded by rākṣasī women."
"You will behold that Maithilī, the daughter of King Janaka, there in Laṅkā — protected on all sides by the ocean."
"Reaching the ocean's far shore, a full hundred yojanas away, and arriving at the southern bank, you will there behold Rāvaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Make haste there at once and strive with valor, O leaping ones! I truly see this with my inner sight — having found her, you will return."
"The first path belongs to the sparrows and those other birds that live on grain; the second to the crows and those that eat tree-fruits."
"The bhāsa birds travel the third path, and the krauñcas together with the kurara birds; hawks travel the fourth, and vultures travel the fifth."
"The sixth path belongs to the swans endowed with strength, valor, beauty, and youth — and beyond that is the way of Vainateya Garuḍa. From Vainateya descends the lineage of all of us, O best of monkeys."
"A reprehensible deed was done by which we became flesh-eaters — yet even standing here, I behold Rāvaṇa and Jānakī with my sight."
"We too possess a divine golden power of vision — and so by the power of our sustenance and by our very nature, O monkeys, we always see as far as a full hundred yojanas and more."
"Our livelihood is ordained by nature to be found at a distance; the livelihood of those who fight on foot is ordained to be found at their very feet."
"Let some means be found for crossing the salt ocean — having reached Vaidehī, you will return with your purpose fulfilled."
"I wish to go with you to the ocean, abode of Varuṇa — I will offer water for my great-souled brother who has gone to heaven."
Then those mighty monkeys of great valor, having carried Saṃpāti — his wings burned away — to the shore of the lord of rivers and streams,
brought back that lord of birds to that very place; and the monkeys became filled with joy, having obtained this news to act upon.
Then, having heard those words of the king of vultures — words sweet as nectar — those foremost of monkeys were filled with joy as he spoke.
Jāmbavān, the foremost of monkeys, together with all the leaping ones, suddenly rose from the ground and addressed the king of vultures.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Where is Sītā? By whom was she seen? Or who has carried off the daughter of Mithilā? Tell us all of this, sir — be a guide to us forest-dwellers."
"Who would not regard the valor of the arrows of Daśaratha's son — falling with the speed of the thunderbolt — and of Lakṣmaṇa himself, who has been spoken of?"
He, pleased, reassuring those monkeys who were filled with affection and attentive to hear of Sītā, spoke these words again.
"Hear now how the abduction of the Vaidehī was heard by me, by whom it was reported to me, and where the wide-eyed one is."
"I, old and my vital strength and prowess diminished, fell long ago upon this difficult mountain extending many yojanas."
"My son, named Supārśva, foremost among birds, sustains me in this condition with food at the proper time."
"Gandharvas are sharp in their desires, serpents sharp in their anger, beasts sharp in their fears — and we birds are sharp in our hunger."
"Once, when the sun had set and I was afflicted by hunger and longing for food, my son came bringing no flesh."
"That youth, foremost among birds, was rebuked by me — overcome by hunger and thirst, and on account of old age and anger."
"He, the joy-increaser, distressed by my withholding of food, paid his respects and then spoke these words truthfully."
"'Father, at the proper time I took to the sky in search of flesh, and stationed myself blocking the gateway of Mount Mahendra."
"'There, facing downward, I alone set myself to obstruct the path of the thousands of creatures that roam the far reaches of the ocean."
"'There I saw someone resembling a heap of broken collyrium, carrying a woman blazing like the rising sun, and going away."
"'I, bent on seizing food, had made my resolve upon seeing them, but I was entreated concerning the path by him with gentle conciliation."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'Indeed, nowhere is there anyone who would strike those who approach with conciliation — not even some person of low birth, much less one like me."
"'He went through the sky with his brilliance, compressing it as it were with his speed. Then I was approached and honored by the aerial beings."
"'"By good fortune you live, father," said the great seers to me. "He who passed with his wife has gone well — there is no doubt."""
"'Thus addressed by those supremely splendid perfected sages, I was informed that he was Rāvaṇa, king of the rākṣasas."
"'He was carrying off the wife of Daśaratha's son Rāma — Janaka's daughter — her ornaments fallen, clad in silk, overcome by the force of grief."
"'She was crying out the names of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, her hair loosened. "This is a waste of time" — so said Supārśva, the foremost among those skilled in speech.'
"Supārśva reported all this matter in full to me. Yet even upon hearing this, my mind had no inclination toward any heroic action."
"For how can a bird without wings undertake any deed? Yet what can be done by me — proceeding by the power of speech and intelligence —"
"Hear what I shall declare, relying on your valor. Through speech and thought I shall accomplish what is dear to all of you, for whatever is the task of Daśaratha's son is indeed mine — of this there is no doubt."
"You are supreme in wisdom, powerful, high-minded, united with the king of monkeys — unapproachable even by the gods."
"And the sharpened arrows of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, feathered with heron-plumes, suffice for protecting and subduing all three worlds."
"Indeed Daśagrīva is endowed with brilliance and strength — yet for you who are capable, nothing whatsoever is difficult."
"Therefore, enough with the delay of time — let a firm resolve of the mind be made. For the wise, such as yourselves, do not hesitate in undertakings."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the leaders of the monkey troops seated themselves on the difficult mountain all around that vulture who had bathed and performed his water-rites.
Saṃpāti, his trust established, spoke again with joy to Aṅgada seated there, surrounded by all those monkeys.
"Let the monkeys fall silent and listen with one-pointed attention. I shall declare truthfully, as I know it, where the daughter of Mithilā is."
"I fell long ago upon the summit of this Vindhya in the forest, my limbs overcome by the heat of the sun, burnt by the rays of the sun."
"Regaining consciousness only after six nights, helpless and bewildered as it were, scanning all directions, I knew nothing at all."
"Then, surveying the oceans, mountains, all rivers and lakes, forests and wilderness regions, my understanding returned."
"Filled with flocks of joyful birds, having peaks and cave-interiors, on the shore of the southern ocean — I concluded: 'This is the Vindhya.'"
"And here there was a holy hermitage, honored even by the gods, in which the sage named Niśākara practiced severe austerities."
"Eight thousand years I dwelt here, O knowers of dharma, without that sage — for Niśākara had gone to heaven."
"Descending with difficulty and slowly from the uneven summit of the Vindhya, I returned with hardship to the earth sharp with kuśa-grass."
"Desirous of seeing that sage, I came with great difficulty; for that sage had been visited many times by Jaṭāyu and by me."
"Near the site of his hermitage, sweet-scented winds blew; no tree was seen that was not flowering or not bearing fruit."
"And having arrived at the holy hermitage and taken shelter at the foot of a tree, desiring to see him, I waited for the blessed Niśākara."
"Then I saw the sage not far off — blazing with energy, having completed his ablutions, irresistible, turned face northward."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Bears, deer, tigers, lions, elephants, and serpents came surrounding him, as living beings approach a benefactor."
"Then, knowing the sage had arrived, those creatures departed, as all the ministers and forces withdraw when the king has entered."
"But the sage, seeing me, was pleased, entered the hermitage again, and after just a moment came out and asked about my purpose."
"'Gentle one, seeing the loss of your feathers I do not comprehend — these two wings of yours are burnt by fire, and your skin too is wounded."
"'Two vultures have been seen by me before, equal to the wind in speed, kings of vultures, brothers who could assume any form at will."
"'You are Saṃpāti the elder, and Jaṭāyu is your younger brother. Assuming a human form, let them both grasp my feet."
"'What is the origin of your affliction? How did the fall of your wings come about? Or has this punishment been imposed by someone? Tell me all, as I ask.'"
Then Saṃpāti narrated to the sage in full that terrible deed done rashly and with difficulty — and likewise the pursuit of the sun.
"Blessed one, on account of my wounds and with senses disturbed by shame, I am exhausted and cannot speak at length."
"Both I and Jaṭāyu, deluded by pride through rivalry, being heroes, soared into the sky wishing to surpass each other's valor."
"Having made a wager on the summit of Kailāsa before the sages, the sun was to be followed until it reached the great western mountain of setting."
"Then we two, arriving simultaneously, looked down at the earth's surface and saw separate cities the size of chariot wheels."
"Somewhere we heard the sounds of musical instruments and the sounds of Vedic recitation, and we saw many women singing, clothed in red garments."
"Swiftly soaring and taking the path of the sun, we two looked back and saw that forest carpeted in green grass."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The earth appeared covered as if by smooth stones — by masses of rock, and the earth was wrapped with rivers as if by threads."
"The Himavat and the Vindhya and the very great mountain Meru appeared on the earth's surface like serpents in a lake."
"Intense perspiration and distress and fear beset us both then; confusion overcame us, and from confusion a terrible swooning."
"The southern direction could not be distinguished, nor the northeastern, nor the western — the world was fixed as at the end of an age, stricken, as if consumed by fire."
"With great effort the sun was perceived once more — the maker of light appeared to us as equal in extent to the entire earth."
"Jaṭāyu, without asking me, plunged down to the earth. Seeing him, I swiftly released myself from the sky."
"Shielded by my wings, Jaṭāyu was not burnt; but through my own negligence I was completely burnt there, falling from the wind-path."
"I suspect that Jaṭāyu fell in Janasthāna; but I fell on the Vindhya, with burnt wings, rendered motionless."
"Bereft of my kingdom, of my brother, of both wings and of my valor, wishing in every way only to die, I shall fall from the mountain peak."
Having spoken thus to that foremost of sages, I wept, greatly afflicted by grief. Then the blessed one, having reflected for a moment, spoke these words.
"Your wings and secondary feathers shall grow anew; and likewise your eyes, your vitality, your valour, and your strength shall be restored to you."
"For I have heard of a great deed yet to come, spoken of in ancient times; I have perceived it through my austerities, and it is known to me from what I have heard."
"There is a king named Daśaratha, a scion of the Ikṣvāku dynasty; his son, of immense splendour, shall be named Rāma."
"He, whose valour is true, being engaged in that task by his father, shall go to the forest along with his brother Lakṣmaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, a demon by birth, invincible to gods and Dānavas, shall steal his wife from Janasthāna."
"Though tempted with pleasures and with foods to eat and drink, the glorious Maithilī, that illustrious one, sunk in sorrow, shall not partake of them."
"But Vāsava, knowing Vaidehī's plight, shall give her food of the highest excellence — food akin to ambrosia and rare even among the gods."
"Receiving that food and recognising it as coming from Indra, Maithilī shall take a portion from the top and scatter it on the ground as an offering to Rāma."
"Saying, 'If my lord, the master, still lives together with Lakṣmaṇa — or even if they have attained divinity — let this food be theirs.'"
"Leaping monkeys, serving as Rāma's messengers, shall come searching for her. You, O bird, must declare to them that she is Rāma's queen."
"In any case you must not go anywhere — where would one in your condition go? Wait for the right place and time; you shall regain your wings."
"I could restore your wings to you even today, but remaining here you shall accomplish a task beneficial to all the worlds."
"Indeed that task must be done by you — it is the task of those two princes, of the Brāhmaṇas, of the gods, of the sages, and of Vāsava himself."
"I too wish to behold the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa; I do not wish to hold on to life much longer — I shall abandon this body."
With these and many other words, that master of speech, having praised me and granted me leave, entered his own hermitage.
Creeping out of the cave of that mountain, slowly and gradually, I climbed the Vindhya and have been awaiting you here.
And now more than a full hundred years of that time have passed; keeping the sage's words in my heart, I have been waiting for the right place and moment.
After Niśākara undertook his great final journey and passed to heaven, grief consumes me, beset as I am by many apprehensions.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The resolve toward death that arises in me I turn back by means of the sage's words; the counsel he gave me for the preservation of my life dispels my sorrow as a blazing tongue of flame dispels darkness.
And knowing the might of evil-souled Rāvaṇa, his son was only threatened with words — why then was Maithilī not rescued?
Having heard her lament, and seeing those two bereft of Sītā, the son born out of Daśaratha's love for me did not perform what was dear to me.
And while Saṃpāti was speaking thus in the company of the monkeys, his two wings suddenly sprouted forth before the eyes of those forest-dwellers.
Seeing his own body adorned with wings spread out and feathered with a reddish hue, he experienced incomparable joy and spoke these words to the monkeys.
"By the power of the great sage Niśākara, of immeasurable soul, my wings, scorched by the rays of the sun, have grown again."
"The valour I possessed in my youth — that very strength and manliness I perceive in myself today."
"Strive by all means — you shall attain Sītā. This regaining of my wings is for you a token of certain success."
Having spoken thus to all those monkeys, Saṃpāti, foremost of fliers, leapt from the summit of the mountain, eager to test his movement through the sky.
Hearing his words, those tiger-like monkeys were overjoyed and delighted in their hearts, and turned their faces toward the rising of their prowess.
Then those best of leapers, with the swiftness of the wind, their manliness recovered, set out in the direction of Abhijit, eager to search for the daughter of Janaka.
Having been told by the king of vultures, the leaping monkeys sprang up together, filled with joy, and roared with the valour of lions.
Having heard Saṃpāti's words regarding the destruction of Rāvaṇa, the joyful monkeys, eager to find Sītā, came to the ocean.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Approaching that place, those monkeys of awesome valour beheld it — standing as if it were a reflection of the entire great world.
Having reached the northern shore of the southern ocean, those foremost of monkeys then encamped together.
They saw the ocean thronged with immense and monstrous creatures of various kinds sporting in the water, with gaping mouths and enormous bodies, and filled with surging waves.
In some places it seemed as if asleep, in other places as if at play, and here and there it was surrounded by masses of water as vast as mountains.
Seeing it crowded with great Dānava lords dwelling in the depths of Pātāla, a sight that made the hair stand on end, those elephant-like monkeys fell into despondency.
Gazing at the ocean, which seemed as uncrossable as the sky itself, all the monkeys suddenly fell into despair, saying, "How shall the task be accomplished?"
Seeing the army thus cast into despondency by the sight of the ocean, the foremost of monkeys consoled those monkeys who were afflicted by fear.
"We have no need of despair; despondency is the greater fault. Despondency destroys a person as an enraged serpent destroys a child."
"This despondency overpowers one when the moment for valiant action arrives; stripped of its energy, the purpose of man cannot be achieved."
When that night had passed, Aṅgada convened another counsel together with the monkeys, assembling with the elder leaders of the monkey host.
That army of monkeys, surrounding Aṅgada, stood resplendent — even as the host of Maruts stands surrounding Vāsava.
"Who else would be capable of steadying that monkey army other than the son of Vālin and other than Hanūmat?"
Then the glorious Aṅgada, the subduer of foes, having paid his respects to those elder monkeys and to the army, spoke words full of purpose.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Who among you, O mighty one, shall now leap over the ocean? Who shall fulfil the purpose of Sugrīva, true to his pledge and the subduer of enemies?"
"What hero, O best of leapers, could vault a hundred yojanas? Who could deliver all these troop leaders from this great peril?"
"By whose grace, having turned back from here with our purpose accomplished, might we joyfully see again our wives, our children, and our homes?"
"By whose grace might we joyfully approach Rāma and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, and the mighty Sugrīva?"
"If any monkey among you is capable of crossing the ocean, let him quickly grant us here the auspicious gift of fearlessness."
Having heard Aṅgada's words, not one of them said anything; that entire monkey army stood there motionless as if frozen.
Again Aṅgada, foremost of monkeys, addressed those monkeys: "You are all the foremost of the powerful, of steadfast valour."
"You are born in distinguished lineages and are honoured repeatedly; there is no obstacle for any of you, at any time, in going across."
"Declare, O best of leapers, whatever capacity each of you has for making the crossing."
Then, having heard the words of Aṅgada, all those foremost of monkeys declared, each in turn, their own eagerness and capacity for the journey.
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Śarabha, Gandhamādana, Mainda and Dvivida, Suṣeṇa, and likewise Jāmbavān—
Gaja spoke up there: "I can leap ten yojanas." Gavākṣa declared he would travel twenty yojanas.
The monkey Gavaya then said to those monkeys: "I shall travel thirty yojanas, O leapers."
The monkey Śarabha then said to those monkeys: "I shall travel forty yojanas—there is no doubt."
The greatly resplendent Gandhamādana said to those monkeys: "I shall travel fifty yojanas—there is no doubt."
The monkey Mainda then said to those monkeys: "I am capable of leaping fully sixty yojanas."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the greatly resplendent Dvivida replied there: "I shall travel seventy yojanas—there is no doubt."
Suṣeṇa, foremost among monkeys, declared to those best of monkeys: "I can leap eighty yojanas, O bulls among leapers."
While they were speaking thus, honoring them all, then Jāmbavān, the eldest among them, spoke in reply.
"Formerly we too had some prowess in speed and movement; but now we have reached the far shore of old age."
"Yet in this situation it is not possible to neglect this task for which the king of monkeys and Rāma are both firmly resolved."
"Know now the movement that is available to me, given the changes of time: I shall travel ninety yojanas—there is no doubt."
And Jāmbavān addressed all those foremost monkeys again: "Indeed my prowess in movement was not merely this much—
"In the past, Viṣṇu the eternal, of great might, striding with his three steps at the sacrifice, was circumambulated by me."
"Now I am old and slow in my leaping; yet in youth at that time my strength was unmatched by any foe."
"Now I reckon my capacity for travel to be this much; yet by this alone the full accomplishment of this task will not come about."
Then the greatly wise Aṅgada, honoring Jāmbavān the great monkey, spoke words of noble import in reply:
"I shall travel this great distance of one hundred yojanas; but whether I have the strength to return is not certain."
The foremost of monkeys, Jāmbavān, skilled in speech, said to him: "Your capacity for the going is well known, O best of monkeys and bears—
"A hundred thousand yojanas even you are capable of traveling and returning—this is not the point that is spoken of here.
"A master who sends others forth should never himself be sent on a mission; all this company is meant to be sent by you, O best of leapers.
"You stand established as our protector in the position of master; a master is the companion of the army—this is the accepted way, O scorcher of foes.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Therefore, dear one, you must always be guarded like a companion; and moreover, O destroyer of enemies, you are the very root of this enterprise.
"The root of an enterprise must be protected—such is the policy of those skilled in affairs; for when the root endures, its qualities flourish like flowers and fruit.
"Therefore you, of true valor, endowed with the strength of both intelligence and might, O scorcher of foes, are the cause in the accomplishment of this enterprise.
"For you are both elder and the son of an elder to us, O foremost of monkeys; relying on you, we are capable of accomplishing the task."
Then Aṅgada, son of Vālin, the great monkey, replied with these words to the greatly wise Jāmbavān who had spoken:
"If I shall not go, and no other bull among monkeys will either, then surely what remains for us is once again to sit in fasting unto death.
"For without fulfilling the command of that wise lord of monkeys, I see no preservation of life even if we were to go there.
"For that monkey lord is supreme in both grace and in wrath; by transgressing his command, destruction would come upon our going.
"Therefore, so that this enterprise does not go otherwise, you who see the purpose clearly are the one who ought to consider this."
Then that heroic bull among leapers, Jāmbavān, having been answered by Aṅgada, spoke these further words to Aṅgada:
"O hero, nothing of this enterprise of yours shall be lacking; I am about to spur on the one who will accomplish it."
Then that hero among monkeys, approaching the foremost among leapers—renowned, sitting apart at ease—urged on that very hero among monkeys, Hanūmān himself.
Beholding thus the monkey host of many hundreds of thousands, dejected, Jāmbavān then spoke to Hanūmān:
"O hero, O best among all who know the scriptures, O Hanūmān—sitting apart in silence, why do you not speak?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Hanūmān, you are the equal of the monkey king Sugrīva, and of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa as well, in splendor and in strength.
"The son of Vinatā, the mighty Garuḍa—renowned as the son of Ariṣṭanemi, foremost of all birds—
"—that great-armed bird of great speed and great renown, I have witnessed many times at the ocean, lifting up serpents with his wings.
"Whatever strength he has in his wings, that same strength is yours in your arms; nor does your prowess and speed fall short of his.
"Strength, wisdom, splendor, and courage, O best of monkeys—you are distinguished above all beings; why do you not know yourself?
"The foremost of apsarās among apsarases, renowned as Puñjikasthalā, known as Añjanā—she became the wife of the monkey Kesarī—
"—by reason of a curse, dear one, she became a monkey-woman able to take any form, the daughter of Kuñjara, the great-souled lord of monkeys.
"While in her monkey nature, lovely in all her limbs, possessed of the power to change form at will, she once took on a human form, adorned with the glory of supreme youth.
"She roamed upon the summit of a mountain like a rain-cloud of the monsoon season, adorned with varied garlands and ornaments, clothed in the finest linen.
"From that wide-eyed one, standing on the mountain's peak, the wind gently carried away her golden garment trimmed in red, fair to behold.
"Then he saw her rounded, well-formed thighs, her full and close-set breasts, and her well-formed, beautiful face.
"Beholding her with broad and ample hips, slender-waisted, of good renown, beautiful in every limb, the Wind God was overcome by desire.
"Pervaded through every limb by the god of love, his mind undone, Māruta embraced that blameless one with his two mighty arms.
"But she, confused and virtuous, spoke these words right there: 'Who wishes to destroy this my vow of fidelity to one husband?'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Having heard the words of Añjanā, Māruta replied: 'I do not violate you, O fair-hipped one—let there be no fear for you, O fortunate one.
"'It is only in mind that I have gone to you; by embracing you, O renowned one, a son endowed with valor and wisdom shall be born to you.'
"Then as a child, beholding the risen sun in the great forest and wishing to seize it thinking it a fruit, you leaped up and flew toward the sky.
"Having traveled three hundred yojanas, O great monkey, scorched by the sun's radiance, yet you fell into no despair.
"Even as you were rushing swiftly through the atmosphere, O great monkey, the wise Indra, seized with rage, hurled his thunderbolt at you.
"Thereupon the left side of your jaw broke against a mountain's rocky peak—and from that very circumstance your name is celebrated as 'Hanūmān.'
"Then, seeing you struck down, the Wind God Vāyu himself, the bearer of fragrance, became greatly enraged and ceased to blow in all three worlds.
"And all the gods, dismayed, the lords of the worlds, when the three worlds were thrown into confusion, sought to appease the enraged Māruta.
"When the Wind was appeased, Brahmā granted you a boon: that in battle, O dear one, O man of true valor, you would be invulnerable to any weapon.
"And seeing you unharmed by the fall of his thunderbolt, the thousand-eyed Indra, gladdened in his heart, granted you an excellent boon:
"'May death come to you only at your own free will,' he declared, O lord. You are the son of Kesarī, born of the field, of terrible valor—
"—the legitimate son of Māruta and equal to him in splendor; you are indeed the son of Vāyu, dear one, and his equal in leaping as well.
"We today are as if our life-force is gone; you at this time among us are endowed with skill and valor—like another king of birds.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"At the time of Viṣṇu's three strides, dear one, I myself circumambulated the earth with its mountains, forests, and groves, twenty-one times in circumambulation.
"At that time we gathered medicinal herbs by divine command, from which the nectar was produced—and by that our great strength was born.
"Now I am old, my prowess diminished; at this present time you are the one among us endowed with all virtues.
"Therefore, O heroic one, rouse yourself—for you are the greatest among leapers; this entire monkey army desires to witness your valor.
"Rise, O tiger among monkeys; leap across the great ocean! For your course, O Hanūmān, is beyond that of all beings.
"All the monkeys are dejected—O Hanūmān, why do you disregard them? Exert your prowess, O greatly swift one, as Viṣṇu exerted his three strides!"
Then, spurred on by Jāmbavān, the son of the Wind God, the monkey of renowned speed, gladdening that army of monkey heroes, assumed a great form of his own.
As Hanūmān was being praised, the mighty one grew in stature; whirling his tail in joy, he attained his full strength.
While he was being extolled by all the bull-like monkeys, filling with his own splendor, his form became matchless.
As a lion fully grown stretches himself in a mountain cave, so now did the true son of Māruta stretch himself.
The face of that wise one as he stretched shone forth—blazing like a sacrificial vessel, like a smokeless fire.
Rising from the midst of the monkeys, his body hair standing up in joy, Hanūmān bowed to the elder monkeys and spoke these words:
"Anila, companion of fire, who splinters mountain peaks, the powerful and immeasurable Wind moving through the sky—
"—I am the true son of that swift-moving, swiftly going, great-souled Māruta; in leaping there is none equal to me.
"I am capable of circling Mount Meru—that vast mountain that seems to scratch the sky—thousands of times without obstruction.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"By the force of my arms' speed I am capable of flooding the entire world—mountains, rivers, and pools—with the sea.
"By the speed of my thighs and legs, the ocean—abode of Varuṇa—will rise up, its great sea monsters thrown into confusion.
"I am capable of circling Vainateyā—the devourer of serpents, flying through the sky, lord of birds—thousands of times.
"I am eager even to reach the blazing, ray-garlanded sun as it departs from its rising, before it has set.
"And then I am capable of returning without touching the earth, by that very great and terrible speed, O bulls among leapers.
"I am capable of surpassing all beings that move through the sky; I shall churn the ocean and split the earth asunder.
"As I leap, O leapers, I shall shake the mountains; and leaping with great speed I shall sweep across the great ocean.
"The blossoms of creepers, plants, and trees of every kind shall follow after me today as I leap through the sky; my path shall be like the path of Svāti through the heavens.
"O monkeys, all beings will watch me moving through the terrible sky, soaring upward, and descending.
"Behold me, O leapers, resembling the great Meru, covering the heavens as I go, as though swallowing the sky.
"I shall scatter the clouds, I shall shake the mountains, I shall churn the ocean as I leap, composed and intent.
"Whether the power of Vainateyā or my own or that of the mighty Māruta—apart from Suparṇa king of birds or the greatly powerful Wind, I see no being who could follow me once I have leaped.
"In the mere twinkling of an eye I shall suddenly fall upon the supportless sky, like lightning rising from a cloud.
"As I leap across the ocean, my form shall be like that of Viṣṇu as he strode out his three great strides.
"I see it clearly in my mind, and my mind's movement accords with it: I shall behold Vaidehī—rejoice, O leapers!

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Equal to Māruta in speed, equal to Garuḍa in swiftness—my resolve is to travel ten thousand yojanas.
