Nāga maidens of noble bearing, their faces like the full moon, were seen by Hanūmat there — but not slender-waisted Sītā.
Nāga maidens seized by force by the lord of rākṣasas and held in subjugation were seen by Hanūmat there — but not that daughter of Janaka.
Not finding her, yet seeing all those other noble women — the mighty-armed Hanūmat, son of the Wind, fell into despondency.
Seeing the great effort of the monkey chiefs and the crossing of the ocean rendered fruitless, the son of the Wind fell once more into anxious thought.
Hanūmat, son of the Wind, descended from the aerial palace and fell into reflection, his mind stricken with grief.
Crossing easily from the aerial palace to the rampart, Hanūmat, swift lord of the monkey host, was like lightning lodged within a cloud.
Having roamed all about Rāvaṇa's dwelling and not found Jānakī Sītā, the monkey spoke these words:
"Laṅkā has been searched most thoroughly in service of Rāma, yet I do not see Vaidehī Sītā, she who is beautiful in every limb."
"Pools, lakes, ponds and rivers, streams with marshy groves along their banks, mountain fastnesses — the whole earth has been searched, yet I do not see Jānakī."
"Here in Rāvaṇa's dwelling Sītā was pointed out by Saṃpāti, king of vultures, yet I do not find her."
"Would Sītā — Vaidehī, Maithilī, daughter of Janaka — ever willingly submit to Rāvaṇa, that wicked-natured one?"
"I think the rākṣasa, fleeing swiftly in terror of Rāma's arrows while carrying Sītā, may have let her fall midway."
"Or else, while being carried along the path frequented by siddhas, the noble lady's heart may have failed upon beholding the ocean below."
"Crushed by the great speed of Rāvaṇa and pressed by his arms, I think that wide-eyed noble lady may have surrendered her life."
"Or perhaps, as Rāvaṇa traversed higher and higher over the ocean, the daughter of Janaka, writhing in his grasp, fell into the sea."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Or perhaps, while guarding her own chastity from this wretched creature, helpless Sītā, that ascetic woman, was devoured by Rāvaṇa."
"Or she of dark eyes, though herself guiltless, may have been devoured by the wives of the rākṣasa king, those women of evil intent."
"Meditating on Rāma's face — like the full moon, with eyes resembling lotus petals — that wretched woman may have perished."
"Crying out again and again 'Oh Rāma! Oh Lakṣmaṇa!' and 'Oh Ayodhyā!', Maithilī Vaidehī may have laid down her body."
"Or perhaps she is confined somewhere in Rāvaṇa's dwelling, piteously murmuring like a myna bird in a cage."
"Born in Janaka's lineage, Rāma's wife, slender-waisted, with eyes like lotus petals — how could she ever submit to Rāvaṇa's will?"
"Whether the daughter of Janaka is destroyed, disappeared, or dead — it is not proper to report such news to Rāma, who loved her as his wife."
"There would be harm in telling him; there would be harm in not telling him. What truly must be done seems difficult to discern."
"With matters thus arrived at this pass, what would be timely and proper?" Hanūmān deliberated thus at length.
"If I return from here to the city of the monkey king without having found Sītā, what human purpose will have been achieved by me?"
"This crossing of the ocean on my part will have been fruitless, as will my entry into Laṅkā and my seeing the rākṣasas."
"What will Sugrīva say, or the assembled monkeys, or those two sons of Daśaratha, when I reach Kiṣkindhā?"
"If I go and report to Kākutstha the most grievous news — that Sītā has not been found by me — he will abandon his life."
"Upon hearing those harsh, terrible, cruel, keen, sense-tormenting, ill words occasioned by Sītā, he will cease to exist."
"Seeing him plunged in anguish, his heart dissolved in death, Lakṣmaṇa — devoted to him most deeply, though wise — will not survive."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Upon hearing that both brothers are dead, Bharata too will die; and seeing Bharata dead, Śatrughna will not survive."
"Looking upon their dead sons, the mothers — Kausalyā, Sumitrā and Kaikeyī — will not survive either; of that there is no doubt."
"Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, grateful and true to his word, will abandon his life upon seeing Rāma thus departed."
"Dejected, distressed, wretched, joyless, tormented by grief for her husband, Rumā will relinquish her life."
"Afflicted by the sorrow caused by Vālin's son and worn by grief, Tārā too will not survive the king's death."
"With the loss of both his parents and Sugrīva's calamity upon him, how will prince Aṅgada maintain his life?"
"Overwhelmed by grief arising from their master's death, the forest-dwellers will beat their heads with palms and fists."
"The monkeys, who were cherished by the glorious monkey king with conciliation, gifts and honor, will cast away their lives."
"The lordly elephants among monkeys, gathered together, will sport no more in forests, on mountains, nor in groves."
"With their sons and wives and ministers, tormented by the calamity that befell their master, they will hurl themselves from mountain peaks and precipices."
"The monkeys will resort to poison, hanging, entering fire, starvation, or the sword."
"I think, if I depart without success, there will be terrible weeping, and the ruin of the Ikṣvāku lineage together with the destruction of the forest-dwellers."
"Therefore I shall not return from here to the city of Kiṣkindhā, for I cannot bear to look upon Sugrīva without Maithilī."
"If I remain here without returning, those two great warriors of righteous soul, and the spirited monkeys, will sustain themselves on hope."
"Taking food only by hand or by mouth, restrained, dwelling at the root of a tree, I shall become a forest ascetic without having found the daughter of Janaka."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"In a place beside the ocean, rich in roots and fruit, I shall build a funeral pyre and enter the fire kindled from the araṇī wood."
"Or, sitting still and properly observing the rites of one who bears the marks of renunciation, crows and beasts of prey will devour my body."
"This too is a departure approved by the seers, I believe: I shall properly enter the waters, if I do not find Jānakī."
"Well-rooted, fortunate, wreathed in glory and fame — this long-standing honor of mine is now shattered, I who have not found Sītā."
"I shall become an ascetic, restrained, dwelling at the root of a tree — I shall not return from here without finding her of dark eyes."
"If I return from here without obtaining Sītā, Aṅgada together with all the monkeys will not survive."
"In dying there are many faults; in living one attains what is good. Therefore I shall preserve my life — while one lives, reunion is certain."
"Thus repeatedly bearing many forms of anguish in his mind, that lordly elephant among monkeys could find no end to his grief."
"Or I shall slay Rāvaṇa, the mighty ten-necked one; let Sītā have been carried off — it shall be requited."
"Or else I shall seize him and carry him above the ocean to Rāma as a sacrificial beast to the lord of sacrificial beasts."
Thus the monkey, having entered upon these deliberations, not having found Sītā, his soul overwhelmed by meditative grief, continued to reflect.
"As long as I do not find Sītā, the glorious wife of Rāma, I shall search this city of Laṅkā again and again."
"And if I bring Rāma here on account of Saṃpāti's word, Rāghava, not finding his wife, would burn all the monkeys."
"I shall remain right here with measured food and restrained senses; let not all those men and monkeys perish on my account."
"There is also this great Aśoka grove with its mighty trees — I shall approach it, for it has not been searched by me."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Paying homage to the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Aśvins and the Maruts, I shall go there as one who augments the grief of the rākṣasas."
"Having conquered the rākṣasas, I shall deliver the queen, delight of the Ikṣvāku lineage, to Rāma the ascetic, proportionate to success."
Having reflected for a moment, his senses knotted with care, the mighty-armed Hanūmān, son of the Wind, arose.
"Homage to Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa; homage to that goddess, the daughter of Janaka; homage to Rudra, Indra, Yama and the Wind; homage to the Moon, the Sun and the hosts of Maruts."
Having paid those homages and to Sugrīva as well, the son of the Wind surveyed all the directions and turned toward the Aśoka grove.
Going first in his mind to the lovely Aśoka grove, the monkey, son of the Wind, then reflected further:
"Surely the Aśoka grove, well-tended with every cultivation, will be full of rākṣasas and crowded with forest creatures."
"Guards are surely appointed there to protect the trees; even the omnipresent lord of all does not blow there with excessive disturbance."
"This form of mine has been contracted for Rāma's sake and for Rāvaṇa's undoing; the gods together with the host of sages will arrange my success here."
"May Brahmā the self-born, the blessed Lord, and the gods grant me success — Agni, Vāyu, and Puruhūta the wielder of the thunderbolt."
"May Varuṇa with his noose, Soma and the Ādityas, the two great-souled Aśvins, and all the Maruts grant me success."
"May all beings grant me success, and he who is the lord of all beings, and whatever others, unseen, range along my path."
"When shall I behold that noble face — with its upturned nose, white teeth, unblemished, with a pure smile, with eyes like lotus petals, appearing like the bright full moon?"
"By that wretched, sinful, cruel-acting one, wearing a most dreadful adornment and garb — overwhelmed by force, that helpless ascetic woman: when will she come within my sight today?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having reflected for a moment and reaching it first in his mind, the greatly resplendent one leaped down to the enclosure wall of that mansion.
Standing on the enclosure wall, every limb thrilled with joy, that great monkey beheld in the early spring various trees flowering at their crests.
Śala trees, aśoka trees, bhavya trees, beautifully blossoming campaka trees, uddālaka trees, nāga trees, mango trees, and kapimukha trees as well —
— he leaped into that tree-garden dense with mango groves and entwined with hundreds of creepers, like an iron arrow loosed from a bowstring.
Entering that wondrous place resounding with birds, surrounded on all sides by silver and golden trees,
— vivid with birds and herds of deer, a grove of marvellous colors, blazing like the risen sun — Hanūmān the monkey beheld it.
Surrounded by trees of every kind laden with flowers and fruit, always frequented by intoxicated kokilas and king-crows —
— in a season delightful to the human heart, teeming with deer and birds, resounding with drunken peacocks, filled with many flocks of birds —
— while searching for that blameless princess of noble bearing, the monkey awakened birds sleeping in comfort.
Struck by the wings of the flocks of birds as they took flight, the śāla trees of many hues released showers of blossoms of every variety.
Strewn with blossoms, Hanūmān son of the Wind shone in the midst of the Aśoka grove like a mountain composed of flowers.
Seeing the monkey moving through the thickets of trees in all directions, all living beings took him for the season of spring.
Strewn with blossoms of every variety fallen from the trees, the earth there blazed like a young woman adorned.
Those trees, shaken with speed by that swift monkey, then shed their many-colored flowers.
With their crests stripped of leaves, their flowers and fruits shed, they were like rogues stripped of their garments and ornaments in defeat.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Those finest of trees, shaken by the swift Hanūmān, quickly shed their flowers, leaves and fruits — those trees so full of blossoms.
Stripped of their flocks of birds, those trees with only trunks remaining became utterly inaccessible, as if shaken by a storm-wind.
Like a young woman with her hair disheveled, her cosmetics smeared, her beautiful lips and teeth drained of color, scratched by nails and teeth —
— so the Aśoka grove, trampled by tail, hands and feet, with its fine trees broken, appeared.
The monkey swiftly scattered the garlands of great creepers as the wind scatters masses of cloud from the Vindhyas in the rainy season.
Roaming there, the monkey beheld ground paved with jewels, charming grounds paved with silver, and grounds paved with gold.
Pools of various shapes filled with the finest water, furnished here and there with stairways of precious gems —
— their sands of pearl and coral, their floors inlaid with crystal, adorned by varied golden trees growing along their banks —
— with groves of blooming lotuses and blue water-lilies, filled with the murmur of cakravāka birds, resounding with the calls of nātyūha birds, echoing with the cries of geese and cranes —
— adorned all around by long streams lined with trees whose water resembled nectar, auspicious streams —
— canopied by hundreds of creepers, covered with santānaka trees, their groves clothed in various shrubs, with spaces made by karavīra plants —
— then he beheld a mountain resembling a rain-cloud, with high peaks, with varied summits, surrounded on all sides by crests —
— canopied by caves in the rock, covered with many kinds of trees: that tiger among monkeys beheld the loveliest mountain in the world.
The monkey also beheld a river fallen from that mountain — like a beloved woman who has sprung from the lap of her beloved and fallen away.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Adorned by trees with their tops plunged into the water, she was like an angry young woman being restrained by her dear kinsmen.
That great monkey beheld her with water turning back again, like a beloved who, now clear-hearted, returns to her beloved once more.
Not far from her, that tiger among monkeys, Hanūmān son of the Wind, beheld lotus ponds filled with many flocks of birds.
He also beheld an artificial pool filled with cool water, its stairways of finest gems, adorned with sands of pearl.
Vivid with various herds of deer, with wonderful colorful groves, adorned all around by grand palaces built by Viśvakarman and by artificial woodlands —
— whatever trees were there bearing flowers and fruit, all were well-furnished with canopies and parasols, all with golden platforms.
Entwined with many spreading creepers and covered with many leaves, that great monkey beheld a single golden śiṃśupā tree.
He saw stretches of ground and gullies with springs; he saw other golden trees resembling peacocks.
By the radiance of those trees, that heroic monkey, great among monkeys, then imagined, as if by the light of Meru, that he himself had become golden.
Seeing that grove fanned by the breeze among its company of golden trees, resounding with hundreds of tinkling bells, he was filled with wonder.
The greatly swift one climbed that śiṃśupā tree — beautiful with fully flowered crest, with tender shoots and sprouts, covered with foliage —
— thinking: "From here I shall see Vaidehī, longing to behold Rāma, wandering here and there, tormented by grief, coming about by chance."
"And this Aśoka grove of the evil-souled one is truly lovely, adorned with campaka, sandalwood and bakula trees."
"And this charming lotus pool, frequented by flocks of birds — Jānakī, the great queen of Rāma, will surely come to this."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"She — Rāma's great queen, always dear to Rāghava, well-versed in roaming through forests — Jānakī will surely come here."
"Or that woman with eyes like a young deer's, knowing this forest well, she who is worn thin by thoughts of Rāma, will come to this grove."
"That goddess of lovely eyes, ever delighting in forest-dwelling, she who ever roams the forest — scorched by grief for Rāma, she will come here."
"Formerly she who is the beloved wife of Rāma, the faithful daughter of Janaka, always yearned for those who roam in the forest."
"At the time of twilight, dark-complexioned Jānakī, of noble hue, will certainly come to this auspicious river for the evening rite."
"And this auspicious Aśoka grove befits her — she who is the consort of the lord of the earth's sons and the match of Rāma."
"If that goddess lives — she whose face resembles the lord of the stars — she will certainly come to this auspicious river."
Thus reasoning, the great-souled Hanūmān, waiting and watching for the wife of the lord of men, concealed in the dense foliage of the fully blossoming tree, surveyed everything.
Standing there, searching for the daughter of Mithilā, he gazed about and surveyed all the ground around him.
He beheld it adorned with Santāna and Kalata trees, endowed with divine fragrance and flavor, beautified on every side.
It resembled Nandana, that grove — thronged with deer and birds, dense with mansions and palaces, filled with the clamorous song of cuckoos.
It was beautified by pools bearing golden lotuses and blue water-lilies, furnished with many seats and carpets, and filled with many-storied houses.
Lovely with flowers of every season and fruit-laden trees, it blazed with the splendor of blooming Aśoka trees like the light of sunrise.
Standing there, the son of Māruta gazed upon it as if blazing — its branches stripped of leaves, made so again and again by birds flying forth in hundreds, wearing blossoms as their garlands.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Aśoka trees — destroyers of sorrow — laden with blossoms from root to crown, bowed down by the weight of their flowers as if touching the earth.
With Karṇikāra trees in bloom and Kiṃśuka trees well flowering, that place seemed lit up everywhere by their radiance.
Puṃnāga, Saptaparṇa, Campaka, and Uddālaka trees — many and deep-rooted — shone beautifully, their flowers in full bloom.
Some of the Aśoka trees there, thousands of them, resembled burnished gold, some were like tongues of flame, and others were like dark collyrium.
Like Nandana, like the variegated garden of Citraratha, it surpassed even the inconceivable — divine, charming, and wrapped in beauty.
It was like a second sky filled with clusters of floral luminaries, variegated with hundreds of floral gems — like a fifth ocean.
The grove was filled with trees of sweet fragrance flowering in all seasons, charming with diverse calls of herds of deer and birds.
With currents of many fragrances, sacred in its scent, enchanting to the mind — rich in perfume like Gandhamādana, a second king of mountains.
Within that Aśoka grove, that bull among monkeys saw, not far away, a grand sanctuary-palace.
It stood in the center supported by a thousand pillars, white as Kailāsa, its stairways made of coral, its platform of molten gold.
It seemed to steal away the eyes, blazing with splendor, pure and lofty, as if scratching the sky with its height.
Then he saw her — clad in soiled garments, surrounded by rākṣasī women, emaciated by fasting, wretched, sighing again and again — pure as the crescent moon at the start of the bright fortnight.
Her beauty, though still alluring, was only faintly visible, like the flame of Agni veiled and obscured by a shroud of smoke.
Clad in a single soiled yellow garment, mud-stained and unadorned — like a lotus pond drained of its lotuses.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Ashamed, tormented by grief, withered, forlorn — like Rohiṇī afflicted by the planet Aṅgāraka.
Her face full of tears, wretched, emaciated by lack of food, absorbed in grief-stricken meditation, pitiable, constantly immersed in sorrow.
Seeing no beloved person, only crowds of rākṣasī women — like a doe separated from her own herd, surrounded by a pack of dogs.
A single braid of hair, dark as a black serpent, fallen along her hip — she who deserved only happiness, burned by grief, the very embodiment of calamity.
Observing her — wide-eyed, exceedingly soiled, emaciated — he surmised her to be Sītā, confirming it by the signs he recognized.
For this woman appeared as she had been seen when carried off by that shape-shifting rākṣasa — the very same form.
Her face was like the full moon, her brows lovely, her breasts beautifully rounded — this goddess whose radiance dispelled darkness in all directions.
Dark-haired, with lips red as Bimba fruit, slender-waisted, well-proportioned — Sītā with eyes like lotus petals, like Rati to Manmatha.
Beloved of all the world, radiant as the full moon — seated on the earth, slender, as composed as an ascetic.
Breathing heavy sighs, timid, like the wife of a great serpent-king — not shining, ensnared in a great web of grief.
Like the flame of fire obscured by a net of smoke — like a memory grown uncertain, like a prosperity that has fallen away.
Like faith that has been struck down, like hope that has been thwarted, like a siddhi beset by obstacles, like an intellect grown turbid.
Like a fame fallen by false slander — afflicted by the anguish of separation from Rāma, wasted by the abduction of the rākṣasa.
Helpless, with eyes like a young deer's, gazing here and there — her dark face with its downcast lashes filled with the water of tears, sighing again and again.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Bearing dirt and grime, wretched, worthy of adornment yet unadorned — like the light of the moon-king veiled by dark clouds.
His mind wavered repeatedly as he gazed upon her — like a sacred science grown slack through disuse.
With difficulty Hanūmān recognized Sītā unadorned — like a word devoid of proper formation that has drifted to another meaning.
Observing that wide-eyed, blameless princess, he concluded it was Sītā, establishing it by means of the signs.
The ornaments on her limbs that Rāma had described one by one — he now recognized those adornments that beautified her body.
The beautifully crafted ear-ornaments, the Śvadaṃṣṭra jewels well set, and the ornaments on her hands variegated with gems and coral.
Darkened now through long wearing, yet retaining their shape — these must be the very ones Rāma described, I believe.
Those which are absent I do not see; those which have not been lost — these are they, without doubt.
That auspicious yellow upper garment, bright as a sheet of gold, slipped off and caught in a tree — the one the monkeys had seen at the time.
And the chief ornaments seen on the ground — cast away by her very self, sounding loud and large.
This garment, more worn from long wearing, is nonetheless still of that color — as splendid as the other one.
This golden-limbed beloved queen of Rāma — even though lost, she does not perish from his mind.
She is the one for whose sake Rāma burns with four fires: compassion, tenderness, grief, and longing.
Compassion because a woman is lost; tenderness because she was his dependent; grief because his wife is gone; longing because she is his beloved.
The beauty of this goddess, the perfection of each of her limbs, and the form of Rāma — she of dark eyes is indeed worthy of him.
This goddess's mind is fixed on him, and his mind is fixed on her — it is for that reason she and that righteous-souled one each live, even for a moment.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Great-armed Rāma does what is difficult indeed — he lives even for a moment without this Sītā whose glance is intoxicating.
Having thus beheld Sītā, the son of Vāyu was overjoyed; in his mind he went to Rāma and praised that lord.
Having praised Sītā who is worthy of all praise, and Rāma who is charming with virtues, that bull among monkeys fell once again into deep reflection.
Having meditated for a moment, his eyes overflowing with tears, the splendid Hanūmān, overcome by his regard for Sītā, lamented aloud.
She who is venerable, dear to the elders, honored even by Lakṣmaṇa who is trained by his elders — if even Sītā suffers such grief, truly time is insurmountable.
The goddess, knowing the resolve of Rāma and the wise Lakṣmaṇa, is not excessively disturbed — like the Gaṅgā at the onset of rains.
Equal in character, age, and conduct, equal in lineage and mark — the Rāghava deserves the daughter of Videha, and this dark-eyed lady deserves him.
Seeing her, resplendent as fresh gold, like Śrī beloved of the world, he went to Rāma in his mind and spoke these words.
For the sake of her, this wide-eyed one, the mighty Vālī was slain and Kabandha — equal to Rāvaṇa in prowess — was struck down.
And Virādha, the rākṣasa of terrible might, was slain in battle — by Rāma striding forward in the forest as great Indra slew Śambara.
Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds were slain at Janasthāna with arrows blazing like tongues of fire.
Khara was slain in battle, Triśiras struck down, and the greatly brilliant Dūṣaṇa — by Rāma, the self-realized one.
The sovereignty of the Vānaras, difficult to obtain, guarded by Vālī — for her sake Sugrīva attained it, honored by all the world.
The illustrious ocean, lord of rivers and streams, was crossed by me, and this city was reconnoitered — all for the sake of her, this wide-eyed one.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Even if Rāma were to overturn the entire earth to its ocean-boundary for her sake, the world too would be right — such is my conviction.
Kingship over the three worlds or Sītā, daughter of Janaka — the whole sovereignty of the three worlds does not match even a fraction of Sītā's worth.
She is the daughter of the virtuous, great-souled king Janaka of Mithilā — Sītā, steadfast in her vow to her husband.
She arose from the earth, from a field furrowed by the plowshare — strewn with auspicious field-dust resembling lotus pollen.
She is the eldest and glorious daughter-in-law of King Daśaratha — who was valiant, noble in character, and never turned back in battle.
She is the beloved wife of Rāma — who knows dharma, is ever grateful, and is self-realized — now fallen into the power of a rākṣasa.
Forsaking all pleasures, driven by the strength of her love for her husband, giving no thought to hardships, she entered the uninhabited forest.
Contented with fruits and roots, devoted to serving her husband — she who found the highest joy even in the forest as if in her own home.
She, this golden-limbed one who always speaks with a sweet smile — now endures this torment, unlucky in suffering these misfortunes.
Rāghava yearns to see this virtuous woman, afflicted by Rāvaṇa — as a thirsty man yearns for a drinking place.
Surely at regaining her, the Rāghava will find joy — like a king fallen from his kingdom who regains the earth.
Abandoned by sensuous pleasures, bereft of her kinsmen, she sustains her body longing for reunion with him.
She does not see these rākṣasī women, she does not see these trees with their flowers and fruits — her heart fixed in one place, she sees only Rāma.
A husband is indeed the supreme ornament of a woman, greater than all ornaments — and deprived of him, she who deserves to shine does not shine.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāma, the lord, does what is difficult indeed — bereft of her, he sustains his body and does not sink under grief.
Seeing her — with dark ends to her hair, eyes like a hundred-petalled lotus, deserving only of happiness yet suffering — even my mind is pained.
Patient as the earth, with eyes resembling a blue lotus, she who was once protected by Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa — is now guarded at the foot of a tree by rākṣasī women with grotesque eyes.
Like a lotus-plant struck by frost, its beauty gone, oppressed by a succession of misfortunes, like a Cakravākī separated from her mate — the daughter of Janaka has fallen into a pitiable state.
Indeed, the Aśoka trees whose tips are bent with blossoms evoke a deep sorrow in her; and with winter's departure the sun has risen, his beams no longer mild but blazing in thousands.
Having pondered the matter thus, the monkey's mind settled into the certainty that this was indeed Sītā; that mighty, swift bull of the monkeys settled himself in that tree.
Then the moon — pure himself, resembling a cluster of Kumuda lotuses — moved through the clear sky, as a swan moves through dark water.
As if rendering assistance, the moon with pure luster, by his cool rays, served the son of Vāyu.
Then he saw Sītā, whose face resembled the full moon, cast down as if by the weight of her grief, like a boat weighed down upon the water.
As Hanūmān, son of Māruta, was eager to behold the daughter of Videha, he saw, not far away, rākṣasī women of terrible aspect.
One-eyed and one-eared, and others whose ears served as coverings; some with no ears, others with ears like pegs; some with nostrils set on top of the head.
Some with enormous bodies and large heads, others with thin and long necks; some with disheveled hair, some bald, others wearing a blanket of hair.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Some with pendulous ears and forehead, pendulous belly and breasts, pendulous lips or chin-like lip, pendulous face and pendulous knees.
Short and tall, hunchbacked and deformed, dwarfish and frightful, crooked in garment, tawny-eyed, with disfigured faces.
Misshapen, tawny, dark-complexioned, wrathful, fond of quarrel — bearing great iron spears, clubs, and maces.
Some with faces of boar, deer, tiger, buffalo, goat, and jackal; others with the feet of elephant, camel, and horse; some with sunken heads.
One-handed and one-footed, some with ears like a donkey's or a horse's, others with ears like a cow's or an elephant's, and yet others with ears like a lion's.
Some noseless, others with oversized noses, some with sideways noses, others entirely without nostrils; some with elephant-like noses, some with nostrils on their foreheads.
Some with elephant's feet, some with great feet, some with cow's feet, some with feet like tufts; some with excessively large heads and necks, others with excessively large breasts and belly.
Some with excessively large mouths and eyes, with long tongues and nails — some with faces of a goat, elephant, cow, or sow.
Rākṣasī women of terrible appearance with faces of horse, camel, and ass — bearing spears and clubs in their hands, wrathful, delighting in strife.
Terrible and smoke-haired rākṣasī women with disfigured faces, constantly drinking, always fond of flesh and wine.
Their bodies smeared with flesh and blood, feeding on flesh and blood — those were the ones that best of monkeys saw, dreadful to behold, causing the hair to stand on end.
Seated around a great shouldering forest tree, encircling it — and beneath it that blameless goddess and princess.
The auspicious Hanūmān fixed his gaze on the daughter of Janaka — lustrous no longer, scorched by grief, her hair matted and filthy.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
As if a star fallen to earth with exhausted merit — rich in the renown of her virtue yet reduced to misery by separation from her husband's sight.
Deprived of her finest ornaments, yet adorned by her husband's love — confined by the lord of rākṣasas, separated from all her kin.
Separated from her herd, hemmed in by a lion, like an elephant cow in bondage — like the crescent of the moon veiled at the edge of clouds by autumn clouds.
Her beauty worn away from lack of touch, like a lute neglected and unplayed — Sītā, devoted to her husband's welfare, unfitting to be under the dominion of rākṣasas.
In the midst of the Aśoka grove, plunged in an ocean of grief, surrounded by those rākṣasī women — like Rohiṇī seized by a planet — Hanūmān saw the goddess, like a creeper stripped of its flowers.
Her body smeared with grime, yet adorned by natural beauty — like a lotus-stalk besmeared with mud, she both shines and does not shine.
The monkey Hanūmān saw that radiant one, doe-eyed, wrapped in a soiled and worn garment.
That goddess with a wretched face, yet inwardly undaunted, protected by her husband's glory and by her own virtue — Sītā of dark eyes.
Seeing Sītā, with eyes resembling those of a young deer, frightened like a young doe, gazing in all directions —
— as if scorching with her sighs the trees bearing new shoots, like a mass of sorrows embodied, like a wave of anguish arisen —
— emaciated, yet with well-proportioned limbs, beautiful even without ornaments —
— the son of Māruta felt an incomparable joy on beholding the daughter of Mithilā; and seeing her of intoxicating eyes, Hanūmān shed tears born of joy, and there he bowed to the Rāghava.
And having bowed to Rāma and to Lakṣmaṇa, that mighty Hanūmān, exhilarated at the sight of Sītā, composed himself.
As he gazed about the grove with its flowering trees and searched for Vaidehī, only a small portion of the night remained.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
In the deep of night he heard the Vedic chanting of Brahmā-rākṣasas — those versed in the six ancillaries of the Veda and sacrificers at the foremost rites.
Then, with the auspicious sounds of musical instruments pleasing to ear and mind, the mighty-armed, greatly powerful Daśagrīva was awakened.
Awakening at the proper hour, the lord of rākṣasas yawned and stretched; his garlands and garments dishevelled, he turned his mind to Vaidehī.
Mightily goaded by the god of love and overcome with passion for her, that rākṣasa could not conceal the desire within himself.
Adorned with every ornament and bearing an unrivalled splendour, he set out toward that garden frequented by various trees laden with every fruit and flower,
surrounded by lotus-ponds adorned with manifold blossoms, filled with perpetually intoxicated birds — a garden wondrous and supremely marvellous.
Encircled by diverse creatures delightful to the eye, and beholding the avenues with their archways of jewels and gold,
he entered the Aśoka grove — densely wooded, thronged with herds of various animals, and carpeted with fallen fruits.
A full hundred women followed him as he walked — that descendant of Pulastya — just as the women of gods and gandharvas follow great Indra.
Some women there took up golden lamps, others held young fly-whisks in their hands, and yet others carried palm-leaf fans.
Some carried water in golden pitchers and went before him; others took up broad-edged swords and followed behind.
One fair lady then took up with her right hand a jewel-studded bowl filled with drink.
Another took up a parasol resembling a royal swan, bright as the full moon, with a golden staff, and went behind him.
Rāvaṇa's noble wives, their eyes heavy with sleep and intoxication, followed their heroic lord as lightning-creepers follow a storm-cloud.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the monkey, son of the Wind, heard the jingling of girdles and the tinkling of anklets of those foremost women.
The monkey Hanūmān saw him — that one of matchless deeds and inconceivable strength and valour — as he reached the gateway.
He was illuminated on all sides by numerous lamps soaked in fragrant oil and held aloft before him.
His eyes oblique, coppery, and wide — suffused with desire, pride, and passion — he appeared like Kāmadeva himself who had cast aside his bow.
His finest garment — white as the foam of churned nectar and free of dust — trailed gracefully behind him, caught loosely on his armlet.
Concealed in the foliage of a branch, hidden by the dense mass of leaves and flowers, Hanūmān began to observe him as he drew near.
As he looked on, that elephant among monkeys saw Rāvaṇa's beautiful women, endowed with beauty and youth.
The king of great renown, encircled by those lovely women, entered the pleasure-grove resounding with the calls of deer and birds.
Intoxicated, adorned with variegated ornaments, with sharp ears, and greatly powerful — this son of Viśravas, the lord of rākṣasas, was thus seen.
Surrounded by those foremost women as the moon is by stars, the greatly resplendent great monkey beheld him — that one of great splendour.
"This is the mighty-armed Rāvaṇa" — thinking thus, the greatly resplendent Hanūmān, son of the Wind, leapt down.
Yet though himself of fierce energy, Hanūmān was overwhelmed by Rāvaṇa's radiance and remained hidden, clinging concealed within the shelter of a leafy hollow.
Rāvaṇa turned and drew near, wishing to behold her — she of dark tresses, beautiful hips, full breasts, and dark-cornered eyes.
At that very moment the blameless princess — she who is endowed with beauty and youth — saw him adorned with the finest of ornaments:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
upon seeing Rāvaṇa, the lord of rākṣasas, Vaidehī — she of noble stature — trembled like a plantain tree in the wind.
Covering her belly with her thighs and her breasts with her arms, the wide-eyed, fair-complexioned woman sat weeping.
Daśagrīva beheld Vaidehī, guarded by the throng of rākṣasī women — wretched, tormented by grief, like a sinking boat upon the ocean.
Seated on the bare ground, firm in her vow, her limbs smeared with dirt in lieu of adornment — she who deserved adornment yet wore none — like a broken branch fallen to the earth from a forest tree.
She seemed to travel on the horses of resolve and longing toward the presence of Rāma — that lion among kings, the knower of the self.
Wasting away, weeping, alone, absorbed in meditation and grief, seeing no end to her sorrow — she who was utterly devoted to Rāma.
Writhing and afflicted — like the wife of the serpent-lord in his coils — tormented as Rohiṇī is by a comet in the grip of a planet.
Born of a family of noble conduct, in a lineage virtuous and righteous — yet brought to such refinement as though born anew in a low family.
Like great fame that has faded, like faith that has been dishonoured, like wisdom that has dwindled, like hope that has been thwarted.
Like a prosperous future destroyed, like a command countermanded, like a direction blazing bright whose time has passed, like an act of worship stolen away.
Like a lotus-pond laid waste, like an army whose heroes have been slain, like a radiance undone by ascetic's curse, like a river running thin.
Like a sacrificial altar defiled, like a flame of fire extinguished, like the full-moon night whose lunar disc is seized by Rāhu.
Like a lotus-pond thrown into confusion — its lotus leaves plucked out, its birds frightened away, disturbed by an elephant's trunk.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Tormented by grief for her husband, withered — like a river drained dry, bereft of all luster, like the night of the dark fortnight.
Delicate, with perfectly formed limbs, fit to dwell in a gem-studded inner chamber — yet scorched as a lotus-stalk only recently uprooted burns in the heat.
Seized and chained to a post, separated from the lord of the herd — sighing, deeply tormented by grief — like the wife of the elephant-king.
Beautiful without effort, adorned by a single long dark braid — like the earth at the passing of the rain-clouds, clothed in a kingdom of forest.
Wasted away by fasting, grief, meditation, and fear — emaciated, wretched, eating little, rich only in austerity.
Afflicted with grief, hands folded like a deity imploring — she prayed with all her being for Rāma, the foremost of the Raghus, to vanquish Daśagrīva.
Gazing and weeping, blameless, her eyes fringed with fine lashes — coppery, wide, and white — utterly devoted to Rāma: Maithilī thus inflamed Rāvaṇa exceedingly, to his own destruction.
Rāvaṇa addressed her — who was surrounded, wretched, joyless, and afflicted — with words that were sweet and full of expressive gestures.
"Upon seeing me, you cover your thighs and belly with your arms, as if wishing out of fear to render yourself invisible."
"I desire you, wide-eyed one; hold me in high regard, my dear — you who are endowed with perfection of every limb, enchanting to all the worlds."
"There are no humans here, nor rākṣasas who take any shape they will. Let the fear that has arisen in you from me depart, O Sītā."
"Among rākṣasas, O timid one, this is in every way their proper law — beyond doubt: either going to the wives of others or carrying them away by force."
"Yet being such, I will not touch you against your will, O Maithilī; let desire play freely in my body as it pleases — but I will not act."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Lady, there is nothing to fear here; place your trust in me, my dear, and give me your love truly — do not thus languish in sorrow."
"A single braid, a bed upon the ground, meditation, soiled garments, and fasting even without purpose — these are not fitting for you."
"Colourful garlands, sandalwood paste, aloe-wood, garments of many kinds, and divine ornaments —"
"— the most precious drinks, conveyances, beds, song, dance, and music: obtain all these by accepting me, O Maithilī."
"You are a jewel among women — do not be thus; adorn your limbs with ornaments. How could you be unworthy, you of such beauty, having attained me?"
"This your youth — so exquisitely arisen — is passing away; that which is past never returns, like the swift current of waters."
"I believe that having made you, the creator of form — the maker of the universe — rested from his labour; for no other exists equal to you in beauty, O fair to behold."
"Having encountered you, O Vaidehī — resplendent with beauty and youth — what man could remain unmoved? Even the Grandfather himself, Brahmā, could not."
"On each and every part of your body that I behold — O you whose face is like the cool-rayed moon, O broad-hipped one — my gaze becomes fixed."
"Become my wife, O Maithilī — cast aside this folly; become the chief queen among the many foremost women I possess."
"All the jewels that have been seized and brought by me from the worlds — all of these are yours, O timid one; this kingdom is yours, and I am yours."
"Having conquered the entire earth, garlanded with its many cities, I shall give it to Janaka for your sake, O graceful one."
"I see no other in this world who could be my equal in strength; behold my exceedingly great valour — without adversary in battle."
"Again and again in battle, gods and asuras alike have been routed by me, their banners crushed — unable to stand against my forces."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Desire me; let the finest adornment be done to you today; let the radiant ornaments be fastened upon your limbs — I see your beauty perfectly suited to such adorning."
"Adorned with all manner of adornment, gracious in bearing, O fair-faced one — enjoy pleasures as you wish, drink, take delight, O timid one, and bestow as you please — even the earth and its wealth."
"Revel in me with confidence and boldly command me; and through my power, as you flourish, let your kinsmen also flourish."
"Behold my prosperity, my glory, and my renown, O fortunate one; what will you do with Rāma, O beautiful one — Rāma who wears bark-cloth?"
"Rāma has renounced his victory, his glory is gone, he wanders the forest, bound by a vow, sleeping on the bare ground — I doubt whether he even lives."
"Rāma will neither see you nor obtain you, O Vaidehī — as a swarm of dark cranes before the clouds conceals the moonlight."
"Nor does Rāghava deserve to recover you from my hands — as Hiraṇyakaśipu could not recover the glory that had passed into Indra's hands."
"O you of lovely smile, lovely teeth, lovely eyes — O graceful one — you steal my mind, O timid one, as Garuḍa seizes a serpent."
"Having seen you — slender, unadorned, clad in a soiled silk garment — I find no pleasure in my own wives."
"However many women dwell in my inner apartments, endowed with every virtue — exercise sovereignty over all of them, O Jānakī."
"For among my dark-tressed women are the foremost ladies of the three worlds; they shall wait upon you as the Apsarases attend upon Śrī."
"The jewels and wealth that belong to Vaiśravaṇa — those, and the worlds themselves, and me, O lovely-browed, broad-hipped one — enjoy all at your pleasure."
"Rāma is not my equal, O lady — not in asceticism, not in strength, not in valour, not in wealth, not in energy, nor in glory."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Drink, roam freely, take delight, enjoy pleasures; I give you wealth in abundance and the earth itself — revel in me at your pleasure, O graceful one, and let your kinsmen gather around you and revel in you."
"Your limbs adorned with necklaces of pure gold, roam with me through the forests along the seashore — forests draped in networks of flowering trees, humming with bees, O timid one."
Having heard the words of that fierce rākṣasa, Sītā, afflicted and with a pitiful voice, softly spoke words of distress in reply.
Sītā, tormented by grief, weeping, trembling, that afflicted woman of noble bearing — devoted wife that she was — thought only of her husband.
Placing a blade of grass between herself and him, she of pure smile replied: "Turn your mind away from me; fix your mind instead upon your own people."
"You are no more fit to desire me than a sinner is fit to attain liberation. I shall not do what must not be done — I am a woman of one husband; having reached a censurable family, born myself in a great and virtuous lineage."
Having spoken thus, Vaidehī — that illustrious woman — turned her back on that rākṣasa Rāvaṇa and spoke again.
"I am another man's wife — I am not a fitting wife for you. Look to righteousness properly; observe the vow of the virtuous properly."
"Just as your own wives are to be protected, so too are the wives of others, O night-wanderer. Taking yourself as the measure, find delight with your own wives."
"The wives of other men bring ruin to one who is unsatisfied with his own wives, who is fickle with unsteady senses, whose understanding is base."
"Either there are no virtuous men here, or you do not heed the virtuous — your soul is led astray, and you do not follow what the wise have declared to be salutary."
"Prosperous kingdoms and cities perish when they obtain a king who has not mastered himself and who delights in unrighteousness."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"So too will this Laṅkā, filled with multitudes of jewels, soon perish because of your single transgression."
"When one of evil deeds is being slain by the fruits of his own actions, O Rāvaṇa of short sight, all creatures rejoice at his destruction."
"Thus will wronged people speak of you, the evil-doer, rejoicing: 'By fate this calamity has come upon the fierce one.'"
"I cannot be tempted by sovereignty or wealth. I am inseparable from Rāghava, as radiance is inseparable from the sun."
"Having rested my head upon the honored arm of that lord of the world, how could I ever rest it upon the arm of any other?"
"I am the fitting wife of that lord of the earth alone — as sacred learning belongs to a brahmin who has bathed at the completion of his vow and who has known the Self."
"Do right, Rāvaṇa: restore me, afflicted as I am, to Rāma, as the lord of elephants returns to his she-elephant calling in the forest."
"That bull among men, Rāma, is one whose friendship is well worth seeking by you who desire your position to endure and who would avoid a terrible death."
"One might escape the thunderbolt once hurled; one might long escape Death itself — but that Rāghava, lord of the world, when enraged, one of your kind could not escape."
"You will hear the great roar of Rāma's bow — like the crash of a thunderbolt released by Indra of a hundred sacrifices."
"Here, soon, arrows bearing the mark of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa — well-jointed, with blazing heads like serpents — will rain down."
"Those arrows, feathered with vulture-plumes, falling everywhere in this city and slaying rākṣasas on all sides, will leave no room for flight."
"That great Garuḍa Rāma will swiftly pluck up the great serpents that are the lords of the rākṣasas, as Vainateya plucks up serpents."
"My husband, the subduer of foes, will swiftly recover me from you, as Viṣṇu recovered the blazing royal splendor from the asuras with his three strides."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"In Janasthāna, that destroyed place, when the host of rākṣasas was slain, this evil deed was done by you who were powerless to face them directly."
"Entering the empty hermitage of those two lion-men while the two brothers had gone to their hunting grounds — thus were you able to carry me off, O vile one."
"You could no more stand in the presence of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa — having merely caught their scent — than a dog could stand before two tigers."
"In battle against those two, your wrestling hold would be as unstable as the seizure of Indra's arms by Vṛtra — only to be overcome by a single arm."
"That lord of mine, Rāma, together with Saumitri, will swiftly take your life with his arrows, as the sun dries up a small pool of water."
"Whether you go to Kubera's mountain or to Vālin's realm, or enter the court of King Varuṇa — you will assuredly not escape from the son of Daśaratha, as a great tree struck down by time does not escape the thunderbolt."
Having heard Sītā's harsh words, the lord of rākṣasas then replied to Sītā — that beautiful-looking woman — with words she would not wish to hear.
"The more a man is gentle and yielding to women, the more he is dominated; the more he speaks what is pleasing, the more he is treated with contempt."
"The desire that has arisen for you restrains my anger, as a skilled charioteer controls galloping horses on the road."
"Love is perverse among humans — it is said that toward the very person in whom one is bound by passion, compassion and affection arise."
"For this reason I do not destroy you, O beautiful-faced one — though you deserve death and disgrace, you who delight in a false renunciation."
"For each and every harsh word you speak to me, a terrible death would befit you, O Maithilī."
Having spoken thus to Vaidehī, Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas, filled with the fury of anger, spoke further to Sītā.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Two months — the term I have set for you — are to be preserved by me. After that, O woman of splendid complexion, you must ascend my bed."
"If, after two months have passed, you still refuse to take me as your husband, my cooks will prepare you as my morning meal."
Seeing Jānakī being threatened by the lord of rākṣasas, those large-eyed daughters of gods and gandharvas were deeply distressed.
Some comforted Sītā — thus threatened by that rākṣasa — with gestures of their lips, others with expressions of their eyes and faces.
Comforted by them, Sītā spoke words beneficial to herself to Rāvaṇa, the lord of rākṣasas, proud of her conduct and virtue.
"Surely there is no one in your company who stands devoted to your highest good — no one who restrains you from this censurable deed."
"Who other than you in all three worlds would even desire me in his mind — the wife of the righteous-souled one, as Śacī belongs to her lord Indra?"
"O vilest of rākṣasas, you have spoken sin against the wife of Rāma of boundless glory — wherever you flee, how will you escape its consequence?"
"As a proud elephant and a hare stand together in the forest, so Rāma is to be reckoned as the elephant and you, O lowly one, as the hare."
"You who revile the lord of the Ikṣvākus here feel no shame — you have not even come within range of his sight."
"These cruel, ugly, dark-reddish eyes of yours — why have they not fallen to the ground, since with them, unworthy as you are, you have gazed at me?"
"O sinner, how does your tongue not crumble as you address me — the wife of that righteous-souled one, the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha?"
"Only because Rāma has given me no such command, and out of preservation of my austerity, do I not reduce you, O ten-necked one, to ashes with my own blazing power."
"I cannot truly be carried off from that wise Rāma. Fate has ordained your destruction — of this there is no doubt."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You who are the brother of Kubera, endowed with heroism and forces — why did you resort to the theft of a wife by luring Rāma away?"
Having heard Sītā's words, Rāvaṇa, the lord of rākṣasas, widening his cruel eyes, gazed at Jānakī.
He was dark as a storm-cloud, with mighty arms and neck, moving with the bearing of a lion, resplendent, with a flaming tongue and fierce eyes.
His towering crown swayed; he was tall, adorned with variegated garlands and unguents, wearing red garlands and garments, and ornamented with blazing armlets.
He was well girt with a great waist-cord made with the mekaka-jewel, bound with the serpent that had produced the nectar of immortality, like Mount Mandara encircled by a serpent.
He was adorned with earrings the color of the newly-risen sun, like a mountain adorned with red-tipped blossoms of the aśoka tree.
Gazing at Vaidehī with eyes reddened by anger, Rāvaṇa spoke to Sītā, hissing like a serpent.
"You who are possessed of unrighteousness, bereft of good judgment, following your vow — I shall destroy you this very day, as the sun destroys the twilight with his brilliance."
Having spoken thus to Maithilī, King Rāvaṇa — the destroyer of enemies — then commanded all the rākṣasī guards of terrible appearance.
He commanded the one-eyed one, the one-eared one, and the one whose ears served as a cloak; the cow-eared, the elephant-eared, the pendant-eared, and the earless one.
He commanded the elephant-footed ones, the dog-footed ones, the cow-footed, and the one with feet small as a talon; the one-eyed one, the one-legged, the broad-footed, and the footless.
He commanded those with exceedingly large heads and necks, those with exceedingly large breasts and bellies, those with exceedingly large mouths and eyes; the long-tongued, the tongueless, the noseless, those with lion-faces, cow-faces, and pig-faces.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Do whatever must be done, all of you rākṣasīs, gathering quickly, so that Jānakī Sītā swiftly comes under my control."
"Turn Vaidehī around by contrary and favorable means, by conciliation, by gifts, and by the threat of punishment."
Having thus commanded them again and again, the lord of rākṣasas, his soul consumed by passion and fury, threatened Jānakī repeatedly.
Then the rākṣasī Dhānyamālinī quickly approached and, embracing the ten-necked one, spoke these words.
"Sport with me, O great king — what use is this Sītā to you? When one who desires courts an unwilling woman, his body is tormented; when one who desires courts a willing woman, joy is fair and full."
Thus addressed by the rākṣasī, that mighty one was lifted up and entered the inner dwelling that blazed with the radiance of the sun.
Then those daughters of gods, gandharvas, and nāgas surrounded the ten-necked one and entered that excellent mansion.
Having threatened Maithilī — who stood firm in her devotion to righteousness, trembling — Rāvaṇa, deluded by passion, abandoned Sītā and entered his own luminous dwelling.
Having spoken thus to Maithilī and having commanded all the rākṣasīs, King Rāvaṇa — the destroyer of enemies — departed.
When the lord of rākṣasas had gone out and returned to the inner apartments, those rākṣasīs of terrible form rushed at Sītā.
Then those rākṣasīs, maddened with rage, approached Sītā and spoke these words to Vaidehī in the harshest of tones.
"Sītā, you do not think highly of becoming the wife of the most excellent Paulastya — the great-souled Rāvaṇa, the ten-necked one."
Then a rākṣasī named Ekajaṭā, red-eyed with anger, addressed Sītā — whose palms were as tender as her belly — and spoke these words.
"Among the six progenitors, the fourth lord of creatures is Pulastya — the mind-born son of Brahmā, renowned by that name."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"And of Pulastya's mind-born son is the illustrious great sage Viśravā by name, equal in splendor to a lord of creatures."
"His son is Rāvaṇa, the destroyer of enemies, O wide-eyed one. You deserve to become the wife of that lord of rākṣasas. The words I have spoken, O beautiful-limbed one — why do you not consent to them?"
Then a rākṣasī named Harijaṭā, with eyes like a cat's, widening them in anger, spoke these words.
"By whom the thirty-three gods and even the king of gods were conquered — you deserve to become the wife of that lord of rākṣasas."
"Of one who is filled with valor, a hero who never retreats from battle, who is powerful and endowed with might — why would you not attain the status of wife?"
"Setting aside his beloved and highly-regarded wives, that king of great might, Rāvaṇa — greatest among all — will come to you."
"Abandoning the inner apartments filled with a thousand women, adorned with jewels of every kind, Rāvaṇa will come to you."
"He who has repeatedly defeated in battle gods, nāgas, gandharvas, and dānavas in combat — he has come to your side."
"Of that great-souled Rāvaṇa, fully prosperous in every way — why do you not desire, O base one, to be the wife of the lord of rākṣasas?"
"The sun does not burn out of fear of him; the wind does not blow in his presence — O woman of lovely glances, why do you not submit to him?"
"Trees out of fear of him let fall a rain of flowers; mountains yield water whenever he wishes; clouds yield rain at his will — O beautiful-browed one."
"Of that king of the nairṛtas, the king of kings, O passionate woman — why do you not turn your mind to becoming the wife of Rāvaṇa?"
"What has been truly told to you, O goddess, is truly well spoken, O passionate one. Accept these words, O sweet-smiling one — otherwise, things will not go well for you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the rākṣasīs, hideous of face, approached Sītā, and those harsh women spoke harsh and unpleasant words to her.
"Sītā, why do you not consent to live in this inner palace — delightful to all beings and furnished with the most worthy couches?"
"You are a mortal woman, and you prize so highly being the wife of a mere mortal. Turn your mind away from Rāma — you will never be his again."
"You are a mortal woman, yet you desire that mortal Rāma — he who has been cast out of his kingdom, whose purpose has not been accomplished, and who is miserable and forlorn, O blameless one."
Having heard the words of the rākṣasīs, Sītā, lotus-eyed, with both eyes brimming with tears, spoke these words.
"What you all say together is hateful to the world; that sinful speech does not take root in my mind."
"A mortal woman does not deserve to be the wife of a rākṣasa. Eat me if you will, all of you — I will not do your bidding. Whether destitute or stripped of his kingdom, whoever is my husband is my lord."
Having heard Sītā's words, the rākṣasīs, overwhelmed with rage and urged on by Rāvaṇa, began to threaten her with harsh words.
Hanūmān, hidden and silent in the śiṃśapā tree, heard those rākṣasīs as they fiercely threatened Sītā.
Rushing at her furiously from all sides as she trembled, they licked their blazing, protruding lips again and again.
And utterly enraged, quickly brandishing their battle-axes, they said: "She does not deserve Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, as her husband."
She — the lovely-faced one — being menaced by those terrible rākṣasīs, wiping away her tears, drew near to that śiṃśapā tree.
Then Sītā, wide-eyed, surrounded by the rākṣasīs, approached that śiṃśapā and stood there, utterly submerged in grief.
Those terrible rākṣasīs fell to threatening her on all sides — her who was thin, wearing a dejected face, and clad in soiled garments.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then a rākṣasī named Vinatā, fearsome to behold, gaunt-bellied and fierce, with the bearing of one enraged, addressed her.
"Sītā, enough — you have shown your love for your husband sufficiently. O auspicious one, excess in all things leads to ruin."
"I am satisfied; well done, the rites due to your mortal husband have been observed. But heed also my words, O Maithilī, who speak for your benefit."
"Embrace Rāvaṇa as your husband — the lord of all rākṣasas, valiant and handsome, like Vāsava the king of gods."
"Forsake the wretched mortal Rāma — noble, generous, and dear-speaking though he be to all — and seek refuge in Rāvaṇa."
"O Vaidehī, anointed with divine perfumes, adorned with divine ornaments, become from this day the mistress of all the worlds — as Svāhā is to Agni, as Śacī to Indra, O beautiful one."
"What is Rāma to you, O Vaidehī — that wretched man whose lifespan is spent?"
"And if you do not act on the words I have spoken, we will devour you this very instant, all of us together."
Then another, named Vikaṭā, with dangling pendulous breasts, angered and roaring, raised her fist and addressed Sītā.
"Many unseemly words from you, O foolish one, have been endured by us out of compassion and gentleness, O Maithilī — yet you still do not act on our timely, beneficial counsel."
"You have been brought by others across the ocean, which is difficult to traverse; you have entered the terrible inner palace of Rāvaṇa, O Maithilī."
"Confined in Rāvaṇa's house and well-guarded by us, not even Purandara himself in person is capable of rescuing you."
"Do as I say, O Maithilī, for I speak what is beneficial. Enough of these flowing tears — abandon this purposeless grief."
"Embrace joy and delight; give up this perpetual wretchedness. Sītā, sport with the king of the rākṣasas as you please."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For you know, O timid one, how fleeting is the youth of women. Before it slips away from you, enjoy pleasure."
"Roam the lovely gardens and mountain-groves together with the king of the rākṣasas, O you of intoxicating eyes."
"Seven thousands of women will remain at your command, O beautiful one. Embrace Rāvaṇa as your husband, the lord of all rākṣasas."
"Or I shall tear out your heart and devour it, O Maithilī, if you do not act on the words I have spoken as I have told you."
Then a rākṣasī named Caṇḍodarī, cruel in appearance, whirling a great spear, spoke these words.
"Upon seeing this woman with eyes like those of a doe, her breasts trembling in terror, abducted by Rāvaṇa, a great craving seized me."
"My mind is set on devouring her liver, her spleen, her heart with its vessels, her entrails, and her head too."
Then a rākṣasī named Praghasā spoke: "Why do we wait? Let us squeeze the throat of this cruel woman."
"Then let it be reported to the king that the mortal woman is dead. There is no doubt he will say: 'Eat her then.'"
Then a rākṣasī named Ajāmukhī spoke: "Slaughter her, then make even morsels of everything."
"Then let us all divide the portions — I have no liking for quarreling. Let drink be fetched quickly, and garlands of many kinds in abundance."
Then a rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā spoke: "What Ajāmukhā has said is exactly what pleases me too."
"And let wine be quickly brought — the destroyer of all sorrow. Having obtained this human flesh, let us dance at the Nikumbhilā shrine."
Thus threatened in this manner by those utterly terrible rākṣasīs, Sītā — who resembled the daughter of a god — abandoned her composure and wept.
As those unsightly rākṣasīs spoke many harsh and dreadful words in this way, the daughter of Janaka wept.
But Vaidehī, that high-minded woman, thus addressed by the rākṣasīs, spoke in a voice choked with tears, utterly trembling with fear.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"A mortal woman does not deserve to become the wife of a rākṣasa. Eat me, all of you, if you will — I will not do your bidding."
She, Sītā — who resembled the daughter of a god — standing in the midst of the rākṣasīs, found no peace, afflicted by grief and threatened by Rāvaṇa.
Sītā shuddered violently, as though her own limbs were failing her — like a doe separated from her herd in the forest and harassed by cuckoos.
She, supporting herself on a large flowering branch of the aśoka tree, thought with grief of her husband, her heart broken.
She, bathing her ample breasts with the flow of tears from her eyes, could find no end to her grief even as she reflected.
Trembling like a plantain tree fallen in a gust of wind, stricken with fear of the rākṣasīs, she became pale of face.
Then the long, thick braid of trembling Sītā was seen quivering like a serpent crawling along.
She, sighing deeply, afflicted by suffering, her senses struck down by grief, distressed, shed tears — Maithilī lamented.
"Ah, Rāma!" she cried, afflicted by pain, then again "Ah, Lakṣmaṇa! Ah, my mother-in-law Kausalyā! Ah, Sumitrā, dear to me!"
"This saying repeated by the wise is indeed true: death is hard to come by at the wrong time, whether for a woman or a man."
"For here I am, tormented by these cruel rākṣasīs in this place, living — bereft of Rāma, suffering — even for a single moment."
"I, this one of little merit, wretched, shall perish without a protector, like a fully laden boat struck by the force of wind in the middle of the ocean."
"Not seeing that husband of mine, having fallen under the power of rākṣasīs, I sink in grief like a river-bank undermined by water."
"Blessed are those who see my lord — he of lotus-petal eyes, lion-like gait, grateful, and dear of speech."
"Bereft in every way of that Rāma of high-souled wisdom, my life is as hard to sustain as though I had swallowed sharp poison."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"What sin did I commit in a previous birth, in another body, on account of which I incur this terrible and most dreadful suffering?"
"Enveloped in great grief, I wish to abandon my life — guarded as I am by rākṣasīs, Rāma cannot be reached by me."
"Shame indeed upon being mortal, shame upon being under another's power — that one cannot abandon life of one's own free will."
Speaking thus, with her face streaming with tears, the young daughter of Janaka, her face cast downward, began to lament.
Grieving, like one maddened, like one bewildered, like one whose mind has wandered, she turned about and rolled upon the ground like a young mare.
"I, belonging to the ever-vigilant Rāghava, have been seized and forcibly brought by the rākṣasa Rāvaṇa, who changes his form at will, though I cried out."
"Having fallen under the power of the rākṣasīs, menaced in a most dreadful manner, reflecting on all this and afflicted by the deepest sorrow, I dare not live."
"I have no use for life, nor for riches, nor for ornaments, dwelling in the midst of rākṣasīs without Rāma, the great warrior."
"Shame on me, ignoble and wicked — who preserves her life even for a moment, having been separated from him; living this sinful life."
"What faith do I have in life or in happiness, without that dear husband of mine, beloved of all the earth bounded by the ocean?"
"Let my body be torn apart or devoured — I am giving it up. For I could not long endure this suffering bereft of my beloved."
"I would not touch the night-wanderer Rāvaṇa even with my left foot — how then could I desire that contemptible one?"
"He who is cruel by nature and desires to court me does not know he has been rejected, nor does he know himself or his own lineage."
"Cut to pieces, torn asunder, divided, or cast into blazing fire — I would still not submit to Rāvaṇa. What is the use of this babble to you at length?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Rāghava is renowned as wise, grateful, and compassionate, virtuous in conduct. I suspect it is from the exhaustion of my own fortune that he shows no compassion."
"He who alone drove away fourteen thousand rākṣasas at Janasthāna — why does that one not come to me?"
"I am confined by Rāvaṇa, a rākṣasa of little true valor. My husband is indeed capable of slaying Rāvaṇa in battle."
"He by whom Virādha, that bull among rākṣasas, was slain in battle in the Daṇḍaka forest — why does that Rāma not come to me?"
"Indeed this Laṅkā in the midst of the ocean may be difficult to assail, yet there exists no obstacle to the passage of Rāghava's arrows."
"What then is the reason why Rāma, of firm valor, does not come for his beloved wife who has been abducted by a rākṣasa?"
"I suspect that Lakṣmaṇa's elder brother does not know I am here. For knowing it, that fiery hero would not tolerate this violation."
"Even the king of the vultures, Jaṭāyu, who found me and would have reported to Rāghava that I had been taken away, has been struck down in battle by Rāvaṇa."
"A great deed was done by old Jaṭāyu, who at that time came to my aid and stood in single combat against Rāvaṇa."
"If that Rāghava knew I am here in this state, he would today, with his arrows, enraged, rid the world of rākṣasas."
"He would scatter the city of Laṅkā and dry up the great ocean, and he would destroy the name and fame of the vile Rāvaṇa."
"Then, searching out the Laṅkā of the rākṣasas, Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa would without doubt cause rākṣasī women in every house, their lords slain, to weep just as I weep now."
"For no enemy seen by those two survives even for an instant. Before long, this Laṅkā would become like a cremation ground, its pathways dense with funeral-pyre smoke and circles of vultures."
"Before long I shall attain my heart's desire. These omens of evil portent foretell the reversal of fortune for all of you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"As for the inauspicious signs that are visible in Laṅkā — before long she will be robbed of her splendor."
"Surely, when the sinful Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, is slain, Laṅkā, formerly invincible, will wither like a widow woman."
"The city of Laṅkā, once prosperous with festivities and celebrations, rākṣasas and all, will become a city whose lord is lost, like a woman whose husband has perished."
"Surely before long I shall hear here the sounds of rākṣasa daughters weeping in grief in every house."
"The city of Laṅkā will be plunged in darkness, stripped of its radiance, its great rākṣasa warriors slain, consumed by Rāma's arrows."
"If only that hero Rāma of red-cornered eyes would come to know that I am dwelling here in Rāvaṇa's abode."
"But the term that was set for me by this cruel and base Rāvaṇa — that time has now arrived."
"These Nairṛtas, doers of evil, who do not know what should not be done — from their unrighteousness a great catastrophe will soon befall."
"These rākṣasas, flesh-eaters, do not know what is right. Surely the rākṣasa will prepare me as his morning meal."
"How shall I, utterly grief-stricken, carry on without him — without seeing that Rāma, lovely to behold, with red-cornered eyes?"
"If there were someone here today who could give me poison, I would quickly behold the god Vaivasvata, separated as I am from my husband."
"That Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa's elder brother, does not know I am alive; for if those two knew, they would not fail to search for me across all the earth."
"Surely that hero, the elder of Lakṣmaṇa, has departed from here to the world of the gods, abandoning his body on the earth, out of grief for me alone."
"Blessed are the gods together with the gandharvas, the siddhas and the great seers, who behold my lord Rāma of lotus eyes."
"Or perhaps for the sake of that wise Rāma, devoted to dharma, that royal sage of the highest spirit — for his sake, as his wife —"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"— when seen, he would rejoice; when unseen, there is no friendship. Ingrates destroy, but Rāma will not destroy."
"Do I then have no virtues whatsoever, or is it the exhaustion of my fortune, that I, Sītā, am separated from Rāma who deserves the best, I who am so passionate?"
"Better for me to die than to live, bereft as I am of that great-souled Rāma of unblemished conduct, that hero who destroys enemies."
"Or perhaps those two best of men, the brothers, have laid down their weapons and roam the forest living on roots and fruits, wandering through the wilderness."
"Or perhaps those two heroes, the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, have been slain by deception by the evil-souled lord of rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa."
"I, with matters having come to this pass, wish in every way to die — yet death is not ordained for me even as I endure this suffering."
"Truly blessed are those great-souled sages who are honored as truthful, who have conquered the self, the greatly fortunate ones, for whom pleasant and unpleasant do not exist."
"From what is dear, grief does not arise; from what is unpleasant arises fear — greater than grief. Homage to those great souls who are free from both."
"I, abandoned here by my dear Rāma of high wisdom, having fallen under the power of the sinful Rāvaṇa, shall give up my life."
Thus harshly addressed by Sītā, the rākṣasīs, overcome with rage, some of them went swiftly to report this to Rāvaṇa.
Then those dreadful-looking rākṣasīs came back to Sītā and spoke harsh words again, all with one purpose — her ruin.
"Now, O ignoble Sītā, O one resolved upon sin, the rākṣasīs will eat this flesh of yours at their pleasure."
Seeing Sītā then being thus threatened by those ignoble ones, the aged rākṣasī Trijaṭā, lying there, spoke these words.
"Devour yourselves, O ignoble ones! You will not eat Sītā — she who is the beloved daughter of Janaka and the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For today I have seen a terrible dream that makes the hair stand on end — portending the destruction of the rākṣasas and the welfare of this one's husband."
Thus addressed by Trijaṭā, the rākṣasīs, overcome with anger and yet afraid, all said these words to her.
"Tell us — what kind of dream did you see in the night?"
Hearing the words that had issued from the mouths of the rākṣasīs, Trijaṭā spoke in due time these words concerning her dream.
"Rāghava himself mounted a divine celestial palanquin fashioned of elephant ivory, moving through the sky, yoked to a thousand horses —"
"— and in the dream today I also saw Sītā clad in white garments, standing upon a white mountain encircled by the ocean, united with Rāma, like the radiance joined with the sun."
"And I saw Rāghava mounted on a great four-tusked elephant, mountain-like, roaming together with Lakṣmaṇa."
"Then those two tiger-like men, blazing with their own splendor, clad in white garlands and garments, drew near to Jānakī."
"Then, at the summit of that elephant standing in the sky, with her husband clasping her, Jānakī rested upon his shoulder."
"Then springing up from her husband's lap, the lotus-eyed one — so I saw — caressed the moon and sun with her two hands."
"Then that best of elephants, mounted by those two princes and by the wide-eyed Sītā, stood above Laṅkā."
"Himself clad in white garlands and garments, he came together with Lakṣmaṇa on a chariot drawn by eight white oxen, with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife Sītā."
"Today Rāvaṇa was seen fallen from the Puṣpaka aerial chariot to the ground, dragged by the hands by a woman, shaven-headed and clad in black garments."
"Adorned with red garlands and unguents, he departed on a chariot yoked with asses toward the southern quarter and entered a pool of mire."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"A dark woman clad in red garments, her body smeared with mire, bound the ten-necked one by the neck and dragged him toward the southern quarter."
"Daśagrīva was carried off on a boar, Indrajit on a porpoise, and Kumbhakarṇa on a camel — all proceeding toward the southern quarter."
"A great assembly took place with the sounds of song and musical instruments, of rākṣasas wearing red garlands and red garments, drinking."
"And this lovely city of Laṅkā, filled with horses and chariots, was seen fallen into the ocean with its gateways and arches shattered."
"Having drunk oil and dancing about, laughing loudly, all the rākṣasa women were in Laṅkā made rough with ash."
"And all these foremost rākṣasas, Kumbhakarṇa and the rest, clad in red garments, entered a pool of cow-dung."
"Depart! Be gone! Rāghava will recover Sītā — he of supreme wrath will slay together with all the rākṣasas."
"Rāghava will not tolerate his beloved, his esteemed wife who followed him faithfully into forest exile, being threatened and terrified thus."
"Therefore enough of cruel words from you — let only gentle speech be spoken. Let us supplicate Vaidehī — this is what pleases me."
"For she who, afflicted with sorrow, beholds such a dream will be freed from many sorrows and attain her most beloved one."
"Even though she has been threatened, seek her favor, O rākṣasīs — what good is further harshness? Terrible fear from Rāghava is now imminent for the rākṣasas."
"For Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, when pleased by obeisance, is capable of protecting the rākṣasīs from great danger."
"And in the limbs of this wide-eyed one I perceive nothing contrary, not even the slightest inauspicious omen."
"Only the dimness of her luster gives me concern — that sorrow has come upon this goddess who does not deserve suffering, this one destined for the sky."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Indeed I see the attainment of Vaidehī's purpose now at hand — the destruction of the lord of rākṣasas and the victory of Rāghava."
"And this is the omen for her to hear great good news — her eye is seen to quiver, lotus-petal-like and long."
"And there is a slight bristling of the hair of her right side which is inauspicious, and suddenly one arm of Vaidehī trembles."
"And her left thigh, incomparable, resembling an elephant's trunk, quivering, seems to point out Rāghava standing before her."
"And a bird that has entered its branch-nest, speaking excellent soothing words, joyfully seems to urge on again and again the utterance of welcoming words."
Hearing those words of Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas — words that were cruel and whose import was cruelty — Sītā, stricken with misery, trembled as a young elephant princess set upon by a lion at the forest's edge.
Surrounded by rākṣasīs and afraid, severely threatened with words by Rāvaṇa, left alone in the midst of a wilderness — Sītā lamented like a young girl abandoned in a deserted forest.
"Truly do the wise say in this world that untimely death does not come — for here am I, wretched and without merit, living even a moment while being reviled thus."
"Deprived of happiness and filled with much sorrow, my heart is surely firm — for it does not today split asunder in a thousand fragments like the peak of a mountain struck by the thunderbolt."
"Surely there is no fault in me that I should be slain by this one of hateful aspect — nor am I able to yield to his desire, as a twice-born man cannot impart a sacred mantra to one who is not twice-born."
"Surely this ignoble lord of rākṣasas will before long sever my limbs with sharp weapons — cutting like an arrow piercing a creature within the womb — since the lord of the worlds does not come."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"How painful indeed are these two months that lie far ahead for me, afflicted as I am — like the night's end for a prisoner condemned to death, a thief who has offended the king."
"Alas Rāma! Alas Lakṣmaṇa! Alas Sumitrā! Alas Rāma, my mother and my birth-mother both — I, wretched and ill-fated, am perishing like a ship on the great ocean tossed by a wayward wind."
"Those two swift sons of the lord of men, those two lion-bulls, were surely slain on my account by that being that held the form of a deer — like two lightning-struck bulls."
"Surely that Time itself in the form of a deer lured me, wretched and ill-fated, at the moment when, deluded, I sent away my lord's son and also Rāma's younger brother, with Lakṣmaṇa going ahead."
"Alas Rāma, keeper of vows and truth, O long-armed one! Alas, you whose face resembles the full moon! Alas, you who are the benefactor and beloved of all living beings — you do not know that I am being condemned to death by the rākṣasas!"
"This devotion to none other than you, this forbearance, this sleeping on the ground, this adherence to dharma, this faithfulness as a wife — all this of mine has been done in vain, like kindness done to ungrateful men."
"Indeed, the dharma I have practiced is in vain, and this fidelity to one husband is without purpose — I who am emaciated and pale do not see you, deprived of you, and without hope of union with you."
"Having dutifully fulfilled your father's command and having returned from the forest with your vow accomplished, I think you are now sporting with large-eyed women, free of fear, your purpose achieved."
"But I, Rāma, who conceived love for you, have long had my heart bound to destruction. Having practiced austerity and vows in vain, I, ill-fated, will abandon my life — fie upon this existence!"
"I would quickly abandon my life — by poison or by a sharp weapon — but there is none here in the rākṣasa's dwelling to give me poison or a weapon."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
