The elephants trumpeted discordantly, the horses fell to the ground, and the earth was strewn with chariots whose housings, standards, and canopies were shattered.
That mighty monkey of fierce valor, having slain those formidable rākṣasas, eager to fight still more rākṣasas, returned once again to that very gateway as a hero.
Rāvaṇa, concealing his inner state, upon learning that the sons of his ministers had been slain by the great-souled monkey, formed a supreme resolve.
He summoned Virūpākṣa, Yūpākṣa, the rākṣasa Durdhara, Praghasa, and Bhāsakarṇa — five leading commanders of his army.
The ten-necked one commanded those heroes, skilled in statecraft, eager for the capture of Hanūmān, who were equal to the wind in battle-speed.
"Go, all of you, at the vanguard of the army, attended by mighty forces, with horses, chariots, and elephants — let that monkey be subdued."
"And whatever outcome befalls them — upon engaging that forest-dweller — an action must be taken that does not contradict the demands of place and time."
"For I do not regard that monkey as merely a monkey when I reason from his deeds — in every way he is a great being attended by great power; he may have been created against us by Indra through the force of his austerities."
"The nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, gods, asuras, and great sages have all been vanquished by me together with all of you."
"By them some offense must certainly be carried out against us — of that there is no doubt; therefore seize him by force."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Nor should you underestimate this monkey of fierce prowess — I have indeed seen monkeys who are swift and of vast valor."
"Vālin and Sugrīva, and Jāmbavān of great might, and Nīla the general, and others beginning with Dvivida —"
"— none of them possess a terrifying speed, nor radiance, nor valor, nor intelligence, nor exuberance of strength, nor a form conceived like this one's."
"This being in the form of a monkey must be known as a great entity — therefore, making great effort, let his capture be accomplished."
"Truly, the three worlds together with Indra, the gods, asuras, and men are not capable of standing before you on the battlefield."
"Nevertheless, by one who is versed in wise counsel and who desires victory in battle, the self must be protected with care — for the outcome of war is uncertain."
All those of great energy received their master's command and rushed forth with great speed, blazing like consecrated fire.
With chariots, with frenzied elephants, with horses of great swiftness, with various sharp weapons, and attended by their full forces.
Then those heroes saw the great monkey blazing, rising like the sun with its rays, crowned with the garland of his own radiant beams.
Standing at the gateway — of great speed, great spirit, great strength, great intelligence, great enthusiasm, great body, great might.
Beholding him, all of them took their positions in every direction and attacked from all sides with their respective terrible weapons.
Five iron arrows, keen and white with golden tips, resembling lotus petals, were shot by Durdhara into his head.
Struck in the head by those five arrows, the monkey leaped up roaring into the sky, making the ten directions resound with his cry.
Then the mighty hero Durdhara, in his chariot with bow readied, raining hundreds upon hundreds of arrows, pressed his attack with great force.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That monkey repelled him in the sky as he poured his rain of arrows, as the wind repels a rain-laden cloud at the end of the monsoon.
Harassed by Durdhara, the son of the wind god uttered another great roar, and increased his own swiftness.
That monkey of great velocity suddenly leaped from a distance and descended upon Durdhara's chariot, like a bolt of lightning upon a mountain.
Then Durdhara, with his eight horses crushed and the axle and yoke of his chariot broken, abandoned it and fell to the ground, his life relinquished.
Virūpākṣa and Yūpākṣa, seeing him fallen to the ground, their wrath kindled, those two irresistible crushers of enemies leaped into the air.
That long-armed monkey, suddenly leaping upward and standing in the clear sky, was struck in the chest by those two with their war-clubs.
The mighty monkey, equal to Garuḍa in valor, repelled the speed of those two swift warriors and descended again to the ground.
Reaching a śāla tree and uprooting it, that monkey, son of the wind god, slew both those rākṣasa warriors.
Then, learning that those three had been slain by the swift monkey, Praghasa of great speed forcibly charged at the monkey.
And the valiant Bhāsakarṇa, enraged, taking up his trident, both of them stood on one side against that tiger among monkeys, that glorious one.
Praghasa struck that best of monkeys with a paṭṭiśa of sharp edge, and the rākṣasa Bhāsakarṇa struck him with his trident.
With his limbs wounded by those two and his body hair smeared with blood, the monkey became furious and blazed with the radiance of the newly risen sun.
Wrenching off a mountain peak together with its deer, serpents, and trees, the heroic Hanūmān, that elephant among monkeys, slew the two rākṣasas.
Then, when those five commanders had fallen, the monkey annihilated the remaining army.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The monkey destroyed horses with horses, elephants with elephants, warriors with warriors, chariots with chariots, as the thousand-eyed Indra destroys asuras.
With the elephants and horses slain, the great chariots with broken axles, and the rākṣasas killed, the earth was blocked in all directions.
Then that monkey, having slain in battle those leaders of the bannered army together with their forces and their vehicles, returned and held that very gateway, a hero who had seized his moment, like Death at the time of the destruction of living beings.
The king, beholding those five commanders slain by Hanūmān together with their retinues and vehicles, looked upon the prince Akṣa — who was eager and ready to rise up into battle — as one unscathed.
Urged on by his father's glance, that prince of great glory, with his bow adorned with gold, sprang forth — as fire is kindled in an assembly by the oblations of foremost twice-born.
Then that bull among rākṣasas, full of valor, mounted a great chariot blazing like the young sun, covered with a network of refined gold, and advanced toward that great monkey.
That chariot earned through accumulated stores of ascetic power, adorned with a network of refined gold, bearing a banner, with its standard jewel-adorned, well-yoked with eight excellent horses swift as thought —
— unconquerable by gods and asuras, moving without obstruction, radiant as the sun, moving through the sky, well-equipped with quivers, furnished with eight attached swords, fitted in order with spears and javelins —
— shining, filled with every equipment, adorned with golden strings, resplendent as the moon and sun, bright as the day-maker — mounting this chariot, he who was equal to the gods in valor went forth.
Filling both the sky and the earth with its mountains with the sounds of horses, elephants, and great chariots, he approached with his assembled forces the capable monkey seated at the gateway.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Approaching that tawny monkey, the tawny-eyed Akṣa, struck with wonder and agitation at the sight of him stationed there like the fire of end-of-age at the time of the annihilation of creatures, regarded him with eyes of deep respect.
That son of a king, mighty himself, pondering the speed and valor of that great-souled monkey among his enemies, and his power in the sky, blazed forth like the sun at the end of winter.
His wrath aroused, beholding that valor which is impossible to restrain in battle, he stood firm and collected in spirit, and provoked Hanūmān in combat with three sharp arrows.
Then Akṣa, his spirit deeply stirred, arrow in hand and bow raised, gazed upon that monkey who was proud, unwearied by exertion, and who had conquered both enemies and exhaustion.
He, adorned with gold necklace, armlets, and beautiful earrings, swiftly advanced in valor toward the monkey — and the encounter between those two was incomparable and caused awe even among gods and asuras.
The earth rumbled, the sun did not blaze, the wind did not blow, the mountain quaked — beholding the combat of the monkey and the prince, the sky roared and the ocean heaved.
Then that hero, a knower of the true principles of concentration, aim, and release, shot three feathered arrows with beautiful faces, gold-plumed, like venomous serpents, and brought them down upon the monkey's head.
Struck on the head simultaneously by those arrows, his eyes wide open and smeared with flowing blood, shining like the newly risen sun, resplendent with arrow-rays, he blazed like the sun with its garland of rays.
Then that foremost among the ministers of the lord of tawny-eyed monkeys, beholding in battle that son of the best of kings, bearing his excellent variegated weapons and adorned bow, was filled with joy and swelled with eagerness for combat.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Like the sun stationed atop Mount Mandara, his wrath fully kindled and united with strength and valor, he then scorched the prince Akṣa together with his forces and his vehicle with the burning rays of the fire of his eyes.
Then he, whose bow was like Indra's bow, who was a cloud of rākṣasas raining arrows in battle, swiftly released his shafts upon that mountain-like lord of monkeys, as a cloud-bank pours rain upon the highest mountain.
Then the monkey, equal to a cloud in valor, beholding in battle the prince Akṣa with his fierce valor in combat and his arrows charged with increasing radiance, strength, and might, roared with joy.
He, proud in his valor despite his youth, his wrath grown great, with eyes like blood, the peerless one approached the monkey in battle like an elephant approaching a great well covered over with grass.
Struck forcibly by those arrows, he whose sound was like the sound of a thundercloud uttered a roar; the son of the wind swiftly leaped into the sky, terrible to behold as he swung his arms and thighs.
That mighty foremost of rākṣasas, full of glory, the chariot-warrior on the best of chariots, charged at him as he leaped upward, raining arrows upon him as a cloud pelts a mountain with a shower of stones.
That heroic monkey, eluding those arrows as they were released, moved along the path frequented by the wind, darting between the arrows like the wind itself, swift as thought, of fierce valor in battle.
The son of the wind god regarded Akṣa — who had seized his bow and was eager for battle, carpeting the sky with various excellent arrows — with eyes of deep regard, and fell into contemplation.
Then the long-armed monkey, his chest pierced by the arrows of that great-souled prince, roaring, being a knower of the true particulars of action, pondered his course of valor in battle.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This mighty one, radiant as the young sun, performs great deeds as if not young at all — yet my mind does not incline toward slaying him who is illustrious in every feat of battle."
"This one is great-souled and vast in valor, composed and most enduring in battle — without doubt, owing to the excellence of his deeds, he is honored by the nāgas, yakṣas, and sages."
"With a spirit swelling with valor and enthusiasm he faces me and stands watching — for his valor would shake the minds even of gods and asuras who act swiftly."
"Certainly this one would not fail to overcome if he were left alone — for his valor grows in battle; therefore slaying him pleases me, for a growing fire cannot safely be neglected."
Reflecting thus upon the other's surging force and arranging his own course of action, the valiant and mighty great monkey then gathered his speed and resolved upon slaying him.
The hero, son of the wind god, slew those eight horses of his — of great speed, steady, capable of bearing great burdens in wheeling — with slaps of his palm along the path traversed by the wind.
Then that great chariot, defeated by the minister of the lord of tawny-eyed monkeys and struck by his palm, with its housing shattered and its yoke-pole broken, fell to the ground from the sky with its horses slain.
He, that great chariot-warrior, abandoning his chariot, with bow and sword, leaped into the sky — that one of fierce valor who by devoted austerity was like a sage — as if leaving his body to enter the abode of the wind-gods.
Then the monkey, equal to the wind in speed and valor, approaching him as he moved in the sky — that sky traversed by Garuḍa, the wind, and the siddhas — seized him firmly by the feet, step by step.
That best of monkeys, whirling him a thousand times as Garuḍa seizes a great serpent, released him with force onto the earth in battle — equal in valor to his father, Vāyu.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That rākṣasa, with arms, thighs, waist, and head broken, streaming blood, his bones and eyes crushed, his joints severed and his sinews scattered, lay slain on the earth by the son of the wind.
The great monkey, having crushed him to the ground, wrought great terror upon the lord of rākṣasas.
With the great sages of great vows who move in circles, and the beings together with the yakṣas and serpents, and the gods with Indra, all greatly stricken with wonder — with the prince slain, the monkey was gazed upon by them all.
Having slain that prince Akṣa, whose radiance was like the son of the Thunderbolt-wielder, his own eyes like blood, that hero returned to that very gateway having seized his moment, like Death at the time of the destruction of living beings.
Then the great-souled lord of rākṣasas, having steadied his mind on learning that young Akṣa had been slain by Hanūmān, in wrath dispatched Indrajit, who resembled Indra himself.
"You are the foremost among those who bear weapons, the master of missile-lore, who has brought grief to gods and asuras alike; your valor is proven against the gods along with Indra, and your arsenal of weapons has been accumulated through worship of the Grandsire."
"When confronted with the force of your missiles, neither asuras nor the Marut hosts — indeed no one in the three worlds — has ever come away unwearied in battle."
"Protected by the might of your arms and shielded by your austerities, knowing the distinction of time and place — you alone are the best in wisdom."
"There is no feat impossible for you in battle, no counsel beyond your deliberate wisdom; there is no one in the three conflicts who does not know your missile-strength and your prowess."
"Your austerity, strength, valor, and missile-might in battle are a fitting match for mine; the mind of one who faces you in the press of war finds no room for fatigue — this is certain."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Slain are all the commanders, the rākṣasa Jambumālī, and the five heroic sons of ministers who led the vanguard of the army."
"Your beloved younger brother, the prince Akṣa, has also been killed; yet I place no great stock in those losses, O slayer of enemies — for you remain."
"Having now seen this great might of the monkey, his power and valor, and having also measured your own essential strength, O wise one, marshal your speed in keeping with your own force."
"As the trampling of one's force subsides when you draw near, just as it ceases when the foe is quelled — weighing your own power against the enemy's, engage now, O foremost among masters of missiles."
"This is certainly not the highest counsel — that I send you forth; yet this is the considered course recognized for kingly duty and for the Kṣatriya code."
"The proficiency in battle with manifold weapons must certainly be employed, O subduer of enemies, and victory in war is to be desired."
Then, having heard his father's words, that hero of unwaning spirit — possessing the prowess of Dakṣa's son — circumambulated his lord, resolved in mind for battle.
Then Indrajit, duly honored by his own dear companions, his martial enthusiasm roused for combat, set out for the battlefield.
The glorious son of the lord of rākṣasas, lotus-petal-eyed, of great splendor, sallied forth like the ocean at the full moon.
Indrajit, resembling Indra, mounted a chariot harnessed with four serpents whose speed equaled that of the king of birds, whose fangs were white and sharp, and whose swiftness was unimpeded.
That chariot-warrior, foremost of archers, expert in weapons, and best among masters of missiles, swiftly rode in his chariot to where Hanūmān stood.
That hero of the monkeys, hearing the rumble of his chariot and the twang of his bow, became all the more elated.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Taking up his great bow and sharp-pointed arrows, the expert in battle advanced toward Hanūmān with clear intent.
As he, arrow in hand, set forth for battle with heightened exultation, all the directions turned turbid and fearsome beasts cried out in many voices.
Nāgas and Yakṣas, great sages, and Siddhas moving in circles gathered there; flocks of birds filled the sky and cried out aloud, supremely excited.
Seeing Indrajit approaching swiftly with his chariot, the swift monkey let out a mighty roar and grew in stature.
Indrajit, mounted on his divine chariot with his variegated bow, twanged his bow with a sound as mighty as a thunderbolt.
Then those two, of exceedingly sharp speed and great strength, fearless in battle — the monkey and the son of the rākṣasa lord — came together, like the kings of gods and asuras locked in enmity.
The immeasurable monkey, grown mighty, deflected the swift rush of arrows of that heroic great-chariot warrior renowned on the battlefield, and ranged about in the path of combat — himself beyond measure, surpassing his father's expectations.
Then that hero, slayer of enemy champions, released arrows with long, sharp heads, well-feathered, with gilded colorful nocks, shot in rapid succession with the speed of a falling thunderbolt.
Hearing the rumble of his chariot, the sound of kettledrums, war-drums, and battle-drums, and the twang of the straining bow, he leapt into the air again.
The great monkey swiftly dodged between the arrows, eluding that adversary's targeting, foiling his aim's concentration.
Spreading out his hands, Hanūmān, son of the Wind, again darted forward in front of those arrows and leapt aloft.
Those two, both endowed with speed and skilled in the arts of war, waged an incomparable battle that captivated the minds of all living beings.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The rākṣasa could find no opening in Hanūmān, nor could Māruti find an opening in that great-souled one; coming together, those two of valor equal to the gods found each other mutually irresistible.
Then, as his mark was missed and his arrows fell in vain, that great-souled one fell into deep deliberation, his mind composed in contemplative concentration.
Then the son of the rākṣasa king formed a resolve regarding that foremost monkey hero — recognizing the monkey's invincibility, how might he be restrained — for the purpose of his capture.
Then that hero of immense splendor, best among masters of missiles, trained the Paitāmaha weapon — the missile of the Grandsire — upon that foremost of monkeys.
Knowing this one to be inviolable, the long-armed Indrajit, conversant with the true nature of missiles, bound the son of the Wind-god with that weapon.
Bound by that weapon of the rākṣasa, the monkey became motionless and fell to the ground.
Then that foremost monkey hero, having recognized the missile's binding through the power of its master, his lesser speed having departed, reflected on the Grandsire's boon and on his own situation.
Then Hanūmān contemplated the Brahmā-weapon enchanted with the spells of Svāyaṃbhuva, and the boon he had received from the Grandsire.
"I have no power to release myself from this missile-bondage, for it comes from the power of the world's preceptor; thus this missile-bondage, being of such a nature, must be honored by me, the son born of the self-existent."
The monkey, having considered the power of the missile and his own capacity for release, and having reflected on the Grandsire's grace, abided by the Grandsire's command.
"Even bound by the missile, no fear arises in me, for I am protected by the Grandsire, by Mahendra, and by the Wind-god."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Moreover, in being captured by the rākṣasas I see a great advantage — a conversation with the king of rākṣasas; let the enemies therefore take me."
His purpose settled — that slayer of enemy heroes — having considered it like a wise elephant, ceased his efforts; restrained by enemies who pressed upon him by force, he roared while being reviled by them with various insults.
Then the rākṣasas, seeing that subduer of enemies motionless, bound him with cords of hemp and with strips of bark from trees twisted together.
He approved of this binding and forcible capture by the enemy warriors, his purpose resolved, out of curiosity — thinking, "If only the lord of rākṣasas might decide to see me."
Bound by that bark cord, he was in fact released by the missile — for the powerful missile-bond does not accompany any other bond.
Then Indrajit the hero, reflecting on that bark-cord binding of that foremost monkey who had been freed from the missile-bond, fell into worry — for one bound by another bond does not remain under the missile's hold.
"Alas, a great deed has been done to no purpose! The rākṣasas did not reflect on the lore of missiles; moreover, when one missile is deployed, no other missile can operate — we are all in doubt."
Hanūmān, freed by the missile, did not realize his own liberation, being dragged by the rākṣasas and oppressed by those bonds.
Then the monkey, beaten by the cruel rākṣasas with fists and wooden clubs, was dragged to the presence of the lord of rākṣasas.
Then Indrajit, closely observing him freed from the missile but bound with bark-cord ropes, presented that immensely powerful monkey hero to the king before his assembled retinue.
The rākṣasas presented that bound foremost-of-monkeys, like a maddened elephant in bonds, to Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas.
"Who is this? Whose is he? Where does he come from? What is his purpose? What is his recourse?" — such discussions arose among the rākṣasa warriors there.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That king, his eyes reddened with anger, spoke this extensive and meaningful speech to Prahasta, the best of ministers, in words suited to the moment.
"Let this wicked-souled one be questioned: where does he come from? What is his motive? What was his purpose in destroying the grove and in threatening the rākṣasī women?"
Hearing Rāvaṇa's words, Prahasta spoke: "Take courage, all good to you; you need have no fear, O monkey."
"If you have been sent by Indra to the abode of Rāvaṇa, tell the truth; let there be no fear for you, O monkey — you shall be released."
"Or if you belong to Vaiśravaṇa, or to Yama, or to Varuṇa — having assumed this lovely form on behalf of Yama or Varuṇa —"
"— or if you have been sent as a messenger by Viṣṇu, who desires victory — for your brilliance is not that of a mere monkey; the form alone is a monkey's —"
"— tell the truth now, and then, O monkey, you shall be released; but if you speak falsely, your life will be hard to preserve."
"Or else — whatever the cause of your entry into the abode of Rāvaṇa —"
Thus addressed, that best of monkeys then spoke to the lord of the rākṣasa host: "I am not of Śakra, nor of Yama, nor of Varuṇa —"
"— I have no alliance with Dhanada, nor was I dispatched by Viṣṇu; this is simply my birth-nature — I am a monkey, and I have come here thus."
"Since an audience with the lord of rākṣasas is difficult to obtain, I destroyed this grove of the rākṣasa king for the purpose of obtaining that audience."
"Then those powerful rākṣasas came, eager for battle; and for the protection of my body I fought back against them in combat."
"I cannot be bound by missile-fetters even by gods or asuras — this very boon has come to me as well from the Grandsire."
"Desiring to see the king, I allowed the missile to have its effect; I was indeed freed from the missile, yet I was greatly tormented by the rākṣasas."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I am to be understood as a messenger of Rāghava of immeasurable might; let this salutary message of mine be heard, O lord."
Beholding that being of immense power, the foremost of monkeys, himself of great courage, composed and unperturbed, spoke words full of meaning to the Ten-faced one.
"I have come to your abode, O lord of rākṣasas, bearing a message from Sugrīva. The lord of monkeys, your brother, has sent you his greetings.
Hear the counsel of your brother, the great-souled Sugrīva — words grounded in righteousness and prudence, beneficial both in this world and the next.
There was a king named Daśaratha, possessor of chariots, elephants, and horses, a kinsman to the world like a father, equal in splendour to the lord of the gods.
His eldest son, a mighty-armed lord, beloved and pleasing, departed at his father's command and entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
That one of great splendour, named Rāma, accompanied by his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife Sītā, followed the path of righteousness.
His wife Sītā, devoted to her husband, the daughter of the great-souled King Janaka of Videha, was lost in the forest.
That prince, searching for the goddess, together with his younger brother, reached Ṛśyamūka and met with Sugrīva.
By him was the search for Sītā pledged, and Rāma in turn granted Sugrīva the kingdom of the monkeys.
Then, having slain Vālin in battle, that prince established Sugrīva as king, lord of the hosts of monkeys and bears.
That lord of monkeys, Sugrīva, true to his pledge and intent on the search for Sītā, dispatched monkeys in all directions.
Thousands, hundreds, and tens of thousands of those monkeys search in all directions, below and above in the sky.
Some are equal to Garuḍa, son of Vinatā; others are comparable to the wind; those heroic monkeys move without obstruction, swift and of great might.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And I am Hanūmān by name, the own-born son of the Wind-god. For Sītā's sake, crossing in an instant the ocean stretching a hundred yojanas, I came here desiring to find her.
Therefore you, who have seen the value of righteousness and profit, who have embraced austerities, O greatly wise one — you ought not to obstruct the wife of another.
For the wise, such as you, do not engage in acts opposed to righteousness, fraught with many perils, and destructive to the very root.
And who is capable of standing before the arrows released by Lakṣmaṇa, following in the wake of Rāma's wrath — even among gods and asuras?
Nor in the three worlds, O king, is there anyone who, having wronged Rāghava, might attain happiness.
Therefore consider this counsel, beneficial in all three times, righteous, and attended by profit: let Jānakī be restored to the lord among men.
For I have seen the goddess — that which was hard to find here has been found. Whatever remaining action follows from this, for that Rāghava is the instrument.
I have marked this Sītā, so wholly given over to grief — she whom you hold without recognising her, as one might grasp a five-hooded serpentess.
She cannot be overcome even by gods together with asuras, like food mixed with poison consumed to excess is fatal to one's vital energy.
This store of righteousness that you have gained through the heat of austerities — it is not proper to destroy it, together with your own life's refuge.
The invulnerability that you perceive for yourself through your austerities — from gods together with asuras — even that is greatly undermined by this very act.
For Sugrīva is neither a god, nor an asura, nor a human, nor a rākṣasa, nor a gandharva, nor a yakṣa, nor a serpent.
Rāghava is a man, O king, and Sugrīva is the lord of monkeys — how then, O king, will you save your life?

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Righteousness does not follow the approach of unrighteousness attended by its fruits; rather, righteousness destroys unrighteousness, and each act bears its own consequence.
You have already reaped the fruit of your righteous deeds — of that there is no doubt; but you shall swiftly obtain the fruit of this unrighteous act as well.
Having understood the slaughter at Janasthāna and the slaying of Vālin, and understanding the alliance of Rāma and Sugrīva — recognise what is beneficial for yourself.
Indeed I alone am capable of destroying Laṅkā with its horses, chariots, and elephants — but that is his resolve.
For Rāma has pledged, in the presence of the hosts of monkeys and bears, the annihilation of enemies — those by whom Sītā has been violated.
For even Purandara himself, should he wrong Rāma, would not attain happiness — what then of a person like you?
She whom you know as Sītā, who stands in your power — know her as the night of death, the destroyer of all Laṅkā.
Enough — Sītā is the very noose of death embodied, clinging of her own accord to your neck; consider well what is fitting for yourself.
Behold this city with its towers and royal highways, scorched by Sītā's blazing power, oppressed by Rāma's wrath, burning even now.
Having heard the unpleasant yet eloquent words of the monkey who spoke without timidity — words elegant and well-composed — the Ten-faced one, his eyes wide with rage, commanded the slaying of that great monkey.
Having heard those words of the great-souled monkey, Rāvaṇa, overcome with fury, commanded his execution.
When the wicked-souled Rāvaṇa had commanded his killing, Vibhīṣaṇa — who had duly announced his embassy — did not approve.
Knowing the lord of rākṣasas to be enraged and the matter at hand to be critical, he reflected on the right course of action, firm in the conduct of duty.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having resolved his purpose, and reverently addressing with gentle words his elder brother the conqueror of enemies, that master of speech spoke words of great benefit.
"O king, the killing of this monkey is contrary to righteousness, censured by the conduct of the world, and unworthy of you, O hero.
Without doubt this enemy is grown mighty and has done an immeasurable wrong; yet the righteous do not prescribe death for an envoy — many punishments have been seen for an envoy, but not death.
Disfigurement of the limbs, flogging with a whip, shaving of the head, and the application of Lakṣmaṇa's brand — these are the punishments prescribed for an envoy; but the slaying of an envoy we have not even heard of.
And how could one such as you, whose mind is schooled in righteousness and prudence, who is firm in discerning what is high and low, remain in the power of anger? For those of firm character restrain their anger.
In discourse on righteousness, in the ways of the world, and in the mastery of the intellect through the śāstras, none equals you, O hero — for you are the supreme one among all gods and asuras.
Nor do I see any benefit in killing this monkey; let this punishment fall upon those by whom this monkey was sent.
Whether righteous or unrighteous, this one has been dispatched by others; speaking on another's behalf, acting under another's authority, an envoy does not deserve death.
Moreover, should this one be killed, O king, I see no other sky-traveller who could come again across the great ocean.
Therefore no effort should be made to kill him, O conqueror of enemy cities; you ought to direct your effort against the gods with Indra at their head.
If this one perishes, I see no other envoy who could rouse those two sons of a human king to battle — those two who love battle, who are proud, and who are kept away by the long path.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
It is not fitting, O delight of the mind, for you who are difficult to conquer even by the valiant, spirited, and courageous gods and asuras, to destroy the war-enterprise of the rākṣasas.
Well-disposed, heroic, composed, born into illustrious lineages, high-minded, foremost among weapon-bearers, sharp at the blade's edge, and well-maintained — such are your warriors.
Let some portion of your forces set out at your command and subdue those two foolish princes, so as to demonstrate your power over your enemies."
Having heard those words, the mighty Ten-necked one spoke in reply to his brother's excellent counsel, fitting to time and place.
"What you have said is correct: the slaying of an envoy is censured. Yet some punishment other than death must certainly be inflicted upon him.
It is said that the tail is dear to monkeys as their ornament — let it be set ablaze at once, and let him depart with it burned.
Then let his allies, kinsmen, relatives, and all his friends behold him wretched, afflicted with the disfigurement of his limbs."
The lord of rākṣasas commanded: "Let him be led by the rākṣasas through the entire city together with its squares, with his tail set ablaze."
Having heard that command, the rākṣasas, hardened with rage, began wrapping his tail in old cotton cloths.
As his tail was being wrapped, the great monkey grew larger, like fire in the forests when it reaches dry fuel.
Then, having drenched it with oil, they set fire to it.
With his tail ablaze, his spirit filled with fury and indignation, his face like the rising sun, he flung those rākṣasas down.
Bound again by the cruel rākṣasas who gathered around him, that foremost of monkeys, that hero, formed a resolve suited to the moment.
"Indeed, these rākṣasas are not capable of binding me; even now, bound as I am, I could cut the bonds, leap up, and slay them.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
I am fully capable of defeating all rākṣasas in battle; yet for Rāma's pleasure I shall endure this circumstance."
"It would be well if I were to survey Laṅkā once more — for at night I did not see it clearly enough in terms of its fortifications and their arrangement; I must certainly examine Laṅkā before night is spent."
"Let the rākṣasas torment me further with bonds and the burning of my tail — my mind feels no weariness."
Then those rākṣasas, joyful, seized that mighty monkey who concealed his feelings — that elephant among monkeys, of great courage — and led him away.
Those rākṣasas of cruel deeds, proclaiming their own acts with the sounds of conch-shells and kettledrums, led him through the city.
Hanūmān was led through the great city of the rākṣasas, and the great monkey observed its wonderful aerial palaces.
The monkey observed the enclosed ground areas, the well-laid-out squares, the streets dense with houses, and the crossroads.
In the public squares, at the crossroads, and along the royal highway, all the rākṣasas proclaimed the monkey a spy.
Then, as the tip of Hanūmān's tail was blazing, those rākṣasa women of distorted eyes reported that unpleasant news to the goddess.
"That copper-faced monkey with whom you conversed, O Sītā — this very one is being led about with his tail set on fire."
Hearing those cruel words, like a seizure of her own self, Vaidehī, burning with grief, approached the fire-god.
With wide eyes, pure and auspiciously disposed, she turned toward the great monkey's well-being and propitiated the bearer of oblations.
"If there is service rendered to my husband, if there is austerity performed, if there is fidelity to one husband — be cool for Hanūmān."
"If that wise one has any compassion for me, if there remains any residue of my fortune — be cool for Hanūmān."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"If that righteous-souled one knows me to be of virtuous conduct and longing for union with him — be cool for Hanūmān."
"If the noble, long-armed Sugrīva, true to his pledge, will rescue me from this suffering — be cool for Hanūmān."
Then the fire, with its sharp flames, undisturbed, with its crest turning rightward, blazed — as though proclaiming auspiciousness for the monkey to the doe-eyed one.
And as his tail burned, the monkey reflected: "This fire is fully kindled — why does it not burn me everywhere?"
"It is seen to have great flames, yet it causes me no pain; it is stationed at the tip of my tail like a touch of cool snow."
"Or rather, this is clearly the same wonder that I witnessed as I flew — through Rāma's power — when Maināka appeared in the ocean, lord of rivers."
"If the ocean and the wise Maināka showed such solicitude for Rāma's purpose, why would fire not do the same?"
"By reason of Sītā's compassion, by the power of Rāghava, and by my father's friendship with him — Pāvaka does not burn me."
Again that elephant among monkeys reflected for a moment, then leaped up with great speed, and the great monkey roared.
Then the glorious son of the Wind-god reached the city gate, lofty as a mountain peak, thronged with rākṣasa guards stationed at their posts.
Becoming mountain-like in an instant, then again self-composed and reduced to the smallest size, he shook off his bonds.
And freed, the glorious one again became like a mountain; looking about, he spied an iron bar resting against the gatehouse arch.
Seizing it, long-armed Māruti — that bar fitted with black iron — slaughtered all those guards once more.
Having slain them, he of fierce prowess in battle, surveying Laṅkā once more, shone resplendent — his tail ablaze making a garland of flames — like the sun with its garland of rays.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the monkey, his desire fulfilled, his enthusiasm growing, gazed upon Laṅkā and reflected on what remained yet to be done.
"What indeed remains for me to do here at present, by which further pain may be inflicted upon these rākṣasas?"
"The grove has been ravaged, distinguished rākṣasas have been slain, a portion of the army has been destroyed — what remains is the destruction of the fortress."
"Once the fortress is destroyed, the task will become one of pleasant effort; with little exertion in this undertaking my labour will bear fruit."
"This fire, the carrier of oblations, blazing on my tail — it is fitting to give it satisfaction with these finest dwellings."
Then, with his tail ablaze, the great monkey moved about the rooftops of Laṅkā's mansions like a thundercloud lit by lightning.
Hanūmān released fire whose flames were like those of the fire of universal dissolution.
Fanned by the wind, that fire blazed with tremendous speed and great force, spreading and growing like the fire of cosmic time.
The wind drove the blazing fire through those dwellings.
Those great mansions adorned with lattices of gold and set with pearls and gems collapsed and fell.
Those shattered palaces fell to the ground like the celestial abodes of Siddhas falling from the sky at the exhaustion of their merit.
He beheld brilliant mineral streams flowing from the mansions — diamond, coral, vaidūrya gem, pearl, and silver, all mingled together.
Just as fire is never sated with wood and grass, so too Hanūmān was not in the least sated with the slaying of those lords of the rākṣasas.
That Laṅkā, enveloped in the flames of fire, her champions slain, her warriors routed, overcome by the furious power of Hanūmān, appeared like a city struck down by a curse.
The great-spirited Hanūmān beheld Laṅkā, her rākṣasas terrified and distraught, blazing with the flames of fire, like the earth struck by the wrath of the Self-born Brahmā.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having slain those many rākṣasas, having broken that grove with its many trees, having set fire to the dwellings of the rākṣasas, that great-souled one turned his mind to Rāma.
Having set all of Laṅkā ablaze, that foremost of monkeys, the best of the vānaras, then extinguished the fire of his tail in the ocean.
Gazing upon the burning, devastated city of Laṅkā, her bands of rākṣasas terrified, the monkey Hanūmān fell into thought.
A great fear arose in him, and self-reproach was born within: "What act have I committed by burning Laṅkā?"
"Blessed are those foremost men, those great souls who restrain anger that has arisen in the mind with intelligence, as water restrains a blazing fire."
"If this Laṅkā has been burned, then surely noble Jānakī too has been burned. By me, not knowing it, the task of my lord has been destroyed."
"The very purpose for which this undertaking was begun has been ruined — for in burning Laṅkā, I did not protect Sītā."
"This was a small matter that needed to be done — of that there is no doubt. But overcome by anger, I have brought about its utter ruin."
"Jānakī is clearly destroyed — not a single spot of Laṅkā is seen unburned; the entire city has been reduced to ashes."
"If indeed this task has been ruined by my perversion of judgment, then laying down my life right here seems most fitting to me."
"Shall I fall into the fire today, or into the submarine fire? Or shall I give my body to the creatures that dwell in the ocean?"
"How can I, who have destroyed the entirety of the task, ever look upon the lord of monkeys, or those two tiger-like men, while still alive?"
"By me, due to the fault of rage, has been displayed what is already renowned in the three worlds — the fickleness and instability of monkeys."
"Shame upon this rājasic nature, uncontrolled and unstable, by which even I, capable of mastery, failed through passion to protect Sītā."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"With Sītā destroyed, those two will perish as well; with their destruction Sugrīva together with his kinsmen will perish."
"Hearing this very news, how will the righteous-souled Bharata, ever devoted to his brothers, along with Śatrughna, be able to survive?"
"With the most righteous Ikṣvāku lineage gone to destruction without doubt, all the subjects will be tormented by grief and anguish."
"Thus I, devoid of fortune, stripped of the accumulation of dharma and artha, my soul overcome by the fault of rage, am clearly the destroyer of the world."
As he was reflecting thus, favorable omens presented themselves — those he had perceived earlier — and he reconsidered.
"Or rather — she of beautiful limbs, that auspicious one, is protected by her own radiance and will not perish; fire does not function within fire."
"Indeed fire cannot rightfully touch, by the law of dharma, the wife of that one of boundless splendor — her who is protected by her own chastity of conduct."
"Surely by the power of Rāma and by the merit of the princess of Videha, this fire — whose very work is burning — did not burn me."
"She who is the deity of the three brothers beginning with Bharata, and who is beloved of Rāma's heart — how could she perish?"
"Or since this imperishable fire, the lord everywhere whose very work is burning, did not burn my tail — how could it scorch that noble lady?"
"By her ascetic practice, by her truthful speech, and by her singular devotion to her husband, she could herself extinguish fire — fire will not burn her."
As he thus reflected upon the queen's embrace of dharma, the great-souled Hanūmān heard the words of the Cāraṇas.
"Ah, truly a deed nearly beyond endurance has been performed by Hanūmān, who again and again unleashed fearsome fire upon the dwellings of the rākṣasas!"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This city of Laṅkā with its watch-towers, ramparts, and gateways has been burned — yet Jānakī has not been burned. This is a wonder and marvel to us!"
By these omens of manifest import, by reasons of great virtue, and by the words of the seers, Hanūmān's heart became glad.
Then the monkey, his desired object attained, knowing the princess to be unharmed, and having seen her again in person, resolved to set out on his return journey.
Then, going to Jānakī who was seated at the foot of the śiṃśapā tree, he saluted her and said: "By good fortune I see you here unharmed."
Then Sītā, gazing again and again upon Hanūmān as he prepared to depart, spoke to him words filled with affection for her husband.
"Truly, you alone are sufficient to accomplish this task. O slayer of enemy heroes, your rise of power is glorious."
"Yet if Kākutstha, the crusher of enemy armies, were to fill Laṅkā with his forces and then lead me away, that would be befitting of him."
"Bring about therefore what is truly befitting of that great-souled hero in battle — cause his valor to manifest as it rightly should."
Having heard those words of hers — purposeful, modest, and supported by reasons — Hanūmān spoke this reply to her.
"Kākutstha will come swiftly, surrounded by the foremost of monkeys and bears, and having conquered your enemies in battle, he will remove your sorrow."
Having thus reassured the princess of Videha, Hanūmān, the son of the wind-god, made up his mind to depart and took leave of Vaidehī.
Then that tiger among monkeys, that crusher of enemies, eager to see his lord, ascended the finest of mountains, Ariṣṭa.
It was adorned with lofty rows of blue padmaka trees, and thickly set with sāla, tāla, āśvakarṇa, and many bamboo groves.
It was ornamented with spreading canopies of flowering creepers, filled with herds of various beasts, and adorned with the flowing streams of mineral ores.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
It was endowed with many waterfalls, made difficult by accumulations of rock, and frequented by great seers, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and serpents.
Its caverns were dense with creepers and trees and troubled by lions; its slopes were crowded with packs of tigers; its trees bore sweet roots and fruits.
That foremost of leaping beings, of surpassing strength, ascended that mountain, spurred on by the joy that was quickened by his eagerness to see Rāma.
Trodden by the soles of his feet on the beautiful mountain ridges, the rocks split apart with a loud crash and were pulverized.
Having climbed that king of mountains, the great monkey grew in size, seeking to leap from the southern to the northern shore of the salt-sea.
Then that hero, son of the wind-god, having mounted the mountain, beheld the fearsome ocean frequented by fish and serpents.
That tiger among monkeys, born of the wind-god, sprang through the sky like the wind itself, traversing from south to north.
That finest of mountains, pressed by that monkey, roared along with the beings dwelling within it and sank into the earth, its peaks trembling and its trees falling.
Churned by the speed of his thighs, flower-bearing trees were uprooted and fell to the ground, as if struck down by Indra's weapon.
The terrifying roar of mighty lions dwelling in the hollows of the caves, disturbed and afflicted, was heard splitting the sky.
Vidyādharī women, their garments loosened and disheveled, their ornaments thrown into disarray, leapt suddenly from the mountain.
Enormous, powerful, blazing-tongued serpents of great venom, their heads and necks pressed down, writhed and coiled about.
Kiṃnaras, serpents, gandharvas, yakṣas, and vidyādharas likewise, abandoning that finest of mountains as it was being crushed, took to the sky.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And that glorious upholder of the earth, pressed by that mighty one, sank into the netherworld, its lofty peaks and trees intact.
That mountain, ten yojanas in breadth and thirty yojanas in height, became level with the earth.
The sky, lovely with the moon and water-lilies, auspicious with the sun and ruddy geese, clustered with the Tiṣya and Śravaṇa stars like kadamba blossoms, its meadows of grass like clouds and river-moss —
— with Punarvasu as its great fish, Mars as its great crocodile, the Airāvata constellation as its great island, stirred by the Svātī star and its swans —
— its waves born of clashing winds, its waters cooled by the moon's rays, its lotuses and water-lilies awakened among serpents, yakṣas, and gandharvas —
— as though swallowing the sky, as though painting the lord of stars, as though sweeping away the firmament together with the stellar hosts and the orb of the sun —
the glorious great monkey Hanūmān, dweller in wind, traveller through the sky, moved as though dragging apart the masses of clouds — the abode of the wind-god.
The great clouds gleamed — some pale and reddish, some dark blue and madder-red, others green and orange-hued.
Entering into the masses of cloud and emerging again and again, now hidden and now revealed, he appeared like the moon.
Roaring with a mighty roar whose sound rivalled the thunder of clouds, the great-spirited one came again across the middle of the ocean.
Having touched the lord of mountains Sunābha, the valiant one of great speed approached like a steel arrow loosed from a bowstring.
Having arrived a little way off and beholding the great mountain that resembled Mahendra and a thundercloud, that bull among monkeys let out a roar.
Hearing the roar of the roaring one, all those monkeys on every side became eager with longing to behold their companion.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Jāmbavān, that foremost of monkeys, his heart thrilled with delight, summoning all the monkeys spoke these words:
"In every respect that Hanūmān has accomplished his task — there is no doubt of this. For one who had not accomplished his task could not produce a roar of this kind."
Hearing the speed of his arms and thighs and the roar of that great-souled one, the monkeys, overjoyed, leapt up from here and there.
Exhilarated, longing to see Hanūmān, they moved from treetop to treetop, from peak to peak.
Delighted, those monkeys grasped the well-flowering branches at the treetops and waved them about like gleaming garments.
Beholding that great monkey descending, resembling a dense mass of cloud, all those monkeys stood with palms joined in reverence.
Then that swift monkey, himself mountain-like, descended upon the tree-covered summit of mount Mahendra.
Then all those bulls among monkeys, their hearts full of joy, gathered around and attended upon the great-souled Hanūmān.
Surrounding him, they all experienced the highest delight, all with gleaming faces, seeing him returned safe and well.
Bringing offerings, roots, and fruits, the monkeys honoured that foremost of monkeys, the son of the wind-god.
Some roared with joy, others made the kila-kila cry; exhilarated, those bulls among monkeys brought down branches of trees.
Then Hanūmān, that great monkey, reverently saluted his elders and seniors headed by Jāmbavān, and also the prince Aṅgada.
Honoured by those two, himself worthy of honour, and gratified by the monkeys, that valiant one reported briefly: "The queen has been found."
Taking the son of Vālin by the hand, he sat down in a pleasant wooded place on mount Mahendra.
Then Hanūmān, joyful, spoke to those bulls among monkeys: "The daughter of Janaka has been seen — she is dwelling in the Aśoka grove."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Guarded by dreadful rākṣasīs, the blameless young woman, wearing her hair in a single braid, longs to behold Rāma; she is exhausted by fasting, soiled, matted-haired, and emaciated."
Then, hearing that great and nectar-like word "she has been seen" from the son of the wind-god, all the monkeys became joyful.
Some hissed, some roared, some of great strength bellowed; others made the kila-kila cry, and still others roared in response.
Some, those elephant-like monkeys, raised their tails in joy; they curled and waved their long, outstretched tails.
And others, those monkeys elephant-like in might, leapt from the mountain peaks and touched Hanūmān with delight.
Then Aṅgada, in the midst of all the monkey heroes, spoke these excellent words to Hanūmān who had just finished speaking:
"In courage and valour there is no monkey equal to you — you who have leapt across the vast ocean and returned again."
"By good fortune you have seen the queen, the glorious wife of Rāma. By good fortune Kākutstha will abandon the grief born of separation from Sītā."
Then the monkeys, surrounding Aṅgada, Hanūmān, and Jāmbavān, joyful, took their places on the broad rocks.
Those foremost of monkeys, eager to hear of the crossing of the ocean, the seeing of Laṅkā, of Sītā, and of Rāvaṇa, all stood with palms joined, their faces turned toward Hanūmān's countenance.
The glorious Aṅgada sat there, surrounded by many monkeys, attended upon like the lord of gods in heaven attended by the celestials.
The lofty, great summit of the mountain, occupied with joy by the renowned and illustrious Hanūmān and by Aṅgada with Aṅgada's arm clasped about him, blazed with splendour.
Then on the summit of that mountain Mahendra, the mighty monkeys with Hanūmān at their head experienced the highest joy.
Then Jāmbavān, himself overjoyed, questioned that joyful great monkey, the son of the wind-god, about what had transpired in the mission.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"How did you see the queen? And how does she fare there? And how has the cruel-actioned Daśānana behaved toward her?"
"Tell us all of this truthfully, O great monkey. Having heard the matter, we shall deliberate further upon the final determination of the course of action."
"And what is the matter that must be told by us when we go there, and what must be protected there — let your honour explain all that to us."
Assigned by him, his body hair standing on end with joy, bowing his head in reverence to the queen Sītā, he replied:
"As you yourselves witnessed, I leapt into the sky from the summit of Mahendra, composed and intent, desiring to reach the southern shore of the ocean.
"As I was going, something that seemed like a dreadful obstacle appeared: I saw a golden peak, divine and exceedingly lovely,
"standing blocking my path — I considered that mountain an obstacle.
"Approaching that divine, golden, foremost of mountains, my mind formed the thought: 'I must break through this.'
"And when struck by my tail, the peak of that great mountain, sun-like in brilliance, was shattered into a thousand fragments.
"And understanding my resolve, that great mountain spoke, as though gladdening my heart, a sweet word: 'Son!'
"'Know me also as your uncle, a friend of Mātariśvan — the one known as Maināka, dwelling in the great ocean.'
"'In former times, O son, the foremost mountains had wings and roamed the earth at will, troubling it on all sides.'
"'Hearing of the conduct of the mountains, the blessed Mahendra, the slayer of Pāka, cut off their wings with his thunderbolt by the thousands.'
"'But I was saved from that by your father, the great-souled Māruta — at that time, O child, I was hurled into the great ocean.'
"'And I must render assistance in the cause of Rāma, O subduer of foes — Rāma, the foremost of upholders of dharma, equal in valour to Mahendra.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Hearing this from the great-souled Maināka, having communicated my mission to the mountain, my mind was roused.
"And being given leave by the great-souled Maināka, adopting my utmost speed, I covered the remaining journey.
"Then for a long time I was advancing rapidly along the path; then I saw the goddess Surasā, mother of serpents.
"That goddess in the midst of the ocean addressed me: 'You, O foremost of monkeys, have been appointed as my prey by the immortals — therefore I shall devour you; you have been ordained for me after a long time.'
"Addressed thus by Surasā, I stood with palms joined, bowing, and with a changed countenance I spoke these words:
"'The glorious Rāma, son of Daśaratha, the scorcher of foes, has entered the Daṇḍaka forest together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and with Sītā.'
"'His wife Sītā has been abducted by the evil-souled Rāvaṇa — by Rāma's command I shall go to her.'
"'You who dwell in this domain, you ought to render assistance to Rāma.'
"'Or else, having seen Maithilī and Rāma the effortless worker, I shall return into your mouth — I promise you truly.'
"Addressed thus by me, that Surasā, who takes any form at will, declared: 'No one may pass beyond me — this is my boon.'
"Addressed thus by Surasā, I became ten yojanas in length; and in an instant I became half that measure in breadth.
"And her mouth was opened wide in proportion to my size. Seeing that gaping mouth, I made my body small.
"And in that moment I became thumb-sized again; swiftly plunging into that mouth, I emerged from it in an instant.
"The goddess Surasā, resuming her own form, said to me again: 'Go, gentle one, O foremost of monkeys, at your ease — may your purpose be accomplished!'
"'And bring together the Vaidehī with the great-souled Rāghava. Be happy, O mighty-armed one — I am pleased with you, monkey.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then praised by all beings with 'Excellent! Excellent!', I soared up into the vast sky like Garuḍa.
"And my shadow was seized, and I could see nothing. With my speed arrested, looking in all ten directions, I could see nothing there by which my movement had been stolen.
"Then a thought arose in me: why has such an obstacle arisen in my passage — one whose form is not visible?
"With sorrowing gaze I cast my sight downward, and then I saw a dreadful rākṣasī lying in the water.
"Laughing a great laugh, I was addressed by that dreadful one — standing unperturbed she spoke these ungracious words:
"'Where are you going, O great-bodied one? You are the coveted prey of me who am hungry — satisfy my body long deprived of food.'
"With the word 'Very well!' I accepted her challenge; then I enlarged my body beyond the measure of her mouth.
"Her great and dreadful mouth grew wide in order to devour me; but she did not perceive me or the transformation I had wrought.
"Then in the twinkling of an eye I contracted my vast form and, tearing out her heart, I soared into the sky.
"That dreadful one, mountain-sized, her heart wrenched out by me, her arms released, fell into the salt ocean.
"And I heard the sky-going beings and siddhas together with cāraṇas: 'The dreadful rākṣasī Siṃhikā has been swiftly destroyed by Hanūmān.'
"Having slain her and remembering my urgent task, I traversed a great distance and saw the southern shore of the ocean adorned with mountains — where that city of Laṅkā lies.
"When the sun had set, I entered the city, the abode of the rākṣasas, unrecognised by the rākṣasas of dreadful might.
"There I searched the entire night for the daughter of Janaka, entering Rāvaṇa's inner apartments, but did not see the slender-waisted one.
"Then, not seeing Sītā in Rāvaṇa's dwelling, I reached a sea of grief and could discern no farther shore.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"And while grieving, I saw, enclosed by a wall stretched with gold, an excellent garden adjoining the palace.
"Leaping over the wall, I saw it filled with many trees.
"In the middle of the Aśoka grove stood a great śiṃśapā tree. Climbing it, I saw a golden grove of banana trees.
"Not far from the śiṃśapā tree I saw a forest-dweller — dark-complexioned, with lotus-petal eyes, her face emaciated by fasting.
"She was surrounded by misshapen and cruel rākṣasīs who subsist on flesh and blood — like a doe surrounded by tigresses.
"Seeing that woman, the blameless wife of Rāma, in such a state, I remained there on that very śiṃśapā tree, watching.
"Then I heard an extremely deep uproar of noise, mingled with the sounds of waist-ornaments and ankle-bells, in Rāvaṇa's dwelling.
"Then I, greatly agitated, contracted my form and sat in the śiṃśapā tree like a bird in the dense foliage.
"Then Rāvaṇa's wives and the mighty Rāvaṇa himself arrived at that place where Sītā stood.
"Seeing the lord of the rākṣasa hosts, the shapely Sītā drew her thighs together and clasped her full breasts with her arms.
"Daśagrīva addressed the deeply sorrowful Sītā, having prostrated with bowed head: 'Think highly of me!'
"'If in your pride and arrogance you do not accept me gladly, O Sītā, then after two months I shall drink your blood.'
"Hearing those words of the evil-souled Rāvaṇa, Sītā, most wrathful, spoke these excellent words:
"'O lowest of rākṣasas, how has your tongue not fallen out while speaking unspeakable words to the wife of Rāma of immeasurable splendour, lord of the Ikṣvāku line, and daughter-in-law of Daśaratha?'
"'What indeed is your valour, O ignoble one, O wicked one — you who abducted me in my husband's absence and came here, unseen by that great-souled one?'
"'You are not the equal of Rāma — you are not even fit to be his slave, nor mine. The Rāghava is worthy of sacrifice, truthful in speech, and renowned in battle.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Addressed thus with harsh words by the daughter of Janaka, Daśānana blazed up suddenly with anger, like fire blazing amid funeral-pyre bones.
"Rolling his cruel eyes and raising his right fist, he began to strike Maithilī — at which the women cried out in alarm.
"Leaping out from among the women, that wicked one's foremost wife, named Mandodarī, restrained him.
"And she, tormented by desire, spoke sweet words to him: 'What business do you have with Sītā, O one equal in valour to Mahendra? Sport with me today — Jānakī is not superior to me.'
"'Sport here, my lord, with the daughters of gods and gandharvas, with the daughters of yakṣas as well — what will you do with Sītā?'
"Then that mighty night-wanderer was suddenly lifted up and led to his own palace by those assembled women.
"When Daśagrīva had departed, the misshapen-faced rākṣasīs threatened Sītā with cruel and dreadful words.
"The daughter of Janaka counted their speech as mere straw, and their threats against Sītā were then utterly fruitless.
"Their roaring and efforts in vain, those flesh-eating rākṣasīs reported to Rāvaṇa Sītā's great resolve.
"Then all of them together, their hopes dashed and their efforts spent, having surrounded her on all sides, fell under the power of sleep.
"And when they had fallen asleep, Sītā, devoted to her husband's welfare, wailing piteously in her misery, grieved deeply, afflicted with sorrow.
"And seeing her in such a state, seeing Sītā's dreadful plight, I rested but my mind found no peace.
"And for the purpose of speaking with the daughter of Janaka, I thought about the method; then the lineage of the Ikṣvāku clan was placed by me in the foreground.
"Having heard the speech I spoke, honoured by the company of royal seers, the queen replied to me with eyes brimming with tears.
"'Who are you? By whom and how have you come here, O bull among monkeys? And what is your bond of affection with Rāma? Please tell me that.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Hearing those words of hers, I too spoke words: 'O queen, your husband Rāma has an ally of dreadful valour — the heroic king of monkeys of great might, named Sugrīva.'
"'Know me as his servant Hanūmān, come here — I have been sent to you by your husband, Rāma the effortless worker.'
"'And this — the glorious Rāma, that tiger among men, son of Daśaratha, has himself given this ring as a token of recognition to you, O illustrious one.'
"'That being so, I wish to be instructed by you, O queen — what shall I do? Shall I carry you to the side of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa? Or is there some other resolution?'
"Hearing and understanding this, Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, said: 'Let the Rāghava come and, having vanquished Rāvaṇa, take me away.'
"Bowing my head in reverence to the noble, blameless queen, I asked for a token of recognition to delight Rāma's heart.
"Addressed thus, the shapely one, most greatly agitated, gave me the foremost, excellent jewel, and instructed me in words.
"Then, bowing reverently to that princess, composed in mind, I performed a clockwise circumambulation, my heart set on returning here.
"She spoke again a further word, having resolved upon it in her mind: 'Hanūmān, you must relate my situation to the Rāghava.'
"'Act in such a way that those two heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sugrīva, come here speedily upon hearing.'
"'If this should be otherwise, my life shall be but two months. Kākutstha will not see me — I shall die here like one without a protector.'
"Hearing that pitiful speech, anger overtook me, and I looked upon the remaining task that must be done next.
"Then my body grew, becoming like a mountain; eager for battle, I began to destroy that grove.
"When the grove was broken and the animals and birds were confused and frightened, the misshapen-faced rākṣasīs woke up and looked about.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"And seeing me in that grove, gathering together from here and there, they quickly went to Rāvaṇa and reported.
"'O king, this formidable grove of yours has been destroyed by that wicked monkey, not knowing your valour, O mighty one.'
"'O lord of kings, command quickly the slaying of that evildoer of wicked intellect who has acted against your pleasure, so that he may come to destruction.'
"Hearing this, the lord of rākṣasas dispatched the rākṣasas called the Kiṃkaras, exceedingly difficult to overcome, who follow Rāvaṇa's will.
"Eighty thousand of them, bearing spears and clubs in their hands, were slain by me in that wooded place with a mace.
"Those remaining survivors among them, swift in their movement, went and reported to Rāvaṇa the army I had slain.
"Then a thought arose in me and I ascended the caitya tower.
"And having slain a hundred rākṣasas there with a pillar, I, who had become the ornament of Laṅkā, destroyed it in anger.
"Then he dispatched Jambumālin, the son of Prahasta.
"That rākṣasa, powerful and skilled in battle, together with his followers I slew with an exceedingly dreadful mace.
"Hearing this, the lord of rākṣasas Rāvaṇa sent the minister's sons, of great might, equipped with infantry forces — I sent all of them to Yama's abode with the very same mace.
"Hearing that the minister's sons, swift in battle, had been slain, Rāvaṇa sent five generals of armies, warriors — all of them together with their armies I slew entirely.
"Then again Daśagrīva sent his son Akṣa of great might together with many rākṣasas into battle.
"But that prince, son of Mandodarī, skilled in battle, who suddenly leapt into the sky — I seized him by the feet and, whirling him around a hundredfold together with his shield and sword, I crushed him.
"Hearing that Akṣa had come and been destroyed, Daśānana Rāvaṇa, most furious, directed his second son named Indrajit, the mighty one, wild with battle-frenzy.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"His entire army and he himself, that bull among rākṣasas — having rendered them powerless in battle, I experienced supreme joy.
"For it was with great confidence that this mighty-armed, mighty one had been sent by Rāvaṇa with heroes intoxicated with pride.
"But he bound me with a Brahmā weapon with great speed; then the rākṣasas there bound me with ropes.
"And taking hold of me, they led me to the presence of Rāvaṇa; being seen, I was addressed by the evil-souled Rāvaṇa.
"And questioned about my coming to Laṅkā and the slaying of those rākṣasas, I declared all of it there: 'It was for the sake of Sītā.'
"'Desirous of seeing her, I came to your abode, O lord — I am the monkey Hanūmān, the direct son of Māruta.'
"'Know me as Rāma's messenger, a monkey, the minister of Sugrīva — I have come here to your presence on Rāma's embassy.'
"'And hear also the message I convey to you — the lord of monkeys speaks to you, O lord of rākṣasas, a composed word, wholesome in dharma, artha, and kāma, beneficial as beneficial food.'
"'While I was dwelling on mount Ṛśyamūka abounding in trees, Rāma the warrior, valiant in battle, came to friendship with me.'
"'He told me, O king: My wife has been abducted by a rākṣasa — for that reason you should make a compact with me for assistance.'
"'The Rāghava along with Lakṣmaṇa made a fire-witnessed alliance of friendship with Sugrīva who had been deprived of his kingdom by Vālin.'
"'By him, having felled Vālin in battle with a single arrow, Sugrīva was made the great king of monkeys, lord of those who leap.'
"'His assistance must be rendered by us here with our entire being — by him I have been sent rightfully to your presence here.'
"'Let Sītā be brought swiftly and given to the Rāghava, before the heroic monkeys scatter your forces.'
"'For the origin of the monkeys has not been known to anyone before — they are those who go to the presence of the gods when invited.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'Thus the king of monkeys speaks to you' — so I addressed him. Then he looked at me with a burning gaze, enraged, as though setting me on fire.
"By that rākṣasa of dreadful deeds I was condemned to death.
"Then his brother, named Vibhīṣaṇa, of great wisdom, petitioned that king of rākṣasas on my account.
"'The killing of a messenger is not found in the treatises on kingship, O rākṣasa; and a messenger must speak truly, as a well-wisher.'
"'Even in the case of a very great offence by a messenger, O one of incomparable might, mutilation is found — but not killing — according to the treatises.'
"Addressed thus by Vibhīṣaṇa, Rāvaṇa commanded those rākṣasas: 'Let this tail of his be set on fire today.'
"Then, hearing his word, my tail was wrapped all around with hemp bark and cotton cloth.
"Then those rākṣasas, ready-armed, of fierce valour, set my tail alight, striking it with wooden clubs.
"Bound as I was with many nooses and controlled by the rākṣasas, I felt no pain whatsoever — I who desired to see the city in daylight.
"Then those heroic rākṣasas, making loud proclamation, led me bound, enveloped in fire, along the royal road to the city gate.
"Then I contracted my very large body once more, freed myself from that bondage, and stood restored to my natural state.
"Seizing an iron club, I slew those guards; then I leapt swiftly to that city gate.
"And with my blazing tail, unperturbed, I burned that city with its towers and gateways, like the fire at the end of an age burning living beings.
"Having burned Laṅkā, again a fear overtook me: while burning Laṅkā, surely Sītā too has been burned — there is no doubt.
"Then I heard the auspicious speech of the cāraṇas who spoke a wondrous message: 'Jānakī has not been burned.'
"Then a thought arose in me after hearing that wondrous speech; the Vaidehī was seen again and I was sent off again by her.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"By the power of the Rāghava, and by your splendour, and for the purpose of Sugrīva's mission, all has been accomplished by me.
"All of this has been duly accomplished by me there — whatever remaining task has not been done here, let all of that now be carried out."
Having narrated all of that account, Hanūmān, son of the wind-god, proceeded to speak a further word:
"The effort of the Rāghava is fruitful, and the diligence of Sugrīva, having encountered the character of Sītā — as is my great leap.
"The character of the noble Sītā is worthy of her, O bulls among leapers — by her ascetic power she could sustain the worlds, or if angered she could burn them utterly.
"In every respect that Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas, has grown excessively powerful — the body of one who has touched her has not been destroyed by her ascetic power.
"What a flame of fire touched by hand could not do, the daughter of Janaka, stirred to the turbulence of extreme anger, could do.
"In the middle of the Aśoka grove of the evil-souled Rāvaṇa, beneath the śiṃśapā tree, the virtuous one sits in pitiable condition.
"Surrounded by rākṣasīs, wasted by grief and anguish, she is like a crescent of the moon surrounded by streaks of cloud — shorn of its lustre.
"The Vaidehī gives no thought to Rāvaṇa who is arrogant with strength; she is devoted to her husband, lovely-hipped, and firm in resolve — Jānakī.
"For the auspicious Vaidehī is devoted to Rāma with her entire being, her mind fixed on Rāma alone — like Paulomī fixed upon Purandara.
"Clothed in a single garment, covered with dust as well, her limbs wasted by grief and anguish, Sītā is devoted to her husband's welfare.
"She was seen by me in the forest, that lady in the midst of rākṣasīs, threatened again and again by the misshapen rākṣasīs.
"Wearing her hair in a single braid, wretched, her every thought absorbed in her husband, sleeping on the ground, her limbs pale — like a lotus pool at the onset of winter.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"She who had turned away from Rāvaṇa's purpose and had resolved to die — that doe-eyed one was somehow brought to trust.
"Then she was spoken to and all the matter was revealed to her; and upon hearing of the friendship of Rāma and Sugrīva, she experienced joy.
"Her conduct is regulated and her devotion to her husband is supreme.
"That the great-souled Daśānana does not slay Daśagrīva — Rāma shall be merely the instrument in his slaying.
"Thus does the greatly blessed Sītā dwell, absorbed in grief — whatever should be done about this, let all of that now be brought to fruition."
Having heard those words, the son of Vālin addressed them all — having taken leave of Jāmbavān and the great monkeys who stood foremost among them.
"Since the mission has gone thus far and has been reported to you all, it is fitting that we now see those two princes together with Vaidehī."
"I alone am sufficient to destroy by force that city of Laṅkā with all its companies of rākṣasas, and Rāvaṇa the mighty as well."
"How much more so when accompanied by heroes — powerful, self-disciplined, skilled in weapons, capable vānara warriors such as yourselves, who are intent on victory!"
"I shall scatter Rāvaṇa in battle together with his army, his vanguard, his sons, and his brothers in arms."
"Even if Indrajit deploys his terrible divine weapons in battle — those of Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Vāyu, and Varuṇa — I shall repel them all and slay the rākṣasas."
"With your approval, my valor shall check him."
"An incomparable and unceasing rain of mountains hurled by me could slay even the gods in battle — what then of those night-roaming demons?"
"Though the ocean should overstep its shores and Mount Mandara should be uprooted, no enemy host in battle could make Jāmbavān tremble."
"The heroic vānara, son of Vāyu — he alone is sufficient for the destruction of all the hosts of rākṣasas, and of the ancient rākṣasas as well."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"At the tremendous onslaught of Panasa and the great-souled Nīla, even Mount Mandara would be shattered to pieces — what then of the rākṣasas in battle?"
"Name a match for Mainda or Dvivida in battles involving gods, asuras, gandharvas, serpents, or birds — you cannot."
"These two best of vānaras, sons of the Aśvins, are of tremendous speed; filled with supreme pride born of the boon granted by the Grandfather."
"For the sake of honoring the Aśvins, the Grandfather of all worlds long ago bestowed upon these two an incomparable immunity from death."
"Intoxicated by the pride of that boon, these two heroic vānaras once overpowered the great army of the gods and drank the immortal nectar."
"These two alone, when roused to fury, are capable of destroying Laṅkā with all her horses, chariots, and elephants — let the other vānaras stand aside."
"Yet it would be improper for us vānaras — who have seen the goddess but not brought her — to go into the presence of the great-souled Rāghava without her."
"To report there merely that 'the goddess was seen but not brought back' — this seems to me improper for you, whose valor is renowned."
"Among you, best of vānaras, none is your equal in leaping and none is your equal in valor throughout the worlds, including among gods and asuras."
"Since the rākṣasa heroes have already been slain thus by Hanūmān, what else remains to be done here? Let us take Jānakī and depart."
Jāmbavān, best of monkeys and one who knows the meaning of things, spoke with great delight to Aṅgada who had thus resolved, speaking words full of purpose.
"This resolve is not incapable — as you see it, O prince. But let your gaze be fixed on the accomplishment of the mission in accordance with the will of Rāma."
Then the forest-dwellers — the heroes headed by Aṅgada and the great monkey Hanūmān — accepted the words of Jāmbavān.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then all of them, filled with joy and with Vāyu's son going before them, the foremost of vānaras leaped away, departing from the summit of Mount Mahendra.
Like Meru and Mandara in their aspect, like great elephants in rut, massive in body and immense in strength, they seemed to cover the sky as they flew.
The beings of the air seemed to carry Hanūmān — honored by them, self-possessed, mighty in strength, and swift in his course — upon their very gazes.
Having secured the accomplishment of Rāghava's purpose and supreme glory for their master, they flew onward — their mission fulfilled, elevated by the success of their deeds.
All of them were eager to bring glad tidings; all delighted in the prospect of battle; all were resolute in purpose regarding vengeance for Rāma — stout-hearted warriors.
Leaping through the sky, those forest-dwellers arrived at a grove filled with trees and creepers that resembled Nandana, the garden of the gods.
This was the Madhuvana — the Honey Grove — so named, guarded and protected by Sugrīva, unapproachable by all creatures, yet delightful to the hearts of all.
It was ever guarded by the great and mighty monkey Dadhimukha — the maternal uncle of the great-souled Sugrīva, chief of the monkeys.
Arriving at that vast and most beloved grove of the lord of monkeys, the vānaras became supremely exuberant.
Then the vānaras, honey-tawny and joyful at seeing the great Madhuvana, approached the young prince Aṅgada and begged him for the honey.
Then the young prince, having obtained the consent of the elder monkeys headed by Jāmbavān, gave them freedom to partake of the honey.
And so, with permission given, all the forest-dwellers were overwhelmed with joy; delighted, they began to dance here and there.
Some sang; some bowed down; some danced; some laughed loudly; some tumbled and rolled; some wandered about; some leaped; some chattered away.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Some leaned upon one another; some boasted against each other; some leaped from tree to tree; some fell from the treetops to the ground.
Some, rising with great speed from the ground, flew up to the tops of great trees; one who was singing approached another laughing, and another laughing approached one who laughed.
One who was weeping approached another weeping; one who was shoving another came and shoved him back. The monkey army was utterly in chaos, the behavior of every creature intoxicated by drinking honey. Not one among them was not drunk; not one among them was not satiated.
Then, seeing the grove being plundered and the trees stripped of their leaves and blossoms, the monkey named Dadhimukha, in his fury, tried to restrain those monkeys.
Threatened by those bold and spirited monkeys, the grove's guardian — elder among the heroic vānaras and fierce in his energy — resolved once more to defend the forest against the monkeys.
He spoke harsh words to some boldly and without restraint; he struck others with his palms; he came to blows with still others; and to yet others he approached with conciliation.
But he was overpowered by those whose onslaught could not be checked for the force of their intoxication, and who themselves could not be stopped — fearless, they came upon him heedless of any fault, and dragged him about.
Stabbing him with their nails, biting him with their teeth, pummeling him with their palms and feet, all the monkeys together, in their drunken state, laid that guardian monkey low and left the great grove utterly ravaged.
Hanūmān, best of monkeys and foremost bull among vānaras, spoke to them: "With minds undisturbed, partake freely of the honey, O monkeys."
Hearing Hanūmān's words, Aṅgada — foremost among monkeys — replied with a clear and cheerful heart: "Let the monkeys drink honey."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The word of Hanūmān — one who has accomplished his mission — must of necessity be honored by me. Even what might otherwise be improper must be done; how much more so a matter such as this."
Hearing those words from the mouth of Aṅgada, the bull-like vānaras responded with joyful acclamation, crying "Excellent! Excellent!" in his honor.
