Having honored Aṅgada, that bull among vānaras, all the monkeys rushed toward the Madhuvana swift as the current of a river.
Elated — they who had seen and heard of Maithilī — and given free rein, those capable warriors overpowered the keepers of the Madhuvana by force.
Then they all leaped up and rushed at the grove-keepers who had assembled, striking them by the hundreds as they stood their ground in the Madhuvana.
Taking up great vessels of honey — droṇa-measures full — they struck one another; others consumed it together in great quantities.
Some honey-tawny monkeys, having drunk their fill, tossed the honey aside; others, intoxicated and unruly, pelted each other with the honeycomb leavings.
Others sat at the roots of trees clutching branches, and then, overcome to excess by the stupor of intoxication, spread leaves and lay down to sleep.
The vānaras, like mad creatures and drunk with honey, flung themselves joyfully at one another, and still others stumbled and reeled about.
Some uttered wild shrieks; some cooed in delight; the monkeys drunk on honey lay stretched out asleep on the ground.
Even the honey-keepers who were servants of Dadhimukha were driven back by those fearsome monkeys and fled in all directions.
Dragged by the knees, shown the sky, and filled with great anguish, they went and spoke these words to Dadhimukha.
"The Madhuvana has been destroyed by force by those given leave by Hanūmān. We ourselves were dragged by the knees and shown the sky."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Dadhimukha the grove-warden, enraged upon hearing that the Madhuvana had been laid waste, pacified those monkeys who had come to him.
"Come, let us go! We shall restrain by force those arrogant monkeys who are consuming the honey."
Hearing these words of Dadhimukha, those heroic bull-like vānaras went once more to the Madhuvana, together with him.
Dadhimukha, in the midst of them and seizing an immense tree, rushed forward swiftly — and all the other vānaras did likewise.
Those monkeys, taking up rocks, trees, and boulders in their anger, came charging toward where the great elephant-like monkeys were.
Those heroes, fixing their master's command in their hearts, rushed forward swiftly, armed with śāla trees, palmyra palms, and rocks.
The grove-guardian warriors, by the thousands, fell upon the monkeys — those perched in trees and those standing on the ground — who were arrogant in their strength.
Then, seeing Dadhimukha enraged, the bull-like vānaras led by Hanūmān charged at him with great speed.
As that great-armed and mighty one came rushing forward with his tree, the furious Aṅgada there struck that elder with both arms.
Blinded by intoxication, he did not recognize that this was his respected elder; swiftly and with great force he slammed him hard into the ground.
With his arm broken, turning away, overwhelmed and drenched in blood, that heroic elephant among monkeys instantly fell senseless for a moment.
That bull among vānaras somehow freed himself from those monkeys, withdrew to one side, and spoke to those servants who had come to him.
"Let these ones stay here; we shall go to where our master, the broad-necked vānara Sugrīva, stands together with Rāma."
"I shall report all of Aṅgada's transgressions to the king. He, the impatient one, upon hearing the words, will have the monkeys put to death."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For this Madhuvana is the beloved grove of the great-souled Sugrīva — inherited from fathers and grandfathers, divine, and unapproachable even by the gods."
"Sugrīva will punish and put to death all these monkeys — greedy for honey, their lives now forfeit — along with their companions."
"These wicked ones who have disregarded the king's command are fit for death. The anger born of our outrage shall bear fruit."
Having spoken thus, the mighty Dadhimukha, together with the grove-keepers, leaped up at once and departed.
In no more than the twinkling of an eye, that forest-dweller arrived at the place where the wise Sugrīva — son of the Sun of a thousand rays — stood.
Seeing Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sugrīva himself, he descended from the sky and alighted on the level ground.
Having landed, that great and mighty monkey Dadhimukha, supreme lord of the grove-keepers, was surrounded by all of those keepers.
With a look of misery on his face and his joined hands raised to his head, he pressed his forehead to the auspicious feet of Sugrīva.
Then the bull among monkeys, seeing the monkey fallen at his feet with bowed head, was troubled at heart and spoke these words.
"Rise, rise! Why have you fallen at my feet? You shall have no fear, O hero — speak only the truth."
Reassured by that great-souled Sugrīva, the highly wise Dadhimukha rose up and spoke.
"O king, this grove was never granted to be enjoyed — not by Ṛkṣarajas, not by you, not by Vālin — yet those monkeys have eaten of it.
Even though the grove-wardens restrained and forbade them, these monkeys, heedless of us, ate and drank the honey.
Some threw away what remained; others ate it; and all of them, when stopped, merely raised their eyebrows in contempt.
The wardens, in trying to bar those best of monkeys from the grove, were then set upon and assaulted by those furious monkey-bulls.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then those many heroic monkeys, eyes reddened with fury, O bull among monkeys, struck down the wardens.
Some were beaten with fists, some struck with knees; others were dragged about at will and shown the sky — hurled through the air.
Thus our brave wardens have been beaten while you, their lord, still reign; and the entire Madhuvana has been eaten by them to their fill.
While Sugrīva, bull among monkeys, was being informed thus, the highly wise Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, questioned him.
"O king, why has this grove-keeper monkey come to present himself before you? Indicating what matter did he speak in distress?"
Thus addressed by the great-souled Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, skilled in speech, replied to him in these words.
"Noble Lakṣmaṇa, the brave monkey Dadhimukha reports that the Madhuvana has been consumed by the heroes led by Aṅgada.
Such boldness as this would not belong to monkeys who had failed in their mission; by entering that grove they have signalled that their task is accomplished.
Without doubt the goddess Sītā has been found — and by none other than Hanūmān; for there is no other agent capable of accomplishing this deed but Hanūmān.
O best of monkeys, success in this mission rests in Hanūmān — the resolve, the valour, the learning, all are firmly established in him.
Where Jāmbavān is the guide, Aṅgada the lord of the host, and Hanūmān the presiding spirit, the outcome cannot be otherwise.
The Madhuvana has been ravaged by the valiant heroes led by Aṅgada — those best of monkeys who have returned having searched the southern quarter.
Having returned, they entered the Madhuvana and the monkeys ravaged the entire grove and enjoyed it to the full; the wardens who tried to stop them together were struck with knees.
It is for this purpose that this sweet-spoken monkey of celebrated prowess, named Dadhimukha, has come here to report."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"O great-armed Saumitri, consider the truth of it: Sītā has been found — see how all the monkeys drink honey upon arriving there!"
"O bull among men, renowned monkeys would not dare to violate the divine grove granted as a boon, without having first found the daughter of Videha."
Then Lakṣmaṇa, righteous in spirit, together with Rāghava, was filled with joy upon hearing the sweet words that flowed from Sugrīva's mouth.
Rāma rejoiced greatly, and so did the greatly glorious Lakṣmaṇa; and Sugrīva, himself overjoyed at hearing Dadhimukha's report, addressed the grove-keeper once more.
"Dear friend, I am pleased that those who have accomplished the work ate of the grove; what those who have done their duty have done is entirely fitting and must be pardoned."
"I desire at once to see those tree-leaping monkeys led by Hanūmān — bold as lions, their mission accomplished — together with the two Rāghavas, and to hear the effort made in finding Sītā."
Thus addressed by Sugrīva, the delighted monkey Dadhimukha paid obeisance to Rāghava, to Lakṣmaṇa, and to Sugrīva.
Having bowed to Sugrīva and to the two mighty Rāghavas, he leapt up into the sky together with his company of brave monkeys.
Just as he had come, so he went back swiftly; descending from the sky to the earth, he entered that grove.
Entering the Madhuvana, he found all the monkey-troop leaders, freed of their intoxication yet still elated, urinating the honey-liquor.
That hero approached them and, joining his cupped palms in añjali, spoke these gentle words in a tone of gladness to Aṅgada.
"Dear lord, let there be no anger over the fact that the wardens who stopped you did so in anger and out of ignorance — they did not know who you were."
"O greatly powerful one, you are the crown prince and lord of this forest; the offence was committed beforehand out of foolishness — it befits you to forgive it."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Just as your father formerly was lord of the monkey host, so too is Sugrīva — no other, O best of monkeys."
"O sinless one, I have gone and reported to your paternal uncle the arrival here of all these forest-wandering monkeys."
"He, upon hearing of your coming together with these monkey-troop leaders, was overjoyed — not at all angry upon hearing that the grove was ravaged."
"Your paternal uncle Sugrīva, lord of monkeys, rejoicing, commanded me the king: 'Send them all here swiftly.'"
Hearing this gentle speech of Dadhimukha, Aṅgada, best of monkeys and skilled in speech, addressed those monkeys with words.
"I think this whole account has been heard by Rāma, O troop-leaders of the monkeys; now that our mission is done, it is not fitting for us to remain here, O afflicters of foes."
"O forest-wanderers, having drunk honey to our satisfaction and rested, what remains but to go there where my elder, Sugrīva, awaits?"
"I shall act in accordance with what all the troop-leaders say when they come together; I am dependent on you all in what must be done."
"I am not fit to issue commands, even though I am crown prince; it would be improper for me to overrule you who have accomplished the mission."
As Aṅgada spoke thus, the forest-dwellers heard his imperishable words and, their hearts filled with joy, spoke these words.
"O king, O bull among monkeys, who, being a master, would speak thus? Every man intoxicated with the pride of lordship thinks only of himself."
"These words are most fitting for you alone, not for any other; your humility proclaims the auspicious fortune that lies ahead for you."
"We are all ready and the moment is right to go there where the undying Sugrīva, lord of the valiant monkeys, abides."
"O best of monkeys, monkeys unsummoned by you cannot move a single step anywhere — this we tell you truly."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
As they spoke thus, Aṅgada replied to them; saying "Very well, let us go," he leapt up from the surface of the earth.
All those monkey-troop leaders leapt up after him as he leapt, filling the sky to overflowing, like flames flung up by a sacrifice.
Those swift-moving monkeys, leaping at once into the sky, roared with great cries, like clouds driven by the wind.
While Aṅgada had not yet arrived, Sugrīva, lord of monkeys, spoke to lotus-eyed Rāma who was afflicted with grief.
"Take heart — good fortune to you! The goddess Sītā has been found, without doubt; they could not have come here if the time allotted had passed."
"The crown prince, great-armed Aṅgada, best among leapers, would not have come to me if the mission had been a failure."
"Even if the conduct of one who had not accomplished the task were such as this, his face would be downcast and his mind wandering and confused."
"This Madhuvana, guarded by our forebears and inherited from father and grandfather, no lord of monkeys bereft of joy would dare to ravage."
"O Rāma of good vows, Kausalyā is blessed in her son — take comfort! The goddess Sītā has been found, beyond doubt, and by none other than Hanūmān; no other agent of that kind could have accomplished this deed."
"O best of the wise, success, intelligence, determination, and valour are fixed in Hanūmān as surely as radiance is fixed in the sun."
"Where Jāmbavān is the guide, Aṅgada the lord of the host, and Hanūmān the presiding spirit, the outcome cannot be otherwise."
"O you of boundless valour, be not prey to anxiety any longer."
Then he heard nearby in the sky the kilakila shout of the forest-dwellers intoxicated with their achievement, roaring as they approached Kiṣkindhā, as if proclaiming their success.
Then, upon hearing that roar of the monkeys, that best of monkeys — his long tail raised and curled — became glad at heart.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Those monkeys came too, eager to see Rāma, placing Aṅgada and the monkey Hanūmān at their head.
Those heroes led by Aṅgada, filled with delight and joy, alighted near the king of monkeys and near Rāghava.
And great-armed Hanūmān, having bowed his head in reverence, announced to Rāghava that the goddess Sītā was well and unharmed.
Then, with the matter resolved in Hanūmān, the son of the Wind, Lakṣmaṇa looked upon the pleased Sugrīva with affection and great esteem.
And Rāghava, slayer of enemy heroes, delighting in his joy, looked upon Hanūmān with the greatest honour and esteem.
Then those monkeys went to Mount Prasravaṇa with its colourful forest and bowed their heads to Rāma and to the mighty Lakṣmaṇa.
Placing the crown prince Aṅgada at their head, and having saluted Sugrīva, they began to report what had happened concerning Sītā.
They told of her confinement in Rāvaṇa's inner chambers, the threats made by the rākṣasī women, her deep devotion to Rāma, and the compact that had been made.
All those monkeys reported this in Rāma's presence; and upon hearing that the daughter of Videha was unharmed, Rāma spoke in reply.
"Where does the goddess Sītā dwell, and how does she bear herself toward me? Tell me everything regarding the daughter of Videha, O monkeys."
Having heard Rāma's words, the monkeys in Rāma's presence urged Hanūmān, who was expert in the particulars of Sītā's situation.
Hearing their words, Hanūmān, the son of the Wind God, skilled in speech, spoke, recounting exactly how he had seen Sītā.
"Having leapt across the ocean stretching a hundred yojanas in breadth, I went searching with longing to see Jānakī Sītā."
"There stands Laṅkā, the city of the evil-souled Rāvaṇa, on the southern shore of the southern ocean."
"There I found Sītā, the virtuous one, in Rāvaṇa's inner chambers, living still, having set all her hope upon you, O Rāma."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I saw her in the midst of rākṣasī women, threatened again and again, guarded by misshapen rākṣasīs in the pleasure grove."
"The goddess, she who is not accustomed to sorrow, suffers great distress, confined in Rāvaṇa's inner chambers and closely guarded by the rākṣasī women."
"She wears her hair in a single braid, wretched, absorbed in thoughts of you, sleeping on the ground, her limbs discoloured — like a lotus pond at the onset of winter."
"The goddess, her desire turned utterly away from Rāvaṇa, resolved to die — thinking of you alone, O Kākutstha, she was somehow found by me."
"O sinless tiger among men, I gradually won her trust by recounting your fame and the glory of the Ikṣvāku lineage."
"Then the goddess was spoken to and shown the full state of affairs; upon hearing of the friendship between Rāma and Sugrīva, she was filled with joy."
"Her devotion and steadfast conduct toward you are unwavering; thus was the greatly blessed daughter of Janaka seen by me, O bull among men, enduring fierce austerity sustained by her devotion to you."
"A token of recognition was given to me by her — the incident as it truly occurred between you and the crow at Citrakūṭa, O Rāghava of great wisdom."
"'The tiger among men, Rāma, should be informed by you, O son of the Wind, of everything that was seen here' — thus Jānakī told me."
"'And this token, carefully preserved, should be given to him' — speaking these words even as Sugrīva listened."
"'This glorious crest-jewel has been guarded by me with great care for you; and also the tika-mark of manaḥśilā mineral — remember that occasion,' she said."
"'This glorious jewel born of water is now rendered up by me to you; seeing this, O sinless one, I shall take joy in my affliction as if I saw you yourself,' she said."
"'I shall sustain my life for one month, O son of Daśaratha; beyond a month I cannot live, fallen under the power of the rākṣasas,' she said."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Thus spoke Sītā to me — slender-limbed, righteous in conduct, imprisoned in Rāvaṇa's inner chambers, her wide eyes like those of a doe."
"All this I have reported to you exactly as it occurred, O Rāghava; now by every means let the crossing of the ocean's waters be arranged."
Both princes having thus found reassurance, and the token having been presented to Rāghava, the son of the Wind narrated in full with complete words, in order, everything that the goddess had related.
Thus addressed by Hanūmān, Rāma, son of Daśaratha, pressing that jewel to his heart, wept together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Beholding that finest of jewels, Rāghava, wasted by grief, his two eyes brimming with tears, spoke these words to Sugrīva.
Just as a tender cow flows with milk out of love for her calf, so too my heart melts at the sight of this precious jewel.
This precious jewel was given to Vaidehī by my father-in-law; fastened as it was at the time of her wedding, it shines most beautifully upon her head.
This jewel, born of water, is honored by the greatest; it was given by the wise Śakra, greatly pleased, at a sacrifice.
Beholding this finest of jewels, O gentle one, today I understand it as the very sight of my father, and likewise of the great king of Videha.
This jewel gleams upon the head of my beloved; today, by the sight of it, I imagine her as if she were present before me.
What did Sītā, the daughter of Videha, say? Tell me again and again, O gentle one—reviving me as if with water, one nearly dead, with the water of her words.
What grief could be greater than this—that I behold this jewel born of water, O son of Sumitrā, without Vaidehī having come with it?
Vaidehī will survive—if she can endure for a month; but I, O gentle one, could not live for even a moment without her, she of the dark eyes.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Take me also to that place where my beloved was seen; having learned of her condition, I could not remain even for a moment.
How does she, my fair-hipped one, the timid, the ever-faithful one, dwell amid the fearsome and terrible rākṣasas who inspire dread?
Surely her face, shrouded by those rākṣasas, no longer shines—like the autumnal moon whose face is veiled by clouds.
What did Sītā say, O Hanūmān? Tell me truthfully—by this I shall live, as a sick man lives by medicine.
The sweet one, sweet of speech—what did my passionate one say, she of noble hips, separated from me? Tell me, O Hanūmān: having attained sorrow upon sorrow, how does Jānakī live?
Thus addressed by the great-souled Rāghava, Hanūmān reported to Rāghava everything that Sītā had spoken.
"This is what the goddess Jānakī said, O bull among men: she gave a token from former events at Citrakūṭa, exactly as they happened."
"Jānakī, having slept pleasantly at your side, awoke before you; a crow suddenly flew up and cried out, pecking between her breasts."
"Then you slept in turn in the goddess's lap, O elder brother of Bharata; and again that bird caused pain to the goddess."
"Then coming again it cried out fiercely; thereupon you were awakened, drenched with her blood."
"Awakened by that very crow which had been tormenting the goddess without ceasing, you, O scorcher of foes, had been sleeping peacefully."
"Seeing her weeping with wounds between her breasts, O mighty-armed one, you breathed heavily like an angry serpent and addressed her."
"'Who, O timid one, has torn the space between your breasts with nail-tips? Who plays with an enraged five-headed serpent?'"
"Looking around suddenly, you saw the crow—standing before you with sharp blood-stained talons—facing you directly."
"That crow was reportedly the son of Śakra, best among birds, roaming between earth and sky, swift as the wind in its flight."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then, O mighty-armed one, O best among the wise, your eyes rolling in anger, you resolved upon a cruel intention against that crow."
"Taking a blade of darbha grass from the spread mat, you charged it with the Brahmāstra; blazing like the fire of dissolution, it flamed toward the bird."
"You hurled that blazing blade of grass at the crow; and then that blazing grass indeed pursued the crow."
"Abandoned by his father, by all the gods, and by the great sages, he wandered through the three worlds and found no protector."
"Him fallen to the ground, O Kākutstha, refuge of the refuge-seeking, though deserving of death, you protected out of compassion."
"The weapon could not be made to go in vain, O Rāghava—thus it destroyed the right eye of that eye-plucking crow."
"Bowing to you, O Rāma, and to king Daśaratha, that crow was then released and returned to the sky as his home."
"You who are the foremost among those who know weapons, possessed of valor, possessed of good character—why do you not employ your weapons against the rākṣasas, O Rāghava?"
"Neither nāgas, nor gandharvas, nor asuras, nor the host of Maruts are capable of standing before you in battle, O Rāma, and withstanding you."
"If you, so mighty, have any concern for me, then let Rāvaṇa be slain swiftly in battle with your well-sharpened arrows."
"And Lakṣmaṇa, the scorcher of foes, acting under his brother's command—why does he, that best of men, that Rāghava, not protect me?"
"Those two tigers among men, equal in splendor to wind and fire, unconquerable even by the gods—why do they disregard me?"
"Surely some great sin of mine exists—there is no doubt—since those two scorchers of foes, capable and united, do not regard me."
"Having heard that pitiful, tear-choked speech of Vaidehī, I again spoke these words to that noble lady."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'Rāma is free of grief for you, O goddess—I swear this to you by truth; and when Rāma is overwhelmed by sorrow, Lakṣmaṇa also burns with pain.'"
"'You have somehow been found—it is not the time for grieving; this very moment you shall see the end of your sorrows, O passionate one.'"
"'Those two tigers among men, princes, destroyers of enemies, roused to eagerness by the prospect of seeing you, will reduce Laṅkā to ashes.'"
"'And having slain the terrible Rāvaṇa along with his kin in battle, the mighty-armed Rāghava will certainly lead you back to his own city.'"
"'Whatever token might let Rāma know—something that will generate delight in him, O blameless one—you should truly give it.'"
"She, gazing in all directions, loosened the excellent binding of her braid and, from her garment, gave me this jewel, O mighty one."
"Receiving that divine jewel for your sake, O best of the Raghus, bowing to her with my head, I hastened in my coming."
"And seeing me roused to eagerness for departure and growing in size, the daughter of Janaka, that fair-complexioned one, her face filled with tears, pitiful, her words choked with weeping, spoke to me."
"'O Hanūmān, convey my greeting of freedom from ill to both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who are like lions, and to Sugrīva together with his ministers, to all of them.'"
"'And you should endeavor to arrange how that mighty-armed Rāghava may rescue me from this flood of sorrow that hems me in.'"
"'And when you reach Rāma's presence, tell him of this fierce surge of my grief and of the taunts of these rākṣasas. May your journey be auspicious, O hero among monkeys.'"
"This is the speech that your noble Sītā spoke to you, O lion among kings of kings, full of despondency. Understanding this, I have told you—believe that Sītā is well and whole."
"Then I was again addressed urgently by the goddess with a further message: 'Out of love for you, O tiger among men, and having obtained your friendship—'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'—you must speak to Rāma, son of Daśaratha, in many such ways, so that he may quickly recover me, having slain Rāvaṇa in battle.'"
"'Or if you think it fit, O hero, O subduer of enemies, stay one day in some hidden place; rested, you shall depart tomorrow.'"
"'And by your nearness to me, O monkey—I who am so bereft of good fortune—there might be for a moment a release from the full ripening of this grief.'"
"'For once you, the mighty, have departed with regard to returning, even my very survival will be in doubt—of this there is no uncertainty.'"
"'The grief born of not seeing you would torment me further—me, overcome by sorrow upon sorrow, fallen low, a sharer in misery.'"
"'Yet this great doubt about your heroes stands as it were before me—a very great doubt, without question, concerning your allies, the monkeys and bears.'"
"'How will those armies of monkeys and bears cross the great ocean, so difficult to cross? Or how will those two sons of the best of men?'"
"'The power to leap over this ocean would belong to only three beings: Vainateya, or Vāyu, or you, O blameless monkey.'"
"'So in this undertaking of heroes, so difficult to accomplish, what solution do you see? Tell me, O best among those who know what must be done.'"
"'Granted, you alone are sufficient for the accomplishment of this task, O slayer of enemy heroes; your rise of power brings you glory.'"
"'But if Rāma, victorious, were to lead me to his own city with his full forces, having slain Rāvaṇa in battle—that would bring him glory.'"
"'Just as I was carried off from the forest by that rākṣasa through guile, Rāghava should not act out of that same fear alone—that would not befit him.'"
"'But if Kākutstha, the crusher of enemy armies, were to overrun Laṅkā with his forces and then lead me away—that would be worthy of him.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'So arrange it in such a way that it may be fitting for that great-souled one's heroism, fitting for the valor of that hero in battle.'"
"Having heard that speech, laden with meaning, humble, joined with reasoning, I then spoke the following further words in reply."
"'O goddess, Sugrīva, lord of the armies of monkeys and bears, best among the leapers, endowed with valor, is firmly resolved for your sake.'"
"'The monkeys who stand under his command are endowed with heroism, possessed of valor, of great strength, swift as the speed of the mind's resolve.'"
"'Their movement is unimpeded above, below, or sideways; and they do not falter in great deeds—those of immeasurable splendor.'"
"'Not once but many times have those greatly fortunate, powerful monkeys, who travel the path of the wind, circumambulated the earth.'"
"'There are forest-dwellers there who are both superior to me and equal to me; none in Sugrīva's company is inferior to me.'"
"'I, at least, have reached here—how much more so those of great power? For it is not the foremost who are sent on missions; it is the lesser folk who are sent.'"
"'Therefore, enough of anguish, O goddess; let your anger depart. The leaders of monkey troops will come to Laṅkā in a single leap.'"
"'And those two—like the risen sun and moon—mounted upon my back, those two lion-men will come into your presence, O greatly fortunate one.'"
"'You will swiftly see Rāghava, the slayer of enemies, like a lion, and Lakṣmaṇa with bow in hand, standing at the gates of Laṅkā.'"
"'You will swiftly see the heroes assembled—armed with nails and fangs, with the stride of lions and tigers, those monkeys resembling lords of monkeys.'"
"'You will soon hear the roar of the chiefs of monkeys, resembling mountains and storm-clouds, roaring upon the slopes of Laṅkā's Malaya hills.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'And you will swiftly see Rāghava—his forest exile over, the subduer of enemies—consecrated as king at Ayodhyā, together with you.'"
"Then, consoled by me with auspicious and pleasing words spoken without despondency, the daughter of the king of Mithilā attained peace—she too, so afflicted by grief on your account."
Having heard Hanūmān's words spoken exactly as they were, Rāma, filled with joy, replied with the following words.
Hanūmān has accomplished an exceedingly great and difficult deed on earth — one that no other being on this earth could even conceive of in mind.
I see no one who could cross the great ocean, save Garuḍa, or the Wind, or Hanūmān.
The city of Laṅkā, which is impregnable to gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, nāgas, and rākṣasas, and which is well-guarded by Rāvaṇa —
— who, having entered it by courage, could emerge alive? Who could enter that city so very hard to assault, guarded by rākṣasas, if he were not equal to Hanūmān in valor and might?
Hanūmān has performed a great service for his master Sugrīva, deploying his own strength in a manner befitting his valor.
A servant who, when assigned by his master to a difficult task, accomplishes it with devotion — such a one is called a foremost among men.
A servant who, though capable, qualified, and charged with the king's task, yet does not perform it — such a one is called the lowest of men.
Hanūmān, appointed to that charge, has fulfilled his duty; he has not made himself small, and Sugrīva too is gratified.
I, scion of the Raghu lineage, and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa have today been saved — rightfully so — by the sight of Vaidehī.
Yet this thought afflicts my wretched heart anew: that here I can render no fitting gift to him who has brought such glad tidings.
This embrace of Hanūmān is my all — given by me to that great soul, availing myself of this moment as the only gift I have.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The search for Sītā has been accomplished — that much is well done. Yet now that we have come to the ocean, my heart is lost once more.
How shall the monkeys reach the southern shore of this vast, hard-to-cross sea? That is the question that weighs upon my mind.
Even though Vaidehī's news has been reported to me, what still remains unsolved is the matter of the monkeys crossing the ocean.
Having spoken thus, Rāma the destroyer of foes, agitated by grief, the long-armed hero, fell into deep contemplation, Hanūmān beside him.
Then glorious Sugrīva spoke words that dispel grief to Rāma, son of Daśaratha, who was scorched by sorrow.
Why do you afflict yourself, O hero, like any ordinary man? Do not be so; abandon your anguish as an ingrate abandons friendship.
I see no occasion for your anguish, O Rāghava, now that news of her has been received and the enemy's abode has been discovered.
You are steadfast, versed in the scriptures, wise, and learned, O Rāghava. Abandon this wicked thought that, like a foe to oneself, corrupts your purpose.
We shall cross the ocean, which teems with great crocodiles, scale Laṅkā, and slay your enemy.
For the man who has lost his energy, who is despondent, whose soul is overwhelmed by grief — all his purposes founder, and calamity overtakes him.
All our monkey chieftains are brave and capable; for your sake they have roused their courage even to the point of entering fire itself.
By their exuberance I know it, and my conviction in this is firm: I shall bring Sītā back by valor, having slain the enemy.
As to how a bridge may be built here, and how we may behold that city of the king of rākṣasas — give your command to that effect, O Rāghava.
Having seen that city of Laṅkā seated on the peak of Trikūṭa, consider Rāvaṇa already slain in battle — take that as certain from the very sight.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Once a bridge is built across the sea and Laṅkā is close at hand, and once the whole army has crossed — consider it conquered.
These monkeys who can assume any form are heroes in battle. Enough then of this faint-hearted thinking, O king, that destroys all purposes.
In this world grief diminishes a man's heroism. What a man must do is hold fast to courage — especially men who are heroes and great souls like yourself.
Whether in ruin or in loss, grief destroys all aims. But you are the foremost among the wise, thoroughly versed in the meaning of all the scriptures.
You ought to conquer the enemy here, together with ministers like me. I see no one in all three worlds, O Rāghava —
— who could stand before you in battle once you have taken up your bow. With the monkeys engaged, your purpose shall not fail.
You shall see Sītā soon, once you have crossed the boundless sea. Enough of clinging to grief — take hold of wrath instead, O lord of the earth.
Sluggish kṣatriyas who take no action — all of them tremble before the fierce. And as for crossing the dreadful lord of rivers, the ocean —
— having come here with us, consider the matter with your keen intellect. For these monkeys who can take any form are heroes in battle.
They will scatter those enemies with showers of rocks and trees. Somehow we do see our way across the abode of Varuṇa.
What more need be said at length? You shall be victorious in every way.
Having heard Sugrīva's well-reasoned speech, Kākutstha, knower of the highest truth, accepted it and then spoke to Hanūmān.
Whether by the swift building of a bridge or by drying up the ocean, I am fully capable in every way of crossing this sea.
How many fortifications does the fortified city of Laṅkā have? Tell me that. I wish to know all of it as if seeing it with my own eyes, O monkey.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The size of the army, the construction of the gates and fortifications, the defensive measures of Laṅkā, and the dwellings of the rākṣasas —
— all that you saw freely and exactly in Laṅkā, recount to me truly. For you are in every way an expert.
Having heard Rāma's words, Hanūmān, son of the Wind, foremost among those skilled in speech, again spoke to Rāma.
"Let me be heard; I shall relate everything, regarding the arrangement of the fortifications, how the city of Laṅkā is protected and how it is guarded by armed forces."
"The surpassing wealth of Laṅkā, the dreadfulness of the ocean, the arrangement of the army's divisions, and the disposition of the war-vehicles —"
"Laṅkā is jubilant and cheerful, crowded with rutting elephants, large, filled with chariots, and thronged with bands of rākṣasas."
"Her four vast gates are of great size, fitted with strongly fastened panels and great iron crossbars."
"On the ramparts stand great and powerful stone-throwing machines, by which any enemy force that arrives there is driven back."
"At the gates, dreadful śataghnis — heavy iron-bolt engines — forged of black iron, sharp and burnished, are ranged by the hundreds, mounted by warrior bands of rākṣasas."
"She has a great golden rampart, hard to assail, whose interstices are inlaid with gems, coral, vaidūrya, and pearls."
"All around are great and terrifying moats, auspicious and vast, filled with cool water, fathomless, and inhabited by crocodiles and fish."
"Over those moats are four very long drawbridges fitted with many great and tightly jointed mechanisms."
"Those drawbridges are raised for defense when an enemy army approaches, and by those mechanisms they are dropped all around into the moats."
"But one bridge is immovable and strong, exceedingly firm and massive, adorned with many golden pillars and parapets."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Rāvaṇa himself, O Rāma, is gifted by nature with martial spirit — ever roused and vigilant in the inspection of his forces."
"The city of Laṅkā is self-sustaining, a fortress of the gods, fearsome; she has all four kinds of natural fortification: riverine, mountainous, forest-based, and artificial."
"She stands on the far shore of the ocean whose opposite shore is far away, O Rāghava; there is no sea-road to her, and she is inaccessible from every direction."
"That fortress-city is built on the summit of a mountain, comparable to the city of the gods, filled with horses and elephants; Laṅkā is supremely difficult to conquer."
"Iron crossbars, śataghnis, and various war-engines adorn the city of Laṅkā belonging to Rāvaṇa, that evil-souled one."
"At the western gate ten thousand rākṣasas are stationed — all of them wielding spears and hard to assail, foremost swordsmen."
"A hundred thousand rākṣasas are stationed at the southern gate — warriors with a four-fold army, and peerless combatants there as well."
"A million rākṣasas are posted at the eastern gate — all bearing shields and swords, and all of them skilled in every weapon."
"Ten million rākṣasas are stationed at the northern gate — charioteers and cavalry, all of them nobly born and highly honored."
"At the central garrison a hundred times a hundred thousand — that is, more than a crore — of yātudhānas, hard to assail, are posted."
"Those drawbridges I have broken, the moats I have filled up, the city of Laṅkā I have burned, and the ramparts I have shattered."
"Whatever route we take to cross the abode of Varuṇa, let it be settled among the monkeys that the city of Laṅkā is as good as slain."
"Aṅgada, Dvivida, Mainda, Jāmbavān, Panasa, Nala, and Nīla the general — with these remaining forces, what more do you need?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Leaping across, they will go to that great city of Rāvaṇa — ramparts, mansions and all — and bring back the Maithilī."
"Therefore, command quickly the full muster of the army and, choosing an auspicious hour, authorize the departure."
Having heard Hanūmat's words duly and in proper order, the greatly resplendent Rāma, whose valour is true, then spoke.
"That city of Laṅkā belonging to that fearsome rākṣasa, which you describe to me — I shall swiftly destroy it. This I say to you as truth."
"In this very moment, O Sugrīva, I choose to set out on the march. The hour is auspicious for victory; the sun has reached the meridian."
"Today is Uttara-Phalgunī; tomorrow the moon will be joined with Hastā. Let us set forth, O Sugrīva, encompassed by all our army divisions."
"And the auspicious omens that are manifesting before me — slaying Rāvaṇa, I shall bring back Sītā, the daughter of Janaka."
"Indeed, this upper eye of mine, twitching as it is, seems to herald my victory and the fulfilment of my heart's desire."
"Let Nīla go in advance of this army to reconnoitre the route, attended by a hundred thousand swift monkeys."
"O Nīla, O general, lead the army swiftly by a path furnished with fruits and roots, with cool woodland streams, and abounding in honey."
"Wicked rākṣasas may defile the roots, fruits, and water along the route; guard against them, remaining ever vigilant."
"Forest-dwellers lurking in ravines, woodland strongholds, and forests might spring forward and scout out the slaughter of our army by the enemy."
"Let the mighty lion-monkeys draw forth the fearsome vanguard, which resembles the flood of the ocean, by the hundreds and by the thousands."
"Let Gaja, who resembles a mountain, and the great-spirited Gavaya, and Gavākṣa march in front, like lordly bulls at the head of a herd of cattle."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Let Ṛṣabha, the lord of leaping monkeys, that bull among monkeys, guard the right flank of the monkey host as it advances."
"Let swift Gandhamādana — fierce as a rutting elephant — take up his post guarding the left flank of the monkey army."
"I shall march in the midst of the army, gladdening the flood of warriors, mounted upon Hanūmat as Indra rides upon Airāvata."
"Let Lakṣmaṇa, who equals Death, advance with Aṅgada — as the lord of beings and the lord of wealth ride with the universal sovereign."
"And let those three — Jāmbavān, Suṣeṇa, and the monkey Vegadarśī, the mighty king of bears — protect the flanks of the army."
Having heard the words of Rāghava, Sugrīva, lord of the army and bull among monkeys, assigned posts to the exceedingly valiant monkeys.
Then all those eager-for-battle monkey hosts swiftly leapt up from caves and mountain peaks and bounded forward.
Then righteous Rāma, honoured by the monkey king and by Lakṣmaṇa, set forth with his army toward the southern quarter.
He marched then encompassed by monkeys resembling elephants, in their hundreds, their hundreds of thousands, their tens of millions, and their ten thousands.
The great monkey army followed behind him as he marched.
Joyful and exultant, all guarded by Sugrīva, the leaping monkeys bounded, leapt, roared, shrieked, and howled as they marched indeed toward the southern quarter.
Eating fragrant honeycombs and fruits, carrying large trees whose blossoms clustered in dense masses,
suddenly spotting one another they dashed and flung each other about; some fell and others leapt up, and still others knocked their companions to the ground.
"Rāvaṇa must be slain by us, and all the night-roaming rākṣasas too" — thus the monkeys roared in the presence of Rāghava.
In the van, the heroic Ṛṣabha and Nīla and also Kumuda were clearing the route together with many monkeys.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
In the centre were King Sugrīva, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa — slayers of foes — surrounded by many powerful warriors.
The heroic monkey Śatabali, attended by ten crores of soldiers, guarded the entire monkey host single-handedly with his firm grasp.
Kesarī, Panasa, Gaja, and the exceedingly mighty Arka, attended by a hundred crores, guarded one flank of the army.
Suṣeṇa and Jāmbavān, surrounded by many bears, placed Sugrīva in front and together guarded the rear of the army.
Their general, heroic Nīla — bull among monkeys, foremost of leapers — guarded that army as it surged forward.
Darīmukha, Prajaṅgha, Jambha, and the monkey Rabhasa — those heroes went on every side urging the monkey soldiers onward.
Moving thus, those tiger-monkeys, swelling with strength, beheld the foremost of mountains, the Sahya, covered with trees and creepers.
That great, fearsome monkey army, resembling the flood of the ocean, poured forth with a tremendous roar, like the ocean with its terrifying momentum.
Those heroic elephant-like monkeys at the side of Daśaratha's son all leapt forward rapidly, like noble steeds urged on.
Borne by the two monkeys, those two bulls among men shone gloriously — as though the moon and the sun were touched by two great sea-monsters.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, riding on Aṅgada, addressed Rāma in auspicious words — he who was full of purposeful thought, possessed of memory, and ready of wit.
"Having recovered Vaidehī who was taken, and having slain Rāvaṇa, you shall return with accomplished purpose to Ayodhyā, which likewise waits with accomplished purpose."
"O Rāghava, I see great and auspicious omens in the sky and upon the earth — all of them heralding the accomplishment of your purpose."
"An auspicious breeze, gentle and pleasant, blows after the army; and these deer and birds cry out in full, sweet voices."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"All the quarters are serene; the sun shines clear and unclouded; and Venus — of brilliant, cloudless flame — follows behind you."
"The cluster of Brahmā shines pure; the great seers shine pure and radiant; all of them blaze forth steadily in the auspicious rightward direction."
"Triśaṅku the royal sage, together with his priest, shines without blemish — that most excellent ancestral star of our great-souled Ikṣvākus."
"Viśākhā also shines bright and undimmed, without affliction — that supreme constellation of our great-souled Ikṣvāku line."
"The constellation of the rākṣasas, Nairṛta, is tormented; Mūla, their own natal star, is afflicted and scorched by a comet with a smoky tail."
"This portends the destruction of the rākṣasas — whose time has come, seized by Death — their star tormented by a planet."
"The divine waters are pure and the rivers are serene; the forests are fruit-laden; fragrances waft most abundantly; trees bloom as in their proper season."
"The arrayed monkey armies blaze brilliantly, O master, like the armies of the gods in the war against Tārakā."
"Having observed all these omens, O noble one, you ought to be joyful." Thus Saumitri, himself elated, spoke these words to reassure his brother.
Then the great host, covering the entire earth, marched onward — accompanied by tiger-bears and tiger-monkeys, armed with claws and fangs.
The dust raised by the tips of the monkeys' hands and feet swallowed the earth, blocking the sun's radiance and enshrouding the world.
That great monkey army marched day and night — a force joyful and exultant, guarded by Sugrīva.
All the monkeys pressed forward swiftly, rejoicing in battle, eager to free Sītā — not halting anywhere even for a moment.
Then they reached the Sahya mountain, thick with trees and teeming with diverse animals, and also the great earth-bearing Malaya.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Even while beholding the variegated forests and the river-springs of Sahya and of Malaya, Rāma pressed on.
The leaping monkeys broke campaka trees, tilaka trees, mango trees, aśoka trees, sinduvāra trees, karavīra trees, and timiśa trees.
The powerful monkeys there consumed fruits with the fragrance of ambrosia, roots, and blossoms of the trees.
Those tawny-brown monkeys, joyful and of a golden hue, marched on drinking honeycombs the size of a droṇa measure that hung pendant from the branches.
The bull-monkeys pressed forward, breaking trees, tearing down creepers, and toppling mountain-boulders.
Other monkeys roared in the trees, drunk with honey; others ran to the trees and still others fell from them.
The earth was filled by those bull-monkeys — like the earth covered with fields of fully bloomed lotuses.
Then reaching Mount Mahendra, lotus-eyed Rāma, long-armed, ascended the summit adorned with trees.
Having climbed the summit, Rāma the son of Daśaratha beheld the expanse of waters teeming with tortoises and fish.
Passing beyond the Sahya and the great mountain Malaya, they reached in due course the ocean, roaring with a terrifying sound.
Rāma — foremost among those who bring delight — descended swiftly and came with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa to the incomparable shore-forest.
Then, having reached the broad shoreline — its rocky surface washed by the sudden surges of water — Rāma spoke these words.
"We have now reached, O Sugrīva, the abode of Varuṇa. Here now arises that anxiety which did not arise before."
"Yonder is the far shore — this ocean, lord of rivers. And this sea cannot be crossed without a means."
"Therefore let the encampment be made here and let counsel be taken here — such that this monkey army may reach the far shore."
Speaking thus, long-armed Rāma — worn by grief over Sītā's abduction — upon reaching the ocean ordered the camp to be established.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The time for counsel has arrived for us regarding the crossing of this ocean. Let each corps be dismissed to its own position; let no one stray in any direction. Let the heroic monkeys go and reconnoitre; the hidden dangers facing us must be known."
Having heard the words of Rāma, Sugrīva together with Lakṣmaṇa encamped the army on the tree-covered shore of the ocean.
That army, encamped near the ocean, blazed in splendour — like a second ocean, its waters pale gold as honey.
Then those bull-monkeys, having come to the shore-forest, settled down there, yearning for the far shore of the great deep.
That monkey army, having reached the great ocean and joyful, gazed upon the great ocean tossed by the force of the wind.
Gazing upon the abode of Varuṇa — its far shore distant, its expanse unobstructed, haunted by hosts of rākṣasas — the monkey troop-leaders sat down.
Fearsome with its violent crocodiles and sea-monsters, churned at the close of day and at moonrise, roiling with moon-halos,
scattered with monstrous sea-beasts lashed by fierce winds, strewn with timitimiṅgila creatures — the abode of Varuṇa seemed blanketed with serpents of blazing coils.
Plunged into by great creatures, filled with many underwater mountains, difficult to ford, treacherous, pathless, fathomless — that dwelling of the asuras.
Churned by makara sea-dragons and serpent coils, reddened by the wind — great masses of water rose up and fell down.
As if scattered with fire-powder, dazzling with the sun's reflections — the charming realm of the sun's enemy, fearsome, forever rendered rough by the underworld.
The ocean appeared like the sky and the sky appeared like the ocean — ocean and sky appeared indistinguishable from one another.
The waters were merged with the sky and the sky was merged with the waters; in that aspect they appeared alike — the stars mingled with the jewels.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Between the ocean with its billowing clouds and its rows of wave-garlands and the sky, no distinction could be made.
The waves of the ocean-king, crashing against one another and intertwined, rang out with terrifying sounds — like great war-drums in battle.
Resounding with the rush of jewel-strewn waters, as if lashed by the wind, as if leaping in rage, teeming with hosts of sea-creatures,
those great-souled heroes beheld the water-abode battered by the wind, as if hurled into the sky by the wind, as if bounding up with its waves — the ocean seemingly churning with the roar of its swirling, wave-tossed waters.
Then that army, with its proper guard duly arranged by Nīla, was well encamped on the northern shore of the ocean.
And both Mainda and Dvivida — those two bull-monkeys — roamed in every direction around that army for its protection.
When the army had encamped on the shore of the lord of rivers and lakes, Rāma, seeing Lakṣmaṇa at his side, spoke these words.
"They say that grief passes away with the passage of time; but mine, as I do not see my beloved, grows greater day by day."
"It is not that my beloved is far — that does not grieve me. It is not that she was taken — that does not grieve me. This alone is what I lament: her youth is passing away."
"Blow, O wind, from wherever that maiden is — touching her, touch me also. Through you I have contact with her body; through the moon I have a meeting of eyes."
"That burns my limbs like poison swallowed and lodged within me — what my beloved cried to me as she was being carried off: 'O my lord!'"
"Fed by that separation as by fuel, blazing with great flames of thought of her, by night and by day my body is consumed by the fire of love."
"I shall plunge into the ocean and sleep, O Saumitri, apart from you; perhaps the blazing passion might burn me even as I lie submerged in the water."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"There is much to sustain life for one who still desires — by this alone: that I and she of beautiful thighs are supported by one and the same earth."
"As a dry field lives by the moisture of the irrigated field beside it, so I live by the mere proximity of her vitality — for I hear that she is alive."
"When indeed shall I see fair-hipped Sītā — her eyes as wide as lotus petals — radiant as Śrī, after vanquishing my enemies?"
"When shall I, like a sick man drinking an elixir, drink from her face which is like a lotus, lifting it gently upward — from those beautiful lips red as the bimba fruit?"
"When indeed shall those two firm, full breasts of hers — resembling the fruits of the tāla palm — trembling, embrace me as she laughs?"
"She — that dark-eyed one with the long eyes, virtuous though surrounded by rākṣasas, who calls me her lord — no doubt finds no protector, as though she were lordless."
"When shall she, shaking off the rākṣasas and rising up free of them, soar aloft — as the crescent moon in autumn shakes free of blue storm-clouds?"
"Sītā, naturally slender, is surely grown yet more slender still through grief and fasting — and by the reversal of her rightful place and season."
"When indeed shall I, having fixed my arrows in the breast of the rākṣasa king, bring Sītā back and cast off this grief from my mind?"
"When indeed shall chaste Sītā — resembling the daughter of the immortals, filled with longing — cling to my neck and shed tears born of joy?"
"When shall I suddenly shed this dreadful grief born of separation from the Maithilī — as one sheds a white garment that has turned otherwise?"
While wise Rāma lamented thus at that place, the sun, his body dimming at the end of the day, descended to the west.
Comforted by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma performed the evening rites — remembering Sītā of lotus-petal eyes, overwhelmed by grief.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
In Laṅkā, having witnessed the fearsome, life-threatening deed wrought by Hanūmat — as by great-souled Śakra himself — the rākṣasa king, his face turned slightly downward in shame, addressed all his rākṣasas.
"Laṅkā, this city so difficult to assail, has been violated and penetrated — by a mere monkey, at that — and Sītā, daughter of Janaka, was seen."
"The pleasure-grove was ravaged, the sacred shrine was violated, eminent rākṣasas were slain, and all of Laṅkā was thrown into turmoil — all by Hanūmat."
"What shall I do? May good befall you all. What is the right course to follow now? Tell me what is fitting — let that be done which, having been done, will prove well done."
"The noble and wise declare that victory has counsel as its root; therefore I choose indeed to take counsel, O mighty ones, regarding Rāma."
"Men in the world are of three kinds — the highest, the lowest, and the middling; of these gathered together I shall speak of their virtues and defects."
"He who, together with counsellors who are well-disposed and capable in resolving deliberations — or with friends of equal purpose, or even with well-wishing kinsmen —"
"— deliberates and then sets forth his undertakings, and also makes effort in what pertains to fate — him they call the highest of men."
"He who deliberates alone on matters of interest, alone sets his mind on dharma, and alone performs his tasks — him they call the middling man."
"He who, without determining the merits and defects, abandoning recourse to the divine, neglects his task with the word 'I shall act' — he is the lowest of men."
"Just as men are forever of three kinds — highest, lowest, and middling — so too counsel itself must be understood to be highest, lowest, and middling."
"Counsel wherein the counsellors, having arrived at unity by means of the eye of śāstra, come to a settled conclusion — that they call the highest counsel."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Counsel wherein the counsellors, even after many opinions have been advanced in determining what is beneficial, yet again arrive at a single conclusion — that is remembered as middling counsel."
"Counsel wherein each upholds his own opinion and speaks against the others, where there is no good outcome in any unity of view — that counsel is called the lowest."
"Therefore, O foremost of counsellors, let you all well deliberate and agree upon what should be done — this is the most urgent matter for me."
"Rāma, surrounded by thousands of heroic monkeys, is advancing upon our city of Laṅkā — he who would lay siege to us."
"And Rāghava shall most certainly cross the ocean with ease — with fitting swiftness, together with his brother and followed by his army."
"With affairs having reached this pass — opposed by the monkeys — let everything beneficial for the city and for the army be deliberated thoroughly on my behalf."
Having been thus addressed by the lord of rākṣasas, those mighty rākṣasas all spoke with folded hands to Rāvaṇa, the lord of rākṣasas.
O king, our great army is filled with iron clubs, spears, javelins, tridents, and broadswords — why then does despondency overtake you?
Kubera, who dwelt on the peak of Kailāsa surrounded by many yakṣas, was reduced to your subjection after great slaughter was wrought.
That guardian of the world, boasting of his friendship with Maheśvara, was defeated by you in fury in battle, O mighty one.
Having slain the hosts of yakṣas, having routed and seized them, you brought away this aerial chariot from the peak of Kailāsa.
Maya, the lord of dānavas, desiring alliance out of fear of you, gave his daughter to be your wife, O bull among rākṣasas.
Madhu by name, the lord of dānavas, proud of his valour and hard to withstand, was seized and brought under your control — he who was the source of joy to Kumbhīnasī.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The nāgas who had retreated to the netherworld were defeated by you, O great-armed one; Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Śaṅkha, and Jaṭī were brought under your subjection.
Those dānavas who are inexhaustible, powerful, heroic, and doubly blessed with boons — you fought them in battle for a full year, O mighty one.
Relying on your own strength, they were brought to subjection, O slayer of foes; and many magical powers were also obtained there, O lord of rākṣasas.
The heroic and mighty sons of Varuṇa, followed by their fourfold armies, were defeated by you in battle, O great-armed one.
Having plunged into the ocean of Yama's army — terrible as the great crocodile of death's rod, adorned by the Śālmalī island — O king,
great victory was obtained and death itself was repelled; by your glorious fighting all the worlds there were thoroughly gratified.
The earth was filled with many heroic kṣatriyas of valour equal to Śakra, like great trees filling a forest.
Those supremely hard-to-conquer ones, in whose might, virtue, and energy Rāghava has no equal in battle — they were forcibly slain by you, O king.
O king, this calamity that has come from an ordinary mortal is unworthy of concern; do not take it to heart — you shall slay Rāghava.
Then Prahasta, a rākṣasa dark as a rain-cloud, that hero who was commander of the army, spoke with folded hands:
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, birds, and serpents are incapable of assailing you — much less vānaras in battle.
All of us were careless and unsuspecting; we were deceived by Hanūmat. That forest-dweller shall not escape alive while I live.
I shall make all the earth up to the ocean, with its mountains, forests, and groves, free of vānaras — let your lordship command me.
I shall also provide protection from the vānaras, O ranger of the night; no grief arising from your own fault shall come upon you.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Durmukha, a rākṣasa in violent rage, declared: "This affront to all of us is truly intolerable —
this further insult to the prosperous lord of rākṣasas and to the city and its inner chambers — the brazen affront of the lord of vānaras.
In this very moment I shall slay the vānaras — whether they have entered the terrible sea, the sky, or the netherworld — and return alone."
Then Vajradaṃṣṭra, immensely strong and in violent rage, seizing a dreadful iron club reddened with flesh and blood, spoke:
"What need have you of that wretched, hapless Hanūmat? While formidable Rāma stands firm with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa,
today I shall come back alone, having routed the army of vānaras and slain Rāma with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa with my iron club."
Then Nikumbha, the heroic and mighty son of Kumbhakarṇa, in supreme fury, spoke to Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry:
"Let all of you remain assembled together with the great king; I alone shall slay Rāghava with Lakṣmaṇa."
Then Vajrahanu, a rākṣasa like a mountain, enraged and licking his mouth with his tongue, spoke:
"Let your lordships attend freely to your affairs without anxiety; I alone shall devour all those chiefs of vānara troops."
"Be at ease, take sport without care, drink honey-wine; I alone shall slay Sugrīva with Lakṣmaṇa, and Aṅgada, Hanūmat, and Rāma, the elephant of the battlefield."
Then Nikumbha, Rabhasas, Sūryaśatru the mighty, Suptaghna, Yajñakopa, Mahāpārśva, and Mahodara —
Agniketu the fierce, Raśmiketu the rākṣasa, and Indrajit of great splendour, the powerful son of Rāvaṇa —
Prahasta, Virūpākṣa, Vajradaṃṣṭra the mighty, Dhūmrākṣa, Atikāya, and Durmukha the rākṣasa —
seizing iron clubs, broadswords, lances, spears, tridents, battle-axes, bows with arrows, and large sharp swords,
those rākṣasas, in supreme fury, leaping up and blazing as if with energy, all spoke to Rāvaṇa:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Today we shall slay Rāma, Sugrīva with Lakṣmaṇa, and the wretched Hanūmat by whom Laṅkā was violated."
Having restrained all of them who had taken up weapons, Vibhīṣaṇa made them sit down again and spoke with folded hands:
"Dear one, the goal which cannot be attained by the three means — conciliation, gifts, and sowing division — has its proper times for the use of force, as the wise declare.
Feats of force succeed, dear one, when performed after due deliberation and in accordance with proper method, against those who are careless, beset by enemies, or struck down by fate.
But how do you wish to assault him who is vigilant, who desires victory, who stands firm in strength, who has conquered his wrath, and who is hard to assail?
Having crossed the terrible ocean, lord of rivers and streams — who could have imagined the feat accomplished by Hanūmat?
The strength and valour of enemies are immeasurable, O rangers of the night; sudden contempt for them must not be shown under any circumstances.
And moreover, what wrong was previously done to Rāma, the glorious one, by the king of rākṣasas — whose wife was carried away from Janasthāna?
If Khara overstepped and was slain by Rāma in battle, the lives of living beings must surely be protected to the best of one's ability.
On account of this, the greatest fear would befall us; the abducted Vaidehī should be surrendered — why perpetuate a quarrel that has been provoked?
It is not fitting for us to wage a pointless war against that valiant one who follows righteousness; let Maithilī be given to him.
Before he shatters the city — with its elephants, horses, and abundant treasures — with his arrows, let Maithilī be given to him.
Before his terrible, great, and invincible army of vānaras descends upon our Laṅkā, let Sītā be given back.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
For the city of Laṅkā and all the heroic rākṣasas will surely perish if the beloved wife of Rāma is not willingly given back.
I implore you out of kinship — act upon my words; I speak what is beneficial and wholesome: let Maithilī be given to him.
Before the prince releases upon you his unfailing arrows — bright as the rays of the autumn sun, freshly fletched, well-strung — for your destruction, let Maithilī be given to the son of Daśaratha.
Abandon wrath, which destroys happiness and righteousness; embrace righteousness, which increases joy and fame; be gracious — let us live with our sons and kinsmen; let Maithilī be given to the son of Daśaratha.
To Vibhīṣaṇa, who had spoken words firmly grounded and well-meaning, Rāvaṇa — urged on by fate — spoke harsh words in return.
One might dwell with a rival, or even with an enraged venomous serpent, but one should never live with a pretended friend who serves the enemy.
I know the nature of kinsmen in all the worlds, O Rākṣasa — kinsmen always rejoice in the misfortunes of their own kin.
Those who are eminent, capable, skilled, or virtuous in conduct, O Rākṣasa — kinsmen despise them and treat even the brave with contempt.
Forever rejoicing in one another's afflictions, perpetrators of harm, concealing their hearts — kinsmen are terrible and cause fear.
Certain verses are said to have been sung by elephants somewhere in a lotus-forest, upon seeing men with nooses in their hands — hear them as I recite them.
Neither fire, nor other weapons, nor nooses are what we fear — but kinsmen, terrible and acting from self-interest, are what truly frighten us.
They will tell others the means of our capture — of that there is no doubt; it is known to us that, among all fears, fear from kinsmen is the most terrible.
Abundance is found in cattle, self-restraint in Brāhmaṇas, fickleness in women — and danger is found from one's own kinsmen.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Therefore, O gentle one, what is unwelcome to you is that I am honored in the world, that I am born of noble lineage, and that I stand with my foot on the heads of my enemies.
Were another to speak such words, O night-wanderer, he would not survive this moment — but shame on you, O defiler of your lineage!
Having been thus spoken to so harshly, Vibhīṣaṇa — the speaker of righteousness — rose up into the air, mace in hand, together with four Rākṣasas.
And then Vibhīṣaṇa — glorious, his anger now roused, stationed in the sky — spoke these words to his brother, the lord of Rākṣasas.
You are my brother, O King — say to me whatever you wish; but these harsh words of yours, untrue as they are, I cannot forgive.
The well-reasoned counsel spoken out of goodwill is not heeded by those of unformed souls who have come under the sway of Time, O ten-faced one.
Men who always speak pleasant things are easily found, O King; but one who speaks — or is willing to hear — what is unpleasant yet beneficial is rare.
I cannot stand by and watch you perish, bound in the noose of Time that carries off all beings, any more than one could ignore a burning dwelling.
I do not wish to see you struck down by Rāma's arrows — those bright shafts blazing like fire and adorned with golden ornaments.
Those who are brave, powerful, and skilled in arms on the field of battle — when fate overtakes them, they collapse like bridges of sand.
Protect yourself in every way, and this city along with all the Rākṣasas. Fare you well — I shall depart. Be happy without me.
When I, acting from goodwill, tried to restrain you, my counsel did not please you, O night-wanderer; for men whose time is run and whose life is spent do not accept benefit though offered by friends.
Having spoken these harsh words to Rāvaṇa, Rāvaṇa's younger brother came in a short time to where Rāma was, together with Lakṣmaṇa.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Those lords of monkeys standing on the earth beheld him stationed in the sky — massive as the peak of Meru, blazing like a bolt of lightning.
Seeing him together with four others as a group of five, Sugrīva — the irresistible lord of monkeys — pondered the matter with the other monkeys, being wise.
Having reflected for a moment, he spoke this excellent speech to all those monkeys, with Hanūmat foremost among them.
This Rākṣasa, bearing all weapons, advances with four Rākṣasas — see! He comes to kill us, there is no doubt.
Hearing Sugrīva's words, all those foremost of monkeys, raising sāla trees and boulders, spoke these words.
Quickly direct us, O King, to slay these wicked-souled ones — let these short-lived beings fall dead to the earth.
While they were thus talking among themselves, Vibhīṣaṇa reached the far shore and stood there, still stationed in the sky.
And Vibhīṣaṇa, greatly wise and great in stature, still stationed in the sky, looked at Sugrīva and those others, and spoke in a mighty voice.
There is a Rākṣasa of wicked conduct named Rāvaṇa, lord of Rākṣasas — I am his younger brother, known as Vibhīṣaṇa.
By him Sītā was carried off from Janasthāna, after slaying Jaṭāyu; she is confined, helpless and wretched, closely guarded by Rākṣasī women.
I remonstrated with him through reasoned arguments and various counsels, again and again: 'Let Sītā be properly restored to Rāma.'
But he, Rāvaṇa, driven by fate, did not accept the beneficial counsel being offered to him — as though it were a bitter medicine.
I, having been spoken to harshly by him and humiliated like a slave, abandoning sons and wife, have taken refuge with Rāghava.
Report to the great-souled Rāghava, the refuge of all worlds, that Vibhīṣaṇa stands present before him and seeks shelter, quickly.
Having heard these words, Sugrīva of swift valor spoke these agitated words to Rāma in the presence of Lakṣmaṇa.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
One who is known as Vibhīṣaṇa, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, together with four Rākṣasas has taken refuge with you, my lord.
Know this Vibhīṣaṇa to be a spy sent by Rāvaṇa — I consider his arrest to be fitting, O best of the forbearing.
This Rākṣasa, directed by a crooked mind, has presented himself — concealed by illusion — to strike once you trust him, O Rāghava.
Let him be seized with severe punishment, along with his counselors — for this is Vibhīṣaṇa, the brother of the cruel Rāvaṇa.
Having spoken thus to Rāma, the agitated commander of the army — himself skilled in speech and knowing the value of words — then fell silent.
Hearing that speech of Sugrīva, Rāma of great might spoke thus to the monkeys nearby, with Hanūmat foremost among them.
What the king of monkeys has said regarding the younger brother of Rāvaṇa — those well-reasoned words of great weight — you all have heard them.
In difficult situations, it is fitting even for a capable and wise friend of good character who desires lasting well-being to offer counsel.
Thus questioned, each of them, without delay, spoke their own opinion to Rāma with due courtesy, each desiring his welfare.
Nothing in the three worlds is unknown to you, O Rāghava — honoring us, O Rāma, you ask us out of friendship.
You are true to your vow, heroic, righteous, of firm valor — you act only after examining, you are mindful, and you give yourself fully to your friends.
Therefore, let your counselors speak one by one, those endowed with sound judgment and capable, with reasons, time and again.
When Rāghava had spoken thus, the wise monkey Aṅgada spoke first, for the purpose of examining Vibhīṣaṇa.
One who has come from the side of the enemy is in every way suspect — Vibhīṣaṇa should not hastily be made worthy of trust.
Those of deceitful mind move about having concealed their true intent, and they strike at moments of vulnerability — that calamity would be very great.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having carefully weighed benefit and harm, one should adopt a course of action — accept someone on the strength of virtues, and reject on account of faults.
If the fault in him is great, let him be cast away without hesitation; or if many virtues are recognized, let acceptance be made, O King.
Then Śarabha, having reflected, spoke words full of meaning: 'Quickly, O tiger among men, let a spy be employed concerning him.'
Having properly set a spy of subtle intelligence, and having examined him thoroughly, then let reception of him be made as is proper.
Then Jāmbavān, discerning, examining with the intelligence of the śāstras, presented a speech full of virtue and free from fault.
Vibhīṣaṇa has come from a sworn enemy and an evil lord of Rākṣasas, arriving at an unsuitable time and place — let him be regarded with suspicion in every way.
Then Mainda, skilled in right and wrong policy, eloquent in speech, after deliberation, spoke words even more reasoned.
This Vibhīṣaṇa is, they say, merely a spokesman for Rāvaṇa — let him be questioned gently and with sweet words, O lord of foremost men.
Having learned his intent, you will then act in accordance with the truth — if he is seen to be innocent or guilty, do so with deliberate mind, O bull among men.
Then Hanūmān, foremost of counselors and endowed with refinement, spoke words that were smooth, meaningful, sweet, and concise.
Even Bṛhaspati himself, were he to speak, would not be able to surpass you — best of minds, most capable, foremost among speakers.
Neither for argument nor contention, neither from pride nor personal desire, will I speak, O King — I will speak truly out of reverence for Rāma.
In what has been said by your counselors on the grounds of benefit and harm, I see a fault — for the proposed course of action does not follow.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Without commission of a task, capability cannot be known — hasty deployment appears to me to be flawed.
What your counselors said — that deployment of a spy is fitting — the reason for that does not hold, given that the goal cannot be achieved thereby.
As for the charge that Vibhīṣaṇa has arrived at an unsuitable time and place — I have something to say about that; hear it as I understand it.
That very place and time become what they become depending on the person encountered; and so too do virtues and faults, passing from person to person.
Having seen the wickedness of Rāvaṇa, and likewise your own valor, his coming here is fitting and consistent with his own discernment.
Regarding what was said — 'Let him be questioned by men in disguised form' — I have a considered opinion about that, upon reflection.
A wise man, when questioned suddenly with suspicion, might speak guardedly — and thereby a friend who came in good faith would be alienated by false questioning.
It is not possible, O King, to know another's inner disposition suddenly — rather, it is by those inner traits that are revealed that one skilled in discernment perceives it deeply.
But even as he speaks, no wickedness of disposition is ever discernible in him — his countenance is serene — and therefore I have no doubt.
One of undisturbed mind, at ease — a deceitful person does not move about in such a manner; his speech too is not crooked — and therefore there is no doubt here.
Demeanor, even when one attempts to conceal it, cannot be fully hidden — it forcibly reveals the inner disposition of men.
An action suited to place and time, O best of those who know what must be done, when undertaken with purposeful application, quickly bears fruit.
Having seen your resolve, having seen Rāvaṇa's false conduct, and having heard of the slaying of Vālin and the consecration of Sugrīva —

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
— desiring a kingdom, he has come here with considered intent; keeping all this in view, his acceptance is appropriate.
What I have said to the best of my ability regarding the Rākṣasa's sincerity — you are the authority for the rest, O best of the wise, having heard it.
Then Rāma — of serene spirit, irresistible, learned, and established in his own self — having heard the son of the Wind, replied.
I too have something to say regarding Vibhīṣaṇa — I wish to hear all of that from you who stand in what is good.
One who has come in the spirit of friendship I would not abandon under any circumstances — even if fault there be in him, this is not censured among the good.
Hearing Rāma's words, Sugrīva — lord of the leaping monkeys — spoke back to the scion of Kākutstha, impelled by warm affection.
What is remarkable in this, O knower of dharma, O crest-jewel of the lords of the world, that you, possessed of true being and standing on the noble path, should speak what is noble?
My own inner self too perceives the purity of Vibhīṣaṇa — from inference, from his disposition, he has been thoroughly examined from every angle.
Therefore, O Rāghava, let the greatly wise Vibhīṣaṇa quickly become our equal and let him enter into friendship with us.
Rāma, having heard and reflected upon that speech of Sugrīva, then spoke more auspicious words to the bull among monkeys.
Whether this night-wanderer be utterly wicked or free of wickedness — how could he ever be capable of doing even the slightest harm to me?
Piśācas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and all the Rākṣasas on earth — I could slay all of them with the tip of my finger, were I so inclined, O lord of the monkey host.
It is heard that a dove, when an enemy sought refuge with him, honored the enemy properly and even invited him with portions of his own flesh.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That dove accepted even him who had come to carry off his wife — then what of a man of my kind, O best of monkeys?
Hear the verses sung of old by Kaṇḍu, son of the sage Kaṇva, that great sage, righteous and truthful in speech.
One should not slay a suppliant who stands with palms joined, pitiable, begging for protection, come seeking refuge — even if he be the greatest enemy — for the sake of non-cruelty, O lord of birds.
Whether afflicted or proud, an enemy who has taken refuge with others must be protected by one of formed soul, even at the sacrifice of his own life.
If he does not protect — out of fear, or delusion, or desire — to the best of his ability and in accordance with truth, that is a sin censured by the world.
If the refugee perishes while the protector watches, the refugee — left unprotected — departs taking with him all the merit of that protector.
Such is the great fault in not protecting those who have surrendered — it leads to exclusion from heaven, to disgrace, and to destruction of strength and valor.
I will fulfill in all truth the excellent teaching of Kaṇḍu — righteous and glorious, it shall yield the fruit of heaven when the time of fruition comes.
To one who has surrendered even once and cries 'I am yours' — I grant freedom from fear from all beings: this is my vow.
Bring him here, O best of monkeys — I have given him my assurance of safety, O Sugrīva, whether it be Vibhīṣaṇa, or even Rāvaṇa himself.
Then, upon hearing those words spoken by the lord of men at the urging of the lord of monkeys, the king of men swiftly went to meet Vibhīṣaṇa, as Purandara meets the king of birds.
When Rāghava had granted him safety, Rāvaṇa's younger brother bowed and, overjoyed, descended from the sky to the earth together with his devoted attendants.
That righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, seeking refuge, fell at Rāma's feet together with four rākṣasas.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
There Vibhīṣaṇa then spoke these words to Rāma — words that were righteous, fitting, timely, and gladdening.
"I am the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, and by him I have been dishonoured. I have come to you for refuge — you who are the refuge of all beings."
"I have abandoned Laṅkā, my friends, and my wealth. My kingdom, my life, and my pleasures are all now surrendered to you."
"I will render assistance in the slaying of the rākṣasas and in the assault upon Laṅkā with all the strength of my life, and I will enter your army."
As he spoke thus, Rāma embraced Vibhīṣaṇa and, filled with joy, said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Bring water from the ocean."
"With it, quickly anoint this greatly wise Vibhīṣaṇa as king of the rākṣasas, O bestower of honour, now that I am pleased with him."
Thus instructed, Saumitri anointed Vibhīṣaṇa as king in the midst of the foremost monkeys, acting on Rāma's command.
Witnessing that gracious act of Rāma, the monkeys at once raised great shouts and cried out, "Well done! Well done!"
Then Hanūmān and Sugrīva asked Vibhīṣaṇa: "How shall we cross the impassable ocean, the abode of Varuṇa?"
"Let us approach by means of some stratagem, so that we may all — together with the army — cross swiftly the lord of rivers and streams, the abode of Varuṇa."
Thus addressed, Vibhīṣaṇa, who knows what is right, replied: "King Rāghava ought to approach the ocean for refuge."
"This measureless great ocean was dug out by Sagara; the great ocean ought therefore to render service to Rāma, his kinsman."
When the wise rākṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa had spoken thus, this course also found favour with Rāghava, who was by nature righteous.
Then that great-spirited one, skilled in proper conduct and seeking to honour the occasion, spoke with a gentle smile to Lakṣmaṇa and to Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Lakṣmaṇa, this counsel of Vibhīṣaṇa pleases me. Speak, you together with Sugrīva — does it please you as well?"
"Sugrīva is ever wise, and you are expert in counsel; having considered the matter, both of you — say what seems best."
Thus addressed, those two heroes, Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa, both spoke this reply, combined with proper courteous form.
"Why would it not please us, O tiger among men, O Rāghava? What Vibhīṣaṇa has said is agreeable and suited to this moment."
"Without building a bridge across this dreadful ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, Laṅkā cannot be reached even by the gods and asuras together with Indra."
"Let the true word of the valiant Vibhīṣaṇa be carried out. Enough delay — let this ocean now be made to serve."
Thus counselled, Rāma then lay down upon the shore of the lord of rivers and streams, which was spread with kuśa grass, like fire resting on a sacrificial altar.
