"Hear, O king, the full account of him whose fiery power was great, who slew his enemies in battle, and how he was unkillable by his foes."
"I shall tell you, O Rāghava, Rāvaṇa's lineage and birth, and likewise the grant of boons that was given to him."
"In former times, in the Kṛta age, O Rāma, there was a lord who was the son of Prajāpati — the brahmarṣi named Pulastya, like Brahmā himself made manifest."
"His virtues in respect of righteousness and conduct cannot be enumerated; he can only be described by name as 'son of Prajāpati.'"
"That foremost of sages, drawn by religious engagement, went to the hermitage of Tṛṇabindu on the slope of the great mountain Meru and dwelt there."
"That righteous-souled sage practiced austerities with his senses restrained through recitation of the Vedas; yet maidens coming to his hermitage created disturbances."
"Daughters of gods and nāgas, daughters of royal sages, and apsarases at play — all these came to that region."
"Because the forest was enjoyable in every season and delightful, those maidens went to that region constantly to sport."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then the great sage, blazing with might, became angered and proclaimed: 'Whatever woman comes into my sight shall bear a child.'"
"All of them, having heard the word of the great-souled one, turned back; fearing a brahmin's curse, they did not approach that region."
"But the daughter of the royal sage Tṛṇabindu did not hear this; she went to his hermitage and wandered there quite without fear."
"At that very time that great sage, son of Prajāpati, was performing his Vedic recitation there, his brilliance blazing with ascetic power."
"She, hearing the sound of the Vedas and seeing that treasury of austerities, became pale in her body, though she was a woman of well-formed limbs."
"Seeing her own form in such a state, she was greatly agitated; thinking 'What is this that has happened to me?' she went and stood before her father."
"Tṛṇabindu, seeing her in that condition, then said: 'Why do you bear this form so unlike your own?'"
"She, distressed, joined her palms and said to that treasury of austerities: 'I do not know the cause, father, by which my form has become like this.'"
"'But earlier I had gone alone to the divine hermitage of the great sage Pulastya, whose soul was purified, in search of my own companions.'"
"'I did not see any companion who had come there; and seeing the transformation of my form, I have come back here.'"
"The royal sage Tṛṇabindu, his brilliance blazing with austerity, entered into meditation and saw therein what had come about through the sage's act."
"Having understood that curse of the great purified-souled sage, he took his daughter and went to Pulastya and said this."
"'Venerable one, accept this daughter of mine, herself adorned with her own virtues, as a gift, O great sage — she offers herself willingly.'"
"'She will always be devoted to your service as you practice your austerities and fatigue your senses — of this there is no doubt.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"As the righteous royal sage spoke those words, the brahmin, wishing to accept the maiden, said simply 'So be it.'"
"Having given her, the king departed to his own hermitage; and the maiden dwelt there, pleasing her husband with her virtues. Delighted, that blazing sage spoke these words."
"'I am thoroughly pleased; may good come to you through the abundance of your virtues. Therefore I shall now produce for you a son equal to me in qualities, who shall perpetuate the lineage of us both, renowned as a son of Pulastya.'"
"'Since the Veda has become famous through being recited by you here in my presence, therefore the son shall be named Viśravas — of this there is no doubt.'"
"Thus addressed, the maiden, with a joyful heart, in no long time gave birth to a son, Viśravas."
"He, renowned through the three worlds, endowed with purity and righteousness, yoked to austerity like his father — Viśravas, that foremost of sages."
Now Pulastya's son Viśravas, that foremost of sages, in no long time was established in austerity just like his father.
He was truthful, virtuous, capable, devoted to Vedic recitation, pure, unattached to all pleasures, and ever intent on righteousness.
The great sage Bharadvāja, knowing his conduct and character, gave his own daughter to Viśravas as a wife — a woman of divine beauty.
Accepting Bharadvāja's daughter in accordance with dharma, Viśravas, that foremost of sages, was filled with the greatest joy.
That righteous-souled one begot upon her a most wondrous offspring endowed with valor and possessed of all the qualities of a brahmin.
At his birth, the Grandfather Brahmā was greatly delighted, and in joy he gave the child his name together with the divine sages at that time.
"Since this is the offspring of Viśravas and resembles Viśravas himself, therefore shall he be renowned by the name Vaiśravaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And Vaiśravaṇa, having gone to the forest of austerities, grew there blazing with great splendor like fire fed with oblations.
Dwelling at his hermitage, this thought arose in the great-souled one's mind: "I shall follow dharma with self-restraint, for dharma is the highest path."
He practiced austerities in the great forest for thousands of years, and at the completion of each thousand years he observed the prescribed rites in their succession.
Living on water alone, then subsisting on air alone, then taking no sustenance at all — in this manner those thousands of years passed as though they were so many rainy seasons.
Then Brahmā, greatly pleased, went together with the host of gods led by Indra to his hermitage and spoke these words.
"I am thoroughly pleased with this conduct of yours, O dear child, O one of good vows. Choose a boon — may good come to you, for you are worthy of a boon in my estimation."
Then Vaiśravaṇa addressed the Grandfather who stood before him: "Venerable one, I desire the guardianship of a world and the protection of wealth."
Then Brahmā, with a thoroughly pleased heart, said to Vaiśravaṇa together with the host of gods, joyfully: "So be it."
"I am indeed prepared to create a fourth guardian of the worlds, for the position alongside Yama, Indra, and Varuṇa is precisely what you desire."
"So it is done — go, O knower of dharma, and obtain lordship over wealth; you shall henceforth be the fourth alongside Yama, Indra, and Varuṇa."
"And accept this celestial vehicle named Puṣpaka, brilliant as the sun, for your conveyance; proceed to equality with the thirty gods."
"May all go well with you; we shall all depart as we came, our purpose fulfilled, dear child, having bestowed upon you this great boon."
When Brahmā and the gods before him had departed to the sky, the lord of wealth humbly bowed and spoke these words to his father.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Venerable father, I have received a boon from the lotus-born Brahmā, but that Prajāpati has not ordained a dwelling place for me."
"Therefore, venerable lord, look out some region for our dwelling — one where no living creature of any kind would be distressed."
Thus addressed by his son, Viśravas, that foremost of sages and knower of dharma, said: "O knower of dharma, hear these words."
"There is a beautiful city named Laṅkā, built by Viśvakarman for the dwelling of the rākṣasas, like Amarāvatī for Indra."
"That delightful city has archways of gold and vaidūrya; it was abandoned long ago by the rākṣasas who were tormented by fear of Viṣṇu, left empty of all the hosts of rākṣasas who had gone down to the depths of the underworld."
"Direct your own mind toward dwelling there; your residence there shall be without fault, and no one shall be harmed."
Hearing his father's most righteous counsel, that righteous-souled one then established himself in Laṅkā on the mountain summit.
By his command, that city was speedily filled with thousands of joyful and ever-rejoicing nairṛtas — the rākṣasa folk.
And there dwelt with delight that righteous-souled lord of the nairṛtas, the son of Viśravas, in Laṅkā girdled by the ocean.
Season after season, humble in spirit, the lord of wealth joyfully came on the Puṣpaka vehicle to visit both his father and his mother.
Praised by hosts of gods and gandharvas, and likewise by siddhas along with cāraṇas, surrounded by his own radiance like the sun encircled by his rays, he proceeded to his father's presence attended by all prosperity.
Hearing the words spoken by Agastya, Rāma was filled with wonder: "So Laṅkā was formerly the birthplace of the rākṣasas."
Then, shaking his head and gazing again and again at Agastya, whose form blazed like the three sacred fires, Rāma smiled and addressed him.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Venerable one, hearing from you that this Laṅkā was formerly also inhabited by flesh-eaters, wonder has arisen in me."
"We had heard that the rākṣasas arose from the lineage of Pulastya; but now you have also recounted yet another origin for them."
"Were those earlier rākṣasas more powerful than Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Prahasta, Vikaṭa, and the sons of Rāvaṇa?"
"Who was their foremost ancestor, O brāhmaṇa? What was his name, and what was the power of his austerities? And having committed what transgression were they driven away by Viṣṇu in the past?"
"Please recount all of this to me in full detail, O sinless one. Dispel the great curiosity that has arisen in me, as the sun dispels darkness."
Hearing those words of Rāghava, adorned with the refinement of learning, Agastya was somewhat astonished, and then addressed Rāghava thus.
"In ancient times, Prajāpati, the lotus-born, having first created the primordial waters, then created living beings for the purpose of protecting those waters."
"Those beings, tormented by hunger, thirst, and fear, approached their maker humbly, saying: 'What shall we do?'"
"Prajāpati, the bestower of honor, addressed those beings as if laughing, saying to them with care: 'Guard and protect these waters.'"
"Some said 'We will guard (rakṣāma)' and others said 'We will worship (yakṣāma),' while yet others said 'We will eat (bhuṅkṣitā)' or 'We will not eat.' Then the creator of beings spoke to them."
"'Those of you who said "We will guard" — let them become rākṣasas; those who said "We will worship" — let them indeed become yakṣas.'"
"Among them, two bulls among rākṣasas were Heti and Praheti, brothers, resembling Madhu and Kaiṭabha in stature, both subduing their enemies."
"Praheti was righteous and had no desire for a wife; but Heti strove with great effort to obtain a wife."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"He of immeasurable soul and great intelligence himself wed Bhayā ('Fear') by name, a maiden who was the sister of Kāla ('Time') and inspiring of fear."
"That bull among rākṣasas, Heti, the foremost among those who have sons, fathered on her a son known as Vidyutkeśa."
"Vidyutkeśa, son of Heti, blazing like a kindled fire, grew up in great splendor, like a lotus in the midst of water."
"When that night-wanderer had reached the prime of youth, his father resolved to arrange his marriage."
"Then Heti, that bull among rākṣasas, for the sake of his son, wooed as a bride the daughter of Saṃdhyā ('Twilight'), who was equal to Saṃdhyā herself in splendor."
"Saṃdhyā reflected: 'A daughter must inevitably be given to another,' and so, O Rāghava, her daughter was given to Vidyutkeśa."
"Having obtained the daughter of Saṃdhyā, the night-wanderer Vidyutkeśa sported with her just as Maghavan (Indra) sports with Paulomī (Śacī)."
"After some time, O Rāma, Sālakaṭaṃkaṭā conceived a child by Vidyutkeśa, just as a line of clouds receives rain from the ocean."
"Then that rākṣasī went to Mount Mandara and gave birth to her child, who shone like the core of a thundercloud, just as the Gaṅgā brought forth Agni's offspring."
"Abandoning that child, she who was desirous of love with Vidyutkeśa sported with her husband, forgetting her own son."
"The infant, abandoned by her, shining like the autumnal sun, placed his hand in his mouth and wept, like a king of clouds thundering."
"Then the lord Hara, riding his bull and traveling in the sky with Umā, looked down and saw the weeping son of the rākṣasa."
"Out of compassion, at the urging of Pārvatī, Bhava, the destroyer of the triple city, then made that son of the rākṣasa equal in age to his own mother."
"And to please Pārvatī, the undecaying, inexhaustible Mahādeva made him immortal and gave him a city that travels through the sky."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Umā also granted a boon to rākṣasī women, O son of a king: that conception of the womb would be immediate, delivery immediate, and attainment of full age immediate — equal to the age of the mother."
"Then Sukeśa, proud of the boons received and having obtained the glory of the lord from Hara's side, that great-minded one traveled everywhere through the sky, having gained a sky-city, like Purandara (Indra)."
"Seeing that righteous rākṣasa Sukeśa, who had obtained the boons, a gandharva named Grāmaṇī, equal in splendor to Viśvāvasu —"
"— he had a daughter named Devavatī, a second Śrī herself; Dakṣa gave her to Sukeśa rightfully, as one gives Śrī."
"Having obtained that beloved husband whose sovereignty was established by the boon, Devavatī was content, like a pauper who has obtained wealth."
"United with her, that night-wanderer shone forth like a great elephant issuing from its tether with its cow-elephant."
"Sukeśa, lord of rākṣasas, fathered on Devavatī, O Rāghava, three rākṣasa sons equal to three-eyed Śiva: Mālyavān, Sumālī, and Māli, foremost among the strong."
"Like the three worlds, steadfast and undisturbed; like the three sacred fires; like three mantras supremely potent; like three terrible diseases."
"These three sons of Sukeśa, blazing like the three sacred fires, grew to full maturity there, like diseases left unchecked."
"Knowing the great sovereignty their father had gained through the receipt of boons, the brothers resolved and went to Mount Meru to perform severe austerities."
"Taking up terrible vows, those rākṣasas, O best of kings, practiced dreadful austerities that inspired fear in all living beings."
"Through austerities on earth that were difficult to perform, combined with truthfulness, uprightness, and self-restraint, they scorched the three worlds along with the gods, asuras, and humans."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then the all-pervading, four-faced one, mounting his excellent aerial vehicle, addressed the sons of Sukeśa and said: 'I am the granter of boons.'"
"Knowing Brahmā to be the granter of boons, all of them with Indra and the hosts of gods standing by, they joined their palms and spoke, trembling like trees in a storm."
"'O god, propitiated by our austerities, if you will grant us a boon, let us be unconquerable, slayers of enemies, long-lived, and supremely powerful' — thus they vowed together with one another."
"Having said 'So shall it be' to the sons of Sukeśa, Brahmā the lord, fond of brāhmaṇas, departed to Brahmaloka."
"Having obtained the boon, then all those night-wanderers, O Rāma, began to afflict the gods and asuras, utterly fearless by virtue of the boon granted."
"The gods along with companies of sages and cāraṇas, being slaughtered by them, found no protector, like men consigned to hell."
"Then those rākṣasas, O best of the Raghu line, assembled with great joy and addressed Viśvakarman, the inexhaustible foremost among craftsmen."
"'You are the builder of the gods' heart-desired homes; so now build a home for us as well, O great-minded one.'"
"'On the Himālayas, or on Meru, or Mandara itself, build for us a great dwelling resembling the abode of Maheśvara.'"
"Then Viśvakarman, mighty-armed, described to those rākṣasas a dwelling place like Indra's Amarāvatī."
"'On the southern shore of the ocean there is a mountain named Trikūṭa; on its middle peak, resembling a cloud, inaccessible even to birds, with all four sides cleft as if by a chisel —'"
"'— a city named Laṅkā, thirty yojanas in extent, with golden walls and gateways, was built by me at Indra's command.'"
"'Dwell in that city, O unconquerable, foremost rākṣasas, just as the celestials led by Indra dwell in Amarāvatī.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'Having gained the fortress of Laṅkā, surrounded by many rākṣasas, you will become invincible, slayers of your enemies.'"
"Hearing Viśvakarman's words, then those rākṣasas, O Rāma, with thousands of attendants, went and inhabited that city of Laṅkā."
"Having obtained Laṅkā with its firm walls and moat, surrounded by hundreds of golden mansions, those night-wanderers sported joyfully."
"There was a gandharvī named Narmadā, enriched by many virtues; she had three daughters, equal in radiance to Intelligence, Śrī, and Fame."
"That gandharvī, no rākṣasī herself, joyfully gave those daughters, their faces like the full moon, to those rākṣasas in order of seniority."
"Three gandharva maidens of great fortune were given by their mother to the three lords of rākṣasas under the auspicious nakṣatra presided over by Bhaga."
"Having thus taken wives, O Rāma, O lord, the sons of Sukeśa sported with their wives just as the immortals sport with apsarases."
"There, the wife of Mālyavān was Sundarī, beautiful by name and nature; learn now what offspring he fathered upon her."
"Vajramuṣṭi, Virūpākṣa, the rākṣasa Durmukha, Suptaghna, Yajñakopa, Matta, Unmatta, and a daughter named Analā — these were born of Sundarī, O Rāma."
"Sumālī's wife also had a face like the full moon; her name was Ketumatī, dearer to him than life itself."
"Learn in order, O great king, what offspring the night-wanderer Sumālī fathered upon Ketumatī."
"Prahasta, Akampana, Vikaṭa, Kālakārmuka, Dhūmrākṣa, Daṇḍa, and the mighty Supārśva —"
"— Saṃhrādi, Praghasa, the rākṣasa Bhāsakarṇa, and daughters Rākā, Puṣpotkaṭā, Kaikasī of pure smile, and Kumbhīnasī — these are remembered as the progeny of Sumālī."
"Māli's wife was a gandharvī named Vasudā, beautiful in form, lotus-petal-eyed, fine-eyed, comparable to the most beautiful of yakṣī women."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Hear from me, O Rāghava, what offspring Māli, the younger brother of Sumālī, fathered upon her, as I shall now recount."
"Anala, Anila, Hara, and Saṃpāti — these night-wanderers, sons of Māli, became the ministers of Vibhīṣaṇa."
"Then those three bulls among rākṣasas, surrounded by night-wanderers and hundreds of sons, proud in their strength and valor, harassed the gods along with Indra, the sages, serpents, and dānavas."
"Roaming the world like the wind, unapproachable in battle, like death itself, resolute, exceedingly arrogant through the gift of boons, they were ever suppressors of the performance of sacrifices."
"The gods and the sages, rich in austerities, being slaughtered by them, fled in fear and sought refuge in Maheśvara, the god of gods."
"Meeting together with Kāmāri, the foe of Tripura, the three-eyed one, the gods with joined palms spoke in voices choked with fear."
"'O blessed one, O guardian of all creatures, O slayer of enemies, all living beings are being afflicted by the sons of Sukeśa, arrogant with the boon granted by Pitāmaha.'"
"'Our hermitages, which were places of refuge, have been made refugeless; Śakra has been expelled from heaven, while they sport in heaven as though they were Śakra.'"
"'"I am Viṣṇu, I am Rudra, I am Brahmā, I am the king of gods, I am Yama, I am Varuṇa, I am the Moon, I am the Sun" — thus those rākṣasas boast.'"
"'Thus those rākṣasas, O god, arrogant through the boon they received, exhilarated by battle, afflict us and those who march at our head.'"
"'Therefore, deign to grant us fearful gods freedom from fear; taking on a terrible form, destroy those thorns of the gods.'"
"Addressed thus by all the gods, Kapardī, the blue-and-red one, with a regard for Sukeśa, the lord addressed the hosts of gods."
"'I will not slay them — those asuras are not to be killed by me. But I will give you a counsel which will indeed bring about their death.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'With this same resolve as your guide, O bulls among gods, go and take refuge in Viṣṇu; the lord will slay them.'"
"Then they cheered Maheśvara with shouts of victory and went to Viṣṇu's presence, tormented by fear of the night-wanderers."
"Bowing to and greatly honoring the god bearing the conch and discus, they spoke hurriedly, afflicted by the sons of Sukeśa."
"'By the three sons of Sukeśa, blazing like the three sacred fires, relying on the strength of their boon, our stations have been seized and taken from us.'"
"'Established in the impregnable city named Laṅkā, situated on the peak of Trikūṭa, those night-wanderers afflict all of us from there.'"
"'Therefore, O Madhusūdana, for our sake slay them; cut their lotus-like faces with your discus and dispatch them to Yama.'"
"'You are our giver of fearlessness in fears — there is none equal to you; dispel our fear, O god, as the sun dispels mist.'"
"Addressed thus by the gods, Janārdana, the god of gods, who grants fear to enemies, having granted fearlessness, spoke to the gods."
"'I know the rākṣasa Sukeśa, arrogant with the boon of the Lord (Śiva); and I know his sons, the eldest of whom is Mālyavān.'"
"'Those vilest of rākṣasas who have transgressed all bounds — I will destroy them in battle; O gods, be free from anxiety.'"
"Addressed thus by the all-powerful Viṣṇu, all those gods went joyfully to their respective abodes, praising Janārdana."
"That night-wanderer Mālyavān, having heard of the mobilization of the gods, spoke these words to his two heroic brothers."
"'The immortals and the sages, having combined their efforts, sought our death and addressed thus the three-eyed Śaṃkara:'"
"'"The sons of Sukeśa, O god, swollen with the power of the boon they received, attack us at every step in terrible forms.""
"'"Overwhelmed by the rākṣasas, we are unable, O lord of Umā, to remain in our own abodes out of fear of those evil-souled ones.""

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'"Therefore for our benefit, O three-eyed one, destroy those rākṣasas; burn them with a mere 'huṃ,' O best among those who burn!""
"Addressed thus by the thirty gods, the slayer of Andhaka, shaking his head and hand, spoke these words:"
"'Those sons of Sukeśa are not to be slain by me in battle, O gods; but I will give you a counsel which will indeed bring about their death.'"
"'He who bears the discus and mace, Janārdana of the yellow garment — he will slay them in battle; take refuge in him.'"
"Not obtaining their wish from Hara (Śiva), they honored Kāmāri (Śiva) and then reached the abode of Nārāyaṇa, to whom they reported everything."
"Then the gods led by Indra were addressed by Nārāyaṇa: 'I will destroy the enemies of the gods; be free from anxiety, O gods.'"
"'The death of us two bulls among rākṣasas has been pledged by Hari to the fear-stricken gods; consider now what course is fitting.'"
"'It was Nārāyaṇa who was the death of Hiraṇyakaśipu and other enemies of the gods; it is impossible to conquer Nārāyaṇa, who now desires to slay us.'"
"Then Sumālī and Māli, having heard Mālyavān's words, addressed their eldest brother like two shares of fortune addressing Vāsava (Indra)."
"'We have studied the scriptures, given gifts, performed sacrifices, guarded our sovereignty, attained long and healthy life, and established our own dharma.'"
"'Plunging into the unperturbed ocean of the gods with floods of weapons, we have always conquered the gods in battle; we have no fear caused by death.'"
"'Even Nārāyaṇa, Rudra, Śakra, and Yama — all of them are afraid to stand before us.'"
"'There is no fault in Viṣṇu here, O lord of rākṣasas; it is by the fault of the gods that Viṣṇu's mind has been stirred to action.'"
"'Therefore today, fully mobilized and surrounded by all our forces, let us seek to destroy the very gods from whom this offence arose.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Thus Māli, Sumālī, and their elder brother Mālyavān the lord, having proclaimed their mobilization, all those rākṣasas marched out for battle, furious as the armies of Jambha and Vṛtra."
"With chariots, lordly elephants, and horses resembling mountains; with donkeys, cows, camels, porpoises, and serpents —"
"— with sea-monsters, tortoises, fish, birds resembling Garuḍa, lions, tigers, boars, sṛmaras, and yaks —"
"— abandoning Laṅkā, all those rākṣasas, proud in their might, enemies of the gods, marched forth to the realm of the gods to fight."
"Seeing the dire upheaval of Laṅkā, the beings that dwelt in Laṅkā, beholding terror, were everywhere dispirited."
"Portents on earth and in the sky, appointed by Time and inspiring fear, swiftly arose to presage the destruction of the lords of rākṣasas."
"Clouds rained bones and hot blood; the ocean overflowed its shores; the greatest of mountains trembled."
"Spirits by the thousands flew about emitting loud laughter equal in sound to the rumbling of thunderclouds, dancing as they went."
"A great wheel of vultures with fire-vomiting beaks circled over the rākṣasas like the wheel of time."
"Those inconceivable and terrible omens — the rākṣasas, proud in their strength, bound by the noose of death, marched on and did not turn back."
"Mālyavān, Sumālī, and Māli, those night-wanderers, marched at the head of their forces, like the fires at the head of sacrificial rituals."
"All those night-wanderers rallied around Mālyavān as if around a mountain, as embodied beings rally around the Creator."
"That army of the lords of rākṣasas, rumbling like a great cloud, obedient to Māli's command, marched toward the realm of the gods, desirous of victory."
"The lord Nārāyaṇa, having learned through the divine messenger of that mobilization of the rākṣasas, then set his mind on battle."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"He, bearing the foremost of weapons — discus, sword, and plough — praised by gods, siddhas, sages, great serpents, chiefs of gandharvas, and apsarases, came face to face with the army of the enemies of immortals."
"That army of the rākṣasa king, its banners whirling, its weapons scattered abroad, its wings driven upward by the wind of Garuḍa's wings, was shaken as the blue lord of mountains when a trembling boulder rolls."
"And then the night-wanderers, whose forms were like the fire of cosmic dissolution, smeared with blood and flesh, surrounding Mādhava from all sides, pierced him by the thousands with their excellent weapons."
Those demon-clouds, roaring, rained down a shower of arrows upon the mountain that was Nārāyaṇa, as storm-clouds rain upon a mountain.
Viṣṇu, dark-complexioned, encircled by those dark-hued foremost night-wanderers as they poured down their shafts, stood like the Añjana mountain wreathed in rain-bearing clouds.
As locusts descend upon a field, as gnats upon a mountain, as souls upon a jar of nectar, as sea-monsters upon the ocean —
— so did the arrows discharged from the bows of the rākṣasas, swift as lightning and wind, enter into Hari as the worlds enter into the sun at the end of an age.
Warriors mounted on chariots drove forward in chariots; those at the fronts of elephants came on elephants; cavalrymen on swift horses; and the foot-soldiers moved through the air.
The rākṣasa lords, mountain-like in size, assailed Hari with arrows, śaktis, ṛṣṭis, and tomaras, leaving him breathless, as breath-control exercises leave a twice-born man breathless.
Tormented by the night-wanderers as a great sea-monster is tormented by fish, he drew the Śārṅga bow and aimed at the bodies of the rākṣasas in that great battle.
With arrows fully drawn and released, bearing tips like thunderbolts and swift as thought, Viṣṇu cut them to pieces, by the hundred, by the thousand.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having dispersed that shower of arrows as the wind disperses a rain-cloud, the Puruṣottama blew his great conch Pāñcajanya.
That lotus-born conch-king, blown by Hari with full breath, resounded with a terrifying roar like a thundercloud at the end of an age.
That sound of the conch-king then struck terror into the rākṣasas as a lion in the forest terrifies rutting elephants.
The horses could not stand still; the elephants lost their rut; warriors fell from their chariots, debilitated by the overwhelming sound of the conch.
The arrows discharged from the Śārṅga bow, their faces like thunderbolts, well-feathered, tore through those rākṣasas and buried themselves in the earth.
Others, the fearsome rākṣasas, split asunder by the arrows released from Nārāyaṇa's bow, fell like mountains struck by the thunderbolt.
With wounds made by the arrows of Adhokṣaja the wound-causer, they streamed blood in rivulets like mountains streaming golden veins of ore.
The sound of the conch-king, and the twang of the Śārṅga bow, and even the clamour of the rākṣasas — all were swallowed by the Vaiṣṇava roar.
As terrible rays stream from the sun, as waves from the ocean, as torrents of serpent-lords from a mountain, as floods of water from a rain-cloud —
— so did the arrows loosed from the Śārṅga and sped by Nārāyaṇa stream forth swiftly, by hundreds and by thousands.
As lions flee before a śarabha, as elephants before a lion, as tigers before an elephant, as leopards before a tiger —
— as dogs before a leopard, as cats before a dog, as serpents before a cat, as mice before a serpent —
— so did those rākṣasas in battle flee before Viṣṇu the all-powerful, routed and laid low upon the earth.
Having slain thousands of rākṣasas, Madhusūdana sounded his lotus-born conch like the king of gods sounds a thundercloud.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The rākṣasa army, struck by Nārāyaṇa's arrows and utterly bewildered by the conch's blast, fled in utter rout toward Laṅkā.
When the rākṣasa force was thus routed and struck down by Nārāyaṇa's arrows, Sumālin checked Hari in battle with a rain of shafts.
Raising his gold-ornamented arm like an elephant raising its trunk, the rākṣasa roared with joy like a thundercloud with lightning.
Even as Sumālin was roaring thus, Hari severed his head with its blazing earrings, and the rākṣasa's charioteer and his horses were thrown into confusion.
Sumālin, lord of rākṣasas, was whirled about by those bewildered horses as a man without self-control is whirled about by his bewildered senses.
Mālin also rushed forward in battle, seizing his arrow-fitted bow; the arrows decorated with gold that flew from Mālin's bow reached Hari and entered him as birds enter the Krauñca mountain.
Though tormented by thousands of arrows released by Mālin, Viṣṇu did not waver in battle, as a man of conquered senses is not shaken by afflictions.
Then the Bhagavān, the nurturer of all beings, wielder of sword and mace, twanged his bowstring and let loose floods of arrows upon Mālin.
Those arrows, gleaming like thunderbolts and lightning, reached Mālin's body and drank his blood as serpents of old drank nectar.
Having turned Mālin to flight, Hari forcibly struck down Mālin's crest, his chariot with its banner, his bow, and his horses.
The foremost night-wanderer Mālin, deprived of his chariot, seized his mace and leapt forward, mace in hand, like a lion leaping from a mountain peak.
With that mace he struck Garuḍa on the forehead in battle as Death strikes Śiva, as Indra strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt.
Garuḍa, sorely struck by Mālin's mace, turned the god away from the battle, overwhelmed by pain.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When the god was turned away by Mālin and Garuḍa, a great tumultuous shout arose from the exulting rākṣasas.
Hearing the clamour of the roaring rākṣasas, the younger brother of Indra's steed — even as he turned away — let fly his discus with the intent to slay Mālin.
That discus, blazing like the solar orb, illuminating the sky with its own radiance, resembling the wheel of Time, severed Mālin's head.
The severed, horrifying head of that rākṣasa lord, cut off by the discus, spouting blood, fell as Rāhu's head fell of old.
Then the gods, greatly rejoiced, uttered with full voice a lion's roar of triumph, crying "Excellent! Excellent, O god!"
Seeing Mālin slain, Sumālin and Mālyavān too, both tormented by grief, fled together with their forces toward Laṅkā.
Garuḍa, great-souled, recovering himself, wheeled back and, enraged, scattered the rākṣasas with the gale of his wings.
Nārāyaṇa too tore apart the night-wanderers with arrow-thunderbolts released from his bow — their hair dishevelled as they fled — as the great Indra tears apart with his lightning-laden thunderbolts.
With parasols shattered, weapons falling, bodies rent and mangled by arrows, entrails streaming out, eyes rolling in terror, that army resembled a host of madmen.
The cries and the speeds of those night-wanderers together with their elephants were like those of elephants crushed by the ancient lion, tormented by a lion.
Covered over by Hari's net of arrows yet discharging their own nets of arrows, the dark-cloud-like night-wanderers fled as dark clouds driven by the wind.
Their heads severed by blows of the discus, their limbs crushed by mace-blows, their bodies split apart in many ways by sword-blows, the rākṣasa lords fell like mountains.
Their lotus-faces cut off by the discus, their chests pounded to pieces by the mace, their necks wrung by the plough-weapon, their skulls shattered by the pestle —

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
— and some cut down by the sword, others struck by arrows, the rākṣasas fell swiftly from the sky into the waters of the ocean.
The sky at that time, with night-wanderers resembling dark storm-clouds falling continuously — their garlands and earrings streaming loose — appeared as though blue mountains were falling without cease.
While that army was being slaughtered from behind by Padmanābha, Mālyavān turned back like an ocean overflowing its shore.
With eyes reddened with rage, his crest quivering, the night-wanderer then spoke these harsh words to Padmanābha:
"O Nārāyaṇa, you do not know the eternal code of the warrior — you who slay us, who have no will to fight and are already broken, as if we were ordinary foes.
O lord of gods, the slayer who kills those turned in flight commits a sin; such a killer does not attain the heaven won by those of righteous deeds.
Or if you have any relish for battle, O bearer of conch, discus, and mace, I stand before you — I am watching. Show whatever strength is yours."
The mighty younger brother of the king of gods answered that lord of rākṣasas: "I have pledged freedom from fear to the gods who are terror-stricken because of you; the extermination of the rākṣasas is the pledge I am upholding.
The welfare of the gods is ever dearer to me than my own life. I shall slay you even if you have gone down to the netherworld."
As the god was speaking thus — his eyes red as blood-red lotuses — the infuriated rākṣasa lord pierced him with a śakti weapon and roared.
The śakti released from Mālyavān's arm, sounding like a bell, blazed upon Hari's chest like a hundred-streaked lightning bolt within a cloud.
Then the lotus-eyed god, beloved of Śakti's bearer Skanda, pulled out that very śakti and hurled it back at Mālyavān.
That śakti, released from Govinda's hand as if hurled by Skanda himself, sped toward the rākṣasa like a great meteor toward the Añjana mountain.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
It fell upon the broad chest of the rākṣasa lord, gleaming with the radiance of his necklaces, like a thunderbolt upon a mountain peak.
His armour pierced by it, he entered into vast darkness; but Mālyavān recovered himself and stood immovable as a mountain.
Then seizing a black-iron trident studded with many spikes, he struck the god firmly between the breasts.
Flushed with battle-lust, he further struck the younger brother of Vāsava with his fist and then retreated a bowshot's distance.
Then a great cry arose in the sky: "Excellent! Excellent!" — for the rākṣasa had struck both Viṣṇu and Garuḍa.
Then the son of Vinatā, Garuḍa, enraged, swept the rākṣasa away with the gale of his wings as a powerful wind sweeps away a heap of dry leaves.
Seeing his elder brother routed by the wing-wind of the king of birds, Sumālin turned toward Laṅkā together with his own forces.
Mālyavān the rākṣasa, blown aloft by the force of the wing-wind, gathered his forces and also went to Laṅkā, wrapped in shame.
Thus, O Rāma, those rākṣasas were many times routed in battle by Hari of the lotus eyes, their foremost commanders slain.
Unable to withstand Viṣṇu, tormented by fear, they abandoned Laṅkā and went to dwell in Pātāla together with their wives.
Those renowned for their valour, O joy of the Raghu line, took refuge with the rākṣasa Sumālin and remained in the lineage of Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa.
Those rākṣasas called Paulastyas whom you slew — Sumālin, Mālyavān, Mālin, and those who were their forerunners — all of them, O illustrious one, were mightier than Rāvaṇa.
There is no other slayer of those rākṣasas, even among the gods, O conqueror of citadels, save the god Nārāyaṇa, bearer of conch, discus, and mace.
You yourself are the god Nārāyaṇa, four-armed, eternal — born to slay the rākṣasas, unconquerable, the imperishable Lord.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, after some time, the rākṣasa named Sumālin wandered all through the mortal world, having come up from Rasātala.
Dark as a blue thundercloud, with earrings of refined gold, he was taking his daughter — like Śrī without her lotus — when he caught sight of the lord of wealth travelling in the Puṣpaka.
Seeing him pass by, resplendent as an immortal, blazing like fire, the rākṣasa then spoke to his daughter Kaikasī by name:
"Daughter, the time for your bestowal has come; your youth is passing. For your sake we are all restrained, dharma-minded in our thoughts.
You, my dear, are endowed with every virtue, like Śrī with her lotus; yet through fear of rejection you have not been accepted by suitors.
The lot of a girl's father is indeed difficult for all who seek honour; for one never knows, my daughter, who will seek a maiden's hand.
A maiden always places in uncertainty these three lineages: her mother's line, her father's line, and the line into which she is given.
Therefore go, my daughter, and choose for yourself Viśravas, the foremost of the best of sages, born of the Prajāpati lineage, of the Paulastya family.
Sons such as that lord of wealth — equal to the sun in splendour — will be yours without doubt, my daughter."
At that very moment, O Rāma, the twice-born son of Pulastya — Viśravas — was tending his sacred fire, blazing like a fourth flame.
Without considering the inauspicious hour, out of reverence for her father, she approached him and stood before him with her face downcast at his feet.
He, blazing with splendour, most magnanimous, looked at her — her face like the full moon, her hips lovely — and spoke:
"Auspicious one, whose daughter are you? Whence have you come here? What is your purpose, and for what reason? Tell me truly, O radiant one."
Thus addressed, the maiden joined her palms and said: "By your own power, O sage, you are able to know my intention.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Yet know this, O brahman: I have come by my father's command. I am named Kaikasī — the rest you are worthy to divine."
The sage entered into meditation and then spoke these words: "I have understood, O auspicious one, the purpose that is in your heart.
But because you have come to me at a dreadful hour, hear, O auspicious one, what manner of sons you shall beget.
You shall bear, O fair-hipped one, rākṣasas who are fierce, fierce in form, beloved of the fierce — cruel in their deeds."
Hearing those words she prostrated herself and said: "O Bhagavān, sons such as these are not fitting from you who are born of Brahmā's line."
Then the sage said: "The last-born of your sons shall be in keeping with my lineage and shall be righteous in spirit."
Thus spoken to, that maiden, O Rāma, after some time brought forth a hideous, most fearsome form of a rākṣasa.
Ten-headed, great-fanged, resembling a heap of dark collyrium, copper-lipped, twenty-armed, vast-mouthed, with blazing hair —
The moment he was born, jackals with blazing mouths and carnivorous birds began circling in the inauspicious direction.
The sky rained blood; the clouds brayed harshly; the sun did not shine in the sky; great meteors fell upon the earth.
Then his father, equal to the Grandfather Brahmā, gave him his name: "Born ten-headed, this one shall be Daśagrīva — the ten-necked."
After him was born Kumbhakarṇa, of immense strength — his measure is not found anywhere in this world.
Then was born one named Śūrpaṇakhā, of hideous face; and Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous in soul, was the last son of Kaikasī.
They grew up there in the great forest, endowed with immense energy. Among them Daśagrīva was fierce, a cause of terror to the worlds.
Kumbhakarṇa, reckless and depraved, wandered about devouring the great sages who were given to dharma, terrorising the three worlds.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
But Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous in soul, was ever established on the path of dharma — devoted to study, regulated in his diet, with his senses restrained.
Then, after some time, the god Vitteśvara — the lord of wealth — came there in his Puṣpaka chariot, of great splendour, to visit his father.
Seeing him blazing with splendour, Kaikasī there took on a rākṣasa mind and spoke to Daśagrīva:
"My son, see Vaiśravaṇa, your brother, invested with splendour — and though you stand equal to him as a brother, see what you yourself are.
O Daśagrīva, O you of immeasurable valour, make such effort so that you, my son, may quickly become the equal of Vaiśravaṇa."
Hearing his mother's words, the illustrious Daśagrīva was seized by unequalled indignation and made a vow:
"I promise you truly: I shall soon become the equal of my brother — or even his superior. Mother, cast away the sorrow in your heart."
Then, impelled by that very wrath, Daśagrīva together with his younger brothers, having resolved "I shall attain my desire through austerity," came to the auspicious hermitage of Gokarṇa for the accomplishment of his purpose.
Then Rāma spoke to the twice-born sage: "How did your brothers practice austerities in the forest, O Brahman? What manner of great vows did they undertake there?"
Then Agastya spoke to Rāma, whose mind was pure and attentive: "Those brothers of his engaged in various ordained rules of dharma there."
Kumbhakarṇa, then ever diligent and devoted to dharma, performed austerities in the summer season seated amid five fires.
In the rainy season, drenched by cloud-waters, he practiced the hero's posture; and in the winter season he constantly dwelt submerged in water.
Thus ten thousand years passed for him as he strove in dharma, fixed upon the straight path.
But Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous in soul, ever devoted to dharma and pure, stood on one foot for five thousand years.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When his vow was completed, the troops of apsarases danced, a rain of flowers fell, and the gods were stirred with joy.
For five thousand years he followed the course of the sun, standing with arms raised and head uplifted, his mind sustained by recitation of the Vedas.
Thus for Vibhīṣaṇa too, whose self was disciplined, ten thousand years passed as if he were in heaven's Nandana grove.
For ten thousand years Daśānana (Rāvaṇa) went without food; and at the completion of each thousand years he offered one of his heads into the fire.
Thus nine thousand years passed for him, and nine of his heads had entered the fire.
Then, at the tenth thousand-year period, just as he was about to sever the tenth head, the Grandsire (Brahmā) arrived there.
The Grandsire, greatly pleased and accompanied by the gods, addressed him: "O child, O child, Daśagrīva — I am pleased with you."
"Ask quickly, O knower of dharma, whatever boon you desire; what wish shall I fulfil for you today? Your toil has not been in vain."
Then Daśagrīva spoke, his inner self filled with delight, bowing his head to the god, his voice choking with joy:
"O blessed one, for living beings there is always no fear other than death; there is no enemy equal to death — therefore I choose immortality."
"May I be forever invincible by Suparṇas (Garuḍas), Nāgas, Yakṣas, Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and the gods, O Lord of creatures."
"I have no concern with other living beings, O you who are worshipped by the immortals — all creatures such as humans are as grass to me."
Thus addressed by Daśagrīva the Rākṣasa, O Rāma, the righteous Grandsire spoke together with the gods:
"It shall be exactly so for you, O foremost of Rākṣasas; and hear further my auspicious and gracious words here."
"Those heads you previously offered into the fire, O sinless one, shall be restored to you just as before, O Rākṣasa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus, as the Grandsire spoke to Daśagrīva the Rākṣasa, those heads that had been offered into the fire rose up again.
Having spoken thus to Daśagrīva, O Rāma, Prajāpati — the Grandsire of the worlds — then spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa:
"Vibhīṣaṇa, O child, by you whose intellect is grounded in dharma, I am fully satisfied; ask a boon, O knower of dharma, O one of good vows."
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous in soul, spoke with joined palms, endowed always with all virtues as the moon is with its rays:
"O blessed one, I am already fulfilled in that the teacher of the worlds is himself pleased with me; yet if a boon is to be given me, hear my wish, O one of good vows."
"Whatever understanding arises in me in whatever circumstances here, may that understanding always be directed toward dharma, and may I uphold that dharma."
"This is the highest and most noble boon I have in mind; for those devoted to dharma, nothing in the world is unattainable."
Then Prajāpati, greatly pleased, said to Vibhīṣaṇa: "As you are most devoted to dharma, O child, so it shall be."
"Since, though born in a Rākṣasa womb, O crusher of enemies, your understanding does not turn toward unrighteousness — immortality I grant you."
But as Prajāpati was about to grant a boon to Kumbhakarṇa, O subduer of enemies, all the gods with joined palms spoke:
"A boon should not be granted to Kumbhakarṇa by you; for you know how this evil-minded one terrifies the worlds."
"Seven apsarases in the Nandana grove, ten attendants of great Indra, O Brahman, and sages and humans — all have been devoured by him."
"Under the guise of a boon, let delusion be granted to him, O one of immeasurable radiance; thus the worlds will prosper and he will be subdued."
Thus spoken to by the gods, Brahmā — born from the lotus — reflected; and as he reflected, the goddess Sarasvatī drew near to his side.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Standing at his side with joined palms, Sarasvatī spoke: "Here I have come, O god — what service shall I render?"
To Sarasvatī thus arrived, Prajāpati spoke: "O Vāṇī (speech personified), enter into the lord of Rākṣasas as that which the gods desire."
Saying "So be it," she entered him; then Prajāpati said: "O Kumbhakarṇa, O mighty-armed one, ask the boon you have in mind."
Hearing those words, Kumbhakarṇa spoke: "To sleep for many years — O god of gods, this is what I desire."
Saying "So be it," the Grandsire together with the gods — and the goddess Sarasvatī having released him — departed to heaven.
But Kumbhakarṇa of evil soul reflected in distress: "What manner of words indeed have now fallen from my mouth?"
Thus all the brothers, having obtained their boons and blazing with splendour, went to the Śleṣmātaka forest and dwelt there in comfort.
Sumālī, learning that those night-rangers had obtained their boons, rose up from Rasātala (the netherworld) together with his followers, having cast off fear.
Mārīca, Prahasta, Virūpākṣa, and Mahodara — the ministers of that Rākṣasa — rose up with great eagerness.
Sumālī, surrounded by all those foremost Rākṣasas, approached Daśagrīva, embraced him, and spoke:
"By good fortune this long-cherished wish of mine for a son has been fulfilled, that you have obtained such a boon, surpassing the three worlds."
"For whose sake we abandoned Laṅkā and went to the netherworld — that great fear created by Viṣṇu which beset us has now passed, O mighty-armed one."
"Time and again shattered by him, we all fled together, abandoning our own abode, and entered the netherworld."
"This city of Laṅkā, formerly inhabited by us Rākṣasas, has been settled by your wise brother, the lord of wealth (Kubera)."
"If it were possible, O sinless one, to reclaim it — whether by conciliation, by gifts, or by force, O mighty-armed one — that would be well done."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You shall become lord of Laṅkā, my child — there is no doubt; and you shall indeed become the master of all of us, O greatly powerful one."
Then Daśagrīva spoke to his grandfather who stood before him: "The lord of wealth (Kubera) is our elder — you should not speak thus."
To Daśagrīva who had spoken thus, the night-ranger Prahasta spoke this humble yet reasoned speech:
"O Daśagrīva, O mighty-armed one, you should not speak like this; among heroes there is no brotherhood — hear these words of mine."
"Aditi and Diti were sisters, it is said, two supremely beautiful wives of Kaśyapa Prajāpati."
"Aditi gave birth to the gods, the lords of the three worlds; Diti, however, bore the Daityas born of Kaśyapa."
"Of the Daityas, O knower of dharma, it is said this city, this earth with its ocean-shores and its mountains — all belonged to them, O hero; they were supremely powerful."
"But having slain them in battle, Viṣṇu the supremely powerful brought this imperishable triple world under the dominion of the gods."
"You alone are not the only one who will reverse this; what the gods themselves did previously — do that; follow these words of mine."
Thus addressed by Prahasta, the evil-souled one, Daśagrīva reflected for a moment and then said simply: "Very well."
With that same joy, on that very day, the valiant Daśagrīva set out for the forest together with those night-rangers.
Stationed at Trikūṭa, the night-ranger Daśagrīva then dispatched Prahasta, skilled in speech, as his emissary.
"Prahasta, go quickly and speak to that foremost of Nairṛtas (Rākṣasas), the lord of wealth, these conciliatory words on my behalf:"
"'This city of Laṅkā, O king, belonging to the great-souled Rākṣasas, has been occupied by you, O gentle one; this is not fitting for you, O sinless one.'"
"'If you were to yield it through conciliation, O one of incomparable prowess, my gratification would be secured and dharma upheld.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus instructed, Prahasta, skilled in speech, went and reported all the words of Daśagrīva to the lord of wealth.
The god Vaiśravaṇa (Kubera), having heard these words from Prahasta, replied to that Prahasta — himself expert in speech:
"Go, tell Daśagrīva: 'This city and this kingdom of mine — O mighty-armed one, it is yours as well; enjoy it; the enemy has been destroyed.'"
"'I shall do all that is good for you, O lord of Rākṣasas, without delay; but meanwhile, wait until I inform my father.'"
Having spoken thus, the lord of wealth went to his father's presence; bowing to that elder, he reported what Rāvaṇa desired.
"O father, this Daśagrīva has dispatched a messenger to me: 'Let the city of Laṅkā, formerly inhabited by the host of Rākṣasas, be given over.' Tell me what I should do here, O one of good vows."
The brahmarṣi Viśravā, that foremost of sages, thus addressed, spoke to the wealth-giver: "Listen, my son, to my words."
"The mighty-armed Daśagrīva spoke in my presence; I repeatedly rebuked him, and that utterly evil-minded one was repeatedly spoken to by me."
"In anger I repeatedly told him to be destroyed; now hear my words, O son, which are directed toward what is best and in accordance with dharma."
"Deluded by the granting of boons, that utterly evil-minded one does not know what is worthy of respect and what is not; and through my curse he has attained a dreadful nature."
"Therefore go, O mighty-armed one, to mount Kailāsa, the bearer of the earth; settle there as your abode, and abandon Laṅkā together with your retinue."
"There is the lovely Mandākinī, the foremost of rivers, her waters covered with golden lotuses bright as the sun."
"Indeed it is not fitting for you to make enmity with that Rākṣasa (Rāvaṇa) who has obtained wealth — for you know what supreme boon he has obtained."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus counselled, and accepting that advice out of reverence for his father, Kubera departed with his wives, his citizens, his ministers, his mounts, and his treasury.
Prahasta, going to Daśagrīva, reported everything: "That city of Laṅkā, thirty yojanas in extent, is empty. Enter it with us and uphold your duty there."
Thus addressed by Prahasta, Rāvaṇa the Rākṣasa then entered the city of Laṅkā together with his brothers and his army of followers.
Anointed by the night-rangers, Daśānana then peopled the city; and that city became filled to satisfaction with night-rangers resembling dark stormclouds.
The lord of wealth, out of reverence for his father's words, then settled a city on that mountain bright as the moon — adorned with beautiful, well-decorated mansions, like Amarāvatī of Purandara (Indra).
The lord of Rākṣasas, having been anointed, then together with his brothers thought about arranging the marriage of his Rākṣasa sister.
He gave that Rākṣasī, his sister Śūrpaṇakhā by name, to Kālakeya, a lord of Dānavas, who bore the name Vidyujjihvā.
Then, having given his sister away, that king while roaming on a hunt saw there, O Rāma, one named Maya, a son of Diti.
Seeing him accompanied by a maiden, the night-ranger Daśagrīva asked: "Who are you, alone in this uninhabited forest wilderness?"
Then Maya, O Rāma, spoke to that night-ranger who had inquired: "Hear — I shall relate to you the full truth of my circumstances."
"An apsaras named Hemā — if you have heard of her, O friend — was given to me by the gods, even as Paulomī was given to Śatakratu (Indra)."
"With mind attached to her, O friend, I spent five hundred years with her; then she, on account of some divine business, departed for fourteen years."
"For her sake, for Hemā, I constructed an entire golden city, variegated with vajra and vaidūrya gems, by my māyā power."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Finding no peace there, bereft of her, deeply sorrowful, I took my daughter and came from that city to the forest."
"This is my daughter, O king, who grew in her womb; I have come seeking a husband to be with her."
"For being the father of a daughter is sorrow for men who aspire to honour; a daughter constantly keeps two families in a state of anxious uncertainty."
"By this wife of mine, however, two sons were born to me: Māyāvī was the first, O friend, and Dundubhi after him."
"All this has been truthfully told to you who asked; how should I now know you, O friend — who are you?"
Thus addressed, the lord of Rākṣasas spoke humbly: "I am a son of Paulastya (Pulastya's lineage), and Daśagrīva is my name."
Knowing him to be the son of a brahmarṣi, Maya was filled with joy and resolved there to give him his daughter.
Smiling, the lord of Daityas spoke these words to the lord of Rākṣasas: "This, O king, is my daughter, carried by the apsaras Hemā — the maiden Mandodarī by name; accept her as your wife."
O Rāma, Daśagrīva said simply "Yes" to him, kindled a fire there, and performed the rite of taking her hand in marriage.
For Maya, O Rāma, knowing the curse of the one rich in austerities, gave her to him knowing his ancestral lineage.
And he gave him his unfailing and supremely wondrous weapon — obtained through the highest austerities — with which Lakṣmaṇa was later struck down.
Thus having taken a wife, that lord and master went to the city of Laṅkā and arranged wives for his brothers as well.
Rāvaṇa arranged as wife for Kumbhakarṇa the granddaughter of Virocana, named Vajrajvālā.
Vibhīṣaṇa, the knower of dharma, obtained as wife Saramā by name, daughter of Śailūṣa, the great-souled king of Gandharvas.
She was born on the shore of the Mānasa lake, and that Mānasa lake, O friend, swelled at the coming of the rains.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Her mother spoke words choked with affection to that girl-child: "O lake, do not swell" — and from that she became Saramā.
Thus those Rākṣasas, having taken wives, sported there delightfully, each with his own wife, like Gandharvas in the Nandana grove.
Then Mandodarī gave birth to a son, Meghanāda — he who is called Indrajit by you.
For the very moment that Rākṣasa's son was born, he cried out and released a mighty roar resembling that of a thundercloud.
When Laṅkā was stupefied by that roar of his, his father himself gave him the name Meghanāda ("Thunder-Roar").
He grew up then, O Rāma, in the auspicious inner apartments of Rāvaṇa, guarded by noble women, concealed like fire within wood.
Then, in the course of time, Sleep in embodied form — sent by Lokeśvara himself — came upon Kumbhakarṇa with great intensity.
Then Kumbhakarṇa spoke to his brother who was seated: "Sleep overpowers me, O king; have a dwelling built for me."
Thereupon craftsmen appointed by the king, skilled as Viśvakarman himself, constructed for Kumbhakarṇa a dwelling equal to Kailāsa.
A yojana in breadth, twice that in length, beautiful to behold and free from any hindrance — such was the dwelling they made for Kumbhakarṇa.
Adorned throughout with variegated columns of crystal and gold, radiant with vaidūrya gems, and hung with networks of tiny bells —
— fitted with gateways of ivory, its terraces of diamond and crystal, pleasant in every season, it was like the sacred cave of Mount Meru.
There the night-roaming Kumbhakarṇa, overtaken by sleep, lay slumbering for many thousands of years without awakening.
While Kumbhakarṇa lay thus overwhelmed by sleep, the ten-headed Rāvaṇa perpetually harassed gods, seers, yakṣas, and gandharvas.
The ten-headed one, filled with fierce anger, would go to the variegated pleasure-groves — Nandana and the rest — and ravage them.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Like an elephant sporting in a river, like the wind scattering trees, like a thunderbolt hurled against mountains, he continually laid waste to all.
Having learned of the conduct of the ten-headed one, O knower of dharma, the lord of wealth Kubera recalled the conduct befitting his own lineage —
— and for the sake of fraternal guidance, and for Rāvaṇa's own welfare, Vaiśravaṇa dispatched a messenger to Laṅkā.
He went to the city of Laṅkā and met Vibhīṣaṇa; honored by him with due courtesy and asked about the purpose of his coming,
— he inquired after the welfare of the king and of kinsmen and relatives, and then had himself presented in the assembly before the seated ten-headed Rāvaṇa.
Seeing the king there blazing with his own splendor, the messenger honored him with words of victory and then remained silent for a moment.
Seated upon a couch that was brought forward, covered with a choice spread, the messenger then spoke these words to the ten-headed one:
"O king, I convey to you everything your brother said — words befitting both of you, O gentle one, in terms of conduct and lineage.
'Enough of this — you have had sufficient sport and made your display of conduct. It is good to establish oneself in dharma, if that be possible.
'I have seen Nandana broken; I hear that seers have been slain. And I have heard of the gods' mobilization against you, O king.
'I have been dismissed by you many times, O lord of rākṣasas. Yet one must protect one's own kinsmen even when they offend, for it is the nature of kinship.
'I, for my part, went to the slopes of the Himālaya to practice dharma, undertaking the severe vrata of Rudra, disciplined and with senses restrained.
'There I beheld the god, the Lord, together with the goddess Umā. And my left eye fell upon the goddess —
'— with the thought "who might this auspicious one be?" and for no other reason, for Pārvatī was playing there having taken on a form of incomparable beauty.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'By the power of the goddess, my left eye was then scorched — its light extinguished as by dust, it became tawny in color.
'Then I went to another vast slope of that mountain, and performed the great vrata there for eight full hundreds of years.
'When that observance was complete, the great god Maheśvara, the Lord, pleased, with a glad heart spoke these words:
'"I am pleased with you, O knower of dharma, O one of excellent vow, through this austerity. This vrata has been performed both by me and by you, O lord of wealth.
'"There is no third person who has performed such a vrata; this vrata, most difficult to undertake, was originated by me alone in former times.
'"Therefore, be pleased to accept friendship with me, O lord of wealth. By your austerity you have overcome all — be my friend, O sinless one.
'"And that left eye of yours which was scorched by the power of the goddess — you shall be called for eternity Ekākṣipiṅgala, 'the tawny one-eyed.'"
'Having thus obtained friendship and leave from Śaṃkara, and upon returning, I have heard of your wicked resolve.'
'Therefore, turn back from these most unrighteous associations, O defiler of your lineage — for the gods together with hosts of seers are devising the means of your destruction.'
Addressed thus, the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, enraged with red-suffused eyes, grinding his hands and teeth together, spoke these words:
"I have understood the words you are speaking, O messenger. You are not what you appear, nor is he truly my brother who has sent you.
"The guardian of wealth does not speak this for my benefit. And you, fool, presume to make me hear of his friendship with Maheśvara!
"He thinks: 'this elder, this senior, must not be slain by me.' But now, having heard my response, this is the resolve I have formed regarding him:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I shall conquer all three worlds relying on the strength of my arms! And this very moment, solely on his account, I shall lead the four Lokapālas to the realm of Yama."
Having spoken thus, the lord of Laṅkā struck the messenger with his sword and gave him over to his wicked rākṣasas to be devoured.
Then Rāvaṇa, having had auspicious rites performed, mounted his chariot desiring the conquest of the three worlds, and set forth toward Kubera, the lord of wealth.
Then he set out with his six ministers, ever mighty in their strength — Mahodara, Prahasta, Mārīca, Śuka, and Sāraṇa —
— and the valiant Dhūmrākṣa, ever eager for battle; accompanied thus, the glorious one marched forth, burning the worlds as it were with his wrath.
Passing over cities, rivers, mountains, forests, and groves in but a moment, he entered Mount Kailāsa.
On hearing that the lord of rākṣasas had encamped on that mountain, the guards said "this is the king's brother" and went to where the lord of wealth Kubera was.
Having gone, they reported to him the entire resolve of his brother; and being authorized by Kubera, they went forth to battle.
Then the stirring of the Nairṛta king's army grew like the swelling of the ocean, shaking the mountain as it were.
Then a battle broke out, thick with yakṣas and rākṣasas; and the ministers of that rākṣasa lord were hard pressed there.
Seeing his army in such a state, the night-roaming Rāvaṇa let out a shout of exhilaration and advanced in fury.
Those ministers of the lord of rākṣasas, terrible in their valor, each fought a thousand thousands of the enemy.
Then Rāvaṇa, even while being struck down with clubs, iron bars, swords, spears, and tomaras, plunged into that army.
The ten-headed one, being battered there as though breathless, was hemmed in on all sides by the lords of yakṣas who rained blows upon him like storm-clouds.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That evil one then raised his mace, equal to the rod of Kāla, and plunged into the army, sending yakṣas to the realm of Yama.
Like fire driven by the wind burning a vast expanse of dry kindling, he burned that army most terribly.
By those ministers of his in battle — Mahodara, Śuka, and the rest — the yakṣas were reduced to a remnant, like clouds scattered by the wind.
Some, their limbs broken by weapons, fell in the field of battle, biting their lips with their own sharp teeth as they were cast to the ground.
Overcome by fear, their weapons fallen away, those yakṣas then sat upon the battleground embracing one another, like river banks battered by water.
For those slain and established in heaven, for those still fighting on earth, for the hosts of seers watching from above — there was no distinction between heaven and earth.
At that moment, O Rāma, a very mighty yakṣa named Saṃyodhakaṇṭaka came forward, commanding vast forces and conveyances.
Struck by that yakṣa as though by Viṣṇu himself, Mārīca fell and touched the earth, like one whose merit is exhausted falling from the sky.
Having regained his senses after a moment and rested, the night-roamer again engaged that yakṣa in combat; and the yakṣa, routed, fled.
Then he entered the gateway that marked the boundary of the gatekeepers — ornamented with gold, dappled with vaidūrya and silver.
Then, O Rāma, as the night-roaming Rāvaṇa was entering, a gatekeeper known as Sūryabhānu barred his way.
Then, having torn out the gateway, the rākṣasa was struck by that yakṣa with the gateway he had hurled — yet he did not fall to the ground, O Rāma, by virtue of the boon granted by the one born of waters.
But Rāvaṇa struck that yakṣa with that same gateway; the yakṣa was no longer seen — he had been reduced to ashes by it.
Then all the yakṣas fled upon seeing this feat of valor, and tormented by fear they took refuge in rivers and caves.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, seeing those yakṣas fleeing in their hundreds of thousands, the superintendent of wealth Kubera himself came forth to battle.
There a yakṣa named Māṇicāra, supremely difficult to conquer, encircled by four thousand yakṣas, gave battle.
Those yakṣas, striking with clubs, pestles, javelins, śaktis, tomaras, and iron hammers in battle, rushed upon the rākṣasas.
Then Prahasta slew a thousand in battle, and Mahodara with his mace slew another thousand.
And the wicked Mārīca in his rage, O Rāma, felled two thousand in merely the interval of a blink.
Engaging Dhūmrākṣa in the great battle, Maṇibhadra struck him on the chest with a pestle in fury — yet he did not waver.
Then Maṇibhadra, swinging his mace, struck the rākṣasa Dhūmrākṣa on the head; overcome, he fell.
Seeing Dhūmrākṣa struck down and fallen, drenched in blood, the ten-headed Rāvaṇa charged at Maṇibhadra in great fury.
That foremost of yakṣas struck him — charging in fury like the fire at the world's end — with three śaktis.
But then struck by the king of rākṣasas with his mace in battle, that blow caused his crown to fall to his side; from that time forward that yakṣa was remembered as Pārśvamauli, 'he whose crown is at his side.'
With that great-souled yakṣa Maṇibhadra having turned back, O Rāma, a tremendous uproar grew on that mountain.
Then from afar appeared the lord of wealth, mace in hand, accompanied by Śukra and Proṣṭhapada, surrounded by the treasure-keepers Śaṅkha and Padma.
Seeing his brother in battle — his dignity forfeited by the curse — the wise one spoke words befitting the lineage of their grandsire Brahmā:
"Though you are restrained by me, you do not understand, O wicked one. Having experienced the fruit of this hereafter, you will come to know it when you are gone to hell.
"Indeed, the man who out of delusion drinks poison and does not understand — that fool comes to know the fruit of his action only at the end.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The gods rejoice in one who is endowed with dharma; it is by that dharma that you have been brought to this state — yet this you do not comprehend.
"Indeed, he who disrespects mothers, fathers, brothers, and teachers — the fruit of that is seen when he has come under the power of the king of the dead.
"In this transient body, he who does not accumulate austerity — that fool suffers afterward, having seen his own destination after death.
"For no one of corrupt intelligence gains good understanding by his own will; whatever action one performs, such is the fruit one reaps.
"Men obtain all things — intelligence, beauty, strength, wealth, sons, and greatness — through their own past deeds and prior actions.
"Thus you are bound for hell, one whose mind is such as this. I shall speak with you no more — this is the verdict for one of wicked conduct."
Having spoken thus, Kubera struck down Rāvaṇa's ministers; all of them, with Mārīca at their head, turned back and fled in all directions.
Then the ten-headed Rāvaṇa was struck on the head by that great-souled lord of yakṣas with his mace — yet he did not flinch from his position.
Then those two, O Rāma, striking each other in the supreme battle, were neither overcome nor wearied, both consumed with indignation.
Then Kubera, the lord of wealth, released the Āgneya weapon in battle; the ten-headed Rāvaṇa countered that weapon with the Varuṇa weapon.
Then the lord of rākṣasas, having entered into his rākṣasa illusion, whirled his great mace and struck Kubera on the head.
Thus struck by him, overcome and drenched in blood, the lord of wealth fell like an aśoka tree with its roots severed.
Then the lord of wealth was revived there by the treasure-keepers — Padma and the rest — who bore Kubera to the Nandana forest.
Then, having conquered Kubera the lord of wealth, O Rāma, the lord of rākṣasas seized his Puṣpaka aerial chariot, the token of victory.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Encircled with golden pillars, its gateways set with vaidūrya gems, covered with networks of pearls, adorned with trees granting every wish —
— that chariot, swift as desire and won by valor: the king mounted it and, having conquered the divine Vaiśravaṇa, descended from Kailāsa.
Having conquered his brother Kubera, O Rāma, the lord of rākṣasas proceeded thence to the Śaravaṇa forest, birthplace of great armies.
Then Daśagrīva beheld that golden Śaravaṇa, wrapped in a network of rays, gleaming like a second sun.
Approaching the mountain, amid a charming grove, he saw there the Puṣpaka chariot, O Rāma, held motionless in the sky.
Seeing the Puṣpaka — that wish-propelled vehicle now rendered motionless — the rākṣasa reflected upon it, surrounded by his ministers.
"What is this? Why does the Puṣpaka not move for me? Hovering above this mountain — whose deed can this be?"
Then Mārīca, wise in understanding, said to Daśagrīva: "It is not without cause, O king, that this Puṣpaka does not move."
Then Nandiśvara, the mighty attendant of the Lord, drawing near to his side, fearlessly addressed the king of rākṣasas thus:
"Turn back, Daśagrīva — Śaṃkara is at sport upon this mountain."
"This mountain has been made inaccessible to suparṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, daityas, dānavas, rākṣasas — to all living beings."
He, his eyes reddened with anger, descended from the Puṣpaka and, saying "Who is this Śaṃkara?", strode to the base of the mountain.
Then he beheld Nandiśvara standing not far away, his lord — gripping a blazing trident, like a second Śaṃkara.
The rākṣasa, seeing his monkey-face and despising him, broke into derisive laughter from sheer foolishness, like a rain-cloud releasing its waters.
The blessed Nandī, wrathful — that other form of Śaṃkara himself — spoke to the rākṣasa Daśagrīva who stood before him:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Because you, O wicked-minded rākṣasa, seeing me in the form of a monkey, have out of foolishness despised me and let loose your mockery —
"— therefore monkeys bearing my form, equal to me in might and energy, shall be born for the destruction of your lineage."
"Yet what can I do to you now, O night-wanderer? You are not to be slain by me — you are already slain, indeed, by your own deeds."
Paying no heed to Nandī's words, the night-wanderer approached the mountain and spoke these words:
"For the sake of that which has cut off my Puṣpaka's flight as it traveled, I shall uproot this very mountain, O lord of cattle!"
"By what power does he sport there like a king? You should know — you do not know — that a danger stands before you."
Having spoken thus, O king, he thrust his arms beneath the mountain and began to lift that peak, replete with deer, serpents, and trees.
Then, O Rāma, the great god Mahādeva, smiling and glancing at what had been done, pressed down upon that mountain with the tip of his toe — as if in play.
Then his arms, thrust beneath the mountain, were crushed, and his ministers who stood there were struck with astonishment.
From the rākṣasa's anger and from the anguish of his crushed arms there burst forth an enormous roar by which the three worlds were filled.
Human beings, terror-struck by the sound, believed it to be the dissolution of the world; the gods too were shaken and disturbed in their several duties.
Then Mahādeva, pleased and standing on the summit of the mountain, released his arms, O king, and addressed Daśānana in these words:
"I am pleased with your valor and your martial spirit, O night-wanderer; the cry released in your pain — that voice — was exceedingly terrible."
"Since all three worlds were made to resound and were seized with fear, therefore you shall henceforth be called Rāvaṇa by name."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Gods, humans, yakṣas, and all others who dwell on the earth's surface shall call you Rāvaṇa — he who makes the world cry out."
"Go, O son of Pulastya, at ease, by whatever path you wish — you are granted leave by me; depart, O lord of rākṣasas."
Thus named in person by Maheśvara, that Rāvaṇa paid homage to Mahādeva and mounted that celestial chariot.
Thereafter, O Rāma, Rāvaṇa roamed across the earth, harassing mighty kṣatriyas here and there.
Then, O king, the long-armed one, wandering over the earth, reached the Himālayan forest and roamed through it — Rāvaṇa.
There he saw a maiden clad in a rough antelope-skin and matted locks, engaged in austerity according to the sage's prescribed rite, like a goddess performing her penance.
Seeing that maiden endowed with beauty and of exceedingly great vows, his mind overpowered by the intoxication of desire, he questioned her as if with a smile:
"Why do you practice this, O fortunate one, which is contrary to your youth? This mode of conduct is not fitting for one of your beauty."
"Whose daughter are you, O fortunate one? Who is your husband, O sinless one? Tell me quickly, as I ask — what is the reason for your pursuit of austerity?"
Thus addressed by that ignoble rākṣasa, the maiden, rich in ascetic power, offered him guest-honor according to the proper rite and spoke:
"My father was named Kuśadhvaja, a brahmarṣi, righteous, the son of Bṛhaspati, glorious, equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom."
"I was born of that great soul as he constantly practiced study of the Vedas — born as a maiden made of speech itself, known by the name Vedavatī."
"Then gods together with gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and serpents — they too went to my father and proposed me as their bride."
"But my father did not give me to any of them, O lord of rākṣasas. I shall tell you the reason — hear it, O great-armed one."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"My father's intended son-in-law was Viṣṇu himself, the best of gods, the lord of the three worlds — to none other would my father give me."
"Learning that the righteous-souled one wished to give me thus, a daitya king named Śambhu, arrogant with power, grew enraged — and that wicked one slew my sleeping father in the night."
"Then my mother, wretched, embracing my father's body, that most noble one entered the fire along with him."
"Then the wish to fulfill my father's true longing regarding Nārāyaṇa settled firmly in my heart: 'I shall accomplish it.'"
"Even for my father who has gone to the realm of the dead I will fulfill his desire — having taken this vow, I practice extensive austerity."
"All this has been told to you by me, O foremost of rākṣasas. Know me to be one who has taken refuge in dharma, with the desire to have Nārāyaṇa as my lord."
"I know who you are, O king. Go, O son of Paulastya's lineage. Through my austerity I know all that transpires in the three worlds."
Then Rāvaṇa, wounded by the arrows of Kandarpа, descended from the prow of his chariot and addressed that maiden of exceedingly great vows:
"You are conceited, O lovely-hipped one, whose mind runs in such a direction — it is old people, O doe-eyed maiden, in whom the accumulation of dharma shines."
"You are endowed with every virtue and do not deserve to do this. You are the most beautiful in all three worlds, O timid one — to follow the ways of old age in youth!"
"And who then is that one whom you speak of as Viṣṇu? In valor, in austerity, in enjoyment, and in strength, he is not my equal, O fortunate one — he whom you desire, O slender-waisted maiden."
"No, do not — do not speak thus!" — so the maiden said to that night-wanderer. But the rākṣasa touched her hair with the tip of his hand.
Then Vedavatī, enraged, cut off her own hair with her hand, kindled a fire, and, resolved upon death, spoke:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Violated by you, O ignoble one, life is no longer mine, O rākṣasa. Therefore I shall enter the fire as you watch."
"And since I, though without sin, have been violated as if unprotected, therefore I shall be born again for the sake of your destruction."
"For you, O wicked one, cannot be slain by a woman — certainly not by me. And if a curse were cast on you, my austerity would be diminished."
"But if there is any deed done, gift given, or oblation offered by me, by that merit may I — virtuous one, not born of a womb — become the daughter of a righteous man."
Having spoken thus, she entered the blazing fire; and from the sky a divine rain of flowers fell all around.
"The enemy struck down by your wrath of old — he who was slain by you when he had taken refuge relying on your mountain-like, superhuman valor —"
"— thus this most blessed one is born again among mortals, drawn forth by a plowshare's tip from the field, upon the sacrificial altar, like a flame of fire."
"This one who was formerly named Vedavatī in the Kṛta age — having reached the Tretā age, born for the slaying of that rākṣasa, she arose as Sītā; she is this Sītā, called again by humans."
When Vedavatī had entered the fire, Rāvaṇa mounted that Puṣpaka chariot and continued to roam the earth.
Then, reaching Uśīrabīja, that rākṣasa saw king Marutta performing a sacrifice together with the gods.
A brahmarṣi named Saṃvarta, the very brother of Bṛhaspati, versed in dharma, was officiating at the sacrifice, surrounded by all the hosts of brahmin priests.
The gods, seeing that rākṣasa who was unconquerable by reason of boons received, assumed various animal forms, fearful of being harassed by him.
Indra became a peacock; the king of dharma became a crow; the lord of wealth became a lizard; Varuṇa indeed became a swan.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Approaching that king, Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas, said: "Give me battle — or else say 'I am defeated.'"
Then king Marutta said to him "Who are you?" — whereupon the rākṣasa, letting out a laugh of contempt, spoke these words:
"I am pleased by your nonchalant manner, O king — you who do not recognize me as Rāvaṇa, the younger brother of Kubera."
"Who is there in the three worlds that does not know my might — I who, having conquered my own brother, seized this chariot?"
Then king Marutta addressed that rākṣasa: "Fortunate indeed are you, by whom your elder brother was conquered in battle!"
"What is accompanied by adharma is not praiseworthy; what is contrary to the world's good is not praiseworthy. Having done a deed of wickedness, you boast of having defeated your own brother."
"Did you first practice dharma alone and then obtain the boon? For I have not heard before of the kind of thing you now proclaim yourself."
