Then that king, seizing his bow and arrows, set forth furiously for battle — but Saṃvarta blocked his path.
The great ṛṣi spoke to Marutta with affection: "If my word is to be heeded, engagement in combat is not appropriate for you."
"This sacrifice to Maheśvara, if left incomplete, would burn up your lineage. How can one who is consecrated engage in war? How can there be cruelty in one who is consecrated?"
"And in battle there is always uncertainty, and this rākṣasa is hard to conquer." Thereupon king Marutta, lord of the earth, turned back at his guru's word, laid aside his arrow-strung bow, composed himself, and faced the sacrifice.
Then Śuka, considering him defeated, proclaimed it aloud — "Rāvaṇa has won!" — and out of joy let loose a shout.
Having devoured the great ṛṣis who were present there, gathered for the sacrifice, and satiated with their blood, he set forth again across the earth.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When Rāvaṇa had departed, the gods, together with Indra, the dwellers in heaven, resumed their own forms; and then they addressed those creatures thus:
Then Indra, out of joy, addressed the peacock with blue plumage: "I am pleased with you for your service, O wise-in-dharma, O bird."
"The thousand eyes that are mine — those shall appear upon your tail-feathers; and when I rain, you shall experience delight — this is the mark of my favor."
"The tail-feathers of peacocks were formerly all blue, O lord of men; having received the boon from the lord of gods, they all took on their variegated splendor."
The king of dharma, O Rāma, addressed the crow perched in the eastern hall: "O bird, I am most pleased with you; hear the word of one who is pleased."
"The various diseases by which other living beings are afflicted at my hand — those shall have no power over you, now that I am pleased — of this there is no doubt."
"You have no fear of death from my boons, O bird — until men slay you, you shall endure."
"And those humans dwelling in my domain who are tormented by hunger — when you have eaten, they too shall be satisfied along with their kinsmen."
Varuṇa then addressed the swan that moves upon the waters of the Gaṅgā: "Hear these words spoken with affection, O lord among winged ones."
"A color enchanting and beautiful, resembling the disk of the moon — it shall arise in you, lofty and gleaming like white foam."
"Having attained likeness to my body, you shall always be beautiful, and you shall obtain incomparable delight — this is the mark of my favor."
"For formerly, O Rāma, the color of swans was not entirely white — their wings were tipped with blue at the ends, their breasts were pure as fresh grass-tips."
Then Vaiśravaṇa addressed the lizard standing on the mountain: "I bestow upon you a golden color — this too is my affection for you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Your head shall always bear wealth upon it, imperishable; this golden hue shall be yours by my favor."
Having thus bestowed boons upon them at that sacrificial festival, the gods, when it was concluded together with the king, returned each to their own abode.
Having vanquished Marutta, the lord of rākṣasas, the ten-faced Daśānana, ever eager for battle, then marched against the cities of other kings.
Approaching those royal lords, who were comparable to Mahendra and Varuṇa, the king of rākṣasas declared: "Give me battle."
"Or else say, 'We are conquered' — that is my firm resolve. For those who do otherwise, there shall be no escape."
Thereupon many wise kings, firm in righteousness, declared "We are conquered," recognizing the superior power of their foe.
Duṣyanta, Suratha, Gādhi, King Gaya, and Purūravas — all these kings declared, O friend, "We are conquered."
Then Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas, approached Ayodhyā, well-guarded by Anaraṇya as Amarāvatī is guarded by Śakra.
He addressed the king: "Give me battle, or else say 'I am conquered' — such is my command here."
Then Anaraṇya, greatly enraged, replied to the lord of rākṣasas: "I grant you single combat, O lord of rākṣasas."
Then that great army of the king, which had been assembled in advance upon hearing the purpose and was prepared, sallied forth intent on slaying the rākṣasas.
Many thousands of elephants and ten thousand horses, together with infantry and chariots, poured forth instantly, covering the earth.
Upon meeting Rāvaṇa's force, the army of that lord of the earth was annihilated, O king, like an oblation cast into fire.
The king watched his great army being destroyed, as five rivers are swallowed up when they reach the great ocean.
Then that king, overwhelmed with rage, himself drawing his bow — brilliant as the bow of Indra — advanced against Rāvaṇa.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The joy of the Ikṣvāku line let fly eight hundred arrows at the head of that king of rākṣasas.
But those arrows, as they fell, made no wound anywhere upon him — like streams of water falling from clouds upon the summit of a mountain.
Then the enraged king of rākṣasas struck the king with his palm upon the head, and the king fell from his chariot.
That king fell to the ground, his limbs convulsed and trembling, like a great sāla tree felled in the forest by a thunderbolt.
Laughing, the rākṣasa addressed that Ikṣvāku lord of the earth: "What fruit have you now obtained by fighting against me?"
"There is none in the three worlds who could give me single combat, O king. I think that, heedless in your pleasures, you have not heard of my might."
As he spoke thus, the king, his breath fading, replied: "What can be done here, when time is insurmountable?"
"I have not been conquered by you, O rākṣasa, self-lauding one — I have been undone by time. You are merely the instrument of my fall."
"Yet what can I now do when my life is ebbing away? Because of the dishonor done to the Ikṣvākus, I shall speak these words, O rākṣasa:"
"If I have given gifts, if I have made oblations, if I have performed austerities rightly, if I have protected my subjects well — then let my words be true:"
"In this very line of the great-souled Ikṣvākus shall be born a king of supreme splendor who will take your life."
Then, when that curse had been uttered, the divine kettledrums resounded like towering rain-clouds being struck, and a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
Then that king, O king of kings, went to his place in the heavenly realm; and when the king had gone to heaven, O Rāma, the rākṣasa turned away.
Then, as he terrorized mortals upon the earth, the lord of rākṣasas encountered in that thick region the foremost of sages, Nārada.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Nārada, the divine sage of great splendor and boundless radiance, standing upon a cloud, addressed Rāvaṇa, who was seated in the Puṣpaka.
"O lord of rākṣasas, gentle one, halt, O son of Viśravas. I am pleased with your mighty exploits and your noble lineage."
"By Viṣṇu with his slaughter of daityas, by Tārkṣya with his routing of serpents, and by you with your crushing of foes in battle — I am greatly gratified."
"I shall say something that deserves to be heard — will you hear it? And having heard it, you should act accordingly, O bull among rākṣasas."
"Why do you slay this world, you who cannot be slain by the gods? This world is already slain when it has fallen under the power of death."
"Behold first, O mighty-armed lord of rākṣasas, this human world, wondrous in its purposes, whose course cannot be known."
"In one place, music and dancing are enjoyed by people full of joy; elsewhere others weep in grief, their faces streaming with tears."
"Bound by the affections of mother, father, son, wife, and cherished kinsmen, this people is ruined by delusion and does not perceive its own suffering."
"Why then afflict this world already undone by delusion? The mortal world is conquered by you already, O gentle one — of this there is no doubt."
Thus addressed, the lord of Laṅkā, blazing as it were with energy, laughed aloud and, saluting Nārada, spoke to him there.
"O great sage, you who roam among gods and gandharvas, you who love battle — I am indeed setting out to descend to the netherworld in quest of victory."
"Having conquered the three worlds and brought nāgas and gods under my sway, I shall then churn the ocean, that abode of nectar, for the sake of amṛta."
Then the blessed sage Nārada addressed the ten-necked one: "By which route now are you going?"
"This route to the city of the king of the dead is exceedingly hard to traverse, O crusher of foes — it leads to Yama's domain and is most formidable."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
But Daśānana released a laugh like an autumnal cloud and, saying "Very well," spoke these words.
"Therefore, O great brahmin, I am proceeding in the southern direction, intent on slaying Vaivasvata, where the son of the Sun holds sway as king."
"For I have vowed in anger, O blessed one, seeking battle, that I will vanquish the four guardians of the worlds, O lord."
"For that reason I am now proceeding to the city of the king of the ancestors — I shall join with death that one who brings affliction to all living beings."
Having spoken thus and saluting the sage, Daśagrīva departed toward the southern quarter together with his exultant ministers.
Then Nārada, the foremost of seers, of great splendor, entered into meditation for a moment and reflected, like fire without smoke.
"He by whom the three worlds, with Indra, with all moving and unmoving beings, are afflicted — and when life-span and dharma are diminished — how is that time-force itself to be destroyed?"
"He from whom the three worlds always flee in terror — how is it that this lord of rākṣasas goes of his own accord toward him?"
"He who is both ordainer and arranger for merit and demerit alike, by whom the three worlds are already conquered — how indeed shall he conquer him?"
"What arrangement will be made differently from this? Stirred by curiosity, I shall go to the abode of Yama."
Having thus reflected, the foremost of seers, swift in valor, went toward the abode of Yama to report what had transpired.
There he saw the god Yama, attended by fire, presiding over the ordained fate of each living being according to its kind.
Seeing the great sage Nārada arrived there, Yama offered him arghya according to the rites and, when the sage was comfortably seated, addressed him.
"Is all well, O divine sage? Is dharma not perishing? What is the purpose of your coming, O one honored by gods and gandharvas?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the blessed sage Nārada spoke: "Hear what I shall say, and let the proper arrangement be made."
"This night-wanderer, named Daśagrīva, O king of the ancestors, is coming by force to bring you, most difficult to conquer, under his sway."
"For this reason I have come hastily, O lord. What will he now do against your rod of punishment?"
In that very interval, from afar the divine aerial vehicle of that rākṣasa was seen approaching — blazing like the risen sun.
That mighty one, with the radiance of the Puṣpaka, having dispelled all darkness from that region, drew near.
The mighty-armed Daśagrīva looked about here and there and saw living beings reaping the fruits of their good deeds and of their evil deeds.
Then Rāvaṇa, the powerful one, by his own valor forcibly released those who were being tormented by their own evil deeds.
As the dead were being freed by that most powerful rākṣasa, the guardians of the dead, greatly enraged, rushed toward the lord of rākṣasas.
Those warriors, hundreds of thousands in number, showered the Puṣpaka with javelins, iron clubs, spears, mallets, śaktis, and tomaras.
They swiftly shattered the seats, pavilions, balustrades, and coverings of the Puṣpaka, like bees swarming upon it.
Yet that celestial craft, the Puṣpaka — though shattered in battle — remained indestructible nonetheless, by virtue of Brahmā's divine power.
Then Rāvaṇa's ministers, those of great valor, fought with all their will and all their strength, and so too did the king Daśānana himself.
Those ministers of the lord of rākṣasas, their limbs smeared with blood and battered by every weapon, waged a mighty battle.
The great ones struck one another in battle with their weapons; the great army of Yama and the ministers of the rākṣasa lord smote each other.
Leaving aside those ministers of the mighty rākṣasa, they charged toward Daśānana himself, raining spears upon him.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the foremost of rākṣasas, his limbs smeared with blood and riddled with blows, shone upon his aerial vehicle like a blossoming aśoka tree.
That powerful one released by force of arms spears, maces, javelins, śaktis, tomaras, arrows, pestles, rocks, and trees.
But gathering up all those missiles and neutralizing those weapons, they — a hundred thousand against one — struck that terrible rākṣasa.
Surrounding him on all sides like massed clouds around a mountain, they left him breathless with stone-hurling slings and spears.
His armor stripped away, enraged, drenched with streams of blood, he abandoned the Puṣpaka and stood upon the earth.
Then the lord of rākṣasas, bow in hand, his arrows readied, having regained his senses after a moment, stood on the earth in fury like Death himself.
Then he fitted the divine Pāśupata weapon to his bow and, calling out to them "Stand! Stand!" drew that bow to its full extent.
That arrow, wreathed in flames and followed by flesh-eating beings in battle, once released, reduced thickets and trees to ash as it blazed forth.
The soldiers of Vaivasvata, scorched by its blazing power, fell upon that battlefield like trees burned down by a forest fire.
Then the rākṣasa of terrible valor, together with his ministers, let out a tremendous roar, shaking the earth as it were.
Hearing that great roar, Yama Vaivasvata reckoned his enemy to be victorious and perceived the decimation of his own army.
Seeing his warriors slain, his eyes blazing with fury, he quickly commanded his charioteer: "Bring up the chariot at once."
His charioteer drew up the divine chariot, whose thunder was tremendous; and that one of great splendour mounted the great car.
Death, noose and club in hand — by whom all three worlds, moving and unmoving, are brought to their end — stood before him.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The staff of Time, embodied and blazing as though with divine lustre — Yama's celestial weapon — stood at his side upon the chariot.
Then the three worlds trembled in terror and the dwellers in heaven shook, beholding Time in wrath, dread to all the three worlds.
The ministers of the lord of rākṣasas, beholding that terrible chariot attended by Death, terrifying to every world—
—all, their senses lost in the lightness of their nature, overcome with fear, cried out "We cannot fight here!" and fled in all directions.
But the rākṣasa, seeing that chariot so terrifying to the worlds, was not agitated; no distress arose in him at all.
Yama, closing on Rāvaṇa and hurling javelins and iron clubs, struck with great fury at the vital points of the rākṣasa.
Rāvaṇa, standing composed, poured a shower of arrows onto Vaivasvata's chariot as a cloud pours a rain of water.
Then, with hundreds of great javelins raining upon his broad chest, the rākṣasa, tormented by those shafts, could no longer retaliate.
Thus assailed with diverse weapons by Yama the crusher of foes, throughout seven nights of battle, he was neither routed nor vanquished.
Then the battle between Yama and the rākṣasa was renewed — both craving victory, neither retreating from the combat.
Then the gods together with gandharvas, the siddhas and the great seers, with Prajāpati at their head, beheld that field of battle.
As those two fought — the foremost of rākṣasas and the lord of the departed — it was as though the dissolution of the worlds had come.
Then the lord of rākṣasas, enraged, drew his bow in the combat and released arrows that filled the sky without interval.
He afflicted Death with four sharp-pointed arrows, the charioteer with seven, and swiftly struck Yama at the vital points with a thousand shafts.
Then, suddenly, from the face of the enraged Yama issued his breath, a garland of flames, the fire of his wrath.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the gods, dānavas and rākṣasas beheld that wonder — the blazing fire born of wrath, seeking to burn the enemy's forces.
Death, utterly enraged, then said to Vaivasvata: "Release me at once, O god; I shall slay the enemy in battle."
"Naraka, Śambara, Vṛtra, Śambhu, Kārtasvara, Balī, Namuci, Virocana, and both Madhu and Kaiṭabha—
—these and many other mighty ones, difficult to assail, I have seen laid low by me. What concern is this night-roamer?"
"Release me rightly, O knower of dharma, until I slay him — for no one I have set eyes upon lives even for a moment."
"This is not merely my power; it is the law of nature — the certainty that whoever I touch does not live."
Hearing those words, the illustrious Dharmarāja replied: "Stay — I myself shall slay this embodiment of death."
Then Vaivasvata the lord, red-eyed in rage, raised in his hand that infallible staff of Time, weighing it.
Along its flanks, unbroken nooses of Time were fixed, and a club embodied stood there, resembling the touch of fire.
By its very sight the vital breaths of living beings are stopped — what then of its striking or pressing upon an embodied soul?
That dreadful staff, encircled in flames, as though drinking up the night-roamer, seized by the powerful hand, blazed terribly in fury.
Then all beings fled from that field of battle, and the gods were shaken beholding Yama with the staff of Time upraised.
But as Yama was about to strike, staff raised against Rāvaṇa, Pitāmaha himself appeared visibly and spoke thus:
"O Vaivasvata, O mighty-armed one of matchless valour, this night-roamer must not be struck by you with this staff.
A boon was indeed granted by me to him, O foremost of the thirty gods; my spoken word must not be made false by you.
For this staff of Time, infallible in felling all creatures, was created by me of old, with Death as its foremost power.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Therefore this must not be hurled by you, O gentle one, upon the rākṣasa's head — for once it falls, none can live even a moment.
For if, once it falls, this rākṣasa does not die — or if Daśagrīva does die — in either case my word would be made untrue.
Restrain this staff upraised for killing from the lord of rākṣasas; uphold my truth, and consider the worlds as well."
Thus addressed, the righteous-souled Yama replied: "This staff is withdrawn; you are our sovereign and master."
"But what can I now do, stationed in this battle, when the rākṣasa who must not be slain by me is puffed up by a boon?"
"Therefore I shall disappear from the sight of this rākṣasa." So saying, with chariot and horses, he vanished on the spot.
Daśagrīva, having conquered him and proclaiming his own name aloud, departed from Yama's abode, exultant, in the Puṣpaka.
Then Vaivasvata, together with the gods led by Brahmā, and the great sage Nārada, went to the third heaven, joyful.
Daśagrīva, having conquered Yama the foremost of the thirty gods, Rāvaṇa, boasting of his victory, surveyed his own companions.
Having celebrated with them in the joy of victory, all of them — Mārīca and the rest — soothed by Rāvaṇa, ascended the Puṣpaka.
Then, exultant, he entered the nether world and the ocean — that abode thronged with hosts of daityas and serpents, well guarded by Varuṇa.
He went to Bhogavatī, the city guarded by Vāsuki, brought the nāgas under his control, and then proceeded to the city of Maṇimatī.
There the daityas known as Nivātakavacas — who had obtained boons — dwelt; the rākṣasa came before them and challenged them to battle.
They, all those mighty daityas, powerful, with diverse weapons, maddened with the pride of battle, engaged him in combat.
As they fought, a full year passed by, and neither side had gained victory or suffered defeat.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Pitāmaha, the imperishable lord who traverses the three worlds, came swiftly, mounted on his excellent aerial vehicle.
Restraining the Nivātakavacas from their act of war, the ancient Pitāmaha spoke these words, knowing the truth of the matter:
"For this Rāvaṇa cannot be conquered in battle by gods and asuras alike; nor can you be brought to destruction by gods and asuras with Indra at their head.
Friendship with this rākṣasa is suitable for you; all affairs are undivided among true friends — of this there is no doubt."
Then Rāvaṇa made friendship with the Nivātakavacas there, with fire as witness, and was filled with affection for them.
Honoured by them in proper fashion, Daśānana dwelt happily for a year, receiving worship indistinguishable from that in his own city.
He, self-possessed, having learned ninety-nine forms of illusion, wandered through the nether world in search of the abode of the lord of waters.
Then he conquered the city called Aśmanagara, guarded by the Kāleyas, in a moment, and slew four hundred daityas.
Then the lord of rākṣasas beheld the divine abode of Varuṇa, resembling a white cloud, standing like Mount Kailāsa.
He saw there the cow Surabhī standing, ever streaming with milk — from whose flowing milk the ocean named Kṣīroda was born.
From that ocean arose the cool-rayed moon, benefactor of creatures; approaching it, the great seers who live on foam sustain themselves; from it arose amṛta and also the wine of the gods.
Circumambulating that most wondrous cow whom people in the world call Surabhī by name, Rāvaṇa entered the great and terrible place guarded by forces of many kinds.
Then he beheld the excellent palace of Varuṇa, streaming with a hundred cascades, resembling an autumnal cloud, perpetually rejoicing.
Then, having slain the commanders of the army in battle while being struck by them in return, he cried: "Where has your king gone? Announce me at once."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Rāvaṇa has come seeking battle; let battle be given to him — or else say with folded hands: 'I am conquered; I have no fear from you.'"
In that interval the sons and grandsons of the great-souled Varuṇa — Gauḥ and Puṣkara as well — came forth in fury.
They, endowed with heroic qualities, surrounded by their own forces, yoked their swift-moving chariots that blazed like the rising sun.
Then a terrible, hair-raising battle arose between the sons of the lord of waters and the rākṣasa Rāvaṇa.
By the ministers of great valour belonging to the rākṣasa Daśagrīva, that entire force of Varuṇa was struck down in an instant.
Seeing their own force in battle, Varuṇa's sons, tormented by the net of arrows, then withdrew from the act of combat.
Driven to the ground and seeing Rāvaṇa in the Puṣpaka, they swiftly entered the sky in their swift-moving chariots.
Then, having attained to an equal position with him, there ensued a great tumultuous aerial battle between them, as between gods and dānavas.
Then they, having turned Rāvaṇa back in battle with arrows resembling fire, shouted various war-cries in exultation.
Then Mahodara, the hero, seeing his king thus assailed, abandoned fear of death and looked about, eager for battle.
Those horses of theirs — swift-moving, swift as the wind — struck by Mahodara with his mace, fell to the earth.
Having slain the warriors and horses of those sons of Varuṇa, he quickly let out a great roar, seeing them standing there deprived of their chariots.
Those chariots of theirs, with their horses and together with their excellent charioteers, struck down by Mahodara, fell to the surface of the earth.
The sons of the great-souled Varuṇa, those heroes, abandoning their chariots and standing in the sky, did not waver in their own power.
Stringing their bows, piercing Mahodara through, they charged Rāvaṇa together in the battle, enraged.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Daśagrīva, enraged, standing like the fire of universal destruction, rained a great swift shower of arrows upon their vital points.
That irresistible one hurled down upon them as he stood above them: diverse clubs, hundreds of broad-headed arrows, swords, javelins, śataghnīs and tomaras.
Then those heroes, pierced and wounded, fell down as foot-soldiers.
Then the rākṣasa, releasing a great roar, slaughtered the followers of Varuṇa with terrible diverse weapons, like a cloud pouring down sheets of rain.
Then all of them, turned back and fallen to the ground, were quickly brought inside their homes by their own men, away from the battle.
Then the rākṣasa commanded: "Let this be reported to Varuṇa." And a minister of Varuṇa named Prabhāsa addressed Rāvaṇa:
"The great-splendoured lord of waters has indeed gone to the world of Brahmā — Varuṇa has gone to hear the gāndharva music — him whom you challenge to battle."
"Then why exhaust yourself in vain, O hero, when the king is gone? The princes who were present here, those heroes, have been defeated by you."
The lord of rākṣasas, hearing that, proclaimed his own name aloud and, releasing a shout of joy, departed from the abode of Varuṇa.
Returning by the very path by which he had come, the rākṣasa turned back and went through the vault of the sky, making for Laṅkā.
Returning in great exultation, that evil-souled Rāvaṇa seized along the way the daughters of kings, seers, gods, and gandharvas.
Whatever lovely maiden or woman the rākṣasa beheld, he slew her kinsmen and placed her in the aerial vehicle.
There Rāvaṇa seized maidens of nāgas, yakṣas, humans, rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas alike.
Long-haired, fair-limbed, moon-faced, all young women bowed down with grief, their breasts bent in sorrow.
Equal to the flickering of fire, trembling, tormented with grief, born of the fire of sorrow and fear, they shed the water of their tears.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
With their sighing, the Puṣpaka with its fire suppressed blazed like a fire-sacrifice, ignited by the sighs of those grieving women.
One, deeply tormented, thought: "He will even kill me." Remembering mothers, fathers, brothers, sons, and fathers-in-law, those women overwhelmed by grief and sorrow wept together.
"How will my son fare without me? How my mother, how my brother — all plunged into an ocean of sorrow?"
"Alas, how shall I live without my husband, my deity? O Death, be gracious — I beg you, take me to the abode of Yama."
"What evil deed did I commit in a former body, that I have been thus violated by him and cast into an ocean of sorrow?"
"I see no end to my suffering in this life. Alas, shame upon the world of humans — there is truly no worse state than this."
"My kinsmen, who were weak, were destroyed by the powerful Rāvaṇa like stars by the risen sun."
"Alas, this rākṣasa, though very powerful, delights in means of slaughter; alas, he does not understand of himself his own evil conduct."
"In every way the valour of this evil-souled one is fitting for him; but this act of violating another's wife is unbecoming."
"Because this evil-minded one lusts after the wives of others, therefore this beast shall meet his death by a cause relating to a woman."
Thus cursed by those women, those devoted wives, faithful and treading the right path, he became stripped of his lustre and brilliance.
While they lamented thus, Rāvaṇa the lord of rākṣasas entered the city of Laṅkā, honoured by the night-roamers.
Then the sister of the king of rākṣasas, deeply distressed, fell at his feet and began to speak.
Then Rāvaṇa, raising up his sister and consoling her, said: "What is this, dear one? Speak to me quickly."
She, the rākṣasī, her eyes choked with tears, spoke these words: "I am ruined, O king; you in your power have made me a widow."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"These daityas slain by you in battle through your might, O king, known as the Kāleyas — they were of great strength and valour."
"There my husband was slain — dearer to me than life itself — killed by you there, O brother, as though you were his enemy."
"I who have been slain by you yourself, O king — by my own kinsman — shall suffer the pain and the name of widowhood given to me by you."
"Surely a son-in-law is to be protected by you even in battles; having slain him in combat, O king, are you not ashamed of yourself?"
Thus addressed by his sister who was crying out, the rākṣasa comforted her and spoke these conciliatory words:
"Enough of grief, my dear; you need have no fear at all. I shall satisfy you always with special gifts of honour."
"Engrossed and distracted in battle, eager for victory, loosing arrows, I do not distinguish in combat friend from foe, O fair one — it was thus that your husband, your brother-in-law, was slain by me in the battle."
"Whatever is appropriate now, I shall do for your benefit. Stay beside your brother Khara, established in lordship."
"He shall be your brother and lord of fourteen thousand mighty rākṣasas in marching and in giving command."
"There your brother Khara, son of your mother's sister, shall be your lord, always acting on whatever you yourself will say."
"Let this hero go swiftly to protect the Daṇḍakas; the mighty Dūṣaṇa shall be his commander of forces."
"For that forest region was cursed long ago by the wrathful Uśanas — it shall become the dwelling of rākṣasas, without doubt."
Having spoken thus, Daśagrīva assigned to him an army: fourteen thousand rākṣasas who could assume any form at will.
Surrounded by all those rākṣasas of terrible appearance, Khara swiftly set out for the Daṇḍakas, fearless on every side.
There he established his rule, free of thorns, and Śūrpaṇakhā dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest, content.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having given that dreadful forest to Khara and having comforted his sister, the ten-necked one grew cheerful and yet more at ease.
Then the great-souled lord of the Rākṣasas entered together with his retinue that great grove of Laṅkā called Nikumbhilā.
There he saw a sacrifice in progress, strewn with hundreds of sacrificial posts and adorned with graceful altars, blazing as it were with sacred splendour.
There he saw his own son Meghanāda, the subduer of enemies, wearing a black antelope-skin and bearing the water-pot and sacrificial fire as his banner.
The lord of the Rākṣasas approached him, embraced him with his arms, and said: "What is this that is going on, my son? Tell me."
Then Uśanas, the preceptor, that foremost of twice-born sages possessed of great austerity, spoke to Rāvaṇa, the foremost of Rākṣasas, for the sake of the success of the sacrifice:
"I shall tell you, O king — hear everything in full. Your son has accomplished seven sacrifices of great extent and detail.
The Agniṣṭoma, the Aśvamedha — the sacrifice rich in gold — the Rājasūya, the Gomedha, and the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice as well —
— and during the performance of the Māheśvara sacrifice, so difficult for men to accomplish, your son has obtained boons here directly from the Lord of creatures Paśupati himself.
A divine chariot that goes wherever one wishes, moving through the sky unfailingly, and the illusion named Tāmasī by which darkness is brought about —
— by this illusion, O lord of Rākṣasas, the movements of one fighting in battle cannot be discerned even by gods and Asuras.
Two inexhaustible quivers, arrows, and a bow most difficult to overcome, and a powerful weapon that destroys enemies in battle —
— having obtained all these boons, this your son, O ten-faced one, has completed the sacrifice today, and I have remained here awaiting you."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the ten-necked one said: "This has not been done well, for the enemies headed by Indra have been honoured with offerings.
Come now — what has been done cannot be undone. Come, my gentle one; let us go to our own palace."
Then Daśagrīva, together with his son and Vibhīṣaṇa, went and caused all those women — all of them distressed with tears — to descend from their conveyances.
Auspicious and jewel-like women of gods, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, adorned with varied ornaments, blazing with their own radiance —
Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous in soul, seeing those women overcome with grief and knowing the mind of his brother, spoke these words:
"With such conduct as this — destructive of honour, purpose, and family — you act according to your own will, causing outrage to living beings.
Having violated the kinswomen and brought these beautiful women here, Kumbhīnasī has been abducted by Madhu, transgressing against you, O king.
Rāvaṇa then said: "I do not understand — what is this? Who is this one whom you have named as Madhu?"
Vibhīṣaṇa, deeply angered, spoke to his brother: "Hear — the fruit of this sinful act has now arrived.
The eldest brother of our maternal grandfather Sumālin, the night-wanderer known as Mālyavān, wise and aged —
— he was the eldest, the noble ancestor on our mother's and father's side; his daughter's daughter was named Kumbhīnasī.
That maiden born of fire is our mother's sister's child; she is thus by dharma a sister to us brothers.
She has been abducted by Madhu, that powerful Rākṣasa, O king, while your son was engaged in the sacrifice and I too was preoccupied within the waters.
Having slain the foremost Rākṣasas who were your trusted ministers, having violated her, he abducted her, O king — she who was under protection in your inner apartments.
"Having heard this, O great king, I endured — and he was not slain — because a maiden must inevitably be given by her givers to a husband. Let this be known and understood by you in respect of what has now come to pass."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then Daśagrīva, enraged, his eyes red, said: "Let my chariot be made ready at once, and let the warriors equip themselves.
My brother Kumbhakarṇa and the principal night-wanderers — let them mount their vehicles, armed with weapons of every kind.
Having slain that Madhu in battle today — Madhu who fears nothing before Rāvaṇa — I shall proceed to the world of Indra, eager for battle, surrounded by friends.
Then, having conquered the triple heaven and brought Purandara under my sway, I shall roam in contentment, glorified by sovereignty over the three worlds.
Four thousand Akṣauhiṇī armies of fierce Rākṣasas bearing weapons of every kind quickly marched out, eager for battle.
Indrajit led the army at the vanguard marshalling the soldiers; the valiant Rāvaṇa was in the middle; and Kumbhakarṇa brought up the rear.
Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous in soul, remained in Laṅkā practising dharma, while all those great and illustrious ones marched toward the city of Madhu.
The Rākṣasas all advanced on chariots, elephants, donkeys, camels, swift horses, and great serpents, making the sky unbroken with their masses.
Hundreds of Daityas who had made enmity with the gods, seeing Rāvaṇa setting out, followed behind him.
But having gone and entered the city of Madhu, the ten-faced one did not find Madhu there; he found only his sister.
Trembling, Kumbhīnasī, the sister of that king of Rākṣasas, bowed with folded hands and cast herself at his feet with her head.
Rāvaṇa, foremost of Rākṣasas, raised her up saying "Fear not", and added: "What shall I do for you?"
She said: "If you are pleased with me, O king of great strength, O bestower of honour, then do not slay my husband here today.
Be true to your word, O lord of kings — regard me as I beseech you; for you yourself said with your own lips, O mighty-armed one, 'Fear not.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāvaṇa then spoke boldly to his sister standing there: "Where is your husband? Let him be brought before me at once."
"I shall go with him to the world of the gods for conquest. Out of compassion and affection for you, I have turned back from slaying Madhu."
Thus addressed, she, the Rākṣasī, woke the sleeping night-wanderer and spoke these wise words as if with joy:
"My brother, the ten-necked night-wanderer, has arrived, desiring to conquer the world of the gods; he chooses you for his ally.
Therefore go together with your kinsmen to serve as his ally, O Rākṣasa — it is fitting to serve the purpose of one who is devoted and affectionate."
Hearing her words, Madhu said "So be it" and, approaching in due form, met the foremost of Rākṣasas.
He honoured Rāvaṇa, the lord of Rākṣasas, according to the rites of hospitality; the valiant ten-necked one, having received due honour in the dwelling of Madhu and having spent one night there, set out once more on his journey.
Then the lord of Rākṣasas, resplendent as Mahendra, reached Mount Kailāsa, the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, and encamped his army.
The valiant Daśagrīva, having arrived there with his army, chose a camp as the sun was setting.
When the pure moon rose, equal in splendour to a great mountain, he beheld in that place virtues and beauties illuminated by the moon's beams.
Divine groves of Karṇikāra trees and dense clusters of Kadamba, lotus-ponds in full bloom, and the waters of the Mandākinī —
— a sweet sound like the ringing of bells was heard — the mingled voices of throngs of Apsarasas singing in the abode of Dhanada.
Trees shaken by the wind poured showers of flowers, as if perfuming that mountain with the fragrance of honey and spring blossoms.
The pleasant breeze blew, carrying an abundant fragrance mingled with the pollen of honey-flowers, kindling desire in Rāvaṇa.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
By the abundance of song and blossoms, by the coolness of the breeze, by the virtues of the mountain, by the advancing night, and by the rising of the moon —
— Rāvaṇa of very great prowess came under the sway of Kāma's arrows and, sighing again and again, gazed upon the moon.
At that moment there appeared Rambhā, the foremost of all Apsarasas, adorned with divine flowers, her face like the full moon —
— wearing fresh beauty-marks and garlands of blossoms from the festival of all six seasons, wrapped in a garment dark as a rain-bearing cloud —
— whose face was like the moon, whose beautiful brows were like bows, whose thighs were like the trunks of elephants, and whose hands were soft as young leaves — she was noticed by Rāvaṇa as she walked through the midst of the army.
The lord of Rākṣasas rose and, overpowered by the force of Kāma's arrow, seized her by the hand as she passed, and smiling, spoke to her:
"Where do you go, O lovely one? What fulfilment do you seek of your own will? Whose auspicious hour is this — he who will enjoy you?
Today, of the juice of your face — fragrant with lotus and blue water-lily, like the taste of nectar and immortal elixir — who today will drink his fill?
Your two breasts, round and auspicious as golden jars, set close together, O timid one — on whose chest will they bestow their touch?
Who today will mount your broad hips, like heaven in form, resembling a golden wheel and wreathed with a golden girdle?
What man is there superior to me — Śakra, Viṣṇu, or the Aśvins? It is not fitting, O timid one, that you pass me by to go to anyone.
Rest yourself, O broad-hipped one, on this auspicious stone floor. There is no sovereign in all three worlds who is my equal.
Therefore this Daśagrīva, who is the lord and master of the three worlds, with folded hands and bowed head, implores you — accept me."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed, Rambhā, trembling, spoke with folded hands: "Be gracious. You ought not to speak thus — you are my elder and guardian.
I should be protected by you even from others; were I to suffer violation, I tell you in truth that by dharma I am your daughter-in-law.
Daśagrīva spoke to her as she stood looking downward at his feet: "If you are the wife of my son, then you would be my daughter-in-law.
Rambhā replied to Rāvaṇa: "Truly so — by dharma I am the wife of your son, O foremost of Rākṣasas.
He is a son more dear than life to your brother Vaiśravaṇa — he who is renowned in all three worlds as Nalakūbara.
He who is a Brāhmaṇa by virtue of dharma, a Kṣatriya by virtue of valour, who is like fire in wrath and like the earth in patience —
— of him, the son of the world-guardian, I have made a tryst; for him alone all this adornment of mine has been made.
His love and no other's rests upon me — by that truth, O king, O subduer of enemies, you ought to release me.
He, the righteous-souled one, is now waiting in longing for me — therefore you ought not to create an obstacle here for your son's beloved. Release me."
"Follow the path trodden by the virtuous, O foremost of Rākṣasas; you are to be honoured by me, and I am to be cherished by you."
Though Rambhā spoke these words full of dharma and reason, the powerful Rākṣasa, scorning them, and overcome by the infatuation of lust, seized her by force and proceeded to violate her.
Rambhā, thus freed, her garlands and ornaments fallen away, was thrown into confusion like a river disturbed by a bull elephant at play.
Trembling, filled with shame and fear, she came to Nalakūbara with joined hands and fell at his feet.
Seeing her in that condition, the great-souled Nalakūbara said: "What is this, dear one? Why have you fallen at my feet?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
She, sighing and trembling, her hands joined, proceeded to tell him everything exactly as it had happened.
"This Daśagrīva, O god, has come intending to go to heaven; the night here is being passed with the help of his army.
As I was coming toward you, I was seen by him, O subduer of enemies; that Rākṣasa seized me and asked me 'Whose are you?'
I told him the whole truth, but his mind overwhelmed by the delusion of desire did not heed those words of mine.
Though I implored him saying 'I am your daughter-in-law, O lord,' he cast all that aside and violated me by force.
Thus you should forgive this transgression against me, O bestower of honour; for the strength of a woman is in no way equal to that of a man, O gentle one."
Hearing this, the son of Vaiśravaṇa became deeply enraged; having heard of that great outrage, he fell into meditation.
Understanding that deed fully, the son of Vaiśravaṇa, his eyes red with wrath after a moment, took water in his hand.
Taking that divine water and touching it in the prescribed manner, he then pronounced a dreadful curse upon the lord of Rākṣasas:
"Because he has violated you, dear one, by force when you were unwilling, therefore he shall never approach another young woman who is unwilling.
When, overcome by desire, he shall violate a woman who is unwilling, his head shall then split into seven pieces."
When that curse blazing like a lit fire was pronounced, the divine kettledrums resounded and a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
All the gods with Prajāpati at their head rejoiced greatly, knowing the entire course of the worlds and the death of that Rākṣasa.
Hearing that hair-raising curse, Daśagrīva no longer delighted in the thought of sexual union with women who were unwilling.
Having crossed Kailāsa, the ten-necked night-wanderer of great splendour advanced with his Rākṣasas and reached the world of Indra.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
As his Rākṣasa army advanced on all sides toward the world of the gods, a sound arose like the crashing of the ocean at dissolution.
Hearing that Rāvaṇa had arrived, Indra rose from his seat and addressed all the gods who had assembled there:
"Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvas, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts — equip yourselves for battle against the wicked Rāvaṇa."
Thus addressed by Śakra, the gods, equal to Śakra in battle, great-souled, filled with eagerness for the fight, armed themselves.
But Mahendra, distressed and frightened before Rāvaṇa, came to Viṣṇu and spoke these words:
"O Viṣṇu of great prowess and valour, what shall we do? That Rākṣasa is powerful and advances intent on battle.
He is powerful by virtue of boons granted — not for any other reason. And the word of Prajāpati must indeed be honoured, O god.
Therefore, as Namuci, Vṛtra, Bali, Naraka, and Śambara were burnt by relying on your intent, so act now.
For in calamities, O god of great strength, the gods have no other recourse or refuge apart from you, O Puruṣottama.
You are Nārāyaṇa the glorious, Padmanābha the eternal; it was by you that I was established in the eternal kingship of the gods.
Therefore tell me in truth yourself, O god of gods — do you, aided by your sword and discus, fight the enemy in battle?"
Thus addressed by Śakra, the lord god Nārāyaṇa replied: "No fear need be entertained by you. Hear my words.
This miscreant cannot be slain in battle by gods or Dānavas, being unconquerable by virtue of the boons he has received.
Yet this Rākṣasa of excessive strength, aided by his son, will in any case accomplish great deeds — this is seen by natural fate.
As for what you say to me — 'Will you fight in battle?' — I shall not fight that Rāvaṇa, the lord of Rākṣasas.
Viṣṇu does not turn back without slaying the enemy; yet today this wish is difficult to fulfil while the Rākṣasa possesses his boon.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
I promise you, O Devendra, O Śatakratu — I alone will be the cause of the death of this Rākṣasa.
I will slay Rāvaṇa together with his sons in battle and satisfy the gods, knowing the appointed time has arrived."
In that interval, at the close of night, a mighty roar was heard on all sides from the army of Rāvaṇa as it engaged in battle.
Then a battle broke out between the gods and the Rākṣasas — dreadful, with a tumultuous uproar and weapons of every kind.
Meanwhile the valiant, fearsome-looking Rākṣasa ministers rushed forward for battle at Rāvaṇa's command.
Mārīca, Prahasta, Mahāpārśva, Mahodara, Akampana, Nikumbha, Śuka, and Sāraṇa —
— Saṃhrādi, Dhūmaketu, Mahādaṃṣṭra, Mahāmukha, Jambumālī, Mahāmālī, and the Rākṣasa Virūpākṣa —
— surrounded by all these warriors of great valour, Sumālī, the noble ancestor of Rāvaṇa, the foremost Rākṣasa, entered the army.
He, enraged, together with those night-wanderers, scattered all the hosts of gods with sharp weapons of every kind.
At that moment the valiant eighth of the Vasus, known as Sāvitra, entered the great battle.
Then a battle broke out between the gods and the Rākṣasas — those Rākṣasas of renown, never retreating in combat.
Then those valiant Rākṣasas struck down the gods standing in battle by hundreds of thousands with dreadful weapons of every kind.
But the gods in turn dispatched the fearsome, mighty Rākṣasas to the abode of Yama in battle with their own valour and various weapons.
At that moment the valiant Rākṣasa named Sumālī, enraged, advanced upon the battlefield with weapons of every kind.
Enraged, he scattered the entire force of the gods with sharp weapons of every kind, as the wind scatters rain-clouds.
Afflicted by great showers of arrows, by dreadful spears and javelins, all the gods could not stand firm, however resolute.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, as the thirty gods were being routed by Sumālī, the eighth of the Vasus, the god Sāvitra, stood his ground.
Covered by his own troops, the great-souled one checked by his valour the night-wanderer who was striking in battle.
Between those two warriors, each of great valour — Sumālī and the Vasu — who never retreated in combat, a most dreadful battle took place in the world.
Then the great-souled Vasu brought down in an instant that great serpent-chariot of Sumālī with his mighty arrows.
Having destroyed his chariot in battle with hundreds of sharp arrows, the Vasu seized a mace in his hand for the purpose of slaying him.
Sāvitra quickly seized that blazing, auspicious mace resembling the staff of Death and brought it down upon Sumālī's head.
As it fell upon his head blazing like a meteor, it shone like a great thunderbolt hurled by the thousand-eyed Indra upon a mountain.
Neither his bones nor his body nor his flesh could be seen thereafter — struck down in that battle, he was reduced to ashes by the mace.
Seeing him slain in battle, all those Rākṣasas fled on all sides together, wailing with a great cry.
Seeing Sumālin slain and reduced to ashes by the divine weapon, and beholding his own army scattered and tormented by arrows,
then that mighty and wrathful son of Rāvaṇa, Meghanāda, turned all the rākṣasas back and took his stand in battle.
That great chariot-warrior charged against that army in a fire-coloured, wish-swift chariot, blazing like a fire consuming forests.
As he entered bearing all manner of weapons, the gods fled in every direction at the mere sight of him.
None remained to face him in battle as he came thirsting to fight; seeing all of them frightened and reeling, Indra spoke.
"Do not be afraid, do not flee — turn back to the battle. My own son goes forth to fight against this unvanquished one."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the divine son of Indra, renowned as Jayanta, advanced toward the battle in a chariot of wondrous make.
Then all the thirty gods surrounded the son of Śacī and drew up in array to engage the son of Rāvaṇa in battle.
A great battle ensued, fitting between gods and rākṣasas, centred on the son of Mahendra and the son of the rākṣasa lord.
Then the rākṣasa's son rained gold-adorned arrows upon Gomukha, the son of Mātali, who was serving as charioteer.
But Jayanta, son of Śacī, equally enraged, pierced his charioteer and Rāvaṇi himself on the battlefield.
Then that great-spirited rākṣasa Rāvaṇi, enraged and eyes blazing wide, overwhelmed Indra's son with a torrent of arrows.
Then Rāvaṇi seized mighty, potent weapons — śataghnīs, lances, javelins, maces, swords, axes — and hurled enormous mountain peaks as well.
Then the worlds were overwhelmed with anguish and a great darkness arose as Rāvaṇa's son struck down his foes.
Then the host of gods, distressed in many ways, ran hither and thither surrounding Śacī's son.
They could not distinguish one another — neither foe from god — as all was confusion everywhere, with all running about on every side.
Meanwhile a mighty Daitya named Pulomā, powerful and heroic, seized him and carried Śacī's son away from battle.
Taking his grandson, he entered the great ocean — he was the maternal grandfather Āryaka, from whose line came Paulomī, the Śacī.
Seeing the exceedingly terrible disappearance of Jayanta, the gods, afflicted and joyless, fled in all directions.
Rāvaṇi, greatly elated and surrounded by his own forces, charged at those gods and let out a tremendous roar.
Seeing his son's disappearance and Rāvaṇa's valour, the lord of gods said to Mātali: "Bring the chariot here."
That divine, most formidable great chariot, swift as thought, was at the ready, brought forward by Mātali.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then clouds with lightning and great thunder moved before that chariot, fickle as the wind, resounding as they went.
Various instruments were played, hymns of praise were intoned with concentration, and hosts of apsarases danced as Vāsava set forth to battle.
Attended by Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Sādhyas, and the Marud hosts bearing manifold weapons, the lord of the thirty gods issued forth.
As Indra went forth, a harsh wind blew, the sun grew dim, and great meteors fell.
Meanwhile the heroic and splendid Daśagrīva, full of power, mounted the divine chariot fashioned by Viśvakarmā.
It was entwined with great-bodied serpents whose very breath made the battle seem ablaze, causing the hair to stand on end.
That divine chariot, surrounded by heroic Daityas and night-wanderers, faced the battlefield and advanced toward Mahendra.
Restraining his son, Rāvaṇa himself took position; and Rāvaṇi, withdrawing from battle, sat down to rest.
Then began the battle of gods against rākṣasas, a terrible downpour of weapons in combat, like clouds in the monsoon.
But Kumbhakarṇa, that evil-souled one, wielding all manner of weapons, was not recognized in battle as he fought with any and all.
With teeth, arms, feet, lances, javelins, and arrows, enraged against anyone at all, he battered the gods.
Then that night-roamer fought together with the great and glorious Rudras and Ādityas, and was cut without cease by their weapons in the battle.
Then that entire rākṣasa army was routed in battle by the thirty gods together with the Marud troops, with sharp and manifold weapons.
Some, struck down by weapons, writhed on the ground; others, still clinging to their mounts, stood in battle.
Chariots, elephants, donkeys, camels, serpents, horses, dolphins, boars, and those with piśāca-faces —
— some night-wanderers, struck through by the gods' weapons, died clinging to them with their arms, raised up stiffly.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That tumult of battle among those rākṣasas slain and fallen senseless on the earth appeared like a vivid painting.
A river flowing at the van of battle ran thick with blood, filled with herons and vultures, bearing away the weapons.
Meanwhile the wrathful and mighty Daśagrīva, beholding his entire army cast down by the gods,
plunging swiftly into that swelling ocean of armies, slaying the thirty gods in battle, advanced directly against Indra.
Then Indra drew his great bow with an immense twang, whose resounding vibration made the ten directions ring.
Drawing that great bow fully, Indra rained down upon Rāvaṇa's head arrows blazing with the brilliance of fire and sun.
And likewise the long-armed Daśagrīva, firmly planted, overwhelmed Indra with torrents of arrows released from his bow.
As the two of them fought, raining arrows on every side, nothing could be distinguished — all was enveloped in darkness.
Then, in that darkness that arose, the rākṣasas and gods together fought, intoxicated with power, slaughtering one another.
Then the divine army left a tenth of the rākṣasa host standing in the battle; the remainder was sent to Yama's realm.
Bound in that darkness, all those gods and rākṣasas could not recognise one another as they fought each other.
Indra, Rāvaṇa, and the immensely powerful Rāvaṇi — these three alone did not fall into confusion, even enveloped in the net of darkness.
Seeing his entire army slain in battle, Rāvaṇa was seized with intense rage and let out a great roar.
In his rage, that formidable one spoke to his charioteer seated in the car: "Drive me to the very end, straight through the enemy's army."
"Today by my own valour in battle I shall destroy from the sky all these thirty gods with great, manifold weapons."
"I will slay Indra, Varuṇa, Dhana-da, and Yama; having swiftly destroyed the thirty gods, I myself shall stand above."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"There is no room for despondency — drive my chariot quickly. I say it to you twice: drive me to the very end today."
"This region where we now stand is the Nandana grove; drive me today to where Mount Udaya lies."
Hearing those words, the charioteer directed the mind-swift horses and drove right through the midst of the enemies.
Understanding his resolve, Indra, lord of the gods, then standing in his chariot, spoke these words to the gods arrayed in battle.
"Gods, hear my words — this is what pleases me: let the rākṣasa Daśagrīva be subdued while still alive."
"For this one of surpassing strength will move through the army with the speed of the wind in his chariot, like a swelling ocean at full tide."
"This one cannot be slain today, being utterly fearless by boon of a blessing; therefore we shall seize the rākṣasa — be alert in combat."
"Just as I enjoy the three worlds by subduing Bali, so it pleases me to subdue this wicked one."
Then Indra, of great splendour, abandoning Rāvaṇa, took position elsewhere and fought on, destroying rākṣasas in battle.
Daśagrīva entered from the north, advancing without turning back; Indra of a hundred sacrifices entered from the southern flank.
Then the lord of rākṣasas, having advanced a hundred yojanas, overwhelmed the entire divine army with torrents of arrows.
Then Indra, observing his own army penetrated, unperturbed, turned it back, surrounding the ten-faced one.
Meanwhile a cry went up from the Dānava and rākṣasa troops: "Alas, we are slain!" — seeing Rāvaṇa encircled by Indra.
Then Rāvaṇi, swooning with rage, mounted his chariot and, most furiously angry, entered that terrible army.
Having entered and employing the māyā formerly bestowed by Gopati, invisible to all beings, he rained missiles upon that army.
Then he abandoned the gods and rushed swiftly against Indra alone; and Mahendra of great splendour could not see the enemy's son.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That swift-handed one struck Mātali and the horses with excellent arrows and overwhelmed Mahendra with a flood of shafts.
Then Indra, abandoning the chariot and releasing Mātali, mounted Airāvata and sought out Rāvaṇi.
But that rākṣasa, by the power of māyā, was not visible in battle, pouring streams of arrows upon Mahendra, whose energy is unbounded.
When Rāvaṇi judged Indra to be exhausted, he bound him by māyā and brought him right to his own army.
Seeing Mahendra thus forcibly seized in battle and carried off by māyā, all the immortals cried out: "What is this?" — for the wielder of māyā by whom he was being led could not be seen.
Meanwhile all the hosts of gods, utterly enraged, rushed upon Rāvaṇa with showers of weapons.
But Rāvaṇa, encountering the Vasus, Ādityas, and Marud hosts, could neither stand in battle nor fight, tormented by their weapons.
Seeing his father exhausted, his body broken by blows, Rāvaṇi, standing invisible in battle, spoke these words to him:
"Come, father, let us go — the work of battle is done. Know that you have conquered; be at ease, be free from distress."
"For I have seized Indra, the master of the divine army and of the three worlds; the gods have been broken in spirit."
"Enjoy the three worlds at your pleasure, having subdued the foe by might. Why exhaust yourself to no purpose? Your battle is fruitless now."
Hearing Rāvaṇi's words, Daśagrīva was composed in mind and withdrew from the work of battle against the divine army.
Then the lord, the master of night-roamers, free of battle's anguish and having won victory, departed joyfully for his palace; and meeting his own son, he spoke:
"By those feats of prowess worthy of supreme strength, the honour of my lineage has been exalted; for you, whose valour rivals the immortals', have defeated the lord of the thirty gods and the thirty gods themselves."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Bring Vāsava here quickly — go to the city, surrounded by your army; I too shall follow swiftly behind you with my ministers as you proceed."
Then that rākṣasa Rāvaṇi, surrounded by his army and bearing the lord of the thirty gods, went to his own abode; joyful in mind, he dismissed the rākṣasas.
When mighty Mahendra had been conquered by Rāvaṇa's son, the gods, placing Prajāpati at their head, went to Laṅkā.
Approaching Rāvaṇa, surrounded by his sons and brothers, Prajāpati stood in the sky and spoke with words of conciliation:
"My dear Rāvaṇa, I am pleased by your son's conduct in battle. How great is his valour and nobility — equal to you, perhaps exceeding you."
"For all three worlds have been conquered by your energy; the vow has borne fruit; I am pleased by my own son indeed."
"And this immensely powerful son of yours, Rāvaṇa's Rāvaṇi — he shall be renowned throughout the world as Indrajit, the Conqueror of Indra."
"This rākṣasa shall be mighty, a conqueror of enemies; relying on him, O king, you have brought the thirty gods under your dominion."
"Therefore let Mahendra, the chastiser of Pāka, be released, O mighty-armed one. And what will the heaven-dwellers give for his release?"
Then great-spirited Indrajit, victorious in battle, spoke: "O god, I choose immortality in exchange for his release."
The lotus-born god then said to Rāvaṇi: "Complete immortality does not exist for any living being on earth."
Then Indrajit spoke to the lotus-born god present there: "Hear what attainment shall be mine in exchange for releasing the lord of a hundred sacrifices."
"What I desire, O god, is that whenever I descend into battle seeking to conquer enemies, I may first duly propitiate Agni with oblations;"
"and if I should enter battle, O god, with the japa-oblation to Vibhāvasu incomplete, then let that be the occasion of my destruction."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For every man wins immortality through austerity; but I have established this immortality through valour."
"So be it," said the god Prajāpati to him; and Indra was released by Indrajit, and the gods departed to the heavens.
Meanwhile Indra, dejected, his garments and garlands dishevelled, fell deep into meditation, his mind entirely absorbed in thoughts of Rāma.
Seeing him in this state, the god Prajāpati said: "O Indra of a hundred sacrifices, why do you grieve? Recall the wrong you committed."
"O lord of immortals, in the beginning I created many creatures — all of one colour, all speaking alike, all of one form in every respect."
"There was no distinction among them in appearance or in marks; thereupon I, with focused mind, reflected on those creatures."
"To create a distinction among them, I fashioned one woman, extracting whatever was the finest feature of each and every creature."
"Thus I fashioned the woman Ahalyā from beauties and virtues; and indeed it was I who gave her the name Ahalyā."
"Having fashioned that woman, O lord of gods, O bull among immortals, I then fell to wondering: whose shall she be?"
"But you, Indra, O lord, O Purandara, claimed that woman in your heart, thinking 'She shall be my wife' on account of your superior station."
"She was placed by me in trust with the great-souled Gautama, entrusted for many years; and she was eventually surrendered to him by me."
"Then, having recognised the steadfastness of that great sage and knowing his perfection in austerity, I bestowed her on him as his wife."
"That righteous great sage dwelt joyfully with her; when she was given to Gautama, the gods lost hope."
"But you, angry and ruled by lust, went to the hermitage of that sage and saw that woman then blazing like a flame of fire."
"She was violated by you, Indra, overcome with desire and consumed by passion; and you were then seen by that supreme sage in his hermitage."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then that one of supreme splendour, enraged, cursed you; by that curse, O lord of gods, you underwent a reversal in a tenth part of your body."
"'Because you have recklessly violated my wife, O Vāsava, therefore, O king, you shall fall into an enemy's hands in battle.'"
"'And this tendency you have set in motion here, O wicked-minded one, will without doubt spread among all human beings as well.'"
"'A great and most powerful adharma will arise there; half of that shall fall upon whoever commits it, and half upon you.'"
"'And you shall have no stable station, O Purandara, by reason of this bond of adharma which you have set in motion here.'"
"'And whoever becomes a supreme Indra shall not remain permanent in that station.' So saying, he released this curse upon you at that time."
"And rebuking his wife severely, that one of immense austerity said: 'O undisciplined woman, vanish from the vicinity of my hermitage!'"
"'Since you, endowed with beauty and youth, were not constant, therefore in the world you shall not be the only beautiful woman.'"
"'And all creatures shall acquire that beauty — so exceedingly rare — which was the occasion of this transgression of yours.'"
"From that time on creatures were abundantly endowed with beauty; all this came about through the release of that sage's curse."
"Remember, O mighty-armed Vāsava, the wrong that you committed — by that, not by anything else, you have fallen into an enemy's grasp."
"Perform the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice quickly, with focused mind; purified by that sacrifice, you will then ascend to the heavens."
"And your son, O lord of gods, has not perished in the great battle; he was carried away and is safely present with Āryaka in the great ocean."
Hearing this, Mahendra performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and once again ascended to the heavens, ruling over the gods.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This, O Rāma, is the might of Indrajit that I have recounted to you; by him the lord of gods himself was conquered — what then of other living beings?"
Then Rāma of great splendor, filled with wonder once again, bowed and spoke these words to Agastya, the foremost of sages.
"Revered one, O best of twice-born men, were the worlds then empty of any realm where Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas, had not come to wreak his ravages?"
"Or were those rulers of the earth lacking in valour? Were many kings excluded by superior weapons and overcome in battle?"
Having heard the words of Rāghava, the venerable sage Agastya smiled and spoke to Rāma as the Grandfather Brahmā himself might address the Lord.
"Thus oppressing kings in this fashion, O bull among kings, O lord of the earth, Rāvaṇa, O Rāma, ranged across the earth.
Then he arrived at a city named Māhiṣmatī, radiant as the city of heaven, where the supreme presence of Vasuretās dwelt.
A king equal in might to Vasuretās himself ruled there — Arjuna by name — in whose quiver fire ever lay sleeping.
On that very day the mighty Arjuna, lord of the Haihayas, had gone to sport on the Narmadā river, accompanied by his wives, like a great lord.
Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, questioned his ministers: "Where is your king Arjuna today? You ought to tell me quickly."
"I am Rāvaṇa, come here desiring battle with that best of men. You must without delay inform him of my arrival."
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, those wise ministers replied to the lord of the rākṣasas that the king was not present.
Hearing from the citizens that Arjuna had gone elsewhere, the son of Viśravā turned away and came to the Vindhya mountain, which resembles the Himālaya.
Rāvaṇa beheld the Vindhya mountain — as if filling the sky, as if churning the earth, as if scratching the heavens with its peaks.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Adorned with a thousand peaks, its caverns haunted by lions, it seemed to burst into loud laughter as its cascading cold waterfalls fell.
Where gods, dānavas, gandharvas, hosts of apsarases, kiṃnaras, and their women played together, it towered to a great height, become like heaven itself.
With rivers flowing freely through it, its waters seeming motionless like something at rest, with quivering-tongued lightning-flashes, it appeared to be vomiting forth its standing waters.
Gazing at the Vindhya mountain — flaring with meteors, riddled with caverns, resembling the Himālaya — Rāvaṇa then proceeded to the Narmadā.
The holy Narmadā, flowing westward to the ocean, her waters stirred by rolling stones — her pools churned by buffaloes, spotted deer, lions, tigers, bears, and the finest elephants, all parched and thirsting under the heat.
Crowded with cakravāka birds and kāraṇḍava ducks, with swans and water-fowl, with sārasa cranes ever intoxicated with joy, and with the cries of kokila birds.
Adorned with blossoming trees as her crown, her bosom formed by pairs of cakravāka birds, her hips the broad sandbanks, her girdle the line of swans.
Her body anointed with pollen of flowers, her garment the pure foam of her waters, pleasant to touch when wading into her current, her eyes the beautiful blossoming blue lotuses.
Quickly descending from the Puṣpaka chariot, the ten-headed one plunged into the Narmadā, best of rivers, as one plunges into a cherished and beautiful woman.
That foremost of rākṣasas, the lord of the rākṣasas, sat down on her beautiful sandbank adorned with many kinds of flowers, together with his ministers, and obtained the joy that comes from beholding the Narmadā.
Then with a playful laugh, Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, spoke there to his ministers Mārīca, Śuka, and Sāraṇa.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The sun, with his thousand rays, having made the world as if golden, fierce in his heat, has taken his stand at the middle of the sky. Knowing that I am seated here, the day-maker now moves toward the moon."
"The wind that blows from the Narmadā is cool, fragrant, and dispels fatigue — it blows thus steadily out of fear of me."
"And this best of rivers, the Narmadā who augments delight, her waves holding fish and birds within them, stands like a woman filled with fear."
"Therefore you, wounded by the weapons of kings equal to Indra in battle, anointed with blood as if with sandal paste —"
"— you all shall plunge into the Narmadā, giver of happiness to men, like great bull-elephants with lotus-like faces, drunk with excitement, entering the Gaṅgā."
"Having bathed in this great river, you shall be released from sin."
"I too shall here, on this sandbank radiant as the autumn moon, slowly offer a floral offering to the lord of Umā."
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, Mārīca, Śuka, Sāraṇa, Mahodara, and Dhūmrākṣa plunged into the Narmadā.
The river Narmadā was churned by those elephant-like lords among the rākṣasas, just as the Gaṅgā is churned by great elephants named Vāmana, Añjana, Padma, and others.
Then those rākṣasas, having bathed in the excellent waters of the Narmadā and emerged therefrom, gathered flowers for Rāvaṇa's offering.
On the beautiful sandbank of the Narmadā, radiant as a white cloud, the lords of the rākṣasas piled up in a moment a mountain of flowers.
Even as the flowers were being brought, Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, descended into the river to bathe, like the elephant Añjana descending into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites and having muttered the most excellent of prayers, Rāvaṇa emerged from those waters of the Narmadā.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seven rākṣasas followed Rāvaṇa as he proceeded with joined palms. Wherever Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, went, a liṅga made of gold was carried thither.
Rāvaṇa installed that liṅga in the midst of a sand altar and worshipped it with fragrant substances and with flowers that smelled like nectar.
Then, having worshipped Hara the supreme — remover of the distress of the good, the granter of boons, adorned with the rays of the moon — that night-wanderer sang aloud and danced, stretching his arms wide.
Not far from that spot on the Narmadā sandbank where Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, was making his floral offering —
— Arjuna, the foremost among the victorious, lord and master of Māhiṣmatī, was at play with his women in the waters of the Narmadā.
King Arjuna, standing in the midst of those women, shone forth like a bull elephant standing in the midst of a thousand she-elephants.
Wishing to test the supreme strength of his thousand arms, Arjuna at that time dammed the current of the Narmadā with those arms.
The pure water, meeting the dam of Kārtavīrya's arms, ran backward in reverse current, eroding the banks.
Filled with fish, crocodiles, and tortoises, scattered with flowers and kuśa grass, that surge of the Narmadā's waters appeared like the onset of the rainy season.
That surge of the water, as if dispatched by Kārtavīrya, swept away entirely all of Rāvaṇa's floral offering.
Rāvaṇa, abandoning the rite half-completed, then looked at the Narmadā as one looks at a beloved woman who has turned contrary.
Seeing from the west the surge of the water growing, resembling the roaring of the ocean, then entering the eastern direction —
— Rāvaṇa then saw the river with her birds no longer startled, abiding in her natural supreme state, appearing like a woman without perturbation.
The ten-faced one, snapping his fingers on his right hand with a loud sound, dispatched Śuka and Sāraṇa to discover the source of the current.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Those two brothers Śuka and Sāraṇa, directed by Rāvaṇa, those two heroes who could travel through the sky, set out facing westward.
Having traveled only half a yojana, those two night-wanderers saw a man at play in the water together with his women.
He was like a great sāla tree in form, his hair disheveled by the water, his eyes red at the corners from intoxication, his radiance like that of the god of love.
He was blocking the river with his thousand arms, that crusher of enemies, like a mountain blocking the earth with a thousand feet.
He was surrounded by a thousand young and beautiful women, like a bull elephant surrounded by a thousand she-elephants in full rut.
Having seen that most wondrous being, the two rākṣasas Śuka and Sāraṇa turned back, approached Rāvaṇa, and spoke to him.
"Who is that being, O lord of the rākṣasas, resembling a great sāla tree, who, having dammed the Narmadā completely, makes the women play?"
"The river, her waters blocked by those thousand arms, repeatedly sends forth surges resembling the roaring of the ocean."
Hearing those two Śuka and Sāraṇa speaking thus, Rāvaṇa exclaimed "It is Arjuna!" and rose up, eager for battle.
As that lord of the rākṣasas set out facing toward Arjuna, a single thunderous roar with a crimson hue was sent forth by the clouds.
Surrounded by Mahodara, Mahāpārśva, Dhūmrākṣa, Śuka, and Sāraṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas came to where that Arjuna was.
In no great length of time that mighty rākṣasa, dark as the elephant Añjana, arrived at that terrible pool of the Narmadā.
There the king of the rākṣasas saw Arjuna, that lord of men, surrounded by women just as a bull elephant is surrounded by she-elephants in rut.
The lord of the rākṣasas, his eyes red with rage, swollen with pride in his strength, spoke these words to the ministers of Arjuna in a deep voice.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Ministers, quickly inform the king of the Haihayas that one named Rāvaṇa has arrived seeking battle."
Hearing Rāvaṇa's words, the ministers of Arjuna rose up armed and spoke these words to Rāvaṇa.
"Well and good, well and good, O Rāvaṇa, your understanding of the right time for battle! You who wish to fight our king when he is intoxicated and surrounded by women — like a tiger wishing to fight a maddened elephant in the midst of she-elephants."
"Forgive us today, O ten-necked one, let the night be spent by you here; if you have determination for battle, then tomorrow, good sir, fight Arjuna in the field."
"Or if you are seized with urgent thirst for battle, then slay us first, and after that you shall engage Arjuna in combat."
Then those ministers of the king were struck down in battle by the ministers of Rāvaṇa, and were devoured by the famished ones.
Then a tumultuous uproar arose along the bank of the Narmadā from the retinue of Arjuna and the ministers of Rāvaṇa.
With arrows, javelin-spears, lances, and thunderbolt-like weapons along with plowshare-clubs, they charged from all sides, afflicting all of Rāvaṇa's host.
The onslaught of the warriors of the Haihaya lord was terrifyingly fierce, like the sound of an ocean filled with fish, crocodiles, and great sea-monsters.
But the ministers of Rāvaṇa — Prahasta, Śuka, and Sāraṇa — blazing with the energy of fire, enraged, burned through the army of Kārtavīrya.
The deed of Rāvaṇa with his ministers was reported to Arjuna, who was still at play, by the men guarding the gates.
Telling the women "Do not be afraid," Arjuna then emerged from those waters, like the elephant Añjana emerging from the waters of the Gaṅgā.
His eyes inflamed by anger, Arjuna then blazed up like fire, most terrifying, like the fire at the end of an age.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Swiftly taking up his mace adorned with excellent golden armlets, he rushed upon the rākṣasas as the sun rushes upon darkness.
Lifting high the great mace for a sweeping arm-blow, and assuming the speed of Garuḍa, Arjuna swooped down.
Blocking his path as the Vindhya mountain blocks the path of the sun, Prahasta stood immovable as the Vindhya itself, armed with his club.
Then Prahasta, swollen with pride and enraged, hurling his terrible iron-bound club, roared like a thundercloud.
At the tip of that club, as it left Prahasta's hand, fire appeared like a garland of aśoka blossoms, as if burning everything.
Kārtavīrya Arjuna, of the valour of an elephant and armed with his mace, skillfully dodged that charging club.
Then the lord of the Haihayas charged at Prahasta, whirling his heavy mace, as tall as five hundred arms.
Struck by it with extreme force, Prahasta fell where he stood, like a mountain struck by Indra's thunderbolt.
Seeing Prahasta fallen, Mārīca, Śuka, Sāraṇa, Mahodara, and Dhūmrākṣa withdrew from the battlefield.
With his ministers retreated and Prahasta felled, Rāvaṇa quickly rushed upon Arjuna, that best of kings.
The dreadful battle between the thousand-armed and the twenty-armed, between the king and the rākṣasa, began there — hair-raising to witness.
Like two agitated oceans, like two mountains with quaking roots, like two suns blazing with energy, like two fires burning everything.
Like two elephants maddened by pride, like two bulls fighting over a cow in heat, like two thunderclouds roaring, like two lions supremely powerful.
Like two wrathful Rudras at the time of dissolution, the rākṣasa and Arjuna struck each other again and again fiercely with their maces.
As mountains endure the terrible blows of Indra's thunderbolt, so those two, man and rākṣasa, endured the blows of each other's maces.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
As an echo arises from thunderclaps among the clouds, so all directions resounded with the fall of their maces.
The mace of Arjuna, falling upon the enemy's chest, made the sky shine like gold, like the lightning of a storm-cloud.
Likewise the mace wielded by Rāvaṇa, falling again and again upon Arjuna's chest, shone like a blazing meteor upon a great mountain.
Neither Arjuna grew weary nor the lord of the rākṣasa hosts; their battle was equal, as the battle of Bali and Indra once was.
Like two great bulls striking each other with their horns, like two elephants striking each other with the tips of their tusks, those foremost of man and rākṣasa struck each other mutually.
Then by the enraged Arjuna, with all his might, the mace was released in the great battle against the space between Rāvaṇa's breasts.
On Rāvaṇa's chest, protected by the boon he had received, that mace broke in two as it fell to the ground, like a weak army.
Rāvaṇa, struck by the mace hurled by Arjuna, stumbled back the distance of a bowshot and sat down, groaning.
Perceiving the ten-necked one to be overcome, Arjuna suddenly seized him as Garuḍa seizes a serpent.
That powerful king, seizing the ten-faced one with force by his thousand arms, bound him, as Nārāyaṇa bound Bali.
As the ten-necked one was being bound, siddhas, cāraṇas, and gods, exclaiming "Well done!", showered flowers upon Arjuna's head.
The Haihaya king, like a tiger carrying off a deer, like the lord of lions carrying an elephant, roared repeatedly with joy like a thundercloud.
But Prahasta, having recovered, seeing the ten-faced one bound, enraged, charged at the king together with those rākṣasas.
The onslaught of those night-wanderers as they charged was like the wondrous swelling of the oceans when summer's heat has passed.
Shouting "Release him! Release him!" and repeatedly "Stand fast! Stand fast!", they hurled clubs and lances at Arjuna.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Even before those weapons reached him, Arjuna, unagitated, that destroyer of enemies, swiftly caught all the weapons of those foes of the immortals.
Then with those very irresistible and superior weapons, he shattered and scattered the rākṣasas as the wind scatters clouds.
Having terrified the rākṣasas, Kārtavīrya Arjuna then, taking Rāvaṇa captive, entered his city surrounded by his friends.
Showered with heaps of flowers and unhusked grain by the twice-born and the citizens, Arjuna, resembling Puruhūta — like thousand-eyed Indra — then entered that city, having indeed subdued Bali.
The sage Pulastya heard of the capture of Rāvaṇa — a capture like the seizing of the wind — as it was being narrated by the gods in heaven.
Then, moved by affection for his son's son and of great steadfastness, the great sage came to see the lord of Māhiṣmatī.
That twice-born one, taking the path of the wind, moving with a speed equal to the wind, driven by the anguish of his mind, arrived at the city of Māhiṣmatī.
