He entered that city resembling Amarāvatī, filled with joyful and prosperous people, as Brahmā might enter Indra's Amarāvatī.
Recognizing him as he came on foot, dazzling to look upon like the sun at its rising, they announced him to Arjuna.
Hearing that word "Pulastya," the lord of the Haihayas raised his joined palms to his head and went forward to meet that best of twice-born men.
His purohita, taking the ceremonial water-offering and the honey-mixture, proceeded in front of the king, as Bṛhaspati before Indra.
Then seeing that sage arriving like the rising sun, Arjuna, beholding his coming, bowed as Indra bows before the Lord.
Causing to be offered to him the honey-mixture, water for the feet, and the arghya gift, that lord of kings spoke to Pulastya with a voice choked with joy.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Today Māhiṣmatī has been made equal to Amarāvatī; today am I indeed blessed, O lord among twice-born, O Indra among sages, because I behold what is so hard to behold."
"Today is my well-being assured, O divine one; today is my lineage exalted — for I bow to those feet of yours which the hosts of gods themselves bow before."
"This kingdom, these sons, these wives, we ourselves — O Brahman, what shall we do? What is to be done? Let your honor command us."
Having then auspiciously inquired of that king about his welfare in matters of dharma, sacred fires, and servants, Pulastya spoke to Arjuna, that king of the Haihayas.
"O king of kings, you of spotless lotus eyes, of a face resembling the full moon — unequalled is your strength, by which the ten-necked one has been conquered by you."
"He of whom the ocean and the wind stand motionless out of fear — that same grandson of mine, most exceedingly difficult to conquer, has today been bound by you."
"Therefore, my son, your fame and name have been made renowned by you — now being besought at my word, dear child, release the ten-faced one today."
Receiving the command of Pulastya without hesitation, that Indra among the lords of the earth, Arjuna, gladly released the lord of the rākṣasas.
Having released that enemy of the thirty gods, Arjuna honored him with divine ornaments, garlands, and garments, entered into a non-aggression friendship with him with fire as witness, bowed to that son of Brahmā, and went home.
The mighty lord of the rākṣasas too, having met with Pulastya, was dismissed by him with an embrace as his act of hospitality, Rāvaṇa feeling ashamed.
And Pulastya, that best of sages, son of the Grandfather Brahmā, having caused the ten-necked one to be freed, went to Brahmaloka.
Thus did Rāvaṇa, having been subjected to humiliation by Kārtavīrya, again obtain his release through the words of Pulastya.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Thus, O joy of the Raghu line, there are those more powerful than the powerful. One who desires his own welfare should never show contempt for another."
Then that king of the flesh-eaters, having obtained the friendship of the thousand-armed one, once again wrought slaughter among men and roamed the entire earth with pride.
Released by Arjuna, Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, roamed the whole earth thus humiliated, yet unbroken in spirit.
Whoever Rāvaṇa heard of — rākṣasa or human — who excelled in strength, him he would approach in arrogance and challenge to battle.
Then one day he went to Kiṣkindhā, the city governed by Vālin, and challenged to battle Vālin of the golden garland.
Then Tāra, the monkey minister, father of Tārā, that lord, spoke these words to Rāvaṇa who had come eager for battle.
"O lord of rākṣasas, Vālin has gone — he who would be your match in strength. No other monkey is capable of standing before you.
Rāvaṇa, he worships the twilight at all four oceans and will return in a moment. Wait but a moment.
"See these heaps of bones, white as conch shells — these, O king, belong to those who came seeking battle and were consumed by the power of the monkey-lord.
"Whatever nectar you have drunk, O Rāvaṇa the rākṣasa, once you encounter Vālin your life will end at that moment.
"Or if you are in haste to die, go to the southern ocean — you will see Vālin there, standing on the earth like the sun itself."
Rebuking Tāra, Rāvaṇa, that lord of rākṣasas, mounted Puṣpaka and flew to the southern ocean.
There Rāvaṇa saw Vālin, whose face glowed like the rising sun, resembling a mountain of gold, absorbed in twilight worship.
Rāvaṇa, dark as collyrium, descended from Puṣpaka and stealthily rushed forward to seize Vālin.
Vālin, who happened to open his eyes, also saw that Rāvaṇa, intent on evil, but did not grow alarmed.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
As a lion does not concern itself with a rabbit, or Garuḍa with a serpent, so Vālin gave no thought to Rāvaṇa of evil resolve.
"I will take this Rāvaṇa of wicked mind who seeks to seize me, tuck him under my arm, and travel the great oceans.
"They shall see my enemy seated in my lap, his garments slipping from his thighs, the ten-necked one dangling like a serpent in Garuḍa's grasp."
Having thus resolved, Vālin, muttering Vedic mantras under his breath, remained still as the king of mountains.
Both that monkey-king and the king of rākṣasas, each intent on seizing the other, proud of their strength, exerted themselves toward that deed.
Judging him close enough to grasp by hand, Vālin, even with his back turned, caught Rāvaṇa by the sound of his footstep, as a bird catches a serpent.
Seizing that lord of rākṣasas who had come to seize him, the monkey leapt skyward with speed, having tucked him under his arm.
Though Rāvaṇa was piercing him again and again with his nails, Vālin, oppressed by him, carried Rāvaṇa as the wind carries a rain-cloud.
Then those terrible rākṣasa ministers, seeing the ten-headed one being carried away and wishing to free him, came rushing and roaring.
Pursued by them, Vālin blazed in the midst of the sky — like the sun in the sky pursued by masses of clouds.
Those foremost rākṣasas, unable to overtake Vālin, exhausted by the force of his arms and legs, fell to the ground.
The mountain lords drew back from Vālin's path as he flew past.
The monkey-lord, of immense speed, outstripping flocks of birds, paid homage to the twilight in succession at all the oceans.
Honoured by sky-dwelling beings, the sky-ranging monkey Vālin reached the western ocean together with Rāvaṇa.
There the monkey worshipped the twilight, bathed, and recited his prayers; then he proceeded to the northern ocean, still bearing the ten-headed one.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having worshipped the twilight at the northern ocean, Vālin went, bearing the ten-headed one, to the great treasure of eastern waters.
There too, having observed the twilight worship, that lord of monkeys, son of Vāsava, turned toward Kiṣkindhā, grasping Rāvaṇa, and came back.
The monkey, having worshipped the twilight at all four oceans, weary from carrying Rāvaṇa, alighted in the forest of Kiṣkindhā.
Then that best of monkeys released Rāvaṇa from his arm and, laughing, asked Rāvaṇa: "Where do you come from?"
Seized by great amazement, looking about with exhausted eyes, the lord of rākṣasas spoke these words to that lord of monkeys:
"O lord of monkeys, radiant as great Indra, I am Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas. I came here eager for battle, and today I have indeed encountered you.
"Ah, what strength! Ah, what heroism! Ah, what composure you possess — by which, seizing me like an animal, you have carried me around the four oceans!
"O hero, O monkey, bearing me thus as if untiring and with such speed — what other hero could traverse thus?
"This speed belongs to only three beings, O leaping one: the mind, the wind, and Suparṇa — or you; of this there is no doubt.
"I, who have now seen your strength, O foremost of monkeys, desire a lasting and deeply affectionate friendship with you, before the sacred fire.
"Wives, sons, city, kingdom, pleasures, garments, food — all of this shall be undivided between us two, O lord of monkeys."
Then the two — monkey and rākṣasa — kindled a fire, attained brotherhood, and embraced one another.
Clasping each other's hands, those two — monkey and rākṣasa — joyfully entered Kiṣkindhā, like two lions entering a mountain cave.
Rāvaṇa dwelt there for a month, like Sugrīva, when his ministers arrived to fetch him — that low one who sought to destroy the three worlds.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Thus was this event of the past, O lord: Rāvaṇa was humbled by Vālin and then also made a brother in the presence of fire.
"The strength of Vālin, O Rāma, was matchless and supreme; yet even he was consumed by that fate, like a moth by fire."
Then Rāma questioned the sage who dwelt in the southern hall; standing with joined palms, endowed with humility, he spoke this meaningful speech:
"The strength of these two — Vālin and Rāvaṇa — was incomparable; yet my view is that neither of them was equal to Hanūmān in valour.
"Courage, dexterity, strength, steadiness, wisdom, mastery of policy, heroism, and power — all these have their home in Hanūmān.
"When the army of monkeys was despondent at the sight of the ocean, he alone reassured the monkeys and then leapt a hundred yojanas.
"He assaulted the city of Laṅkā and the inner apartments of Rāvaṇa; he found Sītā, spoke with her, and reassured her.
"The vanguard of the army, the sons of ministers, the servants, the sons of Rāvaṇa — all these were felled there by Hanūmān alone.
"Released again from captivity, having spoken with the ten-headed one, he reduced Laṅkā to ashes as fire reduces the earth.
"Neither of Kāla, nor of Śakra, nor of Viṣṇu, nor of Kubera are such deeds as Hanūmān's in battle heard of.
"By the arm-strength of this one, I obtained Laṅkā, Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, victory, the kingdom, friends, and kinsmen.
"If Hanūmān, friend of the monkey-lord, were not with me, who would have been capable of obtaining even news of Jānakī?
"Why did Hanūmān, desiring the welfare of Sugrīva, not burn Vālin like a creeper when that enmity arose?
"I believe Hanūmān did not know his own strength, since he merely witnessed the monkey-lord, dear to him, being tormented.
"All of this concerning Hanūmān, O Blessed One, O great sage, O you worshipped by the immortals — tell me in full detail and in truth."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having heard Rāghava's reasoned speech, the sage then spoke these words in the presence of Hanūmān himself:
"This is true, O foremost of the Raghu line, what you say of Hanūmān. In strength there is none equal to him, nor in speed, nor in intelligence.
"But a curse was placed upon him in the past by sages whose curses never fail — that he, though mighty, the crusher of enemies, would not know his own strength.
"Even the deeds performed by him in childhood, O Rāma of great strength, cannot be adequately described on account of his extreme youth at the time.
"But if, O Rāghava, you have desire to hear it, collect your mind, O Rāma, and listen — I shall tell it.
"There is a mountain named Sumeru, of gold granted as a boon by the Sun; there his father — Kesarī by name — governs a kingdom.
"His beloved wife was known as Añjanā. In her, Vāyu begot a most excellent son.
"Having given birth to this one, bright as a śāli-grain husk, Añjanā had gone out roaming the forest, desiring to gather fruits.
"This infant, greatly afflicted by the absence of its mother and by hunger, wept intensely, like the young of the king of śarabhas.
"Then, seeing the rising Vivasvat, resembling a cluster of hibiscus flowers, and tempted by it as a fruit, he leapt upward toward the sun.
"The child, facing the morning sun, himself like the morning sun made manifest, desiring to seize the morning sun, flew through the middle of the sky.
"While Hanūmān was thus flying in his infant state, a very great astonishment arose among the gods, dānavas, and siddhas.
"Neither the wind is so swift, nor Garuḍa, nor the mind — as this son of Vāyu traverses the high sky.
"If even as an infant his speed and stride are like this, what will his swiftness be when he attains the strength of youth?
"Vāyu flew after his own son as he flew, protecting him out of fear of the sun's burning rays, cooling him with masses of frost-cold air.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Traversing many thousands of yojanas through the sky, he reached the proximity of the sun, by the strength of his father and by the recklessness of childhood.
"The day-maker, thinking 'this is a child, unknowing of fault,' and knowing too that a purpose was bound up in this, did not burn him.
"On the very same day that he leapt to seize the sun, Rāhu also was seeking to swallow the day-maker.
"Rāhu, the devourer of moon and sun, touched by this child on top of the sun's chariot, fled in fear.
"The son of Siṃhikā, incensed, went to Indra's palace and, furrowing his brow, spoke to the god surrounded by the host of gods:
"'You gave me moon and sun for appeasing my hunger, O Vāsava — what is this you have now given them to another, O mighty slayer of Vṛtra?
"'Today I came at the conjunction time, wishing to seize the sun; but some other Rāhu, having arrived there, suddenly seized the sun!'"
"Hearing Rāhu's words, Vāsava was seized with agitation; he leapt up from his seat, lifting his golden garland.
"Then the great Airāvata, white as the peak of Kailāsa, with four tusks, streaming with rut-fluid, causing delight, tall, laughing loudly with its golden bell —
"— Indra mounted that king of elephants and, placing Rāhu in front, went to where the sun was, together with Hanūmān.
"Then Rāhu, having rushed forward in great haste and left Vāsava behind, was seen by Hanūmān, who rushed at him like a mountain peak.
"Then, releasing the sun and seeing Rāhu thus, Hanūmān leapt again into the sky to seize the son of Siṃhikā.
"O Rāma, seeing the leaping one rush toward him having released the sun, Rāhu, that one who is nothing but a mouth, turned his face and fled.
"Hoping for Indra as protector, the son of Siṃhikā cried out again and again in terror: 'Indra! Indra!'
"Indra had already noticed the voice of the screaming Rāhu; having heard it, Indra said: 'Do not fear — I shall kill this one.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then, seeing the great Airāvata, thinking 'this too is a fruit,' the son of the wind rushed toward that king of elephants.
"Then, as he rushed to seize Airāvata, his form for a moment became terrible, blazing like Indra and Agni combined.
"The husband of Śacī, not excessively angered, struck with the thunderbolt released from the tip of his hand the one who was rushing thus.
"Then, struck by Indra's thunderbolt, Hanūmān fell upon a mountain; as he fell, his left jaw was broken.
"When the child fell, reeling from the blow of the thunderbolt — to the misfortune of all creatures — Pavana grew furious at Indra.
"That lord entered all living beings, stopping up the cavities of waste and urine, and withheld all creatures, as Vāsava withholds the rains.
"By reason of Vāyu's wrath, all beings everywhere, bereft of breath, with their joints cracking, became like blocks of wood.
"By Vāyu's wrath, the three worlds, devoid of svadha-offerings, devoid of vaṣaṭ-calls, devoid of activity, bereft of dharma, appeared like those fallen to hell.
"Then all creatures — together with gandharvas, gods, asuras, and humans — rushed to Prajāpati, suffering in their misery, seeking happiness.
"The gods, with joined palms and bellies shrunken with fear, said: 'By you, O Blessed Lord, we four kinds of creatures have been created, O lord of creatures.
"'By you, Vāyu was given to us as the lord of life-breath. Having become our lord of prāṇa, why is he today, O best of beings —
"'— blocking and causing suffering, like women shut within the inner apartments? Therefore, afflicted by Vāyu, we have come to you for refuge, O mighty one.
"'Remove this suffering of ours born from the obstruction of Vāyu, O slayer of enemies!'
"Hearing this from the creatures, Prajāpati, the lord of creatures, saying 'I know the reason,' spoke again to them:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'The reason for which Vāyu grew wrathful and obstructed — hear all of that, O creatures, and what is fitting for you yourselves to bear.
"'His son has been struck down today by Indra, king of the immortals, who acted on Rāhu's word — this is why Anila is angry with you all.'
"'Vāyu, bodiless himself, moves through bodies sustaining them; for a body without Vāyu becomes equal to dust.
"'Vāyu is the life-breath, Vāyu is happiness, Vāyu is all this world; a world abandoned by Vāyu finds no happiness.'
"'Today the world has been abandoned by Vāyu, who is life itself; today these beings stand breathless, like wood and walls.'
"'Therefore let us go to where Māruta dwells — for he is the source of your affliction. Lest we perish, let us not fail to propitiate the son of Aditi's co-wife.'
"Then Prajāpati, together with the creatures and with gods, gandharvas, serpents, and guhyakas, went to where Māruta sat, holding his son who had been struck down by the lord of the immortals.
"Then the four-faced one, seeing the son of ever-moving Vāyu in his lap, glowing like sun and fire and gold, was moved to compassion, together with the gods, siddhas, sages, serpents, and rākṣasas.
Then Vāyu, afflicted by the wounding of his son, took up the infant and rose to stand before the Fashioner, the Grandfather.
With earrings, crown, and red-water ornaments trembling, Vāyu fell at the feet of the Creator, composing himself in the three-fold posture of reverence.
That foremost knower of the Vedas, radiant with pendant ornaments, raising Vāyu up by the hand, touched the infant gently.
Merely touched by him who was born from the lotus, the child gracefully regained life, like a crop revived by water.
Seeing this one restored to life, Prāṇa, the sweet-bearing wind, joyfully moved through all beings as before, unobstructed.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Freed from the disease of the wind's restraint, all creatures became joyful, like lotus-ponds freed from cold winds, bearing their flowers again.
Then Brahmā, the triple-aged, three-peaked, three-aboded, worshipped by the thirty gods, spoke to the gods, desiring to please Māruta:
"O Mahendra, Agni, Varuṇa, Lord of wealth, and Maheśvara — I shall speak what is beneficial; though you know it, let it be heard.
"There is a great task for you all to be accomplished by this child. Let all of you give boons to him, the boons that please this Māruta."
Then the thousand-eyed one, his face flushed with joy and beautiful, raising the kuśa-grass garland on which he lay, spoke thus:
"As his jaw (hanu) was injured by the thunderbolt released from my hand, by that name this tiger among monkeys shall be known as Hanūmān.
"I myself shall give him the highest and best boon: from this day forward he shall be invulnerable to my thunderbolt."
"Then the Blessed Lord Mārtāṇḍa, dispeller of darkness, spoke there: 'I give him one-hundredth part of my own radiance.
"'When he shall have the capacity to study the sciences, I shall give him the knowledge of śāstras by which he will become eloquent.'"
Varuṇa also granted a boon: "He shall not die — not for ten million years, and not from my noose, not from water."
Yama too, pleased, granted his boon — immunity from the staff of death, perpetual freedom from disease, and cheerfulness in battle.
"My own mace shall not slay him in battles" — thus spoke the boon-granting one, he of the single tawny eye, Kubera.
"He shall not be slain by me nor by the weapons of those intoxicated with power" — thus the supreme boon was also given by Śaṃkara.
"He shall be invulnerable to all of Brahmā's weapons, long-lived and great-souled" — thus spoke Brahmā.
Viśvakarmā, seeing this infant resembling the infant sun, the foremost of craftsmen, of great wisdom, proclaimed his boon:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Among all the weapons fashioned by me for the gods, he shall be invulnerable to any of them in the time of battle."
Then, seeing him adorned with the boons of the gods, the four-faced one, the teacher of the world, with a pleased countenance, spoke to Vāyu:
"Your son, son of Māruta, shall be the cause of fear to enemies and the giver of fearlessness to friends — unconquerable here.
"He shall accomplish in battle deeds that shall overthrow Rāvaṇa, that shall bring joy to Rāma, and that shall make the hair stand on end."
Having spoken thus and bidding farewell to Māruta, all of them — with the Grandfather at the head — departed with the immortals as they had come.
And Vāyu, the sweet-bearing wind, took his son, brought him home, told Añjanā of the boon that had been granted, and departed.
Having received these boons, O Rāma, he was filled with the power of the granted boons, with strength abiding in himself, as an ocean is filled.
This foremost of monkeys, being filled with strength, fearlessly committed offenses in the hermitages of the great sages.
He would break the ladles and vessels, destroy the agnihotra fires, and scatter the piles of bark garments of the tranquil sages, leaving them broken, torn, and ruined.
The sages, knowing that Brahmā had made him invulnerable to all of Brahmā's weapons, always bore with him.
When even though restrained by Kesarī and by Vāyu and by Añjanā, this monkey continues to transgress all bounds —
— then the great sages, of the lineage of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras, O foremost of the Raghu line, cursed him — not with excessive anger or extreme wrath:
"'O leaping one, you harass us relying on that strength — bewildered by our curse, you shall not know it for a long time.'
Then, with his radiance and power taken away by the power of the great sages' words, he roamed without exceeding his bounds, having attained a gentle nature.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Now there was one named Ṛkṣarājā, father of Vālin and Sugrīva, king of all the monkeys, blazing in splendour like the sun.
That lord of monkeys, having long governed the kingdom of the monkeys, passed away in the course of time — that one named Ṛkṣarājā met his death by the law of Time.
When he had set, Vālin was made king in his father's place by ministers skilled in counsel, and Sugrīva in Vālin's place.
With Sugrīva, his friendship was undivided, without flaw, unshakeable — like that of Anila with fire.
It is only by the power of the curse that he did not know his own strength — when the enmity between Vālin and Sugrīva arose, O Rāma.
"For, O Rāma, Sugrīva, even while being tormented by Vālin, did not know it, and Māruti did not know the strength within himself.
"In valour, energy, intellect, and splendour, in virtue, sweetness, policy and its opposite, in gravity, cleverness, heroism, and steadfastness — who in this world surpasses Hanūmān?
"Long ago, to learn grammar, this immeasurable king of monkeys, facing the sun, moving backward, went from the rising mountain to the setting mountain, bearing that great text.
"Who shall stand before Hanūmān — like the ocean that seeks to flood the worlds, like fire that seeks to burn them, like Antaka at the time of the world's destruction?
"He and the other great monkey-lords — Sugrīva, Mainda, Dvivida, together with Nīla, together with Tāra, Tāreya, Nala — all of these, O Rāma, were created by the gods for your sake.
"All of this has been told — what you asked of me. The deeds of Hanūmān in his childhood have been narrated by me.
"You have been seen, O Rāma, and spoken with. We shall go." Having spoken thus, all those sages departed as they had come.
Then Rāma, having deliberated, embraced his fearless friend Pratardana, lord of Kāśī, and spoke these words.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Affection has been shown by you, supreme friendship has been shown, and great effort has been made, O king, by you together with Bharata."
"Therefore let Your Honour now go to Vārāṇasī, the city of the Kāśīs, that beautiful city protected by you, with its fine ramparts and splendid gateways."
Having said so much, the righteous-souled Kākutstha rose from his exalted seat and embraced that friend, pressing him close to his chest.
Having dismissed that companion, Rāghava, smiling, addressed the kings who had come as guests with words of sweet syllables.
"Your unwavering affection has been guarded by your valour; dharma has ever been constant for you, and so has truth, always."
"Through your might and through the valour of your great selves, Rāvaṇa the wicked-souled, evil-minded lord of rākṣasas has been slain."
"I was merely the instrument there; by your collective splendour, Rāvaṇa with his horde in battle, with his sons and all his kinsmen, was destroyed."
"And you were all assembled by the great-souled Bharata upon hearing that the daughter of the king of Janaka had been abducted in the forest."
"A very long time has passed for all the striving great-souled kings in this undertaking; let your minds be inclined toward departure."
The kings, filled with great joy, replied to him: "By good fortune you are victorious, Rāma, and your kingdom too is firmly established."
"By good fortune Sītā has been recovered; by good fortune the enemy has been defeated. This is our highest desire; this is our supreme glory."
"That we behold you victorious, Rāma, your enemies slain — and it is fitting, O Kākutstha, that you should praise us."
"For those worthy of praise know how to speak such praise. We take our leave; we shall depart. You dwell in our hearts always."
"And may your affection for us, O great king, endure eternally."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Those great-souled kings, those heroes, departed in all directions, making the earth tremble, heading joyfully to their own cities.
Gathered with thousands of akṣauhiṇī armies in manifold ways, all those who had assembled for Rāghava's sake returned home, rejoicing.
And the rulers of the earth, proud of their strength, declared: "We never even got to see Rāvaṇa standing before us in battle!"
"We were assembled afterwards by Bharata to no purpose at all — the rākṣasas there would surely have been slain by the kings, of that there is no doubt."
"Protected by the arm-strength of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, we could have fought with ease on the far shore of the ocean, free from anxiety."
Speaking these and thousands of other such stories, those great chariot-warriors entered their respective kingdoms.
Arriving at their own cities, those kings, desiring to please Rāma, presented various gems as offerings to him.
Horses, gems, garments, elephants overflowing with rut, divine sandalwood, and divine ornaments.
Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and the great chariot-warrior Śatrughna took those gems and returned again to Ayodhyā.
Having arrived at the beautiful city of Ayodhyā, those bulls among men presented all the gems to the great-souled Rāghava.
Receiving all that with joy, Rāghava distributed all of it to the great-souled Sugrīva.
He gave also to Vibhīṣaṇa, and to those other bears and vānaras headed by Hanūmat — those heroes — and to the mighty rākṣasas.
All of them, joyful of heart, then bore those gifts given by Rāma upon their heads and in their arms, those of great strength.
They drank fragrant mead of various kinds, and savoured well-prepared meats and fruits.
As they resided thus, more than a month passed — all of it seemed but a moment, sustained as they were by devotion to Rāma.
Rāma took pleasure with those vānaras of wish-assuming form, with those kings of great valour, and with those mighty rākṣasas.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus a second winter month passed happily for all those rejoicing vānaras and rākṣasas alike.
As those bears, vānaras, and rākṣasas were dwelling there in that manner, the great-resplendent Rāghava said this to Sugrīva:
"Go, dear friend, to Kiṣkindhā, impregnable to gods and asuras. Rule your kingdom together with your ministers, now that its thorns have been removed."
"And, O mighty-armed one, look with the greatest affection upon Aṅgada, upon Hanūmat, and upon the supremely powerful Nala."
"Upon Suṣeṇa your heroic father-in-law, upon Tāra the best among the strong, upon the irresistible Kumuda, and upon the supremely powerful Nīla."
"Upon the heroic Śatabali, upon Mainda and Dvivida, upon Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, and the mighty Śarabha."
"Look with affection upon the irresistible king of bears, the mighty Jāmbavān, and upon Gandhamādana as well."
"And those other great souls who laid down their lives for my sake — look upon them with affection, and do nothing that would displease them."
Having spoken thus and having praised Sugrīva again and again, Rāma then addressed Vibhīṣaṇa with sweet speech:
"Rule Laṅkā righteously — for you are the acknowledged king, O lord of the earth, of the city of the rākṣasas, equal to your brother Vaiśravaṇa."
"And never, O king, under any circumstance, turn your mind to unrighteousness. For the wise among kings do surely inherit the earth."
"And, O king, remember me always together with Sugrīva, with the highest affection. Go now, free from anxiety."
Hearing the words of Rāma, the bears, vānaras, and rākṣasas praised Kākutstha saying "Well done! Well done!" again and again.
"Your wisdom, O mighty-armed one, your wondrous valour, and your supreme sweetness of nature, Rāma, are ever like those of the Self-born Brahmā."
While the vānaras and rākṣasas were speaking thus, Hanūmat bowed down and addressed Rāghava with these words:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"My highest love, O king, is permanently established in you; my devotion is constant, O hero — my heart goes nowhere else."
"As long as I shall hear the story of Rāma upon this earth, O hero, so long shall my life-breaths dwell within my body — of this there is no doubt."
Hearing Hanūmat speak thus, the lord of kings rose from his seat, embraced him, and then spoke these words:
"So shall it be, O best of monkeys — of this there is no doubt. As long as the worlds shall endure, so long shall my story endure."
"As long as this story of mine shall travel through the worlds, so long shall your life-breaths dwell in your body — of this there is no doubt."
Then Rāghava removed from his own neck a garland bright as the moon, trembling with vaidūrya gems, and fastened it with affection upon Hanūmat.
With that garland bound upon his chest, that great monkey shone like the lord of golden mountains with the moon crowning his summit.
Hearing this from Rāghava, the vānaras rose up one after another, bowed their heads to his feet, and those mighty ones departed.
The mighty-armed Sugrīva was embraced by Rāma, and the righteous-souled Vibhīṣaṇa was held close to his chest.
And all of them, their voices choked with tears, their eyes filled with tears, bewildered, as if stupefied by grief, departed from Rāghava then.
Having dismissed the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, the mighty-armed Rāma, together with his brothers, rejoiced in perfect happiness.
Then, in the afternoon, Rāghava along with his brothers heard a sweet voice speaking down from the sky.
"Gentle Rāma, look upon me with your gracious countenance. Know me, O lord, as Puṣpaka, arrived from the peak of Kailāsa.
"Following your command, O best of men, I went to wait upon Dhanada, the lord of wealth, and he spoke to me thus.
"'You have been won back by the king of men, the great-souled Rāghava, who slew in battle the terrible Rāvaṇa, lord of rākṣasas.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'My own supreme delight, O gentle one, is in the slaying of that wicked Rāvaṇa together with his troops, his sons, ministers, and kinsmen.
"'You who were won in Laṅkā by the supremely noble Rāma — O gentle one, serve him alone: this I command you.
"'This is my highest wish: that you carry Rāghava, the joy of the world, wherever he desires. Go now, free from all care."
"Having learnt this command of the great-souled lord of wealth, I have come again to your presence. Accept me thus, O lord."
"So be it" — with these words the scion of Kākutstha duly honoured Puṣpaka with fried grain, unbroken rice, flowers, and fragrant perfumes.
"Go wherever you please, and return when I recall you" — thus dismissed by Rāma, Puṣpaka departed once more, adorned with blossoms, in the direction of its desire.
When that wondrous Puṣpaka had disappeared from sight, Bharata, with joined palms, spoke these words to the delight of the Raghus.
"Exceedingly marvellous things appear while you govern the kingdom — the utterances of non-human beings are heard again and again.
"And from freedom from disease among mortals — this full month has now passed, O Rāghava, and even old creatures have not met with death.
"Women give birth to fine sons, and men are handsome of form; and the joy of the city-dwelling people is extraordinarily great, O king.
"Indra showers rain in season, rain akin to nectar, and breezes blow that are pleasant to the touch and bestow comfort.
"'May such a king be ours for long' — so speak the citizens in the city, O lord of men, and the people in the countryside.
Having heard these exceedingly sweet words uttered by Bharata, Rāma, filled with joy, rejoiced in utter happiness.
Then Rāma, the mighty-armed, having dismissed the gold-adorned Puṣpaka, entered the Aśoka grove.
It was beautified on all sides with sandalwood, agaru, mango, tall kāleyaka, and forests of devadāru trees.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
It was covered with priyaṅgu, kadamba, kurabaka, jambū, pāṭalī, and kovidāra trees.
At all times it was lovely with beautiful flowers, laden with fruits, delightful, rich with charming shoots and blossoms, and thronged with maddened bees.
It was adorned with cuckoos, bhṛṅgarājas, birds of many colours, and hundreds of variegated mango trees as its ornaments.
There the trees shone — some resembling refined gold, some like tongues of fire, and others like blue collyrium.
There were ponds of various forms, filled with the finest water, with steps of precious gems and floors inlaid with crystal.
They were adorned with groves of blooming lotuses and blue water-lilies, graced by cakravāka birds, and beautified by enclosures of various forms and stone pavements.
Here and there in the woodland's expanse were lawns resembling vaidūrya gems, adorned most excellently, set about with flowering trees.
Rāma's grove had been laid out to resemble Indra's Nandana, and likewise Brahmā's Caitraratha garden.
Entering that flourishing Aśoka grove — abounding in pavilions and arbours, enveloped with bowers of creepers — the delight of the Raghus took his seat.
Rāma seated himself upon a fine-formed seat adorned with clusters of flowers and spread with a woollen coverlet.
Taking Sītā into his arms, the scion of Kākutstha gave her the finest sweet wine to drink, as Indra gives nectar to Śacī.
Attendants quickly brought diverse kinds of meat and various fruits for Rāma's enjoyment.
Young and beautiful women skilled in dance and song danced before the king, yielding to the sway of wine.
Thus Rāma, filled with joy, delighted Vaidehī — the daughter of Videha, whose face was most lovely — day after day, in the manner of a god.
While the great-souled king of men, Rāghava, was thus taking his pleasure, the lovely cool season passed by.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
In the forenoon, having discharged his civic duties righteously, the knower of dharma would spend the remaining half of the day's portion within the inner apartments.
And Sītā, having performed her morning religious observances, would stand with joined palms before all her mothers-in-law without distinction.
Then she would come to Rāma adorned with varied and manifold ornaments, as Śacī comes to the thousand-eyed Indra seated in heaven.
Seeing his wife endowed with every auspicious quality, Rāghava was filled with incomparable delight and said, "Well done, well done."
"O Vaidehī, the gaining of offspring is now at hand for me. Tell me what you desire — what is your wish? Let it be done for you."
Then Vaidehī, smiling gently, spoke these words to Rāma: "I desire to see the holy forest hermitages, O Rāghava.
"Those that are established on the banks of the Gaṅgā, belonging to the sages who perform meritorious deeds and live on fruits and roots — O hero, to dwell at the feet of such sages.
"This is my supreme desire — O scion of Kākutstha, that I might dwell even for a single night among those meritorious ones who live on roots and fruits."
"So be it" — this was promised by Rāma of untiring deeds. "Be assured, O Vaidehī — you will go tomorrow, without doubt."
Having spoken thus to Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, Rāma, the scion of Kākutstha, went out into the middle courtyard surrounded by his friends.
There, skilled raconteurs of many kinds of stories — men who provoke laughter — attended upon the king as he sat, on all sides.
Vijaya, Madhumatta, Kāśyapa, Piṅgala, Kuśa, Surāji, Kāliya, Bhadra, Dantavakra, and Samāgadha —
— these men joyfully narrated to the great-souled Rāghava stories of many kinds, full of jests and amusing tales.
Then, in the course of some conversation, Rāghava asked: "What stories, O Bhadra, are circulating in the city and in the countryside?

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"What do the townspeople and country folk say regarding me? And what regarding Sītā, and what regarding Bharata, and what of Lakṣmaṇa?
"And what regarding Śatrughna, and my mother Kaikeyī? For kings in a new reign do become subjects of public speech."
Thus addressed by Rāma, Bhadra, with joined palms, replied: "Auspicious stories, O king, circulate among the city-dwellers —
"— but this victory of yours, O gentle one, pertaining to the slaying of the ten-necked one, is what is talked of most by the citizens in the city, O bull among men.
Thus addressed by Bhadra, Rāghava spoke: "Tell me everything truthfully and completely, holding nothing back.
"The words — both good and ill — that the city-dwellers speak: having heard them now, I shall act on what is good and refrain from what is ill.
"Speak openly, without fear, free from all anxiety, exactly as the citizens speak, and as the people speak in the countryside."
Thus spoken to by Rāghava, Bhadra, standing with joined palms and fully composed, replied to the mighty-armed king with these well-chosen words:
"Hear, O king, how the citizens speak — both good and ill — at crossroads, in markets, on the streets, in forests and in gardens.
"'Rāma accomplished the formidable feat of building a bridge across the ocean — something never done before by any predecessors, not even by gods or dānavas.
"'And the terrible Rāvaṇa was slain together with his army and forces; monkeys were brought to submission, and bears together with rākṣasas.
"'Having slain Rāvaṇa in battle and recovered Sītā, Rāghava set his anger aside and brought her back to his own home.
"'What kind of pleasure in his heart can there be from enjoying Sītā — she who was formerly seized by force and placed in Rāvaṇa's lap?
"'She who was carried away again to Laṅkā, who went to the Aśoka grove, who fell under the power of the rākṣasas — how is it that Rāma does not reject her?

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'This will become something to be tolerated in our own wives as well — for as the king does, so the subjects follow.'
"Thus do the city-dwellers speak in many ways, O king, in all the cities and throughout the countryside."
Hearing these words of his, Rāghava, in the deepest anguish, said to all his friends: "How shall this be conveyed?"
But all of them, bowing low to the ground with their heads and prostrating themselves, replied to the grief-stricken Rāghava: "It is even so, without doubt."
Having heard the words uttered by all of them, the scion of Kākutstha, the tormentor of enemies, then dismissed them all.
Having dismissed the company of friends and resolved in his mind, Rāghava spoke these words to the doorkeeper who was seated nearby.
"Quickly bring Saumitri Lakṣmaṇa of auspicious marks, and the long-armed Bharata, and the unconquered Śatrughna."
Having heard Rāma's command, the doorkeeper placed his joined palms upon his head and went to Lakṣmaṇa's house, entering without obstruction.
And then he spoke with joined palms raised in salutation: "The king desires to see you; go there without delay."
"Indeed, so be it" — hearing Rāghava's command, Saumitri mounted his chariot and hastened to Rāghava's dwelling.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa depart, the doorkeeper approached Bharata nearby and said with joined palms: "The king desires to see you."
But Bharata, hearing the word of Rāma conveyed by the doorkeeper, leapt up swiftly from his seat and went there on foot.
Seeing Bharata departing, the doorkeeper hastened with joined palms to Śatrughna's residence and spoke these words.
"Come, O best of the Raghus, the king desires to see you; for Lakṣmaṇa has already gone, and so has the greatly renowned Bharata."
Hearing that message — the command of Rāma — Śatrughna bowed his head to the ground in reverence and went to where Rāghava was.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing that the princes had arrived, with his faculties disturbed by anguish, his head bowed low and his mind dejected, Rāma spoke to the doorkeeper.
"Bring the princes quickly to my presence; my life resides in them — they are my vital breaths that walk abroad."
Thus directed by the lord of men, the princes, clad in white garments, entered humbly with joined palms, composed and attentive.
But they, seeing his face like the moon in eclipse, like the sun at dusk stripped of its radiance,
and beholding the tear-filled eyes of wise Rāma, and seeing his face like a lotus bereft of its beauty —
— they then quickly bowed their heads to Rāma's feet in obeisance and all stood composed, while Rāma shed tears.
The mighty-armed one embraced them with both arms, raised them up, said "Be seated," and then spoke these words.
"You are my all, you are my life; it is by you that this kingdom has been made, and I now protect it, O lords of men.
"You are well-versed in the meaning of the śāstras and thoroughly grounded in discernment; together you must seek out this matter that concerns me, O lords of men."
When they had all sat down, their hearts full of sorrow, Kākutstha spoke with a parched face.
"All of you listen, blessings upon you; do not turn your minds otherwise. Regarding Sītā, such is the report that circulates among the citizens toward me:
"A very great reproach from the townspeople and likewise from the countryside is directed at me — a hateful reproach that cuts into my very vitals.
"'He is born in the lineage of the great-souled Ikṣvākus — how could he bring back to his city a Sītā of wicked conduct?'
"For you know, dear Saumitri, how Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa in the desolate forest of Daṇḍaka, and how he was destroyed by me.
"Before your very eyes, O Saumitri, Havyavāhana — the fire of the gods — and Vāyu who moves through the sky declared that Maithilī was without sin.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"And Candra and Āditya too testified in the presence of all the gods and all the seers, long ago, that the daughter of Janaka was blameless.
"She thus certified as pure in conduct was placed into my hand by great Indra on the island of Laṅkā, in the presence of gods and gandharvas.
"And my inner soul knows Sītā to be pure and illustrious. Having taken Vaidehī back, I came to Ayodhyā.
"Yet this great dispute and grief remains in my heart — the very great reproach of the citizens and of the countryside alike.
"Any being in this world of whom infamy is sung falls into the lowest realms for as long as that report is remembered.
"Infamy is condemned by the divine ones; glory is honoured among the gods; and every undertaking of great-souled persons is for the sake of glory.
"I would even abandon my life, or abandon you, O bulls among men, out of fear of disgrace — how much more then the daughter of Janaka.
"Therefore let all of you behold me fallen into an ocean of grief; for I see no sorrow greater than this.
"Tomorrow at dawn, O Saumitri, mount the chariot driven by Sumantra, take Sītā aboard, and abandon her at the border of the realm.
"On the far bank of the Gaṅgā, the hermitage of the greatly noble Vālmīki, divine in its appearance, is situated on the bank of the Tamasā river.
"There, in a lonely forest thicket, abandon her, O Raghunandana, and return quickly, O Saumitri — carry out my command.
"And I am not to be spoken to in any manner concerning Sītā; my displeasure would be extreme if I were opposed in this.
"And I adjure you by my arms and my life: whoever would speak to dissuade me or seek to placate me in any manner —
"— let them show me honour only if they abide by my command. From here today let Sītā be taken; carry out my command.
"She had formerly expressed to me a wish to visit the great hermitages along the Gaṅgā's bank; let this desire of hers also be fulfilled."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having spoken thus, Kākutstha — that righteous soul — with eyes closed by tears, withdrew and entered, surrounded by his brothers.
Then, when the night had passed, Lakṣmaṇa, his heart dejected, spoke to Sumantra with a parched face.
"O charioteer, quickly yoke the horses to the finest chariot, well-spread with cushions, and bring also a beautiful seat from the royal palace for Sītā."
"For Sītā must be taken by me from the royal palace to the hermitage of the holy-actioned great seers; let the chariot be brought quickly."
Sumantra, saying "So be it," brought the chariot yoked with the finest horses — a chariot gleaming most beautifully, its floor spread soft for comfort.
Having brought it, he said to Saumitri — the increaser of joy among friends — "The chariot stands ready, my lord; let whatever must be done be done."
Addressed thus by Sumantra, that bull among men, Lakṣmaṇa, entered the royal palace, approached Sītā, and spoke.
"O goddess, you must be brought quickly to the auspicious hermitage of the sages on the bank of the Gaṅgā by me — by command of our lord the king."
Thus addressed by the great-souled Lakṣmaṇa, Vaidehī experienced incomparable delight and consented gladly to the journey.
Taking precious garments and various jewels, Vaidehī made ready for departure.
"These ornaments I shall give to the wives of the sages." Saumitri said "So be it," and having helped Maithilī mount the chariot, set forth with swift horses, bearing in mind Rāma's command.
And then Sītā said to Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of prosperity: "I see many ill omens today, O Raghunandana.
"My eye throbs today, trembling arises throughout my limbs, and my heart, O Saumitri, I perceive to be unwell.
"And my anxiety is extreme, my restlessness profound; the earth itself, O wide-eyed one, I see as though it were empty.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"May all be well with that brother of yours together with his brothers, and likewise with all of my mothers-in-law without exception, O hero.
"And may all living beings in city and countryside likewise be well." So praying, Sītā made the añjali gesture toward the deities.
Lakṣmaṇa, hearing that meaning, bowed his head in reverence to Maithilī and said "All will be auspicious" — outwardly composed but with his heart drying up within.
Then, having halted for the night at a hermitage on the bank of the Gomatī, Saumitri rose again at dawn and addressed the charioteer.
"Yoke the chariot quickly; today I shall bear the waters of the Bhāgīrathī upon my head, as the Three-Eyed Lord bears the river on the mountain."
Having quickly seen to the horses and yoked those swift-as-thought steeds to the chariot, the charioteer said to Vaidehī with joined palms: "Please mount."
At the charioteer's words, Sītā mounted the finest chariot together with Saumitri and the wise Sumantra.
Then, having traveled half a day and glimpsing the waters of the Bhāgīrathī, Lakṣmaṇa, overcome with grief, broke into loud weeping.
Sītā, utterly devoted, seeing Lakṣmaṇa distressed, addressed him: "O knower of dharma, why do you weep like this?"
"Having arrived at the bank of the Jāhnavī — long desired by me — why do you cause me distress at a moment of joy, O Lakṣmaṇa?
"You always abide at Rāma's feet, O bull among men — have you perhaps come to grief at being separated from him for two nights?
"Rāma is dear to me too, even more than life, O Lakṣmaṇa — yet I do not grieve so; do not be so childish.
"Take me across the Gaṅgā and show me the ascetics; then I shall give them wealth, garments, and ornaments.
"Then, having paid appropriate homage to the great seers, spending one night there, we shall return to that city."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having heard her words, wiping her beautiful eyes, Lakṣmaṇa, wishing to cross the blessed Gaṅgā, brought a boat.
Then Rāghava's younger brother, having first helped Maithilī board, himself boarded the well-appointed, spacious Niṣāda boat.
Lakṣmaṇa, burning with grief, said to Sumantra together with his chariot, "Stay here," and said to the boatman, "Row on."
Then, having reached the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words to Maithilī, his palms joined in reverence, his voice choked with tears.
"There is a great thorn lodged in my heart, O Vaidehī, that I have been made an instrument of public reproach by the noble and wise one on this account."
"Death today, or whatever lies beyond death, would be better for me. I should not have been employed in such a task as this, which is condemned by all the world."
"Be gracious to me; you ought not to be angry with me, O lady of excellent vows." Saying so, with joined palms, Lakṣmaṇa fell to the ground.
Seeing him weeping, his palms joined, desiring his own death, Maithilī was seized with great distress and spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"I do not understand this at all — tell me the truth, Lakṣmaṇa. I see that you yourself are not at ease. Is the king well?"
"Were you cursed by the king, that you are afflicting yourself with such grief? Tell me in my presence. I command you."
Thus urged by Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, his heart broken, face cast downward, his throat thick with tears, spoke these words.
"Having heard a most terrible reproach spoken in the midst of the assembly, and likewise throughout the city and the countryside, on account of you, O daughter of Janaka —"
"— those words which the king laid to heart, casting indignation behind him, are not to be spoken by me before you, my lady."
"You, who are blameless, have been abandoned by the king through fear of the citizens' censure — it cannot be otherwise, my lady — and I am the one entrusted with this."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I am to leave you at the edge of the hermitages, having received the king's command — such, indeed, is the cruel wrong done to you."
"But this is the sacred and beautiful forest of austerity of the brahmarṣis on the bank of the Jāhnavī — do not give way to despair, O auspicious one."
"This foremost of sages, the supremely renowned brāhmaṇa Vālmīki, is the dear friend of King Daśaratha, my father."
"Come to the shelter of this great soul's feet and dwell there happily, O daughter of Janaka, intent on fasting and spiritual practice."
"By abiding in the vow of devotion to your husband, and keeping Rāma ever in your heart, your highest good, O lady, will come about by doing thus."
Having heard Lakṣmaṇa's terrible words, the daughter of Janaka, Vaidehī, fell to the ground overcome by the deepest anguish.
She lay as if unconscious for a moment, her eyes clouded with tears; then the daughter of Janaka spoke to Lakṣmaṇa in a faint voice.
"This body of mine was surely created for sorrow by the Creator, Lakṣmaṇa, since the very form of suffering is so manifest in me today."
"What sin was committed in a former life, or what husband was I separated from, that I, a chaste woman of pure conduct, have been abandoned by a king?"
"Before, O Saumitre, I lived in the hermitage following at the feet of Rāma, and yet even while attending upon him I was plunged in sorrow."
"How, O gentle one, shall I dwell in a hermitage forsaken and alone? And to whom shall I tell my grief, I who am wholly immersed in sorrow?"
"What shall I say among the sages? What wrong have I done the king? For what reason have I been abandoned by the great-souled Rāghava?"
"Indeed I would relinquish my life today in the waters of the Jāhnavī, O Saumitre, but the royal lineage of my husband would become an object of ridicule."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Do as commanded, O Saumitre; leave me, who am the companion of sorrow. Let the king's command be obeyed — but hear this word of mine."
"Bow your head and, with joined palms upraised, reverently salute the feet of all my mothers-in-law without distinction, and convey my good wishes to the king."
"As you conduct yourself toward your brothers, so conduct yourself always toward the citizens — this is the highest dharma, and this would be matchless glory."
"Whatever you may win from the citizens through righteousness — O bull among men, O joy of the Raghus — I do not grieve for my own body as I do for the censure of your citizens."
While Sītā was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa, his heart broken, bowed his head to the earth and was unable to utter a single word.
Having made a reverential circumambulation of her, he boarded the boat again, weeping loudly, and urged the boatman on.
Having crossed to the northern bank, weighed down with the burden of grief, dazed as it were by sorrow, he swiftly mounted the chariot.
Turning back again and again to look at Sītā standing helpless on the far bank, wringing her hands, Lakṣmaṇa then departed.
As Sītā, distressed, gazed again and again at the chariot growing distant and at Lakṣmaṇa, grief entered into her deeply.
That ascetic woman, bearer of glory, bowed down by the burden of sorrow, seeing no lord at her side, wept with a great cry of anguish in that forest resounding with the cries of peacocks, she the chaste one wholly consumed by grief.
Seeing Sītā weeping there, the young disciples of the sages ran to where the blessed Vālmīki, foremost in wisdom, was seated.
The sons of sages, having saluted the sage's feet, all reported to the great seer the sound of her weeping.
"Blessed one, a woman never seen here before, the wife of some great soul, is crying out in distress like Śrī bewildered, her voice broken."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Blessed one, kindly look upon her — she is like a goddess fallen from the sky; we do not know her to be a mortal woman. Let proper honor be rendered to her."
Hearing their words, the knower of dharma, his inner sight acquired through austerity, having ascertained the truth with his wisdom, hurried to where Maithilī was.
The great sage, having gone a little way on foot toward that place and taken his welcoming offering, reached the lovely bank of the Jāhnavī, and there he saw Sītā, the beloved wife of Rāghava, standing helpless.
Vālmīki, foremost of sages, spoke gentle words to Sītā, afflicted by the weight of grief, as if refreshing her with his radiance.
"You are the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha, the faithful queen-consort of Rāma, the daughter of King Janaka — welcome to you, O lady devoted to your husband."
"Even as you were coming, you were known to me through my absorption in dharma; and the entire cause of this has been perceived in my heart."
"I know you to be sinless, Sītā, through the sight gained by austerity. You are of pure heart, O Vaidehī — now you are under my care."
"The female ascetics established in penance not far from my hermitage will care for you always, dear child, as a calf is cared for."
"Accept this welcoming gift; be at ease, freed from anxiety. Come as if arriving at your own home, and do not give way to grief."
Having heard the sage's words, most wonderful indeed, Sītā saluted his feet with bowed head and said "So be it," with joined palms.
Sītā, with joined palms, followed behind the departing sage; she followed to where the female ascetics, ever constant in dharma, dwelt in composure.
Seeing the sage arriving with Vaidehī following him, they came forward filled with joy and spoke these words.
"Welcome to you, O foremost of sages; long has it been since you came, O master. We all salute you — speak, what shall we do?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing their words, Vālmīki said to them: "This Sītā has come — she is the wife of the wise Rāma."
"She is the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha, the virtuous daughter of Janaka, sinless, abandoned by her husband — she is to be protected by me always."
"You all look upon her with the deepest affection. Out of respect for my word, let her be honored by you especially."
Having consoled Vaidehī again and again, the greatly renowned sage of great austerity returned to his own hermitage, accompanied by his disciples.
Having seen Sītā, daughter of Mithilā, led into the hermitage, Lakṣmaṇa, his heart afflicted, was seized with dreadful anguish.
And that great-spirited one spoke to Sumantra, the charioteer who was also a counsellor: "Behold the grief born of Sītā's suffering that afflicts the wise Rāma."
"What greater sorrow could befall Rāghava than this — that he has abandoned the daughter of Janaka, his wife of pure conduct?"
"Clearly I think it is fate that causes Rāghava's separation from Vaidehī, O charioteer; for fate is indeed impossible to transgress."
"He who, when angered, could slay gods together with gandharvas, asuras and rākṣasas — that Rāghava now follows the dictates of fate."
"Formerly, by the command of my father, he dwelt in the dreadful desolate Daṇḍaka forest for nine years and five."
"Yet even more grievous than that seems to me the exile of Sītā, upon hearing the cruel words of the townspeople."
"What support of righteousness, O charioteer, can be found in this honour-destroying act toward Maithilī, carried out on account of the lowly words of the townspeople?"
Having heard these many words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, Sumantra joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words:
"You should not grieve, O Saumitri, concerning Maithilī; this was foreseen before by the brāhmaṇas in the presence of your father, O Lakṣmaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Rāma will surely be one whose lot is mostly sorrow and little happiness; the righteous great one will abandon you and Maithilī, and likewise Śatrughna and Bharata, after a great span of time."
"But this should not be told to you, O Saumitri, nor to Bharata — for what Durvāsas once said was not spoken by the king as a communication to you."
"Those words were spoken by the sage in the presence of the great king, of myself, O bull among men, and in the presence of Vasiṣṭha."
"Having heard the sage's words, that bull among men said to me: 'O charioteer, this must never be told by you in any gathering of people.'"
"I, with concentrated mind, accepted those words of that guardian of the world; I would never act falsely toward them — such is my conviction, O gentle one."
"There is nothing at all that I ought not speak before you, O gentle one; if you have faith in hearing it, let it be heard, O delight of the Raghu line."
"Even though I was formerly made to hear this secret by the king of men, I shall nonetheless recount it — for fate is impossible to transgress."
Having heard his speech, profound in meaning and weighty, Saumitri then spoke these words to the charioteer: "Speak the truth."
Thus urged by the great-souled Lakṣmaṇa, the charioteer began to relate the words that had been spoken by the sage.
"Long ago, the great sage Durvāsas, son of Atri, dwelt through the rainy season in the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha."
"Your father, of great splendour and most exalted fame, went there himself, wishing to see that great-souled priest."
"Seeing the great sage seated at the left side of Vasiṣṭha, blazing with energy like the sun, he reverently saluted those two sages, foremost among ascetics."
"The king, honoured by them with a welcome, a seat, water for the feet, and fruits and roots, sat there with the sages."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"As they sat there, those most noble sages exchanged many sweet conversations while the sun passed its midday course."
"Then, in the midst of a certain conversation, the king, with joined palms and restrained manner, addressed that great-souled son of Atri, rich in austerity."
"'Revered one, how extensive will my lineage be? What will be the lifespan of my Rāma, and what the lifespans of my other sons?'"
"'What lifespan will the sons of Rāma have? Out of devotion, revered one, tell me the course of this my lineage.'"
"Hearing the words spoken by King Daśaratha, Durvāsas of immense energy began to speak."
"'Rāma will be lord of Ayodhyā for a long time; his younger brothers too will be prosperous and happy.'"
"'For a certain reason the righteous one will abandon you and the glorious Maithilī after a great span of time.'"
"'Having attended to his kingship for ten thousand years and ten hundred years, Rāma will depart to the world of Brahmā.'"
"'Having worshipped with prosperous aśvamedha sacrifices, the conqueror of enemy cities, the scion of Kākutstha, will establish many royal lineages.'"
"Having narrated in full all the comings and goings of this royal lineage, that sage of immense energy and great brilliance fell silent."
"When the sage had fallen silent, King Daśaratha then saluted those two great souls and returned to the finest of cities."
"These words spoken by the sage there long ago were heard by me and laid up in my heart; it shall not be otherwise than this."
"Things being so, you ought not fall into grief, O Rāghava — whether for Sītā's sake or for Rāghava's sake; be resolute, O best of men."
Hearing the most wonderful words spoken by the charioteer, he was seized with incomparable joy and said: "Well spoken, well spoken!"
As the charioteer and Lakṣmaṇa conversed thus along the road, the sun went to its setting; and those two then spent the night at the Gomatī river.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having passed that night there at the Gomatī, the delight of the Raghu line, Lakṣmaṇa, rose again at dawn and then set forth.
Then, when midday arrived, that great warrior entered Ayodhyā, filled with jewels and thronged with joyful and prosperous people.
But Saumitri, that most great-minded one, was overcome with the deepest wretchedness: "What shall I say when I stand before the feet of Rāma — 'I have gone and done it'?"
As he brooded thus, before him appeared the most magnificent palace of Rāma, resembling the moon.
That best of men descended at the gate of the king's palace, and entered with downcast face and grieving heart, unhindered.
He saw Rāghava, sorrowful and seated upon the high seat; with eyes full of tears he beheld his elder brother before him.
Lakṣmaṇa, his heart afflicted, clasped his feet, and spoke with a despondent voice, with joined palms, composed in manner:
"Having placed foremost the command of the noble one, and having abandoned the daughter of Janaka at the auspicious hermitage of Vālmīki on the bank of the Gaṅgā as directed, I have come again, O hero, to attend at your feet."
"Do not grieve, O tiger among men; such is the way of time. Men of your kind — those possessed of courage and wisdom — do not grieve.
"All accumulations end in diminishment; all that rises ends in falling; all unions end in separation; and life ends in death."
"You are capable of conquering yourself — and indeed all worlds — by the mind alone, O scion of Kākutstha; how much more then a sorrow such as this?"
"Bulls among men of your kind are not bewildered by such things as that for which Maithilī was abandoned — out of fear of censure, O king."
"Therefore you, O tiger among men, steadfast in fortitude, abandon this weakness of mind; do not allow yourself to be consumed by anguish."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Thus addressed by the great-souled Lakṣmaṇa, the scion of Kākutstha spoke with the highest affection to Saumitri, who was devoted as a friend:
"It is exactly as you say, O best of men, O Lakṣmaṇa; and I am satisfied, O hero, by your guidance in my duty."
"Contentment has been made, O gentle one, and anguish has been dispelled; by your very sweet words I have been consoled, O Lakṣmaṇa."
Then Sumantra, having come, said to Rāghava: "These ascetics, O king, have been stopped and stand at the gate."
"The great seers, placing the Bhārgava named Cyavana at their head, are urgently requesting an audience with you, O great king — they are eager and pleased, O tiger among men, they who dwell on the banks of the Yamunā."
Hearing those words of his, Rāma, the knower of dharma, said: "Let those great-souled twice-born ones, with the Bhārgava at their head, be admitted."
The doorkeeper, honouring the king's command, with joined palms raised to his head, then admitted the many revered ascetics.
More than a hundred of those great-souled ascetics, blazing with their own inner radiance, then entered the royal palace.
Those twice-born ones brought in abundance to Rāma full water-pots honoured with water from all sacred fords, and also fruits and roots.
Rāma, filled with affection, received all of it — all the sacred-ford waters and the various fruits.
And the mighty-armed one addressed all those great sages: "Pray be seated, each according to his rank, on these finest of seats."
Hearing Rāma's words, all those great seers sat down on the beautiful golden cushioned seats.
Seeing the seers seated there, the conqueror of enemy cities, Rāghava, with a pure heart and joined palms, spoke these words.
"What is the purpose of your coming? What may I do for you, O wealth-of-austerity ones? I am at the command of the great seers, the glad fulfiller of every wish."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"This entire kingdom and the life dear to my heart — all of this is for the sake of the twice-born. I speak this truth to you."
Hearing his words, there arose a great cry of "well said!" from those fierce-austerity seers dwelling on the bank of the Yamunā.
And those great-souled ones, filled with great joy, said: "This is fitting for you alone in this world, O best of men, and no other."
"Many mighty kings have passed away, O king, who, not heeding the gravity of duty, did not deign to make such a pledge."
"But you, out of reverence for the brāhmaṇas, have made this pledge without looking for reasons — now fulfil it. You are capable of it, there is no doubt. You ought to protect the seers from this great terror."
While the seers were speaking thus, Kākutstha said: "Tell me what the task is. I shall destroy the fear that afflicts you."
As Kākutstha spoke thus, the Bhārgava said: "Hear, O lord of men, the root-cause of our fear and of this land's fear."
"In former times, in the Kṛta age, O Rāma, there was a Daiteya of immense power, the eldest son of Lolā, a great asura named Madhu."
"He was devoted to the brāhmaṇas, a provider of refuge, accomplished in wisdom, and the most supremely noble gods held incomparable affection for him."
"That Madhu, endowed with valour and deeply established in dharma, was given by Rudra, out of great esteem, a wondrous boon."
"The great-souled one, greatly pleased, drew from his own trident the mighty, exceedingly radiant spear and gave it, and spoke these words:"
"'This matchless and auspicious dharma has been practised by you through my grace. Filled with supreme affection, I give you this supreme weapon.'"
"'So long as you do not quarrel with the gods or the brāhmaṇas, O great asura, this trident shall be yours; otherwise it will be destroyed.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'Whoever challenges you to battle without fear — the trident, having reduced him to ashes, will return to your hand.'"
"Having thus received the boon from Rudra, the great asura again prostrated before Mahādeva and spoke these words:"
"'O Blessed One, may this supreme trident remain perpetually in my lineage, O god — for you are the lord of the gods.'"
"To Madhu speaking thus, the god, Śiva, lord of all beings, Mahādeva, replied: 'It shall not be so in this manner.'"
"'Let not your auspicious words, made by my grace, be fruitless. This trident shall pass to one son of yours.'"
"'As long as this trident remains in the hand of your son, he shall be invincible by all beings, the trident-bearer.'"
"Thus Madhu, having received from the god this most wondrous great boon, the foremost among asuras had a splendid abode built."
"His beloved wife, the highly fortunate Kumbhīnasī, was the offspring of Viśvāvasu, born of Analā, of great radiance."
"Her son, of great valour, named Lavaṇa, was ferocious; from childhood his soul was wicked and he committed only evil deeds."
"Seeing that undisciplined son, Madhu was filled with grief and fell into sorrow, yet he said nothing to him."
"He, leaving this world, entered the abode of Varuṇa; having placed the trident in Lavaṇa's care, he conveyed to him the boon."
"He, by the power of the trident and likewise by the wickedness of his own nature, torments the three worlds, and the ascetics in particular."
"Such is the might of Lavaṇa, and such is the nature of that trident — knowing this authority, O Kākutstha, you are our highest refuge."
"Many kings, O Rāma, were in former times beseeched by fear-stricken seers for refuge, O hero, yet we found no protector."
"We, having heard that Rāvaṇa together with his forces and army has been slain, acknowledge you, O Rāma, as our protector and no other king on earth. Thus we, tormented by fear, desire to be rescued from Lavaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When they had spoken thus, Rāma, with joined palms, replied to those seers: "What does Lavaṇa eat? What are his habits? And where does he dwell?"
Hearing Rāghava's words, all those seers then reported to him how Lavaṇa had grown powerful.
"His food is all living creatures, the ascetics in particular. His conduct is perpetual ferocity. His abode is always in the Madhuvana forest."
"Slaying ten thousand lions, tigers, deer, and elephants, as well as human beings, he makes his daily meal each day."
"Then that mighty one devours still other creatures — like Death at the time of universal dissolution, with gaping mouth."
Hearing that account, Rāghava said to those great sages: "I shall slay that rākṣasa. Let your fear depart."
Having thus given his pledge to those fierce-lustred sages, the joy of the Raghu-line then addressed all his brothers assembled together.
"Who among you heroes shall be the slayer of Lavaṇa? To whom shall that assignment be given — to the mighty-armed Bharata, or again to Śatrughna?"
Thus addressed by Rāghava, Bharata spoke: "I shall slay him. Let that assignment be given to me."
Hearing the words of Bharata, full of courage and valour, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa — Śatrughna — rose from his golden seat.
And Śatrughna, prostrating before the king, spoke — the mighty-armed middle son among the Raghu-joys who had already accomplished great deeds:
"Indeed, in former times the noble one guarded the empty city of Ayodhyā, bearing anguish in his heart in anticipation of the noble one's return."
"And many sorrows have been endured here, O king — the great-souled one lying on beds of sorrow in Nandigrāma."
"Subsisting on fruit and roots, wearing matted locks and bark garments, this son of Raghu endured such suffering. With me, your servant, now present, O king, he should not suffer any more hardship."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
As Śatrughna spoke thus, Rāghava replied again: "So be it, O Kākutstha — let my command be carried out."
"I shall consecrate you as king in the beautiful city of Madhu; establish Bharata there, O mighty-armed one, if you regard my word."
"You are a hero, accomplished in learning, and capable of establishing that city frequented by Madhu, as well as the fair provinces."
"For he who uproots a royal lineage and at its extinction does not install a king there — that man goes to hell."
"Therefore you, having slain Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu, that one of evil resolve, rule the kingdom by dharma — if you regard my word."
"And do not speak in return, O hero, interrupting my words. The command of an elder brother must be carried out by a younger — there is no doubt in this matter."
"And accept, O Kākutstha, the consecration prepared by me, preceded by rites and mantras performed by Vasiṣṭha and the other brāhmaṇas."
Thus addressed by Rāma, Śatrughna—endowed with heroic valour—was overcome by deep embarrassment and spoke slowly, word by word.
"O bull among men, your command must certainly be carried out; O greatly blessed one, your command is impossible to transgress. I am your willing servant, O king, O bull among men."
When the heroic and great-souled Śatrughna had spoken thus, the delighted Rāma addressed Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata.
"Bring with careful attention the materials for the consecration; today itself I shall consecrate this tiger among men, this invincible hero."
"O ye two of Kākutstha's line, by my command summon the chief priest, the city elders, the officiating priests, and all my ministers."
Knowing the king's command, the great chariot-warriors acted accordingly; placing the chief priest at their head and setting the consecration rites in motion, they entered the royal palace, which resembled the abode of Indra.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then the auspicious consecration of the great-souled Śatrughna grew in grandeur, bringing great rejoicing to Rāghava's city.
Then, seating the consecrated Śatrughna upon his lap, Rāghava spoke sweet words to him, filling him with radiant energy.
"This arrow of yours is unfailing and divine, the conqueror of enemy citadels; with this, O gentle one, O delight of Raghu's line, you shall slay Lavaṇa."
"This arrow, O Kākutstha, was fashioned when the self-born, unconquered god lay upon the great ocean—he whom neither gods nor asuras could behold."
"Invisible to all creatures, he—when overcome by wrath for the destruction of those two evil-souled ones, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were engaged in wreaking havoc—fashioned this supreme arrow, O hero."
"Desiring to create the three worlds, he slew those two in battle with this weapon; with this foremost of arrows, he then brought the worlds into being."
"This arrow was not released by me earlier when I sought to slay Rāvaṇa, O Śatrughna, lest great terror befall all creatures."
"And there is that great trident given by the mighty three-eyed god for the destruction of enemies—Madhu's supreme weapon."
"Having stored that weapon in his dwelling, worshipping it again and again, he ranges in all directions, surveying them, and thereby obtains food for himself."
"But when someone challenges him, desiring battle, then the rākṣasa seizes that trident and reduces the challenger to ashes."
"Therefore, O tiger among men, before he re-enters his citadel and while he is without his weapon, stand at the gateway bearing your arms."
"And when he has not yet entered his dwelling, O bull among men, O mighty-armed one, challenge him to battle; then you shall slay the rākṣasa."
"If it is done otherwise, he will be invincible; but if it is done in this manner, O hero, he will meet his destruction."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"All this has been explained to you, including the counter to the trident; for the deed of the glorious blue-throated one is impossible to transgress."
Having spoken thus to Kākutstha and praised him again and again, the delight of Raghu's line spoke yet further words.
"O bull among men, four thousand horses, two thousand chariots, and a hundred elephants—"
"—and market convoys adorned with goods of every kind, and likewise entertainers and dancers, let them accompany you, Śatrughna."
"Taking ten thousand pieces of silver and gold, go forth, O Śatrughna, O bull among men, abundantly supplied with wealth and conveyances."
"And the army, well-maintained, joyful, and well-fed, unsurpassed—O foremost of men, please and gratify them with kind words and generous gifts."
"For wealth does not abide there, nor wife, nor kinsmen—O Rāghava, only the corps of well-gratified servants endures."
"Therefore, having dispatched that great army thronging with rejoicing men, go you alone, bow in hand, to the forest of Madhu."
"So that Lavaṇa, son of Madhu, does not recognise you as you approach, seeking battle, go without arousing suspicion."
"For no other death exists for him, O bull among men; whoever comes to face him is surely slain by Lavaṇa."
"When the summer has passed and the rainy season is at hand, then slay Lavaṇa, O gentle one; for that is the time of this evil-minded one's vulnerability."
"Let your soldiers march with great sages at their head, so that with what remains of the summer season they may cross the waters of the Jāhnavī."
"Then, having stationed all the forces on the riverbank with composure, go forward yourself with bow in hand, O swift-striding one."
Thus instructed by Rāma, Śatrughna summoned those mighty commanders of the army and then addressed them with these words.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"These are your designated halting places, wherever you shall encamp; you must conduct yourselves without causing obstruction, so that no one is harassed."
Having given them such instruction and sent the great army forth, he paid his respects to Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and Kaikeyī.
Having circumambulated Rāma with reverential right-hand salutation and bowed his head to him, and having been given leave by his lord, Śatrughna the afflicitor of enemies—
—Śatrughna, of disciplined spirit and mighty strength, prostrated himself with joined palms before Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata, and then, having circumambulated the chief priest Vasiṣṭha, departed.
Having dispatched that entire army and himself halting only a month along the road, Śatrughna then went forward swiftly and alone with haste.
After halting for two nights along the way, the hero and delight of Raghu's line came to the holy hermitage of Vālmīki, that most excellent of abodes.
He greeted the great-souled Vālmīki, that foremost of sages, and then, standing with joined palms, spoke these words.
"O venerable one, I wish to stay here tonight; I have come hither on a task for my lord, and at dawn tomorrow I shall proceed toward the western quarter, the domain of Varuṇa."
Hearing Śatrughna's words, that bull among sages smiled and replied to the great-souled one: "Welcome to you, O greatly renowned one."
"This hermitage is verily the home of the Rāghava lineage, O gentle one; accept without hesitation the seat, the water for feet, and the guest-offering that I extend."
Then Kākutstha accepted the honour and ate the food of fruits and roots, and was filled with utmost satisfaction.
Having eaten, the mighty-armed one then asked the great sage: "In former times, to whose hermitage near here did the splendour of the sacrifice belong?"
Hearing that question of his, Vālmīki spoke these words: "O Śatrughna, listen—learn to whom this sacred precinct formerly belonged."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"An ancestor of your line, the son of the great-souled Sudāsa, named Mitrasaha—valiant and supremely righteous—"
"—this Saudāsa, even as a youth, took to the hunt; and the hero beheld a pair of rākṣasas prowling about."
"Terrible in the form of tigers, they were devouring many thousands of deer and yet were not satisfied, never reaching fullness."
"Seeing those two rākṣasas and finding the forest stripped of deer, he was seized by great wrath and slew one of them with a mighty arrow."
"Having struck down that one, Saudāsa the bull among men, his fever of rage spent and his fury gone, looked upon the slain rākṣasa."
"Seeing him gazing thus, the companion of that rākṣasa was filled with terrible anguish and spoke these words to Saudāsa:"
"'Because you have slain my companion who had committed no offence, therefore, O most wicked one, I shall repay you in kind.'"
"Having spoken thus, that rākṣasa vanished on the spot; and in the course of time King Mitrasaha came to reign."
"The king too performed a sacrifice—the great Aśvamedha sacrifice—near that hermitage; Vasiṣṭha supervised that ritual."
"There the great sacrifice lasting for many years and groups of years prospered with the highest splendour and was the equal of a sacrifice of the gods."
