"Then, at the close of the sacrifice, remembering his former enmity, the rākṣasa assumed the form of Vasiṣṭha and thus addressed the king:"
"'At the conclusion of the sacrifice today, let food containing meat be given to me quickly—there is to be no deliberation in this matter.'"
"Hearing those words spoken by the rākṣasa who could take any form at will, the lord of the earth—skilled in the preparation of food—addressed his cook:"
"'Prepare quickly a dish of oblation-food containing meat so as to be tasty, in such a way that the guru may be well pleased.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"At the command of the lord of kings, the cook—his mind agitated—went about his task; and that rākṣasa there again took on the disguise of the cook."
"He then presented human flesh to the king, announcing: 'This tasty oblation-food with meat has been brought.'"
"He brought that food—tampered with by the rākṣasa, O tiger among men—to present to Vasiṣṭha together with his wife Madayantī."
"The brahmin, knowing that the food brought was human flesh, was seized by great wrath and began to utter a curse."
"'Because you, O king, wish to give me this as food, therefore this food shall be yours—there is no doubt of this.'"
"That king, together with his wife, prostrated himself again and again and then explained to Vasiṣṭha what had been said by one who had assumed the form of a brahmin."
"Having heard the account of the lord of kings and that the matter had been distorted by the rākṣasa, Vasiṣṭha again addressed the king, that bull among men:"
"'This word I have uttered in the grip of rage cannot be made void; yet I shall grant you a boon:"
"'The duration of this curse shall be twelve years; and by my grace, O lord of kings, you shall not remember what has passed.'"
"Thus that king, the crusher of enemies, having endured that curse, regained his kingdom and thereafter protected his subjects."
"This auspicious precinct of the sacrifice of that Kalmāṣapāda is the one near this hermitage about which you ask, O Rāghava."
"Having heard that most terrible story of that lord of kings, and having paid his respects to the great sage, he entered the leaf-hut."
That very same night on which Śatrughna entered the leaf-hut, that very same night Sītā too gave birth to a pair of boys.
Then, at the middle of the night, the young disciples of the sage joyfully announced to Vālmīki the auspicious birth of Sītā's children: "O mighty one, perform for them the protective rite that dispels evil spirits."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing those words of theirs, the sage was filled with joy; and he performed for those two a protective rite with the demon-slaying, demon-destroying charm.
Taking a handful of kuśa grass and a blade of lava grass as well, the twice-born Vālmīki bestowed upon the two of them the protection that destroys evil spirits.
The one of the two born first was to be cleansed with kuśa grass consecrated by sacred mantras; and from this, his name shall be Kuśa.
And the other of the two, to be carefully cleansed by the elder women with a blade of lava grass — he shall bear the name Lava.
Thus those two, born as twins, shall be known by the names Kuśa and Lava — the two names bestowed by me — and they shall attain great renown.
Those pure-souled ones, composed and reverent, received the protective ritual from the sage's hand, and then those blameless ones duly performed the protective rite for the two infants.
Even as that protective rite was being performed, along with the recitation of lineage and name, and the glorification of Rāma's name, came the auspicious birth-sons of Sītā.
At midnight, Śatrughna, who had gone to the leaf-hut that night, heard the most welcome of tidings; he exclaimed, "How fortunate! How fortunate!"
And for that great-souled, overjoyed Śatrughna, the rainy-season night of Śrāvaṇa, light of step, quickly passed.
At dawn, the mighty hero completed his morning rituals, took leave of the sage with joined palms, and set out again, turning back westward.
Having journeyed to the bank of the Yamunā, he spent seven nights along the way, taking lodging in the hermitages of sages of holy renown.
There, together with the sages headed by Cyavana of the Bhārgava lineage, that greatly glorious king passed his time in many kinds of conversation.
When night had come, Śatrughna asked the brāhmaṇa Cyavana, joy of the Bhṛgu lineage, about the strength and weakness of Lavaṇa.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"What is the power of his trident, O brāhmaṇa? Who before now have been slain — who came to single combat at the point of this trident?"
Having heard those words of the great-souled Śatrughna, the mighty Cyavana replied to that scion of the Raghu line.
"His deeds are beyond counting, O bull among men. Hear from me what transpired at the rise of the Ikṣvāku dynasty."
"In Ayodhyā of old there was a mighty king, son of Yuvanāśva, renowned throughout the three worlds for his valor — known as Māndhātā."
"Having brought the entire earth under his dominion, that lord of the earth, the king, undertook a campaign to conquer the world of the gods."
"When Māndhātā set out with desire to conquer the celestial world, Indra and all the great-souled gods were seized with intense fear."
"Honored by the host of gods with half of Indra's throne and half of his kingdom, that king of earth mounted a solemn pledge."
"Knowing his sinful intention, the chastiser of Pāka, Indra, spoke these appeasing words to the son of Yuvanāśva."
"'You are a king in the human world, O bull among men — you desire the kingdom of the gods here without yet having made the entire earth obedient to you.'"
"'If, O hero, the entire earth, whole and complete, is truly under your sway, then rule over the kingdom of the gods here, together with your troops, forces, and conveyances.'"
"Then Māndhātā spoke these words to Indra as he spoke thus: 'Where on the face of the earth has my command been repelled, O Śakra?'"
"To him, the thousand-eyed one replied: 'Lavaṇa — a rākṣasa, son of Madhu, dwelling in the Madhu forest — does not observe your command, O sinless king.'"
"Hearing those harsh and unwelcome words spoken by Indra, the king was ashamed, bowed his head downward, and was unable to speak."
"Taking leave of the thousand-eyed Indra, the glorious lord of men returned somewhat shame-faced to this world below."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Harboring indignation in his heart, that blameless one came with his troops, forces, and conveyances to bring the son of Madhu under his power."
"Desiring to fight Lavaṇa, that bull among men dispatched a messenger to Lavaṇa's presence."
"The messenger went and spoke many harsh and unwelcome words to the son of Madhu; while speaking thus, that messenger was devoured by the rākṣasa."
"When the messenger was long delayed, the king, filled with wrath, assailed that rākṣasa on all sides with a shower of arrows."
"Then Lavaṇa laughed aloud, took his trident in hand, and hurled that supreme weapon to slay the king along with all his followers."
"That blazing trident reduced the king, together with his troops, forces, and conveyances, to ashes, and then returned once more to the hand of Lavaṇa."
"In this manner that great king was slain together with his forces and conveyances. The power of the trident, O hero, is immeasurable and unsurpassed."
"Tomorrow at dawn you shall without doubt slay Lavaṇa — catch him quickly before he takes up his weapon; victory is then certain for you."
As they conversed and eagerly awaited auspicious victory, the night passed quickly for that great-souled Śatrughna.
Then, at that bright and clear dawn, the rākṣasa warrior went out from the city, driven by hunger in search of prey.
Meanwhile, the heroic Śatrughna crossed the river Yamunā and stood at the gate of Madhupura, bow in hand.
Then, when midday had arrived, that cruel-deeded rākṣasa came back, bearing the weight of many thousands of living creatures.
Then he saw Śatrughna standing at the gate, holding his weapon. The rākṣasa then said to him: "What will you do with this?"
"Thousands like you, armed as you are, O basest of men, have been devoured by me in fury. Are you awaiting your appointed time?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"My meal today is also not yet complete, O most despicable of men. How have you, having come on your own, walked into my very mouth, O fool?"
As he spoke thus and laughed again and again, Śatrughna, full of valor, shed tears of rage.
From that great-souled Śatrughna, overcome by rage, rays of fiery energy blazed forth from every limb of his body.
And Śatrughna, deeply enraged, said to that night-wanderer: "I wish to fight you in single combat, O evil-minded one."
"I am the son of Daśaratha, the brother of the wise Rāma. My name is Śatrughna — Śatrughna, come here desiring your death."
"Let single combat be granted to me who desire battle. You are the enemy of all living beings — you shall not escape me alive."
While he spoke thus, the rākṣasa laughed aloud and replied to that foremost of men: "By good fortune you have come, O fool."
"My mother's sister's brother — the rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa — was slain by Rāma, O evil-minded one, for the sake of a woman, O basest of men."
"All of that — the destruction of Rāvaṇa's clan — I have endured, keeping contempt before me, especially toward you and your kind."
"All of you have not been slain — you are despised like blades of grass — those who exist, those who shall exist, and you too, O basest of men."
"To you who desire battle I shall give battle, O fool — the kind you desire — wait while I make ready my weapon."
Then Śatrughna said to him: "Where will you go from me alive? Even a weakened enemy who has come must not be released by a man of steadfast soul."
"For he who, with a confused mind, gives an enemy room to maneuver is destroyed by his own weak-mindedness, like a coward."
Hearing those words of the great-souled Śatrughna, Lavaṇa roused fierce anger and cried out repeatedly, "Stand! Stand!"
Slapping palm against palm and grinding his teeth, Lavaṇa challenged the tiger of the Raghu line again and again.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
To Lavaṇa of terrible valour who spoke thus, Śatrughna, destroyer of enemies, spoke these words.
"Śatrughna was not yet born when others were conquered by you; but today, struck by my arrow, go to the abode of Yama."
"Today, O evil-souled one, let the sages, the learned brāhmaṇas, and the gods witness you slain in battle by me, even as they witnessed Rāvaṇa."
"When you, O night-roamer, are scorched by my arrow and fallen today, this city and the countryside will be at peace."
"Today the arrow released from my arm, its face like a thunderbolt, will enter your lotus-heart as a ray enters that of the sun's son."
Addressed thus, Lavaṇa, swooning with rage, hurled a great tree at the chest of Śatrughna; the hero cut it to a hundred pieces.
Seeing that act rendered fruitless, the powerful rākṣasa seized a great many trees and hurled them again at Śatrughna.
The brilliant Śatrughna severed those many oncoming trees one by one with three or four arrows whose joints were smooth.
Then Śatrughna, endowed with valour, discharged a rain of arrows at the rākṣasa's body, yet the rākṣasa was not distressed.
Then Lavaṇa laughed and, uprooting a tree with ease, struck the hero on the head; his limbs went limp and he fell into a swoon.
When that hero fell, a great cry of "Ah! Ah!" arose from the hosts of sages, gods, Gandharvas, and Apsarases.
Disdaining Śatrughna, though struck down and prostrate on the earth, the rākṣasa, even with the opportunity secured, did not enter his own dwelling.
Nor did he take up his trident, seeing him fallen on the ground; thinking him slain, he then went off to gather his food.
But within a moment Śatrughna recovered consciousness and stood again, weapon in hand, at the rākṣasa's gate, honoured by the sages.
Then he took up that supreme, infallible, divine arrow — blazing with energy, terrible, filling all ten directions.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Its face was like a thunderbolt, its speed like a thunderbolt, its weight equal to Meru and Mandara; smooth at every joint, unconquered in all battles.
Its body smeared with blood-red sandalwood, with beautiful feathering; dreadful to lords of Dānavas, lords of mountains, and Asuras.
Seeing it blazing like the fire of Time arrived at the end of an age, all beings were overcome with terror.
The entire world — with gods, Asuras, Gandharvas, sages, and hosts of Apsarases — was uneasy and approached the Grandsire.
And they said to the god of gods, the boon-granting great-grandsire: "Has the dissolution of the worlds come, O god, or the conflagration of the age?"
"Such a thing has never been seen or heard before, O great-grandsire — the terror and bewilderment of the gods, the destruction of the worlds, O lord."
Hearing those words, Brahmā, the grandsire of the worlds, who dispels fear, declared to the gods the cause of their terror.
"For the slaying of Lavaṇa in battle, the arrow held by Śatrughna — by whose radiance all you best of gods have been bewildered —"
"— this is the primordial, eternal, radiant arrow of the god who created the worlds, dear ones, by which this fear has come upon you."
"This great arrow was created by that great-souled one for the sake of slaying Kaiṭabha and Madhu — for the destruction of those two Daityas."
"Know this to be the radiant arrow of Viṣṇu; and this Śatrughna is likewise the former body of that great-souled Viṣṇu."
"Go from here and witness the foremost of rākṣasas, Lavaṇa, being slain by the great-souled hero, the younger brother of Rāma."
Hearing those sweet words of the god of gods, they went to the place where Śatrughna and Lavaṇa were both fighting.
All beings saw that arrow, divine in appearance, held in Śatrughna's hand, risen like the conflagration at the end of an age.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Seeing the sky filled with gods, the son of Raghu's line roared repeatedly with the roar of a lion and beheld Lavaṇa once more.
Challenged by the great-souled Śatrughna, Lavaṇa, filled with rage, presented himself for battle.
Drawing that bow to his ear, that best of archers released the great arrow at Lavaṇa's broad chest; cleaving his chest swiftly, it entered the netherworld.
Having gone to the divine netherworld, that arrow, worshipped by the gods, swiftly returned again to the delight of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
Pierced through by Śatrughna's arrow, that night-roaming Lavaṇa fell suddenly to the ground like a mountain struck by the thunderbolt.
And that great divine trident, when the rākṣasa Lavaṇa was slain, in the sight of all beings, returned to the power of Rudra.
Having slain with a single arrow the terror of all three worlds, the foremost hero of Raghu's line shone forth with bow and arrow raised, even as the thousand-rayed sun dispels darkness.
When Lavaṇa was slain, the gods — with Indra at their head and Agni foremost among them — spoke sweet words to Śatrughna, scorcher of enemies.
"By good fortune is your victory, dear one; by good fortune the rākṣasa Lavaṇa is slain. O best among tigers of men, O Rāghava, ask a boon."
"We are all gathered here as granters of boons, O mighty-armed one, desiring your victory; indeed our vision is never without fruit."
Hearing the words of the gods, the valiant, great-armed Śatrughna, with hands joined above his head, replied with a disciplined mind.
"Let me quickly establish settlement in this lovely Madhupurī, sweet Madhurā, created by the gods — this let my boon be, so I think."
The gods, with hearts full of joy, said "So be it" to the Rāghava: "A lovely city it shall be — Śūrasenā, without doubt."
Having spoken thus, those great-souled ones ascended to heaven; and the greatly radiant Śatrughna brought up his army.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That army came quickly on hearing Śatrughna's command, and Śatrughna began the founding of the settlement by his decree.
That city, divine in appearance, auspicious, was established in the twelfth year, and the territory of the Śūrasenas became free from all fear.
The fields were full of crops, Indra rained in season, the people were free of disease and vigorous, protected by the arms of Śatrughna.
Shaped like a half-moon, graced by the bank of the Yamunā, adorned with foremost mansions, adorned with market squares and bazaars.
Whatever great emptiness had been made by Lavaṇa formerly, the hero beautified that with abundance of various commodities.
Śatrughna, the younger brother of Bharata, himself prosperous in wealth, surveyed that prosperous city and was supremely pleased, overcome with supreme joy.
The thought arose in his mind: having established the city of Madhurā, "I should behold the feet of Rāma in this auspicious twelfth year."
Then, in the twelfth year, Śatrughna desired to go to Ayodhyā, protected by Rāma, accompanied by a small retinue and force.
Having dismissed his ministers, the chiefs of the army, and the chaplain, he went in a splendid chariot harnessed with horses.
Traversing seven or eight calculated stages of travel, the son of Raghu's line quickly reached Ayodhyā, eager to behold the Rāghava.
Entering the lovely city, that glorious, great-armed delight of the Ikṣvāku line went to where the greatly resplendent Rāma was.
He saluted the great-souled one blazing as it were with energy, and standing with palms joined, spoke to Rāma of true valour.
"Whatever was commanded, O great king, all of that I have done: that wicked Lavaṇa is slain, and that city has been established."
"Twelve years have passed without you, O delight of Raghu's line; I could not bear to dwell separated from you, O king."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Grant me your favour, O Kākutstha, O you of boundless valour; without you I wander abroad like a calf bereft of its mother."
Embracing Śatrughna who spoke thus, Rāma said: "Do not grieve, O hero; this is not the conduct befitting a kṣatriya."
"Kings do not despair during sojourns abroad, O Rāghava; and subjects must be protected through the dharma of the kṣatriya, O Rāghava."
"Come to Ayodhyā to see me from time to time, O hero, O best of men, and then return to your own city."
"You are dearer to me even than life itself, without doubt; yet the protection of the kingdom must inevitably be carried out."
"Therefore, O Kākutstha, dwell with me for five nights; after that you shall go to Madhurā with your servants, army, and conveyances."
Hearing these words of Rāma, righteous and pleasing to the mind, Śatrughna said with a sorrowful voice, "So be it."
That mighty archer, the Kākutstha, having dwelt there five nights by the Rāghava's command, made ready for departure.
Having taken leave of the great-souled Rāma of true valour, and of Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa as well, he mounted his great chariot.
Accompanied for a long distance by the great-souled Lakṣmaṇa and by Bharata, Śatrughna then quickly went to his city.
Having dispatched Śatrughna along with his brothers, Rāghava rejoiced contentedly, governing the kingdom by righteousness.
Then, after a few days, an aged brahmin of the land came to the royal gate, bearing the corpse of a child.
Weeping, he uttered manifold words filled with tears of affection, crying out again and again, "My son, my son!"
"What evil deed did I commit in a former body in a previous life, that I now see you, my only son, gone to death?"
"A child who had not yet reached youth, only five years of age — you have met death untimely, for my grief, O my dear son."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Without doubt, within a few days I and your mother shall both go to death, slain by grief for you, O my son."
"I do not recall having spoken falsehood, nor do I recall having done harm — by what evil deed of mine has my son, while yet a child, been carried to the abode of Vaivasvata without having performed the rites due to his forefathers?"
"Never before have I seen or heard of so dreadful a sight — the death of those who have not yet reached their time, in Rāma's kingdom."
"Without doubt some great sin has been committed by Rāma. O king, restore this child to life who has fallen under the sway of death."
"O king of great might, may you attain long life together with your brothers. We have lived happily in your kingdom."
"Now the realm of the great-souled Ikṣvākus is left without a protector, having found in Rāma a king who brings about the death of children."
"The subjects perish through the faults of a king when they are not protected according to proper law; and when a king is of wicked conduct, people die before their time."
"When people in cities and in the countryside commit unlawful acts and there is no protection, then comes the calamity wrought by untimely death."
"This killing of a child — whether in the city or in the country — shall without doubt plainly prove to be the king's fault."
Thus, with many such words, again and again blaming the king, tormented by grief, he embraced his son.
Rāghava heard all of that pitiful lamentation of the brahmin, filled with pain and grief.
Deeply afflicted by sorrow, he summoned his ministers, Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, his brothers, and the guild leaders together.
Then eight brahmins were ushered in together with Vasiṣṭha; they said to the king, who was resplendent as a god, "May you be well."
They were Mārkaṇḍeya, Maudgalya, Vāmadeva, Kāśyapa, Kātyāyana, Jābāli, Gautama, and likewise Nārada.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
All these foremost among the twice-born were seated in the assembly fires, and the ministers and guild leaders likewise took their places as was fitting.
When all of them, blazing with splendor, had taken their seats, Rāghava related everything — the reason why the brahmin was weeping.
Hearing that speech of the distressed king, Nārada replied with an auspicious word to the king in the presence of the sages.
"Hear, O king, how this destruction of a child has come about in this age. Having heard, O hero, O delight of the Raghu line, do what must be done."
"In the Kṛta age of old, O Rāma, only brahmins were ascetics; in that age, O king, no one who was not a brahmin was an ascetic under any circumstances."
In that age, blazing with brahmic power, unclouded, all were immortal and far-sighted in birth.
Then came the age known as the Tretā, of embodied human beings, wherein kṣatriyas are born, endowed with the austerity of a prior birth.
Those great-souled humans who excelled by valor and austerity in a previous birth — it was they who lived in that Tretā age.
All that brahmin and kṣatriya order — whatever existed in both the earlier and the latter of those two ages — was of equal power and endowed with equal might.
Yet seeing no further special distinction therein, they then established everywhere the institution of the four varṇas.
Then adharma cast one foot upon the earth; and because the twice-born became associated with adharma, they grew dull.
Then a limit was established for the span of life, and people, devoted to truth and righteousness, practiced only virtuous deeds.
In the Tretā age, while brahmins and kṣatriyas practiced austerity, the remaining people rendered service.
That supreme dharma then came down to the vaiśya and śūdra; and śūdras especially performed worship on behalf of all the varṇas.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then adharma set down its second foot, and thereupon arose that age reckoned as the Dvāpara.
In that age numbered as the Dvāpara, as the yuga drew toward its end, adharma and untruth both increased, O bull among men.
In that same Dvāpara age, austerity entered into the vaiśyas; a śūdra does not attain the fierce austerity of dharma, O bull among men.
One born in a lower varṇa, O best of men, will practice very great austerity — for the practice of austerity by those born in a śūdra womb shall come in the Kali age."
"Supreme adharma in the Dvāpara, O Rāma, rests upon a śūdra. Indeed, O king, at the border of your realm there is a śūdra of wicked mind practicing great austerity — it is because of him that this death of a child has come about."
"For whatever wicked-minded man commits adharma or an unlawful act in the realm of a king, whether in the city — that man quickly goes to hell, as does the king himself, without doubt."
"Therefore, O tiger among men, search your own realm; wherever you find wrongdoing, there make every effort to act."
"Thus there shall be for you an increase of dharma, a lengthening of people's lifespan, O best of men, and the restoration of life to this child."
Having heard Nārada's words, which were as if full of nectar, he felt incomparable joy, and spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Go, dear Lakṣmaṇa, comfort the foremost brahmin, and place that child's body in a vessel of oil."
"With the most excellent fragrant substances and with sweet-smelling oils, let it be arranged, dear one, so that the child does not deteriorate."
"Act in such a way that no decay or decomposition comes to the body of the child who is thus preserved, O one of unblemished deeds."
Having so instructed Lakṣmaṇa of auspicious marks, the great-famed Kākutstha, the scion of Kākutstha's line, mentally called upon the Puṣpaka, thinking, "Come."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Understanding that sign, the golden-adorned Puṣpaka came within a moment to the presence of Rāghava.
Bowing down, it said: "Here I am, O lord of men. I, your obedient servant, am present, O mighty-armed one."
Hearing the pleasant words of Puṣpaka, the lord of men saluted those great sages and boarded the celestial chariot.
Taking his bow, his quiver, and his sword of brilliant radiance, having left in the city both heroes — Saumitri and Bharata —
— he set out toward the west, searching the desert regions on all sides, and then the glorious one went to the northern direction, girt by the Himālayas.
Finding not even the slightest wrongdoing there either, the lord of men then surveyed the entire eastern direction as well.
Then that son of a royal sage advanced toward the southern direction, and on the northern slope of mount Śaivala he saw a very great lake.
In that lake, the glorious Rāghava saw an ascetic performing very great austerity, hanging with his face downward.
Approaching him as he practiced the highest austerity, Rāghava spoke these words: "You are blessed, O observer of good vows."
"In what womb were you born, O firm and courageous one, that you advance in austerity? I ask you out of curiosity — I am Rāma, son of Daśaratha."
"What is the desired object you have in mind — the attainment of heaven, or the obtaining of a boon? What purpose have you taken refuge in, for which this austerity has been performed? I wish to hear, O ascetic."
"Are you a brahmin — blessings to you — or an invincible kṣatriya? Are you a vaiśya, or are you a śūdra? Tell me the truth of this."
Hearing that speech of Rāma, whose deeds are effortless, the one who had been standing with bowed head in that same posture now spoke these words.
"I was born in the womb of a Śūdra woman, and I have undertaken fierce austerity. O Rāma of great renown, I seek to attain divinity in this very body."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I speak no falsehood, O king, in my desire to conquer the world of gods. Know me to be a Śūdra, O Kākutstha; by name I am called Śambūka."
While that Śūdra was still speaking, Rāghava drew his sword of beautiful brilliance, bright and pure from its scabbard, and severed his head.
At that very moment, the boy was reunited with life.
Then Rāma, lotus-eyed, went to the hermitage of Agastya, and having bowed to him with proper reverence, rejoiced happily.
Having saluted the great-souled sage who blazed as if with splendor, that lord of men received the highest hospitality and sat down.
The greatly resplendent Kumbhayoni, of great austerity, said to him: "Welcome to you, O best of men; by good fortune you have come, O Rāghava."
"You are held in great esteem by me, O Rāma, for your many excellent virtues; you are a guest worthy of honor, O king, and you dwell in my heart."
"The gods indeed speak of you as having arrived as the slayer of the Śūdra; and in accordance with the duty owed to a Brāhmaṇa, you have restored his son to life."
"Let one night be spent here in my presence, O Rāghava; at dawn you shall go to your own city in the Puṣpaka."
"And this ornament, O gentle one, fashioned by Viśvakarmā, divine, blazing with its own brilliance in divine form — accept it, O Kākutstha; do what is dear to me, O Rāghava."
"For the gift of something already given is said to yield very great fruit; therefore I shall present it according to due rite — receive it, O bull among men."
Then Rāma accepted from that great-souled sage the divine and wondrous ornament, blazing like the sun.
Having received that excellent ornament, Rāma then proceeded to ask about the origin of that divine object.
"This is most wondrous, O Brahman, endowed with an excellent form — how did the revered one come to possess it, and whence, and by whom was it brought?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Out of curiosity I ask you, O Brahman of great renown; for you are indeed the supreme treasury of many marvels."
When Kākutstha spoke thus, the sage then replied: "Hear, O Rāma, the full account of what happened long ago in the Tretā age that has passed."
"Long ago in the Tretā age there was a forest of great extent, one hundred yojanas in every direction, devoid of beasts and free of birds."
"While performing supreme austerity in that uninhabited forest, O gentle Rāma, I came to traverse that wilderness."
"The appearance of that forest was impossible to describe: it had fruits and roots of delicious taste, and trees of many varieties."
"In the middle of that forest was a lake extending a yojana, filled with lotuses and blue water-lilies, and completely free of algae."
"It was as if a supreme wonder, of incomparable delightfulness, free of dust, likewise undisturbed, adorned with flocks of beautiful birds."
"Near that lake was a great and wondrous hermitage, ancient, exceedingly holy, and utterly devoid of any ascetics."
"There I spent a night of the hot season, O bull among men; rising early at dawn I approached that lake."
"Then I beheld a corpse there, plump and ageless, standing somewhere at that body of water in great splendor, O king."
"Pondering that matter, O Rāghava, I stood for a moment on the bank of the lake thinking: 'What can this be?' O lord."
"Then after a moment I saw a divine and wonderful sight: an aerial chariot of supreme magnificence, yoked with swans, swift as thought."
"In that chariot, O joy of the Raghu line, O hero, a heavenly being of great distinction was attended by a thousand celestial nymphs adorned with divine ornaments; some sang charming songs while others played instruments."
"As I watched, O Rāma, O joy of the Raghu line, that heavenly being descended from the aerial chariot and began to eat that corpse."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then, having eaten as much flesh as he desired, in abundance and with full satisfaction, the heavenly being descended and proceeded to touch the water of the lake."
"Having performed his ablutions in the proper manner, that heavenly being, O bull among men, proceeded to ascend his excellent and supreme aerial chariot."
"Seeing him who resembled a god ascending, O bull among men, I then spoke these words to him."
"'Who are you, O one who resembles a god? And why do you partake of this reprehensible food, O gentle one? You ought to explain the purpose of this.'"
"'It is a wonder that one of such nature — resplendent, honored among the gods — should take reprehensible food, O gentle one; I wish to hear the truth of this.'"
"Having eaten and hearing my auspicious words, O Rāma, O joy of the Raghu line, that heavenly being replied with joined palms:"
"'Hear, O Brahman, the full account of this matter of my joy and sorrow, which is indeed difficult to transcend, since you ask me, O twice-born one.'"
"'In former times there was a king of the Vidarbha country, my father of great renown, known as Sudeva, mighty in the three worlds.'"
"'He had two sons born of two wives, O Brahman; I am known as Śveta, while the younger was Suratha.'"
"'When my father had gone to heaven, the citizens consecrated me; there I governed the kingdom with righteousness and complete composure.'"
"'Thus thousands of years passed, O one of excellent vows, O Brahman, as I administered the kingdom and protected the subjects with righteousness.'"
"'When for some reason I came to know my lifespan, O best of twice-born ones, I placed the law of Time in my heart and then went to the forest.'"
"'I entered this difficult forest, devoid of beasts and birds, to practice austerity near the blessed lake.'"
"'Having consecrated my brother Suratha as lord of men over the kingdom, I reached this lake and performed austerity for a long time.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'After performing three thousands of years of most arduous austerity, O great sage, I attained the unsurpassed world of Brahmā.'"
"'Then, while I was dwelling in heaven, O best of twice-born ones, O supremely noble one, hunger and thirst tormented me; and so my senses were afflicted.'"
"'Going to the Grandfather, best of the three worlds, I said: "O revered one, is not this Brahmaloka free from hunger and thirst?"'"
"'"By what deed is this attained? I am subject to hunger and thirst — what is my food, O god? Tell me that, O Grandfather."'"
"'Then the Grandfather said to me: "O son of Sudeva, your food is the sweet flesh of your own body — eat of that perpetually."'"
"'"The body nourished by you while performing supreme austerity grows back without ever having been planted, O Śveta of great mind — it never fails to regenerate."'"
"'"You made not even the smallest gift in that forest inhabited by living creatures; therefore, O dear child, even having gone to heaven you are tormented by hunger and thirst."'"
"'"Therefore eat your own excellent body, well nourished by your austerities, whose essence is like ambrosia — that will bring you satisfaction."'"
"'"When, O Śveta, the great and invincible sage Agastya comes to traverse that forest, then you will be released from this ordeal."'"
"'"For he is capable of rescuing even the hosts of gods, O gentle one — how much more so you, O mighty-armed one, who have fallen under the sway of hunger and thirst!"'"
"'Thus I, having heard the determination of the revered god of gods, take my reprehensible food — my own body — O best of twice-born ones.'"
"'For many groups of years, O Brahman, O brahmarṣi, this body that I eat does not diminish, and my satisfaction is also complete.'"
"'Release me, who am in this distressful plight, from this ordeal; for there is no refuge for others here except the twice-born Kumbhayoni.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'Accept this ornament, O gentle one, O best of twice-born ones, for the purpose of my deliverance; O brahmarṣi, you ought to show grace.'"
"I, having heard those words of that heavenly being filled with sorrow, accepted that excellent ornament for the purpose of his deliverance."
"When that auspicious ornament was accepted by me, the former human body of that royal sage perished then and there."
"When that body had perished, that royal sage — satisfied and filled with great joy, the king delighted — departed once more to the triple heaven."
"That divine and wondrous ornament was given to me, for that reason, by him who is equal to Indra, O Kākutstha."
Having heard that most wondrous speech of Agastya, the Rāghava, out of both reverence and amazement, began to inquire further.
"Blessed one, that dreadful forest where Śveta, the king of Vidarbha, practises austerities — how did it come to be devoid of deer and birds?
That forest has become utterly lifeless, empty, and abandoned by men; yet he entered it to perform ascetic practice. I desire to hear the truth of this."
Having heard Rāma's words filled with curiosity, that supremely resplendent one began to speak.
"Long ago, Rāma, in the Kṛta age, there was the lord Manu, wielder of the rod of punishment. His great son was Ikṣvāku, the increaser of the lineage.
Placing that son in the ancestral kingdom on earth, that unconquerable realm, he said: 'Be the founder of royal lineages upon the earth.'
And that was assented to by the son, pledging 'so be it' to his father, O Rāghava. Then Manu, greatly delighted, spoke again.
'I am pleased; you are a doer of the most excellent deeds — of this there is no doubt. Protect the subjects by the rod of chastisement, but do not apply the rod without cause.'
'The punishment that is inflicted upon erring men, when it is administered lawfully and duly, leads the king to heaven.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'Therefore, O mighty-armed one, be diligent in the matter of the rod of punishment, my son; for in so doing the highest dharma in the world will accrue to you.'
Having thus instructed his son at length with composure, Manu departed joyfully to the triple heaven, to the unsurpassed world of Brahmā.
After Manu had departed to heaven, the boundlessly radiant Ikṣvāku became absorbed in the thought: 'How shall I beget sons?'
By various and manifold acts, that son of Manu, righteous in soul, begot one hundred sons resembling the sons of gods.
Of all of them the youngest, dear child, O Delight of the Raghu line, was foolish, unlearned, and did not serve his elders obediently.
His father gave him the name Daṇḍa, that one of little lustre, saying: 'Surely the falling of the rod of punishment upon his body will come to pass.'
Seeing that dreadful fault in his son, O Rāghava, O Subduer of Foes, Ikṣvāku gave him a kingdom between the Vindhya and the Śaivala mountains.
Daṇḍa became king there on that beautiful mountain terrain, and he founded a matchless, superb city, O Rāma.
He gave the city the name Madhumanta, O lord, and he chose the virtuous Uśanas as his royal chaplain.
Thus that king governed his kingdom together with his chaplain, thronged with joyful people, like the kingdom of the gods in heaven.
Having narrated this to Rāma, the great seer born of the water-jar proceeded in this same tale to speak another word.
Then that Daṇḍa, O descendant of Kākutstha, that dull-minded one, ruled his kingdom there for many thousands of years, with its enemies subdued.
Then at a certain time, the king approached the charming hermitage of Bhārgava in the pleasant month of Caitra.
There Daṇḍa saw the daughter of Bhārgava, incomparable in beauty upon the earth, wandering in a secluded part of the forest, that most excellent one.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That one of very dull wit, seeing her and smitten by the arrow of the bodiless god of love, approached her in great agitation and spoke these words to the maiden.
'From where are you, O fair-hipped one? Whose daughter are you, O auspicious one? Tormented by the bodiless god, I ask you, O slender-waisted one.'
To him speaking thus, that lustful one maddened by delusion, the daughter of Bhārgava replied to the king with these gentle, conciliatory words.
'Know me as the daughter of Bhārgava, that divine one of unwearied actions; I am the eldest, called Arajā, dwelling in the hermitage, O king of kings.'
'My father is your elder and teacher, O king of kings, and you are a pupil of that great-souled one; he is a great ascetic who, when angered, would bring very great calamity upon you.'
'If anything is to be done with me in a righteous manner, on the proper path, then, O best of kings, seek my father's consent — that one of great radiance.'
'Otherwise a dreadful consequence would befall you; for my father in his wrath could burn up even the three worlds.'
Thus addressed by Arajā, Daṇḍa, pierced by the arrow of desire, intoxicated with passion, replied, placing his joined hands upon his head.
'Show me favour, O fair-hipped one; you should not waste the moment. On your account my very life is being torn asunder, O one of auspicious face.'
'Even death or dreadful sin upon obtaining you — honour me who am devoted, O timid one, devoted and utterly overwhelmed.'
Having spoken thus to the maiden, that mighty one seized her by force with his arms, and as she struggled, he proceeded to violate her according to his desire.
Having committed that great outrage, most terrible and cruel, Daṇḍa quickly went back to his superb city of Madhumanta.
And Arajā too, weeping, waited in great terror not far from the hermitage for her father, that one resembling a god.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
After a short while the divine seer of boundless radiance, accompanied by his disciples, hungry and afflicted, returned to his own hermitage.
He saw Arajā, dejected, covered with dust, like moonlight obscured by the red glow of dawn, no longer shining.
Wrath arose in him, especially since he was afflicted with hunger, as if burning up the three worlds, and he spoke these words to his disciples.
'Behold the calamity of the perverted Daṇḍa who has not known his own self — terrible to behold, like an enraged tongue of fire.'
'Destruction has come upon this evil-minded, wicked-souled one together with his retinue — he who desires to touch the blazing flame of the sacred fire.'
'Because he has committed such a dreadful-to-behold sin, therefore that dull-minded one shall reap the fruit of his sinful deed.'
'Within seven nights that king, that evil-minded one, doer of sinful deeds, together with his servants, army, and conveyances, shall meet his death.'
'The kingdom of this evil-minded one, a hundred yojanas in every direction, shall be burnt up by the great rain of dust sent by the Chastiser of Pāka.'
'All beings here, both the stationary and the moving, shall entirely perish by the great rain of dust.'
'The entirety of Daṇḍa's kingdom shall become invisible as if turned to dust within seven nights.'
Having spoken thus, burning with wrath, he said to the people dwelling in that hermitage: 'Let them remain at the borders of the realm.'
Having heard the word of Uśanas, those people dwelling in the hermitage departed from his kingdom and took up residence outside it.
Having spoken thus to the assembly of sages, he said to Arajā: 'Remain here, O one of lovely limbs, in the hermitage, with a composed mind.'
'This lake, extending a yojana in compass, of most lovely radiance, enjoy it, O Arajā, free from grief, and let the time be awaited here.'

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
'And whatever beings come to dwell near you on that night, they shall be forever exempt from destruction by the rain of dust.'
Having spoken thus, Bhārgava went to take up residence elsewhere. Within seven days it was reduced to ashes, as had been declared by that speaker of sacred truth.
That kingdom of Daṇḍa on the ridges of the Vindhya and Śaivala mountains was cursed long ago by that brahmarṣi when that transgression of dharma was committed.
'From that time forward, O descendant of Kākutstha, it is called the Daṇḍaka forest; where ascetics dwelt, and where there was Janasthāna.'
'All that you asked of me, O Rāghava, has been told. The time for performing the twilight devotion passes, O hero; it must not be neglected.'
'All these great seers with their water vessels filled stand on all sides; having performed the water rite, they attend upon the sun, O tiger among men.'
'Attended upon by those seers together, those best of brahman-knowers, the sun has set, O Rāma; go and touch the water.'"
Heeding the sage's word, Rāma set out to perform the twilight rite at the sacred lake frequented by the apsarases.
Having touched the water there and performed the evening twilight observance, Rāma entered the hermitage of the great-souled Kumbhayoni — Agastya, born of a jar.
For him Agastya prepared abundantly rich fruits, roots, medicinal herbs, and pure pot-herbs for the evening meal.
That foremost of men ate of that food resembling nectar, and, gratified and fully content, spent that night there.
Rising early at dawn, having performed his daily morning duties, the best of the Raghu line — the subduer of foes — approached the sage to take his leave.
Saluting the great sage born of the kumbha — the jar — Rāma said: "I take my leave of you; I shall depart. Be pleased to give me your permission."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I am blessed, I have been favoured by the sight of the great-souled one. And I shall come here again to behold you, for the purification of my own self."
As the descendant of Kākutstha spoke these words, wondrous to behold, the sage rich in austerities, whose eye is dharma, answered in utmost delight:
"This speech of yours, O Rāma, is altogether wonderful, auspicious in every syllable. You yourself, O joy of the Raghu line, are the purifier of all worlds."
"Those beings who behold you even for a single moment, O Rāma, are purified and become as heaven itself; they are worshipped by the gods in the celestial realm."
"But those living beings on earth who gaze upon you with hostile eyes are struck down forthwith by the rod of Yama and go directly to hell."
"Go then, untroubled, upon a path free from all peril. Rule your kingdom by dharma, for you are the very refuge of the world."
Thus addressed by the sage, the wise king, composed and with palms joined in reverence, paid obeisance to that sage of holy conduct.
After reverencing the foremost among sages and all those who were rich in austerities, the unperturbed hero ascended that Puṣpaka chariot adorned with gold.
As he departed, the hosts of sages honoured him on all sides with blessings, as the immortals honour thousand-eyed Indra blazing like Mahendra.
Serene, Rāma was a sight to behold upon the gold-adorned Puṣpaka, like the moon stationed near a cloud in the season of rain.
Then, when midday had arrived, honoured from every quarter, the descendant of Kākutstha reached Ayodhyā and descended from the aerial car.
Then, having dismissed the beautiful Puṣpaka that travels at will, Rāma addressed a doorkeeper stationed in the inner courtyard:
"Go to Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata — both of swift step — inform them of my arrival and then announce me for a long while."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing that speech of Rāma — whose deeds cause no affliction — the doorkeeper summoned the two princes and reported it to the descendant of Raghu.
Seeing the beloved Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa arrive, the descendant of Raghu — Rāma — embraced them and then spoke these words:
"I have duly performed the most excellent duty owed to the twice-born; yet I wish to build the bridge of dharma still further, O descendants of Raghu."
"Together with you two, who are as my own selves, I desire to perform the most excellent Rājasūya sacrifice — for therein eternal dharma resides."
"Mitra, the destroyer of foes, having sacrificed at the Rājasūya with well-offered oblations and a well-conducted rite, attained the sovereignty of Varuṇa."
"And Soma too, knower of dharma, having sacrificed rightly by the Rājasūya, attained everlasting glory among all worlds and an eternal station."
"Whatever is most beneficial on this day — let it be deliberated together with me; what is wholesome, what is fitting — you should speak freely, with care."
Having heard these words of the descendant of Raghu, Bharata — skilled in the art of speech — joined his palms together and spoke these words:
"In you, O virtuous one, dharma supreme resides; in you the entire earth is established, O mighty-armed one; and in you rests glory, O you of immeasurable valour."
"All the great-souled guardians of the earth look to you as the immortals look to Prajāpati — as the lord of worlds — just as we do."
"And the subjects regard you as a father, O great-powered king; you are the refuge on this earth for all living beings, O descendant of Raghu."
"How can you, O king, perform such a sacrifice in which the destruction of royal lineages throughout the earth is foreseen?"
"Those men of prowess upon the earth, O king — for all of them there will be destruction there, like the universal dissolution at the end of all things."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You, O tiger among men, of matchless valour and virtue — you should not destroy the earth, for it stands already under your sway."
Hearing those words of Bharata, sweet as nectar, Rāma of true valour was filled with incomparable joy.
And he spoke an auspicious word to the one who increased Kaikeyī's delight: "I am pleased, I am fully content by your speech today."
"This word spoken by you, O tiger among men, is without feebleness, grounded in dharma, and is truly the protection of the earth."
"From that intention, O knower of dharma, I now desist from the Rājasūya, that best of sacrifices, indeed by virtue of your well-spoken words."
"The protection of subjects is the dharma of kings, equal in worth to sacrifice. Therefore I heed your word, well and wisely spoken."
While Rāma was speaking thus and Bharata, the great-souled one, had spoken, Lakṣmaṇa too spoke an auspicious word to the joy of the Raghu line:
"The Aśvamedha — the great sacrifice, purifier of all sins — let that foremost of rites find favour with you, O invincible one; it shall purify you too."
"For it is heard in the tradition of former times that the great-souled Vāsava — Śakra — when enveloped by the sin of brahmanicide, was purified by the Aśvamedha."
"In ancient times, O mighty-armed one, there was in the great gathering of gods and asuras a great Daitya named Vṛtra, revered by all the worlds."
"A hundred yojanas in breadth and three times that in height, he regarded the three worlds with affection and looked upon all with tender love."
"Knowing dharma and knowing gratitude, perfected in intellect, he ruled all the earth steadily by dharma."
"While he was reigning, the earth yielded all desires; roots and fruits were produced full of nourishment."
"The earth ripened without tilling, abundantly rich; that great-souled one enjoyed a kingdom so prosperous and wondrous to behold."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Then a resolve arose in his mind: I shall practise the most excellent austerity, for austerity is the highest good, austerity is the highest bliss."
"Entrusting his eldest son as supreme lord over the citizens, he undertook fierce austerity, scorching all the gods with its heat."
"While Vṛtra was performing austerities, Vāsava, exceedingly troubled, approached Viṣṇu and spoke these words:"
"'By his austerities, O mighty-armed one, the worlds have been conquered by Vṛtra; he is powerful and virtuous in soul — I am not able to vanquish him."
"'If he continues his austerities still further, O lord of gods, then as long as the worlds endure they will be subject to his sway."
"'And you, of immense power, hold this most magnanimous one in disregard — yet Vṛtra would not last even a moment were you wrathful, O lord of gods."
"'For ever since I entered into the bond of friendship with you, O Viṣṇu, I have obtained from that time forward the lordship over all the worlds."
"'You then, O one of surpassing glory, extend your grace to the worlds; for by your action the entire universe would become at peace and free from decay."
"'All these dwellers in heaven look to you, O Viṣṇu; by the great slaying of Vṛtra render them your aid."
"'For you have always rendered aid to these great-souled ones; this burden is unbearable for others — you are the refuge of those who have no other refuge.'"
Having heard those words of Lakṣmaṇa, the destroyer of enemies [Rāma] said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Recount to me in full the slaying of Vṛtra."
Thus addressed by Rāghava, Lakṣmaṇa — the increaser of Sumitrā's joy — once again narrated the divine tale.
Having heard the words of the thousand-eyed Indra and of all the celestials, Viṣṇu addressed all the gods, with Indra at their head, saying:
"I was formerly bound in friendship with the great-souled Vṛtra; therefore, for the sake of your welfare, I will not myself slay the great asura.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Yet the highest good of all of you must certainly be accomplished; therefore I shall declare the means by which you shall slay Vṛtra.
I shall divide myself into three parts, O best of gods; by that means the thousand-eyed one shall slay Vṛtra — of this there is no doubt.
One portion shall enter Vāsava [Indra], the second shall enter the thunderbolt itself, and the third shall enter the earth; thus Śakra shall slay Vṛtra."
When the lord of the gods spoke thus, the gods then replied: "It shall be exactly as you say — there is no doubt — O slayer of the daityas."
"May it be well with you; we shall go, intent on slaying the asura Vṛtra. Do you bestow your own energy upon the supremely noble Vāsava."
Then all those great-souled ones, with the thousand-eyed Indra at their head, advanced into that forest where the great asura Vṛtra dwelled.
They beheld that foremost of asuras blazing with his own radiance, as though drinking up the three worlds and burning the very sky.
At the very sight of that foremost asura the gods were seized with terror, [wondering:] "How shall we slay him? How shall we avoid defeat?"
While they stood there deliberating, Sahasrākṣa Purandara grasped the thunderbolt with both arms and hurled it at the head of Vṛtra.
As though scorched by the dreadful fire of cosmic dissolution blazing with great flames, the world was terrified when [the thunderbolt] struck Vṛtra's head.
Contemplating that inconceivable slaying of Vṛtra, the lord of the wise gods — the greatly renowned one — quickly fled to the far end of the world.
The sin of Brahmin-slaughter [brahmahatyā] followed swiftly after that fleeing Indra and fell upon his limbs; grief entered into that Indra.
The gods, their foe slain but their Indra vanished, with Agni at their head, praised Viṣṇu — the best of the three worlds — again and again.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"You are the supreme refuge, O god; you are the primordial lord of the universe; you have attained the state of Viṣṇu for the benefit and sustenance of all beings."
"And this Vṛtra has been slain by you; yet the sin of Brahmin-slaughter afflicts Vāsava. O tiger among gods, prescribe the means of his liberation."
Hearing those words of the gods, Viṣṇu said: "Let Śakra worship me alone; I shall purify the wielder of the thunderbolt."
"Having worshipped me with the meritorious horse-sacrifice, Pākaśāsana [Indra] shall regain the sovereignty over the gods, free from fear from any quarter."
Having thus instructed the gods with those nectar-like words, Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods, departed to the highest heaven while being hymned with praises.
Having thus fully narrated the entire slaying of Vṛtra, that best of men, Lakṣmaṇa, proceeded to take up the remainder of the tale.
Then, with the mighty Vṛtra — who had been the terror of the gods — slain, Śakra, the slayer of Vṛtra, was enveloped in the sin of Brahmin-slaughter and could not recover his senses.
Having sought refuge at the end of the worlds, bereft of awareness and consciousness, he dwelt there for some time, writhing like a serpent.
Then, with Sahasrākṣa [Indra] disappeared, the world became filled with distress; the earth appeared devastated, without moisture, with dried-up forests.
The clouds shed no water, the lakes and rivers alike ran dry, and there was upheaval among all creatures, caused by the absence of rain.
While this world was wasting away, the gods, their minds agitated, set about performing that sacrifice which Viṣṇu had previously prescribed.
Then all the hosts of gods, together with their preceptors and the sages, went in a body to that place where Indra lay stupefied by terror.
Seeing Sahasrākṣa stupefied by the sin of Brahmin-slaughter, they placed him at their head and performed the horse-sacrifice on behalf of the lord of the gods.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then that great horse-sacrifice of the great-souled Mahendra grew and flourished for the purpose of purifying him from the sin of Brahmin-slaughter, O lord of men.
Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the Brahmin-slaughter [brahmahatyā] of the great-souled one approached [the gods] and said: "Where shall you assign me a dwelling place?"
Then the gods, satisfied and filled with delight, said to her: "Divide yourself into four parts of your own accord, O formidable one."
Having heard the words of the great-souled gods, Brahmin-slaughter, the dreadful one, sought to choose a different abode in their presence.
"With one portion I shall dwell in rivers swollen with water; with a second portion in trees — I tell you this as truth."
"This third portion of mine shall dwell in women in the flush of youth, for the three nights [of their monthly season] when they are intoxicated with pride — I, the destroyer of pride."
"Those who deliberately slay Brahmins that are blameless — with that fourth portion shall I take refuge in them, O bulls among gods."
The gods then replied to her: "Let it all be exactly as you say, O terrible one; accomplish what you desire."
Then the gods, filled with joy, paid homage to Sahasrākṣa; and Vāsava became free from fever and purified of sin.
And when Sahasrākṣa was reinstated, the entire world became calm; then Śakra duly honored that wondrous sacrifice.
"Such indeed is the power of the horse-sacrifice, O joy of the Raghu lineage; do you, O greatly blessed sovereign, perform the horse-sacrifice."
Having heard those words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, the greatly resplendent Rāghava, skilled in speech, replied with a smile.
"It is exactly so, O best of men, just as you say, Lakṣmaṇa — [you have narrated] the full account of the slaying of Vṛtra and whatever is the fruit of the horse-sacrifice."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For it is heard, O gentle one, that in former times there was a son of Kardama Prajāpati — Ila by name, the lord of the Bāhlīkas, glorious and supremely righteous."
"That greatly renowned king, having brought the entire earth under his sway, governed his kingdom like a father cares for his son, O tiger among men."
"By the supremely noble gods, by the daityas and the great asuras, by the nāgas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and the great-souled yakṣas —"
"— he was constantly honored by them all, stricken with fear, O gentle one, O joy of the Raghu lineage; and the three worlds trembled before that great-souled one when he was wrathful."
"Such was that king — steadfast in righteousness and valor, supremely noble in intellect, the greatly renowned lord of the Bāhlīkas."
"That long-armed one set out on a hunt in a beautiful forest during the delightful month of Caitra, together with his retinue, army, and elephants."
"That king slew deer in the forest by the hundreds of thousands; yet even having slain so many, that great-souled king felt no satisfaction."
"While ten thousand beasts of various kinds were being slain by that great-souled one, he came upon the region where great Skanda [Mahāsena] was born."
"In that place, Hara — the lord of the lords of gods — was sporting with Pārvatī [the daughter of the mountain king] together with all his formidable attendants."
"The lord of Umā, he whose banner bears the bull, having transformed himself into a woman, desiring to please the goddess, [dwelt] in that mountain cascade."
"And whatever creatures there were in that region of the forest that were called male, and whatever else existed there — all of it became feminine in nature."
"Meanwhile, the king Ila, son of Kardama, slaying thousands of deer, arrived at that very region."
"He saw that everything there — serpents, deer, and birds — had been made feminine, and that he himself along with his retinue had likewise become female, O joy of the Raghu lineage."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"He was seized with great grief on seeing himself reduced to such a state, and knowing it to be the act of Umāpati [Śiva], he was overcome with terror."
"Then the king, together with his retinue, army, and elephants, took refuge with that great-souled god — the blue-throated one, Kapardī [Śiva with matted locks]."
"Then the boon-granting one, greatly renowned, smiling and together with the goddess, himself spoke these words to the son of Prajāpati:"
"'Arise, arise, O royal seer, O son of Kardama, O greatly powerful one! Choose a boon, O gentle one of good vows — any boon except manhood [itself].'"
"Then that king, afflicted with grief, having been refused by the great-souled one, did not accept any other boon from that best of gods, while remaining in female form."
"Then, with great grief, the king prostrated himself before Mahādevī — the daughter of the king of mountains — with his whole inner self."
"'You are the sovereign and bestower of boons upon the worlds, O beautiful one; O goddess of unerring vision, O gentle one, I adore you — homage be to you!'"
"Knowing what was in the heart of that royal seer, the goddess — honored by Rudra — spoke these auspicious words in the presence of Hara:"
"'The god grants boons of one half, and I likewise grant boons of the other half; therefore take the half boon [available from me] — alternating between womanhood and manhood for as long as you wish.'"
"Having heard that most wondrous and unsurpassed boon from the goddess, the king, his mind filled with great delight, then spoke:"
"'If you, O goddess — peerless in beauty on earth — are pleased with me, then [may I] having passed one month in womanhood, again become a man for one month.'"
"Knowing his desire, the goddess of lovely countenance spoke these auspicious words: 'So shall it be.'"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"'O king, when you are in the form of a man you shall not remember your female existence, and when you are in the form of a woman for the other month you shall not remember your manhood.'"
"Thus that king, the son of Kardama, having been a man for one month, became for one month a woman beautiful as the three worlds — she became Ilā."
Having heard that tale connected with Ilā, as narrated by Rāma, both Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata were filled with the utmost wonder.
With folded hands they asked Rāma once more to tell them in full detail about the nature of that great-souled king's condition.
How did that king endure his wretched state when he had become a woman? And when he became a man again, how did he conduct himself?
Hearing their words, filled as they were with eager curiosity, Kākutstha narrated the full course of that king's story just as it had unfolded.
During that very first month, having become a woman of surpassing beauty, she wandered surrounded by those followers of hers who had likewise become women.
The woman of incomparable beauty, her eyes like lotus petals, plunged swiftly into that forest thick with trees, shrubs, and creepers, and roamed it on foot.
Having abandoned all her mounts on every side, Ilā took her pleasure in the hollow of that mountain's broad flank.
Then, in that woodland region not far from the mountain, she beheld a lake of wondrous beauty, thronged with flocks of birds of every kind —
— and there in that lake Ilā saw Budha, the son of Soma, blazing with his own radiance like the full moon when it rises.
He was performing fierce austerities within the water, unapproachable, moving at will, standing in the full bloom of his youth.
Astonished, she stirred the entire lake into commotion together with those former men who had become women, O joy of the Raghu lineage.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
But Budha, gazing upon her and pierced by the arrows of desire, lost command of himself at that moment and trembled in the water.
Gazing upon the radiant Ilā, who surpassed in beauty even the goddesses of the three worlds, he fell into deep thought: "Who is this being who exceeds even the divine?"
"I have never before seen anyone — not among the goddesses, not among the Nāgī women, not among the Asura women, not even among the Apsarases — adorned with this beauty."
"She would be a fitting match for me, if she belongs to no other." Settling his mind on this resolve, he came up from the water onto the bank.
Having come to the hermitage, the righteous-souled one called out to four of the women; they, in turn, paid homage to him.
The righteous one asked them: "Whose is this woman of incomparable beauty? For what purpose has she come here? Tell me the truth without delay."
Hearing those words of his, auspicious and sweet, with syllables gentle as honey, all those women replied in equally sweet voices.
"This fair-hipped one is always our mistress and our lord. She has no husband; she roams the forest glades with us."
Hearing those words of the women, whose meaning was unclear, that twice-born one mentally recited the holy recollective spell called Āvartanī.
Having thereby learned the full truth of the king's story just as it had come about, the foremost of sages addressed all those women.
"Were men, O fortunate ones, dwelling on the slope of this mountain? You shall remain on this mountain; let a dwelling be prepared."
"You shall all live always on roots, fruit, and bulbs; and you women shall obtain as husbands beings known as Kiṃpuruṣas."
Hearing the words of the son of Soma, those many women, transformed into Kiṃpuruṣī females, thenceforth attended upon that mountain in many different ways.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having heard the origin of the Kiṃpuruṣas, both Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata exclaimed "How wonderful!" to Rāma, lord of the people.
Then Rāma of great renown, righteous of soul, once more narrated this tale about the son of Prajāpati.
Seeing all those women flee, that best of sages addressed the woman endowed with incomparable beauty, almost as if smiling.
"I am the beloved son of Soma, O fair-faced one; worship me, O beautiful-limbed woman, with devoted and tender eyes."
Hearing his words, abandoned by her own people and alone in that wilderness, Ilā answered that great luminary of wondrous splendor.
"I am free to act as I will, O gentle one; I am under your power. Command me, O son of Soma; do with me as you desire."
Hearing those words of hers, so wondrous in their tenor, the son of the Moon, filled with joy and consumed by love, sported with her.
For Budha the month of Mādhava passed like an instant, as he delighted exceedingly with that bright-faced Ilā, so great was his passion.
Then, when the month was complete, the glorious son of Prajāpati, his face like the full moon, awoke upon his bed.
He saw Budha, the son of Soma, there performing austerities in the lake, arms raised, unsupported; and the king addressed him.
"Revered one, I entered a difficult mountain together with my retinue, but I cannot see that army. Where have those who belong to me gone?"
Hearing those words of that royal seer who had lost his memory, Budha replied with gentle, reassuring speech.
"Your retainers were struck down by a great shower of stones, and you fell asleep in this hermitage, afflicted by fear of the wind and rain."
"Be reassured; good fortune to you — be without fear, free of grief. Live here, O hero, eating fruit and roots, at your ease."
Reassured by those words, that king of great renown replied with gentle words, yet grieved at the loss of his retainers.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"I shall abandon my own kingdom; I cannot endure even a moment without my retainers. O Brahmin, you should permit me to depart."
"My eldest son, devoted to righteousness and of great renown, O Brahmin, known as Śaśabindu — let him receive my kingdom."
"For I could not bear to go and speak any ill word to my retainers' wives who live in comfort, O great and radiant one."
While the lord of kings spoke thus, Budha said something most wondrous by way of consolation: "Let your dwelling here be pleasing to you."
"You must not grieve, O son of Kardama, O great and mighty one. After you have dwelt here a full year, I will accomplish what is beneficial for you."
Hearing those words of Budha of untiring deeds, the king resolved to remain, as the expounder of sacred knowledge had said.
For one month he would become a beautiful woman and take pleasure without cease; for one month he would take on the form of a man and turn his mind to dharma.
Then, in the ninth month, the fair-hipped Ilā gave birth to a son — Purūravas — begotten by the son of Soma.
No sooner was he born than the fair-hipped one placed him in his father's hands — that mighty son of Ilā, equal in complexion to Budha.
Budha, self-possessed, also comforted the king when he had resumed his male form, entertaining him with stories full of righteousness.
While Rāma spoke thus of that wondrous birth, Lakṣmaṇa and the greatly renowned Bharata spoke up again.
"Having dwelt a full year as the beloved of the son of Soma, what did she do, O best of men? You should relate that to us."
Listening to the sweetness of those words from the two who questioned him, Rāma then narrated this story about the daughter of Prajāpati.
When the hero had passed into the state of manhood, Budha of supreme intelligence and great renown summoned the supremely noble Saṃvarta.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
And also Cyavana, the son of Bhṛgu, and the sage Āriṣṭanemi, and Pramodana the gladdener, and then the sage Durvāsas.
Having assembled all of them — skilled in speech and seers of truth — he addressed all his friends with composure and steadiness of mind.
"This great-armed king is Ila, the son of Kardama. Know his true situation and let what is beneficial for him be arranged."
Even as they were conversing, Kardama of immense splendor came to that hermitage together with great-souled twice-born sages.
Pulastya, Kratu, Vaṣaṭkāra, and the greatly splendid Oṃkāra also came to that hermitage.
All of them, their minds gladdened at meeting one another, well-wishers of the lord of Bāhli, then each spoke separately.
But Kardama spoke words supremely beneficial for the sake of his son: "O twice-born ones, hear my words, for they are what is best for the king."
"I see no remedy except the Lord whose banner bears the bull; and no sacrifice is higher than the Aśvamedha, which is also dear to that great-souled one."
"Therefore let us all perform that most formidable sacrifice for the sake of the king." Thus addressed by Kardama, all the foremost of the twice-born approved of that sacrifice as a means of propitiating Rudra.
The royal seer Marutta, conqueror of enemy citadels, the disciple of Saṃvarta and renowned by that name, then brought forward the materials for that sacrifice.
Then a great sacrifice was performed near the hermitage of Budha, and Rudra of great renown came, filled with supreme satisfaction.
Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the lord of Umā, pleased and filled with the greatest joy, spoke thus to all the twice-born regarding Ilā.
"I am delighted by the Hayamedha and by your devotion, O best of the twice-born. What good and pleasing thing shall I do for this lord of Bāhli?"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
While the lord of the gods spoke thus, those twice-born with concentrated minds propitiated the lord of the gods so that Ilā might become a man.
Then Rudra, his heart delighted, of immense splendor, bestowed manhood once more upon Ilā, and having given this boon, vanished from sight.
When the Hayamedha was concluded and Hara had disappeared, all those far-sighted twice-born returned whence they had come.
The king, abandoning Bāhli, established a city renowned for its glory, Pratiṣṭhāna, in the most excellent Madhyadeśa.
Śaśabindu, conqueror of enemy citadels, became king in Bāhli, while the mighty Ila, son of Prajāpati, became king at Pratiṣṭhāna.
Ila in due time attained the unsurpassed world of Brahmā, and the king Purūravas, son of Ila, obtained Pratiṣṭhāna.
"Such indeed is the power of the Aśvamedha, O you two bulls among men: one who had become a woman thereby regained manhood — and other boons difficult to obtain besides."
Having related all this, Kākutstha of immeasurable splendour then spoke again to Lakṣmaṇa among his brothers, these words rooted in righteousness.
"Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, and Jābāli, and likewise Kaśyapa, and all the foremost of the twice-born who are to be honoured at the Aśvamedha—
having summoned all of them and taken counsel, O Lakṣmaṇa, I shall release the horse, auspiciously appointed, with full concentration of mind."
Hearing those words spoken by Rāghava, Lakṣmaṇa of swift valour summoned all the twice-born and presented them before Rāghava.
Beholding Rāghava, who shone like a god and was utterly unapproachable, they who had reverenced his feet honoured him with blessings.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, Rāghava addressed those most excellent of twice-born with words pertaining to righteousness and bearing on the Aśvamedha.
Having heard the wondrous and illuminating counsel of those foremost twice-born regarding the Aśvamedha, he became greatly pleased.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Understanding their considered opinion, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: "O mighty-armed one, dispatch a message to the great-souled Sugrīva:
"'Come swiftly with many great monkeys and their attendants, for your welfare, to partake in this most excellent sacrifice.'
"And let the mighty-armed Vibhīṣaṇa of swift valour, surrounded by many rākṣasas who move at will, come to attend the Aśvamedha."
"And the kings, O tiger among men, who desire to do what is dear to me—let them come promptly with their retinues to that unsurpassed sacrificial ground."
"And those twice-born devoted to righteousness who have gone to other lands—invite all of them, O Lakṣmaṇa, to the Aśvamedha."
"And the sages, O mighty-armed one, the ascetics whose wealth is their austerity—those who have gone to other lands, and the great seers with their wives—let them be summoned."
"And a very great sacrificial enclosure on the Gomatī in the Naimiṣa forest—let it be ordered, O mighty-armed one; that place is sacred and unsurpassed."
"A hundred thousand cart-loads of choice rice, and ten thousand loads of sesame and lentils—let these proceed in advance, O mighty one."
"Many crores of gold coins and hundreds more of silver—let the great-minded Bharata go in front, placing all these before him."
"The rows of shops along the streets, all the actors and dancers, the townspeople, children and the elderly, and the twice-born who are well composed in mind—"
"and the skilled artisans and craftsmen learned in their arts, and all my mothers, and the princes and the inner apartments—"
"and my golden wife, worthy of initiation into the sacrificial rite—let the great-minded Bharata go forth placing all of them before him."
Having promptly dispatched all of that in its entirety, the elder brother of Bharata released the auspicious dark-spotted horse.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Having appointed Lakṣmaṇa together with the officiating priests in charge of the horse, Kākutstha then set out with his army toward Naimiṣa.
Beholding the sacrificial enclosure, which was supremely wondrous, the mighty-armed and glorious king felt incomparable joy and exclaimed thus.
While he was residing at Naimiṣa, all the kings came from every kingdom, and Rāma duly honoured them in return.
The foremost of men, blazing with great splendour, assigned suitable and richly appointed quarters to those great-souled kings together with their retinues.
Food and drink and garments for those great-souled ones with their retinues—Bharata, together with Śatrughna, swiftly distributed these.
And the great-souled monkeys, together with Sugrīva, all bowing humbly to the brāhmaṇas, performed the service of distributing food.
And Vibhīṣaṇa, surrounded by many garlanded rākṣasas, placed himself as a servant in attendance upon the sages of fierce austerity.
Thus well arranged, the horse-sacrifice proceeded; and the course of the horse, guarded by Lakṣmaṇa, was set in motion.
No other sound was to be heard at that horse-sacrifice of the great-souled king but "Give as you please, give freely"—and as far as the supplicants were satisfied, so far was the giving by monkeys and rākṣasas to be seen.
There was no one there who was impure, wretched, or emaciated at that best of sacrifices of the king, which was filled with joyful and well-nourished people.
And the great-souled sages of long life who were present there could not recall any such sacrifice, adorned with torrents of gifts.
Of silver, gold, gems, and garments being given ceaselessly—no end of them was to be perceived.
"Not of Śakra, nor of Soma, nor of Yama, nor of Varuṇa has such a sacrifice been seen before"—thus spoke the ascetics of great austerity.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Everywhere the monkeys stood, and everywhere the rākṣasas too, their hands filled, giving garments and riches abundantly to those who desired them.
Such was the sacrifice of that lion among kings, endowed with every virtue; it continued for a full year and more, and did not diminish.
While such a supremely wondrous sacrifice was in progress, the foremost of sages, Vālmīki, came swiftly with his disciples.
Beholding the sacrifice that appeared divine and wonderful to behold, he had auspicious leaf-huts made in a secluded spot among the hermitages of the sages.
Joyfully he spoke to his two disciples: "Go, the two of you, composed and attentive, and sing the complete Rāmāyaṇa poem with the greatest delight."
"In the sacred hermitages of the sages, in the dwelling-places of brāhmaṇas, in the lanes and royal roads, in the houses of kings—"
"at the gate of Rāma's palace, wherever the ritual acts are being performed, and especially before the officiating priests—there it should be sung in particular."
"And these sweet and varied fruits that grow here on the mountaintops—eating and tasting them, you shall sing."
"You shall not come to fatigue, my dear ones, having eaten the fruits and choice roots; you shall accept nothing from the city."
"If Rāma, the lord of the earth, should summon you to sing before him as the sages are seated, then let the singing begin."
"Twenty cantos are to be sung each day with the greatest joy, with the many metres there, as was taught by me previously."
"And no greed whatsoever is to be entertained, not even a little, out of desire for wealth. What use is wealth to those who dwell in hermitages and subsist on fruits and roots?"
"If Kākutstha should ask you, 'Children, of whom are you?', say to the lord of men: 'We are disciples of Vālmīki.'"
"Having attuned these strings to the sweetest pitch, or the mode shown before, sing with utmost sweetness, free from anxiety."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"The singing should proceed from the beginning, and without disrespecting the king; for the king is by right the father of all beings."
"Therefore, the two of you, with joyful hearts, sing tomorrow at dawn with full concentration the sweet song accompanied by the melody of the lute."
Having instructed them thus many times, the sage Prācetasa, Vālmīki of surpassing generosity and great renown, then fell silent.
The two princes, having placed that wondrous and auspicious instruction of the sage within their hearts, passed the night happily and with eager anticipation, even as the two Aśvins refined by the teaching of Bhārgava.
Those two, at the dawning of the night into day, having bathed and offered oblations into fire as previously instructed by the sage, sang [the poem] here and there [throughout the grounds].
Kākutstha [Rāma] heard from various places that earlier narrative — a recitation genre unprecedented [in its kind], adorned with melody.
Hearing it composed in many metres and accompanied by the rhythm of the lute, Rāghava [Rāma] became wholly absorbed in wonder.
Then, in a pause between ritual acts, the king — that tiger among men — assembled the great sages, the kings, the learned scholars, and the Vedic experts,
the Purāṇa specialists, the grammarians, and the elder twice-born — having gathered all of them together, he had the two singers take their seats [before the assembly].
The groups of sages there, and the kings of great splendour, were filled with delight — drinking in, as it were, with their eyes both the king and those two singers.
