Then all of them spoke to one another at once: "Both of these resemble Rāma — as if one image were drawn from another image."
"Were they not wearing matted locks, were they not clad in bark garments, we could find no difference between these two singers and Rāghava [himself]."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
While the listeners conversed in this way, growing in joy, those two sons of the sage commenced their song there, increasing [the audience's] delight.
Then there arose a sweet celestial music surpassing the human — and none of the listeners reached satiation with the wealth of that song.
Beginning from the very beginning — from the cantos opened by the vision of Nārada — they sang forward from there, up to twenty cantos.
Then in the late afternoon, having heard those twenty cantos, Rāghava — who was affectionate toward his brothers — spoke to Bharata:
"Give quickly eighteen thousand [coins] of gold to these two noble souls, O Kākutstha — let the effort of these boys not go unrewarded."
But those two bards [Kuśa and Lava] did not accept the gold being offered, and the noble-souled pair spoke in astonishment: "What is this to us?"
"We are forest-dwellers fully content with wild fruits and roots. What use have we for gold or precious metal in the forest?"
As the two spoke thus, the listeners and Rāma alike — all of them — filled with curiosity and were greatly astonished.
And Rāma, the greatly resplendent, eager to hear the full extent of that poem, asked those two sons of the sage:
"What is the measure of this poem? What is the foundation [topic] of this great noble work? Who is he — that foremost sage who is the author of this great poem?"
The two sons of the sage replied to Rāghava's questioning words: "The venerable Vālmīki is the author — he who has come to be near the sacrifice — and it is he who has revealed this entire story to you in full."
"From the very beginning, O lord of kings, [it extends through] five hundred cantos. Its subject, O king, is whatever is auspicious and inauspicious throughout [your] life."
"If your mind is resolved to hear [it], O king, O great warrior — being called to a moment's pause between ritual acts — then listen to it together with your younger brothers."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Rāma said "So be it," and those two, having received permission from Rāghava, went joyfully to the dwelling where that foremost sage resided.
And Rāma too, having savoured the sweetness of that song, returned to the ritual hall together with the sages and the great-souled kings.
For many days together Rāma listened to that supremely wondrous song — in the company of the sages, the kings, and the monkeys.
Then, recognising Kuśa and Lava as Sītā's sons from that song, Rāma spoke words in the midst of that assembly:
"Convey my words and go into the presence of the venerable [Vālmīki]:"
"'If [Sītā] is pure in conduct, if she is indeed free of all stain, let her establish her own purity here, having gained the great sage's sanction.'"
"'Having ascertained the sage's pleasure and the inner intent of Sītā — who is willing to give proof — then report to me promptly.'"
"'Tomorrow morning, let Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, take her oath in the midst of the assembly — for the purpose of [her] vindication and of mine here as well.'"
Having heard this supremely wondrous speech of Rāghava, the messengers hastened to the grove where that foremost sage dwelt.
They bowed before the great-souled one blazing with boundless radiance and spoke to him Rāma's words — gentle and sweet.
Having heard their report and understood the inner intention of Rāma, the sage of very great splendour then spoke:
"May it be so — blessings upon you. As Rāghava wishes, so shall Sītā act; for the husband is the deity of a woman."
Thus addressed by the sage, all of Rāma's messengers — those of great strength — returned and reported the sage's words to Rāghava.
Then Kākutstha, greatly delighted upon hearing the words of the great-souled sage, addressed the sages assembled there and the kings as well:
"Let the venerable sages together with their disciples, and the lords of men with their retinues, witness the oath of Sītā — and whoever else desires to.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
On hearing those words of the great-souled Rāghava, there arose a great cry of "bravo!" from all the foremost sages.
The great-souled kings too praised Rāghava: "This befits you alone, O best of men — nowhere else on earth."
Having thus made this decision — "It shall be tomorrow" — Rāghava, the slayer of enemies, then dismissed all of them.
When that night had passed, the king Rāghava — greatly resplendent — having gone to the sacrificial arena, summoned all the sages.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and then Kaśyapa; Viśvāmitra of long austerities, and Durvāsas of great ascetic power;
Agastya, and likewise Āśakti, the Bhārgava Vāmana, Mārkaṇḍeya of long life, and Maudgalya of great austerities;
The Bhārgava Cyavana, Śatānanda who is learned in dharma, the radiant Bharadvāja, and Agniputra of great lustre —
these and many other sages of sharpened vows, and kings — those tigers among men — all assembled together.
Rākṣasas of great valour and monkeys of great strength — all those noble souls — came together out of eager curiosity.
Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras by the thousands — all of them assembled together for the purpose of witnessing Sītā's oath.
Hearing that all had thus assembled — still as a motionless mountain — the foremost sage quickly approached together with Sītā.
Sītā followed behind that sage with downcast face, hands folded in reverence, tears flowing, having placed Rāma in her heart.
Seeing Sītā approaching behind Vālmīki like Śrī following Brahmā, there arose a great acclamation [from the assembly].
Then a tumultuous clamour arose from all — those whose hearts were agitated by a vast grief born of sorrow [for her].
Some cried "Well done, Sītā!", others cried "Well done, Rāma!" — while yet others there said "Well done, well done!" [meaning both].
Then, entering the midst of the throng of people, that foremost sage Vālmīki — with Sītā beside him — thus spoke to Rāghava:

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"O son of Daśaratha, this Sītā — of excellent vows and virtuous conduct — sinless, was abandoned by you near my hermitage.
"O Rāma, O upholder of great vows — out of fear of public censure you [cast her out]; Sītā shall now give proof [of her purity]. You should grant her permission to do so.
"These two sons of Jānakī, born as twins — they are your sons indeed, O unconquerable one. I speak this truth to you.
"I am the tenth son of Pracetas [Varuṇa], O joy of the Rāghava clan — I do not recall ever speaking a falsehood; and likewise, these two are your sons.
"For many thousands of years I have performed austerities — may I reap the fruit of that [penance] insofar as Maithilī is sinless.
"Having contemplated, O Rāghava, through [my knowledge of] the five elements together with the mind as sixth, that Sītā is pure — it was thus that I took her in at the forest stream.
"This woman of pure conduct, sinless, who holds her husband as her deity — she shall give you proof, who feared the censure of the world."
Thus addressed by Vālmīki, Rāghava replied with palms joined in the midst of the assembly, having beheld that one of divine complexion.
"So it is, O highly blessed one, O knower of dharma, exactly as you declare. I am convinced, O Brahman, by your words that are without blemish."
"Proof was indeed given formerly by Vaidehī in the presence of the gods. Yet knowing her to be without sin, I abandoned Sītā out of fear of what the world would say, O Brahman — may you forgive that."
"And I know these two sons of mine, Kuśa and Lava, born as twins; may I now have the joy of being reunited with Maithilī, whose purity has been proclaimed in the midst of the world."
Understanding the intention of Rāma, the foremost of the gods, all of them assembled together with the Grandfather Brahmā at their head.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedeva, troops of Maruts, the two Aśvins, the seers, the Gandharvas, the hosts of Apsarases, the Sādhya gods — all of them — and all the great seers came.
Then an auspicious, holy, divinely fragrant, and delightful wind, the best of the celestials, gladdened that multitude of people on every side.
The people assembled from all the realms gazed upon that wondrous, inconceivable event with concentrated minds, as in the Kṛtayuga of old.
Sītā, clad in an ochre robe, beholding all who had gathered, spoke words with palms joined, her gaze lowered and her face cast downward.
"As I have never even in mind thought of any man other than Rāghava, so may the goddess Mādhavī — the Earth — grant me an opening."
As Vaidehī was thus taking this oath, that wonder appeared: from the surface of the earth rose a divine, incomparable throne.
It was borne on the heads of serpents of immeasurable might, divine in its divine form, adorned with all kinds of jewels.
And upon it the goddess Earth, taking Maithilī in her arms, welcomed her with a greeting and caused her to be seated on that throne.
Beholding her seated on the throne and descending into the netherworld, an unceasing shower of divine flowers rained down upon Sītā.
A very great cry of "bravo!" arose at once from the gods: "Bravo, bravo, O Sītā, whose virtue is of such a nature!"
In this manner the gods who were stationed in the sky uttered many such words with joyful minds, having witnessed the descent of Sītā.
And the sages who had gathered at the sacrificial enclosure, as well as the kings, those tigers among men, could not cease from their amazement.
In the sky and on the earth, all beings, both stationary and moving, the great-bodied Dānavas, the lords of serpents in the underworld —
— some cried out in great joy, some were absorbed in meditation, some gazed at Rāma, some were rendered senseless gazing at Sītā.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
At the sight of Sītā's descent, there was a great gathering of those beings; and at that moment the entire world was utterly overwhelmed.
At the conclusion of that sacrifice, Rāma, deeply grief-stricken, seeing Vaidehī no more, considered this world empty. Overcome utterly by sorrow, he could find no peace of mind.
He dismissed all the kings, the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, and sent away the assembled throng of Brahman-led seers, richly laden with gifts.
Having dismissed them all, Rāma, the lotus-eyed, then entered Ayodhyā carrying Sītā in his heart.
That scion of Raghu took no other wife beyond Sītā; at every sacrifice a golden image of Jānakī served as the ritual consort.
For ten thousand years he performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and Vājapeya sacrifices ten times that number, together with many sacrifices endowed with great gold.
That glorious one performed also the Agniṣṭoma, the Atirātra, the Gosava with great wealth, and other rites in which the sacrificial fees were duly rendered.
In this manner a very great span of time passed for Rāghava, the great-souled one, who was established in his kingdom and who strove ever in the path of dharma.
The bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas remained under Rāma's authority; the kings were attached to Rāghava day by day.
Rain fell in season, abundance prevailed, the directions were clear; the city and the countryside were filled with people who were joyful and well-nourished.
No one died before his time, no disease afflicted living beings, and there was no adharma whatsoever while Rāma was governing the kingdom.
Then, after a long time, Rāma's illustrious mother, surrounded by her sons and grandsons, attained the fate decreed by time — she died.
Sumitrā also followed, and the illustrious Kaikeyī; having performed dharma in its many forms, they were established in the three heavens.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
All of them were established in heaven and were reunited with King Daśaratha, those highly blessed ones together attained dharma.
Rāma made great offerings for them in due seasons, for his mothers without distinction, among Brāhmaṇas and ascetics.
Rāma, whose soul was established in dharma, performed ancestral rites with many jewels and sacrifices of the utmost magnificence, thereby honoring the ancestors and the gods.
Now after some time, Yudhājit, king of the Kekayas, sent his own preceptor to the great-souled Rāghava.
He sent the brahmarṣi Gārgya, son of Aṅgiras, of immeasurable splendor, and ten thousand horses as an incomparable gift of affection.
The king presented to Rāma also blankets, jewels, choice embroidered garments, and many ornaments.
Hearing that the great seer Gārgya had arrived — the beloved envoy of his maternal uncle Aśvapati —
— Kākutstha went out to meet him, accompanied by his retinue, to a distance of a krośa, and honored Gārgya, receiving that wealth.
Having asked in a pleasing manner after the welfare of his maternal uncle, Rāma began to question the highly blessed one when he was seated.
"What message does my maternal uncle convey? For what purpose has the blessed one come here, O best among those versed in speech, like Bṛhaspati himself in person?"
Hearing the words of Rāma, the brahmarṣi, wondrous in appearance, began to narrate to Rāghava the full details of the matter.
"Your maternal uncle Yudhājit speaks this message, O mighty-armed one, O bull among men — may it please you to hear it, full of affection."
"This Gandharva territory, adorned with fruits and roots, a most beautiful region on both banks of the Sindhu —"
"— it is guarded by Gandharvas, armed and skilled in battle, sons of Śailūṣa, thirty million heroes of great might."
"Having conquered them, O Kākutstha, O mighty-armed one, please establish two well-ordered cities in that auspicious Gandharva territory."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"No other man's path leads there; that region is supremely beautiful. May it please you, O mighty-armed one — I do not speak falsely to you."
Hearing this, Rāghava was pleased with the great seer and with his maternal uncle's message, and said "So be it," glancing then toward Bharata.
The pleased Rāghava, with folded hands, said to the twice-born sage: "These two princes will conquer that territory, O brahmarṣi."
"The two heroic sons of Bharata — Takṣa and Puṣkala — well protected by their maternal uncle, and both intent on dharma."
"With Bharata going in front, the two princes, accompanied by their forces and retinue, will slay the sons of the Gandharvas and then divide between them the two cities."
"Having established those two excellent cities and settled his own sons there, the most righteous Bharata will return once more to my side."
Having spoken thus to the brahmarṣi, he then commanded Bharata along with his army and retinue, and consecrated the two princes.
Under an auspicious lunar asterism, placing the son of Aṅgiras at their head, Bharata set forth with his army and with the two princes.
That army, like Indra's own forces, marched out through the city gates, escorted far by Rāghava, and was formidable to gods and asuras alike.
Flesh-eating creatures and very great rākṣasas also followed Bharata, thirsting for blood.
And many hosts of spirits, flesh-eating, exceedingly fierce, numbering in the thousands, desirous of feasting on the flesh of the Gandharva's sons, followed along.
Many thousands of lions, tigers, and jackals, as well as birds of the air, went in front of the army.
The army, healthy and unimpeded, having spent a month and a half on the road, arrived at Kekaya, filled with men who were cheerful and well-provisioned.
Hearing that Bharata, the commander of the army, had arrived together with Yudhājit of the Gārgya lineage, the lord of the Kekayas felt surpassing delight.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
That lord of the Kekayas sallied forth with a great host of people, advancing swiftly against the Gandharvas who resembled the gods in form.
Bharata and Yudhājit, united and swift of stride, arrived at the Gandharva city together with their armies and retinues of foot-soldiers.
Hearing that Bharata had arrived, those Gandharvas of great valor assembled together, eager for battle, crying out on all sides.
Then a tumultuous, hair-raising battle ensued — terrible and lasting seven nights — and neither side gained victory.
Then Bharata, the younger brother of Rāma, enraged, discharged against the Gandharvas the dreadful weapon of Kāla called Saṃvarta.
Bound by the noose of Kāla and torn apart by the Saṃvarta weapon, thirty million of them were struck down in an instant by that great-souled one.
That slaughter, terrible to behold — such a deed of great-souled men accomplished in merely the twinkling of an eye — the dwellers of heaven do not recall its like.
When those warriors had been slain, Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, then established two most excellent and prosperous cities: Takṣa in Takṣaśilā and Puṣkara in Puṣkarāvatī.
That beautiful Gandharva country, the Gāndhāra territory, was filled within five years with provinces and urban settlements.
Filled with floods of wealth and jewels, adorned with groves, the two cities rivaled each other in every excellence, vying with one another to excel in virtues.
Both were renowned for their great beauty, distinguished by spotless commerce, thronged with throngs of gardens and vehicles, with marketplaces well laid out in their quarters.
Both were splendid foremost cities, lovely and adorned with wide expanses, graced with principal mansions of great beauty and palatial structures of matching splendor.
Adorned too with the splendid expanse of shrines to the gods — having settled the land in five years, Bharata the younger brother of Rāghava, the mighty-armed son of Kaikeyī, returned to Ayodhyā.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The illustrious Bharata paid homage to the great-souled Rāghava — who was like Dharma incarnate — even as Vāsava pays homage to Brahmā.
And he reported in full detail the great slaughter of the Gandharvas and the settlement of the country. Hearing this, Rāghava was well pleased with him.
Hearing that, Rāghava was filled with joy together with his brothers, and Rāghava spoke to his brothers words that were wonderful to behold.
"O Saumitri, these two princes of yours, Aṅgada and Candraketu, accomplished in dharma and firm-bowed, are worthy of kingdoms."
"I shall consecrate these two to kingdoms — let a suitable territory be arranged — one that is pleasant and uncrowded, where the two archers may dwell in happiness."
"A territory should be found, dear one, where there would be no injury to kings and no destruction of hermitages — so that we commit no offense."
When Rāma had spoken thus, Bharata replied: "This territory along the Kārāpatha road is exceedingly beautiful and free from affliction."
"Let a city be established there for the great-souled Aṅgada, and likewise a beautiful, wholesome city called Candrakānta for Candraketu."
Rāghava accepted the words spoken by Bharata, and having brought that territory under control, he settled it for Aṅgada.
The lovely city known as Āṅgadīyā was founded for Aṅgada — beautiful and well-protected — by Rāma of tireless deeds.
And Candraketu was settled in the wrestling-ground of Malla, in the Malla country — the city famed as Candrakānta, divine like a city of heaven.
Then Rāma, Bharata, and Lakṣmaṇa — those invincible ones in battle — were filled with great joy and performed the consecration rites.
Having consecrated the two princes and dispatched them with their armies and retinues — Aṅgada toward the western land and Candraketu toward the north —

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, followed after Aṅgada, while Bharata became the rear-guard for Candraketu.
Lakṣmaṇa dwelt in Āṅgadīyā for a full year; once that invincible prince was established, he returned again to Ayodhyā.
Bharata likewise dwelt there for a year and more, and then returning to Ayodhyā, he came to the feet of Rāma.
Both Saumitri and Bharata, devoted to the feet of Rāma and supremely righteous, did not notice time passing, so great was their love.
Thus ten thousand years passed for them as they strove constantly in dharma and in the affairs of the city every day.
Having enjoyed the world with minds fully content and encompassed by glory, those three stood firm upon the highest path of dharma — like three blazing sacrificial fires of brilliant splendor kindled well at a great sacrifice.
Then, after some time had passed, while Rāma stood firm upon the path of dharma, Kāla — Time personified — came to the royal gate in the form of an ascetic.
He spoke to the steadfast and illustrious Lakṣmaṇa: "Announce me to Rāma — I have come on a matter of great importance."
"For I am the messenger of a most powerful great seer of immeasurable might. O mighty one, I have come desiring to see Rāma on a matter of urgency."
Hearing those words, Saumitri hastened and reported to Rāma what the ascetic wished to say.
"Be victorious by dharma in both worlds, O king of great splendor. An ascetic bright as the sun has come as a messenger wishing to see you."
Hearing the words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma said: "Dear one, let the sage of great power, the bearer of his message, be admitted."
Saumitri said "So be it" and ushered in that sage who blazed as if with flames and scorched with his very radiance.
Approaching the foremost of the Raghu line who blazed with his own effulgence, the seer spoke to Rāghava with sweet voice: "May you flourish!"

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
The great-resplendent Rāma offered him worship preceded by the arghya libation, and then calmly proceeded to inquire of his welfare.
Asked of his welfare by Rāma, the best among speakers and greatly renowned, he took his seat upon the divine golden throne.
Then Rāma spoke to him: "Welcome, great sage. Now deliver the words on account of which you have come as a messenger."
Prompted by that lion among kings, the sage began to speak: "What is to be said must be said in a private meeting — and the spoken word must not be wounded by any eye."
"Whoever listens or looks upon this, O Rāghava, shall be worthy of death — if, that is, you value the word of this foremost of sages."
Having pledged "So be it," Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa: "O mighty-armed one, stand at the door and dismiss the door-keeper."
"For he shall truly deserve death, O Saumitri, who sees or hears this private discourse between the sage and me."
Then, having stationed Lakṣmaṇa, the scion of Kākutstha, at the keeping of the door, Rāghava said to the sage: "Speak."
"Whatever words are in your mind, on account of which you have come with such focused resolve — speak them without hesitation; they dwell in my heart as well."
Listen, O Rāma, mighty-armed one, great in strength — for what purpose I have been commissioned and sent here by the god Pitāmaha.
I am your son from your prior existence, O conqueror of enemy cities; O hero, brought forth through māyā — I am Kāla, the all-consumer.
And the blessed Pitāmaha, lord of worlds and sovereign, said: 'The time has come for you, O mighty-armed one, to protect the celestial realms.'
Having once contracted the worlds through māyā yourself, lying upon the great ocean on the waters, you formerly brought me forth.
Then, having created through māyā Ananta, the mighty serpent lying in the water, and also two mighty beings —

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
— Madhu and Kaiṭabha, by whose heaped bones this earth, crowded with mountains, came to be formed —
— producing me from your navel upon the divine lotus blazing like the sun, you entrusted to me all the creative work of Prajāpati.
Thus I, having laid down my burden, worship you, lord of the universe; grant protection to beings — you are the source of my splendor.
And you, the invincible one, from that eternal state assumed the nature of Viṣṇu for the protection of all beings.
Born of Aditi as a mighty son, you who increase the joy of your brothers — whenever deeds arise, you stand ready to aid the world.
You, the best of the worlds, with your subjects in terror, desiring the slaying of Rāvaṇa, turned your mind toward birth among humans.
You yourself ordained for yourself, of old, the measure of your sojourn — ten thousand years and ten hundred years.
You, whose son is mind-born, having fulfilled your allotted lifespan among men here — the time has come to approach, O best of best men.
If, O great king, you wish to tend your subjects yet longer, then dwell on — O hero, may it be well with you; thus spoke Pitāmaha.
Or if you have the desire to conquer the realm of the gods, O Rāghava, let the gods be protected by Viṣṇu and freed from affliction.
Having heard the words spoken by Pitāmaha and conveyed by Kāla, Rāghava, smiling, spoke to Kāla, the all-withdrawer.
"I have heard the supremely wondrous words of the god of gods; great delight has arisen in me from your coming."
"May it be well with you. I shall go to that very place whence I have come — for you have truly entered my heart now that you have arrived; I have no hesitation in this."
"For in all the affairs of the gods who are subject to me, I must stand firm at the final withdrawal of all — just as Pitāmaha has declared."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
While those two were thus conversing, the blessed sage Durvāsas, desirous of an audience with Rāma, approached the gate of the palace.
Approaching Saumitri, that foremost of sages said: "Show me Rāma at once — my purpose will lapse if delayed."
Hearing the sage's words, Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, saluted the great-souled one and spoke these words.
"Tell me, revered one, what is the matter — what is the purpose, what should I do? Rāghava is occupied, O brahmin; please wait but a moment."
Hearing this, that tiger among sages, inflamed with anger, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa with words that seemed to burn him with a glance.
"This very instant, O Saumitri, announce me to Rāma — otherwise I shall curse you, your realm, your city, and Rāghava as well."
"And Bharata, O Saumitri, and all your posterity — for I am no longer able to hold back my anger in my heart."
Hearing those fearsome-seeming words of that great-souled one, Lakṣmaṇa reflected in his mind on the import of those words.
"Let death be mine alone; let there be no destruction of all" — having resolved this in his understanding, he announced it to Rāghava.
Hearing Lakṣmaṇa's words, Rāma dismissed Kāla and, stepping out swiftly, the king beheld the son of Atri.
Bowing to that great-souled one blazing as it were with splendor, Kākutstha, with hands folded in reverence, asked: "What is the purpose?"
Hearing those words spoken by Rāghava, the great sage and lord Durvāsas replied to Rāma: "Hear me, O you who cherish righteousness."
"Today marks the completion of my thousand-year vow, O Rāghava; I, O sinless one, desire food — whatever is prepared in your household."
Hearing those words, Rāma, filled with great delight, offered to the foremost of sages the food that had been prepared.
That best of sages, having eaten that food comparable to nectar, addressed Rāma with "Well done, Rāma" and returned to his own hermitage.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
When he had departed, the greatly resplendent Rāghava, whose mind had been glad, recalled the words of Kāla and was then overcome with sorrow.
Deeply tormented by grief, recalling that terrible encounter, he stood with downcast face, dejected in mind, unable to speak.
Then Rāghava of great renown, having resolved in his mind the words of Kāla, said only "This is not to be" — and sat in silence.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, seeing Rāghava downcast and wretched like the moon overcome by eclipse, joyfully spoke sweet words.
"You ought not to grieve on my account, O mighty-armed one — for such is the course of Kāla, bound by the ordinance laid down of old."
"Slay me, O gentle one, without hesitation, and uphold your vow — for men who fail in their vows descend to hell, O Kākutstha."
"If there is love in you, O great king, if I am worthy of your favor — slay me without hesitation, O Rāghava, and let righteousness flourish."
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, with agitated senses, summoned his ministers and likewise the chief priest.
And the lord of men recounted to them, in their midst, all that had happened — both the arrival of Durvāsas and the vow that had been made with the ascetic.
Hearing this, all the ministers together with the preceptors sat in assembly; then Vasiṣṭha of great splendor spoke these words.
"This has been foreseen, O mighty-armed Rāma of great renown — your end, which causes the hair to stand on end, and your separation from Lakṣmaṇa."
"Abandon him — Kāla is powerful; do not render your vow futile, for when a vow is destroyed, righteousness goes to ruin."
"And when righteousness is destroyed, all that is movable and immovable in the three worlds, together with the hosts of gods and sages, would perish — of this there is no doubt."
"Therefore you, tiger among men, who are the protector of the three worlds — render the world whole today by the death of Lakṣmaṇa."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Hearing that counsel of those assembled — fraught with righteousness and purpose — Rāma, in the midst of the assembly, addressed Lakṣmaṇa.
"I release you, O Saumitri — let there be no inversion of righteousness; for the righteous, renunciation and death are equally ordained, and both are the same."
When Rāma had spoken those words, Lakṣmaṇa, his eyes blurred with tears, departed in haste — but he did not enter his house.
He went to the bank of the Sarayū, sipped its waters, and with hands folded in reverence, restrained all his vital channels and breathed not a breath.
As he stood thus absorbed, not breathing — all the gods together with Śakra and the troops of apsarasas, together with the hosts of sages, showered him with flowers.
As he became invisible to all his younger brothers, Śakra took up Lakṣmaṇa — mighty in strength and still in his body — and entered heaven.
Then the best of gods, all rejoicing and delighted, together with the sages, honored the fourth part of Viṣṇu that had returned.
Having dismissed Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, filled with grief and sorrow, addressed the chaplain, the ministers, and the citizens thus:
"Today I shall consecrate Bharata, devoted to dharma, the heroic lord of Ayodhyā, to the kingdom; thereafter I myself shall depart to the forest."
"Bring in the consecration materials so that no time be lost — today itself I shall go the way that Lakṣmaṇa has gone."
Hearing what Rāghava had spoken, all the subjects bowed their heads deeply to the ground and became as though bereft of life.
Bharata too lost consciousness upon hearing Rāma's words; he denounced the kingdom and spoke thus to Rāghava:
"By truth I swear, O king — not even in the heavenly world do I desire the kingdom without you, O joy of the Raghu lineage."
"Anoint these two bards, Kuśa and Lava, O king, lord of men — the heroic Kuśa over the Kosalas, and Lava over the northern realm."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"Let swift-striding messengers go to Śatrughna and without delay announce to him this departure of ours to heaven."
Hearing what Bharata had said, and seeing the citizens downcast and burning with sorrow, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words:
"Dear Rāma, behold — all these subjects have prostrated themselves on the earth. Knowing what they desire and require, do not act contrary to their wishes."
At Vasiṣṭha's words, Kākutstha raised up the assembled subjects and addressed them all, asking: "What shall I do?"
Then all the subjects spoke to Rāma: "We shall follow you wherever you go, O Rāma."
"This is our supreme joy; this is deemed our highest dharma; the satisfaction dwelling in our hearts is always firm in following you."
"If you have love and unsurpassed affection for your citizens, then, O Kākutstha, lead us along the true path together with our sons and wives."
"Whether to a forest of austerities, or a stronghold, or a river, or the ocean — if we are not to be abandoned by you, lead us all, O Lord."
He, knowing their resolve, and perceiving the decree of fate as well as the citizens' unwavering devotion, said simply: "So be it."
Having made this decision, on that very day Rāghava consecrated the heroic Kuśa over the Kosalas and Lava over the northern realm —
— anointing both those great-souled princes, Kuśa and Lava; and he gave to each three thousand chariots, ten thousand elephants,
and ten thousand horses as gift to each — endowing both with abundant jewels and great wealth, surrounded by joyful and prosperous people.
Having consecrated those two heroes and dispatched them to their own cities, he then sent swift messengers to the great-souled Śatrughna.
Those messengers, urged by Rāma's command and swift of stride, proceeded quickly to Madhurā and did not halt on the way.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
Then, arriving at Madhurā within three days and nights, they reported to Śatrughna everything exactly as it had occurred:
— the abandonment of Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava's resolve, the consecration of his two sons, and likewise the citizens' intention to follow him.
The charming city of Kuśa, established on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains by the wise Rāma, was named Kuśāvatī.
And the beautiful city of Lava was proclaimed Śrāvatī; and Ayodhyā was left deserted, with Bharata following Rāghava.
Having thus swiftly reported everything to the great-souled Śatrughna, those messengers then fell silent, saying: "Hasten, O king."
Hearing of this dreadful-seeming dissolution of the lineage now at hand, he assembled his subjects and his chaplain Kāñcana,
and, as a joy of the Raghu line, he narrated to them everything that had taken place and the reversal of his own fortune that was to come, along with his brothers.
Then that heroic lord of men consecrated his two sons: Subāhu received Madhurā, and Śatrughnātī received Vaidiśā.
Dividing that army from Madhurā between his two sons, he established both princes well-stocked with wealth and grain.
Then, having bade farewell to the king Śatrughnātī at Vaidiśā, that Rāghava hastened to Ayodhyā in a single chariot.
He saw the great-souled Rāma blazing like fire, clad in fine linen garments, accompanied by imperishable sages.
He then saluted Rāma with palms joined and senses controlled, and spoke these words — he who knew dharma, meditating on dharma alone:
"Having duly consecrated both the sons of the Rāghava line with proper gifts, know me, O king, as fully resolved to accompany you."
"There is nothing more to be said in this matter — your command is irresistible. You should not abandon me, O hero, especially as I am devoted to you."
Understanding his resolute and unfaltering mind, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, said to Śatrughna simply: "So be it."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
At the conclusion of his speech, monkeys assuming any form at will, and multitudes of bears and rākṣasas, converged there in great numbers.
Sons of gods, sons of sages, and sons of Gandharvas — all of them, knowing Rāma's dissolution was at hand, had all gathered together.
All assembled, they saluted Rāma and said: "We have come, O king of great renown, desiring to accompany you."
"If you were to depart without us, O bull among men, it would be as though you had struck us down with the rod of Yama himself."
Hearing those words of the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, he then spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa in gentle and sweet tones:
"As long as people endure, so long shall you, Vibhīṣaṇa, O lord of rākṣasas, great in valour, abide in Laṅkā and rule your realm."
"Protect your subjects according to dharma; you need say nothing further."
Having spoken thus to him, Kākutstha then said to Hanūmat: "You have resolved to live on — do not break the vow you have taken."
"As long as my stories circulate in the world, O lord of monkeys, so long shall you sustain your life and honour your pledge."
Having spoken thus, Kākutstha then said to all those bears and monkeys: "Come, travel with me" — so did Rāghava address them then.
When night had given way to dawn, broad-chested Rāma of great renown, lotus-eyed, then addressed the chaplain:
"Let the sacred fire of the agnihotra, blazing with clarified butter, proceed ahead, along with the royal parasol of the Vājapeya sacrifice, adorning the great path."
Then the radiant Vasiṣṭha performed the entire rite of the Great Departure — the mahāprāsthānika — completely and according to proper injunction.
Then, clad in linen garments and silently reciting the supreme Brahman within, Rāma took kuśa grass in both hands and, inclining forward, set out.
Speaking not a word, making no gesture anywhere, beyond pleasure on the path, he went forth from that house blazing like the sun.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
On Rāma's left side walked Padmā Śrī, calm and composed; on his right walked Hrī of wide eyes; and Vyavasāya walked ahead of him.
His arrows of various kinds and his bow of elongated form followed Kākutstha, all of them bearing human shapes.
The Vedas in the form of brāhmaṇas, Sāvitrī the all-protecting, Oṃkāra, and Vaṣaṭkāra — all of them followed Rāma in devotion.
The great-souled sages and all the gods of the earth followed Kākutstha as he approached the gate of heaven.
The women of the inner palace followed him as he went, along with the elderly, children, and maidservants, and attendants of all ranks and servants bearing tribute.
And Bharata with his inner household, accompanied by Śatrughna, went forth — having embraced Rāma's vow, they followed Rāghava in complete devotion.
Then the great-souled brāhmaṇas, bearing their sacred fires and composed in mind, followed the highly-minded Kākutstha with their sons and wives.
The ministers and the ranks of servants, with their sons, kinsmen, and retinues, all followed Rāghava joyfully.
Then all the subjects, surrounded by joyful and prosperous people, followed Rāghava as he went forward, their hearts enraptured by his virtues.
All had bathed and were joyful, bearing splendid garlands of flowers, proud and resounding with joyful shouts, all following Rāma in devotion.
No one there was wretched, or ashamed, or sorrowful; all were joyful and elated — it was supremely wondrous.
Country folk who had come wishing to see the king's departure — they too, upon merely seeing it, followed along together with all the others.
The bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, and the citizens of the city, followed behind with supreme devotion, fully composed in mind.
Having travelled a yojana and a half, the delight of the Raghu line beheld the river whose waters are sacred — the Sarayū, flowing toward the west.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
At that very moment Brahmā, the grandfather of all worlds, surrounded by all the gods and by great-souled sages,
came to the place where Kākutstha stood ready to ascend to heaven — attended by hundreds of millions of divine celestial chariots.
A great torrential shower of flowers fell, released by the wind like a vast flood.
While hundreds of instruments resounded and the place was thronged with Gandharvas and Apsarases, Rāma stepped on foot into the waters of the Sarayū.
Then the grandfather spoke from the sky: "Come, O Viṣṇu — may good befall you! By good fortune have you arrived, O Rāghava."
"Together with your brothers who are equal to gods, O great-radiant one, enter your own form — that eternal Vaiṣṇava body and that everlasting sky."
"For you, O lord, are the refuge of all worlds. None know you truly, O wide-eyed one, except through that primal Māyā which you previously assumed."
"You are the inconceivable great being, imperishable, the totality of all. O greatly radiant one, of your own will enter whatever form you desire."
Having heard the grandfather's words and having resolved upon it, the great-minded one, together with his brothers and still in his bodily form, merged into the radiance of Viṣṇu.
Then the gods worshipped the divine one who had entered Viṣṇu — the Sādhyas, the host of Maruts, Indra and the others, with Agni at their head.
The divine companies of sages, the Gandharvas and Apsarases, Garuḍas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, and the Daityas, Dānavas and Rākṣasas —
— all were rejoicing, all were delighted, all had their heart's desire fulfilled. "Well done! Well done!" cried all of them, free of sin, as they rose to the triple heaven.
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendour, spoke to the grandfather: "O faithful one, you should grant worlds to these multitudes of people."

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
text:
"For all these noble ones have followed me out of love; they are devoted and deserve a fitting reward, having surrendered themselves for my sake."
Hearing the words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the lord and preceptor of all worlds, declared: "These assembled ones shall go to the worlds called Sāntānika."
"And whatever being, even among the lower creatures, meditating on Rāma alone, shall give up its life in devotion — it shall dwell in the offspring, endowed with all virtues, in the realm next to Brahmaloka."
The Vānaras and the bears likewise returned to their own respective origins.
Those who had been born from gods and others, from sages, Nāgas and Yakṣas — each returned to those very origins from which they had come forth.
When the lord of gods had spoken thus, all of them came to the ford called Gopratāra and entered the Sarayū, their eyes swimming with tears of joy.
Every living being that plunged into the waters, filled with great delight, cast off its human body and ascended a celestial chariot.
Even those born in lower wombs, upon reaching the waters of the Sarayū, became divine; with celestial forms they shone like gods ablaze with light.
The stationary and the mobile — all, upon reaching the waters of the Sarayū and being immersed in that sacred flood, attained the world of the gods.
Whatever divine origin the Vānaras, bears and Rākṣasas had — each one of them entered back into that very origin, having cast off their bodies in the waters.
Having thus sent all to heaven, the great-minded preceptor of the worlds, himself rejoicing, departed to the sky together with the rejoicing gods.
This alone is the narrative, together with the Uttara-kāṇḍa, honoured by Brahmā, known as the Rāmāyaṇa — the foremost work composed by Vālmīki.
